"That is the voice of Xīsī."
Then he hanged himself.
Duke Mǐn
was the son of Shū Jiāng, the younger sister of Āi Jiāng,
therefore the men of Qí established him.
Gòngzhòng had illicit relations with Āi Jiāng,
and Āi Jiāng wished to establish him.
At Duke Mǐn's death,
Āi Jiāng was privy to the knowledge,
therefore she fled to Zhū.
The men of Qí seized her and put her to death at Yí,
and brought back her corpse.
Duke Xí requested and buried her.
B4.2.4 When Chéng Jì was about to be born,
Duke Huán had the father of Bǔ Chǔqiū
divine about it.
He said:
"It is a boy.
His name will be Yǒu.
He will be at the duke's right hand;
between the two altars of the soil,
he will be a support to the ducal house.
When the Jì clan perishes,
then Lǔ will not flourish."
They also consulted the stalks,
and met with Dà Yǒu changing to Qián.
It was said:
"He is the same as his father,
respected as if in the ruler's place."
When he was born,
there was a mark on his hand like the character 'Yǒu',
and so they named him thus.
B4.2.5 In winter, in the twelfth month,
the Dí people attacked Wèi.
Duke Yì of Wèi was fond of cranes;
some cranes rode in carriages.
When they were about to fight,
the men of the state who had received armor all said:
"Send the cranes!
The cranes truly have emoluments and positions;
how can we fight?"
The duke gave a jade ring to Shí Qízǐ,
and gave arrows to Nìng Zhuāngzǐ,
ordering them to guard,
saying:
"Use these to assist the state,
choose what is advantageous and act."
He gave an embroidered robe to his wife,
saying:
"Listen to these two gentlemen!"
Qú Kǒng drove the war chariot,
Zǐ Bó was the right-hand man;
Huáng Yí led the van,
Kǒng Yīngqí brought up the rear.
They fought with the Dí people at Yíngzé,
the army of Wèi was utterly defeated,
and they thereupon extinguished Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi did not remove his banner,
and therefore was badly defeated.
The Dí people imprisoned the scribes Huá Lónghuá and Lǐ Kǒng
to pursue the men of Wèi.
The two men said:
"We
are grand scribes,
and in fact preside over their sacrifices.
If we do not go first,
the state cannot be obtained."
So they went first.
When they arrived,
they told the defenders:
"You cannot wait."
At night they went out with the people of the state.
The Dí entered Wèi,
and then pursued them,
and again defeated them at the river.
Formerly,
when Duke Huì came to the throne he was young,
and the men of Qí made Zhāo Bó have intercourse with Xuān Jiāng.
He was unwilling,
but they forced him.
They begot Qízǐ, Duke Dài, Duke Wén, the wife of Duke Huán of Sòng, and the wife of Duke Mù of Xǔ.
Duke Wén, because of Wèi's many troubles,
first went to Qí.
When they were defeated,
Duke Huán of Sòng met them at the river,
and they crossed by night.
The surviving people of Wèi, men and women, numbered seven hundred and thirty.
Adding to them the people of Gòng
and Téng,
they became five thousand.
They established Duke Dài and made a temporary capital at Cáo.
The wife of Duke Mù of Xǔ composed the "Zài Chí".
The Marquis of Qí sent the duke's son, Wúkuī, to lead three hundred chariots
and three thousand armored soldiers to garrison Cáo.
He presented to the duke a team of horses, five sets of sacrificial robes, three hundred each of oxen, sheep, pigs, chickens, and dogs, and timber for gates.
He presented to the lady a fish-skin carriage and thirty pairs of heavy brocade.
B4.2.6 The people of Zhèng disliked Gāo Kè,
and sent him to lead an army and station it on the river,
and after a long time did not recall him.
The army disbanded and returned,
and Gāo Kè fled to Chén.
The people of Zhèng composed the "Qīng Rén" about this.
B4.2.7 The Marquis of Jìn sent his heir apparent, Shēnshēng, to attack the Gāoluò clan of the Eastern Mountains.
Lǐ Kè remonstrated, saying:
"The heir apparent presents the offerings of the ancestral temple
and the altars of soil and grain,
and morning and evening attends to the ruler's meals;
therefore he is called the 'heir'.
When the ruler travels, he guards;
if there is a guard, he follows.
To follow is called 'soothing the army';
to guard is called 'overseeing the state'.
This is the ancient rule.
To lead an army,
to decide plans alone;
to administer oaths to the troops —
these are matters for the ruler and the chief ministers of state to deliberate.
They are not the business of the heir apparent.
An army is about controlling commands;
to receive commands lacks authority,
to issue commands alone is unfilial.
Therefore the ruler's designated heir should not lead an army.
If the ruler loses the proper office,
and the army leader lacks authority,
what use is it?
Moreover, your servant has heard the Gāoluò clan are about to fight.
May you, my lord, abandon this!"
The duke said:
"I have sons,
but do not yet know whom to establish!"
He did not reply and withdrew.
He saw the heir apparent.
The heir apparent said:
"Am I to be deposed?"
He replied:
"He has charged you with overseeing the people,
and instructed you in military affairs.
You should fear only not being reverent.
For what reason would you be deposed?
Moreover, you should fear being unfilial,
do not fear not being established.
Cultivate yourself and do not blame others,
then you will avoid calamity."
The crown prince led the army,
and the duke clothed him in a parti-colored robe,
and adorned him with a metal jué-ring.
Hú Tū drove the war chariot,
with Xiān Yǒu as the right-hand guard.
Liáng Yúzǐ Yǎng drove for Hǎn Yí,
with Xiān Dānmù as the right-hand guard.
Yángshé Dàfū served as commandant.
Xiān Yǒu said:
"Clothed in a robe that is half the duke's own,
and holding the crucial command of the army,
on this campaign,
you, sir, should exert yourself!
A half-robe from one's own body harbors no malice,
and military authority wards off disaster;
with such closeness, there will be no calamity—
what is there to worry about?"
Hú Tū sighed and said:
"The season
is a sign of affairs;
clothing
is the adornment of the person;
ornaments
are the banners of the heart.
Thus, to show respect for an affair,
one gives the command at the proper beginning;
to honor the person,
one clothes him in pure garments;
to employ his loyalty,
one adorns him with appropriate ornaments.
Now the command is given at the end of the season,
blocking the affair;
he is clothed in a parti-colored robe,
distancing him from his person;
he is adorned with a metal jué-ring,
casting aside his loyalty.
The clothing distances him,
the season blocks him;
parti-colored means coolness,
winter
means killing,
metal
means cold,
jué
means separation—
how can one rely on this?
Even if one wishes to exert oneself,
can the Dí be completely exterminated?"
Liáng Yúzǐ Yǎng said:
"One who leads an army
receives the command in the ancestral temple,
receives the sacrificial meat at the altar of the soil,
and has regular robes.
Not obtaining these but instead wearing parti-colored robes—
the command can be understood.
To die would be unfilial;
it would be better to flee."
Hǎn Yí said:
"Parti-colored robes are irregular and inconstant,
and a metal jué-ring does not return.
Even if one returns, what would be the use?
The ruler has intentions."
Xiān Dānmù said:
"This clothing
even a madman would find suspicious.
Saying
'exterminate the enemy and return'—
can the enemy be completely exterminated?
Even if the enemy were exterminated,
there would still be slanderers within;
it would be better to disobey."
Hú Tū wished to depart.
Yángshé Dàfū said:
"You cannot.
To disobey a command is unfilial,
to abandon one's duty is disloyal.
Even though you know it is cold-hearted,
wickedness cannot be chosen.
You, sir, should die for it!"
The crown prince was about to engage in battle,
when Hú Tū admonished him, saying:
"You cannot.
In the past, Xīn Bó counseled Zhōu Huán Gōng, saying:
'When inner favorites are made equal to the queen,
outer favorites control the government,
favored sons are matched with the heir,
and great cities rival the state—
these are the roots of disorder.'
The Duke of Zhōu did not follow this,
and thus met with disaster.
Now the roots of disorder have fully formed;
can your establishment be certain?
Be filial and bring peace to the people—
you, sir, should consider this!
Rather than endangering your person
and hastening your condemnation."
B4.2.8 Chéng Fēng heard the prophecy concerning Chéng Jì,
and so served him,
and entrusted Duke Xī to him;
therefore, Chéng Jì established him.
B4.2.9 In the first year of Duke Xī,
Duke Huán of Qí moved Xíng to Yíyí.
In the second year,
he established Wèi in Chǔqiū.
The people of Xíng moved as if returning home;
the state of Wèi forgot its destruction.
B4.2.10 Duke Wén of Wèi wore robes of coarse cloth
and caps of plain silk,
devoted himself to materials and instructed the farmers,
facilitated commerce and benefited artisans,
respected education and encouraged learning,
and appointed methods and employed the capable.
In the first year [of his reign],
he had thirty war chariots;
by the final year,
he had three hundred chariots.
A5.1 The Classic of the First Year of Duke Xī
A5.1.1 First year, spring,
the royal first month.
A5.1.2 The armies of Qí,
Sòng,
and Cáo stationed at Nièběi,
to rescue Xíng.
A5.1.3 In summer, the sixth month,
Xíng moved to Yíyí.
A5.1.4 The armies of Qí,
Sòng,
and Cáo walled Xíng.
A5.1.5 In autumn, the seventh month, on Wùchén,
the lady, Lady Jiāng, died in Yí,
and the men of Qí brought her back.
A5.1.6 The men of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
A5.1.7 In the eighth month,
the duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
and a man of Zhū at Chéng.
A5.1.8 In the ninth month,
the duke defeated the army of Zhū at Yǎn.
A5.1.9 In winter, the tenth month, on Rénwǔ,
Gōngzǐ Yǒu led the army and defeated the army of Jǔ at Lì,
capturing Jǔ Nú.
A5.1.10 In the twelfth month, on Dīngsì,
the funeral of the lady arrived from Qí.
B5.1 The Commentary of the First Year of Duke Xī
B5.1.1 First year, spring,
it is not recorded that he ascended the throne,
because the duke had been driven out.
That the duke was driven out and then returned
is not recorded,
to conceal it.
Concealing the state's disgrace
is according to ritual.
B5.1.2 The feudal lords rescued Xíng.
The people of Xíng were routed,
and fled to the armies.
The armies then drove away the Dí people,
gathered the vessels and implements of Xíng
and moved them,
and the armies took nothing for themselves.
B5.1.3 In summer,
Xíng moved to Yíyí,
and the feudal lords walled it for them,
to rescue them from calamity.
In all cases, when a feudal lord or hegemon
rescues from calamity,
shares in disaster,
or punishes offenses,
it is according to ritual.
B5.1.4 In autumn,
the men of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
because Zhèng had drawn close to Qí.
They made a covenant at Luò,
to plan the rescue of Zhèng.
B5.1.5 In the ninth month,
the duke defeated the army of Zhū at Yǎn—
these were the defenders of Xūqiū who were about to return.
B5.1.6 In winter,
men of Jǔ came to seek bribes,
and Gōngzǐ Yǒu defeated them at Lì,
capturing Nú, the younger brother of the Viscount of Jǔ.
— —He was not a minister,
but [the record] praises the capture.
The duke granted Jì Yǒu the fields of Wènyáng and Fèi.
B5.1.7 The coffin of the Lady of the Rén clan arrived from Qí.
The gentleman considered that the Qí people's execution of Āi Jiāng was excessive.
A woman
follows others.
A5.2 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 2 of Duke Xī
A5.2.1 In the second year, in spring, the royal first month,
we fortified Chǔqiū.
A5.2.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on the Xīnsì day,
we buried our junior consort Āi Jiāng.
A5.2.3 The army of Yú and
the army of Jìn destroyed Xiàyáng.
A5.2.4 In autumn, in the ninth month,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the men of Jiāng,
and the men of Huáng made a covenant at Guàn.
A5.2.5 In winter, in the tenth month,
there was no rain.
A5.2.6 The men of Chǔ invaded Zhèng.
B5.2 The Commentary of Zuo, Year 2 of Duke Xī
B5.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
the feudal lords fortified Chǔqiū and established the state of Wèi there.
The record does not list those who met,
because our ruler was late.
B5.2.2 Xún Xī of Jìn requested to borrow a route through Yú, offering the horses from Qūchǎn and the jade from Chuíjí
in order to attack Guó.
The Duke said:
"These are my treasures."
He replied:
"If we obtain a route through Yú,
it is as if they were stored in an outer treasury."
The Duke said:
"Gōng Zhīqí is there."
He replied:
"Gōng Zhīqí's character is such that
he is timid and cannot remonstrate forcefully;
moreover, having grown up with the ruler from a young age,
the ruler is overly familiar with him;
even if he remonstrates,
the ruler will not listen."
Thereupon, he sent Xún Xī to borrow a route through Yú,
saying:
"Jì acted without principle,
entering from Diānlíng,
attacking the three gates of Míng.
Since Jì has already been punished,
it was solely for your sake.
Now Guó acts without principle,
relying on its inns,
to invade the southern borders of our humble state.
We dare to request to borrow a route
to demand an accounting from Guó."
The Duke of Yú agreed,
and further requested to attack Guó first.
Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated,
but he did not listen,
and then raised an army.
In summer,
Lǐ Kè and Xún Xī of Jìn led their troops
to join the army of Yú,
attacked Guó,
and destroyed Xiàyáng.
Yú is recorded first,
because of the bribe.
B5.2.3 In autumn,
they made a covenant at Guàn,
to subdue Jiāng
and Huáng.
B5.2.4 The eunuch Diāo of Qí first
leaked military information at Duōyú.
B5.2.5 The Duke of Guó defeated the Róng at Sāngtián.
Bǔ Yǎn of Jìn said:
"Guó is sure to perish.
Losing Xiàyáng and not fearing,
and moreover achieving merit,
this is Heaven depriving them of a mirror,
and increasing their malady.
They are sure to despise Jìn
and not comfort their people.
It will not take five harvests."
B5.2.6 In winter,
the men of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and Dòu Zhāng captured Zhèng's Nián Bó.
A5.3 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 3 of Duke Xī
A5.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
the royal first month,
there was no rain.
A5.3.2 In summer, the fourth month, there was no rain.
A5.3.3 The men of Xú took Shū.
A5.3.4 In the sixth month, it rained.
A5.3.5 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the men of Jiāng,
and the men of Huáng met at Yánggǔ.
A5.3.6 In winter,
the Duke's son Yǒu went to Qí to attend a covenant.
A5.3.7 The men of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B5.3 The Commentary of Zuo, Year 3 of Duke Xī
B5.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
there was no rain.
In summer, in the sixth month,
it rained.
From the tenth month
there was no rain until the fifth month.
It is not called a drought,
because it did not constitute a disaster.
B5.3.2 In autumn,
they met at Yánggǔ,
to plan an attack on Chǔ.
B5.3.3 The Marquis of Qí, because of the meeting at Yánggǔ, came to renew the covenant.
In winter,
the Duke's son Yǒu went to Qí to attend the covenant.
B5.3.4 The men of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng wished to make peace.
Kǒng Shū said it was not permissible,
stating:
"Qí is just now diligently aiding us;
to abandon their virtue
is inauspicious."
B5.3.5 The Marquis of Qí and his consort Cài Jī were boating in the park,
and she rocked the boat.
The Duke was frightened,
and his countenance changed;
he forbade her,
but she would not stop.
The Duke was angry,
and sent her back,
but did not sever relations completely.
The men of Cài married her to another.
A5.4 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 4 of Duke Xī
A5.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
our Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo to invade Cài.
Cài collapsed,
and then they attacked Chǔ,
halting at Xíng.
A5.4.2 In summer,
the Baron of Xǔ, Xīn Chén, died.
A5.4.3 Qū Wán of Chǔ came to make a covenant with the army,
and they made a covenant at Shàolíng.
A5.4.4 The men of Qí seized Yuán Táotú of Chén.
A5.4.5 In autumn,
together with the men of Jiāng
and the men of Huáng, they attacked Chén.
A5.4.6 In the eighth month,
our Duke arrived from the attack on Chǔ.
A5.4.7 They buried Duke Mù of Xǔ.
A5.4.8 In winter, in the twelfth month,
Gōngsūn Zī led troops to join the men of Qí,
the men of Sòng,
the men of Wèi,
the men of Zhèng,
the men of Xǔ,
and the men of Cáo to invade Chén.
B5.4 The Commentary of Zuo, Year 4 of Duke Xī
B5.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí led the armies of the feudal lords
to invade Cài.
Cài collapsed,
and then they attacked Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent a messenger to speak with the army, saying:
"You dwell in the northern sea,
and I dwell in the southern sea;
even horses and cattle in heat do not reach each other.
I did not expect your lordship to tread upon my land.
What is the reason?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"In the past, Duke Kāng of Shào commanded our former lord, the Grand Duke, saying:
'The Five Marquises
and the Nine Earls,
you are to campaign against them,
in order to assist the Zhōu house!'
He granted our former lord jurisdiction over the lands,
eastward reaching to the sea,
westward reaching to the Hé River,
southward reaching to Mùlíng,
northward reaching to Wúdì.
Your tribute of bundled thatch grass is not presented,
the king's sacrifices are not supplied,
there is nothing with which to strain the wine,
and I am here to demand it.
King Zhāo campaigned southward and did not return,
and I am here to inquire about it."
The reply was:
"The failure to present tribute
is our ruler's crime,
how dare we not supply it?
As for King Zhāo's not returning,
you should inquire about that by the waterside!"
The army advanced,
and encamped at Xíng.
In summer,
the ruler of Chǔ sent Qū Wán to the army.
The army withdrew,
and encamped at Shàolíng.
The Marquis of Qí arrayed the armies of the feudal lords,
and rode with Qū Wán to observe them.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Is this not for my sake?
It is to continue the friendship of our former lords.
What would you say to joining me in friendship?"
The reply was:
"If you, my lord, in your kindness, seek blessings from the altars of our humble state,
and deign to receive our ruler,
it is our ruler's wish."
The Marquis of Qí said:
"With this multitude to do battle,
who can withstand it?
With this to attack cities,
what city cannot be taken?"
The reply was:
"If you, my lord, use virtue to soothe the feudal lords,
who would dare not submit?
If you, my lord, use force,
the state of Chǔ has Fāngchéng for its walls,
and the Hàn River for its moat.
Even with your multitude,
there is no place to use it."
Qū Wán made a covenant with the feudal lords.
B5.4.2 Yuán Táotú of Chén said to Shēn Hóu of Zhèng:
"If the army passes between Chén and
Zhèng,
our states will certainly suffer greatly.
If it goes out to the east,
displays arms to the Eastern Yí,
and returns along the coast,
that would be acceptable."
Shēn Hóu said:
"Good."
Táotú reported this,
and the Marquis of Qí
agreed to it.
Shēn Hóu had an audience,
and said:
"The army is weary.
If it goes out to the east and encounters the enemy,
I fear it will not be usable.
If it passes between Chén and
Zhèng,
they can supply its provisions and grain,
and sandals,
that would be acceptable."
The Marquis of Qí was pleased,
and gave him Hǔláo.
He arrested Yuán Táotú.
B5.4.3 In autumn,
they attacked Chén,
to punish its disloyalty.
B5.4.4 Duke Mù of Xǔ died in the army,
and was buried with the rites of a marquis,
which was according to ritual.
Whenever a feudal lord dies at court or
at a meeting,
he is given one rank higher;
if he dies in the king's service,
he is given two ranks higher.
Thus there was the use of a dragon robe for his burial.
B5.4.5 In winter,
Dàifú Shūsūn led troops
to join the armies of the feudal lords in invading Chén.
Chén made peace,
and Yuán Táotú was returned.
B5.4.6 Earlier,
Duke Xiàn of Jìn wanted to make Lí Jī his principal wife.
He divined by shell,
and it was not auspicious;
he divined by stalks,
and it was auspicious.
The duke said:
"Follow the stalks."
The diviner said:
"The stalks are short, the tortoise is long;
it is better to follow the long.
Moreover, its verse says:
'If you favor her exclusively, it will change;
you will lose your fine ram.
One fragrant, one foul,
for ten years the smell will still linger.'
It must not be done!"
He did not listen,
and established her.
She gave birth to Xī Qí,
and her younger sister gave birth to Zhuó Zǐ.
When he was about to establish Xī Qí as heir,
having already formed a plan with the middle-ranking officers,
Jī said to the crown prince:
"The lord dreamed of Qí Jiāng;
you must sacrifice to her quickly!"
The crown prince sacrificed at Qūwò,
and brought the sacrificial meat to the duke.
The duke was hunting,
and Jī placed it in the palace for six days.
When the duke arrived,
she poisoned it and presented it.
The duke poured a libation on the ground,
and the ground swelled up.
He gave it to a dog,
and the dog died.
He gave it to a minor servant,
and the minor servant also died.
Jī wept and said:
"The villainy comes from the crown prince."
The crown prince fled to Xīnchéng.
The duke killed his tutor, Dù Yuánkuǎn.
Someone said to the crown prince:
"If you explain yourself,
the lord will certainly discern the truth."
The crown prince said:
"If the lord is without Lady Jī,
he cannot rest peacefully,
nor eat his fill.
If I explain myself,
Jī will certainly be found guilty.
The lord is old;
I would again be unhappy."
He said:
"Will you then flee?"
The crown prince said:
"The lord does not truly discern my crime;
bearing this name to go out,
who would take me in?"
On the wùshēn day of the twelfth month,
he hanged himself at Xīnchéng.
Jī then slandered the two princes,
saying:
"They both knew about it."
Chóng'ěr fled to Pú,
and Yíwú fled to Qū.
A5.5 《The Fifth Year of Duke Xī, the Classic》
A5.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn killed his heir, Shēnshēng.
A5.5.2 The Elder Jī of Qǐ came to present her son at court.
A5.5.3 In summer,
Gōngsūn Zī went to Móu.
A5.5.4 The duke, together with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo, met with the king's heir at Shǒuzhǐ.
A5.5.5 In autumn, in the eighth month,
the feudal lords made a covenant at Shǒuzhǐ.
A5.5.6 The Earl of Zhèng escaped and returned, not joining the covenant.
A5.5.7 The men of Chǔ destroyed Xián,
and the ruler of Xián fled to Huáng.
A5.5.8 In the ninth month, on the first day, wùshēn,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A5.5.9 In winter,
the men of Jìn arrested the Duke of Yú.
B5.5 《The Fifth Year of Duke Xī, the Commentary》
B5.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year, in the royal first month, on the Xīnhài day, the new moon,
the sun reached its southernmost point.
The Duke, having observed the new moon,
then ascended the observation tower to gaze out,
and recorded it,
which was according to ritual.
At each equinox,
solstice,
beginning,
and closing,
he must record the cloud formations and phenomena,
for the sake of preparedness.
B5.5.2 The Marquis of Jìn sent someone to report the reason for killing Crown Prince Shēnshēng.
Earlier,
the Marquis of Jìn had sent Shì Wěi
to build the cities of Pú and Qū for the two princes,
but he was not careful,
placing firewood in the walls.
Yíwú complained about it.
The Duke sent someone to reprimand him.
Shì Wěi kowtowed and replied:
"Your servant has heard it said:
'To grieve without a death,
sorrow will surely find its match;
to build walls without warfare,
the match will surely guard them.'
If enemies are to guard them,
then why be careful?
To abandon one's official duty and disobey orders
is disrespectful;
to firmly secure them for enemies
is disloyal.
Lacking loyalty and respect,
how can one serve his lord?
The Odes say:
'Cherishing virtue brings peace,
the clan's sons are the wall.'
May my lord cultivate virtue
and strengthen the clan's sons,
what wall can compare to that?
In three years, he will be seeking troops,
why use caution?"
He withdrew and composed a verse:
"Fox-furs, shaggy and thick,
one state with three lords,
to whom should I turn?"
When the calamity came,
the Duke sent the eunuch Pī to attack Pú.
Chóng'ěr said:
"One does not resist the command of father and lord."
Then he announced:
"Those who resist,
are my enemies."
He climbed over the wall and fled.
Pī cut off his sleeve.
He then fled to Dí.
B5.5.3 In summer,
Gōngsūn Zī went to Móu,
to take a wife there.
B5.5.4 They met at Shǒuzhǐ,
meeting with the royal crown prince Zhèng,
to plan for the pacification of Zhōu.
B5.5.5 Chén Yuán Xuānzhòng
resented Zhèng Shēnhóu for opposing him at Zhàolíng,
so he urged him to fortify the city granted to him as a fief,
saying:
"To beautify its walls
is a great name,
your descendants will not forget.
I will help you request it."
He then requested it from the various lords on his behalf
and they fortified it,
beautifully.
He then slandered him to the Earl of Zhèng,
saying:
"He beautified the walls of his granted fief,
intending to rebel."
Because of this, Shēnhóu incurred offense.
B5.5.6 In autumn,
the various lords made a covenant.
The King sent Zhōu Gōng to summon the Earl of Zhèng,
saying:
"I will support you in following Chǔ,
assisted by Jìn,
you can have a little peace."
The Earl of Zhèng was pleased with the King's command,
but feared he would not pay court to Qí,
so he fled back without joining the covenant.
Kǒng Shū stopped him,
saying:
"A ruler of a state cannot act lightly,
acting lightly will cause him to lose allies;
losing allies,
calamity is sure to arrive.
To be in distress and then beg for a covenant,
what is lost will be great.
My lord will surely regret it."
He did not listen,
fled from his army and returned.
B5.5.7 Chǔ Dòu Gòuyútú destroyed Xián,
the Viscount of Xián fled to Huáng.
At that time, Jiāng, Huáng, Dào, and Bó were on friendly terms with Qí,
all were related by marriage to Xián.
The Viscount of Xián relied on this
and did not serve Chǔ,
nor did he prepare defenses,
therefore he perished.
B5.5.8 The Marquis of Jìn again borrowed a passage through Yú
to attack Guó.
Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated, saying:
"Guó
is the outer shield of Yú,
if Guó perishes,
Yú will surely follow.
Jìn cannot be given an opening,
enemies cannot be treated lightly.
Once is already excessive,
can it be done a second time?
The proverb says
'the cheekbone and the jawbone depend on each other,
when the lips are gone the teeth are cold'
refers to
Yú and
Guó."
The Duke said:
"Jìn
is of our same clan,
how could they harm us?"
He replied:
"Tàibó
and Yúzhòng
were sons of Tàiwáng;
Tàibó did not follow,
therefore he did not succeed.
Guózhòng
and Guóshū
were sons of Wángjì;
they served as ministers for King Wén,
their merit was in the royal house,
recorded in the covenant repository.
If he is about to destroy Guó,
what love would he have for Yú?
Moreover, can Yú be closer than the Huán and Zhuāng clans?
If he loved them,
what crime did the clans of Huán and Zhuáng commit?
That they were made to be slaughtered?
Was it not solely because they were pressing close?
Close relatives, honored and pressing close,
he still harmed them,
how much more a state?"
The Duke said:
"My sacrificial offerings are abundant and pure,
the spirits will surely support me."
He replied:
"Your servant has heard it said,
the ghosts and spirits do not actually favor people,
they rely solely on virtue.
Therefore the Zhōu Shū says:
'The August Heaven has no favorites,
it assists only the virtuous.'
It also says:
'Millet and grain are not the fragrance,
bright virtue is the fragrance.'
It also says:
'The people do not change the offerings,
only virtue is the offering.'
Thus,
if there is no virtue,
the people will not be harmonious,
and the spirits will not accept the offerings.
What the spirits rely upon
will be virtue.
If Jìn takes Yú,
and with bright virtue
presents fragrant offerings,
would the spirits spit them out?"
He did not listen,
and granted the Jìn envoy's request.
Gōng Zhīqí left with his clan,
saying:
"Yú will not have its year-end sacrifice.
On this campaign,
Jìn will not need to raise arms again."
In the eighth month, on the Jiǎwǔ day,
the Marquis of Jìn besieged Shàngyáng.
He asked Bǔ Yǎn, saying:
"Will I succeed?"
He replied:
"You will overcome it."
The Duke said:
"When?"
He replied:
"A children's rhyme says:
'On the morning of Bǐng,
the dragon's tail hides in the dawn;
uniforms all splendid,
they take Guó's banners.
The quail stars, bright and bold,
the Tiāncè star, dim and faint,
when the fire star is at mid-heaven, the army forms, the Duke of Guó will flee.'"
It must have been at the juncture of the ninth and tenth months!
At dawn on the bǐngzǐ day,
the sun was in the Tail constellation,
the moon in the Winnowing Basket constellation,
and the Firebird was at the zenith—
it must have been at that time.”
In winter, in the twelfth month, on the first day of the month, which was bǐngzǐ,
Jìn destroyed Guó.
Duke Chǒu of Guó fled to the capital.
The army returned,
lodged in Yú,
then attacked Yú by surprise and destroyed it.
They captured the Duke of Yú and his grandee Jǐng Bó,
using them as attendants for Lady Mù of Qín,
and restored the sacrifices of Yú,
moreover returning its tribute duties to the king.
Therefore, the record says:
“The men of Jìn captured the Duke of Yú,”
to blame Yú,
and also to indicate the ease of the capture.
A5.6 《The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Sixth Year of Duke Xī》
A5.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
the royal first month.
A5.6.2 In summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Earl of Cáo to attack Zhèng,
besieging Xīnchéng.
A5.6.3 In autumn,
the men of Chǔ besieged Xǔ,
and the feudal lords thereupon rescued Xǔ.
A5.6.4 In winter,
the Duke arrived from the attack on Zhèng.
B5.6 《The Commentary of Zuo: The Sixth Year of Duke Xī》
B5.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Jiǎ Huá to attack Qū.
Yí Wú could not hold it,
made a covenant and departed.
He was about to flee to Dí,
when Xì Ruì said:
“To leave later and go to the same place is a crime;
it would be better to go to Liáng.
Liáng is near Qín and enjoys its favor.”
So he went to Liáng.
B5.6.2 In summer,
the feudal lords attacked Zhèng
because it had fled the covenant of Shǒuzhǐ.
They besieged Xīnmì,
which Zhèng had fortified at an improper time.
B5.6.3 In autumn,
the Viscount of Chǔ besieged Xǔ in order to rescue Zhèng.
The feudal lords rescued Xǔ,
and he then withdrew.
B5.6.4 In winter,
Marquis Mù of Cài was about to bring Duke Xī of Xǔ
to see the Viscount of Chǔ at Wǔchéng.
The Earl of Xǔ bound his hands behind his back,
held a jade disk in his mouth,
his grandees wore mourning garments and hempen bands,
and the officers carried a coffin.
The Viscount of Chǔ asked Péng Bó about this.
He replied:
“In the past, when King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
Wēizǐ Qǐ acted thus.
King Wǔ personally released his bonds,
accepted his jade disk and purified it,
burned his coffin,
treated him with courtesy and commanded him,
restoring him to his former position.”
The Viscount of Chǔ followed this.
A5.7 《The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Seventh Year of Duke Xī》
A5.7.1 In the seventh year, in spring,
the men of Qí attacked Zhèng.
A5.7.2 In summer,
the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū came for an audience.
A5.7.3 Zhèng put to death its grandee Shēn Hóu.
A5.7.4 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the heir of Chén, Kuǎn,
and the heir of Zhèng, Huá,
and made a covenant at Níngmǔ.
A5.7.5 The Earl of Cáo, Bān, died.
A5.7.6 Gōngzǐ Yǒu went to Qí.
A5.7.7 In winter,
Duke Zhāo of Cáo was buried.
B5.7 《The Commentary of Zuo: The Seventh Year of Duke Xī》
B5.7.1 In the seventh year, in spring,
the men of Qí attacked Zhèng.
Kǒng Shū said to the Earl of Zhèng:
“There is a proverb that says:
‘If the heart is not strong,
why fear sickness?’
Since we can neither be strong
nor be weak,
this is the way to ruin.
The state is in danger;
I beg to submit to Qí in order to save the state.”
The Duke said:
“I know where this is coming from;
please wait for me a little while.”
He replied:
“We cannot wait from morning till evening—
how can we wait for you?”
B5.7.2 In summer,
Zhèng put Shēn Hóu to death to please Qí,
and also because of the slander of Chén’s Yuán Táotú.
Earlier, Shēn Hóu,
born of a woman from Shēn,
was favored by King Wén of Chǔ.
When King Wén was about to die,
he gave him a jade disk
and sent him away,
saying:
“Only I know you.
You are devoted to profit and never satisfied,
taking and seeking as you please,
yet I do not find fault with you.
Those who come after will demand more from you;
you will surely not escape.
When I die,
you must leave quickly.
Do not go to a small state,
for they will not tolerate you.”
After the burial,
he fled to Zhèng
and was again favored by Duke Lì.
When Zǐ Wén heard of his death,
he said:
“The ancients had a saying:
‘No one knows a minister like his ruler.’
This cannot be changed.”
B5.7.3 In autumn,
they made a covenant at Níngmǔ
to deliberate about Zhèng.
Guǎn Zhòng said to the Marquis of Qí:
“I have heard:
‘Win over the wavering with ritual,
and cherish the distant with virtue.
If virtue and ritual do not change,
no one will fail to be cherished.’”
The Marquis of Qí cultivated ritual among the feudal lords,
and the feudal lords’ officials received local products.
The Earl of Zhèng sent his heir, Huá,
to receive commands at the meeting.
He said to the Marquis of Qí:
“The three clans of Xiè,
Kǒng,
and Zǐrén
are truly disobeying your command.
If you remove them to achieve peace,
I will regard Zhèng as your inner minister,
and you will have nothing unfavorable.”
The Marquis of Qí was about to agree.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“You have united the feudal lords with ritual and good faith,
yet would end with treachery—
is this not unacceptable?
That father and son do not transgress is called ritual;
keeping commands and serving the times is called good faith.
To violate these two—
there is no greater treachery.”
The Duke said:
“The feudal lords have attacked Zhèng
without success;
now if there is an opening,
to follow it—
is this not acceptable?”
He replied:
“If you pacify them with virtue
and add instruction,
and they refuse,
then lead the feudal lords to attack Zhèng.
Zhèng will be too busy facing destruction—
how would they dare not fear?”
If you lead a host of criminals to threaten them,
Zhèng will have grounds for argument,
so what is there to fear?
Moreover, assembling the feudal lords
is to honor virtue.
To hold a meeting and place a traitor among them—
how can this serve as an example for future generations?
When the feudal lords gather,
their virtue,
punishments, rites,
and righteousness
are recorded by every state.
If the position of a traitor is recorded,
the lord's covenant will be undermined.
To act without leaving a record
is not the way of great virtue.
My lord, you must not consent!
Zhèng will surely accept the covenant.
Since Zǐ Huá is the crown prince,
yet seeks the intervention of a great state to weaken his own country,
he too will inevitably not escape misfortune.
Zhèng has Shū Zhàn,
Dǔ Shū,
and Shī Shū—three capable ministers governing—
so there is no opening to exploit."
The Marquis of Qí declined the request.
Zǐ Huá thereby incurred offense from Zhèng.
B5.7.4 In winter,
the Earl of Zhèng sent a request to form a covenant with Qí.
B5.7.5 In the intercalary month,
King Huì passed away.
King Xiāng, fearing the troubles caused by Prince Dài,
and apprehensive that he might not be established,
did not announce the mourning,
but reported the difficulties to Qí.
A5.8 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Eighth Year of Duke Xí"
A5.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the Duke met with the king's representative,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Earl of Cáo,
and the heir of Chén, Kuǎn,
and formed a covenant at Táo.
The Earl of Zhèng begged to join the covenant.
A5.8.2 In summer,
the Dí attacked Jìn.
A5.8.3 In autumn, the seventh month,
a dì sacrifice was held in the grand temple,
to bring in the Lady.
A5.8.4 In winter, on the dingwèi day of the twelfth month,
the Heavenly King passed away.
B5.8 "The Commentary of Zuo: The Eighth Year of Duke Xí"
B5.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the covenant was formed at Táo,
to deliberate on the affairs of the royal house.
The Earl of Zhèng begged to join the covenant,
seeking to submit.
King Xiāng secured his position
and only then announced the mourning.
B5.8.2 Lǐ Kè of Jìn led the army,
with Liáng Yóumǐ as charioteer,
and Guó Shè as the right-hand guard,
and defeated the Dí at Cǎisāng.
Liáng Yóumǐ said:
"The Dí are shameless;
if we pursue them,
we are sure to achieve a great victory."
Lǐ Kè said:
"It is enough to intimidate them;
do not provoke all the Dí tribes."
Guó Shè said:
"Within a year, the Dí are sure to come again,
for we have shown them weakness."
In summer,
the Dí attacked Jìn,
in retaliation for the battle at Cǎisāng.
This occurred exactly one year later.
B5.8.3 In autumn,
the dì sacrifice
was used to bring in Āi Jiāng,
which was contrary to ritual.
Generally, for a lady,
if she does not die in her chamber,
is not laid in state in the ancestral temple,
no obituary is sent to allied states,
and she is not enshrined with her husband's mother,
then she should not be brought in.
B5.8.4 In winter,
a royal messenger came to announce the mourning,
delayed due to the troubles,
hence the tardiness.
B5.8.5 The Duke of Sòng fell ill,
and the crown prince Zīfù firmly requested,
saying:
"Mù Yí is older and benevolent;
my lord, you should establish him!"
The duke ordered Zǐ Yú.
Zǐ Yú declined,
saying:
"To be able to yield the state—
what benevolence could be greater?
I am not his equal,
and moreover, it would be improper."
Thereupon, he hurried away and withdrew.
A5.9 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Ninth Year of Duke Xí"
A5.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
on the dīngchǒu day of the third month of the royal calendar,
the Duke of Sòng, Yù Yuè, passed away.
A5.9.2 In summer,
the Duke met with the Chief Minister Zhōu Gōng,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Viscount of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo at Kuíqiū.
A5.9.3 In autumn, on the yǐyǒu day of the seventh month,
Bó Jī passed away.
A5.9.4 In autumn, on the wùchén day of the ninth month,
the feudal lords formed a covenant at Kuíqiū.
A5.9.5 On the jiǎzǐ day,
the Marquis of Jìn, Guǐ Zhū, passed away.
A5.9.6 In winter,
Lǐ Kè of Jìn killed his lord's son, Xī Qí.
B5.9 "The Commentary of Zuo: The Ninth Year of Duke Xí"
B5.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
Duke Huán of Sòng passed away.
Before the burial, Duke Xiāng met with the feudal lords,
hence he was referred to as
"Viscount."
Generally, during mourning,
the king is called
"the little child,"
and dukes and marquises are called
"Viscount."
B5.9.2 In summer,
the meeting at Kuíqiū
renewed the covenant,
and also fostered good relations,
which was in accordance with ritual.
The king sent Chief Minister Kǒng
to present sacrificial meat to the Marquis of Qí,
saying:
"The Son of Heaven has performed sacrifices to King Wén
and King Wǔ,
and sends me, Kǒng, to present sacrificial meat to the Elder Uncle."
The Marquis of Qí was about to descend and bow.
Kǒng said:
"And there is a further command.
The Son of Heaven sends me, Kǒng, to say:
'As the Elder Uncle is aged,
and has rendered additional service,
you are granted one rank higher,
and need not descend to bow!'"
The Marquis replied:
"The awe of Heaven is not distant from my face by even a foot;
I, Xiǎo Bái,
how dare I presume upon the Son of Heaven's command
and not descend to bow?
—I fear to stumble and fall below,
bringing shame upon the Son of Heaven.
How dare I not descend to bow?"
He descended,
bowed;
ascended,
and received.
B5.9.3 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí formed a covenant with the feudal lords at Kuíqiū,
saying:
"All of us who are allies here,
after this covenant is made,
let us return to good relations."
Chief Minister Kǒng returned first,
and encountered the Marquis of Jìn,
saying:
"There is no need to attend the meeting.
The Marquis of Qí does not devote himself to virtue
but diligently pursues distant campaigns;
thus he attacked the Shānróng in the north,
attacked Chǔ in the south,
and now holds this meeting in the west."
As for the east, it is unknown whether they have attacked,
but the west certainly has not.
The trouble lies in the chaos!
Your lordship should focus on pacifying the chaos,
and not be hasty in your actions.”
The Marquis of Jìn then turned back.
B5.9.4 In the ninth month,
Marquis Xiàn of Jìn passed away.
Lǐ Kè and Pī Zhèng wanted to install Duke Wén,
so they used the followers of the three princes to start a rebellion.
Earlier,
Marquis Xiàn had appointed Xún Xī as tutor to Xī Qí.
When the marquis fell ill,
he summoned him and
said:
“I entrust this young orphan to you, a great officer,
what will you do?”
Xún Xī bowed his head to the ground and replied:
“I will exert all my strength,
adding to it loyalty
and steadfastness.
If we succeed,
it will be due to your lordship’s spirit;
if we do not succeed,
I will follow with my death.”
The marquis asked:
“What do you mean by loyalty
and steadfastness?”
He replied:
“To know what benefits the ducal house and do it without fail—
that is loyalty;
to escort the deceased and serve the living,
with neither harboring suspicion—
that is steadfastness.”
When Lǐ Kè was about to kill Xī Qí,
he first informed Xún Xī, saying:
“The resentment of the three princes is about to erupt,
with Qín and Jìn supporting them.
What will you do?”
Xún Xī said:
“I will die for it.”
Lǐ Kè said:
“It will be of no use.”
Xún Shū said:
“I have made a promise to the late ruler,
and I cannot break it.
How can one desire to keep one’s word yet cherish one’s life?
Even if it is of no use,
how can I avoid it?
Moreover, if people desire goodness,
who is not like me?
I wish to be without duplicity—
can I tell others to stop?”
In the tenth month of winter,
Lǐ Kè killed Xī Qí at his residence.
The record says
“killed his ruler’s son”—
because the marquis had not yet been buried.
Xún Xī was about to die for it,
when someone said:
“It would be better to install Zhuó Zǐ
and assist him.”
Xún Xī installed Prince Zhuó
and buried the marquis.
In the eleventh month,
Lǐ Kè killed Prince Zhuó at court.
Xún Xī died for it.
The gentleman says:
“As the Odes say:
‘A flaw in a white jade scepter
can still be ground away;
a flaw in these words
cannot be undone.’
Xún Xī was such a man.”
B5.9.5 The Marquis of Qí led the armies of the various states to attack Jìn,
reaching Gāoliáng before turning back—
this was to punish the chaos in Jìn.
The order did not reach Lǔ,
so it was not recorded.
B5.9.6 Xì Ruì of Jìn had Yí Wú offer heavy bribes to Qín
in order to gain entry,
saying:
“Others truly possess the state—
why should we begrudge it?
Once inside, we can win the people;
what does it matter about the land?”
Yí Wú followed this advice.
Xí Péng of Qí led troops to join the Qín army
and installed Duke Huì of Jìn.
The Earl of Qín said to Xì Ruì:
“On whom does the prince rely?”
He replied:
“I have heard that
an exile has no faction;
if he has a faction, he must have enemies.
Yí Wú was weak and did not enjoy play;
he could fight but not excessively;
as he grew older, he did not change—
I know nothing else about him.”
The earl said to Gōngsūn Zhī:
“Will Yí Wú stabilize the state?”
He replied:
“I have heard:
‘Only by following principles can one stabilize a state.’
The Odes say:
‘Without knowledge or awareness,
they follow the rules of God.’
This refers to King Wén.
It also says:
‘Without error or harm,
few do not take it as a rule.’
This means having no preferences or aversions,
no jealousy or aggression.
Now his words are full of jealousy and aggression—
it will be difficult!”
The earl said:
“Jealousy leads to much resentment;
how then can he prevail?
This is to our advantage.”
B5.9.7 Duke Xiāng of Sòng ascended the throne.
Considering Prince Mùyí benevolent,
he appointed him as Left Marshal to handle governance,
and thus Sòng was well-governed.
Hence, the Yú clan for generations served as Left Marshal.
A5.10 The Tenth Year of Duke Xī (Spring and Autumn Annals)
A5.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
in the royal first month,
the duke went to Qí.
A5.10.2 The Dí destroyed Wēn,
and the Viscount of Wēn fled to Wèi.
A5.10.3 Lǐ Kè of Jìn assassinated his ruler Zhuó and his great officer Xún Xī.
A5.10.4 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Baron of Xǔ attacked the Northern Róng.
A5.10.5 Jìn killed its great officer Lǐ Kè.
A5.10.6 In autumn, the seventh month.
A5.10.7 In winter,
there was heavy snow.
B5.10 The Tenth Year of Duke Xī (Commentary)
B5.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
the Dí destroyed Wēn
because the Viscount of Sū was untrustworthy.
The Viscount of Sū betrayed the king and allied with the Dí,
but he also could not get along with the Dí.
The Dí attacked him,
and the king did not rescue him,
so he was destroyed.
The Viscount of Sū fled to Wèi.
B5.10.2 In the summer, the fourth month,
Zhōu Gōng Jìfù
and Prince Dǎng joined Xí Péng of Qí
to install the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn killed Lǐ Kè
to justify himself.
When he was about to kill Lǐ Kè,
the duke sent someone to tell him:
“Without you,
I would not have reached this position.
Nevertheless,
you have killed two rulers and one great officer—
for one who is your ruler,
is it not difficult?”
He replied:
“If there had been no removal,
how could you, my lord, have risen?
If you wish to add a crime,
will there be no words for it?
I have heard your command.”
He fell on his sword and died.
At that time, Pī Zhèng was on a mission to Qín,
and also to apologize for delaying the bribes,
so he was not involved.
B5.10.3 The Marquis of Jìn reburied the Crown Prince Gòng.
In autumn,
Hú Tū went to the lower capital
and encountered the crown prince.
The crown prince had him mount
as charioteer
and told him:
“Yí Wú has been disrespectful;
I have obtained permission from God.
I will give Jìn to Qín,
and Qín will sacrifice to me.”
He replied:
“I have heard:
‘Spirits do not enjoy sacrifices from those not of their kind;
the people do not sacrifice to those not of their clan.’
Will your sacrifice not be cut off?”
Moreover, what crime have the people committed?
You have failed to administer punishment,
and you have neglected the sacrifices.
Please consider this, my lord!"
The lord said,
"Very well.
I will make another request.
In seven days,
there will be a shaman at the western outskirts of Xīnchéng
who will appear to me."
He agreed,
and then disappeared.
When the time came, he went and
informed him, saying:
"The Emperor has permitted me to punish the guilty,
and they will be defeated at Hán."
When Pī Zhèng went to Qín,
he spoke to the Earl of Qín, saying:
"Lǚ Shēng,
Xì Chēng,
and Jì Ruì
are truly disloyal.
If you send them lavish gifts to summon them,
I will drive out the ruler of Jìn,
and you can install Chóng'ěr,
and nothing will fail."
In winter,
the Earl of Qín sent Líng Zhì to deliver gifts and
inquiries,
and to summon the three men.
Xì Ruì said:
"The gifts are lavish and the words are sweet—
they are luring us."
Thereupon, they killed Pī Zhèng,
Qí Jǔ, and the seven yú grandees:
Zuǒháng Gònghuá,
Yòuháng Jiǎhuá,
Shū Jiān,
Zhuī Chuán,
Léi Hǔ,
Tè Gōng,
and Shān Qí,
all of whom were partisans of Lǐ Kè and
Pī Zhèng.
Pī Bào fled to Qín
and spoke to the Earl of Qín, saying:
"The Marquis of Jìn has betrayed his great lord
and harbors resentment over minor grievances,
so the people do not support him.
If you attack him,
he will certainly be driven out."
The Duke said:
"If he has lost the support of the masses,
how can he be killed?
If he avoids disaster,
who can drive out the ruler?"
A5.11 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Eleventh Year of Duke Xī"
A5.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
Jìn killed its grandee Pī Zhèngfù.
A5.11.2 In summer,
the Duke and his wife, Lady Jiāng, met with the Marquis of Qí at Yánggǔ.
A5.11.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
there was a great rain-seeking sacrifice.
A5.11.4 In winter,
the people of Chǔ attacked Huáng.
B5.11 "The Commentary of Zuo: The Eleventh Year of Duke Xī"
B5.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent messengers to report the rebellion of Pī Zhèng.
B5.11.2 The Son of Heaven sent Duke Shào Wǔ and
the Neishi Guò
to confer a mandate upon the Marquis of Jìn.
He received the jade sluggishly.
Guò returned
and reported to the King, saying:
"The Marquis of Jìn will likely have no descendants!
The King conferred a mandate upon him,
yet he was sluggish in receiving the auspicious token.
He has already abandoned himself first—
how can he have successors?
Ritual
is the trunk of the state,
and reverence
is the carriage of ritual.
Without reverence,
ritual cannot be carried out;
if ritual cannot be carried out,
then superiors and inferiors will be in chaos.
How can he endure for generations?"
B5.11.3 In summer,
the Róng tribes of Yáng, Jù,
Quán, Gāo,
Yī, and Luò jointly attacked the capital,
entered the royal city,
and burned the eastern gate.
This was because Prince Dài had summoned them.
Qín and Jìn attacked the Róng to rescue Zhōu.
In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn made peace between the Róng and the King.
B5.11.4 The people of Huáng did not send tribute to Chǔ.
In winter,
the people of Chǔ attacked Huáng.
A5.12 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Twelfth Year of Duke Xī"
A5.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
on the third month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
there was a solar eclipse.
A5.12.2 In summer,
the people of Chǔ extinguished Huáng.
A5.12.3 In autumn, in the seventh month.
A5.12.4 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
the Marquis of Chén, Chǔjiù, died.
B5.12 "The Commentary of Zuo: The Twelfth Year of Duke Xī"
B5.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
the feudal lords fortified the outer wall of Wèi's Chǔqiū,
fearing disaster from the Dí.
B5.12.2 The people of Huáng relied on the harmony between the feudal lords and Qí
and did not fulfill their duties to Chǔ,
saying:
"From Yǐng to us is nine hundred lǐ—
how can they harm us?"
In summer,
Chǔ extinguished Huáng.
B5.12.3 The King, because of the Róng disaster,
punished Prince Dài.
In autumn,
Prince Dài fled to Qí.
B5.12.4 In winter,
the Marquis of Qí sent Guǎn Yíwǔ to make peace between the Róng and the King,
and sent Xí Péng to make peace between the Róng and Jìn.
The King entertained Guǎn Zhòng with the rites for a shàngqīng.
Guǎn Zhòng declined, saying:
am a humble official.
There are the two guardians appointed by the Son of Heaven, Guó and
Gāo, in place.
If, according to the seasonal rituals of spring and autumn, they come
to receive the King's command,
how could I be treated with such rites?
I, a péichén, dare to decline."
The King said:
"Uncle!
I praise your merits!
You respond with your virtuous conduct,
and I command that it be remembered without fail.
Go and fulfill your duties,
and do not disobey my command!"
Guǎn Zhòng ultimately accepted the rites for a xiàqīng
and returned.
The gentleman said:
"It is fitting that the Guǎn clan sacrifices generation after generation!
He yielded and did not forget his superiors.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The amiable and upright gentleman
is blessed by the spirits.'"
A5.13 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Thirteenth Year of Duke Xī"
A5.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Dí invaded Wèi.
A5.13.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
the funeral of Duke Xuān of Chén was held.
A5.13.3 The Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo at Xián.
A5.13.4 In autumn, in the ninth month,
there was a great rain-seeking sacrifice.
A5.13.5 In winter,
Gōngzǐ Yǒu went to Qí.
B5.13 "The Commentary of Zuo: The Thirteenth Year of Duke Xī"
B5.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí sent Zhòngxì Jiǎo on a mission to Zhōu,
and also to speak about Prince Dài.
When the matters were concluded,
he did not speak with the King.
He returned,
He returned and reported, saying:
"Not yet.
The king's anger has not subsided;
perhaps it will take ten years?
If not ten years,
the king will not summon him."
B5.13.2 In summer,
a meeting was held at Xián,
because the Huáiyí were troubling Qǐ,
and also to deliberate on the affairs of the royal house.
B5.13.3 In autumn,
due to the difficulties caused by the Róng,
the feudal lords garrisoned Zhōu.
Qí Zhòngsūn Jiǎo oversaw this.
B5.13.4 In winter,
Jìn suffered repeated famines,
and sent to request grain from Qín.
The Earl of Qín said to Zǐsāng:
"Shall we give it to them?"
He replied:
"If you generously bestow aid and they repay it,
what more will you seek from them?
If you generously bestow aid and they do not repay it,
their people will certainly become disaffected;
when they are disaffected and you then attack them,
having no popular support,
they are sure to be defeated."
He said to Bǎilǐ:
"Shall we give it to them?"
He replied:
"Natural disasters are widespread,
and states encounter them in turn.
Relieving calamities
and showing compassion to neighbors
is the proper way.
To act according to the way
brings blessings."
Pī Zhèng's son Bào was in Qín,
and urged an attack on Jìn.
The Earl of Qín said:
"Their ruler is hateful,
but what crime have their people committed?"
Qín then transported grain to Jìn,
in an unbroken line from Yōng to Jiàng,
and it was called the Campaign of the Boats.
A5.14 The Spring and Autumn Annals, the Fourteenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.14.1 In the fourteenth year, in spring,
the feudal lords walled Yuánlíng.
A5.14.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
Jì Jī and the Viscount of Zēng met at Fáng.
She made the Viscount of Zēng come to court.
A5.14.3 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the xīnmǎo day,
Shālù collapsed.
A5.14.4 The Dí invaded Zhèng.
A5.14.5 In winter,
Marquis Xī of Cài died.
B5.14 The Commentary of Zuo, the Fourteenth Year of Duke Xī
B5.14.1 In spring of the fourteenth year,
the feudal lords walled Yuánlíng and moved Qǐ there,
but the record does not name the persons involved,
indicating an omission.
B5.14.2 Jì Jī of Zēng came home on a visit,
but the duke was angry
and detained her,
because the Viscount of Zēng had not come to court.
In summer,
they met at Fáng,
and she made him come to court.
B5.14.3 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the xīnmǎo day,
Shālù collapsed.
Bǔ Yǎn of Jìn said:
"Within a year there will be a great calamity,
nearly destroying the state."
B5.14.4 In winter,
Qín suffered famine,
and sent to request grain from Jìn,
but the men of Jìn refused to give it.
Qìng Zhèng said:
"To reject a kindness
is to lose friendship;
to gloat over another's calamity
is inhumanity;
to be covetous and selfish
is inauspicious;
to anger a neighbor
is unrighteous.
When these four virtues are all lost,
how can one preserve the state?"
Guó Shè said:
"If the skin is gone,
to what shall the hair adhere?"
Qìng Zhèng said:
"To discard good faith
and reject a neighbor—
who will sympathize with our troubles?
Without good faith,
troubles arise;
without aid,
we are sure to perish.
This is indeed so."
Guó Shè said:
"It will not lessen their enmity,
but will strengthen the enemy;
it is better not to give."
Qìng Zhèng said:
"To reject a kindness
and gloat over calamity—
this is what the people abandon.
Even close ones will become enemies,
how much more those who are already resentful foes?"
They did not listen.
Withdrawing, he said:
"The ruler will surely regret this!"
A5.15 The Spring and Autumn Annals, the Fifteenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
the duke went to Qí.
A5.15.2 The men of Chǔ attacked Xú.
A5.15.3 In the third month,
the duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo,
and made a covenant at Mǔqiū,
then encamped at Kuāng.
Gōngsūn Áo led troops and the officers of the feudal lords to rescue Xú.
A5.15.4 In summer, in the fifth month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A5.15.5 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the army of Qí
and the army of Cáo attacked Lì.
A5.15.6 In the eighth month,
there was a plague of locusts.
A5.15.7 In the ninth month,
the duke returned from the meeting.
A5.15.8 Jì Jī went back to Zēng.
A5.15.9 On the jǐmǎo day, the last day of the month,
lightning struck the temple of Yí Bó.
A5.15.10 In winter,
the men of Sòng attacked Cáo.
A5.15.11 The men of Chǔ defeated Xú at Lóulín.
A5.15.12 In the eleventh month, on the rénxū day,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Earl of Qín fought at Hán,
and the Marquis of Jìn was captured.
B5.15 The Commentary of Zuo, the Fifteenth Year of Duke Xī
B5.15.1 In spring of the fifteenth year,
the men of Chǔ attacked Xú,
because Xú had drawn close to the Zhūxià states.
In the third month,
a covenant was made at Mǔqiū,
renewing the covenant of Kuíqiū,
and also to rescue Xú.
Mèng Mùbó led troops and the armies of the feudal lords to rescue Xú,
and the feudal lords encamped at Kuāng to await them.
B5.15.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
The record does not give the first day of the month or the day of the eclipse,
due to an error by the officials.
B5.15.3 In autumn,
they attacked Lì,
in order to rescue Xú.
B5.15.4 When the Marquis of Jìn entered his state,
Lady Mù of Qín entrusted Jiǎ Jūn to him,
and also said:
"Take back all the ducal sons."
The Marquis of Jìn had illicit relations with Jiǎ Jūn,
and also did not take back the ducal sons,
so Lady Mù resented him.
The Marquis of Jìn had promised bribes to the high officials,
but afterward went back on it all.
He promised the Earl of Qín five cities in the region beyond the Yellow River,
extending east to Guóluè,
south to Huàshān,
and inside to Xièliáng City,
but afterward did not give them.
When Jìn suffered a famine,
Qín supplied them with grain;
when Qín suffered a famine,
Jìn closed its grain markets to them.
Therefore, the Earl of Qín attacked Jìn.
Bǔ Túfǔ performed a divination by yarrow stalks,
and the result was auspicious:
"Crossing the river,
the marquis's chariot will be wrecked."
The earl questioned him.
He replied:
"This is actually greatly auspicious.
After three defeats,
you are sure to capture the ruler of Jìn.
The hexagram encountered was 'Gǔ'
䷑, which says:
'A thousand chariots thrice depart,
after thrice departing,
capture their male fox.'
Now the fox of 'Gǔ'
must refer to their ruler.
The inner trigram of 'Gǔ'
is wind;
the outer trigram
is mountain.
The season is now autumn,
we will cause their fruits to fall,
and take their timber,
this is why we will overcome.
When the fruits have fallen
and the timber is lost,
if they are not defeated,
what can they await?"
After three defeats, the Qín army reached Hán.
The Marquis of Jìn said to Qìng Zhèng:
"The enemy has penetrated deep,
what is to be done?"
He replied:
"It is you, my lord, who have caused them to penetrate deep,
what can be done!"
The marquis said:
"Insolent!"
They divined for the right-hand charioteer,
and Qìng Zhèng proved auspicious.
But he was not employed.
Bù Yáng drove the war chariot,
and Jiāpú Tú served as the right-hand charioteer.
They used small steeds from Zhèng.
Qìng Zhèng said:
"In ancient times, for great affairs,
one must use horses bred in one's own land,
born of its water and soil,
and thus knowing the hearts of its people;
accustomed to its training,
and familiar with its ways;
wherever they are driven,
they fulfill one's will.
Now we use horses of foreign breed
for military action;
when they become frightened and change,
they will resist their driver.
Their breath will become disordered and rebellious,
their blood will surge throughout,
their veins will swell and burst forth,
outwardly strong but inwardly exhausted.
They will be unable to advance or retreat,
incapable of maneuvering.
You will certainly regret it."
He did not listen.
In the ninth month,
the Marquis of Jìn went to meet the Qín army,
and sent Hán Jiǎn to observe their forces.
He returned and said:
"Their army is smaller than ours,
but their fighting men are twice our number."
The marquis said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"When you left Jìn, you relied on their resources;
when you entered, you enjoyed their favor;
in famine, you ate their grain.
They have bestowed three favors without receiving recompense,
and thus they have come.
Now if we attack them again,
we will be sluggish,
while Qín will be vigorous;
twice our number is not even the limit."
The marquis said:
"A single man cannot be provoked with impunity,
how much less a state?"
He then sent a messenger to request battle,
saying:
"I, though unworthy,
can gather my multitudes but cannot disperse them.
If you, my lord, do not withdraw,
there is no escape from your command."
The Earl of Qín sent Gōngsūn Zhī to reply,
saying:
"Before you, my lord, had entered Jìn,
I feared for you;
after you entered but before your position was settled,
I still worried for you.
Now that your position is settled,
how dare I not accept your command?"
Hán Jiǎn withdrew
and said:
"I am fortunate if I can be taken prisoner."
On the rénxū day,
they fought at Hányuán.
The warhorses of Jìn became mired in the mud and halted.
The marquis called for Qìng Zhèng.
Qìng Zhèng said:
"Obstinate in rejecting advice,
defying the divination,
you certainly sought this defeat;
how can you escape it now?"
He then left him.
Liáng Yóumǐ drove for Hán Jiǎn,
with Guó Shè as the right-hand charioteer;
they intercepted the Earl of Qín's chariot
and were about to capture him.
Qìng Zhèng, by coming to rescue the marquis, caused them to err,
and they thus lost the Earl of Qín.
Qín captured the Marquis of Jìn and returned with him.
The great officers of Jìn, with hair disheveled and tents pitched,
followed him.
The Earl of Qín sent a messenger to address them,
saying:
"Why are you gentlemen so sorrowful?
My accompanying your ruler westward
is merely to fulfill Jìn's ominous dream;
how dare I go to extremes?"
The great officers of Jìn bowed three times and touched their heads to the ground, saying:
"You tread upon the earth
and are crowned by heaven;
heaven and earth
truly hear your words.
We, your servants, dare to remain below the wind."
Mù Jī heard that the Marquis of Jìn was about to arrive;
taking the heir apparent Yīng,
Hóng, and her daughter Jiǎn Bì, she ascended a tower
and stood upon firewood.
She sent someone to meet the earl in plain mourning garments with hempen girdles,
and announced:
"Heaven has sent down disaster,
causing our two rulers to meet not with jade and silk,
but with raised weapons.
If the ruler of Jìn enters in the morning,
then this handmaid will die in the evening;
if he enters in the evening,
she will die in the morning.
Only you, my lord, can decide!"
He then lodged him at the Língtái.
The great officers requested that he be brought into the capital.
The earl said:
"Capturing the Marquis of Jìn
was a rich gain to bring home;
if now I bring home a funeral,
what use is that?
And what would the great officers gain from it?
Moreover, the people of Jìn, in sorrow and anxiety,
move me,
and invoke heaven and earth to bind me.
If I do not consider Jìn's grief,
I will double their anger;
if I break my word,
I betray heaven and earth.
Doubled anger
is hard to bear;
betraying heaven
is inauspicious.
I must return the ruler of Jìn."
Prince Zhí said:
"It would be better to kill him,
and not let wickedness gather."
Zǐsāng said:
"Return him and take his heir apparent as hostage,
and you will surely achieve great success.
Jìn cannot yet be destroyed,
and killing its ruler
would only create enmity.
Moreover, Shǐ Yì has said:
'Do not start calamity,
do not rely on disorder,
do not double anger.'
Doubled anger
is hard to bear;
oppressing others
is inauspicious."
He then agreed to make peace with Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Qǐ
to inform Xiàlǚ Yísheng,
and to summon him.
Zǐjīn taught him what to say,
saying:
"Assemble the people of the state
and distribute rewards in the ruler's name.
And tell them:
'Though I have returned,
I have brought disgrace upon the altars of soil and grain;
you should divine about making Túyǔ your ruler.'"
The multitude all wept,
and Jìn thereupon instituted the yuántián system.
Lǚsheng said:
"Our ruler does not grieve over his own exile,
but is concerned about his ministers and officers;
this is the utmost in kindness.
What shall we do for our ruler?"
The multitude said:
"What should we do?"
He replied:
"Levy taxes and repair weapons
to assist the young heir.
When the feudal lords hear of this,
they will know that though we have lost a ruler, we have another;
that our ministers and officers are harmonious and united;
and that our armor and weapons are increasing.
Those who are friendly to us will be encouraged,
and those who hate us will be afraid.
Perhaps this will be beneficial!"
The multitude was pleased,
and Jìn thereupon instituted the zhōubīng system.
Earlier,
when Marquis Xiàn of Jìn performed a divination by milfoil about marrying his elder daughter Bó Jī to Qín,
he obtained the hexagram Guīmèi changing to Kuí.
The diviner Sū interpreted it,
saying:
"It is not auspicious.
The verse says:
'The man stabs the sheep,
but there is no blood;
the woman carries the basket,
but there is no offering.
Reproaches from the western neighbor,
cannot be repaid.
Guīmèi changing to Kuí,
means there will be no assistance.'
Zhèn changing to Lí,
is also Lí changing to Zhèn.
'It is thunder, it is fire;
it is Yíng defeating Jī.
The chariot loses its axle strap,
fire burns its banners;
it is not favorable for marching the army,
they will be defeated at Zōngqiū.
Guīmèi and Kuí signify isolation,
the enemy draws his bow.
The nephew follows his aunt;
after six years he will flee,
escape back to his own state,
and abandon his family.
The next year he will die at the ruins of Gāoliáng.'"
When Duke Huì was in Qín,
he said:
"If the former ruler had followed the diviner Sū's interpretation,
I would not have come to this!"
Hán Jiǎn, who was in attendance,
said:
"Tortoise shells
show images,
milfoil stalks
show numbers.
Things are born and then have images;
from images they multiply,
and from multiplication come numbers.
The former ruler's failed virtue,
could it be numbered?
Diviner Sū's interpretation of this,
what good would it have done not to follow it?
The Odes say:
'The calamities of the people below,
do not descend from Heaven.
Chattering together, hating behind backs,
the strife is truly caused by men.'"
B5.15.5 Thunder struck the temple of Yí Bó,
which was to punish him,
for the Zhǎn clan had hidden faults.
B5.15.6 In winter,
the men of Sòng attacked Cáo,
to settle an old grievance.
B5.15.7 Chǔ defeated Xú at Lóulín,
because Xú relied on rescue.
B5.15.8 In the tenth month,
Jìn's Yīnyísheng met with the Earl of Qín,
and they made a covenant at Wángchéng.
The Earl of Qín said:
"Is the state of Jìn harmonious?"
He replied:
"It is not harmonious.
The petty men are ashamed of losing their ruler
and grieve over the loss of their relatives;
they do not fear levying taxes and repairing weapons
to establish Túyǔ as ruler,
saying:
'We must take revenge,
even if it means serving the Róng and Dí.'
The noblemen love their ruler
and acknowledge his guilt;
they do not fear levying taxes and repairing weapons
to await Qín's command,
saying:
'We must repay virtue,
even if it means death, we will not have two hearts.'
Because of this, they are not harmonious."
The Earl of Qín said:
"What does the state say about your ruler?"
He replied:
"The petty men are distressed,
saying he will not be spared;
the noblemen are forgiving,
believing he will certainly return.
The petty men say:
'We have poisoned Qín,
how could Qín return our ruler?'
The noblemen say:
'We acknowledge our guilt,
Qín will certainly return our ruler.
When he was disloyal, they seized him;
when he submitted, they released him.
There is no virtue greater than this,
no punishment more awe-inspiring than this.
Those who submit will cherish the virtue,
those who are disloyal will fear the punishment.
With this single action,
Qín can become hegemon.
To install him and not stabilize him,
to depose him and not establish another,
turning virtue into resentment,
Qín would not do such a thing.'"
The Earl of Qín said:
"This is my heart's desire."
He changed the lodging of the Marquis of Jìn,
and presented him with seven sets of sacrificial animals.
É Xī said to Qìng Zhèng:
"Why not flee?"
He replied:
"Having caused my ruler's defeat,
if I do not die after the defeat,
and further cause the loss of punishment,
I would not be a proper minister.
A minister who is not a proper minister,
where could I go?"
In the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Jìn returned.
On Dīngchǒu,
he killed Qìng Zhèng and then entered.
That year,
Jìn again suffered famine,
and the Earl of Qín again supplied them with grain,
saying:
"I resent their ruler,
but I pity their people.
Moreover, I have heard that when Tángshū was enfeoffed,
Jīzǐ said:
'His descendants will surely become great.'
How can Jìn's future be hoped for?
Let us temporarily cultivate virtue,
and wait for capable men."
Thereupon, Qín began to levy taxes in Jìn's Hédōng region,
and established offices and officials there.
A5.16 The Classic of the Sixteenth Year of Duke Xī
A5.16.1 In the sixteenth year, in spring,
the first month, on the first day Wùshēn,
five meteorites fell in Sòng.
In this month,
six fishhawks flew backward,
passing over the capital of Sòng.
A5.16.2 In the third month, on Rénshēn,
the nobleman Jì Yǒu died.
A5.16.3 In summer, the fourth month, on Bǐngshēn,
Jì Jī of Zēng died.
A5.16.4 In autumn, the seventh month, on Jiǎzǐ,
Gōngsūn Zī died.
A5.16.5 In winter, the twelfth month,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Marquis of Xíng,
and the Earl of Cáo at Huái.
B5.16 Commentary on Duke Xi, Year 16
B5.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
five stones fell in Sòng.
These were fallen stars.
Six herons flew backwards,
passing over the capital of Sòng.
This was due to the wind.
Shū Xìng, the Neishi of Zhōu, was on a diplomatic mission to Sòng.
Duke Xiāng of Sòng asked him,
saying:
"What omen is this?
Wherein lies good or ill fortune?"
He replied:
"This year Lǔ will suffer many great bereavements.
Next year Qí will have turmoil.
You, my lord, will gain the allegiance of the feudal lords,
but not to the end."
After withdrawing, he told others:
"The lord asked the wrong question.
These are matters of yīn and yáng,
not the source of good or ill fortune.
Good and ill fortune come from men.
I did not dare to contradict the lord, that is all."
B5.16.2 In summer,
Qí attacked Lì,
but did not subdue it.
They went to rescue Xú and then returned.
B5.16.3 In autumn,
the Dí invaded Jìn.
They took Hú,
Chú, and Shòuduó.
They crossed the Fén River,
and reached Kūndū,
taking advantage of Jìn's defeat.
B5.16.4 The King informed Qí of the troubles with the Róng.
Qí summoned the feudal lords to garrison Zhōu.
B5.16.5 In winter, on the yǐmǎo day of the eleventh month,
Zhèng killed Zǐ Huá.
B5.16.6 In the twelfth month,
a meeting was held at Huái,
to deliberate about Zēng,
and also to campaign eastward.
While fortifying Zēng,
the laborers became distressed.
Someone climbed a mound at night and cried out:
"Qí has turmoil!"
The fortification was not completed, and they returned.
A5.17 The Annals of Duke Xi, Year 17
A5.17.1 In the seventeenth year, in spring,
men of Qí
and men of Xú attacked the Yīngshì.
A5.17.2 In summer,
Xiàng was destroyed.
A5.17.3 In autumn,
the Lady Jiāng, the wife [of the Duke], met with the Marquis of Qí at Biàn.
A5.17.4 In the ninth month,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A5.17.5 In winter, on the yǐhài day of the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí, Xiǎo Bái, died.
B5.17 Commentary on Duke Xi, Year 17
B5.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
men of Qí attacked the Yīngshì for Xú's sake,
in retaliation for the battle of Lóulín.
B5.17.2 In summer,
Yǔ, the Heir of Jìn, became a hostage in Qín.
Qín returned the lands east of the [Yellow] River to Jìn
and gave him a wife.
When Duke Huì of Jìn was in Liáng,
Earl Liáng gave him a wife.
Liáng Yíng became pregnant,
and passed the expected date.
Bǔ Zhāofǔ and his son divined about it.
His son said:
"She will give birth to a boy and a girl."
Zhāo said:
"Yes.
The boy will be a servant,
the girl will be a concubine."
Therefore, they named the boy Yǔ ("stable-boy"),
and the girl Qiè ("concubine").
When Zǐ Yǔ went west as a hostage,
Qiè became a palace maid.
B5.17.3 An army destroyed Xiàng.
At the meeting at Huái,
the Duke [of Lǔ] was occupied with the affairs of the feudal lords,
and had not yet returned,
when [someone] took Xiàng.
The men of Qí held him responsible for this,
and detained the Duke.
B5.17.4 In autumn,
because of the Duke's situation, Shēng Jiāng
met with the Marquis of Qí at Biàn.
In the ninth month,
the Duke arrived.
The Annals record it as
"arrived from the meeting,"
because he was still occupied with the affairs of the feudal lords,
and also to conceal the matter.
B5.17.5 The Marquis of Qí had three principal wives:
Wáng Jī,
Xú Yíng,
and Cài Jī.
None had a son.
The Marquis of Qí was fond of women,
and had many favorites.
Among his favored concubines, six were treated like principal wives:
The elder Wèi Jī,
who bore Wǔ Mèng;
the younger Wèi Jī,
who bore Duke Huì;
Zhèng Jī,
who bore Duke Xiào;
Gé Yíng,
who bore Duke Zhāo;
Mì Jī,
who bore Duke Yì;
and Sòng Huázi,
who bore the prince Yōng.
The Duke, together with Guǎn Zhòng, entrusted Duke Xiào to Duke Xiāng of Sòng,
to be made Heir.
Yōng Wū was favored by Wèi Gòng Jī (the elder Wèi Jī).
Through the eunuch Diāo,
he presented delicacies to the Duke,
and also gained favor.
The Duke promised him he would establish Wǔ Mèng.
When Guǎn Zhòng died,
the five princes all sought to be established.
In winter, on the yǐhài day of the tenth month,
Duke Huán of Qí died.
Yì Yá entered,
and together with the eunuch Diāo, using the influence of the inner favorites,
killed many officials,
and established Prince Wúkuī.
Duke Xiào fled to Sòng.
On the yǐhài day of the twelfth month,
the death announcement was sent.
On the xīnsì day,
he was interred at night.
A5.18 The Annals of Duke Xi, Year 18
A5.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Earl of Cáo,
men of Wèi,
and men of Zhū attacked Qí.
A5.18.2 In summer,
an army went to rescue Qí.
A5.18.3 In the fifth month, on the wùyín day,
the army of Sòng and the army of Qí fought at Yǎn.
The army of Qí was utterly defeated.
A5.18.4 The Dí rescued Qí.
A5.18.5 In autumn, on the dīnghài day of the eighth month,
Duke Huán of Qí was buried.
A5.18.6 In winter,
men of Xíng
and men of Dí attacked Wèi.
B5.18 Commentary on Duke Xi, Year 18
B5.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng led the feudal lords to attack Qí.
In the third month,
the men of Qí killed Wúkuī.
B5.18.2 The Earl of Zhèng for the first time paid court to Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ bestowed metal upon him,
but afterwards regretted it.
He made a covenant with him, saying:
"Do not use it to cast weapons!"
Therefore, he used it to cast three bells.
B5.18.3 The men of Qí wished to establish Duke Xiào,
but could not overcome the faction of the four princes.
Consequently, they fought with the men of Sòng.
In summer, in the fifth month,
Sòng defeated the army of Qí at Yǎn,
established Duke Xiào, and returned.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
Duke Huán of Qí was buried.
B5.18.4 In winter,
men of Xíng and
men of Dí attacked Wèi,
besieging Tùpǔ.
The Marquis of Wèi offered the state to his father's generation, his brothers, his sons and his nephews.
When he faced the multitude at court,
he said:
"If anyone can govern it,
I, Huǐ, will follow him."
The multitude did not consent,
and afterwards he stationed the army at Zǐlóu.
The Dí army withdrew.
B5.18.5 The Earl of Liáng enlarged his capital
but could not populate it,
naming it Xīnlǐ.
Qín seized it.
A5.19 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 19 of Duke Xī
A5.19.1 In the nineteenth year, in spring,
in the king's third month,
men of Sòng seized Yīng Qí, the Viscount of Téng.
A5.19.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
the Duke of Sòng,
men of Cáo,
and men of Zhū made a covenant at the south of Cáo.
A5.19.3 The Viscount of Zēng went to Zhū to join the covenant.
On the jǐyǒu day,
men of Zhū seized the Viscount of Zēng,
and used him.
A5.19.4 In autumn,
men of Sòng besieged Cáo.
A5.19.5 Men of Wèi attacked Xíng.
A5.19.6 In winter,
they met with men of Chén,
men of Cài,
men of Chǔ,
and men of Zhèng to make a covenant in Qí.
A5.19.7 Liáng perished.
B5.19 The Zuo Commentary, Year 19 of Duke Xī
B5.19.1 In the nineteenth year, in spring,
they then built a walled city and dwelt there.
B5.19.2 Men of Sòng seized the Duke Xuān of Téng.
B5.19.3 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng ordered Duke Wén of Zhū to use the Viscount of Zēng at the altar of Cì Suī,
wishing thereby to attach the Eastern Yí.
Simǎ Zǐyú said:
"In ancient times, the six domestic animals were not used for one another,
and for minor affairs great sacrificial victims were not used;
how much less would they dare to use men?
Sacrifices are for the sake of men.
The people are the masters of the spirits.
To use men,
who would enjoy it?
Duke Huán of Qí preserved three perishing states
to attach the various lords,
yet righteous men still said his virtue was shallow.
Now at a single meeting
he has cruelly treated the rulers of two states,
and further uses them for licentious and benighted spirits.
To seek hegemony thereby,
is it not difficult?
To obtain a natural death would be fortunate."
B5.19.4 In autumn,
men of Wèi attacked Xíng,
to repay the campaign at Tùpǔ.
At this time, Wèi had a great drought.
They divined about performing sacrifices to the mountains and rivers,
but it was not auspicious.
Nìng Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Formerly, Zhōu suffered famine,
but when they conquered Yīn, the year was abundant.
Now Xíng is just without the Way,
and among the various lords there is no hegemon.
Is it perhaps that Heaven wishes to have Wèi punish Xíng?"
They followed this.
When the army was raised, rain fell.
B5.19.5 Men of Sòng besieged Cáo,
punishing its disobedience.
Zǐyú spoke to the Duke of Sòng, saying:
"King Wén heard that Chóng was virtuous but in disorder and attacked it.
The army was there for thirty days, yet it did not submit.
He withdrew, cultivated instruction, and then attacked again.
Thereupon, from their ramparts they submitted.
The Odes says:
'He gave a pattern to his wife,
extended it to his brothers,
and so governed the family and state.'
Now your lordship's virtue is perhaps still somewhat deficient,
yet you attack others.
What of it?
Why not for the time being look inward and examine your virtue?
When there is no deficiency, then act."
B5.19.6 Duke Mù of Chén requested to cultivate good relations with the various lords,
so as not to forget the virtue of Duke Huán of Qí.
In winter,
they made a covenant in Qí,
cultivating the good relations of Duke Huán.
B5.19.7 Liáng perished.
The record does not name its ruler,
because it brought it upon itself.
Earlier,
the Earl of Liáng was fond of earthworks,
repeatedly building walled cities but not dwelling in them.
The people were exhausted and could not bear it.
Then he said:
"A certain enemy is about to arrive."
He then dug a moat around the ducal palace,
saying:
"Qín is about to surprise-attack us."
The people were terrified and scattered.
Qín then seized Liáng.
A5.20 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 20 of Duke Xī
A5.20.1 In the twentieth year, in spring,
the southern gate was newly built.
A5.20.2 In summer,
the Viscount of Gào came for an audience.
A5.20.3 In the fifth month, on the yǐsì day,
the Western Palace suffered a fire.
A5.20.4 Men of Zhèng entered Huá.
A5.20.5 In autumn,
men of Qí
and men of Dí made a covenant in Xíng.
A5.20.6 In winter,
men of Chǔ attacked Suí.
