B5.20 The Zuo Commentary, Year 20 of Duke Xī
B5.20.1 In the twentieth year, in spring,
the southern gate was newly built.
The record
is because it was not in season.
In all cases of opening
or closing,
one follows the season.
B5.20.2 The people of Huá rebelled against Zhèng
and submitted to Wèi.
In summer,
the Zhèng prince Shì
and Xiè Dǔkòu led an army and entered Huá.
B5.20.3 In autumn,
Qí and Dí made a covenant in Xíng,
to plan for Xíng's difficulties with Wèi.
At this time, Wèi was just troubling Xíng.
B5.20.4 Suí, with the various lords east of the Hàn River, rebelled against Chǔ.
In winter,
Dòu Gǔwūtú of Chǔ led an army to attack Suí,
obtained an agreement and returned.
A gentleman said:
"Suí being attacked
was due to not measuring its strength.
If one measures strength and then acts,
his errors are few.
Success or failure lies with oneself;
can it lie with others?
The Odes says:
'Is it not that I would go early and late,
but I say the road is full of dew.'"
B5.20.5 Duke Xiāng of Sòng wished to assemble the various lords.
Zāng Wénzhòng heard of it,
and said:
"To make one's own desires follow those of others
is permissible;
to make others follow one's own desires
seldom succeeds."
A5.21 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 21 of Duke Xī
A5.21.1 In the twenty-first year, in spring,
Dí invaded Wèi.
A5.21.2 Men of Sòng,
men of Qí,
and men of Chǔ made a covenant at Lùshàng.
A5.21.3 In summer,
there was a great drought.
A5.21.4 In autumn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Earl of Cáo met at Yú.
They seized the Duke of Sòng to attack Sòng.
A5.21.5 In winter,
the Duke attacked Zhū.
A5.21.6 The men of Chǔ sent Yí Shēn to come and present spoils of war.
A5.21.7 In the twelfth month, on the Guǐchǒu day,
the Duke met with the feudal lords and made a covenant at Bó,
and released the Duke of Sòng.
B5.21 The Commentary of the Twenty-First Year of Duke Xī
B5.21.1 In the spring of the twenty-first year,
the men of Sòng made the covenant at Lùshàng,
to seek the allegiance of the feudal lords from Chǔ.
The men of Chǔ agreed to it.
The prince Mùyí said:
"For a small state to contend for the covenant,
is calamity.
Will Sòng perish!
It would be fortunate if it only meets with defeat later."
B5.21.2 In summer,
there was a great drought.
The Duke wanted to burn the wizards and
the hunchbacks.
Zāng Wénzhòng said:
"This is no preparation against drought.
Repairing the city walls,
reducing food,
economizing on expenditures,
encouraging agriculture,
and urging mutual aid—
these are the proper tasks.
What can the wizards and hunchbacks do?
If Heaven wished to kill them,
then it would be as if they had not been born;
if they could cause drought,
burning them would only make it worse."
The Duke followed his advice.
In this year,
there was famine but no harm.
B5.21.3 In autumn,
the feudal lords met with the Duke of Sòng at Yú.
Zǐyú said:
"Is the calamity not here!
Your desire, my lord, is excessive,
how can they bear it?"
Thereupon, Chǔ seized the Duke of Sòng to attack Sòng.
In winter,
they met at Bó to release him.
Zǐyú said:
"The calamity is not yet over,
this is not enough to chastise our lord."
Sù, Xūjù,
and Zhuānyú
were of the Fēng surname,
and indeed were in charge of the sacrifices to Tàihào and the Jì River,
serving the various Xià states.
The men of Zhū destroyed Xūjù.
The ruler of Xūjù came fleeing,
relying on Chéngfēng.
Chéngfēng spoke to the Duke on his behalf,
saying:
"To honor the bright sacrifices,
and protect the small and weak,
is the ritual of Zhōu;
for the barbarians to disturb the Xià,
is a calamity for Zhōu.
If you enfief Xūjù,
it would be to honor Hào
and Jì
and restore the sacrifices,
and alleviate calamity."
A5.22 The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Twenty-Second Year of Duke Xī
A5.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
the Duke attacked Zhū,
and took Xūjù.
A5.22.2 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Baron of Xǔ,
and the Viscount of Téng attacked Zhèng.
A5.22.3 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the Dīngwèi day,
[our army] fought with the men of Zhū at Shēngxíng.
A5.22.4 In winter, in the eleventh month, on the first day Jǐsì,
the Duke of Sòng fought with the men of Chǔ at Hóng,
and the army of Sòng was utterly defeated.
B5.22 The Commentary of the Twenty-Second Year of Duke Xī
B5.22.1 In the spring of the twenty-second year,
[the Duke] attacked Zhū,
took Xūjù,
and restored its ruler,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B5.22.2 In the third month,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ.
B5.22.3 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng attacked Zhèng.
Zǐyú said:
"The so-called calamity is here."
B5.22.4 Formerly,
when King Píng moved east,
Xīn Yǒu went to Yīchuān,
and saw people with disheveled hair sacrificing in the wilds.
He said:
"In less than a hundred years,
this will become Róng territory!
Its rituals have already perished."
In autumn,
Qín
and Jìn moved the Lùhún Róng to Yīchuān.
B5.22.5 The crown prince of Jìn, Yǔ, was a hostage in Qín.
He was about to flee back [to Jìn],
and said to Lady Yíng:
"Will you go back with me?"
She replied:
"You, sir,
are the crown prince of Jìn,
and are humiliated in Qín.
Your desire to return,
is it not appropriate?
My humble lord sent this handmaid to serve you with towel and comb,
to secure your position.
To follow you and return
would be to abandon my lord's command.
I dare not follow,
nor dare I speak of it."
Thereupon he fled back.
B5.22.6 Fù Chén spoke to the King, saying:
"I request to summon the Grand Uncle.
The Odes say:
'Be harmonious with your neighbors,
and marriage relations will be greatly friendly.'
If we brothers are not harmonious,
how can we blame the feudal lords for not being friendly?"
The King was pleased.
Prince Dài returned from Qí to the capital,
for the King had summoned him.
B5.22.7 The men of Zhū, because of the affair of Xūjù,
sent out an army.
The Duke despised Zhū,
and without making preparations, resisted them.
Zāng Wénzhòng said:
"A state, however small,
cannot be taken lightly.
Without preparations,
even if numerous,
one cannot rely on it.
The Odes say:
'Trembling with fear and caution,
as if approaching a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice.'
They also say:
'Be reverent, be reverent!
Heaven's will is clear,
and the mandate is not easily maintained!'
The bright virtue of the former kings
still found nothing not difficult,
nothing not fearful,
how much more for our small state!
My lord, do not say that Zhū is small;
wasps and scorpions have poison,
how much more a state!"
He did not listen.
On the Dīngwèi day of the eighth month,
the Duke fought with the army of Zhū at Shēngxíng,
and our army was utterly defeated.
The men of Zhū captured the Duke's helmet,
and hung it at the Yú Gate.
B5.22.8 The men of Chǔ attacked Sòng to rescue Zhèng.
The Duke of Sòng was about to give battle.
The Grand Minister of War, Gù, remonstrated, saying:
"Heaven has abandoned Shāng for a long time;
if you, my lord, are going to revive it,
it will not be pardonable."
He did not listen.
In winter, on the first day Jǐsì of the eleventh month,
the Duke of Sòng fought with the men of Chǔ at Hóng.
The men of Sòng had already formed their ranks,
but the men of Chǔ had not yet fully crossed the river.
The Minister of War said:
"They are many, we are few;
while they have not yet fully crossed,
I request to attack them."
The Duke said:
"No."
After they had crossed but had not yet formed ranks,
he again reported.
The Duke said:
"Not yet."
After they had formed their battle array, he then attacked them,
and the army of Sòng was utterly defeated.
The Duke was wounded in the thigh.
The gate guards were annihilated.
All the people of the state blamed the Duke.
The Duke said:
"A noble man does not inflict a second wound,
nor does he capture those with grey hair.
In ancient warfare,
one did not take advantage of an enemy's disadvantageous position.
Although I am but the remnant of a fallen state,
I will not drum the attack before the enemy has formed ranks."
Zǐyú said:
"You do not understand warfare.
When a formidable enemy
is in a narrow pass and unable to form ranks,
Heaven is aiding us.
To press the advantage and drum the attack—
is that not permissible?
Even then, there is still reason for caution.
Moreover, those who are formidable today
are all our enemies.
Even if they reach old age,
if captured, they should be taken—
what consideration is there for grey hair?
To clarify shame
and teach warfare
is to seek the killing of the enemy.
If a wound has not yet caused death,
why not inflict another?
If you pity inflicting a second wound,
then it would be better not to wound at all;
if you pity their grey hair,
then it would be better to submit to them.
The three armies are to be used to advantage;
gongs and drums are to rouse the spirit with their sound.
When it is advantageous to use them,
exploiting a narrow pass is permissible;
when the sound is full and stirs the will,
drumming against disorderly ranks is permissible."
B5.22.9 On the morning of Bǐngzǐ day,
Lady Mǐshì, wife of Duke Wén of Zhèng, and Lady Jiāngshì
greeted the King of Chǔ at Kēzé.
The King of Chǔ had Shī Jìn show them the captives and severed ears.
The noble man said:
"This is contrary to ritual.
Women do not go beyond the gate to send off or welcome guests;
they do not cross the threshold to see their brothers;
military affairs should not be brought near women's implements."
On Dīngchǒu day,
the King of Chǔ entered Zhèng for a feast,
where nine rounds of toasts were offered,
the courtyard was filled with a hundred displays of gifts,
and six additional varieties of food in bamboo and wooden containers were added.
After the feast concluded,
he departed at night,
and Wén Mǐ saw him off to the army camp.
He took two royal ladies of Zhèng and returned with them.
Shū Zhān said:
"Will the King of Chǔ not die a natural death!
In performing the rites, he ends with no distinction.
Without distinction, it cannot be called ritual.
How then will he die a natural death?"
The feudal lords thereby knew he would not succeed in becoming hegemon.
A5.23 The Classic of the Twenty-Third Year of Duke Xī
A5.23.1 In the twenty-third year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Sòng
and besieged Mín.
A5.23.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on Gēngyín day,
Duke Zīfù of Sòng died.
A5.23.3 In autumn,
the men of Chǔ attacked Chén.
A5.23.4 In winter, in the eleventh month,
the Viscount of Qǐ died.
B5.23 The Commentary of the Twenty-Third Year of Duke Xī
B5.23.1 In the twenty-third year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Sòng
and besieged Mín,
to punish it for not joining the covenant with Qí.
B5.23.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng died,
due to the wound he received at Hóng.
B5.23.3 In autumn,
Chǔ's Chéng Déchén led an army to attack Chén,
to punish it for being disloyal to Chǔ and siding with Sòng.
He then took Jiāo
and Yí,
fortified Dùn, and returned.
Zǐwén considered this his achievement
and made him Lìngyǐn.
Shūbó said:
"What will you do for the state?"
He replied:
"I use this to bring peace to the state.
When one has great merit
but no high office,
how many of such men can bring peace?
Are there any?"
B5.23.4 In the ninth month,
Duke Huì of Jìn died.
Duke Huái was established,
and he ordered that no one should follow the fugitives.
He set a deadline;
if they did not return by the deadline,
there would be no pardon.
Hú Tū's sons, Máo and Yǎn, were following Chóng'ěr in Qín,
and he did not summon them.
In winter,
Duke Huái arrested Hú Tū,
saying:
"If your sons return, you will be spared."
He replied:
"When a son is able to serve,
his father teaches him loyalty—
this is the ancient rule.
To have one's name recorded
and present gifts of introduction
means that disloyalty is a crime.
Now my sons' names
are recorded under Chóng'ěr,
and it has been several years.
If I summon them now,
I would be teaching them disloyalty.
If a father teaches his sons disloyalty,
how can he serve his ruler?
If punishment is not excessive,
it shows the ruler's wisdom,
and that is my wish.
If one indulges in punishment to gratify oneself,
who then is without fault?
I have heard your command."
So he was killed.
Bǔ Yǎn claimed illness and did not go out,
saying:
"The *Zhōushū* says:
'Only when one is greatly enlightened,
do the people submit.'
If one is not enlightened oneself,
yet kills people to gratify oneself,
is that not difficult?
If the people see no virtue,
but only hear of slaughter,
how can there be posterity?"
B5.23.5 In the eleventh month,
Duke Chéng of Qǐ died.
It is recorded as
"Viscount,"
because Qǐ
is an Eastern Yi state.
His personal name is not recorded,
because there was no covenant alliance.
Whenever feudal lords are in a covenant alliance,
upon death, the announcement is made with the personal name—
this is ritual.
If the announcement is made with the personal name,
then it is also recorded;
otherwise, it is not,
to avoid inaccuracy.
B5.23.6 When Prince Chóng'ěr of Jìn encountered disaster,
the men of Jìn attacked him at Púchéng.
The people of Púchéng wished to fight,
but Chóng'ěr would not allow it,
saying:
"I rely on my father the ruler's command
and enjoy the livelihood he provides,
and thereby gain followers.
To have followers and yet oppose him—
no crime could be greater.
I shall flee."
So he fled to Dí.
His followers were Hú Yǎn,
Zhào Cuī,
Diān Jié,
Wèi Wǔzǐ,
and Sīkōng Jìzǐ.
The Dí attacked Qiánggāorú,
captured two of their women,
Shū Wěi
and Jì Wěi,
and presented them to the prince.
The prince took Jì Wěi,
who gave birth to Bó Tiáo
and Shú Liú;
he gave Shū Wěi to Zhào Cuī as wife,
and she gave birth to Dùn.
When he was about to go to Qí,
he said to Jì Wěi:
"Wait for me twenty-five years;
if I do not return by then, remarry."
She replied:
"I am twenty-five now,
and if I remarry after another such period,
I will be entering my coffin.
I beg to wait for you."
He stayed among the Dí for twelve years and then departed.
Passing through Wèi,
Duke Wén of Wèi did not treat him with courtesy.
Leaving Wǔlù,
he begged for food from a rustic,
who gave him a clod of earth.
The prince was angry
and wanted to whip him.
Zǐfàn said:
"It is a gift from Heaven."
He bowed his head to the ground, accepted it,
and carried it away.
Arriving in Qí,
Duke Huán of Qí gave him a wife,
and he had twenty teams of horses.
The prince became content there.
His followers considered this unacceptable.
As they were about to depart,
they plotted beneath a mulberry tree.
A silkworm maid was above them
and reported it to Jiāngshì.
Jiāngshì killed her
and said to the prince:
"You have ambitions for the four quarters.
As for the one who overheard it,
I have killed her."
The prince said:
"I have no such ambitions."
Jiāng said:
"Go!
Attachment and comfort
truly ruin one's name."
The prince would not agree.
Jiāng plotted with Zǐfàn,
got him drunk, and sent him off.
When he awoke,
he pursued Zǐfàn with a spear.
Arriving in Cáo,
Duke Gòng of Cáo heard that his ribs were fused together,
and wanted to see him naked.
While he was bathing,
they approached and watched him.
The wife of Xí Fùjī said:
"I observe that the followers of the Jìn prince
are all sufficient to be ministers of state.
If they assist him,
that man is sure to return to his state.
If he returns to his state,
he is sure to achieve his ambition among the feudal lords.
Achieving his ambition among the feudal lords,
he will punish those who showed him discourtesy,
and Cáo will be the first.
Why do you not early on show yourself different from the rest?"
So he sent a tray of food,
placing a jade disc in it.
The prince accepted the food but returned the jade.
Arriving in Sòng,
Duke Xiāng of Sòng presented him with twenty teams of horses.
Arriving in Zhèng,
Duke Wén of Zhèng also did not treat him with courtesy.
Shū Zhàn remonstrated, saying:
"Your servant has heard that those whom Heaven opens the way for,
men cannot match.
The Jìn prince has three such signs.
Perhaps Heaven is about to establish him.
May my lord treat him with courtesy!
Men and women of the same surname,
their offspring do not flourish.
The Jìn prince
is born of a Jī,
and yet has survived to this day —
this is the first.
Having suffered the calamity of exile abroad,
and Heaven not granting peace to Jìn,
it is likely about to open the way for him —
this is the second.
He has three men of talent,
sufficient to be superior to others,
and they follow him —
this is the third.
Jìn and Zhèng are of equal rank;
when their sons and younger brothers pass through,
they should certainly be treated with courtesy,
how much more one for whom Heaven has opened the way!"
He did not listen.
Arriving in Chǔ,
the Viscount of Chǔ feasted him,
saying:
"If you, Prince, return to Jìn,
then with what will you repay me?"
He replied:
"Slaves, maidens, jade, and silk,
you, my lord, already possess;
feathers, furs,
ivory, and hides,
are produced in your land.
What spreads to Jìn,
are your leftovers;
with what then can I repay you?"
He said:
"Even so,
what will you repay me with?"
He replied:
"If by your divine favor,
I am able to return to Jìn.
Should Jìn and Chǔ engage in warfare,
meeting on the central plains,
I will withdraw three days' march for you.
If I do not then obtain your command to desist,
I will grasp whip
and bow in my left hand,
and carry quiver
and bow-case on my right,
to engage with you in contest."
Zǐyù requested to kill him.
The Viscount of Chǔ said:
"The Jìn prince is broad-minded yet frugal,
cultured and courteous.
His followers are respectful and tolerant,
loyal and capable.
The Marquis of Jìn has no close kin,
and is hated both abroad and at home.
I have heard that among the Jī surname,
the descendants of Tángshū,
theirs will be the last decline.
Is it not likely to be through this Jìn prince?
If Heaven is about to raise him up,
who can overthrow him?
To oppose Heaven
is sure to bring great calamity."
So he sent him to Qín.
The Earl of Qín gave him five women,
Huáiyíng being among them.
She held the basin for him to wash his hands,
and afterwards he shook off the water.
Angered,
she said:
"Qín
and Jìn are equals;
why do you demean me?"
The prince was afraid,
removed his outer garments, and confined himself as a prisoner.
Another day,
the duke feasted him.
Zǐfàn said:
"I am not as cultured as Cuī;
I request that Cuī accompany you."
The prince recited the poem "Hé Shuǐ".
The duke recited the poem "Liù Yuè".
Zhào Cuī said:
"Chóng'ěr, bow in thanks for the gift!"
The prince descended the steps,
bowed, and touched his head to the ground.
The duke descended one step
and declined the honor.
Cuī said:
"My lord, by invoking what assists the Son of Heaven, you have commanded Chóng'ěr;
how dare Chóng'ěr not bow?"
A5.24 The Spring and Autumn Annals, the 24th Year of Duke Xī
A5.24.1 In the 24th year, in spring,
the royal first month.
A5.24.2 In summer,
the Dí attacked Zhèng.
A5.24.3 In autumn,
in the seventh month.
A5.24.4 In winter,
the Heavenly King left and resided in Zhèng.
A5.24.5 The Marquis of Jìn, Yíwú, died.
B5.24 The Commentary of Zuo, the 24th Year of Duke Xī
B5.24.1 In the 24th year, in spring,
the royal first month,
the Earl of Qín sent him into Jìn.
It is not recorded in the Annals,
because notification of his entry was not given.
Reaching the Yellow River,
Zǐfàn handed a jade disc to the prince,
saying:
"Your servant, bearing the tether of a follower,
has roamed the world with you, my lord.
My offenses are many indeed.
Even I know them,
how much more you, my lord?
I beg to take my leave from here."
The prince said:
"If I am not of one heart with my maternal uncle,
may the White River be my witness!"
He threw the jade disc into the river.
Crossing the river,
they besieged Línghú,
entered Sāngquán,
and took Jiǔcuī.
On the day jiǎwǔ in the second month,
the Jìn army encamped at Lúliǔ.
The Earl of Qín sent his son Zhí to the Jìn army.
The army withdrew,
and encamped at Xún.
On the day xīnchǒu,
Hú Yǎn, along with the great officers of Qín and
Jìn, made a covenant at Xún.
On the day rényín,
the Jìn prince entered the Jìn army.
On the day bǐngwǔ,
he entered Qūwò.
On the day dīngwèi,
he entered Jiàng,
and held court at the Wǔ Palace.
On the day wùshēn,
he had Duke Huái killed at Gāoliáng.
This was not recorded,
nor was it reported.
Lǚ and
Xì, fearing persecution,
planned to set fire to the duke's palace and assassinate the Marquis of Jìn.
The eunuch Pī requested an audience.
The duke sent to reprimand him,
and refused him,
saying:
"At the battle of Púchéng,
the ruler's command was for one night's delay,
yet you arrived immediately.
Afterwards, when I was following the Dí lord
hunting along the Wèi River,
you came on behalf of Duke Huì to seek to kill me;
the command was for three nights' delay,
yet you arrived by the second night.
Though you had the ruler's command,
why were you so swift?
The sleeve you cut off is still here.
You had better leave!"
He replied:
"I thought that when you, my lord, returned,
you would understand such matters.
If you still do not,
you will again face calamity.
A ruler's command admits no second thoughts;
this is an ancient rule.
To remove the ruler's enemies,
one must exert all one's strength.
Whether they were men of Pú
or men of Dí,
what concern were they of mine?
Now that you, my lord, have ascended the throne,
will there not be
men of Pú and Dí?
Duke Huán of Qí set aside the matter of the arrow-hook,
and made Guǎn Zhòng his minister.
If you, my lord, act differently,
why trouble to command me?
Those who will leave are many;
how could it be only this mutilated servant?"
The duke granted him an audience,
and he reported the plot.
In the third month,
the Marquis of Jìn secretly met the Earl of Qín at Wángchéng.
On the last day of the month, jǐchǒu,
the duke's palace caught fire.
Xiáshēng and
Xì Ruì, failing to capture the duke,
went to the riverbank,
where the Earl of Qín lured them and killed them.
The Marquis of Jìn welcomed his wife, Lady Yíng, and returned with her.
The Earl of Qín sent three thousand men as guards to Jìn,
who were in fact stewards of discipline.
Earlier,
the Marquis of Jìn's page Tóuxū,
who was the keeper of the treasury,
when the duke went into exile,
stole from the treasury and fled,
using all the funds to seek the duke's restoration.
When the duke returned,
Tóuxū sought an audience.
The duke refused him, saying he was washing his hair.
Tóuxū said to the attendant:
"When washing the hair, the heart is turned upside down;
when the heart is upside down, plans are reversed.
No wonder I cannot get an audience.
Those who stayed guarded the altars of soil and grain,
those who went into exile served as traveling servants;
both are acceptable.
Why must those who stayed be blamed?
If a ruler of a state makes enemies of common men,
those who will fear are many."
The attendant reported this,
and the duke hastily granted him an audience.
The Dí people returned Jì Wěi to Jìn,
but requested to keep her two sons.
Duke Wén gave a wife to Zhào Cuī,
who bore Yuántóng,
Píngkuò,
and Lóuyīng.
Lady Zhào requested to bring back Dùn and his mother,
but Zǐyú refused.
Lady Zhào said:
"To gain favor and forget the old,
how can one command others?
You must bring them back!"
She insisted,
and he agreed.
When they came,
considering Dùn talented,
she firmly requested the duke
to make him the heir,
and placed her own three sons beneath him;
she made Shū Wěi the principal wife,
and placed herself beneath her.
The Marquis of Jìn rewarded those who had followed him in exile.
Jiè Zhītuī did not speak of emolument,
and emolument did not reach him.
Tuī said:
"Duke Xiàn had nine sons,
and only our lord remains.
Duke Huì and Duke Huái had no kin,
and were abandoned by all, inside and out.
Heaven has not cut off Jìn,
so there must be a ruler.
Who will preside over the sacrifices of Jìn
if not our lord?
Heaven indeed placed him there,
yet these few men consider it their own achievement;
is this not false?
To steal another's wealth
is still called theft;
how much more so to claim Heaven's merit
as one's own achievement?
Those below justify their crime,
those above reward their treachery;
high and low deceive each other,
making it difficult to live among them."
His mother said:
"Why not also seek reward?
To die thus,
who would pity you?"
He replied:
"To condemn and yet imitate them,
is an even greater crime.
Moreover, having uttered complaints,
I will not eat their food."
His mother said:
"Then let them know,
what of it?"
He replied:
"Words are
the ornament of the person.
Since I am about to hide my person,
why use ornament?
That would be seeking prominence."
His mother said:
"Can you truly do this?
I will hide with you."
They hid away and died.
The Marquis of Jìn sought them but could not find them.
He made Miánshàng their fields,
saying:
"To record my fault,
and to honor a good man."
B5.24.2 When Zhèng entered Huá,
the people of Huá submitted.
When the army withdrew,
they again allied with Wèi.
Zhèng's princes Shì and
Xiè Dǔyúmí led an army to attack Huá.
The king sent Bó Fú and
Yóu Sūnbó to Zhèng to plead for Huá.
The Earl of Zhèng resented King Huì for entering
and not giving Duke Lì a cup,
and also resented King Xiāng for allying with Wèi and Huá.
Therefore, he did not obey the king's command,
and detained the two envoys.
The king was angry,
and planned to use the Dí to attack Zhèng.
Fù Chén remonstrated, saying:
"It cannot be done.
I have heard that
the highest way is to soothe the people with virtue,
the next is to draw close to kin,
so that they support each other.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu grieved that the two uncles were not harmonious,
so he enfeoffed relatives
to protect and screen Zhōu.
Guǎn, Cài,
Chéng, Huò,
Lǔ, Wèi,
Máo, Dān,
Gào, Yōng,
Cáo, Téng,
Bì, Yuán,
Fēng, and Xún—
these are the sons of King Wén.
Yú, Jìn,
Yīng, and Hán
were descendants of King Wǔ.
Fán, Jiǎng,
Xíng, Máo,
Zuò, and Zhài
were descendants of the Duke of Zhōu.
Duke Mù of Shào, reflecting that the virtue of Zhōu was not as it should be,
therefore gathered the royal clan in Chéngzhōu
and composed a poem,
saying:
'The blossoms of the cherry tree,
how brilliant they are.
Among all men today,
none are like brothers.'
Its fourth stanza says:
'Brothers may quarrel within the walls,
but they ward off insult from without.'
Thus,
though brothers may have minor resentments,
they do not cast aside their close kin.
Now the Son of Heaven cannot bear a minor resentment
and casts aside the kinship of Zhèng.
What is to be done about this?
Rewarding merit, being affectionate to kin, being intimate with the near, and honoring the worthy—
these are the great aspects of virtue.
Approaching the deaf, following the ignorant, associating with the obstinate, and employing the treacherous—
these are the great aspects of villainy.
Casting aside virtue
and exalting villainy—
these are the great aspects of calamity.
Zhèng has the merit of
King Píng
and King Huì,
and also the kinship of
King Lì and King Xuān.
Casting aside favorites
and employing the three good men,
among the various Jī clans it is the closest.
All four virtues are present.
Ears that do not hear the harmony of the five notes
are deaf;
eyes that do not distinguish the patterns of the five colors
are blind;
a heart that does not follow the principles of virtue and righteousness
is obstinate;
a mouth that does not speak words of loyalty and trustworthiness
is treacherous.
The Dí people all follow these,
and all four villainies are present.
When Zhōu possessed excellent virtue,
it still said
'none are like brothers,'
and therefore established fiefdoms.
In its efforts to pacify and embrace all under heaven,
it still feared there might be external insults;
for warding off insults,
nothing is like being affectionate to kin,
and therefore it used kin to screen Zhōu.
Duke Mù of Shào also said this.
Now the virtue of Zhōu has already declined,
and yet it further betrays
the Dukes of Zhōu and Shào,
to follow various villains.
Is this not unacceptable?
The people have not forgotten past calamities,
and the King is again stirring them up.
What will he say to Kings Wén
and Wǔ?"
The King did not listen,
and sent Tuí Shū
and Táo Zǐ to lead out the Dí army.
In summer,
the Dí attacked Zhèng
and took Lì.
The King felt grateful to the Dí people
and intended to take one of their women as his queen.
Fù Chén remonstrated, saying:
"This cannot be done.
Your servant has heard it said:
'The one who repays grows weary,
but the one who bestows is never satisfied.'
The Dí are inherently greedy,
and the King is further encouraging them.
A woman's virtue knows no bounds,
a wife's resentment has no end.
The Dí will certainly become a calamity."
The King again did not listen.
Earlier,
Duke Zhāo of Gān was favored by Queen Huì,
and Queen Huì intended to establish him [as heir],
but she died before she could do so.
Duke Zhāo fled to Qí.
The King restored him,
and he also had an affair with Lady Wěi.
The King deposed Lady Wěi.
Tuí Shū
and Táo Zǐ said:
"It was we who actually caused the Dí to come;
the Dí will surely resent us."
Thereupon they supported the Grand Uncle
to attack the King.
The King's guards were about to resist them,
but the King said:
"What would my deceased mother think of me?
I would rather let the feudal lords deal with this."
The King then left,
and when he reached Kǎnkǎn,
the people of the capital brought him back in.
In autumn,
Tuí Shū
and Táo Zǐ, supporting the Grand Uncle, led the Dí army to attack Zhōu,
greatly defeated the Zhōu army,
and captured the Duke of Zhōu Jìfù,
the Earl of Yuán,
the Earl of Máo,
and Fù Chén.
The King left and went to Zhèng,
residing at Fàn.
The Grand Uncle took Lady Wěi and resided at Wēn.
B5.24.3 Zǐ Huá of Zhèng's younger brother Zǐ Zāng fled to Sòng.
He was fond of collecting egret-feather caps.
The Earl of Zhèng heard of this and disliked him,
and sent bandits to lure him.
In the eighth month,
bandits killed him between Chén and Sòng.
The gentleman says:
"If clothing is not appropriate,
it is a disaster for the person.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'That man there,
does not match his clothing.'
What happened to Zǐ Zāng
was because he did not match [his station]!
The *Book of Songs* says:
'He brought sorrow upon himself.'
This refers to Zǐ Zāng.
The *Book of Xià* says:
'The earth was leveled and heaven completed.'
This is about matching."
B5.24.4 Sòng made peace with Chǔ,
and Duke Chéng of Sòng went to Chǔ.
On his return,
he entered Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng was about to host a feast for him,
and inquired about the rites from Huáng Wǔzǐ.
He replied:
"Sòng
is the descendant of a former dynasty,
and is a guest to Zhōu.
When the Son of Heaven has sacrificial ceremonies,
they send them meat;
when there is mourning,
they are bowed to.
It is permissible to be generous."
The Earl of Zhèng followed this,
and feasting Duke of Sòng
with added ceremony
was in accordance with ritual.
B5.24.5 In winter,
the King sent a messenger to report his difficulties,
saying:
"I, lacking in virtue,
have offended against my mother's favored son, Dài,
and am now in the humble place of Fàn in Zhèng territory.
I venture to inform my uncle."
Zāng Wénzhòng replied:
"When the Son of Heaven is covered with dust abroad,
how dare I not hasten to inquire after the officials in charge?"
The King sent Jiǎn Shīfù to report to Jìn,
and sent Zuǒ Yānfù to report to Qín.
The Son of Heaven does not leave [his state];
the record says
"the Heavenly King left and resided in Zhèng,"
because he was avoiding the trouble caused by his mother's son.
The Son of Heaven wearing mourning garments
and lowering his name
is in accordance with ritual.
B5.24.6 The Earl of Zhèng, along with Kǒng Jiàngchú,
Shí Jiǎfǔ,
and Hóu Xuānduō, inspected the officials
and supplies at Fàn,
and afterwards attended to his own government affairs.
This was in accordance with ritual.
B5.24.7 The people of Wèi were about to attack Xíng.
Lǐ Zhì said:
"If we do not gain control of their guard,
we cannot take the state.
I request that my brothers take office there."
So he went
and obtained office.
A5.25 *The Classic Text of the 25th Year of Duke Xī*
A5.25.1 In the 25th year, in spring,
in the first month, on the bǐngwǔ day,
the Marquis of Wèi, Huǐ, destroyed Xíng.
A5.25.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on the guǐyǒu day,
the Marquis of Wèi, Huǐ, died.
A5.25.3 Dàng Bójī of Sòng came to meet the bride.
A5.25.4 Sòng put its senior minister to death.
A5.25.5 In autumn,
the men of Chǔ besieged Chén,
and installed the viscount of Dùn in Dùn.
A5.25.6 The funeral of Duke Wén of Wèi was held.
A5.25.7 In winter, in the twelfth month, on Guǐhài,
our duke met with the viscount of Wèi
and Qìng of Jǔ,
and made a covenant at Táo.
B5.25 The Commentary for the Twenty-fifth Year of Duke Xī
B5.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
the men of Wèi attacked Xíng.
The two Lǐs followed Guózǐ
as he inspected the city walls.
They seized him by the arms and threw him over the wall,
killing him.
In the first month, on Bǐngwǔ,
Marquis Huǐ of Wèi extinguished Xíng.
Because it was of the same surname,
he recorded his name.
Lǐ Zhì made an inscription
which said:
"I seized and killed Guózǐ;
no one dared to stop me."
B5.25.2 The earl of Qín stationed his army on the Yellow River,
intending to escort the king back.
Hú Yǎn said to the marquis of Jìn:
"If you wish to seek the allegiance of the feudal lords,
nothing is better than diligently serving the king.
The feudal lords will trust you,
and it is moreover a great act of righteousness.
To continue the task of King Wén,
and to establish trust and prestige among the feudal lords,
now is the time to do it."
He sent the diviner Yǎn to divine by tortoise shell,
who said:
"Auspicious.
It encountered the omen of the Yellow Emperor fighting at Bǎnquán."
The duke said:
"I am not worthy of this."
He replied:
"The rites of Zhōu have not changed;
the king of today
is the emperor of antiquity."
The duke said:
"Divine by milfoil!"
He divined by milfoil,
and encountered the hexagram Dàyǒu ䷍ changing to Kuí
He said:
"Auspicious.
It encountered
the hexagram where 'the duke is received in audience by the Son of Heaven'
Victory in battle and the king's feast,
what auspiciousness could be greater?
Moreover, in this hexagram,
Heaven becomes a marsh to receive the sun;
the Son of Heaven humbles his heart to welcome the duke.
Is this not acceptable?
Dàyǒu departs and Kuí returns,
which is also its proper place."
The marquis of Jìn declined the Qín army
and proceeded downstream.
In the third month, on Jiǎchén,
he encamped at Yángfán.
The right army besieged Wēn,
and the left army went to meet the king.
In summer, in the fourth month, on Dīngsì,
the king entered Wángchéng.
They captured Tàishū from Wēn,
and killed him at Xíchéng.
On Wùwǔ,
the marquis of Jìn had audience with the king.
The king feasted him with sweet wine,
and commanded that he be presented with gifts.
He requested the use of the subterranean passage for burial,
but it was not granted.
The king said:
"That is a royal prerogative.
There is no one who has replaced the virtue [of the Zhōu],
yet there would be two kings;
this is also something my uncle would dislike."
He gave him the lands of Yángfán, Wēn, Yuán, and Cuánmáo.
Jìn then for the first time opened up Nányáng.
Yángfán did not submit,
so he besieged it.
Cāng Gé cried out:
"Virtue is used to soothe the central states,
punishment is used to awe the barbarians of the four quarters.
It is fitting that we dare not submit.
Here, who is not a relative or in-law of the king?
How can you take them captive?"
So he let the people leave.
B5.25.3 In autumn,
Qín and Jìn attacked Ruò.
Dòu Kè and Qū Yùkòu of Chǔ led the armies of Shēn and Xī to garrison Shāngmì.
The men of Qín passed by Xī, and from a hidden bend
they entered and bound some carters,
then proceeded to besiege Shāngmì.
At dusk they approached the walls.
At night,
they dug a pit, smeared blood on a covenant document,
and pretended to have made a covenant with Zǐyí and Zǐbiān.
The people of Shāngmì were afraid,
and said:
"Qín has taken Xī!
The garrison troops have turned against us!"
So they surrendered to the Qín army.
The Qín army took the lords' sons Yí of Shēn and Biān of Xī captive and returned with them.
The Chief Minister of Chǔ, Zǐyù, pursued the Qín army,
but did not catch up.
He then besieged Chén,
and installed the viscount of Dùn in Dùn.
B5.25.4 In winter,
the marquis of Jìn besieged Yuán,
and ordered provisions for three days.
When Yuán did not surrender,
he ordered the troops to withdraw.
A spy came out,
and said:
"Yuán is about to surrender."
The army officers said:
"Please wait for it."
The duke said:
"Trustworthiness
is the treasure of a state,
and what the people rely upon.
To gain Yuán but lose trustworthiness,
what would they rely on then?
The loss would be even greater."
He withdrew one stage
and Yuán surrendered.
He moved Yuán Bó Guàn to Jì.
Zhào Cuī was made senior minister of Yuán,
and Hú Zhēn was made senior minister of Wēn.
B5.25.5 The men of Wèi mediated peace between Jǔ and us.
In the twelfth month,
they made a covenant at Táo,
to renew the good relations of Duke Wén of Wèi,
and also to make peace with Jǔ.
B5.25.6 The marquis of Jìn asked the eunuch Bódī about who should guard Yuán.
He replied:
"Formerly, Zhào Cuī followed you with a pot of cooked food,
and though he went hungry on the byways, he did not eat it."
Therefore he was sent to reside at Yuán.
A5.26 The Text for the Twenty-sixth Year of Duke Xī
A5.26.1 In the twenty-sixth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
on Jǐwèi,
our duke met with the viscount of Jǔ
and Nìng Sù of Wèi, and made a covenant at Xiàng.
A5.26.2 The men of Qí invaded our western borders.
Our duke pursued the Qí army,
reached Xī,
but did not catch up.
A5.26.3 In summer,
the men of Qí attacked our northern borders.
A5.26.4 The men of Wèi attacked Qí.
A5.26.5 The duke's son Suì went to Chǔ to beg for troops.
A5.26.6 In autumn,
the men of Chǔ extinguished Kuí,
and took the viscount of Kuí back with them.
A5.26.7 In winter,
the men of Chǔ attacked Sòng,
and besieged Mín.
Our duke, using Chǔ troops, attacked Qí,
and took Gǔ.
A5.26.8 Our duke arrived from attacking Qí.
B5.26 The Commentary for the Twenty-sixth Year of Duke Xī
B5.26.1 In the twenty-sixth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
our duke met with Zīpīgōng of Jǔ
and Nìng Zhuāngzǐ,
and made a covenant at Xiàng,
to renew the covenant of Táo.
B5.26.2 The Qí army invaded our western borders,
to protest against these two covenants.
B5.26.3 In summer,
Duke Xiào of Qí attacked our northern borders.
The men of Wèi attacked Qí,
because of the covenant at Táo.
Our lord sent Zhǎn Xǐ to present provisions to the army,
having him receive instructions from Zhǎn Qín.
Before the Marquis of Qí had entered our territory,
Zhǎn Xǐ went to meet him,
saying:
"My humble lord has heard that you, my lord, have personally raised your precious feet,
and are about to disgrace our poor city.
He has sent his lowly minister to present provisions to your attendants."
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Are the men of Lǔ afraid?"
He replied:
"The petty men are afraid,
but the noble men are not."
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Your houses are like suspended chimes [empty],
your fields have no green grass,
what do you rely on to be unafraid?"
He replied:
"We rely on the command of the former kings.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu
and the Grand Duke [of Qí]
were the arms and legs of the Zhōu house,
assisting King Chéng from both sides.
King Chéng rewarded their labors,
and granted them a covenant,
saying:
'For generations of descendants,
do not harm each other!'
It is recorded in the covenant repository,
and the Grand Preceptor is in charge of it.
Therefore, Duke Huán assembled the feudal lords,
and planned for their lack of harmony,
mended their breaches,
and rescued them from their disasters,
thus making manifest the old duties.
When you, my lord, ascended the throne,
the expectations of the feudal lords said:
'He will follow the achievements of Duke Huán!'
Therefore, our poor city did not dare to gather and guard [against you],
saying:
'How could it be that in the ninth year of his succession,
he would abandon the command and neglect the duty?
What would he do about his former lord?
Our lord certainly would not do so.'
Relying on this, we are not afraid."
The Marquis of Qí then withdrew.
B5.26.4 Dōngmén Xiāng Zhòng
and Zāng Wénzhòng went to Chǔ to beg for troops.
Zāngsūn met Zǐ Yù
and urged him to attack Qí
and Sòng,
because of their lack of allegiance.
B5.26.5 The Viscount of Kuí did not sacrifice to Zhùróng and Yù Xióng,
and the men of Chǔ reproached him.
He replied:
"Our former king, Xióng Zhì, was ill,
and the ghosts and spirits did not forgive him,
so he fled to Kuí.
Thus we lost Chǔ,
so why sacrifice [to its ancestors]?"
In autumn,
Chéng Déchén of Chǔ
and Dòu Yíshēn led an army and destroyed Kuí,
taking the Viscount of Kuí back [as captive].
B5.26.6 Because Sòng was on good terms with the Marquis of Jìn,
it turned against Chǔ and allied with Jìn.
In winter,
the Chief Minister of Chǔ, Zǐ Yù,
and the Minister of War, Zǐ Xī,
led an army to attack Sòng,
surrounding Mín.
Our lord used the Chǔ army to attack Qí,
and took Gǔ.
In general, when an army
can be directed left and right, it is called
"using" it.
They placed Duke Huán's son, Yōng, in Gǔ,
with Yì Yá serving him, making him a support for Lǔ.
Shēn Gōng Shū Hóu of Chǔ garrisoned it.
Duke Huán had seven sons,
who became seven great officers in Chǔ.
A5.27 The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Twenty-Seventh Year of Duke Xī
A5.27.1 In the twenty-seventh year, in spring,
the Viscount of Qǐ came to our court.
A5.27.2 In summer, in the sixth month, on the day Gēngyín,
the Marquis of Qí, Zhāo, died.
A5.27.3 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
Duke Xiào of Qí was buried.
A5.27.4 On the day Yǐsì,
Gōngzǐ Suì led an army and entered Qǐ.
A5.27.5 In winter,
men of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
and the Baron of Xǔ besieged Sòng.
A5.27.6 In the twelfth month, on the day Jiǎxū,
our lord met with the feudal lords,
and made a covenant in Sòng.
B5.27 The Commentary: The Twenty-Seventh Year of Duke Xī
B5.27.1 In the twenty-seventh year, in spring,
Duke Huán of Qǐ came to our court.
He used barbarian rites,
therefore he is called 'Viscount'.
Our lord looked down on Qǐ,
because Qǐ was not respectful.
B5.27.2 In summer,
Duke Xiào of Qí died.
Though there was enmity with Qí,
we did not neglect the mourning observances,
which was according to ritual.
B5.27.3 In autumn,
we entered Qǐ,
to reprimand them for their lack of ritual.
B5.27.4 The Viscount of Chǔ was about to besiege Sòng.
He sent Zǐ Wén to drill troops at Kuí,
which was finished by the end of the morning,
without punishing a single man.
Zǐ Yù again drilled troops at Wěi,
which took the whole day to finish,
he flogged seven men,
and pierced the ears of three men.
The senior statesmen all congratulated Zǐ Wén.
Zǐ Wén gave them wine.
Wěi Jiǎ was still young,
he arrived late,
and did not offer congratulations.
Zǐ Wén asked him about it.
He replied:
"I do not know what to congratulate.
You, sir, handed over the government to Zǐ Yù,
saying:
'In order to pacify the state.'
If he pacifies it internally but is defeated externally,
what gain is there?
If Zǐ Yù is defeated,
it is due to your recommendation.
Recommending someone who brings defeat to the state—
what is there to congratulate?
Zǐ Yù is stubborn and without ritual,
he cannot govern the people.
If he commands over three hundred chariots,
he will likely be unable to return.
If he does return, then congratulations,
what would be late about that?"
In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ and the feudal lords besieged Sòng.
Gōngsūn Gù of Sòng went to Jìn
to report the emergency.
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Repaying kindness,
saving from distress,
gaining prestige,
and establishing hegemony—
it lies in this."
Hú Yǎn said:
"Chǔ has just obtained Cáo,
and newly formed a marriage alliance with Wèi.
If we attack Cáo
and Wèi,
Chǔ is sure to rescue them,
then Qí
and Sòng will be spared."
Thereupon, they held a great hunt at Bèilú,
formed three armies,
and deliberated on the supreme commander.
Zhào Cuī said:
"Xì Hú is suitable.
I have frequently heard his words,
he delights in ritual
and music,
and is earnest about the Odes and Documents.
The Odes and Documents
are the storehouse of righteousness;
ritual and music
are the rules of virtue;
virtue and righteousness
are the roots of benefit.
The Book of Xià says:
'Collect and employ according to their words,
clearly test them by their achievements,
and reward them with chariots and robes according to their service.'
My lord, please try him!"
Then he appointed Xì Hú to command the central army,
with Xì Zhēn as his deputy.
He appointed Hú Yǎn to command the upper army,
but Hú Yǎn yielded to Hú Máo,
and instead served as his deputy.
He ordered Zhào Cuī to be a minister,
but Zhào Cuī yielded to Luán Zhī
and Xiān Zhěn.
He appointed Luán Zhī to command the lower army,
with Xiān Zhěn as his deputy.
Xún Línfù drove the war chariot,
and Wèi Chōu served as the right-hand guard.
When the Marquis of Jìn first returned to his state, he instructed his people.
After two years,
he wished to employ them.
Zǐfàn said:
"The people do not yet understand righteousness,
and are not settled in their dwellings."
Therefore,
he went out to secure King Xiāng on his throne,
and at home he devoted himself to benefiting the people.
The people then cherished life.
He was about to employ them.
Zǐfàn said:
"The people do not yet understand trustworthiness,
and have not yet fully developed their capacities."
Therefore, he attacked Yuán
to demonstrate trustworthiness to them.
Among the people, those who exchanged goods
did not seek excessive profit,
and their words were clearly reliable.
The Duke said:
"Is it permissible now?"
Zǐfàn said:
"The people do not yet understand ritual,
and have not yet developed a sense of reverence."
Therefore, he held a great hunt
to demonstrate ritual to them,
and established the office of Zhízhì
to regulate the officials.
The people obeyed without confusion,
and only then did he employ them.
He expelled the garrison from Gǔ,
lifted the siege of Sòng,
and with one battle achieved hegemony—
all due to the teachings of Wén.
A5.28 The Classic of the 28th Year of Duke Xī
A5.28.1 In the 28th year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn invaded Cáo,
and the Marquis of Jìn attacked Wèi.
A5.28.2 Gōngzǐ Mǎi was garrisoning Wèi;
he did not complete the garrison duty,
and was executed.
A5.28.3 The men of Chǔ rescued Wèi.
A5.28.4 On Bǐngwǔ day in the third month,
the Marquis of Jìn entered Cáo
and captured the Earl of Cáo,
delivering him to the men of Sòng.
A5.28.5 In summer, on Jǐsì day in the fourth month,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the army of Qí,
the army of Sòng,
and the army of Qín fought with the men of Chǔ at Chéngpú;
the army of Chǔ was utterly defeated.
A5.28.6 Chǔ put to death its senior officer Dé Chén.
A5.28.7 The Marquis of Wèi fled to Chǔ.
A5.28.8 On Guǐchǒu day in the fifth month,
our Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Viscount of Wèi,
and the Viscount of Jǔ,
and made a covenant at Jiàntǔ.
A5.28.9 The Marquis of Chén attended the meeting.
A5.28.10 Our Duke had an audience with the King at his temporary residence.
A5.28.11 In the sixth month,
the Marquis of Wèi, Zhèng, returned from Chǔ to Wèi.
Wèi Yuánxuān fled to Jìn.
A5.28.12 The Marquis of Chén, Kuǎn, died.
A5.28.13 In autumn,
Lady Jǐ of Qǐ came.
A5.28.14 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí.
A5.28.15 In winter,
our Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Viscount of Chén,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and the men of Qín at Wēn.
A5.28.16 The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng.
A5.28.17 On Rénshēn day,
our Duke had an audience with the King at his temporary residence.
A5.28.18 The men of Jìn seized the Marquis of Wèi
and sent him to the capital.
Wèi Yuánxuān returned from Jìn to Wèi.
A5.28.19 The feudal lords then besieged Xǔ.
A5.28.20 The Earl of Cáo, Xiāng, returned to Cáo,
and then joined the feudal lords in besieging Xǔ.
B5.28 The Commentary of the 28th Year of Duke Xī
B5.28.1 In the 28th year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn was about to attack Cáo
and requested passage through Wèi.
The men of Wèi refused.
He turned back,
crossed at the southern bend of the Yellow River,
invaded Cáo, and attacked Wèi.
On Wùshēn day in the first month,
he took Wǔlù.
In the second month,
Jìn's Xì Hú died.
Yuán Zhěn was appointed to command the central army,
and Xū Chén was made deputy of the lower army—
this was to honor virtue.
The Marquis of Jìn
and the Marquis of Qí made a covenant at Liǎnyú.
The Marquis of Wèi requested to join the covenant,
but the men of Jìn refused.
The Marquis of Wèi wished to side with Chǔ,
but the people of the state did not want this,
so they expelled their ruler
to please Jìn.
The Marquis of Wèi went out and resided at Xiāngniú.
B5.28.2 Gōngzǐ Mǎi was garrisoning Wèi,
and the men of Chǔ came to rescue Wèi,
but were unsuccessful.
Our Duke, fearing Jìn,
killed Zǐ Cóng to please them.
He told the men of Chǔ:
"He did not complete his garrison duty."
B5.28.3 The Marquis of Jìn besieged Cáo
and attacked its gates,
suffering many casualties.
The men of Cáo displayed the corpses on the city walls,
and the Marquis of Jìn was troubled by this.
He listened to the plan of the cart-drivers,
who proclaimed
"we will camp among the tombs."
The army moved there.
The men of Cáo were terrified,
and for those they had obtained,
they placed them in coffins and sent them out.
Taking advantage of their terror, he attacked them.
On Bǐngwǔ day in the third month,
he entered Cáo,
rebuking them for not employing Xī Fùjī
while three hundred men rode in carriages,
and further said,
"present your merits!"
He ordered that no one enter Xī Fùjī's residence,
and exempted his clan—
this was to repay past kindness.
Wèi Chōu
and Diān Jié were angry,
saying:
"He gives no thought to our toils,
what repayment is there for us?"
They set fire to Xī Fùjī's house.
Wèi Chōu was wounded in the chest.
The Duke wished to kill him,
but cherished his talent.
He sent to inquire,
and also to observe him.
If he was seriously ill, he would kill him.
Wèi Chōu bound his chest and appeared before the messenger,
saying:
"By the grace of our lord,
I am not unwell!"
He leaped forward three hundred times,
and bent and leaped three hundred times.
Then he released him.
He had Diān Jié executed and his corpse paraded before the army,
and appointed Zhōu Zhīqiáo
as the commander of the right flank.
The people of Sòng sent Mén Yǐnbān to the Jìn army to report the urgency.
The Duke said:
"The people of Sòng report urgency;
if we abandon them, they will be cut off;
if we ask Chǔ for help, they will not agree.
I wish to fight,
but Qí and Qín are not yet willing.
What should we do?"
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Have Sòng abandon us and bribe Qí
and Qín,
and rely on them to ask Chǔ for help.
We will capture the ruler of Cáo,
and divide the lands of Cáo
and Wèi
to bestow upon the people of Sòng.
Chǔ cherishes Cáo
and Wèi,
so they will certainly not agree.
Delighted by the bribes
and angered by the obstinacy,
how can we avoid fighting?"
The Duke was pleased,
captured the Earl of Cáo,
and divided the lands of Cáo
and Wèi
to give to the people of Sòng.
The King of Chǔ entered and resided in Shēn,
ordered Shēn Shū to withdraw from Gǔ,
and ordered Zǐ Yù to withdraw from Sòng,
saying:
"Do not pursue the Jìn army!
The Marquis of Jìn was abroad
for nineteen years,
and indeed obtained the state of Jìn.
The dangers and hardships,
he has fully experienced them;
the true and false of the people,
he knows them completely.
Heaven granted him years,
and removed his harms.
What Heaven has established,
can it be overthrown?
The *Military Annals* say:
'When appropriate, return.'
It also says:
'Know difficulty and retreat.'
It also says:
'One with virtue cannot be opposed.'
These three records
refer to Jìn."
Zǐ Yù sent Bó Fén
to request battle,
saying:
"I dare not claim to achieve merit,
but I wish to use this opportunity to silence the mouths of slanderers."
The King was angry,
gave him few troops,
only the Western Guard,
the Eastern Palace, and the six units of Ruò'áo followed him.
Zǐ Yù sent Wǎn Chūn to report to the Jìn army, saying:
"Please restore the Marquis of Wèi
and reestablish Cáo,
and I will also lift the siege of Sòng."
Zǐ Fàn said:
"Zǐ Yù is without courtesy!
The ruler takes one,
the minister takes two;
we cannot miss this opportunity."
Xiān Zhěn said:
"You should agree with him!
To settle others is called courtesy.
Chǔ with one word settles three states,
we with one word destroy them.
We would be without courtesy;
how then can we fight?
If we do not agree to Chǔ's words,
we abandon Sòng;
to rescue and then abandon them,
what will we say to the feudal lords?
Chǔ has three acts of grace,
we have three resentments.
With many resentments and enmities,
how can we fight?
It is better to secretly agree to restore Cáo
and Wèi
to win them over,
capture Wǎn Chūn to anger Chǔ,
and plan after the battle."
The Duke was pleased.
Then he detained Wǎn Chūn in Wèi,
and secretly agreed to restore Cáo
and Wèi.
Cáo
and Wèi declared a break with Chǔ.
Zǐ Yù was angry,
and pursued the Jìn army.
The Jìn army retreated.
The military officers said:
"For a ruler to avoid a minister
is disgraceful;
moreover, the Chǔ army is weary,
why retreat?"
Zǐ Fàn said:
"An army is strong when it is righteous,
and weary when it is unrighteous.
How can it depend on duration?
Without Chǔ's favor,
we would not have reached this point.
Retreating three *shè* to avoid them
is how we repay it.
To betray favor and break promises,
to oppose their enmity,
we would be unrighteous and Chǔ righteous.
Their troops have long been well-fed,
they cannot be called weary.
If we retreat and Chǔ returns,
what more shall we seek?
If they do not return,
the ruler retreats,
the minister offends;
the unrighteousness lies with them."
They retreated three *shè*.
The Chǔ troops wished to stop,
but Zǐ Yù would not allow it.
In the summer, on the fourth month, Wùchén day,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
Qí's Guó Guīfù,
Cuī Yāo,
and Qín's Xiǎozi Yìn encamped at Chéngpú.
The Chǔ army camped with their backs to Xī,
and the Marquis of Jìn was troubled by this.
He heard the commoners chanting:
"The fields are lush and abundant,
abandon the old
and plan for the new."
The Duke was doubtful.
Zǐ Fàn said:
"Fight!
If we fight and win,
we will surely gain the feudal lords.
If we do not win,
with mountains and rivers as our defense,
there will surely be no harm."
The Duke said:
"What about Chǔ's favor?"
Luán Zhēnzǐ said:
"The various Jī clans north of the Hàn River,
Chǔ has indeed wiped them out.
To think of small favors and forget great shame,
it is better to fight."
The Marquis of Jìn dreamed of wrestling with the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ pinned him down
and sucked his brains,
so he was afraid.
Zǐ Fàn said:
"Auspicious.
We gain Heaven,
Chǔ submits to its crime,
and we will soften them."
Zǐ Yù sent Dòu Bó to request battle,
saying:
"I request to play with your lordship's soldiers;
your lordship may lean on the chariot rail and watch,
and Déchén will also observe."
The Marquis of Jìn sent Luán Zhī to reply,
saying:
"Our humble lord has heard your command.
The favor of the King of Chǔ,
we have not dared to forget,
and that is why we are here.
For the great officer, we retreat;
how dare we oppose the ruler?
Since we have not received permission,
we dare trouble the great officer
to tell your several gentlemen:
'Prepare your chariots,
respect your ruler's affairs,
tomorrow morning we shall meet.'"
Jìn had seven hundred chariots,
with all their harnesses and trappings.
The Marquis of Jìn ascended the ruins of Yǒushēn
to observe the army,
saying:
"The young and old have courtesy,
they can be used."
Then they cut down the trees
to augment their weapons.
On Jǐsì day,
the Jìn army arrayed north of Shēn,
Xū Chén, as assistant of the lower army,
faced Chén
and Cài.
Zǐ Yù led the central army with the six companies of Ruò'áo,
saying:
"Today there will certainly be no Jìn."
Zǐ Xī commanded the left wing,
Zǐ Shàng commanded the right wing.
Xū Chén covered the horses with tiger skins,
and first attacked Chén and
Cài.
Chén and
Cài fled,
and the right division of Chǔ collapsed.
Hú Máo set up two banners and retreated.
Luán Zhī had the chariots drag brushwood and feigned flight,
the Chǔ army pursued them,
Yuán Zhěn and
Xì Zhēn with the central army's ducal clan attacked them from the flank.
Hú Máo and
Hú Yǎn with the upper army attacked Zǐ Xī from both sides,
and the left division of Chǔ collapsed.
The Chǔ army was utterly defeated.
Zǐ Yù gathered his troops and halted,
therefore he was not defeated.
The Jìn army for three days lodged and
fed,
and by Guǐyǒu they returned.
On Jiǎwǔ,
they arrived at Héngyōng,
and built a royal palace at Jiàntǔ.
Three months before the campaign,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ,
to present his army.
Because the Chǔ army was already defeated and he was afraid,
he sent Zǐrén Jiǔ to negotiate peace with Jìn.
Jìn's Luán Zhī entered to make a covenant with the Earl of Zhèng.
On the Bǐngwǔ day of the fifth month,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Héngyōng.
On Dīngwèi,
they presented Chǔ captives to the King:
one hundred chariots with armored teams,
and a thousand foot soldiers.
The Earl of Zhèng assisted the King,
using the ritual of peace.
On Jǐyǒu,
the King offered sweet wine,
and commanded the Marquis of Jìn to partake.
The King commanded Yǐn Shì and Prince Zǐ Hǔ,
and the Inner Scribe Shū Xīngfǔ to record the command appointing the Marquis of Jìn as Hegemon,
bestowing upon him the robes for the grand chariot,
the robes for the war chariot,
one vermilion bow and a hundred vermilion arrows,
a thousand black bows and arrows,
one yǒu of black millet aromatic wine,
and three hundred tiger warriors,
saying:
"The King says to Uncle,
'Respectfully obey the King's command,
to pacify the four states,
and correct and remove the King's evil.'"
The Marquis of Jìn declined three times,
then accepted the command,
saying:
"Chóng'ěr dares to bow twice and knock his head,
to receive and proclaim the Son of Heaven's great and illustrious grace
and command."
He received the recorded command and went out.
He entered and exited three times for audience.
The Marquis of Wèi heard that the Chǔ army was defeated,
was afraid,
fled to Chǔ,
then went to Chén,
and sent Yuán Xuān to escort Shū Wǔ
to receive the covenant.
On Guǐhài,
Prince Zǐ Hǔ made a covenant with the feudal lords in the King's court,
the essential words said:
"All shall assist the royal house,
and not harm each other!
If anyone violates this covenant,
the bright spirits will strike him,
causing his army to fall,
he will not be able to preserve his state,
and down to his great-great-grandsons,
none will be spared, old or young."
The gentleman says that this covenant was trustworthy,
and says that Jìn in this campaign
was able to attack with virtue.
B5.28.4 Earlier,
Chǔ's Zǐ Yù made for himself a jade cap and
jade tassels,
but had not yet worn them.
Before the battle,
he dreamed the River God said to him:
"Give them to me!
I will give you the marshlands of Mèngzhū."
He did not give them.
Dà Xīn and Zǐ Xī sent Róng Huáng to remonstrate,
but he did not listen.
Róng Jì said:
"If dying benefits the state,
one might still do it,
how much more so jade?
It is but dung and soil.
Yet it can aid the army,
what is there to cherish?"
He did not listen.
Going out,
he told the two men,
saying:
"It is not the spirits who defeated the Lingyǐn,
the Lingyǐn did not diligently serve the people,
he truly brought defeat upon himself."
After the defeat,
the King sent someone to say to him:
"If you, Great Officer, return,
what will you say to the elders of Shēn and
Xī?"
Zǐ Xī and
Sūn Bó said:
"Dé Chén is about to die.
We two ministers stopped him,
saying:
'The ruler will surely execute you.'"
He reached Liángǔ and died.
The Marquis of Jìn heard of it,
and then his joy could be known,
saying:
"No one can harm me anymore.
Wěi Lǚchén is indeed the Lingyǐn,
but he attends only to himself,
and does not care for the people."
B5.28.5 Someone accused Yuán Xuān to the Marquis of Wèi, saying:
"He has set up Shū Wǔ."
His son Jiǎo followed the Duke,
the Duke sent someone to kill him.
Xuān
did not abandon his mission,
but escorted Yí Shū to enter and guard.
In the sixth month,
the men of Jìn restored the Marquis of Wèi.
Nìng Wǔzǐ made a covenant with the men of Wèi at Yuānpú,
saying:
"Heaven brought disaster upon Wèi,
ruler and ministers were not harmonious,
leading to this distress.
Now Heaven guides our hearts,
causing all to humble their hearts and follow each other.
If there were no stayers,
who would guard the altars of soil and grain?
If there were no goers,
who would defend the herds and pastures?
Because of the lack of harmony,
we now clearly beg for a covenant before you, great spirits,
to guide Heaven's heart.
From this day onward,
after the covenant is made,
let the goers not boast of their strength,
and the stayers not fear their guilt.
If anyone violates this covenant,
to oppose each other,
the bright spirits and former rulers
will correct and strike them."
The people of the state heard this covenant,
and thereafter were not divided.
The Marquis of Wèi entered ahead of schedule,
Nìngzǐ went first,
Cháng Zāng guarded the gate,
thinking he was an envoy,
and entered with him in the chariot.
Prince Chuǎn Quǎn and
Huá Zhòng were the vanguard,
Shū Sūn was about to wash his hair,
heard the ruler had arrived,
was joyful,
grabbed his hair and ran out,
the vanguard shot and killed him.
The Duke knew he was innocent,
laid his head on his thigh and wept for him.
Chuǎn Quǎn ran out,
the Duke sent someone to kill him.
Yuán Xuān fled to Jìn.
B5.28.6 In the battle of Chéngpú,
Jìn's central army was caught in the wind in the marsh,
and lost the left banner of the great standard.
Qí Mán violated orders,
the Minister of War killed him,
and displayed him to the feudal lords,
sending Máo Fá to replace him.
The army returned.
On Rénwǔ,
they crossed the river.
Zhōu Zhī Qiáo returned first,
Shì Huì acted as charioteer.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on Bingshēn,
the army was reorganized,
and they returned to Jìn with triumphant songs.
Captives were presented,
and severed ears were offered.
A victory feast was held,
and great rewards were bestowed.
Meetings were convened,
and those who were disloyal were punished.
Zhōu Zhīqiáo was executed and his corpse displayed in the capital,
and the people were greatly awed.
The gentleman says of Duke Wén
"He was capable of administering punishments;
after three criminals were punished, the people submitted.
The Odes say:
'Show kindness to this central state,
and thereby pacify the four quarters.'
This refers to not failing in rewards
and punishments."
B5.28.7 In winter,
a meeting was held at Wēn,
to punish those who were disobedient.
B5.28.8 The Marquis of Wèi and Yuán Xuǎn engaged in a lawsuit.
Nìng Wǔzǐ acted as his assistant,
Qián Zhuāngzǐ
as his representative in court,
and Shì Róng as the chief prosecutor.
The Marquis of Wèi lost the case.
Shì Róng was executed,
Qián Zhuāngzǐ had his feet amputated,
and Nìng Yú was deemed loyal
and pardoned.
The Marquis of Wèi was seized
and sent to the capital,
where he was confined in a deep chamber.
Nìngzǐ was responsible for providing him with food and clothing.
Yuán Xuǎn returned to Wèi
and installed Prince Xiá.
B5.28.9 At this meeting,
the Marquis of Jìn summoned the King,
presenting him to the feudal lords,
and had the King go hunting.
Zhòngní said:
"For a minister to summon his sovereign
is not something to be taken as an example."
Therefore, the record states:
"The Heavenly King hunted at Héyáng,"
indicating it was not the proper place,
and to clarify virtue.
B5.28.10 On Rénshēn,
the Duke paid court to the King at his temporary residence.
B5.28.11 On Dīngchǒu,
the feudal lords besieged Xǔ.
B5.28.12 The Marquis of Jìn fell ill.
The page of the Earl of Cáo, Hóu Nòu, bribed the diviner,
making him say that the illness was due to Cáo:
"Duke Huán of Qí held meetings
and enfeoffed those of different surnames,
yet now you, my lord, hold meetings and extinguish those of the same surname.
Cáo Shū Zhènduó
was a descendant of King Wén;
our former lord, Táng Shū,
was a descendant of King Wǔ.
Moreover, to assemble the feudal lords and extinguish a fraternal state
is contrary to ritual.
To share a command with Wèi
yet not share in its restoration
is contrary to good faith.
To punish the same crime differently
is contrary to justice.
Ritual is used to enact righteousness,
good faith to uphold ritual,
and justice to correct evil.
If you abandon these three,
what will you do, my lord?"
The Duke was pleased,
restored the Earl of Cáo,
and then met with the feudal lords at Xǔ.
B5.28.13 The Marquis of Jìn established three infantry divisions to defend against the Dí.
Xún Línfǔ commanded the central division,
Tú Jī commanded the right division,
and Xiān Miè commanded the left division.
A5.29 The Twenty-Ninth Year of Duke Xī, the Classic
A5.29.1 In the twenty-ninth year, in spring,
Jiè Gélú came.
A5.29.2 The Duke arrived from the siege of Xǔ.
A5.29.3 In summer, in the sixth month,
he met with the King's representative,
the man of Jìn,
the man of Sòng,
the man of Qí,
the man of Chén,
the man of Cài,
and the man of Qín,
and made a covenant at Díquán.
A5.29.4 In autumn,
there was heavy hail.
A5.29.5 In winter,
Jiè Gélú came.
B5.29 The Twenty-Ninth Year of Duke Xī, the Commentary
B5.29.1 In the twenty-ninth year, in spring,
Jiè Gélú came to court
and stayed at Chāngyǎn.
The Duke was at a meeting,
so he sent him fodder
and grain,
which was according to ritual.
B5.29.2 In summer,
the Duke met with Prince Zǐhǔ, Hú Yǎn of Jìn, Gōngsūn Gù of Sòng, Guó Guīfǔ of Qí, Yuán Táotú of Chén, and Xiǎozi Yìn of Qín,
and made a covenant at Díquán,
renewing the covenant of Jiàntǔ
and planning an attack on Zhèng.
The ministers are not recorded,
to censure them.
According to ritual,
ministers do not meet with dukes and marquises;
they may meet with earls, viscounts, and barons.
B5.29.3 In autumn,
there was heavy hail,
which was a disaster.
B5.29.4 In winter,
Jiè Gélú came,
and because he had not yet seen the Duke,
he came again to court.
He was treated with ritual,
and additional feasts and gifts were given.
Jiè Gélú heard an ox lowing
and said:
"This one bore three sacrificial oxen,
and all have been used.
Its sound says so."
They inquired and found it to be true.
A5.30 The Thirtieth Year of Duke Xī, the Classic
A5.30.1 In the thirtieth year, in spring,
it was the royal first month.
A5.30.2 In summer,
the Dí invaded Qí.
A5.30.3 In autumn,
Wèi killed its great officer Yuán Xuǎn and Prince Xiá.
The Marquis of Wèi, Zhèng, returned to Wèi.
A5.30.4 The men of Jìn
and the men of Qín besieged Zhèng.
A5.30.5 The men of Jiè invaded Xiāo.
A5.30.6 In winter,
the Heavenly King sent the Chief Minister, the Duke of Zhōu, on a courtesy visit.
A5.30.7 Prince Suì went to the capital,
and then went to Jìn.
B5.30 The Thirtieth Year of Duke Xī, the Commentary
B5.30.1 In the thirtieth year, in spring,
the men of Jìn invaded Zhèng
to observe whether it could be attacked or not.
The Dí, taking advantage of Jìn's concern about Zhèng,
in summer,
invaded Qí.
B5.30.2 The Marquis of Jìn sent Physician Yǎn to poison the Marquis of Wèi.
Nìng Yú bribed the physician,
making him dilute the poison,
so he did not die.
The Duke interceded for him,
presenting jade to the King and the Marquis of Jìn,
each ten pairs,
and the King granted it.
In autumn,
he released the Marquis of Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi sent bribes to Zhōu Chuán
and Yě Jǐn, saying:
"If you can restore me,
I will make you ministers."
Zhōu and Yě killed Yuán Xuǎn, Zǐ Shì,
and Zǐ Yí.
When the Duke entered,
and sacrificed to the former lords,
Zhōu and Yě, having donned their court robes,
were about to receive their appointments,
when Zhōu Chuán entered first,
and upon reaching the gate,
fell ill and died.
Yě Jǐn declined the ministership.
B5.30.3 In the ninth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn and
the Earl of Qín besieged Zhèng,
because it had been disrespectful to Jìn,
and also because it was disloyal and sided with Chǔ.
The Jìn army was stationed at Hánlíng,
and the Qín army was stationed south of Fàn.
Yì Zhīhú said to the Earl of Zhèng:
"The state is in danger.
If you send Zhú Zhīwǔ to see the ruler of Qín,
the army will certainly withdraw."
The Duke followed his advice.
(Zhú Zhīwǔ) declined, saying:
"In my prime,
I was still not as capable as others;
now I am old,
I am incapable of doing anything."
The Duke said:
"I could not employ you, sir, earlier;
now in urgency I seek your help,
this is my fault.
However, if Zhèng perishes,
you, sir, will also suffer disadvantage."
He consented.
At night, he was let down by a rope from the city wall and went out.
He saw the Earl of Qín and said:
"Qín and
Jìn are besieging Zhèng;
Zhèng already knows it is doomed.
If the destruction of Zhèng would be beneficial to you, my lord,
I would venture to trouble your officers with it.
But to cross another state to make a distant borderland your own,
you, my lord, know the difficulty of that.
Why then use the destruction of Zhèng to increase your neighbor's territory?
The neighbor's strength is
your lordship's weakness.
If you spare Zhèng and make it your host on the eastern route,
when your envoys come and go,
(Zhèng can) supply their deficiencies,
and you, my lord, would suffer no harm.
Moreover, you, my lord, once granted favors to the ruler of Jìn;
he promised you Jiāo and
Xiá,
yet he set up fortifications the morning after crossing the river (and reneged),
as you, my lord, know.
That Jìn,
how could it ever be satisfied?
Having already made Zhèng its eastern border,
it will wish to extend its western frontier.
If it does not encroach upon Qín,
from where will it take territory?
Encroaching upon Qín to benefit Jìn—I ask you, my lord, to consider this."
The Earl of Qín was pleased,
made a covenant with the men of Zhèng,
sent Qǐzǐ, Péng Sūn, and Yáng Sūn to guard it,
and then returned.
Zǐ Fàn requested to attack them.
The Duke (of Jìn) said:
"It cannot be.
Without that man's strength, I would not have reached this position.
To rely on another's strength and then to harm him
is unrighteous;
to lose one's ally
is unwise;
to replace order with chaos
is un-martial.
Let us return."
He also withdrew from there.
Earlier,
the Zhèng prince Lán had fled to Jìn,
and followed the Marquis of Jìn to attack Zhèng.
He requested not to participate in the siege of Zhèng.
This was granted,
and he was ordered to wait for commands in the east.
Shí Jiǎfǔ and
Hóu Xuānduō of Zhèng went to receive
him to be the crown prince,
in order to seek peace with Jìn.
The men of Jìn agreed.
B5.30.4 In winter,
the King sent Zhōu Gōng Yuè to come on a courtesy visit.
At the feast there were chāngchōu (fermented rice drink),
báihēi (rice and millet cakes), and xíngyán (tiger-shaped salt).
He declined, saying:
"For a ruler of a state,
whose civil virtues are sufficient to shine forth,
and whose martial might is awe-inspiring,
then there are prepared offerings for the feast,
to symbolize his virtue;
presenting the five flavors,
offering the fine grains,
and tiger-shaped salt,
to manifest his achievements.
How can I bear this?"
B5.30.5 Dōngmén Xiāng Zhòng was about to go on a courtesy visit to Zhōu,
and thus for the first time paid a courtesy visit to Jìn.
A5.31 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, the 31st Year of Duke Xī*
A5.31.1 In the 31st year, in spring,
we took the fields west of Jǐ.
A5.31.2 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Jìn.
A5.31.3 In summer, in the fourth month,
we divined four times about the suburban sacrifice,
and it was not favorable,
so we released the sacrificial animal.
We still performed the three望 sacrifices.
A5.31.4 In autumn, in the seventh month.
A5.31.5 In winter,
the lady of Qí, Bó Jī, came to seek a wife.
A5.31.6 The Dí besieged Wèi.
In the twelfth month,
Wèi moved to Dìqiū.
B5.31 *The Commentary of Zuo, the 31st Year of Duke Xī*
B5.31.1 In the 31st year, in spring,
we took the fields west of Jǐ,
which was dividing the territory of Cáo.
(The Duke) sent Zāng Wénzhòng to go,
and he lodged at the Chóng guesthouse.
The keeper of the Chóng guesthouse advised him, saying:
"Jìn has newly gained the allegiance of the feudal lords,
and will certainly be close to those who come first.
If you do not hurry,
you will not make it in time."
He followed this advice.
The division of Cáo's territory
extended from south of Táo,
eastward bordering on Jǐ,
comprising all of Cáo's territory.
B5.31.2 Xiāng Zhòng went to Jìn,
to express thanks for the fields of Cáo.
B5.31.3 In summer, in the fourth month,
we divined four times about the suburban sacrifice,
and it was not favorable,
so we released the sacrificial animal—
this was contrary to ritual.
We still performed the three望 sacrifices—
this was also contrary to ritual.
For regular sacrifices, one does not divine about whether to perform them,
but divines about the sacrificial animal and
the day.
When the ox is divined for the day, it is called the 'shēng' (victim).
When the victim is ready and then one divines about the suburban sacrifice,
this shows negligence and
disrespect from above.
The望 sacrifices
are a minor part of the suburban sacrifice.
If the suburban sacrifice is not performed,
then there should be no望 sacrifices either.
B5.31.4 In autumn,
Jìn held a military review at Qīngyuán,
and formed five armies to defend against the Dí.
Zhào Cuī became a minister.
B5.31.5 In winter,
the Dí besieged Wèi,
and Wèi moved to Dìqiū.
A divination said
(it would last) three hundred years.
Duke Chéng of Wèi dreamed that Kāng Shū said:
"Xiàng is seizing my offerings."
The Duke ordered sacrifices to Xiàng.
Nìng Wǔzǐ said it could not be done,
saying:
"Spirits and deities, if they are not of the same clan,
do not enjoy their sacrifices.
What have Qǐ and Zēng to do with it?
Xiàng has not received sacrifices here for a long time;
it is not Wèi's fault.
We cannot interfere with the sacrificial mandates of King Chéng and
the Duke of Zhōu.
I ask to change the sacrificial order."
B5.31.6 Xiè Jià of Zhèng disliked the prince Xiá,
and the Earl of Zhèng also disliked him,
so Prince Xiá fled to Chǔ.
A5.32 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, the 32nd Year of Duke Xī*
A5.32.1 In the 32nd year, in spring,
it was the royal first month.
A5.32.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
the Earl of Zhèng, Jié, died.
A5.32.3 The men of Wèi invaded Dí. In autumn, the men of Wèi made a covenant with Dí.
A5.32.4 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
the Marquis of Jìn, Chóng'ěr, died.
B5.32 *The Commentary of Zuo, the 32nd Year of Duke Xī*
B5.32.1 In the 32nd year, in spring,
Dòu Zhāng of Chǔ requested peace with Jìn,
and Yáng Chǔfǔ of Jìn reciprocated the visit,
and Jìn and Chǔ began to have communications.
B5.32.2 In summer,
the Dí tribe was in turmoil.
The men of Wèi invaded the Dí,
and the Dí requested peace.
In autumn,
the men of Wèi made a covenant with the Dí.
B5.32.3 In winter,
Duke Wén of Jìn died.
On the gēngchén day,
they were about to place his coffin in the ancestral temple at Qūwò.
As they left Jiàng,
a sound like an ox came from the coffin.
Bǔ Yǎn had the great officers bow,
and said:
"Our lord commands a great affair:
a western army will pass by and overstep our borders;
attack them,
and you will certainly win a great victory."
Qǐzǐ, from Zhèng, sent a message to Qín,
saying:
"The men of Zhèng have put me in charge of the key to their northern gate.
If you secretly send an army here,
you can obtain the state."
Duke Mù consulted Jiǎn Shū about it.
Jiǎn Shū said:
"To weary an army by attacking a distant state—
I have never heard of such a thing.
The army will be wearied and its strength exhausted,
and the distant lord will be prepared for it.
Is this not perhaps unfeasible?
What the army does,
Zhèng is sure to know of it.
To labor without gain,
will surely breed resentment.
Moreover, to march a thousand lǐ,
who will not know of it?"
The duke rejected his advice.
He summoned Mèng Míng, Xīqǐ, and Báiyǐ,
and ordered them to lead the army out beyond the eastern gate.
Jiǎn Shū wept for them,
saying:
"Mèngzǐ!
I see the army going out, but I shall not see it coming back!"
The duke sent someone to say to him:
"What do you know?
If you had died at a middling age,
the trees on your grave would be big enough to clasp by now."
Jiǎn Shū's son was with the army.
He wept as he saw him off,
saying:
"The men of Jìn will certainly intercept the army at Xiáo.
At Xiáo there are two ridges.
The southern ridge
is the tomb of Xiàhòu Gāo;
the northern ridge
is where King Wén sheltered from wind and rain.
You will surely die between them.
I will gather your bones there!"
The Qín army then marched eastward.
A5.33 The Classic of the 33rd Year of Duke Xī
A5.33.1 In the 33rd year, in spring,
in the king's second month,
men of Qín entered Huá.
A5.33.2 The Marquis of Qí sent Guó Guīfǔ on a courtesy visit.
A5.33.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on the xīnsì day,
men of Jìn and the Jiāngróng defeated the Qín army at Xiáo.
A5.33.4 On the guǐsì day,
they buried Duke Wén of Jìn.
A5.33.5 The Dí invaded Qí.
A5.33.6 Our duke attacked Zhū and took Zīlóu.
A5.33.7 In autumn,
the duke's son Suì led an army to attack Zhū.
A5.33.8 Men of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jī.
A5.33.9 In winter, in the tenth month,
our duke went to Qí.
A5.33.10 In the twelfth month,
our duke arrived from Qí.
A5.33.11 On the yǐsì day,
our duke died in his small chamber.
A5.33.12 Frost fell but did not kill the grass.
Plum trees bore fruit.
A5.33.13 Men of Jìn,
Chén,
and Zhèng attacked Xǔ.
B5.33 The Commentary of the 33rd Year of Duke Xī
B5.33.1 In spring of the 33rd year,
the Qín army passed by the northern gate of the Zhōu capital.
Those on the left and right of the chariots took off their helmets and descended,
then three hundred chariots leaped back on.
Wángsūn Mǎn was still young.
Observing this,
he spoke to the king, saying:
"The Qín army is presumptuous and without propriety;
it is sure to be defeated.
Presumption leads to lack of strategy;
lack of propriety leads to carelessness.
To enter perilous ground carelessly,
and moreover to lack strategy—
can it avoid defeat?"
When they reached Huá,
a merchant of Zhèng named Xián Gāo, who was about to trade in Zhōu,
encountered them.
He first presented four hides,
then twelve oxen to provision the army,
saying:
"My unworthy ruler has heard that you, sir, are marching your army past our humble state.
I venture to provision your followers.
Our humble state is not wealthy,
but for your followers' stay,
if you lodge we will prepare a day's provisions,
and if you march we will provide a night's guard."
Moreover, he sent a swift messenger to report to Zhèng.
Duke Mù of Zhèng sent someone to inspect the guest quarters,
and found them packing their loads,
sharpening their weapons,
and feeding their horses.
He sent Huáng Wǔzǐ to dismiss them with words,
saying:
"You, sirs, have lingered long in our humble state.
Our supply of dried meat and provisions
is exhausted.
Since you, sirs, are about to depart,
Zhèng has its Yuánpǔ park,
just as Qín has its Jùpǔ park.
You, sirs, may take its deer,
to give our humble state some respite.
How would that be?"
Qǐzǐ fled to Qí,
Féng Sūn
and Yáng Sūn fled to Sòng.
Mèng Míng said:
"Zhèng is prepared;
we cannot hope for success.
To attack and not conquer it,
to besiege it without reinforcements—
we should return."
They destroyed Huá and returned.
B5.33.2 Guó Zhuāngzǐ of Qí came on a courtesy visit.
From the greeting at the outskirts to the presentation of gifts upon departure,
the ceremonies were completed and executed with diligence.
Zāng Wénzhòng spoke to our duke, saying:
