"Guózǐ administers affairs;
Qí still has propriety.
You, my lord, should pay a court visit there!
I have heard it said:
'To submit to those who have propriety
is a safeguard for the altars of soil and grain.'"
B5.33.3 Yuán Zhěn of Jìn said:
"Qín disobeyed Jiǎn Shū,
and through greed has wearied its people—
Heaven is presenting them to us.
A presentation from Heaven must not be lost;
an enemy must not be let go.
To let go an enemy
gives rise to calamity;
to disobey Heaven
is inauspicious.
We must attack the Qín army!"
Luán Zhī said:
"We have not yet repaid Qín's kindness,
yet we attack its army—
is this not forgetting our deceased lord?"
Xiān Zhěn said:
"Qín does not grieve for our mourning,
but attacks our kinsmen.
Qín is thus without propriety—
what kindness is there to repay?
I have heard it said:
'To let go an enemy for a single day
is the calamity of many generations.'
To plan for our descendants—
can this be called forgetting our deceased lord!"
Thereupon they issued the command
and hastily raised the Jiāngróng.
The heir apparent dyed his mourning garments black.
Liáng Hóng drove the commander's chariot,
and Lái Jū served as the right-hand guard.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the xīnsì day,
they defeated the Qín army at Xiáo,
and captured Bǎilǐ Mèngmíng Shì, Xīqǐ Shù, and Báiyǐ Bǐng, and brought them back.
They then wore black to bury Duke Wén,
and Jìn from this time began the practice of wearing black mourning.
Wén Yíng requested the three commanders,
saying:
"They were the ones who truly incited discord between our two rulers.
If our ruler could capture and eat them,
he would not be satisfied.
Why trouble yourself to punish them?
Let them return to be executed in Qín,
to fulfill our ruler's wish.
What do you think?"
The duke agreed.
Xiān Zhěn came to court,
and asked about the Qín prisoners.
The duke said:
"The lady requested it,
so I released them."
Xiān Zhěn was furious,
saying:
"The warriors exerted their strength to capture them on the battlefield,
yet a woman's momentary plea released them within the capital.
This ruins the army's achievements and fosters the enemy's hatred.
Our destruction is not far off!"
He turned away and spat.
The duke sent Yáng Chǔfǔ to pursue them.
When he reached the river,
they were already in the boat.
He untied the left-side horse,
and under the duke's order, presented it to Mèng Míng.
Mèng Míng bowed his head to the ground and said:
"It is your grace
that we, the bound captives, were not used to smear the drums with blood,
but were sent back to be executed in Qín.
If our ruler considers us worthy of execution,
we will die without regret.
If, following your grace, we are spared,
in three years we shall come to thank you for your gift."
The Earl of Qín, dressed in plain clothes, waited in the suburbs,
facing the army and weeping,
saying:
"I disobeyed Jiǎn Shū,
and brought disgrace upon you, my officers.
This is my crime."
He did not dismiss Mèng Míng,
saying:
"It is my fault.
What crime have you, my officers, committed?
Moreover, I will not let one fault overshadow great virtue."
B5.33.4 The Dí invaded Qí,
taking advantage of Jìn's mourning period.
B5.33.5 The duke attacked Zhū,
capturing Zīlóu,
in retaliation for the Shēngxíng campaign.
The people of Zhū did not prepare defenses.
In autumn,
Xiāng Zhòng again attacked Zhū.
B5.33.6 The Dí attacked Jìn,
reaching Jī.
On the wùzǐ day of the eighth month,
the Marquis of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jī.
Xì Quē captured the leader of the Bái Dí.
Xiān Zhěn said:
"A commoner vented his anger before his ruler,
yet was not punished.
How dare I not punish myself?"
He removed his helmet and entered the Dí army,
and died there.
The Dí returned his head,
his face looking as if alive.
Earlier,
when Jiù Jì was on a mission,
he passed through Jì,
and saw Jì Quē weeding,
while his wife brought him food.
They were respectful,
treating each other like guests.
He brought him back,
and spoke to Duke Wén, saying:
"Respect
is the accumulation of virtue.
One who can be respectful must possess virtue.
Virtue is used to govern the people.
I beg you, my lord, to employ him!
I have heard it said:
'When leaving the house, act as if receiving a guest;
when undertaking affairs, act as if performing a sacrifice.'
This is the rule of benevolence."
The duke said:
"His father was guilty.
Is it permissible?"
He replied:
"Shun punished Gǔn for his crime,
yet promoted Yǔ for his merit.
Guǎn Jìngzhòng was an enemy of Duke Huán,
yet he truly served as his minister and achieved success.
The 'Kāng Gào' says:
'If the father is not kind,
the son is not reverent;
if the elder brother is not friendly,
the younger brother is not respectful;
these do not implicate each other.'
The 'Shī' says:
'When gathering mustard greens and radish leaves,
do not reject them because of their roots.'
You, my lord, may select the good points."
Duke Wén appointed him as a lower army officer.
Upon returning from Jī,
Duke Xiāng, with a triple command, appointed Xiān Qiějū to command the central army.
With a double command, he awarded the district of Xiānmáo to Xū Chén,
saying:
"Recommending Xì Quē
was your achievement."
With a single command, he appointed Xì Quē as a minister,
and restored to him the territory of Jì,
though he still did not hold a military rank.
B5.33.7 In winter,
the duke went to Qí.
He paid court,
and also condoled regarding the Dí invasion.
On his return,
he died in his small chamber,
having sought comfort there.
Chén, and Zhèng attacked Xǔ,
punishing it for turning toward Chǔ.
B5.33.9 The Chǔ prime minister Zǐ Shàng invaded Chén and Cài.
Chén and Cài made peace,
so he then attacked Zhèng,
intending to install Prince Xiá.
They attacked the Jiédié Gate.
Xiá fell into the pond of the Zhōu family,
and the outer servant Kūn Tún captured him
and presented him.
Lady Wén collected his body and buried him beneath Kuàichéng.
B5.33.10 Jìn's Yáng Chǔfǔ invaded Cài.
Chǔ's Zǐ Shàng came to its aid,
and the two armies faced each other across the Zhì River.
Yángzǐ was troubled by this,
and sent a message to Zǐ Shàng, saying:
"I have heard:
'In civil matters, do not oppose what is proper;
in military matters, do not avoid the enemy.'
If you wish to fight,
then I will withdraw thirty lǐ,
and you may cross and array your forces.
The timing is at your command.
Otherwise,
ease our position.
To weary the troops and waste resources
is of no benefit either."
He then harnessed his chariot and waited.
Zǐ Shàng wished to cross,
but Dà Sūnbó
said:
"It cannot be done.
The people of Jìn are untrustworthy.
If they attack us when we are halfway across,
what use is regret after defeat?
It is better to ease their position."
So they withdrew thirty lǐ.
Yángzǐ announced:
"The Chǔ army has fled."
And then returned.
The Chǔ army also returned.
Crown Prince Shāngchén slandered Zǐ Shàng, saying:
"He accepted a bribe from Jìn and avoided them.
This is a disgrace to Chǔ.
No crime is greater."
The king executed Zǐ Shàng.
B5.33.11 When Duke Xí was buried,
the delay
in making the spirit tablet
was contrary to ritual.
Whenever a ruler dies,
the burial is completed and then the accompanying sacrifice is held.
After the accompanying sacrifice, the spirit tablet is made.
Special sacrifices are offered to the tablet,
while the seasonal and grand sacrifices are held in the temple.
A6.1 The First Year of Duke Wén (Classic)
A6.1.1 First year, spring,
the royal first month,
the duke ascended the throne.
A6.1.2 Second month, guǐhài day,
there was a solar eclipse.
A6.1.3 The Heavenly King sent Shū Fú to attend the burial.
A6.1.4 Summer, fourth month, dīngsì day,
we buried our ruler, Duke Xí.
A6.1.5 The Heavenly King sent Máo Bó to confer a mandate upon the duke.
A6.1.6 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Wèi.
A6.1.7 Shūsūn Déchén went to the capital.
A6.1.8 The people of Wèi attacked Jìn.
A6.1.9 In autumn,
Gōngsūn Áo met with the Marquis of Jìn at Qì.
A6.1.10 In winter, on the dīngwèi day of the tenth month,
Shāngchén, the heir apparent of Chǔ, murdered his ruler, Yún.
A6.1.11 Gōngsūn Áo went to Qí.
B6.1 The Commentary for the First Year of Duke Wén
B6.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
the King sent the Neishi Shūfú to attend the funeral.
Gōngsūn Áo heard that he was skilled in physiognomy,
and presented his two sons to him.
Shūfú said:
"Gǔ will provide for you,
Nán will bury you.
Gǔ has a full jaw,
he will surely have descendants in the state of Lǔ."
B6.1.2 At this time, there was an intercalary third month,
which was contrary to ritual.
The former kings in rectifying the seasons,
established the beginning at the start,
set the correct points in the middle,
and placed the surplus at the end.
Establishing the beginning at the start,
ensures the sequence is not disordered;
setting the correct points in the middle,
ensures the people are not confused;
placing the surplus at the end,
ensures affairs are not perverse.
B6.1.3 In summer, on the dīngsì day of the fourth month,
Duke Xí was buried.
B6.1.4 The King sent Máobó Wèi to come and confer the royal mandate upon the Duke.
Shūsūn Déchen went to Zhōu to express gratitude.
B6.1.5 In the later years of Duke Wén of Jìn,
the feudal lords paid court to Jìn.
Duke Chéng of Wèi did not pay court,
but sent Kǒng Dá to invade Zhèng,
attacking Mián, Zī, and Kuāng.
After Duke Xiāng of Jìn had completed the mourning rites,
he sent word to the feudal lords and attacked Wèi,
reaching Nányáng.
Xiān Qiějū said:
"To imitate wrongdoing
is calamity.
I request my lord to pay court to the King,
while I follow the army."
The Marquis of Jìn paid court to the King at Wēn.
Xiān Qiějū and Xū Chén attacked Wèi.
On the first day, the xīnyǒu day, of the fifth month,
the Jìn army besieged Qì.
On the wùxū day of the sixth month,
they captured it,
and took Sūn Zhāozǐ prisoner.
The men of Wèi sent word to Chén.
Duke Gòng of Chén said:
"Attack them again,
and I will intercede for you."
Kǒng Dá of Wèi led an army to attack Jìn.
The gentleman considered this crude.
In ancient times,
one did not scheme across states.
B6.1.6 In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn demarcated the fields of Qì,
therefore Gōngsūn Áo met with him.
B6.1.7 Earlier,
the ruler of Chǔ intended to make Shāngchén his heir apparent,
and consulted the Lingyǐn Zǐshàng about it.
Zǐshàng said:
"Your age is not yet advanced,
and you have many favorites;
to depose him later would cause disorder.
In the selection for Chǔ,
it has always been among the younger ones.
Moreover, this man
has the eyes of a wasp and the voice of a jackal;
he is a cruel man,
and should not be established."
He did not listen.
Later,
he again wished to establish Prince Zhí,
and depose the heir apparent Shāngchén.
Shāngchén heard of this but had not verified it,
and told his tutor Pān Chóng:
"How can I verify it?"
Pān Chóng said:
"Entertain Jiāng Mǐ
but show her no respect."
He followed this advice.
Jiāng Mǐ angrily said:
"Bah!
Menial!
No wonder the king wishes to depose you and establish Zhí."
He told Pān Chóng:
"It is true."
Pān Chóng said:
"Can you serve him?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"Can you flee?"
He said:
"I cannot."
"Can you undertake a great affair?"
He said:
"I can."
In winter, in the tenth month,
he used the palace guards to surround King Chéng.
The King requested to eat bear's paw and then die.
He did not listen.
On the dīngwèi day,
the King hanged himself.
They posthumously titled him
"Líng",
but his eyes did not close;
they said
"Chéng",
and then his eyes closed.
King Mù was established,
and gave Shāngchén's residence as heir apparent to Pān Chóng,
making him Grand Tutor,
and also put him in charge of the Ring Guard.
B6.1.8 Mùbó went to Qí,
beginning diplomatic visits,
which was according to ritual.
Whenever a ruler ascends the throne,
his ministers go out to pay visits,
to renew old friendships,
secure external support,
foster good relations with neighboring states,
in order to protect the altars of soil and grain.
This is the way of loyalty, good faith, humility, and deference.
Loyalty
is the correctness of virtue;
good faith
is the firmness of virtue;
humility and deference
are the foundation of virtue.
B6.1.9 At the battle of Xiáo,
after the men of Jìn had returned the Qín commanders,
the great officers and attendants of Qín all said to the Earl of Qín:
"This defeat
was the fault of Mèng Míng;
you must kill him."
The Earl of Qín said:
"This is my fault.
The poem of Ruì Liángfū of Zhōu says:
'The great wind has its path,
the greedy man ruins his kind.
When he hears words he answers,
when he recites words he is as if drunk.
He does not use the good,
but turns and makes me perverse.'
This is because of greed,
and refers to me.
I, through greed, brought calamity upon that man;
what fault has that man?"
He again put him in charge of government.
A6.2 The Text for the Second Year of Duke Wén
A6.2.1 In the spring of the second year,
on the jiǎzǐ day of the second month of the royal calendar,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Qín army fought at Péngyá,
and the Qín army was utterly defeated.
A6.2.2 On the dīngchǒu day,
the spirit tablet of Duke Xí was made.
A6.2.3 On the yǐsì day of the third month,
a covenant was made with Chǔfù of Jìn.
A6.2.4 In summer, in the sixth month,
Gōngsūn Áo met with the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Earl of Zhèng,
and Shì Hú of Jìn to covenant at Chuílǒng.
A6.2.5 From the twelfth month there was no rain,
until the seventh month of autumn.
A6.2.6 On the dīngmǎo day of the eighth month,
a great sacrifice was held in the grand temple,
elevating Duke Xí.
A6.2.7 In winter,
men of Jìn,
Sòng,
Chén,
and Zhèng attacked Qín.
A6.2.8 Prince Suì went to Qí to present betrothal gifts.
B6.2 The Commentary for the Second Year of Duke Wén
B6.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
Mèng Míng Shì of Qín led an army to attack Jìn,
to avenge the battle of Xiáo.
In the second month,
the Marquis of Jìn resisted him.
Xiān Qiějū commanded the central army,
with Zhào Cuī as his assistant.
Wángguān Wúdì drove the war chariot,
and Hú Jūjū served as the right-hand guard.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
they engaged the Qín army at Péngyá,
and the Qín army was defeated.
The people of Jìn called the Qín army
"the army that came to thank us for the gift."
At the battle of Xiáo,
Liáng Hóng of Jìn drove the war chariot,
and Lái Jū served as the right-hand guard.
The day after the battle,
Duke Xiāng of Jìn had the Qín prisoners bound,
and ordered Lái Jū to behead one with a dagger-axe.
The prisoner cried out,
and Lái Jū dropped the dagger-axe.
Láng Shěn picked up the dagger-axe and beheaded the prisoner,
then captured him and followed the duke's chariot.
He was then made the right-hand guard.
At the battle of Jī,
Xiān Zhěn dismissed him,
and appointed Xù Jiǎnbó in his place.
Láng Shěn was angry.
His friend said:
"Why not die for this?"
Shěn said:
"I have not yet found a worthy cause to die for."
His friend said:
"I will join you in making trouble."
Shěn said:
"The Zhōu Zhì says:
'If courage is used to harm superiors,
one will not be admitted to the bright hall.'
To die for an unrighteous cause
is not true courage.
To be employed for a common purpose is called courage.
I attained the position of right-hand guard through courage;
being dismissed for lacking courage
is also fitting.
yet my dismissal was appropriate,
then he does understand me.
You should wait and see."
At Péngyá,
after the battle lines were formed,
he led his own troops in a charge against the Qín army,
and died there.
The Jìn army followed him,
and greatly defeated the Qín army.
The gentleman said
"Láng Shěn in this acted as a gentleman.
The Shī says:
'If the gentleman is angered,
disorder is quickly stopped.'
It also says:
'The king blazed with anger,
and so marshaled his hosts.'
He was angered but did not create disorder,
instead following the army
—he may be called a gentleman."
The Earl of Qín still employed Mèng Míng.
Mèng Míng diligently improved the state's governance,
and generously bestowed benefits upon the people.
Zhào Chéngzǐ said to the great officers:
"If the Qín army comes again,
we must avoid them.
Fear leads them to increase their virtue,
and they cannot be withstood.
The Shī says:
'Think of your ancestors,
and cultivate their virtue.'
Mèng Míng thinks of this.
Thinking of virtue without slackening,
how can he be opposed?"
B6.2.2 On the dīngchǒu day,
the spirit tablet of Duke Xī was made.
The record
indicates it was not done at the proper time.
B6.2.3 The people of Jìn came to reproach
because the duke had not paid court,
and the duke went to Jìn.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the jǐsì day,
the people of Jìn sent Yáng Chǔfǔ to make a covenant with the duke,
to humiliate him.
The record says:
"Made a covenant with Chǔfǔ of Jìn,"
to show disapproval.
The journey to Jìn is not recorded,
to conceal it.
B6.2.4 Before the duke returned,
in the sixth month,
Mù Bó met with the feudal lords
and the Minister of Works of Jìn, Shì Hú, to make a covenant at Chuílǒng,
because Jìn was reproaching Wèi.
The record
"Shì Hú"
indicates he was competent for the task.
The Marquis of Chén pleaded with Jìn on behalf of Wèi for peace,
and seized Kǒng Dá to appease them.
B6.2.5 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the dīngmǎo day,
a great sacrifice was held in the grand temple,
elevating Duke Xī,
which was a reverse order of sacrifice.
At this time, Xiàfù Fújì was the Minister of Rituals.
He honored Duke Xī,
and moreover declared openly:
"I see that the new ghost is large,
and the old ghost is small.
Putting the large first and the small after
is accordance.
Elevating the sage and worthy
is illumination.
Illumination and accordance
are ritual."
The gentleman considered this a violation of ritual:
"Ritual always follows proper order.
Sacrifice
is a great affair of the state,
yet to reverse its order,
can this be called ritual?
Even if a son is wise and sagely,
he does not precede his father in the sacrifices for a long time.
Thus Yǔ did not precede Gǔn,
Tāng did not precede Xiè,
and King Wén and King Wǔ did not precede Bù Zhú.
Sòng honors Dì Yǐ as ancestor,
and Zhèng honors King Lì as ancestor,
still honoring the higher ancestor.
Therefore the Lǔ Sòng says:
'In spring and autumn without cease,
the offerings and sacrifices are without error,
to the great and august Lord on High,
and the august ancestor Hòu Jì.'
The gentleman says
'ritual,'
meaning he honored Hòu Jì as close ancestor
yet put the Lord on High first.
The Shī says:
'I inquire after my aunts,
and then proceed to my elder sisters.'
The gentleman says
'ritual,'
meaning he honored his sisters as close
yet put his aunts first."
Zhòngní said:
"Zāng Wénzhòng
had three instances of lacking benevolence,
and three of lacking wisdom.
Demoting Zhǎn Qín,
abolishing the six passes,
and having his concubines weave mats—
these are the three lacking benevolence.
Creating empty vessels,
indulging in reverse sacrifices,
and sacrificing to the Yuānjū bird—
these are the three lacking wisdom."
B6.2.6 In winter,
Xiān Qiějū of Jìn, Prince Chéng of Sòng, Yuán Xuǎn of Chén, and Prince Guīshēng of Zhèng attacked Qín,
captured Wāng and Péngyá and returned,
to avenge the battle of Péngyá.
The ministers are not recorded,
for the sake of Duke Mù,
to honor Qín,
which is called exalting virtue.
B6.2.7 Xiāng Zhòng went to Qí to present betrothal gifts,
which was ritual.
Whenever a ruler ascends the throne,
to foster good relations with maternal uncles,
to arrange marriages,
and to take a principal wife to oversee the grain offerings
is filial piety.
Filial piety is the beginning of ritual.
A6.3 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Third Year of Duke Wén
A6.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
Shūsūn Déchén joined with men of Jìn,
men of Sòng,
men of Chén,
men of Wèi,
and men of Zhèng to attack Shěn.
Shěn collapsed.
A6.3.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
Prince Zǐhǔ died.
A6.3.3 Men of Qín attacked Jìn.
A6.3.4 In autumn,
men of Chǔ besieged Jiāng.
A6.3.5 Locusts rained down in Sòng.
A6.3.6 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn.
In the twelfth month, on the jǐsì day,
the Duke and the Marquis of Jìn made a covenant.
A6.3.7 Yáng Chùfǔ of Jìn led an army to attack Chǔ in order to rescue Jiāng.
B6.3 Commentary on the Third Year of Duke Wén
B6.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
Zhuāng Shū joined the armies of the feudal lords to attack Shěn,
because it had submitted to Chǔ.
Shěn collapsed.
Whenever the people flee from their superiors, it is called "collapse";
when the superiors flee, it is called "flight."
B6.3.2 The Marquis of Wèi went to Chén,
to express gratitude for Jìn's peacemaking.
B6.3.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on the yǐhài day,
Wángshū Wéngōng died.
The news of his death was sent,
and condolences were offered as for an ally,
which was according to ritual.
B6.3.4 The Earl of Qín attacked Jìn,
crossed the Yellow River and burned his boats,
captured Wángguān and Jiāo,
but the people of Jìn did not come out.
He then crossed at Máojīn,
buried the corpses at Xiáo and returned.
Thereupon he became hegemon over the Western Róng,
because of Mèng Míng.
The gentleman therefore knew
that "as for Duke Mù of Qín being a ruler,
he was comprehensive in selecting men,
and consistent in employing them;
as for Mèng Míng being a minister,
he was untiring,
and capable of fearful reflection;
as for Zǐsāng's loyalty,
he understood men,
and was capable of promoting the good.
The Odes say,
'Where gather the white southernwood?
In the pools, in the islets.
Where use it?
In the affairs of the duke and marquis.'
Duke Mù of Qín had this.
'Early and late, never slackening,
to serve the one man.'
Mèng Míng had this.
'He bequeaths plans to his grandsons,
to secure and assist his sons.'
Zǐsāng had this."
B6.3.5 In autumn,
locusts fell like rain in Sòng,
because they fell and died.
B6.3.6 The army of Chǔ besieged Jiāng.
Xiān Pú of Jìn attacked Chǔ to rescue Jiāng.
In winter,
Jìn reported the matter of Jiāng to Zhōu.
Wángshū Huángōng
and Yáng Chùfǔ of Jìn attacked Chǔ to rescue Jiāng.
They attacked the gate at Fāngchéng,
encountered Zǐ Zhū, the Earl of Xī, and returned.
B6.3.7 The people of Jìn, fearing they had been discourteous to the Duke,
requested to renew the covenant.
The Duke went to Jìn,
and made a covenant with the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn feasted the Duke,
and recited "Lush and Luxuriant Is the Artemisia."
Zhuāng Shū made the Duke descend
and bow.
He said:
"A small state receiving commands from a great state,
how dare it not be careful of ceremony?
You, my lord, have bestowed a great ceremony upon us,
what joy can compare to this?
Moreover, the joy of a small state
is the kindness of a great state."
The Marquis of Jìn descended,
and declined.
They ascended,
and completed the bow.
The Duke recited "Excellent and Happy."
A6.4 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Fourth Year of Duke Wén
A6.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A6.4.2 In summer,
a bride, Jiāng, was welcomed from Qí.
A6.4.3 The Dí invaded Qí.
A6.4.4 In autumn,
the people of Chǔ extinguished Jiāng.
A6.4.5 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Qín.
A6.4.6 The Marquis of Wèi sent Nìng Yú to come on a friendly mission.
A6.4.7 In winter, in the eleventh month, on the rényín day,
the lady, née Fēng, died.
B6.4 Commentary on the Fourth Year of Duke Wén
B6.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the people of Jìn returned Kǒng Dá to Wèi,
considering him an excellent man of Wèi,
and therefore pardoned him.
B6.4.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Wèi went to Jìn to express gratitude.
B6.4.3 The Earl of Cáo went to Jìn to settle dues.
B6.4.4 A bride, Jiāng, was welcomed from Qí,
but a minister did not go,
which was contrary to ritual.
The gentleman therefore knew that Chū Jiāng would not find favor in Lǔ,
saying:
"To betroth her with honor but welcome her with disrespect,
to treat her as a ruler's wife but demean her,
to establish her and then cast her aside,
to abandon good faith
and ruin her position,
in the state there will surely be disorder,
in the family there will surely be ruin.
It is fitting that she did not find favor!
The Odes say:
'Stand in awe of Heaven's majesty,
and thus preserve it.'
This refers to revering one's position."
B6.4.5 In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn attacked Qín,
besieging Yuán
and Xīnchéng,
in retaliation for the battle of Wángguān.
B6.4.6 The people of Chǔ extinguished Jiāng.
The Earl of Qín on account of this put on plain garments,
moved out of his chamber,
did not have music played,
and exceeded the proper number of days.
His ministers remonstrated.
The Duke said:
"An ally has been extinguished;
though I could not rescue it,
how dare I not show compassion?
I am myself fearful."
The gentleman said:
"The Odes say:
'Only those two states,
their governance did not succeed;
only these four states,
they then examined and measured.'
This refers to Duke Mù of Qín."
B6.4.7 Nìng Wǔzǐ of Wèi came on a friendly mission.
The Duke feasted with him,
and for him recited "Heavy Dew" and "Red Bow."
He did not decline,
nor did he respond with a recitation.
The Duke sent an envoy to inquire privately.
He replied:
"Your servant thought it was practice
that occasioned it.
Formerly, when the feudal lords came to the king at the beginning of the year,
the king feasted and entertained them,
and then recited 'Heavy Dew,'
for the Son of Heaven faces the sun,
and the feudal lords obey his commands.
When the feudal lords shared the king's hatred,
and presented their achievements,
the king then bestowed upon them one red bow,
one hundred red arrows,
one thousand black bows and arrows,
to reward them for the feast.
Now your servant, a mere attendant minister, has come to renew the old friendship;
you, my lord, have condescended to bestow this upon me.
How dare I presume upon the great ceremony and bring blame upon myself?"
B6.4.8 In winter,
Chéngfēng died.
A6.5 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Fifth Year of Duke Wén
A6.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
the king sent Róng Shū to present the jade for the mouth,
and also funeral gifts.
A6.5.2 In the third month, on the xīnhài day,
we buried our little ruler's wife, Chéngfēng.
A6.5.3 The king sent Shào Bó to come and attend the burial.
A6.5.4 In summer,
Gōngsūn Áo went to Jìn.
A6.5.5 The people of Qín entered Ruò.
A6.5.6 In autumn,
the people of Chǔ extinguished Lù.
A6.5.7 In winter, in the tenth month, on the jiǎshēn day,
the Viscount of Xǔ, Yè, died.
B6.5 The Commentary of Duke Wen, Year 5
B6.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
the King sent Róng Shū to bring the jade for the mouth and funeral gifts. Zhào Zhāogōng came to attend the burial.
This was according to ritual.
B6.5.2 Formerly,
Ruò had rebelled against Chǔ and allied with Qín,
but then became disloyal to Chǔ.
In summer,
men of Qín entered Ruò.
B6.5.3 The people of Lù rebelled against Chǔ and allied with the Eastern Yi.
In autumn,
Chǔ's Chéng Dàxīn
and Zhòng Guī led an army and extinguished Lù.
B6.5.4 In winter,
Chǔ's prince Xiè extinguished Liǎo.
Zāng Wénzhòng heard that Lù and Liǎo were extinguished,
and said:
"Gāo Yáo
and Tíngjiān have suddenly had their sacrifices cut off.
They did not establish virtue,
and the people had no support.
How lamentable!"
B6.5.5 Jìn's Yáng Chǔfǔ went on a diplomatic mission to Wèi.
On his return, he passed through Níng.
Níng Yíng followed him.
But when they reached Wēn, he returned.
His wife asked him about it.
Yíng said:
"Because he was rigid.
The *Shāng Shū* says:
'For those who are deep and weak, use firmness to overcome; for those who are lofty and brilliant, use gentleness to overcome.'
This man is uniformly one,
will he not perish?
Heaven, with its firm virtue,
still does not interfere with the seasons,
how much more should this be so among men?
Moreover, showy without substance,
this is what gathers resentment.
To offend and gather resentment
is no way to secure one's person.
I feared I would not gain benefit from him but would encounter his calamity,
and therefore left him."
Jìn's Zhào Chéngzǐ, Luán Zhēnzǐ, Huò Bó, and Jiù Jì all died.
A6.6 The Annals of Duke Wen, Year 6
A6.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the burial of Xǔ Xǐgōng took place.
A6.6.2 In summer,
Jìsūn Xíngfú went to Chén.
A6.6.3 In autumn,
Jìsūn Xíngfú went to Jìn.
A6.6.4 In the eighth month, on day Yǐhài,
Jìn Hóu Huān died.
A6.6.5 In winter, the tenth month,
Gōngzǐ Suì went to Jìn.
A6.6.6 The burial of Jìn Xiānggōng took place.
A6.6.7 Jìn killed its senior officer Yáng Chǔfǔ.
A6.6.8 Jìn's Hú Yègǔ fled to the Dí.
A6.6.9 In the intercalary month, the announcement of the new moon was not made,
but court was still held at the temple.
B6.6 The Commentary of Duke Wen, Year 6
B6.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
Jìn held a military review at Yí,
and abolished two armies.
They made Hú Yègǔ command the central army,
with Zhào Dùn as his assistant.
Yáng Chǔfǔ arrived from Wēn,
changed the review to be held at Dǒng,
and altered the central army command.
Master Yáng
was a follower of Chéng Jì,
and therefore was a partisan of the Zhào clan.
Moreover, he considered Zhào Dùn capable,
saying:
"To employ the capable
is to the state's benefit."
Therefore he placed him above.
Xuānzǐ thereupon began to administer the state's governance.
He established regulations for affairs,
rectified laws and penalties,
clarified legal cases and punishments,
supervised fugitives,
followed contracts and essentials,
reformed old corruptions,
based himself on ritual and precedence,
continued regular offices,
and promoted those who were submerged.
When this was completed,
he presented it to the Grand Tutor Master Yáng and the Grand Preceptor Jiǎ Tuó,
to have it implemented throughout the state of Jìn,
to serve as the constant law.
B6.6.2 Because of the amity between Chén and Wèi,
Zāng Wénzhòng wished to seek good relations with Chén.
In summer,
Jì Wénzǐ
went on a diplomatic mission to Chén,
and also took a wife there.
B6.6.3 Qín Bó Rènhǎo died.
He had the three sons of the Zǐjū clan—Yǎnxī, Zhòngháng, and Zhènhǔ—buried with him as attendants in death.
They were all excellent men of Qín.
The people of the state mourned them,
and composed the ode "Huáng Niǎo" for them.
A nobleman said:
"It is fitting that Qín Mù did not become a covenant leader!
In death he abandoned the people.
When the former kings departed the world,
they still bequeathed models of law,
how much more should they not have taken away good men?
The *Odes* say:
'When men are gone,
the state is utterly distressed.'
This speaks of having no good men.
How could he take them away?
The ancient kings knew that life is not long,
and therefore they established sages and wise men together,
set up for them reputations and influence,
distributed to them insignia and emblems,
recorded for them words and speeches,
made for them laws and measures,
displayed for them standards and limits,
guided them with models and examples,
gave them statutes and regulations,
instructed them with codes and canons,
taught them to guard against profit,
entrusted them with regular duties,
led them with ritual and rules,
so that they would not lose what was appropriate for the land,
and the multitude of officers relied on them.
Only then did they approach their mandate's end.
The sage kings were alike in this.
Now, even if he had no laws
to bequeath to his successors,
to furthermore gather up his excellent men and put them to death
makes it difficult to remain above."
The nobleman therefore knew
that Qín would not again campaign eastward.
B6.6.4 In autumn,
Jì Wénzǐ was about to go on a diplomatic mission to Jìn.
He had someone seek out the rituals for encountering mourning
to take with him.
His officer said:
"What use will these be?"
Wénzǐ said:
"To prepare for the unforeseen
is a good teaching of antiquity.
To seek and not have them is truly difficult.
What harm is there in seeking them in excess?"
B6.6.5 In the eighth month, on day Yǐhài,
Jìn Xiānggōng died.
Línggōng was young.
The people of Jìn, because of the difficult situation,
wished to establish an older ruler.
Zhào Mèng said:
"Establish prince Yōng.
He is fond of goodness and is older.
The former ruler loved him,
and he is close to Qín.
Qín
is an old ally.
To establish a good man makes it secure,
to serve an older one is accordant,
to establish a loved one is filial,
to bind with an old ally brings peace.
Because of the difficult situation,
we therefore wish to establish an older ruler.
With these four virtues,
the difficulty will surely be relieved."
Jiǎ Jì said:
"It would be better to establish prince Lè.
Chén Yíng was favored by two rulers.
To establish her son,
the people will surely be at peace with it."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Chén Yíng was lowly,
her rank was ninth among the consorts.
How could her son command awe?
Moreover, to be favored by two rulers
is wantonness.
As a son of the former ruler,
he could not seek a great state
but went out to a small state.
This is base."
The mother is licentious and the son depraved,
lacking authority;
Chén is small and distant,
offering no support—
how then can he be settled?
Dù Qí, for the sake of the ruler,
yielded to Bī Jí and placed her above herself;
and because of the Dí,
yielded to Jì Wěi, taking a lower position herself,
thus her rank was fourth.
For this reason, the former ruler loved her son
and had him serve in Qín,
where he became Assistant Minister.
Qín is large and near,
sufficient to provide support;
the mother is righteous and the son beloved,
sufficient to awe the people.
To establish him—
is this not appropriate?"
He sent Xiān Miè and Shì Kuì to Qín to welcome the Gōngzǐ Yōng.
Jiǎ Jì also sent someone to summon Gōngzǐ Lè from Chén,
but Zhào Mèng had him killed at Bì.
B6.6.6 Jiǎ Jì resented Yángzǐ for changing his rank,
and knowing he had no support in Jìn,
in the ninth month,
Jiǎ Jì sent Xù Jūjū to kill Yáng Chǔfù.
The record says:
"Jìn killed its great officer,"
because he encroached on official duties.
B6.6.7 In winter, the tenth month,
Xiāng Zhòng went to Jìn for Duke Xiāng's burial.
B6.6.8 On the bǐngyín day of the eleventh month,
Jìn killed Xù Jiǎnbó.
Jiǎ Jì fled to the Dí.
Xuānzǐ sent Yú Pián to escort his family.
At the Yí hunt,
Jiǎ Jì had humiliated Yú Pián,
and Yú Pián's followers wanted to kill all of the Jiǎ clan in revenge.
Yú Pián said:
"It cannot be.
I have heard the former records say:
'Enmity and favor
do not pass to descendants—
this is the way of loyalty.'
Our master treats Jiǎ Jì with courtesy;
if I use his favor to repay a private grudge,
would that not be improper?
To rely on another's favor
is not courage.
To reduce enmity
only to increase hatred
is not wisdom.
To harm the public for private ends
is not loyalty.
If I abandon these three principles,
how can I serve our master?"
He fully provided for Jiǎ Jì's family and their utensils, goods, and valuables,
personally led a guard for them,
and escorted them to the border.
B6.6.9 In an intercalary month, not announcing the first day—
this is contrary to ritual.
Intercalation is to correct the seasons;
the seasons are to guide affairs;
affairs are to enrich the people's livelihood.
The way of nurturing the people lies herein.
Not announcing the intercalary first day
is to abandon the seasonal governance—
how then can one govern the people?
A6.7 《The Seventh Year of Duke Wén's Spring and Autumn Annals》
A6.7.1 In the seventh year, spring,
the duke attacked Zhū.
A6.7.2 On the jiǎxū day of the third month,
he took Xūqú.
A6.7.3 Then he fortified Wú.
A6.7.4 In summer, the fourth month,
the Sòng duke Wángchén died.
A6.7.5 The people of Sòng killed their great officer.
A6.7.6 On the wùzǐ day,
men of Jìn and men of Qín fought at Línghú.
Xiān Miè of Jìn fled to Qín.
A6.7.7 The Dí invaded our western borders.
A6.7.8 In autumn, the eighth month,
the duke met with the feudal lords
and the great officers of Jìn, making a covenant at Hù.
A6.7.9 In winter,
Xú attacked Jǔ.
A6.7.10 Gōngsūn Áo went to Jǔ to attend the covenant.
B6.7 《The Commentary to the Seventh Year of Duke Wén》
B6.7.1 In the seventh year, spring,
the duke attacked Zhū,
taking advantage of Jìn's troubles.
B6.7.2 On the jiǎxū day of the third month,
he took Xūqú
and settled a son of Duke Wén there—
this was contrary to ritual.
B6.7.3 In summer, the fourth month,
Duke Chéng of Sòng died.
At this time, Gōngzǐ Chéng became Yòu Shī,
Gōngsūn Yǒu became Zuǒ Shī,
Yuè Yù became Sīmǎ,
Lín Guàn became Sītú,
Gōngzǐ Dàng became Sīchéng,
and Huá Yùshì became Sīkòu.
Duke Zhāo intended to remove all the ducal sons,
but Yuè Yù said:
"It cannot be.
The ducal clan
is the branches and leaves of the ducal house.
If you remove them,
then the trunk and roots will have nothing to shelter them.
Even the gé lěi vine can shelter its own roots;
thus the gentleman takes it as a metaphor—
how much more so a ruler of a state?
This is what the proverb calls
'to shelter it
yet wield an axe against it.'
It must not be done.
You must not.
May Your Lordship consider this!
Treat them with virtue,
and they will all be your limbs and supports—
who would dare to be disloyal?
Why remove them?"
He did not listen.
The clans of Dukes Mù and Xiāng
led the people of the state to attack the duke,
killing Gōngsūn Gù and Gōngsūn Zhèng in the ducal palace.
The six ministers reconciled with the ducal house,
and Yuè Yù gave up the position of Sīmǎ
to yield to Gōngzǐ Áng.
Duke Zhāo then assumed the throne and held the burial.
The record says: "The people of Sòng killed their great officer"—
not naming them,
because they were many,
and also to indicate they were not guilty.
B6.7.4 Duke Kāng of Qín escorted Gōngzǐ Yōng to Jìn,
saying:
"When Duke Wén entered
he had no guard,
hence there were the troubles of Lǚ and Xì."
Thus he gave him many foot guards.
Mù Yíng daily carried the heir apparent
and wailed in the court,
saying:
"What crime did the former ruler commit?
What crime did his heir commit?
To abandon the rightful heir and not establish him,
seeking a ruler from outside instead—
where will you place this child?"
Leaving the court,
she then carried him to the Zhào house,
and kowtowed to Xuānzǐ,
saying:
"The former ruler entrusted this child to you,
saying:
'If this child is capable,
I shall receive your grace;
if incapable,
I shall hold you accountable.'
Now though the ruler has passed,
his words still ring in our ears—
yet you abandon him.
How can this be?"
Xuānzǐ and all the great officers were troubled by Mù Yíng,
and fearing coercion,
they turned against Xiān Miè
and established Duke Líng,
to resist the Qín army.
Jī Zhèng remained to guard the capital.
Zhào Dùn commanded the central army,
with Xiān Kè as his assistant;
Xún Línfǔ assisted the upper army;
Xiān Miè commanded the lower army,
with Xiān Dū as his assistant.
Bù Zhāo drove the commander's chariot,
with Róng Jīn as the right-hand guard.
They reached Jǐnyīn.
Xuānzǐ said:
"If we accept Qín,
then Qín is a guest;
if we do not accept,
they are invaders.
Since we have not accepted,
yet we delay our troops,
Qín will harbor ill intent."
To seize the enemy's resolve before they act is
the best strategy in warfare.
To pursue invaders as if chasing fugitives is
the best policy in warfare."
He trained the soldiers,
sharpened the weapons,
fed the horses,
provided an early meal,
and moved the army secretly at night.
On the day Wùzǐ,
they defeated the Qín army at Línghú,
pursuing them as far as Kūshǒu.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
Xiān Miě fled to Qín,
and Shì Huì followed him.
When Xiān Miě was sent on his mission,
Xún Línfǔ tried to stop him,
saying:
"The ruler's wife and crown prince are still here,
yet you seek a ruler from outside—
this will certainly not succeed.
Why not decline on grounds of illness?
What do you think?
Otherwise,
disaster will strike you.
You could send an acting minister to go,
that would be acceptable.
Why must it be you?
Those who serve together in office are colleagues.
I once served as your colleague—
how dare I not do my utmost?"
He did not listen.
Xún Línfǔ recited the third stanza of the poem "Bǎn" for him,
but again he did not listen.
After his flight,
Minister Xún sent all his family, belongings, and wealth to Qín,
saying:
"This is because we were colleagues."
Shì Huì remained in Qín for three years
without meeting Shì Bó.
Someone said to him:
"One who can help a man flee his state,
yet cannot meet him here—
what use is that?"
Shì Jì replied:
"I share the same guilt with him;
it is not out of righteousness.
What would meeting accomplish?"
When he later returned,
he still did not meet him.
B6.7.5 The Dí people invaded our western borders,
and the Duke sent word to Jìn.
Zhào Xuānzǐ sent Jiǎ Jì to question Fēng Shū,
and also to reprimand him.
Fēng Shū asked Jiǎ Jì:
"Who was more worthy, Zhào Cuī or Zhào Dùn?"
He replied:
"Zhào Cuī
was like the sun in winter;
Zhào Dùn
was like the sun in summer."
B6.7.6 In autumn, the eighth month, the Marquis of Qí, Duke of Sòng, Marquis of Wèi, Marquis of Chén, Earl of Zhèng, Baron of Xǔ, and Earl of Cáo met with Jìn's Zhào Dùn and formed an alliance at Hù,
because the Jìn ruler had been established.
Our Duke arrived late,
so the record does not specify the participants.
In general, when meetings of feudal lords are recorded,
not specifying the participants
indicates lateness.
If one arrives late,
his state is not recorded,
to avoid inaccuracy.
B6.7.7 Mù Bó took a wife from Jǔ,
named Dài Jǐ,
who gave birth to Wén Bó;
her younger sister Shēng Jǐ gave birth to Huì Shū.
When Dài Jǐ died,
he sought another bride from Jǔ.
The people of Jǔ declined on account of Shēng Jǐ,
so he arranged a betrothal for Xiāng Zhòng instead.
In winter,
Xú attacked Jǔ,
and the people of Jǔ came to request an alliance.
Mù Bó went to Jǔ to oversee the alliance,
and also to fetch a bride for Zhòng.
When he reached Yānlíng,
he climbed the city wall and saw her—
she was beautiful—
and took her for himself.
Zhòng requested to attack him,
and the Duke was about to agree,
but Shūzhòng Huì Bó remonstrated,
saying:
"I have heard it said:
'When arms are raised within, it is rebellion;
when raised outside, it is invasion.
An invasion may still affect others,
but rebellion brings harm upon oneself.'
Now, if a subject rebels and the ruler does not stop it,
thus inviting external enemies,
what is to be done?"
The Duke stopped him.
Huì Bó mediated the matter,
making Zhòng give her up
and Gōngsūn Áo return her,
so they became brothers again as before.
They followed this advice.
B6.7.8 Jìn's Xì Quē said to Zhào Xuānzǐ:
"Formerly, Wèi was not friendly,
so we took its territory.
Now it is friendly;
we should return it.
If we do not punish rebellion,
how can we demonstrate authority?
If we do not show kindness to those who submit,
how can we demonstrate benevolence?
Without authority or benevolence,
how can we demonstrate virtue?
Without virtue,
how can we lead alliances?
You are the chief minister,
charged with leading the feudal lords.
If you do not strive for virtue,
what will become of us?
The *Xià Shū* says:
'Admonish them with goodness,
oversee them with authority,
encourage them with the *Nine Songs*,
and do not let them go astray.'
The virtues of the nine achievements can all be sung—
these are called the *Nine Songs*.
The six treasuries and three affairs
are called the nine achievements.
Water, fire, metal, wood, earth, and grain
are called the six treasuries;
correct virtue, beneficial use, and abundant life
are called the three affairs.
When these are practiced righteously,
they are called virtue and ritual.
Without ritual, there is no harmony,
and from this rebellion arises.
If your virtue, sir,
cannot be sung,
who will come to you?
Why not let the friendly states sing of you?"
Xuānzǐ was pleased with this.
A6.8 *The Eighth Year of Duke Wén's Classic*
A6.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the royal first month.
A6.8.2 Summer, the fourth month.
A6.8.3 Autumn, the eighth month, on Wùshēn,
the Heavenly King passed away.
A6.8.4 Winter, the tenth month, on Rénwǔ,
Gōngzǐ Suì met with Jìn's Zhào Dùn,
and they formed an alliance at Héngyōng.
A6.8.5 On Yǐyǒu,
Gōngzǐ Suì met with the Luòróng tribes,
and they formed an alliance at Bào.
A6.8.6 Gōngsūn Áo went to the capital,
but did not reach it and returned.
On Bǐngxū,
he fled to Jǔ.
A6.8.7 There was a plague of locusts.
A6.8.8 The people of Sòng killed their grand master, the Minister of War.
The Minister of Works of Sòng came fleeing.
B6.8 *The Eighth Year of Duke Wén's Commentary*
B6.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xiè Yáng to return the lands of Kuāng and
Qī to Wèi,
and also restored the fief of the Duke's Son-in-Law Chí,
from Shēn to the borders of Hǔláo.
B6.8.2 In summer,
the people of Qín attacked Jìn,
capturing Wǔchéng,
in retaliation for the battle of Línghú.
B6.8.3 In autumn,
King Xiāng passed away.
B6.8.4 The people of Jìn came to demand an explanation for the Hù alliance.
In winter,
Xiāng Zhòng met with Jìn's Zhào Mèng
and formed an alliance at Héngyōng,
in response to the Hù alliance.
He then met with the Yīluòróng tribes.
The record says "Gōngzǐ Suì"
to honor him.
B6.8.5 Mù Bó went to Zhōu to offer condolences for the mourning,
but did not reach it;
he took the gifts and fled to Jǔ,
to follow his own desires there.
B6.8.6 The Lady of Duke Xiāng of Sòng was
the elder sister of King Xiāng.
Duke Zhāo treated her without propriety.
The Lady, relying on the Dài clan,
had the grandsons of Duke Xiāng, Kǒng Shū and Gōngsūn Zhōnglí, and the Grand Marshal, the prince Áng, killed,
all of whom were partisans of Duke Zhāo.
The Marshal died holding his tally of authority,
therefore he was recorded by his office.
The Minister of Works, Dàng Yìzhū, came fleeing,
and returned his tally of authority to the keeper of the storehouse before leaving.
The Duke received him according to his official rank,
and all his positions were restored.
He was also recorded by his office,
in both cases to honor them.
B6.8.7 At the military review at Yí,
the Marquis of Jìn intended to promote Jī Zhèngfǔ and Xiān Dū,
and to make Shì Hú and Liáng Yì'ěr command the Central Army.
Xiān Kè said:
"The merits of Hú and Zhào
cannot be set aside."
They followed him.
Xiān Kè seized fields from Kuǎi Dé at Jǐnyīn.
Therefore, Jī Zhèngfǔ, Xiān Dū, Shì Hú, Liáng Yì'ěr, and Kuǎi Dé started a revolt.
A6.9 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Wén Year 9
A6.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
the Earl of Máo came to request gold.
A6.9.2 The Lady, Jiāng Shì, went to Qí.
A6.9.3 In the second month,
Shūsūn Déchén went to the royal capital.
On the xīnchǒu day,
King Xiāng was buried.
A6.9.4 Men of Jìn killed their Great Officer Xiān Dū.
A6.9.5 In the third month,
the Lady Jiāng Shì arrived from Qí.
A6.9.6 Men of Jìn killed their Great Officers Shì Hú and Jī Zhèngfǔ.
A6.9.7 Men of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
A6.9.8 The prince Suì met with men of Jìn,
men of Sòng,
men of Wèi,
and men of Xǔ to rescue Zhèng.
A6.9.9 In summer,
the Dí invaded Qí.
A6.9.10 In autumn, in the eighth month,
the Earl of Cáo, Xiāng, died.
A6.9.11 In the ninth month, on the guǐyǒu day,
there was an earthquake.
A6.9.12 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Jiāo to come on a friendly mission.
A6.9.13 Men of Qín came to present burial garments for Duke Xī
and Chéngfēng.
A6.9.14 Duke Gòng of Cáo was buried.
B6.9 The Commentary of Zuo, Duke Wén Year 9
B6.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
in the royal first month, on the jǐyǒu day,
they sent assassins to kill Xiān Kè.
On the yǐchǒu day,
men of Jìn killed Xiān Dū and Liáng Yì'ěr.
B6.9.2 The Earl of Máo, Wèi, came to request gold,
which was contrary to propriety.
It was not recorded as a royal command
because the king had not yet been buried.
B6.9.3 In the second month,
Zhuāng Shū went to Zhōu
for the burial of King Xiāng.
B6.9.4 In the third month, on the jiǎxū day,
men of Jìn killed Jī Zhèngfǔ,
Shì Hú,
and Kuǎi Dé.
B6.9.5 Fàn Shān said to the Viscount of Chǔ:
"The ruler of Jìn is young,
and his mind is not on the various lords.
The north can be planned for."
The Viscount of Chǔ stationed his army at Láng Yuān to attack Zhèng.
They imprisoned the princes Jiān and Máng, and Yuè Ěr.
Zhèng made peace with Chǔ.
B6.9.6 The prince Suì met with Zhào Dùn of Jìn, Huá Ŏu of Sòng, Kǒng Dá of Wèi, and a Great Officer of Xǔ to rescue Zhèng,
but they did not catch up with the Chǔ army.
The high ministers were not recorded
because they were tardy,
to punish their lack of respect.
B6.9.7 In summer,
Chǔ invaded Chén,
capturing Húqiū,
because it had submitted to Jìn.
B6.9.8 In autumn,
the prince Zhū of Chǔ attacked Chén from the Eastern Yí region,
but the men of Chén defeated him,
capturing the prince Fá.
Chén became fearful,
and then made peace with Chǔ.
B6.9.9 In winter,
Chǔ's Zǐ Yuèjiāo came on a friendly mission,
and held the ceremonial gifts arrogantly.
Shūzhòng Huìbó said:
"This man will surely bring destruction to the Ruò'áo clan.
To be arrogant towards his former rulers
means the spirits will not bless him."
B6.9.10 Men of Qín came to present burial garments for Duke Xī
and Chéngfēng,
which was according to propriety.
When lords offer condolences or congratulations to one another,
even if it is not timely,
if it is done with propriety,
it is recorded,
so as not to forget old friendships.
A6.10 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Wén Year 10
A6.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
in the royal third month, on the xīnmǎo day,
Zāngsūn Chén died.
A6.10.2 In summer,
Qín attacked Jìn.
A6.10.3 Chǔ killed its Great Officer Yí Shēn.
A6.10.4 From the first month there was no rain,
until autumn, the seventh month.
A6.10.5 A covenant was made with the Viscount of Sū at Nǚlì.
A6.10.6 In winter,
the Dí invaded Sòng.
A6.10.7 The Viscount of Chǔ
and the Marquis of Cài stationed themselves at Juéhé.
B6.10 The Commentary of Zuo, Duke Wén Year 10
B6.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
men of Jìn attacked Qín,
capturing Shàoliáng.
B6.10.2 In summer,
the Earl of Qín attacked Jìn,
capturing Běizhēng.
B6.10.3 Formerly,
the Fàn shaman Yù Sì of Chǔ said to King Chéng and to Zǐ Yù and
Zǐ Xī:
"All three of you lords will die a violent death."
At the battle of Chéngpú,
the king remembered this,
and therefore sent someone to stop Zǐ Yù, saying:
"Do not die."
He did not arrive in time.
He stopped Zǐ Xī;
Zǐ Xī had hanged himself but the rope broke,
and the king's messenger arrived just then,
so he was stopped,
and was made the Duke of Shāng.
He went down the Hàn River and up the Jiāng,
intending to enter Yǐng.
The king was at the Zhǔ Palace,
came down,
and saw him.
He was afraid,
and excused himself, saying:
"I escaped death,
but again there are slanderous words,
saying I was about to flee.
I have returned to die before the Minister of Justice."
The king made him the Minister of Works,
but he again plotted with Zǐ Jiā to assassinate King Mù.
King Mù heard of it,
and in the fifth month,
killed Dòu Yí Shēn and Zhòng Guī.
B6.10.4 In autumn, in the seventh month,
a covenant was made with the Viscount of Sū at Nǚlì,
because King Qǐng had been established.
B6.10.5 The Marquis of Chén and the Earl of Zhèng met with the Viscount of Chǔ at Xī.
In winter,
they then, together with the Marquis of Cài, stationed themselves at Juéhé,
intending to attack Sòng.
Huá Yùshì of Sòng said:
"Chǔ wishes to weaken us.
Should we first show ourselves weak to them?
Why must we wait for them to entice us?
We ourselves are incapable,
but what crime have the people committed?"
They then went to meet the Viscount of Chǔ,
offered him provisions and listened to his commands.
They then guided him to hunt at Mèngzhū.
The Duke of Sòng commanded the right wing of the hunt,
and the Earl of Zhèng commanded the left wing.
Fù Suì, Lord of Qīsī, served as Right Marshal,
while Zǐ Zhū and Wén Zhī Wúwèi served as Left Marshals.
They were ordered to harness the chariots at dawn and carry fire-drills.
The Duke of Sòng violated the order,
and Wúwèi flogged his charioteer as a public warning.
Someone said to Zǐ Zhōu:
"One should not humiliate a ruler of a state."
Zǐ Zhōu replied:
"I acted according to my official duty.
What does it matter if he was powerful?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'He does not spit out the hard,
nor does he swallow the soft.'
'Do not indulge the crafty and fawning,
to restrain the boundless.'
This is also about not evading the strong.
How dare I cherish my life and thereby disrupt official duties?"
B6.10.6 At the meeting at Jué Mò,
the Viscount of Jūn fled back home.
A6.11 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, the Eleventh Year of Duke Wén*
A6.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
the Viscount of Chǔ invaded Jūn.
A6.11.2 In summer,
Shū Péngshēng met with Xì Quē of Jìn at Chéngkuāng.
A6.11.3 In autumn,
the Earl of Cáo came for an audience.
A6.11.4 Gōngzǐ Suì went to Sòng.
A6.11.5 The Dí tribe invaded Qí.
A6.11.6 In winter, in the tenth month, on the jiǎwǔ day,
Shūsūn Déchen defeated the Dí tribe at Xián.
B6.11 *The Commentary of Zuo, the Eleventh Year of Duke Wén*
B6.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
the Viscount of Chǔ invaded Jūn.
Chéng Dàxīn
defeated the army of Jūn at Fángzhǔ.
Pān Chóng again invaded Jūn,
reaching Xíxué.
B6.11.2 In summer,
Shúzhòng Huìbó met with Xì Quē of Jìn at Chéngkuāng,
to plan regarding the states that were following Chǔ.
B6.11.3 In autumn,
Duke Wén of Cáo came for an audience,
as he had just ascended the throne
and came to present himself.
B6.11.4 Xiāng Zhòng visited Sòng on a diplomatic mission,
and spoke on behalf of Sīchéng Dàng Yìzhū, restoring him to his position.
He also congratulated them on the Chǔ army not causing harm.
B6.11.5 Sōumán invaded Qí,
and then attacked us.
Our duke divined about sending Shūsūn Déchen to pursue them,
and it was auspicious.
Hóu Shūxià drove for Zhuāng Shū,
Mián Fángshēng served as the right-hand guard,
and Fùfǔ Zhōngshēng served as the fourth man on the chariot.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the jiǎwǔ day,
they defeated the Dí tribe at Xián,
capturing the tall Dí warrior Qiáorú.
Fùfǔ Zhōngshēng stabbed his throat with a dagger-axe,
and killed him.
They buried his head at the Zǐjū Gate.
They named Xuān Bó after him.
Earlier,
in the time of Duke Wǔ of Sòng,
Sōumán invaded Sòng.
Minister of Works Huángfǔ led an army to resist them.
Ér Bān drove for Huángfǔ Chōngshí,
Gōngzǐ Gǔshēng served as the right-hand guard,
and Minister of Justice Niúfǔ served as the fourth man on the chariot.
They defeated the Dí tribe at Chángqiū,
capturing the tall Dí warrior Yuánsī.
Two of Huángfǔ's sons died there,
so the Duke of Sòng awarded Ér Bān a gate,
allowing him to collect its tolls.
It was called the Ér Gate.
When Jìn destroyed Lù,
they captured Qiáorú's younger brother Fénrú.
In the second year of Duke Huì of Qí,
Sōumán invaded Qí.
Qí's Wángzǐ Chéngfù captured his younger brother Róngrú.
They buried his head at the north gate of Zhōushǒu.
The people of Wèi captured his youngest brother Jiǎnrú.
Sōumán thus perished.
B6.11.6 The crown prince of Chéng, Zhūrú, settled himself at Fúzhōng,
but the people of the state did not submit to him.
A6.12 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, the Twelfth Year of Duke Wén*
A6.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
the Earl of Chéng fled to us.
A6.12.2 The Earl of Qǐ came for an audience.
A6.12.3 In the second month, on the gēngzǐ day,
Zǐ Shūjī died.
A6.12.4 In summer,
the men of Chǔ besieged Cháo.
A6.12.5 In autumn,
the Viscount of Téng came for an audience.
A6.12.6 The Earl of Qín sent Shù to visit on a diplomatic mission.
A6.12.7 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the wǔwǔ day,
men of Jìn
and men of Qín fought at Héqū.
A6.12.8 Jìsūn Xíngfǔ led an army to fortify Zhū and Yùn.
B6.12 *The Commentary of Zuo, the Twelfth Year of Duke Wén*
B6.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
the Earl of Chéng died,
and the people of Chéng set up a new ruler.
The crown prince fled to us with Fúzhōng and the jade tablet of Chéng.
Our duke received him with the rites due to a feudal lord,
which was contrary to ritual.
Therefore, the record says:
"The Earl of Chéng fled to us."
It does not record the place,
to show respect for a feudal lord.
B6.12.2 Duke Huán of Qǐ came for an audience,
as it was his first audience with our duke.
He also requested to repudiate Shūjī
without breaking off the marriage alliance.
Our duke agreed.
In the second month,
Shūjī died.
It does not say "of Qǐ,"
because she was repudiated.
It records "Shūjī,"
indicating she was not a maiden.
B6.12.3 The Chief Minister of Chǔ, Dàsūn Bó, died,
and Chéng Jiā became Chief Minister.
The various Shū tribes rebelled against Chǔ.
In summer,
Zǐ Kǒng captured the Viscount of Shū, Píng, and the Chief of Zōng,
and then besieged Cháo.
B6.12.4 In autumn,
Duke Zhāo of Téng came for an audience,
also for the first time with our duke.
B6.12.5 The Earl of Qín sent Xīqí Shù to visit on a diplomatic mission,
and to announce they would attack Jìn.
Xiāng Zhòng declined the jade gift,
saying:
"Your lord does not forget the friendship of our former rulers,
shining upon the state of Lǔ,
bringing stability and peace to its altars of soil and grain,
and further honors us with great vessels.
My humble ruler dares to decline the jade."
The guest replied:
"Our paltry vessel
is not worth declining."
The host declined three times.
The guest answered:
"My humble ruler wishes to seek blessings from the Duke of Zhōu and the Duke of Lǔ in order to serve you.
This paltry vessel of our former ruler
is sent by this humble minister to your officers,
as a token of auspicious covenant,
to secure a friendly agreement,
thereby lending authority to my humble ruler's command,
and to cement the friendship between our two states.
Therefore, I dare to present it."
Xiāng Zhòng said:
"If there were no gentlemen,
could a state endure?
The state is not uncivilized."
He gave him generous gifts.
B6.12.6 Because of the battle of Línghú,
in winter,
the Earl of Qín invaded Jìn,
and captured Jīmǎ.
The men of Jìn resisted them.
Zhào Dùn commanded the central army,
with Xún Línfǔ as his assistant.
Xì Quē commanded the upper army,
with Yú Pián as his assistant.
Luán Dùn commanded the lower army,
with Xū Jiǎ as his assistant.
Fàn Wúxù drove the commander's chariot,
and they followed the Qín army to Héqū.
Yú Pián said:
"The Qín army cannot last long.
Let us deepen our ramparts and strengthen our defenses
to await them."
They followed his advice.
The men of Qín wished to fight.
The Earl of Qín said to Shì Huì:
"How should we fight?"
He replied:
"The Zhào clan has newly promoted one of their subordinates named Yú Pián,
and he is certainly the one who devised this plan,
intending to weary our army.
The Zhào clan has a collateral relative named Zhào Chuān,
who is the son-in-law of the Jìn ruler,
favored but immature,
and not versed in military affairs;
he is fond of valor and reckless,
and moreover, he detests Yú Pián's assistance to the Upper Army.
If we send light troops to provoke them,
it might work."
The Earl of Qín offered a jade disc to pray for victory by the Yellow River.
On the wǔwǔ day of the twelfth month,
the Qín army launched a surprise attack on the Jìn Upper Army.
Zhào Chuān pursued them,
but did not catch up.
Returning,
he angrily said:
"Carrying provisions and sitting in armor,
we are here precisely to seek the enemy.
The enemy has come, yet we do not attack;
what are we waiting for?"
The military officers said:
"We are waiting for the right moment."
Chuān said:
"I do not understand these schemes;
I will go out alone."
Then he led his own troops out.
Xuānzǐ said:
"If Qín captures Chuān,
they will have captured a high minister.
If Qín returns victorious,
how shall we repay this?"
So they all went out to fight,
and the armies engaged briefly before disengaging.
A Qín envoy warned the Jìn army at night, saying:
"The soldiers of both rulers are not yet weary;
let us meet tomorrow."
Yú Pián said:
"The envoy's eyes were shifting and his speech was agitated;
he fears us,
and they are about to flee.
If we press them against the river,
we are sure to defeat them."
Xū Jiǎ
and Zhào Chuān blocked the army gate and shouted:
"The dead and wounded have not been collected, and you would abandon them.
This is not benevolent.
Not waiting for the appointed time
and pressing the enemy in a perilous place,
shows no courage."
So they stopped.
The Qín army fled by night.
They again invaded Jìn,
entering Xiá.
B6.12.7 The walls of Zhū and Yùn were fortified,
recorded
because it was timely.
A6.13 The Thirteenth Year of Duke Wén's Spring and Autumn Annals
A6.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the royal first month.
A6.13.2 In summer, on the rénwǔ day of the fifth month,
Marquis Shuo of Chén died.
A6.13.3 Zǐ Qúchú of Zhū died.
A6.13.4 From the first month there was no rain,
until autumn, the seventh month.
A6.13.5 The roof of the Great Chamber collapsed.
A6.13.6 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn.
The Marquis of Wèi met the Duke at Tà.
A6.13.7 The Dí invaded Wèi.
A6.13.8 On the jǐchǒu day of the twelfth month,
the Duke and the Marquis of Jìn made a covenant.
A6.13.9 The Duke returned from Jìn,
and the Earl of Zhèng met the Duke at Fěi.
B6.13 The Commentary on the Thirteenth Year of Duke Wén
B6.13.1 In spring of the thirteenth year,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Zhān Jiā to reside at Xiá,
to guard the pass of Táolín.
B6.13.2 The men of Jìn were troubled by Qín's employment of Shì Huì.
In summer,
the six ministers met at Zhūfú.
Zhào Xuānzǐ said:
"Suí Huì is in Qín,
Jiǎ Jì is in Dí;
trouble will come daily.
What should we do?"
Zhōngxíng Huánzǐ said:
"I request to recall Jiǎ Jì;
he is capable in external affairs,
and moreover, he has past merits."
Xì Chéngzǐ said:
"Jiǎ Jì caused disorder,
and his crimes are great;
he is not as good as Suí Huì.
He can be humble and has a sense of shame,
gentle yet not to be trespassed against;
his wisdom is sufficient for employment.
Moreover, he is without crime."
So they sent Wèi Shòuyú to pretend
to be a rebel from Wèi,
in order to lure Shì Huì.
They detained his family in Jìn,
and let him escape at night.
He requested to surrender to Qín,
and the Earl of Qín agreed.
He stepped on Shì Huì's foot at court.
The Earl of Qín stationed his army west of the river,
while the men of Wèi were east of it.
Shòuyú said:
"I request someone from the east who can speak with those two or three officers;
I will go with him first."
They sent Shì Huì.
Shì Huì declined,
saying:
"The men of Jìn
are tigers and wolves;
if they go back on their word,
I will die,
and my wife and children will be killed;
it will be of no benefit to you, my lord,
and there will be no way to regret it."
The Earl of Qín said:
"If they go back on their word,
and I do not return your family to you,
may the river bear witness!"
Then he set out.
Rào Cháo gave him a whip as a gift,
saying:
"Do not say that there are no capable men in Qín;
it is just that my counsel was not followed."
Once they had crossed the river,
the men of Wèi made a clamor and returned.
The men of Qín sent his family back.
Those of his clan who remained took the surname Liú.
B6.13.3 Duke Wén of Zhū
divined about moving the capital to Yì.
The scribe said:
"It is beneficial for the people but not beneficial for the ruler."
The Lord of Zhū said:
"If it benefits the people,
that is my benefit.
Heaven gave birth to the people and set up rulers over them,
to benefit them.
If the people are already benefited,
I am sure to share in it."
His attendants said:
"Your life can be prolonged;
why does my lord not do it?"
The Lord of Zhū said:
"My mandate is to nurture the people.
Whether death comes early or late,
is a matter of timing.
If it truly benefits the people,
then moving the capital,
nothing could be more auspicious!"
So they moved the capital to Yì.
In the fifth month,
Duke Wén of Zhū died.
The gentleman says:
"He understood the mandate."
B6.13.4 In autumn, the seventh month,
the roof of the Great Chamber collapsed;
it was recorded
because it showed a lack of reverence.
B6.13.5 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn,
to pay court,
and to renew the covenant.
The Marquis of Wèi met the Duke at Tà,
requesting peace with Jìn.
When the Duke returned,
the Earl of Zhèng met the Duke at Fěi,
also requesting peace with Jìn.
The Duke accomplished both.
The Earl of Zhèng feasted with the Duke at Fěi;
Zǐjiā recited the "Hóng Yàn."
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"Our ruler has not yet escaped such a situation."
Wénzǐ recited the "Sì Yuè";
Zǐjiā recited the fourth stanza of "Zǎi Chí."
Wénzǐ recited the fourth stanza of "Cǎi Wēi."
The Earl of Zhèng bowed.
The Duke returned the bow.
A6.14 The Annals of Duke Wen, Year 14
A6.14.1 In the fourteenth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
the duke arrived from Jìn.
A6.14.2 Men of Zhū attacked our southern borders.
Shū Péngshēng led an army to attack Zhū.
A6.14.3 In summer, in the fifth month, on the yǐhài day,
the Marquis of Qí, Pān, died.
A6.14.4 In the sixth month,
the duke had a meeting with the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Earl of Cáo,
and Zhào Dùn of Jìn.
On the guǐyǒu day,
they made a covenant together at Xīnchéng.
A6.14.5 In autumn, in the seventh month,
a comet entered the Northern Dipper.
A6.14.6 The duke arrived from the meeting.
A6.14.7 Men of Jìn sought to install Jié Zī in Zhū,
but were unsuccessful in installing him.
A6.14.8 In the ninth month, on the jiǎshēn day,
Gōngsūn Áo died in Qí.
A6.14.9 The Qí nobleman, Gōngzǐ Shāngrén, murdered his ruler, Shě.
A6.14.10 Zǐ'āi of Sòng came fleeing.
A6.14.11 In winter,
Dān Bó went to Qí.
A6.14.12 Men of Qí seized Dān Bó.
A6.14.13 Men of Qí seized Zǐ Shūjī.
B6.14 The Commentary of Duke Wen, Year 14
B6.14.1 In spring of the fourteenth year,
King Qǐng died.
Zhōu Gōng Yuè and Wángsūn Sū contended for power,
therefore no death announcement was sent.
In all cases of a king's death
or a feudal lord's death,
if no announcement is sent,
it is not recorded.
Calamities
or blessings,
if not reported,
are also not recorded.
This is to punish disrespect.
B6.14.2 When Duke Wén of Zhū died,
the duke sent condolences,
but did so disrespectfully.
Men of Zhū came to demand satisfaction,
attacking our southern borders.
Therefore, Huì Bó attacked Zhū.
B6.14.3 Zǐ Shūjī was the consort of Duke Zhāo of Qí,
and bore Shě.
Shūjī was not favored,
and Shě lacked authority.
Gōngzǐ Shāngrén repeatedly distributed largesse in the state.
He gathered many knights,
exhausting his own household,
and borrowed from the public treasury to continue.
In summer, in the fifth month,
Duke Zhāo died,
and Shě succeeded to the position.
B6.14.4 Duke Wén of Zhū's principal consort was Qí Jiāng,
who bore Duke Dìng.
His second consort was Jìn Jī,
who bore Jié Zī.
When Duke Wén died,
the men of Zhū established Duke Dìng.
Jié Zī fled to Jìn.
B6.14.5 In the sixth month,
they made a covenant together at Xīnchéng,
because those who had followed Chǔ submitted,
and also to plan about Zhū.
B6.14.6 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the yǐmǎo day,
at night,
Shāngrén of Qí murdered Shě,
and offered the position to Yuán.
Yuán said:
"You have sought this for a long time.
I can serve you,
but you cannot afford to store up much resentment.
Would you spare me?
You do it!"
B6.14.7 A comet entered the Northern Dipper.
Shūfú, the Neishi of Zhōu, said:
"Before seven years have passed,
the rulers of Sòng, Qí, and Jìn will all die in disorder."
B6.14.8 Zhào Dùn of Jìn, with the armies of the feudal lords amounting to eight hundred chariots, sought to install Jié Zī in Zhū.
The men of Zhū declined, saying:
"Jué Qiě, born of a Qí mother, is the elder."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Their words are reasonable.
Not to follow them
would be inauspicious."
So he returned.
B6.14.9 Zhōu Gōng was about to bring a lawsuit against Wángsūn Sū in Jìn.
The king turned against Wángsūn Sū,
and sent Yǐn Shì and Dān Qǐ to plead Zhōu Gōng's case in Jìn against him.
Zhào Xuānzǐ settled the affairs of the royal house
and restored them.
B6.14.10 When King Zhuāng of Chǔ was established,
Zǐ Kǒng and Pān Chóng were about to attack the various Shū tribes.
They left Gōngzǐ Xiè and Zǐ Yí in charge of the capital,
and went to attack Shū Liǎo.
The two men revolted.
They fortified Yǐng,
and sent assassins to kill Zǐ Kǒng,
but were unsuccessful and returned.
In the eighth month,
the two men took the ruler of Chǔ and left.
As they were about to go to Shāngmì,
Lú Jí Lí and Shū Mí tricked them,
and then killed Dòu Kè and Gōngzǐ Xiè.
Earlier,
Dòu Kè had been held prisoner in Qín.
After Qín's defeat at Xiáo,
they sent him back to seek peace.
Peace was made, but he was discontented.
Gōngzǐ Xiè sought to be Lingyǐn but did not obtain it.
Therefore, the two men revolted.
B6.14.11 When Mù Bó followed Jǐ Shì,
the men of Lǔ established Wén Bó.
Mù Bó had two sons in Jǔ,
and sought to return.
Wén Bó made the request on his behalf.
Xiāng Zhòng made him not attend court
to receive orders.
He returned but did not go out.
After three years, he went back to Jǔ with his entire household.
Wén Bó became ill,
and requested:
"My son Gǔ is young.
I ask that Nán be established."
This was granted.
Wén Bó died,
and Huì Shū was established.
Mù Bó requested to give heavy bribes in order to return.
Huì Shū made the request on his behalf,
and it was granted.
As he was about to come,
in the ninth month,
he died in Qí.
His death was announced,
and burial was requested,
but it was not granted.
B6.14.12 Gāo'āi of Sòng was the fēngrén of Xiāo.
He was made a qīng,
but, deeming the Duke of Sòng unrighteous, he left,
and so came fleeing.
The record says, "Zǐ'āi of Sòng came fleeing,"
esteeming him.
B6.14.13 The men of Qí established Duke Yì.
They sent word to announce the calamity,
therefore it was recorded under
"the ninth month."
Gōngzǐ Yuán of Qí
disapproved of Duke Yì's conduct of government.
To the end, he did not call him "duke,"
but called him "that man."
B6.14.14 Xiāng Zhòng sent a message to the king,
asking to use the king's favor to seek Zhāo Jī from Qí.
He said:
"He killed her son;
what use is her mother?
I ask to receive her and punish her."
In winter,
Dān Bó went to Qí to request Zǐ Shūjī.
Men of Qí seized him.
They also seized Zǐ Shūjī.
A6.15 The Annals of Duke Wen, Year 15
A6.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
Jìsūn Xíngfú went to Jìn.
A6.15.2 In the third month,
Huá Sūn, the Sīmǎ of Sòng, came to make a covenant.
A6.15.3 In summer,
the Earl of Cáo came for an audience.
A6.15.4 Men of Qí returned the body of Gōngsūn Áo.
A6.15.5 In the sixth month, on the xīnchǒu day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Drums were beaten and a sacrifice of animals was made at the altar of soil.
A6.15.6 Dān Bó arrived from Qí.
A6.15.7 Jìn's Xì Quē led troops to attack Cài.
On Wùshēn,
they entered Cài.
A6.15.8 In autumn,
men of Qí invaded our western borders.
A6.15.9 Jì Sūn Xíngfú went to Jìn.
A6.15.10 In winter, the eleventh month,
the feudal lords made a covenant at Hù.
A6.15.11 In the twelfth month,
men of Qí came to return Zǐ Shūjī.
A6.15.12 The Marquis of Qí invaded our western borders,
then attacked Cáo,
entering its outer wall.
B6.15 Commentary on the Fifteenth Year of Duke Wén
B6.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Jìn,
on account of Dān Bó and Zǐ Shūjī.
B6.15.2 In the third month,
Sòng's Huá Ǒu came to make a covenant,
and all his officials followed him.
The record says, "Sòng's Minister of War, Huá Sūn,"
to honor him.
The duke feasted with him.
He declined, saying:
"Your servant's late ancestor Dū offended Duke Shāng of Sòng,
and his name is recorded in the registers of the feudal lords.
Your servant, inheriting his sacrifices,
how dare I disgrace Your Lordship?
I beg to receive your command from the Yàlǚ."
The men of Lǔ considered him quick-witted.
B6.15.3 In summer,
the Earl of Cáo came for an audience,
which was according to ritual.
Feudal lords paid mutual visits every five years,
to carry out the king's commands,
an ancient institution.
B6.15.4 Some men of Qí plotted for the Mèng clan,
saying:
"Lǔ,
your relatives,
decorate the coffin and place it at Tángfù;
Lǔ will surely take it."
They followed this.
The people of Biàn reported it.
Huì Shū, still emaciated from mourning,
made a request,
standing at court to await the command.
It was granted.
They took
and encoffined it.
The men of Qí sent it.
The record says:
"Men of Qí returned Gōngsūn Áo's remains,"
for the Mèng clan,
and also a matter of state.
The burial followed that of Gòng Zhòng.
Shēng Jǐ did not look upon it,
but wept behind a screen in the hall.
Xiāng Zhòng wished not to wail.
Huì Bó said:
"Death
is the end of kinship;
though one cannot have a good beginning,
a good end is possible.
Shǐ Yì had a saying:
'Brothers should show their finest feelings.
Relieve want, congratulate goodness, condole disaster,
offer sacrifices with reverence, mourn with grief;
though the feelings differ,
do not cut off affection—
this is the way of kinship.'
If you do not lose the Way,
what resentment can you have against others?"
Xiāng Zhòng was pleased.
He led his brothers to wail for him.
In later years,
his two sons came,
Mèng Xiànzǐ loved them,
and it was known throughout the state.
Someone slandered them,
saying:
"They will kill you."
Xiànzǐ reported it to Jì Wénzǐ.
The two sons said:
"Our master is known for loving us;
we are known for planning to kill him—
is this not far from ritual?
Being far from ritual is worse than death."
One guarded the gate at Jùméng,
one guarded the gate at Lìqiū, and both died.
B6.15.5 In the sixth month, on the first day Xīnchǒu,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Drums were beaten and animals sacrificed at the altar of soil,
which was contrary to ritual.
When there is an eclipse of the sun,
the Son of Heaven does not feast,
but beats drums at the altar of soil;
feudal lords use silk at the altar of soil,
and beat drums at court,
to make clear service to the spirits, instruct the people, and serve the ruler,
showing distinctions in dignity,
an ancient way.
B6.15.6 The men of Qí granted Dān Bó's request and pardoned him,
sending him to deliver their message.
The record says, "Dān Bó arrived from Qí,"
to honor him.
B6.15.7 At the covenant of Xīnchéng,
the men of Cài did not participate.
Jìn's Xì Quē with the upper army
and lower army attacked Cài,
saying:
"Our ruler is young,
we must not be negligent."
On Wùshēn,
they entered Cài,
and returned after making a covenant beneath its walls.
In general, to conquer a state
is called 'destroying' it;
to capture a great city
is called 'entering' it.
B6.15.8 In autumn,
men of Qí invaded our western borders,
so Jì Wénzǐ reported it to Jìn.
B6.15.9 In winter, the eleventh month, the Marquis of Jìn, Duke of Sòng, Marquis of Wèi, Marquis of Cài, Marquis of Chén, Earl of Zhèng, Baron of Xǔ, and Earl of Cáo made a covenant at Hù,
renewing the covenant of Xīnchéng,
and planning to attack Qí.
The men of Qí bribed the Marquis of Jìn,
so they returned without success.
Because there was trouble with Qí,
our duke did not attend.
The record says, "The feudal lords made a covenant at Hù,"
meaning they were unable to act.
In general, when feudal lords meet,
if our duke does not participate,
it is not recorded,
to conceal the ruler's fault.
If he participates but it is not recorded,
it is because he was late.
B6.15.10 The men of Qí came to return Zǐ Shūjī,
on account of the king.
B6.15.11 The Marquis of Qí invaded our western borders,
thinking the feudal lords incapable.
Then he attacked Cáo,
entering its outer wall,
punishing it for coming to court.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"Will the Marquis of Qí not avoid calamity?
He himself is without ritual,
yet punishes those who have ritual,
saying:
'Why do you practice ritual?'
Ritual follows Heaven,
which is the Way of Heaven.
He himself opposes Heaven,
and yet punishes others—
he will hardly avoid calamity.
The Odes say:
'Why have no fear?
Have no fear of Heaven.'
That a gentleman does not oppress the young and lowly
is from fear of Heaven.
In the 'Zhōu Sòng' it says:
'Fear the majesty of Heaven,
and thus preserve it.'
If one does not fear Heaven,
how can one preserve anything?
He seized the state through disorder,
and upholds ritual to guard it,
yet still fears he will not end well;
if he commits many acts without ritual,
he will not last."
A6.16 The Sixteenth Year of Duke Wén
A6.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
Jì Sūn Xíngfú met with the Marquis of Qí at Yánggǔ,
but the Marquis of Qí did not conclude a covenant.
A6.16.2 In summer, the fifth month,
the duke four times did not observe the first day of the month.
A6.16.3 In the sixth month, on Wùchén,
Gōngzǐ Suì and the Marquis of Qí made a covenant at Qīqiū.
A6.16.4 In autumn, the eighth month, on Xīnwèi,
the lady Jiāng shì died.
A6.16.5 The Quán Terrace was demolished.
A6.16.6 The people of Chǔ,
the people of Qín,
and the people of Bā destroyed Yōng.
A6.16.7 In winter, in the eleventh month,
the people of Sòng assassinated their ruler, Chǔjiù.
B6.16 The Commentary for the Sixteenth Year of Duke Wén
B6.16.1 In the spring of the sixteenth year,
in the royal first month,
[Lǔ] made peace with Qí.
The Duke was ill,
and sent Jì Wénzǐ to meet with the Marquis of Qí at Yánggǔ.
[Jì Wénzǐ] requested a covenant,
but the Marquis of Qí refused,
saying:
"Please wait until your lord has recovered."
B6.16.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
the Duke did not hold the fourth announcement of the new moon [at the ancestral temple],
due to illness.
The Duke sent Xiāng Zhòng to present bribes to the Marquis of Qí,
and therefore they made a covenant at Cīqiū.
B6.16.3 There were snakes that emerged from the Quán Palace,
entering the capital,
matching the number of former rulers.
In autumn, on the xīnwèi day of the eighth month,
Shēng Jiāng passed away.
The Quán Terrace was demolished.
B6.16.4 Chǔ suffered a great famine.
The Róng attacked its southwest,
reaching Fùshān,
and encamped at Dàlín.
They also attacked its southeast,
reaching Yángqiū,
to invade Zīzhī.
The people of Yōng led the various Mán tribes to rebel against Chǔ.
The people of Jūn led the Bǎipú tribes to gather at Xuǎn,
intending to attack Chǔ.
At this time, the northern gates of Shēn and Xī were not opened.
The people of Chǔ planned to move to Bǎngāo.
Wěi Jiǎ said:
"That will not do.
If we can go there,
the enemy can also go there.
It would be better to attack Yōng.
As for Jūn and the Bǎipú, they think that due to the famine we cannot raise an army,
and therefore they attack us.
If we send out our army,
they will surely become fearful and return home.
The Bǎipú live scattered,
each will flee to their own settlements,
who will have the leisure to plot against others?"
Then they sent out the army.
After fifteen days,
the Bǎipú dispersed.
From Lú onward,
they opened the granaries and shared the food.
They encamped at Gōushì.
They sent Lú Jílí to invade Yōng,
reaching Yōng's Fāngchéng.
The people of Yōng pursued them,
and captured Zǐ Yángchuāng.
After three nights he escaped,
and said:
"The Yōng army is numerous,
and the various Mán tribes are gathered there.
It would be better to bring back the main army,
and also mobilize the king's troops,
combine them and then advance."
Shī Shū said:
"That will not do.
For now, let us engage them again to make them arrogant.
When they are arrogant and we are enraged,
then we can defeat them.
This was how former ruler Fén Mào subdued Xíngxí."
They engaged them again,
and in seven encounters all retreated,
only the people of Bēi, Tiáo, and Yú actually pursued them.
The people of Yōng said:
"Chǔ is not worth fighting against."
Consequently, they made no defensive preparations.
The Viscount of Chǔ rode in a relay carriage,
assembled the army at Línpǐn,
divided it into two columns:
Zǐ Yuè from Shíxī and
Zǐ Bèi from Rèn attacked Yōng.
The people of Qín and Bā followed the Chǔ army.
The various Mán tribes made a covenant with the Viscount of Chǔ,
and subsequently they destroyed Yōng.
B6.16.5 The Sòng prince Bào was courteous to the people of the state.
When Sòng suffered famine,
he exhausted his grain stores to lend to them.
For those aged seventy and above,
there was none to whom he did not give gifts,
and he regularly added delicacies and rare foods.
Not a day passed without him visiting the gates of the six ministers.
The talented men of the state,
there was none he did not serve;
from the descendants of Huán downward,
there was none he did not show compassion to.
