Prince Bào was handsome and striking.
The Lady Xiāng wished to have relations with him,
but could not,
so she assisted him in his benefactions.
Duke Zhāo was without virtue.
The people of the state supported Prince Bào
through the Lady.
At this time, Huá Yuán was the Right Marshal,
Gōngsūn Yǒu was the Left Marshal,
Huá Ŏu was the Minister of War,
Lín Guàn was the Minister of Land,
Dàng Yìzhū was the Minister of Works,
and Prince Zhāo was the Minister of Justice.
Earlier,
when the Minister of Works Dàng died,
Gōngsūn Shòu declined the position of Minister of Works,
and requested that Yìzhū be appointed to it.
Afterwards, he told someone:
"The ruler is without virtue.
My office is close [to the ruler],
I fear being implicated.
If I abandon my office,
then the clan will have no protection.
A son
is a second self.
Let him temporarily postpone death for me.
Even if I lose my son,
the clan will still not be lost."
Later,
the Lady planned to have the Duke hunt at Mèngzhū and kill him.
The Duke knew of this,
and took all his treasures with him when he left.
Dàng Yìzhū said:
"Why not go to one of the feudal lords?"
The Duke said:
"I am unable to get along with the great officers, up to the ruler's grandmother, and with the people of the state.
Which feudal lord would accept me?
Moreover, having already been a ruler of men,
to then become a subject of another,
it would be better to die."
He gave all his treasures to his attendants
and sent them away.
The Lady sent word to the Minister of Works to leave the Duke.
He replied:
"To be his minister and flee his calamity,
how could I face a future ruler?"
In winter, on the jiǎyín day of the eleventh month,
when Duke Zhāo of Sòng was about to hunt at Mèngzhū,
before he arrived,
the Lady Wáng Jī sent the Commander of the Royal Hunt to attack and kill him.
Dàng Yìzhū died for him.
The record says:
"The people of Sòng assassinated their ruler, Chǔjiù,"
because the ruler was without virtue.
Duke Wén took the throne,
and made his full brother Xū the Minister of Works.
When Huá Ŏu died,
he made Dàng Huǐ the Minister of War.
A6.17 The Text for the Seventeenth Year of Duke Wén
A6.17.1 In the seventeenth year, in spring,
men of Jìn,
Wèi,
Chén,
and Zhèng attacked Sòng.
A6.17.2 In summer, on the guǐhài day of the fourth month,
we buried our Lady, Shēng Jiāng.
A6.17.3 The Marquis of Qí attacked our western borders.
On the guǐwèi day of the sixth month,
our Duke and the Marquis of Qí made a covenant at Gǔ.
A6.17.4 The feudal lords met at Hù.
A6.17.5 In autumn,
our Duke arrived from Gǔ.
A6.17.6 In winter,
Prince Suì went to Qí.
B6.17 The Commentary for the Seventeenth Year of Duke Wén
B6.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
Xún Línfǔ of Jìn, Kǒng Dá of Wèi, Gōngsūn Níng of Chén, and Shí Chǔ of Zhèng attacked Sòng,
denouncing them, saying:
"Why did you assassinate your ruler?"
Nevertheless, they established Duke Wén and returned.
The ministers are not recorded,
because they failed in their duty.
B6.17.2 In summer, on the guǐhài day of the fourth month,
Shēng Jiāng was buried.
Because there was trouble from Qí,
it was delayed.
B6.17.3 The Marquis of Qí attacked our northern borders.
Xiāng Zhòng requested a covenant.
In the sixth month,
they made a covenant at Gǔ.
B6.17.4 The Marquis of Jìn held a military review at Huángfù,
and subsequently reassembled the feudal lords at Hù,
to bring peace to Sòng.
Our lord did not attend the meeting,
because of the trouble from Qí.
The record says "the feudal lords,"
indicating they achieved nothing.
At this time, the Marquis of Jìn refused to see the Earl of Zhèng,
believing him to be disloyal and siding with Chǔ.
Zhèng's Zǐjiā sent a messenger
and with him a letter,
to inform Zhào Xuānzǐ,
saying:
"When our humble ruler ascended the throne, in his third year,
he summoned the Marquis of Cài
to join him in serving your ruler.
In the ninth month,
the Marquis of Cài entered our humble state to proceed.
Our humble state was then facing the troubles of Hóu Xuānduō,
so our ruler was unable to accompany the Marquis of Cài.
In the eleventh month,
we managed to suppress Hóu Xuānduō,
and then followed the Marquis of Cài
to present ourselves before your officers.
In the sixth month of his twelfth year,
Guīshēng assisted our ruler's legitimate heir, Yí,
in inviting the Marquis of Chén from Chǔ, and they came to pay court to your lord.
In the seventh month of his fourteenth year,
our ruler again paid court
to complete the affairs concerning Chén.
In the fifth month of his fifteenth year,
the Marquis of Chén went from our humble state to pay court to your lord.
In the first month of last year,
Zhú Zhīwǔ went, accompanying Yí to court.
In the eighth month,
our ruler again went to pay court.
Considering that Chén and Cài are in close proximity to Chǔ,
yet dared not be disloyal,
this is due to the efforts of our humble state.
Even though our humble state serves your lord in this manner,
why are we not exempt from blame?
During his reign,
he once paid court to Xiāng,
and twice appeared before your lord.
Yí and two or three of my humble self's colleagues have successively been to Jiàng.
Although we are a small state,
our service cannot be surpassed.
Now your great state says:
"'You have not satisfied our wishes.'
Our humble state faces destruction,
and can do no more.
The ancients had a saying:
'If one fears the head and fears the tail,
how much of the body remains?'
They also said:
'A dying deer does not choose its cry.'
When a small state serves a great state,
if the great state is virtuous,
then the small state acts as a man should;
if it is not virtuous,
then the small state is like a deer,
rushing desperately into danger—
in extremity, how can it choose?
If your commands are without limit,
we also know we are doomed.
We will then muster all our forces and await at Tiáo,
awaiting only your officers' commands.
In the sixth month, on the Rénshēn day, of the second year of Duke Wén,
we paid court to Qí.
In the second month, on the Rénxū day, of the fourth year,
we attacked Cài on behalf of Qí,
and also secured a settlement with Chǔ.
Situated between great states,
and compelled to follow forceful commands,
is this really our crime?
If your great state does not consider this,
we have no way to escape your orders."
Jìn's Gǒng Shuò went to Zhèng to negotiate a settlement,
and Zhào Chuān and Gōngxù Chí were sent as hostages.
B6.17.5 In autumn,
Gān Chù of Zhōu defeated the Róng at Shěn Chuí,
attacking them while they were drinking.
B6.17.6 In winter, in the tenth month,
Zhèng's heir-apparent Yí
and Shí Chǔ went to Jìn as hostages.
B6.17.7 Xiàng Zhòng went to Qí,
to acknowledge the covenant at Gǔ.
Upon his return, he reported:
"Your servant heard that the men of Qí are about to consume Lǔ's wheat.
From what your servant observed,
they will not be able to.
The ruler of Qí's words are frivolous.
Zāng Wénzhòng had a saying:
'If the ruler of the people is frivolous,
he is sure to die.'"
A6.18 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Wén's Eighteenth Year*
A6.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
in the king's second month, on the Dīngchǒu day,
the duke died beneath the terrace.
A6.18.2 The Earl of Qín, Yīng, died.
A6.18.3 In summer, in the fifth month, on the Wùxū day,
men of Qí murdered their ruler, Shāngrén.
A6.18.4 In the sixth month, on the Guǐyǒu day,
we buried our ruler, Duke Wén.
A6.18.5 In autumn,
the prince Suì
and Shūsūn Déchén went to Qí.
A6.18.6 In winter, in the tenth month,
the son died.
A6.18.7 The lady Jiāngshì returned to Qí.
A6.18.8 Jìsūn Xíngfǔ went to Qí.
A6.18.9 Jǔ murdered its ruler, Shùqí.
B6.18 *The Commentary of Zuo, Duke Wén's Eighteenth Year*
B6.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí set the date for mobilizing his army,
but then fell ill.
The physician said:
"He will not live until autumn,
he will die."
The duke heard of this,
performed divination,
and said:
"I hope he dies before the date!"
Huì Bó presented the tortoise shell.
The diviner Chǔqiū interpreted the cracks,
saying:
"The Marquis of Qí will not live until the date,
but not from illness;
you, my lord, will also not hear of it.
The one who presented the shell will have misfortune."
In the second month, on the Dīngchǒu day,
the duke died.
B6.18.2 When Qí's Duke Yì was still a prince,
he contended with Bǐng Chù's father over fields,
and did not win.
When he ascended the throne,
he had the corpse dug up and cut off its feet,
and then made Chù serve as his carriage driver.
He took Yán Zhí's wife for himself,
and made Zhí serve as his carriage attendant.
In summer, in the fifth month,
the duke went on an excursion to Shēnchí.
The two men were bathing in the pool.
Chù struck Zhí with a whip.
Zhí was angry.
Chù said:
"Someone took your wife and you were not angry;
one strike at you,
what harm is there?"
Zhí said:
"How does that compare with one who had his father's feet cut off and could not resent it?"
They then plotted to murder Duke Yì,
and hid his body among the bamboos.
They returned,
set out their wine vessels, and then fled.
The men of Qí set up Prince Yuán as ruler.
B6.18.3 In the sixth month,
Duke Wén was buried.
B6.18.4 In autumn,
Xiàng Zhòng and Zhuāng Shū went to Qí,
because Duke Huì had been established,
and also to acknowledge the burial.
Duke Wén had two consorts. Jìng Yíng gave birth to Duke Xuān.
Jìng Yíng was favored,
and privately served Xiàng Zhòng.
Duke Xuān was the elder,
and she entrusted him to Xiàng Zhòng.
Xiàng Zhòng wished to establish him,
but Shū Zhòng would not agree.
Zhòng had an audience with the Marquis of Qí
and requested his support.
The Marquis of Qí, newly established,
and wishing to be close to Lǔ,
granted it.
B6.18.5 In winter, in the tenth month,
Zhòng killed È and Shì,
and established Duke Xuān.
The record says
"the son died,"
concealing the truth.
Zhòng, using the ruler's command, summoned Huì Bó,
His steward Gōng Rǎn Wùrén tried to stop him,
saying,
"If you enter, you will certainly die."
Shū Zhòng said,
"To die in obedience to the ruler's command is permissible."
Gōng Rǎn Wùrén said,
"If it is the ruler's command,
you may die for it;
if it is not the ruler's command,
why listen to it?"
He did not listen,
and entered,
where he was killed and buried in horse dung.
Gōng Rǎn Wùrén took Shū Zhòng's wife and children and fled to Cài,
but later the Shū Zhòng clan was restored.
B6.18.6 Lady Jiāng, the wife [of the late ruler], returned to Qí,
for it was a final return.
As she was about to depart,
she wept while passing through the marketplace,
saying,
"Heaven!
Zhòng acted without principle,
killing the rightful heir and establishing a concubine's son."
All the people in the marketplace wept.
The people of Lǔ called her Āi Jiāng.
B6.18.7 Jǔ's Duke Jì had a son, the heir apparent Pú,
and also had Jì Tuó.
He favored Jì Tuó and deposed Pú,
and moreover committed many acts of impropriety in the state.
Pú, relying on the people of the state, assassinated Duke Jì,
and taking his precious jades, came fleeing [to Lǔ],
presenting them to Duke Xuān.
The duke ordered that he be granted a city,
saying,
"Today it must be conferred!"
Jì Wénzǐ sent the Minister of Justice to expel him beyond the borders,
saying,
"Today it must be carried out!"
The duke asked the reason.
Jì Wénzǐ had the Grand Historian Kè reply, saying:
"The late senior official Zāng Wénzhòng
taught Xíngfǔ the ritual of serving one's ruler,
and Xíngfǔ has upheld it in all his dealings,
not daring to neglect or deviate from it.
He said:
'When you see one who shows respect to his ruler,
serve him
as a filial son cares for his parents;
when you see one who shows disrespect to his ruler,
punish him,
as a hawk or sparrowhawk pursues small birds.'
The former ruler, the Duke of Zhōu, established the "Zhōu Rituals,"
saying:
'Use them to observe virtue,
use virtue to handle affairs,
use affairs to measure achievement,
use achievement to nourish the people.'
He composed the "Oath Mandate," saying:
'To destroy the rules is to be a traitor;
to conceal a traitor is to be a receiver.
To steal goods is to be a thief;
to steal vessels is to be a villain.
To bear the name of receiver,
to rely on the use of villainy,
is a great inauspicious virtue.
There are fixed punishments,
with no pardon.
They are recorded in the Nine Punishments, not to be forgotten.'
Xíngfǔ, upon examining Jǔ Pú,
finds nothing in him to emulate.
Filial piety, respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness are auspicious virtues;
thievery, villainy, receiving, and villainy are inauspicious virtues.
As for Jǔ Pú's filial piety and respect,
he assassinated his ruler and father;
as for his loyalty and trustworthiness,
he stole precious jades.
His person
is that of a thief and villain;
his vessels
are evidence of villainy.
To protect and benefit him
is to be a receiver.
To use him as a model would bring confusion;
the people would have no standard to follow.
He does not measure up to goodness,
but is entirely within inauspicious virtue.
Therefore, we have removed him."
"In former times, Gāoyángshì
had eight talented sons:
Cāng Shū, Tuí Ái, Táo Yǎn, Dà Lín,
Máng Jiàng, Tíng Jiān, Zhòng Róng, Shū Dá.
They were orderly, sagely, broad, and profound,
intelligent, sincere, earnest, and honest.
The people of the world called them the 'Eight Kǎi.'
Gāoxīnshì
had eight talented sons:
Bó Fèn, Zhòng Kān, Shū Xiàn, Jì Zhòng,
Bó Hǔ, Zhòng Xióng, Shū Bào, Jì Lí.
They were loyal, reverent, diligent, and virtuous,
kind, compassionate, benevolent, and harmonious.
The people of the world called them the 'Eight Yuán.'
These sixteen clans
generation after generation continued their excellence,
not letting their fame fade.
Down to the time of Yáo,
Yáo was unable to promote them.
Shùn served as minister under Yáo,
promoted the Eight Kǎi,
and set them to oversee the land,
to manage all affairs,
so that everything was timely and orderly,
and the earth was level and heaven accomplished.
He promoted the Eight Yuán,
and set them to spread the five teachings throughout the four quarters:
righteousness for the father, kindness for the mother, friendliness for the elder brother,
respect for the younger brother, and filial piety for the son,
so that there was peace within and accomplishment without.
"In former times, Dìhóngshì
had an untalented son,
who suppressed righteousness and concealed villainy,
delighting in practicing inauspicious virtue;
he gathered together vile and evil creatures.
Stubborn, deceitful, and unfriendly,
he associated with them,
and the people of the world called him 'Hùndùn.'
Shàohàoshì
had an untalented son,
who destroyed trust and abandoned loyalty,
glorifying and adorning evil speech;
calm in slander and habitual in perversity,
devoted to calumny and harboring wickedness,
he slandered those of great virtue.
The people of the world called him 'Qióngqí.'
Zhuānxūshì had an untalented son,
who could not be taught or instructed,
and did not understand speech;
when admonished, he was stubborn;
when left alone, he was deceitful.
He was arrogant and defiant toward illustrious virtue,
throwing into chaos the constant ways of heaven.
The people of the world called him 'Táowù.'
These three clans
generation after generation continued their wickedness,
increasing their evil fame,
down to the time of Yáo,
and Yáo was unable to remove them.
Jīnyúnshì
had an untalented son,
greedy for food and drink,
avaricious for goods and wealth;
his encroaching desires were extravagant,
impossible to satisfy.
He amassed and hoarded, accumulating goods,
knowing no limit or measure.
He did not share with the orphaned and widowed,
nor did he pity the poor and destitute.
The people of the world compared him to the three villains,
and called him 'Tāotiè.'
Shùn served as minister under Yáo,
received guests at the four gates,
and banished the four villainous clans—
Hùndùn, Qióngqí, Táowù, and Tāotiè—
casting them out to the four wild regions,
to guard against chīmèi.
Therefore, when Yáo passed away,
the world was as one,
united in heart in supporting Shùn,
making him the Son of Heaven,
because he had promoted the sixteen ministers
and removed the four villains.
Thus, the Yú Shū recounts Shùn's achievements,
saying: 'He carefully displayed the five constant virtues,
and the five constant virtues were all followed.'
This means there was no violation of teaching.
It says:
'He brought them into all affairs of government,
and all affairs of government were timely and orderly.'
This means there was no neglect of affairs.
It says:
'He received guests at the four gates,
and the four gates were reverent.'
This means there were no wicked men.
"Shùn had twenty great achievements
and became the Son of Heaven.
Now, although Xíngfǔ has not obtained a single good man,
he has removed one wicked one.
Compared to Shùn's achievements,
it is one-twentieth,
perhaps enough to avoid blame!"
B6.18.8 The Wǔ clan of Sòng guided the son of Duke Zhāo,
intending to support Sīchéng Xū to start a rebellion.
In the twelfth month,
the Duke of Sòng killed his own younger brother Xū and the son of Duke Zhāo,
and sent the Dài, Zhuāng, and Huán clans to attack the Wǔ clan at the residence of Simǎ Zǐbó.
Thereupon, he expelled the Wǔ and Mù clans.
He appointed Gōngsūn Shī as Sīchéng.
When Gōngzǐ Cháo died,
he appointed Yuè Lǚ as Sīkòu,
to pacify the people of the state.
A7.1 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 1 of Duke Xuān
A7.1.1 In the first year, in spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A7.1.2 The Duke's son Suì went to Qí to meet the bride.
A7.1.3 In the third month,
Suì arrived from Qí with the lady, the wife, Jiāng.
A7.1.4 In summer,
Jìsūn Xíngfú went to Qí.
A7.1.5 Jìn exiled its senior officer Xū Jiǎfǔ to Wèi.
A7.1.6 The Duke met with the Marquis of Qí at Píngzhōu.
A7.1.7 The Duke's son Suì went to Qí.
A7.1.8 In the sixth month,
men of Qí took the fields west of Jǐ.
A7.1.9 In autumn,
the Viscount of Zhū came for an audience.
A7.1.10 The Viscount of Chǔ and
men of Zhèng invaded Chén,
and subsequently invaded Sòng.
Zhào Dùn of Jìn led an army to relieve Chén.
The Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Earl of Cáo met the Jìn army at Fěilín,
and attacked Zhèng.
A7.1.11 In winter,
Zhào Chuān of Jìn led an army to invade Chóng.
A7.1.12 Men of Jìn
and men of Sòng attacked Zhèng.
B7.1 The Commentary, Year 1 of Duke Xuān
B7.1.1 In the first year, in spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke's son Suì went to Qí to meet the bride.
This was to honor the ruler's command.
B7.1.2 In the third month,
Suì arrived from Qí with the lady, the wife, Jiāng.
This was to honor the lady.
B7.1.3 In summer,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Qí,
presenting bribes to request a meeting.
B7.1.4 The men of Jìn punished those who had disobeyed orders,
exiling Xū Jiǎfǔ to Wèi.
They established Xū Kè in his place.
Xiān Xīn fled to Qí.
B7.1.5 The meeting at Píngzhōu
was to secure the Duke's position.
B7.1.6 Xiānmén Xiāngzhòng went to Qí
to acknowledge the settlement.
B7.1.7 In the sixth month,
men of Qí took the fields west of Jǐ.
This was because, for the sake of establishing the Duke,
they had given bribes to Qí.
B7.1.8 When the men of Sòng murdered Duke Zhāo,
Xún Línfǔ of Jìn led the armies of the various states
to attack Sòng.
Sòng made peace with Jìn,
and Duke Wén of Sòng accepted a covenant with Jìn.
(Jìn) also met with the various lords at Hù,
intending to attack Qí on behalf of Lǔ,
but they all took bribes
and returned.
Duke Mù of Zhèng said:
"Jìn is not worth allying with."
He then accepted a covenant with Chǔ.
When Duke Gòng of Chén died,
the men of Chǔ did not observe the proper rites.
Duke Líng of Chén accepted a covenant with Jìn.
In autumn,
the Viscount of Chǔ invaded Chén,
and subsequently invaded Sòng.
Zhào Dùn of Jìn led an army to relieve Chén and Sòng.
They met at Fěilín,
in order to attack Zhèng.
Wěi Jiǎ of Chǔ came to relieve Zhèng,
and they encountered (the Jìn army) at Běilín,
capturing Xiè Yáng of Jìn.
The men of Jìn then withdrew.
B7.1.9 Jìn wished to seek peace with Qín.
Zhào Chuān said:
"Let us invade Chóng.
Qín is concerned about Chóng,
and will certainly rescue it.
We can then seek peace."
In winter,
Zhào Chuān invaded Chóng.
Qín did not make peace.
B7.1.10 The men of Jìn attacked Zhèng,
to retaliate for the battle at Běilín.
At this time, the Marquis of Jìn was extravagant,
and Zhào Xuānzǐ was in charge of the government.
He repeatedly remonstrated but (the Marquis) would not listen,
therefore (Jìn) could not compete with Chǔ.
A7.2 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 2 of Duke Xuān
A7.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
on the Rénzǐ day of the royal second month,
Huà Yuán of Sòng led an army and Gōngzǐ Guīshēng of Zhèng led an army,
and they fought at Dàjí.
The Sòng army was utterly defeated,
and Huà Yuán of Sòng was captured.
A7.2.2 A Qín army attacked Jìn.
A7.2.3 In summer,
men of Jìn,
men of Sòng,
men of Wèi,
and men of Chén invaded Zhèng.
A7.2.4 In autumn, on the Yǐchǒu day of the ninth month,
Zhào Dùn of Jìn murdered his ruler Yígāo.
A7.2.5 In winter, on the Yǐhài day of the tenth month,
the Son of Heaven passed away.
B7.2 The Commentary, Year 2 of Duke Xuān
B7.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
Gōngzǐ Guīshēng of Zhèng, having received orders from Chǔ, attacked Sòng.
Huà Yuán and Yuè Lǚ of Sòng defended against him.
On the Rénzǐ day of the second month,
they fought at Dàjí.
The Sòng army was utterly defeated.
Huà Yuán was taken prisoner,
Yuè Lǚ was captured, along with four hundred and sixty armored chariots, two hundred and fifty prisoners, and one hundred slain (whose left ears were taken).
Kuáng Jiǎo encountered a man of Zhèng,
who fell into a well.
(Kuáng Jiǎo) reversed his halberd and pulled him out,
but was himself captured by the man.
The gentleman says:
"He lost propriety and disobeyed commands,
it is fitting that he was captured.
In war,
to manifest resolution and firmness
in obeying commands is called propriety.
To kill the enemy is resolution;
to carry out resolution is firmness.
To reverse this is to invite punishment."
Before the battle, Huà Yuán slaughtered sheep to feed his officers,
but his charioteer Yáng Zhēn did not receive any.
When the battle came,
he said:
"The sheep yesterday
was your affair;
today's affair
is mine."
He drove (the chariot) straight into the Zhèng army,
therefore (Sòng) was defeated.
The gentleman says
Yáng Zhēn "was not human.
Because of his private resentment,
he ruined the state and brought calamity upon the people.
What punishment could be greater than this?
The Odes says
'the man without goodness'
— does it not refer to Yáng Zhēn?
He brought calamity upon the people to gratify himself."
The men of Sòng offered one hundred war chariots and one hundred teams of dappled horses to ransom Huà Yuán from Zhèng.
Half had been delivered,
when Huà Yuán escaped and returned.
He stood outside the gate,
announced himself, and then entered.
He saw Shū Zāng,
and said:
"It was your horses, wasn't it?"
He replied:
"It was not the horses,
it was the man."
After this exchange, (Shū Zāng) came and fled (to Sòng).
When Sòng was fortifying its walls,
Huà Yuán was in charge of the work,
and inspected the progress.
The wall-builders sang:
"With glaring eyes,
and bulging belly,
he threw away his armor and came back.
Oh the beard, oh the beard,
he threw away his armor and came back again."
He had him ride in his chariot and said to him:
"Oxen have hides,
rhinoceroses are still plentiful,
so what does it matter if we discard our armor?"
The laborer said:
"Even if there are hides,
what about the red lacquer?"
Huá Yuán said:
"Let's go!
Their mouths are many, ours are few."
B7.2.2 The Qín army attacked Jìn
to avenge the defeat at Chóng,
and then besieged Jiāo.
In summer,
Jìn's Zhào Dùn came to rescue Jiāo,
and then from Yīndì,
together with the armies of the various states, invaded Zhèng
to avenge the battle of Dàjí.
Chǔ's Dòu Jiāo came to rescue Zhèng,
saying:
"Can one desire the allegiance of the feudal lords
yet dislike the difficulties involved?"
He then encamped at Zhèng
to await the Jìn army.
Zhào Dùn said:
"That clan of his is contending with Chǔ,
and will likely perish soon.
Let us for now aggravate their troubles."
He then withdrew.
B7.2.3 Duke Líng of Jìn was not acting as a ruler should:
He heavily taxed the people to carve and decorate his walls,
shot pellets at people from a tower,
and watched them dodge the pellets;
When the cook stewed bear's paws and they were not done,
he killed him,
placed him in a basket,
and had a woman carry it past the court.
Zhào Dùn and Shì Jì saw the hand,
asked the reason,
and were troubled by it.
They were about to remonstrate.
Shì Jì said:
"If we remonstrate and he does not accept it,
then no one will follow us.
Let me go first;
if he does not accept it,
then you follow me."
He advanced three times
until he reached the eaves,
and only then did the duke look at him,
saying:
"I know my faults,
and will change them."
Shì Jì bowed his head to the ground and replied:
"Who among men is without faults?
Having faults and being able to change them
is the greatest good.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'All have a beginning,
but few can bring it to an end.'
If it is like this,
then those who can make amends for their faults are few.
If you, my lord, can bring it to an end,
then the altars of soil and grain will be secure,
and it is not only your ministers who will rely on it.
It also says:
'When the imperial robe has a flaw,
only Zhòng Shānfǔ can mend it.'
This is about being able to make amends for faults.
If you, my lord, can make amends for your faults,
the imperial robe will not be discarded."
Still, he did not change.
Xuānzǐ (Zhào Dùn) repeatedly remonstrated,
and the duke, troubled by him,
sent Chú Ní to assassinate him.
Chú Ní went in the morning;
the bedroom door was open,
and Zhào Dùn, dressed in full court attire, was about to go to court.
It was still early,
so he sat and dozed.
Chú Ní withdrew,
sighed, and said:
"Not forgetting reverence and respect,
he is the master of the people.
To assassinate the master of the people
is disloyal;
to abandon the ruler's command
is untrustworthy.
Having either one of these,
it is better to die."
He dashed his head against a locust tree and died.
In autumn, the ninth month,
the Marquis of Jìn invited Zhào Dùn to drink,
concealed armed men,
and planned to attack him.
His right-hand attendant, Tímí Míng, knew of it,
hurried forward and ascended,
saying:
"A minister attending his lord at a feast,
after three cups,
is contrary to ritual."
He then helped Zhào Dùn down.
The duke set a fierce dog on him;
Míng fought with it and killed it.
Dùn said:
"Abandoning men and using dogs,
though fierce, what can they do!"
He fought his way out.
Tímí Míng died in the fight.
Earlier,
Xuānzǐ was hunting at Shǒushān,
and rested at Yìsāng,
where he saw Líng Zhé starving,
and asked about his illness.
He said:
"I have not eaten for three days."
Xuānzǐ fed him,
but he set aside half.
Xuānzǐ asked him.
He said:
"I have been away as a retainer for three years,
and do not know if my mother is still alive.
Now I am near home,
I beg to leave this for her."
Xuānzǐ had him eat it all,
and prepared for him a basket of food and meat,
placing it in a bag to give to him.
Later, he became one of the duke's guards,
reversed his halberd to ward off the duke's men,
and thus saved Xuānzǐ.
Xuānzǐ asked the reason.
He replied:
"I am the starving man of Yìsāng."
Xuānzǐ asked his name and residence,
but he did not tell him and withdrew,
and then went into exile himself.
On yǐchǒu day,
Zhào Chuān killed Duke Líng at Táoyuán.
Xuānzǐ had not yet left the mountains when he returned.
The Grand Historian wrote:
"Zhào Dùn assassinated his ruler,"
and displayed it in court.
Xuānzǐ said:
"It was not so."
He replied:
"You are the chief minister;
when you fled, you did not cross the border;
when you returned, you did not punish the assassin.
If it was not you, then who was it?"
Xuānzǐ said:
"Alas!
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Because of my longing,
I brought this sorrow upon myself.'
This refers to me."
Confucius said:
"Dǒng Hú
was a good historian of old;
his recording method did not conceal the truth.
Zhào Xuānzǐ
was a good minister of old;
he suffered condemnation for the sake of the rule.
It is a pity
that he did not cross the border, for then he would have been exempt."
Xuānzǐ sent Zhào Chuān to welcome Prince Hēitún from Zhōu and established him.
On rénshēn day,
he held court at Wǔgōng.
B7.2.4 Earlier,
during the turmoil of Lì Jī,
a curse was made not to keep the ducal sons in groups,
and from then on, Jìn had no public clan.
When Duke Chéng ascended the throne,
he then made the legitimate sons of the ministers into officials
and gave them lands,
making them the public clan.
He also made their other sons into officials,
and they became the "other sons";
their illegitimate sons became the "public retinue."
Thus, Jìn then had the public clan, other sons, and public retinue.
Zhào Dùn requested that Kuò be made a member of the public clan,
saying:
"He is the beloved son of Lady Jī.
If not for Lady Jī,
I would be a man of the Dí."
The duke agreed.
In winter,
Zhào Dùn became the leader of the chariot troops,
and had Píng Jì lead his former clan as the Grand Master of the Public Clan.
A7.3 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Third Year of Duke Xuān*
A7.3.1 In the third year, spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the mouth of the ox for the suburban sacrifice was injured,
and another ox was divined for.
The ox died,
and so the suburban sacrifice was not held.
Nevertheless, the three望 sacrifices were performed.
A7.3.2 Duke Kuāng was buried.
A7.3.3 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked the Lùhún Róng.
A7.3.4 In summer,
the men of Chǔ invaded Zhèng.
A7.3.5 In autumn,
the Red Dí invaded Qí.
A7.3.6 The army of Sòng besieged Cáo.
A7.3.7 In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Bǐngxū,
the Earl of Zhèng, Lán, died.
A7.3.8 They buried Duke Mù of Zhèng.
B7.3 Commentary on Duke Xuān, Year 3
B7.3.1 In the spring of the third year,
they did not perform the Suburban Sacrifice,
but performed the Wàng sacrifice.
Both were contrary to ritual.
The Wàng sacrifice
is a type of Suburban Sacrifice.
If they did not perform the Suburban Sacrifice,
then they should not have performed the Wàng sacrifice either.
B7.3.2 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng
and reached Yán.
Zhèng made peace with Jìn,
and Shì Huì entered to conclude the covenant.
B7.3.3 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked the Lùhún Róng,
and then proceeded to Luò,
where he displayed his troops on the borders of Zhōu.
King Dìng sent Wángsūn Mǎn to greet the Viscount of Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ asked about the size and
weight of the Nine Tripods.
He replied:
"It lies in virtue, not in the tripods.
In the past, when the Xià dynasty was virtuous,
distant regions depicted their strange creatures,
the Nine Pastors contributed metal,
and tripods were cast bearing images of these creatures,
so that all creatures were represented and made ready,
enabling the people to recognize spirits and evil things.
Therefore, when the people entered rivers, marshes, mountains, and forests,
they did not encounter anything unfavorable.
Chīmèi and wǎngliǎng [demons and monsters],
none could encounter them.
Thus they were able to harmonize above and below,
to receive Heaven's blessings.
Jié had depraved virtue,
and the tripods were transferred to Shāng,
for a span of six hundred years.
King Zhòu of Shāng was cruel and oppressive,
and the tripods were transferred to Zhōu.
When virtue is splendid and enlightened,
even if [the tripods] are small,
they are heavy.
When there is wickedness, perversity, delusion, and disorder,
even if [the tripods] are large,
they are light.
Heaven blesses enlightened virtue,
and there is a fixed limit.
King Chéng fixed the tripods at Jiárǔ,
divined that [the dynasty] would last for thirty generations,
and divined that it would last for seven hundred years.
This is the mandate of Heaven.
Although the virtue of Zhōu has declined,
the mandate of Heaven has not yet changed.
The weight of the tripods
may not be inquired about."
B7.3.4 In summer,
the men of Chǔ invaded Zhèng,
because Zhèng had drawn close to Jìn.
B7.3.5 Duke Wén of Sòng had been on the throne for three years
when he killed his uterine younger brother Xū and the sons of Duke Zhāo.
This was the plot of the Wǔ lineage.
He sent the Dài and Huán lineages to attack the Wǔ lineage at the residence of Minister of War Zǐbó,
and completely expelled the Wǔ and Mù lineages.
The Wǔ and Mù lineages, with the army of Cáo, attacked Sòng.
In autumn,
the army of Sòng besieged Cáo,
in retaliation for the disorder caused by the Wǔ lineage.
B7.3.6 In winter,
Duke Mù of Zhèng died.
Formerly,
Duke Wén of Zhèng had a low-ranking concubine named Yān Jí.
She dreamed that a heavenly envoy gave her an orchid,
saying:
'I am Bó Tiáo.
I
am your ancestor.
Take this as your son.
Because the orchid has the fragrance of the state,
people will cherish and adore it like this.'
Afterwards, Duke Wén saw her,
gave her an orchid, and had intercourse with her.
She declined, saying:
'Your handmaid is without talent,
but if I am fortunate enough to bear a child,
and you do not believe it,
may I dare to use the orchid as proof?'
The Duke said:
'Agreed.'
She gave birth to Duke Mù,
and named him Lán (Orchid).
Duke Wén also had relations with the consort of the Zhèng Zǐ, named Chén Guī,
who bore Zǐ Huá and Zǐ Zāng.
Zǐ Zāng offended [the Duke] and left.
[The Duke] lured Zǐ Huá
and killed him at Nánlǐ,
and sent assassins to kill Zǐ Zāng between Chén and Sòng.
He also took a wife from Jiāng,
who bore the prince Shì.
When [Shì] went to court in Chǔ,
the men of Chǔ poisoned him,
and he died when he reached Yè.
He also took a wife from Sū,
who bore Zǐ Xiá and Zǐ Yúmí.
Yúmí died early.
Xiè Jià hated Xiá,
and Duke Wén also hated him,
so he was not established.
The Duke expelled all the princes.
Prince Lán fled to Jìn,
and followed Duke Wén of Jìn to attack Zhèng.
Shí Guǐ said:
'I have heard that the Jī and Jí clans are a good match,
and their descendants are sure to flourish.
Jí
is an auspicious clan;
it was the principal consort of Hòu Jì.
Now Prince Lán
is a nephew of the Jí clan.
Heaven may be opening the way for him;
he is sure to become ruler,
and his descendants are sure to flourish.
If we take the lead in welcoming him,
we can secure great favor.'
Together with Kǒng Jiāngchú and Hóu Xuānduō, they welcomed him,
made a covenant in the Great Temple,
and established him,
thereby making peace with Jìn.
Duke Mù fell ill,
and said:
'When the orchid dies,
I will die, will I not?
It is the reason for my life.'
He cut down the orchid and died.
A7.4 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Xuān, Year 4
A7.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
the Duke and the Marquis of Qí mediated peace between Jǔ and Tán.
The people of Jǔ refused.
The Duke attacked Jǔ,
and took Xiàng.
A7.4.2 The Earl of Qín, Dào, died.
A7.4.3 In summer, in the sixth month, on the day Yǐyǒu,
the Zhèng prince Guīshēng assassinated his ruler, Yí.
A7.4.4 The Red Dí invaded Qí.
A7.4.5 In autumn,
the Duke went to Qí.
A7.4.6 The Duke arrived from Qí.
A7.4.7 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B7.4 Commentary on Duke Xuān, Year 4
B7.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
the Duke and the Marquis of Qí mediated peace between Jǔ and Tán,
but the people of Jǔ refused.
The Duke attacked Jǔ,
and took Xiàng.
This was contrary to ritual.
One brings peace to states through ritual,
not through disorder.
To attack and not to bring order
is disorder.
To use disorder to bring peace to disorder—
what order can there be?
Without order,
how can one practice ritual?
B7.4.2 The men of Chǔ presented a giant soft-shelled turtle to Duke Líng of Zhèng.
Prince Sòng and Zǐjiā were about to have an audience.
Zǐgōng's index finger moved,
and he showed it to Zǐjiā,
saying:
'On other days when I have been like this,
I have always tasted some unusual delicacy.'
When they entered,
the cook was about to cut up the turtle.
They looked at each other and smiled.
The duke asked about it,
and Zǐjiā told him.
When the turtle soup was served to the high officials,
he summoned Zǐgōng but did not give him any.
Zǐgōng was angry.
He dipped his finger in the cauldron,
tasted it, and went out.
The duke was angry
and wanted to kill Zǐgōng.
Zǐgōng plotted with Zǐjiā to strike first.
Zǐjiā said:
"Even an old domestic animal,
one hesitates to kill it;
how much more so a ruler?"
[Zǐgōng] in turn slandered Zǐjiā.
Zǐjiā, in fear, went along with him.
In summer,
they assassinated Duke Líng.
The record says: "Zhèng's prince Guīshēng assassinated his ruler Yí,"
because his authority was insufficient.
The gentleman says:
"Benevolent but not martial,
he was unable to succeed."
In general, when an assassination of a ruler is recorded,
if the ruler is named,
it is because the ruler was without the Way;
if the minister is named,
it is the minister's crime.
The people of Zhèng set up Zǐliáng.
He declined, saying:
"If it is for worthiness,
then Qùjí is insufficient;
if it is for order of succession,
then Prince Jiān is the elder."
So they set up Duke Xiāng.
Duke Xiāng intended to expel the Mù clan,
but to spare Zǐliáng.
Zǐliáng would not agree,
saying:
"If the Mù clan ought to be preserved,
then that is certainly my wish.
If they are to be driven to ruin,
then let us all be ruined together.
What would Qùjí be doing [if spared alone]?"
So he spared them,
and they all became high officials.
B7.4.3 Formerly,
Chǔ's Minister of War Zǐliáng gave birth to Zǐ Yuèjiāo.
Zǐwén said:
"You must kill him!
This child
has the appearance of a bear or tiger and the voice of a jackal or wolf.
If you do not kill him,
he will certainly wipe out the Ruò'áo clan.
The proverb says:
'The cub of a wolf has a wild heart.'
This is a wolf indeed.
How can it be reared?"
Zǐliáng would not agree.
Zǐwén considered it a great sorrow.
When he was about to die,
he gathered his clan
and said:
"If Jiāo comes to administer the government,
then leave quickly,
lest you be caught in the disaster."
And weeping, he said:
"Even ghosts seek food.
Will not the ghosts of the Ruò'áo clan go hungry!"
When Chief Minister Zǐwén died,
Dòu Bān became Chief Minister,
and Zǐyuè became Minister of War.
Wěi Jiǎ became Minister of Works.
He slandered Zǐyáng and had him killed.
Zǐyuè became Chief Minister,
and he himself became Minister of War.
Zǐyuè in turn hated him.
So, using the clan of Ruò'áo,
he imprisoned Bó Yíng in Liáoyáng and killed him.
Then he took up position at Zhēngyě,
intending to attack the king.
The king sent the sons of three kings as hostages,
but he would not accept them.
He encamped his army at Zhāngshì.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the wùxū day,
the ruler of Chǔ fought with the Ruò'áo clan at Gāohǔ.
Bó Fén shot at the king.
The arrow flew over the chariot pole,
reached the drum stand,
and stuck in the bronze bell.
He shot again.
The arrow flew over the chariot pole,
and pierced through the hub-cover.
The army was afraid
and retreated.
The king sent someone to circulate among the troops, saying:
"Our former ruler King Wén conquered Xī,
and obtained three arrows there.
Bó Fén stole two of them.
They are now all used up."
They beat the drums and advanced,
and thus annihilated the Ruò'áo clan.
Formerly,
Ruò'áo took a wife from Yún,
and she gave birth to Dòu Bóbǐ.
When Ruò'áo died,
he followed his mother and was reared in Yún.
He had illicit relations with the daughter of the ruler of Yún,
and she gave birth to Zǐwén.
The lady of Yún had him abandoned in the Mèng marshes.
A tiger suckled him.
The ruler of Yún was hunting
and saw him.
He was frightened and returned.
His lady told him about it,
and he then had the child taken in.
The people of Chǔ call 'suckle' gǔ,
and call 'tiger' wūtú.
Therefore they named him Gǔ Wūtú.
He gave his daughter in marriage to Bóbǐ.
This was Chief Minister Zǐwén.
His grandson, the admonishing official Kèhuáng, was on a mission to Qí.
On his return, when he reached Sòng,
he heard of the rebellion.
His attendants said:
"You cannot go back."
The admonishing official said:
"If I abandon my ruler's command,
who alone would accept me?
The ruler
is Heaven.
Can one escape Heaven?"
So he returned,
reported on his mission,
and then turned himself in to the Director of Justice.
The king, remembering Zǐwén's governance of the state of Chǔ,
said:
"If Zǐwén has no posterity,
how can we encourage goodness?"
He restored him to his position,
and changed his name to Shēng.
B7.4.4 In winter,
the ruler of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
because Zhèng had not submitted.
A7.5 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Xuān Year 5
A7.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
the duke went to Qí.
A7.5.2 In summer,
the duke arrived from Qí.
A7.5.3 In autumn, in the ninth month,
Qí's Gāo Gù came to meet Shū Jī.
A7.5.4 Shūsūn Déchén died.
A7.5.5 In winter,
Qí's Gāo Gù and Zǐ Shū Jī came.
A7.5.6 The men of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B7.5 The Zuo Tradition, Duke Xuān Year 5
B7.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
the duke went to Qí.
Gāo Gù made the marquis of Qí detain the duke,
to request Shū Jī.
B7.5.2 In summer,
the duke arrived from Qí.
The record
is because of his transgression.
B7.5.3 In autumn, in the ninth month,
Qí's Gāo Gù came to fetch the bride,
doing it for himself.
Therefore the record says "fetched Shū Jī,"
because a high minister fetched her himself.
B7.5.4 In winter,
they came,
to return the horses.
B7.5.5 The ruler of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
Chén made peace with Chǔ.
Jìn's Xún Línfǔ rescued Zhèng
and attacked Chén.
A7.6 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Xuān Year 6
A7.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
Jìn's Zhào Dùn
and Wèi's Sūn Miǎn invaded Chén.
A7.6.2 In summer, in the fourth month.
A7.6.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
there were locusts.
A7.6.4 In winter, in the tenth month.
B7.6 Commentary on the Sixth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
Jìn and Wèi invaded Chén,
because Chén had allied with Chǔ.
B7.6.2 In summer,
King Dìng sent Zǐfú to Qí to seek a queen.
B7.6.3 In autumn,
the Red Dí attacked Jìn,
besieging Huái and Xíngqiū.
The Marquis of Jìn wished to attack them.
Zhōngháng Huánzǐ said:
"Let them inflict harm upon their own people,
until their excesses reach the limit.
Then they can be destroyed.
The Book of Zhōu says:
'Destroy the great Yīn,'
referring to this kind of situation."
B7.6.4 In winter,
Zhào Huángōng went to Qí to welcome the queen.
B7.6.5 The people of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
obtained a covenant and returned.
B7.6.6 Zhèng's nobleman Mán Mǎn spoke with Wángzǐ Bó Liào,
wishing to become a minister.
Bó Liào told someone:
"Without virtue yet greedy,
this corresponds to the hexagram Fēng (䷶) changing to Lí (䷝) in the Zhōuyì,
he will not pass beyond this."
After one year,
the people of Zhèng killed him.
A7.7 Text of the Seventh Year of Duke Xuān
A7.7.1 In the seventh year, in spring,
the Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū to form an alliance.
A7.7.2 In summer,
the Duke joined the Marquis of Qí in attacking Lái.
A7.7.3 In autumn,
the Duke returned from attacking Lái.
A7.7.4 There was a great drought.
A7.7.5 In winter,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
and the Earl of Cáo at Hēirǎng.
B7.7 Commentary on the Seventh Year of Duke Xuān
B7.7.1 In the seventh year, in spring,
Wèi's Sūn Huánzǐ came to form an alliance,
beginning diplomatic relations.
And they planned to meet with Jìn.
B7.7.2 In summer,
the Duke joined the Marquis of Qí in attacking Lái,
but he was not part of the planning.
In general, when troops are dispatched,
if involved in the planning it is called "joined with,"
if not involved in the planning it is called "met with."
B7.7.3 The Red Dí invaded Jìn,
and took the grain of Xiàngyīn.
B7.7.4 Zhèng made peace with Jìn,
which was due to the planning of Gōngzǐ Sòng,
so he assisted the Earl of Zhèng at the meeting.
In winter,
they made a covenant at Hēirǎng.
Wángshū Huángōng oversaw it,
to address the discord.
When the Marquis of Jìn was established,
the Duke did not pay court,
nor did he send a great officer on a courtesy visit,
so the men of Jìn detained the Duke at the meeting.
They made a covenant at Huángfù,
but the Duke did not participate in the covenant.
He was released through a bribe.
Therefore, the covenant at Hēirǎng was not recorded,
to conceal it.
A7.8 Text of the Eighth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.8.1 In the eighth year, in spring,
the Duke returned from the meeting.
A7.8.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
Gōngzǐ Suì went to Qí,
but upon reaching Huáng he returned.
A7.8.3 On Xīnsì,
there was a ceremony at the Grand Temple,
and Zhòng Suì died at Chuí.
On Rénwǔ,
the supplementary ceremony was still held.
The Wàn dance was performed,
but the Yuè pipes were omitted.
A7.8.4 On Wùzǐ,
Lady Yíngshì died.
A7.8.5 The army of Jìn
and the White Dí attacked Qín.
A7.8.6 The people of Chǔ destroyed Shūliǎo.
A7.8.7 In autumn, in the seventh month, on Jiǎzǐ,
there was an eclipse of the sun,
which was total.
A7.8.8 In winter, in the tenth month, on Jǐchǒu,
we buried our junior queen Jìng Yíng.
It rained, so the burial could not be completed.
On Gēngyín,
by midday the burial was completed.
A7.8.9 The walls of Píngyáng were fortified.
A7.8.10 The army of Chǔ attacked Chén.
B7.8 Commentary on the Eighth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.8.1 In the eighth year, in spring,
the White Dí made peace with Jìn.
In summer,
they joined Jìn in attacking Qín.
The men of Jìn captured a Qín spy,
killed him in the market of Jiàng,
and after six days he revived.
B7.8.2 There was a ceremony at the Grand Temple,
and after Xiāng Zhòng died the supplementary ceremony was held,
which was contrary to ritual.
B7.8.3 Because the various Shū tribes had rebelled,
Chǔ attacked Shūliǎo
and destroyed it.
The Viscount of Chǔ fixed its borders.
Reaching Huáruì,
he made a covenant with Wú and Yuè and returned.
B7.8.4 Xū Kè of Jìn suffered from a gu illness,
and Xì Quē was in charge of government.
In autumn,
he dismissed Xū Kè,
and appointed Zhào Shuò as assistant commander of the lower army.
B7.8.5 In winter,
they buried Jìng Yíng.
There was a drought, and there was no hemp,
so for the first time they used géfú.
It rained,
so the burial could not be completed,
which was in accordance with ritual.
According to ritual,
when divining for a burial date,
the more distant day is chosen first,
to avoid appearing unaffectionate.
B7.8.6 The walls of Píngyáng were fortified,
recorded
because it was timely.
B7.8.7 Chén made peace with Jìn.
The army of Chǔ attacked Chén,
obtained a covenant and returned.
A7.9 Text of the Ninth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
the Duke went to Qí.
A7.9.2 The Duke returned from Qí.
A7.9.3 In summer,
Zhòngsūn Miè went to the capital.
A7.9.4 The Marquis of Qí attacked Lái.
A7.9.5 In autumn,
they took Gēnmóu.
A7.9.6 In the eighth month,
the Viscount of Téng died.
A7.9.7 In the ninth month,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
and the Earl of Cáo met at Hù.
A7.9.8 Xún Línfǔ of Jìn led an army to attack Chén.
A7.9.9 On Xīnyǒu,
the Marquis of Jìn, Hēitún, died at Hù.
A7.9.10 In winter, in the tenth month, on Guǐyǒu,
the Marquis of Wèi, Zhèng, died.
A7.9.11 The people of Sòng besieged Téng.
A7.9.12 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
A7.9.13 Jìn's Xì Quē led troops to rescue Zhèng.
A7.9.14 Chén executed its senior official Xiè Yě.
B7.9 Commentary for Duke Xuān Year 9
B7.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
the King sent a messenger to request a courtesy visit.
In summer,
Mèng Xiànzǐ visited the Zhōu court.
The King considered him to be well-mannered,
and bestowed generous gifts upon him.
B7.9.2 In autumn,
they captured Gēnmóu.
This is recorded to indicate it was easy.
B7.9.3 Duke Zhāo of Téng died.
B7.9.4 They met at Hù,
to discuss measures against those not in harmony.
The Marquis of Chén did not attend the meeting.
Jìn's Xún Línfù led the armies of the various states to attack Chén.
The Marquis of Jìn died at Hù,
and so they returned.
B7.9.5 In winter,
the men of Sòng besieged Téng,
taking advantage of its mourning period.
B7.9.6 Duke Líng of Chén, along with Kǒng Níng and Yí Xíngfù, had illicit relations with Xià Jī.
They all wore her undergarments next to their skin,
and joked about it at court.
Xiè Yě remonstrated, saying:
"When lords and ministers openly engage in lewdness,
the people have nothing to emulate,
and moreover, it creates an unseemly reputation.
My lord, you should put a stop to this!"
The Duke said:
"I am able to reform."
The Duke informed the two men.
The two men requested to kill him,
the Duke did not forbid it,
and so they killed Xiè Yě.
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'When the people are full of wickedness,
do not set up laws for yourself.'
This refers to Xiè Yě, does it not!"
B7.9.7 The Viscount of Chǔ, because of the affair of the Lì campaign,
attacked Zhèng.
B7.9.8 Jìn's Xì Quē rescued Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng defeated the Chǔ army at Liǔfén.
All the people of the state were pleased,
only Zǐliáng was worried, saying:
"This is a disaster for the state,
my death is not far off."
A7.10 The Spring and Autumn Annals for Duke Xuān Year 10
A7.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
the Duke went to Qí.
A7.10.2 The Duke arrived from Qí.
A7.10.3 The men of Qí returned to us the fields west of Jǐ.
A7.10.4 In summer, the fourth month, on day Bǐngchén,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A7.10.5 On day Jǐsì,
Duke Huì of Qí, Yuán, died.
A7.10.6 The Cuī clan of Qí fled to Wèi.
A7.10.7 The Duke went to Qí.
A7.10.8 In the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from Qí.
A7.10.9 On day Guǐsì,
Xià Zhēngshū of Chén assassinated his ruler, Píngguó.
A7.10.10 In the sixth month,
the army of Sòng attacked Téng.
A7.10.11 Gōngsūn Guīfù went to Qí.
They buried Duke Huì of Qí.
A7.10.12 Men of Jìn,
men of Sòng,
men of Wèi,
and men of Cáo attacked Zhèng.
A7.10.13 In autumn,
the Son of Heaven sent Wáng Jìzǐ to pay a courtesy visit.
A7.10.14 Gōngsūn Guīfù led troops to attack Zhū,
and captured Yì.
A7.10.15 There was a great flood.
A7.10.16 Jìsūn Xíngfù went to Qí.
A7.10.17 In winter,
Gōngsūn Guīfù went to Qí.
A7.10.18 The Marquis of Qí sent Guó Zuǒ to pay a courtesy visit.
A7.10.19 There was a famine.
A7.10.20 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
B7.10 Commentary for Duke Xuān Year 10
B7.10.1 In the spring of the tenth year,
the Duke went to Qí.
The Marquis of Qí, because we had submitted,
returned the fields west of Jǐ.
B7.10.2 In summer,
Duke Huì of Qí died.
Cuī Zhù was favored by Duke Huì.
The Gāo and Guó clans feared his pressure,
and upon the Duke's death, they expelled him.
He fled to Wèi.
The record says "the Cuī clan,"
because it was not his fault;
moreover, they announced him by his clan name,
not his personal name.
Whenever a senior official of a feudal state leaves,
they announce to the other feudal lords, saying:
"So-and-so of such-and-such clan, the guardian minister,
has failed in his duty to guard the ancestral temple,
we dare to announce."
They announce it to all envoys bearing jade and silk gifts;
if not,
then they do not.
B7.10.3 The Duke went to Qí to attend the funeral.
B7.10.4 Duke Líng of Chén, along with Kǒng Níng and Yí Xíngfù, drank at the Xià household.
The Duke said to Xíngfù:
"Zhēngshū resembles you."
He replied:
"He also resembles you, my lord."
Zhēngshū was incensed by this.
As the Duke was leaving,
Zhēngshū shot and killed him from his stable.
The two men fled to Chǔ.
B7.10.5 The people of Téng relied on Jìn and did not serve Sòng.
In the sixth month,
the army of Sòng attacked Téng.
B7.10.6 Zhèng made peace with Chǔ.
The armies of the various states attacked Zhèng,
obtained a settlement and returned.
B7.10.7 In autumn,
Liú Kānggōng came to return the courtesy visit.
B7.10.8 The army attacked Zhū,
and captured Yì.
B7.10.9 Jì Wénzǐ for the first time paid a courtesy visit to Qí.
B7.10.10 In winter,
Zǐjiā went to Qí,
because of the attack on Zhū.
B7.10.11 Guó Wǔzǐ came to return the courtesy visit.
B7.10.12 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
Jìn's Shì Huì rescued Zhèng,
and pursued the Chǔ army north of Yǐng.
The armies of the various states garrisoned Zhèng.
B7.10.13 Zhèng's Zǐjiā died.
The people of Zhèng investigated the disorder during the time of Duke Yōu.
They hacked open Zǐjiā's coffin,
and expelled his clan.
They reburied Duke Yōu,
and gave him the posthumous title
"Líng."
A7.11 The Spring and Autumn Annals for Duke Xuān Year 11
A7.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
it was the royal first month.
A7.11.2 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Chén,
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Chénlíng.
A7.11.3 Gōngsūn Guīfù joined with the men of Qí to attack Jǔ.
A7.11.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn met with the Dí at Cuánhán.
A7.11.5 In winter, the tenth month,
the men of Chǔ killed Xià Zhēngshū of Chén.
A7.11.6 On day Dìnghài,
the Viscount of Chǔ entered Chén.
A7.11.7 He installed Gōngsūn Níng
and Yí Xíngfù in Chén.
B7.11 Commentary for Duke Xuān Year 11
B7.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng and reached Lì.
Zǐ Liáng said:
"Jìn and Chǔ do not devote themselves to virtue
but contend by force of arms.
We may follow whichever comes to us.
Jìn and Chǔ are without good faith;
how can we alone have good faith?"
He then submitted to Chǔ.
In summer,
Chǔ made a covenant at Chénlíng,
because Chén and Zhèng had submitted.
B7.11.2 The Left Premier of Chǔ, Zǐ Zhòng, invaded Sòng.
The king waited for him at Yán.
B7.11.3 The Prime Minister, Wěi Àiliè, walled the city of Yí.
He ordered the border officers to plan the work,
and submitted their plans to the Minister of Works.
They calculated the labor and set the time,
distributed the materials,
leveled the boards and pillars,
balanced the baskets and rammers,
measured the earth and materials,
considered the distances,
surveyed the foundations,
prepared the provisions,
and assigned the officers.
The work was completed in thirty days,
without exceeding the original plan.
B7.11.4 Jìn's Xì Chéngzǐ sought to make peace with the multitude of Dí tribes.
The multitude of Dí tribes hated the service imposed by the Red Dí,
and so submitted to Jìn.
In autumn,
they met at Cuánhán,
and the multitude of Dí tribes submitted.
On this occasion,
the great officers wished to summon the Dí.
Xì Chéngzǐ said:
"I have heard that
without virtue,
nothing is better than diligence.
Without diligence,
how can one seek others?
If one can be diligent,
there will be a following.
Let us follow this.
The Odes say:
'King Wén was indeed diligent.'
If King Wén was still diligent,
how much more should we, who are deficient in virtue, be so?"
B7.11.5 In winter,
because of the disorder caused by the Xià clan in Chén, the Viscount of Chǔ
attacked Chén.
He told the people of Chén,
"Do not be alarmed!
I am going to punish the Shǎoxī clan."
He then entered Chén,
killed Xià Zhēngshū,
and tore him apart with chariots at the Lì Gate.
He then annexed Chén as a county.
The Marquis of Chén was in Jìn.
Shěn Shūshí had been on a mission to Qí.
On his return,
after reporting his mission
he withdrew.
The king sent to reproach him,
saying:
"Xià Zhēngshū acted without principle,
murdering his ruler.
I, with the other princes, punished and executed him.
The other princes and the county lords all congratulated me.
You alone did not congratulate me.
What is the reason?"
He replied:
"May I still offer an explanation?"
The king said:
"You may!"
He said:
"Xià Zhēngshū murdered his ruler;
his crime was great.
To punish and execute him
was the duty of a ruler.
However, people also have a saying:
'A man leads an ox to trample another's field,
and the other seizes his ox.'
The man who led the ox to trample
was indeed at fault;
but to seize his ox
is too heavy a punishment.
The other princes followed you,
saying they were punishing a crime.
Now you have annexed Chén as a county,
coveting its wealth.
You summoned the princes to punish a crime,
but you end by coveting wealth.
Is this not improper?"
The king said:
"Excellent!
I had not heard this.
To restore it,
is it possible?"
He replied:
"We humble folk have a saying:
'Take it from his bosom and give it to him.'"
The king then restored Chén as a state.
From each district he took one man and returned with them,
calling it the Xià Prefecture.
Therefore, the record says: "The Viscount of Chǔ entered Chén.
He sent Gōngsūn Níng and Yí Xíngfǔ back to Chén."
The record
shows that it was according to propriety.
B7.11.6 At the battle of Lì,
the Earl of Zhèng fled back,
and from that time Chǔ had not achieved its aim.
Zhèng had accepted the covenant at Chénlíng,
but also secretly served Jìn.
A7.12 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Twelfth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
Duke Líng of Chén was buried.
A7.12.2 The Viscount of Chǔ laid siege to Zhèng.
A7.12.3 In summer, in the sixth month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Xún Línfǔ of Jìn led an army and fought with the Viscount of Chǔ at Bì.
The army of Jìn was utterly defeated.
A7.12.4 In autumn, in the seventh month.
A7.12.5 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day Wùyín,
the Viscount of Chǔ extinguished Xiāo.
A7.12.6 Men of Jìn,
Sòng,
Wèi,
and Cáo made a covenant together at Qīngqiū.
A7.12.7 An army of Sòng attacked Chén.
Men of Wèi went to the rescue of Chén.
B7.12 The Commentary of Zuǒ, Twelfth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
the Viscount of Chǔ laid siege to Zhèng.
After seventeen days,
the people of Zhèng divined about suing for peace,
and it was not auspicious.
They divined about weeping in the great temple,
and also about bringing out chariots in the lanes,
and it was auspicious.
The people of the state wept greatly,
and those guarding the walls all cried.
The Viscount of Chǔ withdrew his army.
The people of Zhèng repaired their walls.
He advanced and again besieged it,
and in the third month, he captured it.
He entered by the Huáng Gate,
and reached the main road.
The Earl of Zhèng, baring his shoulder and leading a sheep,
came to meet him,
saying:
"I, not favored by Heaven,
have been unable to serve you,
causing you, my lord, to harbor anger
and bring it to my humble city.
This is my crime.
How dare I not listen to your commands?
If you take me captive to the south of the river
to populate the seacoast,
I will obey.
If you divide my land and bestow it on the other princes,
making me and my people their servants,
I will obey.
But if, in your kindness, you remember our former friendship,
and seek blessings from the spirits of Lì, Xuān, Huán, and Wǔ,
not extinguishing my altars of soil and grain,
but allowing me to change and serve you,
placing me among your nine counties,
that would be your kindness,
and my wish,
though I dare not hope for it.
I venture to lay bare my heart;
may you, my lord, consider it."
The king's attendants said:
"Do not grant it.
To gain a state, there should be no pardon."
The king said:
"Their ruler can humble himself before others;
he will surely be able to trust and employ his people.
How can we hope to seize his state?"
He withdrew thirty li
and granted them peace.
Pān Wāng entered to make the covenant,
and Zǐ Liáng went out as a hostage.
B7.12.2 In the summer, in the sixth month,
the Jìn army went to rescue Zhèng.
Xún Línfù commanded the central army,
with Xiān Hú as his assistant;
Shì Huì commanded the upper army,
with Xì Kè as his assistant;
Zhào Shuò commanded the lower army,
with Luán Shū as his assistant.
Zhào Kuò and Zhào Yīngqí were the senior officers of the central army,
Gǒng Shuò and Hán Chuān were the senior officers of the upper army,
Xún Shǒu and Zhào Tóng were the senior officers of the lower army.
Hán Jué was the Marshal.
When they reached the Yellow River,
they heard that Zhèng had already made peace with Chǔ.
Huánzǐ wished to turn back,
saying:
"If we cannot reach Zhèng in time and yet exhaust the people,
what use is it?
Let Chǔ return, and then we can act,
it will not be too late."
Suí Wǔzǐ said:
"Good.
I have heard that in employing an army,
one observes the cracks and then acts.
If virtue, punishments, governance, affairs, statutes, and rites are not neglected,
they cannot be opposed,
and one should not campaign against them.
The ruler of Chǔ chastised Zhèng,
angered by its duplicity
and pitying its humility.
He attacked when it rebelled,
and spared it when it submitted.
Thus, virtue and punishments were accomplished.
Attacking the rebellious
is punishment;
being gentle with the submissive
is virtue.
Both are established.
Last year he entered Chén,
this year he entered Zhèng,
yet the people are not weary,
and the ruler has no resentment or slander,
so governance has its constant principles.
When they raise the army with the Jīngshī formation,
merchants, farmers, artisans, and traders
do not abandon their occupations,
and the infantry and charioteers are harmonious,
so affairs are not disrupted.
Wěi Áo, as Prime Minister,
selected the excellent statutes of the state of Chǔ.
When the army marches,
the right flank guards the chariots,
the left gathers bedding,
the vanguard scouts for ambushes,
the center makes decisions,
the rear provides strong support.
All officers act according to their signals,
and military administration is prepared without orders,
so they are able to use the statutes.
In the ruler's appointments,
among those of the same surname, he selects from among his kin;
among those of different surnames, he selects from the old families.
In appointments, he does not neglect virtue;
in rewards, he does not neglect merit.
The aged receive added kindness,
travelers receive hospitality.
Noble and commoner,
each has distinguishing garments and insignia.
The noble have constant dignity,
the humble have degrees of authority,
so rites are not violated.
Virtue established, punishments carried out,
governance accomplished, affairs timely,
statutes followed, rites in order—
how can one oppose them?
Advance when you see the opportunity,
retreat when you know the difficulty,
this is the good way of the army.
Annex the weak, attack the benighted,
this is the good constant principle of warfare.
You should rather put your army in order and manage your warfare!
There are still those who are weak and benighted,
why must it be Chǔ?
Zhònghuǐ had a saying:
'Seize the disordered, subdue the perishing,'
that is annexing the weak.
The 'Zhuó' ode says:
'Oh, splendid the king's host!
It nurtures the times of darkness,'
that is attacking the benighted.
The 'Wǔ' ode says:
'None can rival such achievements.'
To soothe the weak and attack the benighted,
in order to strive for the achievements' domain,
is permissible."
Zhìzǐ said:
"It cannot be.
The reason Jìn became hegemon
was due to martial armies and forceful ministers.
Now to lose the feudal lords
cannot be called forceful;
to have an enemy and not pursue
cannot be called martial.
To lose hegemony because of us
is worse than death.
Moreover, we have raised a full army and set out;
to hear the enemy is strong and retreat
is not manly.
To be appointed army commander,
and end up being unmanly—
only you gentlemen are capable of that,
I will not do it."
He then crossed the river with the assistant of the central army.
Zhī Zhuāngzǐ said:
"This army is in peril!
The Zhōuyì has it,
in the hexagram Shī ䷆ changing to Lín ䷒,
it says:
'An army sets out with discipline;
if not good,
it is ominous.'
For affairs to proceed smoothly and succeed is good;
to go against this is not.
The multitude scattered becomes weak,
a river blocked becomes a marsh.
Having discipline means being able to control oneself,
hence it is called discipline. If not good,
it means discipline is exhausted.
Full and then exhausted,
obstructed and not unified,
that is why it is ominous.
Not proceeding is called Lín,
having a commander but not following him—
what Lín is greater than this?
This refers to it.
If they indeed meet the enemy,
they will certainly be defeated.
Zhìzǐ will bear the blame for it;
even if he escapes and returns,
he will surely have great misfortune."
Hán Xiànzǐ said to Huánzǐ:
"Zhìzǐ has led a contingent force to disaster,
your crime is great.
You are the supreme commander;
if the army does not obey orders,
whose crime is it?
To lose an ally and destroy an army
is a crime already heavy;
it would be better to advance.
If the affair is not successful,
the blame will be shared.
Rather than bearing the crime alone,
if the six of us share it,
is that not better?"
The army then crossed the river.
The ruler of Chǔ moved his army north and halted at Yán.
Shěn Yǐn commanded the central army,
Zǐ Zhòng commanded the left,
Zǐ Fǎn commanded the right.
They were about to water their horses at the river and return.
Hearing that the Jìn army had already crossed,
the king wished to turn back,
but his favorite Wǔ Shēn wished to fight.
The Prime Minister Sūnshū Áo did not wish to,
saying:
"Last year we entered Chén,
this year we entered Zhèng,
it is not that we have had no affairs.
If we fight and are not victorious,
will Shēn's flesh be enough to eat?"
Shēn said:
"If the affair is successful,
then Sūnshū will be without strategy.
If not successful,
Shēn's flesh will be with the Jìn army,
how could you eat it?"
The Prime Minister turned his chariot southward
and reversed the banners.
Wǔ Shēn spoke to the king, saying:
"Jìn's administrators are new,
and cannot enforce orders.
Their assistant Xiān Hú is stubborn, cruel, and unkind,
and unwilling to obey orders.
As for their three commanders,
they act arbitrarily without achieving results.
They listen but have no superior,
to whom should the multitude turn?
On this campaign,
the Jìn army is sure to be defeated.
Moreover, for a ruler to flee from a minister,
what would become of the altars of soil and grain?"
The king was troubled by this,
and told the Prime Minister to change the chariots' direction
and head north,
halting at Guǎn to await them.
The Jìn army was between Áo and Qiāo.
Huáng Xū of Zhèng sent an envoy to the Jìn army,
saying:
"Zhèng's alignment with Chǔ is
a matter of state survival,
and they harbor no disloyalty.
The Chǔ army, having won sudden victories, has grown arrogant;
their troops are weary,
and they are unprepared.
If you attack them,
with the Zhèng army as reinforcement,
the Chǔ army is sure to be defeated."
Zhìzǐ said:
"Defeating Chǔ and subduing Zhèng—it all depends on this.
We must agree to it!"
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"Since Chǔ conquered Yōng,
its ruler has not a day failed to admonish his people, instructing them on the hardships of livelihood,
the unpredictability of calamity,
and the necessity of vigilance without slackening.
In the military,
he has not a day failed to inspect the troops
and warn them
that victory cannot be taken for granted,
citing Zhòu's hundred victories yet ultimate lack of heirs,
and instructing them with the examples of Ruò'áo
and Fén Mào,
who opened up mountains and forests with rough carts and humble attire.
His admonition is:
'The people's livelihood lies in diligence;
diligence ensures no want.'
This cannot be called arrogance.
The late senior official Zǐ Fàn once said:
'An army in the right is strong;
in the wrong, it is weak.'
We, lacking virtue,
have provoked resentment from Chǔ.
We are in the wrong, Chǔ is in the right;
this cannot be called weakness.
Their ruler's army is divided into two divisions,
each division has a company,
and each company has its subunits.
The right division begins at dawn,
counting until noon,
then the left takes over,
continuing until dusk.
Inner officers take turns on night duty
to guard against emergencies.
This cannot be called unprepared.
Zǐ Liáng,
an outstanding man of Zhèng,
and Shī Shū,
a respected figure of Chǔ,
with Shī Shū entering into an alliance
and Zǐ Liáng in Chǔ,
shows Chǔ and Zhèng are close.
They come urging us to fight—
if we win, they will come to us;
if not, they will go to Chǔ,
using us as a test!
Zhèng cannot be followed."
Zhào Kuò and Zhào Tóng said:
"Since leading the army here,
we have sought only the enemy.
To defeat the enemy and gain an ally—
what more is there to wait for?
We must follow Zhìzǐ!"
Zhì Jì said:
"Yuán and Píng are followers of calamity."
Zhào Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Luán Bó is excellent!
If his words are implemented,
they will surely benefit Jìn long-term."
The Chǔ junior minister went to the Jìn army,
saying:
"Our ruler, having suffered misfortune in youth,
is not skilled in rhetoric.
Hearing that two former rulers traveled this route,
it was to instruct and pacify Zhèng;
how dare we seek offense from Jìn?
Gentlemen, do not linger long!"
Suí Jì replied:
"Formerly, King Píng commanded our late ruler Wén Hóu:
'Together with Zhèng, assist the Zhōu royal house,
and do not neglect the king's commands!'
Now Zhèng does not comply,
so our ruler has sent his ministers to question Zhèng;
how dare we trouble your envoy?
We respectfully acknowledge your ruler's message."
Zhìzǐ considered this flattery,
sent Zhào Kuò to amend it,
saying:
"The envoy misspoke.
Our ruler sent his ministers to move the great state's tracks from Zhèng,
saying:
'Do not avoid the enemy!'
His ministers cannot evade this command."
The Chǔ ruler again sent to seek peace with Jìn,
and the Jìn people agreed,
setting a date for the covenant.
Chǔ's Xǔ Bó drove for Yuè Bó,
with Shè Shū as chariot right,
to challenge the Jìn army.
Xǔ Bó said:
"I have heard that in challenging,
the driver lowers banners, grazes the enemy ramparts, and returns."
Yuè Bó said:
"I have heard that in challenging,
the left shoots with fine arrows,
takes the reins from the driver,
the driver dismounts,
adjusts the horses and reins, and returns."
Shè Shū said:
"I have heard that in challenging,
the right enters the enemy ramparts,
cuts off ears, captures prisoners, and returns."
Each performed as they had heard and returned.
The Jìn pursued them,
attacking from left and right.
Yuè Bó shot horses on the left
and men on the right,
halting the pursuit.
He had but one arrow left.
A deer appeared ahead;
he shot it, hitting the spine.
Jìn's Bào Guǐ was behind them;
Shè Shū offered the deer,
saying:
"As the season is not right
and game offerings have not arrived,
I dare present this to your followers."
Bào Guǐ stopped them,
saying:
"Their left is skilled in shooting,
their right eloquent—
they are gentlemen."
Thus they escaped.
Jìn's Wèi Qí sought a ducal clan position
but failed,
and in anger,
wished to ruin the Jìn army.
He requested to challenge,
but was refused.
He requested to be an envoy,
and was permitted.
He went,
requested battle,
and returned.
Chǔ's Pān Dǎng pursued him;
reaching Yíng Marsh,
seeing six deer,
he shot one and turned to offer it,
saying:
"You have military affairs;
perhaps your hunters lack fresh game?
I dare offer this to your followers."
Shū Dǎng ordered him to leave.
Zhào Zhān sought a minister rank but failed,
and was angry about missing the Chǔ challengers;
he requested to provoke battle,
but was refused.
He requested to summon a covenant,
was permitted,
and went with Wèi Qí under orders.
Xì Xiànzǐ said:
"Two resentful men have gone;
if unprepared,
we will surely be defeated."
Zhìzǐ said:
"The Zhèng people urged battle,
but we dared not follow;
the Chǔ seek peace,
yet we cannot befriend them.
The army has no fixed orders—
what use is much preparation?"
Shì Jì said:
"Preparation is wise.
If those two anger Chǔ,
and Chǔ attacks us,
we will lose the army soon—
better to prepare.
If Chǔ means no harm,
removing preparation to covenant
harms friendship little;
if they come with malice,
with preparation,
we will not be defeated.
Moreover, even when lords meet,
guards are not withdrawn—
as a precaution."
Zhìzǐ would not agree.
Shì Jì had Gǒng Shuò and Hán Chuān lead seven ambushes before Áo,
so the upper army was not defeated.
Zhào Yīngqí had his men prepare boats by the river first,
so they crossed first after defeat.
Pān Dǎng, having pursued Wèi Qí,
and Zhào Zhān arriving at the Chǔ camp at night,
spread a mat outside the camp gate,
and sent his men inside.
The King of Chǔ had thirty chariots for the "expansive" formation,
divided into left and right divisions.
The right division would harness the horses at cockcrow,
and rest at midday;
the left division would then take over,
resting at sunset.
Xǔ Yǎn drove the chariot for the right division,
with Yǎng Yóujī as the right-hand warrior;
Péng Míng drove the chariot for the left division,
with Qū Dàng as the right-hand warrior.
On the day yǐmǎo,
the king rode in the left division chariot
to pursue Zhào Zhān.
Zhào Zhān abandoned his chariot and fled into the woods,
Qū Dàng grappled with him,
and seized his armor skirt.
The men of Jìn, fearing that the two commanders would provoke the Chǔ army,
sent armored chariots to meet them.
Pān Dǎng, seeing the dust they raised,
sent a galloping messenger to report:
"The Jìn army is coming!"
The men of Chǔ also feared that their king would enter the Jìn ranks,
and so they advanced to deploy their battle lines.
Sūn Shū said:
"Advance!
It is better that we press upon others,
than that others press upon us.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Ten great war chariots,
to lead and open the march'—
this is to take the initiative.
The *Military Annals* says:
'Taking the initiative can seize the enemy's resolve'—
we should press the attack."
So they swiftly advanced their troops,
chariots charging, soldiers running,
and fell upon the Jìn army.
Huánzǐ, not knowing what to do,
had the drums beaten in the army, saying:
"Whoever crosses the river first will be rewarded!"
The central and lower armies fought for the boats,
and the fingers of those in the boats could be scooped up by the handful.
The Jìn army shifted to the right,
but the upper army did not move.
Gōng Yǐn Qí led the soldiers of the right flank
to pursue the lower army.
The King of Chǔ sent Táng Jiǎo and Cài Jiūjū to inform Marquis Huì of Táng, saying:
"I, lacking virtue and being greedy,
have encountered a great enemy—
this is my fault.
However, if Chǔ is not victorious,
it would be your shame as well.
I dare to borrow your divine power
to aid the Chǔ army."
He ordered Pān Dǎng
to lead forty reserve chariots,
to follow the Marquis of Táng
as the left flank,
to pursue the upper army.
Jū Bó said:
"Shall we wait for them?"
Suí Jì said:
"The Chǔ army is now at its peak;
if they concentrate on us,
our army will surely be wiped out.
It is better to gather our forces and withdraw.
To share the blame and preserve the people—
is that not acceptable?"
They covered the rear of their troops and retreated,
and were not defeated.
The king saw the right division,
and was about to mount it.
Qū Dàng blocked the door,
saying:
"Your Majesty began with this,
and must also end with it."
From then on, in Chǔ, the left division took precedence in the "expansive" formation.
Some men of Jìn had their chariots stuck in a rut,
and could not advance;
the men of Chǔ taught them to remove the crossbar.
They advanced a little,
but the horses turned around;
they were again taught to pull out the pennants
and throw them on the yoke,
and only then got out.
Looking back, they said:
"We are not as practiced at fleeing as a great state."
Zhào Zhān
used his two fine horses to ferry his elder brother and uncle across,
and returned with other horses.
Encountering the enemy and unable to escape,
he abandoned his chariot and fled into the woods.
Minister Féng was riding with his two sons,
and told his sons not to look back.
They looked back and said:
"Old Zhào is behind."
He was angry with them,
made them get down,
pointed to a tree and said:
"I will recover your bodies here."
He handed Zhào Zhān the reins,
and thus saved him.
The next day,
he went to the marked spot to recover the bodies,
and both were found dead under the tree.
Chǔ's Xióng Fújī captured Zhī Yīng,
and Zhī Zhuāngzǐ
led his clan back to rescue him,
with Chú Wǔzǐ driving the chariot,
and many soldiers of the lower army following them.
Every time he shot an arrow,
he would draw it,
select it,
and put it in Chúzǐ's quiver.
Chúzǐ angrily said:
"You are not seeking your son,
but are fond of arrow shafts—
the rushes of Dǒngzé,
could they ever be exhausted?"
Zhī Jì said:
"If I do not capture someone else's son,
how can I get my own son back?
This is why I cannot shoot carelessly."
He shot Lián Yǐn Xiānglǎo,
captured him,
and carried off his corpse;
he shot Prince Gǔchén,
and took him prisoner.
He returned with both of them.
By dusk,
the Chǔ army was encamped at Bì.
The remnants of the Jìn army could not maintain formation,
and crossed the river at night,
making noise throughout the night.
On the day bǐngchén,
the Chǔ supply train reached Bì,
and then encamped at Héngyōng.
Pān Dǎng said:
"Why does Your Majesty not build a martial mound
and collect the Jìn corpses to make a jīngguàn?
I have heard
that after defeating an enemy, one must show one's descendants,
so as not to forget the martial achievements."
The King of Chǔ said:
"This is not something you understand.
In writing,
'stopping spears' makes the character for 'martial'.
When King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
he composed the *Odes*, saying:
'We gather up our shields and spears,
we sheathe our bows and arrows.
We seek virtuous conduct,
to spread throughout this Xià—
truly, the king preserves it.'
He also composed *Wǔ*,
whose final stanza says:
'To firmly establish your achievements.'
Its third stanza says:
'Spreading this continuously,
we go forth only seeking stability.'
Its sixth stanza says:
'Pacifying the myriad states,
repeatedly having abundant years.'
The martial,
is to prohibit violence, to cease weapons, to preserve greatness,
to establish merit, to pacify the people,
to harmonize the masses, to enrich wealth—
therefore, we cause our descendants not to forget its principles.
Now I have caused the bones of two states to be exposed—
this is violence;
displaying troops to intimidate the feudal lords—
this is not ceasing weapons;
being violent and not ceasing weapons—
how can we preserve greatness?
With Jìn still existing,
how can we establish merit?
There are still many desires of the people that we go against—
how can the people be pacified?
Lacking virtue yet forcibly contending with the feudal lords—
how can we harmonize the masses?
Taking advantage of others' crises
and finding peace in others' chaos,
considering it one's own glory—
how can we enrich wealth?
The martial has seven virtues,
and I have none of them—
what can I show to my descendants?
Let us build a temple for the former rulers,
to report the completion of the affair, that is all.
The martial is not my achievement.
In ancient times, enlightened kings attacked the disrespectful,
took their leaders and buried them,
making a great execution,
and thus had jīngguàn
to punish the wicked.
Now there is no crime to be found,
and the people were all loyal
and died fulfilling their lord's commands—
what reason is there to make a jīngguàn?"
He sacrificed at the Yellow River,
built a temple for the former rulers,
reported the completion of the task, and returned.
B7.12.3 In this campaign,
Shí Zhì of Zhèng actually brought the Chǔ army into the city,
intending to partition Zhèng,
and establish Gōngzǐ Yúchén.
On Xīnwèi,
Zhèng killed Pú Shū and Zǐfú.
The gentleman says:
"What Shǐ Yì meant by
'do not rely on disorder'
refers to this kind of situation.
The *Shī* says:
'In the chaos and distress of separation,
where shall we find our home?'
It is to those who rely on disorder that it returns!"
B7.12.4 The Earl of Zhèng and the Viscount of Xǔ went to Chǔ.
B7.12.5 In autumn,
the Jìn army returned.
Huánzǐ requested death,
and the Marquis of Jìn intended to grant it.
Shì Zhēnzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"It cannot be done.
At the battle of Chéngpú,
the Jìn army feasted for three days,
yet Duke Wén still wore a worried expression.
His attendants said:
'To be worried when there is joy,
is that like being joyful when there is worry?'
The duke said:
'Dé Chén is still alive,
my worry is not yet over.
A cornered beast will still fight,
how much more a chief minister of a state?'
When Chǔ killed Zǐ Yù,
then the duke's joy became evident.
He said:
'No one can harm me anymore.'
This was Jìn's second victory
