and Chǔ's second defeat,
and because of this, Chǔ did not contend for two generations.
Now Heaven may be giving Jìn a great warning,
and if we kill Línfù
to double Chǔ's victory,
will we not perhaps long fail to contend?
Línfù in serving his lord,
when advancing thinks of exhausting his loyalty,
when retiring thinks of mending his faults.
He is a defender of the altars of soil and grain.
How can we kill him?
His defeat
is like an eclipse of the sun or moon;
what does it diminish of their brightness?"
The Marquis of Jìn restored him to his position.
B7.12.6 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Xiāo.
Huá Jiāo of Sòng, with men of Cài, went to rescue Xiāo.
The men of Xiāo imprisoned Xióngxiàng Yíliáo and Gōngzǐ Bǐng.
The king said:
"Do not kill them,
and I will withdraw."
The men of Xiāo killed them.
The king was enraged,
and thereupon besieged Xiāo.
Xiāo collapsed.
Shēn Gōng Wūchén said:
"The troops are suffering much from the cold."
The king inspected the three armies,
patting and encouraging them,
and the officers and men of the three armies all felt as if clad in silk wadding.
Thereupon they pressed close to Xiāo.
Huán Wúshè spoke with Sīmǎ Mǎo,
and called out to Shēn Shūzhǎn.
Shūzhǎn said:
"Do you have wheat yeast?"
He replied:
"No."
"Do you have mountain xióngqióng?"
He replied:
"No."
"What about the bellyache from river fish?"
He replied:
"Look into the dry well and save me."
"If you make a straw cord,
and weep by the well, I will come."
The next day,
Xiāo collapsed.
Shēn Shū looked into the well,
and there was the straw cord,
so he called out and brought him out.
B7.12.7 Yuán Hú of Jìn, Huá Jiāo of Sòng, Kǒng Dá of Wèi, and men of Cáo made a covenant together at Qīngqiū,
saying:
"Compassion for the distressed,
punishment for the disloyal."
Here the ministers are not recorded,
because they did not fulfill their words.
B7.12.8 Because of the covenant,
Sòng attacked Chén.
The men of Wèi rescued them,
and Kǒng Dá said:
"Our former ruler had a covenant with them.
If a great state punishes us,
I will die for it."
A7.13 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Xuán, Year 13*
A7.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the army of Qí attacked Jǔ.
A7.13.2 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Sòng.
A7.13.3 In autumn,
there were locusts.
A7.13.4 In winter,
Jìn killed its great officer Xiān Hú.
B7.13 *The Commentary of Zuo, Duke Xuán, Year 13*
B7.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the army of Qí attacked Jǔ,
because Jǔ relied on Jìn and did not serve Qí.
B7.13.2 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Sòng,
because they had rescued Xiāo.
The gentleman says:
"Of the covenant at Qīngqiū,
only Sòng could be exempt from blame."
B7.13.3 In autumn,
the Red Dí attacked Jìn,
reaching Qīng,
because Xiān Hú had summoned them.
B7.13.4 In winter,
the men of Jìn investigated the defeat at Bì and the army at Qīng,
laid the blame on Xiān Hú and killed him,
exterminating his entire clan.
The gentleman says:
"'When evil comes,
one brings it upon oneself'—
this refers to Xiān Hú, does it not!"
B7.13.5 Regarding the covenant at Qīngqiū,
Jìn, because Wèi had rescued Chén,
punished them.
They sent a man who did not leave,
saying:
"If the guilt is not assigned to anyone,
we will bring our army against you."
Kǒng Dá said:
"If it benefits the altars of soil and grain,
I beg to offer myself as the scapegoat.
The guilt lies with me.
I am the one in charge of government,
and to resist the punishment of a great state—
on whom shall the responsibility fall?
I will die for it."
A7.14 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Xuán, Year 14*
A7.14.1 In the fourteenth year, in spring,
Wèi killed its great officer Kǒng Dá.
A7.14.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on Rénshēn,
the Earl of Cáo, Shòu, died.
A7.14.3 The Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng.
A7.14.4 In autumn, in the ninth month,
the Viscount of Chǔ besieged Sòng.
A7.14.5 They buried Duke Wén of Cáo.
A7.14.6 In winter,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the Marquis of Qí at Gǔ.
B7.14 *The Commentary of Zuo, Duke Xuán, Year 14*
B7.14.1 In the fourteenth year, in spring,
Kǒng Dá hanged himself and died.
The men of Wèi used this to satisfy Jìn
and were spared.
Thereupon they announced to the various states:
"Our unworthy ruler had a disobedient minister, Dá,
who stirred up trouble between our humble city and the great state.
He has now suffered for his crime.
We dare to announce this."
The men of Wèi, considering his past service,
again gave him a wife for his son,
and restored him to his position.
B7.14.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng,
because of the affair at Bì.
He announced it to the various states,
held a review, and returned.
This was the plan of Zhōngháng Huánzǐ,
who said:
"Show them our order,
and let them plan and come to us."
The people of Zhèng were afraid,
and sent Zǐ Zhāng to replace Zǐ Liáng in Chǔ.
The Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ,
to plan regarding Jìn.
Zhèng considered Zǐ Liáng to be well-mannered,
and therefore summoned him.
B7.14.3 The King of Chǔ sent Shēn Zhōu on a diplomatic mission to Qí,
saying:
"Do not ask for passage through Sòng."
He also sent Prince Féng on a mission to Jìn,
without asking for passage through Zhèng.
Shēn Zhōu, because of the incident at Mèng Zhū, bore a grudge against Sòng,
and said:
"Zhèng is clear-sighted, Sòng is deaf.
The Jìn mission will come to no harm,
but I will certainly die."
The King said:
"If they kill you,
I will attack them."
[Shēn Zhōu] presented his son Xī and then departed.
When he reached Sòng,
the people of Sòng detained him.
Huá Yuán said:
"To pass through our territory without asking for passage
is to treat us as a border state.
To treat us as a border state
means our destruction.
If we kill their envoy,
they will certainly attack us.
If they attack us,
we will also be destroyed.
Destruction is the same in either case."
They then killed him.
When the King of Chǔ heard of this,
he flung back his sleeves and rose.
His attendants caught up with him with his shoes at the Zhì Huáng gate,
with his sword at the outer gate of his sleeping quarters,
and with his chariot at the market of Pú Xū.
In autumn, in the ninth month,
the King of Chǔ besieged Sòng.
B7.14.4 In winter,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the Marquis of Qí at Gǔ,
and saw Yàn Huánzǐ.
He spoke with him about Lǔ,
and was pleased.
Huánzǐ told Gāo Xuānzǐ:
"Zǐjiā will likely perish!
He is attached to Lǔ.
Attachment leads to greed,
and greed leads to scheming against others.
If one schemes against others,
others will also scheme against oneself.
If a whole state schemes against him,
how can he avoid perishing?"
B7.14.5 Mèng Xiànzǐ said to the Duke:
"Your servant has heard that when a small state seeks to avoid trouble from a large state,
it sends missions and presents gifts;
thus there are a hundred kinds of court offerings;
when it attends court and presents its achievements,
thus there are elegant appearances and fine decorations,
excellent and beautiful, with additional gifts,
planning how to avoid trouble.
If punishment is inflicted and then bribes are offered,
it will be too late.
Now Chǔ is at Sòng,
may Your Lordship consider this!"
The Duke was pleased.
A7.15 The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Fifteenth Year of Duke Xuān
A7.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the King of Chǔ at Sòng.
A7.15.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
the people of Sòng and the people of Chǔ made peace.
A7.15.3 In the sixth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
the army of Jìn destroyed the Red Dí of Lù,
and brought the Earl of Lù, Yīng'ér, back with them.
A7.15.4 The people of Qín attacked Jìn.
A7.15.5 Wáng Zházǐ killed Shào Bó
and Máo Bó.
A7.15.6 In autumn,
there was a plague of locusts.
A7.15.7 Zhòngsūn Miè met with Qí's Gāo Gù at Wúlóu.
A7.15.8 For the first time, land tax was levied according to the area of fields.
A7.15.9 In winter,
caterpillars were produced.
A7.15.10 There was famine.
B7.15 The Commentary: The Fifteenth Year of Duke Xuān
B7.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
Gōngsūn Guīfù met with the King of Chǔ at Sòng.
B7.15.2 The people of Sòng sent Yuè Yīngqí to report their urgent situation to Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn wished to rescue them.
Bó Zōng said:
"It cannot be done.
The ancients had a saying:
'Even if the whip is long,
it does not reach the horse's belly.'
Heaven is now granting power to Chǔ,
we cannot contend with them.
Even with Jìn's strength,
can we go against Heaven?
A proverb says:
'High or low depends on the mind.'
Rivers and marshes receive filth,
mountains and marshes conceal venomous creatures,
fine jade hides flaws,
and a ruler of a state endures disgrace;
this is the Way of Heaven.
May Your Lordship wait!"
He then stopped.
He sent Xiè Yáng to go to Sòng,
to tell them not to surrender to Chǔ,
saying:
"The army of Jìn has all been raised,
and will arrive soon."
The people of Zhèng captured him and presented him to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ offered him rich bribes,
to make him say the opposite.
He refused.
After three times, he agreed.
They had him mount a siege tower chariot,
to call out to the people of Sòng and inform them.
He then conveyed his lord's command.
The King of Chǔ was about to kill him,
and sent someone to say to him:
"You already agreed to my proposal,
but then went back on it;
what is the reason?
It is not that I am untrustworthy,
but you abandoned it.
Quickly go to your punishment!"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that
a ruler who can issue commands acts righteously,
a minister who can receive commands acts faithfully,
and faith carrying out righteousness brings benefit.
To plan without losing benefit,
in order to protect the altars of soil and grain,
is the master of the people.
Righteousness does not admit of double faith,
faith does not admit of double commands.
For Your Lordship to bribe your servant
is to not understand commands.
Having received a command to go forth,
I would rather die than fail;
how could I be bribed?
Your servant's agreement with Your Lordship
was to accomplish the command.
To die and accomplish the command
is your servant's good fortune.
If my humble lord has a faithful minister,
and I, your humble servant, achieve completion
in death,
what more could I seek?"
The King of Chǔ released him and let him return.
In summer, in the fifth month,
the army of Chǔ was about to leave Sòng,
when Shēn Xī knocked his head on the ground before the King's horses,
saying:
"Wú Wèi knew he would die
but did not dare to neglect the King's command;
the King has abandoned his word."
The King could not reply.
Shēn Shūshí was driving,
and said:
"Build houses,
send back the farmers to their fields,
and Sòng will certainly obey your command."
He followed this advice.
The people of Sòng were afraid,
and sent Huá Yuán to enter the Chǔ army at night.
He climbed onto Zǐ Fǎn's bed,
roused him,
and said:
"My humble lord has sent Yuán to report our distress,
saying:
'Our poor city exchanges children to eat,
and splits bones for fuel.
Even so,
a treaty made under the city walls,
even if it means the state perishes,
we cannot accept.
If you withdraw thirty lǐ from us,
we will obey your command.'"
Zǐ Fǎn was afraid,
made a covenant with him,
and reported to the king.
They withdrew thirty li,
and Sòng made peace with Chǔ.
Huá Yuán served as a hostage.
The covenant said:
"We shall not deceive you,
and you shall not be suspicious of us."
B7.15.3 The wife of Lùzǐ Yīng'ér
was the elder sister of Jìn Jǐnggōng.
Fēng Shū, who was in charge of the government, killed her,
and also injured the eyes of Lùzǐ.
The Marquis of Jìn was about to attack him.
All the great officers said:
"It cannot be done.
Fēng Shū has three outstanding talents;
it would be better to wait for his successor."
Bó Zōng said:
"He must be attacked.
The Dí have five crimes;
though their talents are many,
what good does it do?
They do not sacrifice,
this is the first.
They are addicted to wine,
this is the second.
They abandoned Zhòng Zhāng and seized the lands of the Lí clan,
this is the third.
They cruelly treated our Bó Jī,
this is the fourth.
They injured their ruler's eyes,
this is the fifth.
They rely on their outstanding talents,
and do not cultivate virtue;
this increases their crimes.
Their successors perhaps will reverently uphold virtue and righteousness
to serve the spirits and the people,
and thereby strengthen their mandate;
how can we wait for that?
Not to punish the guilty,
saying 'we will wait for the successor,'
if the successor then has justifications and we attack,
would that not be unacceptable?
To rely on talent and numbers
is the way to perish.
King Zhòu of Shāng followed this,
and therefore was destroyed.
When Heaven goes against the seasons, it causes calamities;
when Earth goes against its products, it causes prodigies;
when the people go against virtue, it causes disorder.
Disorder then gives rise to prodigies and calamities.
Thus in writing,
the character for 'correct' turned upside down becomes the character for 'deficient.'
All of this is present in the Dí."
The Marquis of Jìn followed him.
In the sixth month, on Guǐmǎo,
Jìn Xún Línfǔ defeated the Red Dí at Qūliáng.
On Xīnhài,
he extinguished Lù.
Fēng Shū fled to Wèi;
the men of Wèi delivered him to Jìn,
and the men of Jìn killed him.
B7.15.4 Wángsūn Sū contended for power with the Shào and
Máo clans.
He sent Wángzǐ Jié to kill Shào Dàigōng and Máo Bó Wèi,
and finally established Shào Xiāng.
B7.15.5 In autumn, in the seventh month,
Qín Huángōng attacked Jìn
and halted at Fǔshì.
On Rénwǔ,
the Marquis of Jìn drilled his troops at Jì,
to seize Dí territory,
established the Marquis of Lí, and returned.
When he reached Luò,
Wèi Kē defeated the Qín army at Fǔshì
and captured Dù Huí,
a man of great strength from Qín.
Earlier,
Wèi Wǔzǐ had a favored concubine,
who had no son.
When Wǔzǐ fell ill,
he commanded Kē, saying:
"You must marry her off."
When his illness became critical,
he then said:
"You must use her for burial!"
When he died,
Kē married her off,
saying:
"When the illness was critical, he was confused;
I follow his lucid command."
At the battle of Fǔshì,
Kē saw an old man tying grass
to trip Dù Huí.
Dù Huí stumbled and fell,
and so was captured.
At night, he dreamt of the old man, who said:
"I am the father of the woman you married off.
You followed your father's lucid command,
and therefore I repay you."
B7.15.6 The Marquis of Jìn rewarded Huánzǐ with a thousand households of Dí captives,
and also rewarded Shì Bó with the district of Guāyǎn,
saying:
"I obtained Dí territory;
it was your achievement.
Without you,
I would have lost Bó Shì."
Yángshé Zhí praised this reward,
saying:
"What the Zhōu Shū calls
'employing the employable and revering the reverent'
refers to this kind of thing.
Shì Bó employed Zhōngháng Bó;
the ruler trusted him,
and also employed Shì Bó.
This is what is called illustrious virtue.
The means by which King Wén founded Zhōu
did not exceed this.
Therefore the Shī says:
'He spread his gifts and founded Zhōu,'
meaning he was able to bestow.
Following this way,
what would not succeed?"
B7.15.7 The Marquis of Jìn sent Zhào Tóng to present Dí captives to Zhōu,
but he was disrespectful.
Liú Kānggōng said:
"Within ten years,
Yuán Shū will certainly have a great calamity.
Heaven has taken away his spirit."
B7.15.8 For the first time, land tax was levied per acre;
this was contrary to ritual.
Grain should not be taken beyond the traditional levy,
in order to enrich resources.
B7.15.9 In winter,
locust larvae appeared,
causing famine.
This was considered fortunate.
A7.16 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Xuān 16th Year
A7.16.1 In the sixteenth year, in spring,
the royal first month.
The men of Jìn extinguished the Red Dí tribes of Jiǎshì and Liúxū.
A7.16.2 In summer,
the Xuān Pavilion in Chéngzhōu caught fire.
A7.16.3 In autumn,
Bó Jī of Tán returned home.
A7.16.4 In winter,
there was a great harvest year.
B7.16 The Commentary of Zuǒ, Duke Xuān 16th Year
B7.16.1 In the sixteenth year, in spring,
Jìn Shì Huì led an army and extinguished the Red Dí tribes of Jiǎshì, Liúxū, and Duóchén.
In the third month,
he presented the Dí captives.
The Marquis of Jìn requested from the king,
and on Wùshēn,
with the fúmiǎn robe and crown, commanded Shì Huì to command the central army
and also be Grand Tutor.
Thereupon, the robbers of Jìn fled to Qín.
Yángshé Zhí said:
"I have heard it said:
'Yǔ promoted good men,
and the not-good men kept away'—
this refers to this situation.
The Shī says:
'Trembling with fear and caution,
as if facing a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice'—
this is when good men are in high position.
When good men are in high position,
then the state has no people who rely on luck.
A proverb says:
'When the people have much luck,
it is the state's misfortune'—
this refers to there being no good men."
B7.16.2 In summer,
the Xuān Pavilion in Chéngzhōu caught fire;
it was set by people.
In all cases of fire,
fire set by people is called 'fire,'
fire from Heaven is called 'calamity.'
B7.16.3 In autumn,
Bó Jī of Tán returned home;
she had been divorced.
B7.16.4 Because of the troubles with the Máo and
Shào clans,
the royal house was again in disorder,
and Wángsūn Sū fled to Jìn.
The men of Jìn restored him.
In winter,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Huì to pacify the royal house.
King Dìng hosted a feast for him.
Yuán Xiānggōng assisted with the rituals.
The meat was served in large, uncut pieces.
Wǔ Jì privately asked about the reason for this.
The king heard of it,
summoned Wǔzǐ, and said:
"Jìshì!
Have you not heard?
For royal feasts, there is the formal presentation of the whole sacrificial animal;
for banquets, the meat is divided on the stand.
A duke is entitled to the formal feast,
a minister to the banquet.
Such are the rituals of the royal house."
Wǔzǐ returned
and studied the canonical rituals,
in order to revise the laws of the state of Jìn.
A7.17 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 17 of Duke Xuān*
A7.17.1 In the seventeenth year, in spring,
in the king's first month, on the Gēngzǐ day,
Xǔ Nán Xīwǒ died.
A7.17.2 On the Dīngwèi day,
Cài Hóu Shēn died.
A7.17.3 In summer,
we buried Duke Zhāo of Xǔ.
A7.17.4 We buried Duke Wén of Cài.
A7.17.5 In the sixth month, on the Guǐmǎo day,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A7.17.6 On the Jǐwèi day,
our duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
and the Viscount of Zhū,
and they formed an alliance at Duàndào.
A7.17.7 In autumn,
our duke arrived from the meeting.
A7.17.8 In winter, in the eleventh month, on the Rénwǔ day,
our duke's younger brother Shū Xī died.
B7.17 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, Year 17 of Duke Xuān*
B7.17.1 In the seventeenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Kè to summon the state of Qí to a meeting.
The Duke of Qí Qìng had women hidden behind a curtain
and made them watch.
When Xìzǐ ascended,
the women laughed in the side chamber.
Xiànzǐ was enraged,
went out and swore, saying:
"If I do not avenge this,
may I never cross the river!"
Xiànzǐ returned first,
leaving Luán Jīnglú to await orders in Qí,
saying:
"If you do not secure Qí's compliance,
do not report back."
When Xìzǐ arrived,
he requested to attack Qí.
The Marquis of Jìn did not permit it.
He requested to use his own private forces,
but again it was not permitted.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gāo Gù, Yàn Ruò,
Cài Cháo, and Nánguō Yǎn to the meeting.
When they reached Liànyú, Gāo Gù fled back.
In summer,
they met at Duàndào,
to punish those with divided loyalties.
They swore an alliance at Juǎnchǔ,
excluding the men of Qí.
The men of Jìn seized Yàn Ruò at Yěwáng,
seized Cài Cháo at Yuán,
and seized Nánguō Yǎn at Wēn.
Miáo Bēnhuáng was on a mission,
and saw Yàn Huánzǐ.
Upon returning,
he spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"What crime did Yànzǐ commit?
In the past, when the feudal lords served our former lord,
they all acted as if they could not do enough,
but now they all say that our ministers are untrustworthy,
and the feudal lords all have divided loyalties.
The ruler of Qí feared he would not be treated with proper courtesy,
so he did not come out
but sent these four men.
His attendants tried to dissuade him,
saying:
'If you do not go out,
they will certainly seize our envoys.'
Therefore, Gāozǐ fled when he reached Liànyú.
These three men said:
'If it means severing our ruler's goodwill,
we would rather return and die.'
For this reason, they braved the danger and came.
If we had kindly welcomed them
to comfort those who would come.
Instead, we seized them,
thus confirming Qí's dissuaders,
have we not already erred?
To err and not correct it,
and to prolong it further,
until they come to regret it—
what benefit is there in that?
It allows those who turned back to have an excuse,
and harms those who came,
frightening the feudal lords.
What use is that?"
The men of Jìn relaxed their guard,
and they escaped.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
the Jìn army returned.
B7.17.2 Fàn Wǔzǐ was about to retire,
and summoned Wénzǐ, saying:
"Xiè!
I have heard that
those whose joy and anger follow proper patterns are few,
while those who are easily swayed are many.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'If the gentleman is angered,
disorder may quickly be stopped.
If the gentleman is pleased,
disorder may quickly cease.'
The joy and anger of a gentleman
are to stop disorder.
If they do not stop it,
they will certainly increase it.
Perhaps Xìzǐ wishes to stop disorder in Qí.
If not,
I fear he will increase it.
I am about to retire,
so let Xìzǐ fulfill his ambition;
perhaps then there will be relief.
You, follow the several ministers with respect."
He then requested to retire.
Xì Xiànzǐ took charge of the government.
B7.17.3 In winter,
our duke's younger brother Shū Xī died.
He was a full brother by the same mother.
In general, for the full brothers of the crown prince,
if the duke is alive, they are called 'gōngzǐ';
if he is not alive, they are called 'dì'.
In general, when they are called 'dì',
they are all full brothers by the same mother.
A7.18 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 18 of Duke Xuān*
A7.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn
and the heir of Wèi, Zāng, attacked Qí.
A7.18.2 Our duke attacked Qǐ.
A7.18.3 In summer, in the fourth month.
A7.18.4 In autumn, in the seventh month,
men of Zhū murdered the Viscount of Zēng in Zēng.
A7.18.5 On the Jiǎxū day,
Chǔzǐ Lǚ died.
A7.18.6 Gōngsūn Guīfù went to Jìn.
A7.18.7 In winter, in the tenth month, on the Rénxū day,
our duke died in the main chamber.
A7.18.8 Guīfù returned from Jìn,
reached Shēng,
and then fled to Qí.
B7.18 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, Year 18 of Duke Xuān*
B7.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn
and the heir of Wèi, Zāng, attacked Qí,
reaching Yánggǔ.
The Marquis of Qí met with the Marquis of Jìn,
swore an alliance at Zēng,
and sent his son, Gōngzǐ Qiáng, as a hostage to Jìn.
The Jìn army then returned.
Cài Cháo
and Nánguō Yǎn escaped back.
B7.18.2 In summer,
our duke sent someone to Chǔ to request troops,
intending to attack Qí.
B7.18.3 In autumn,
men of Zhū murdered the Viscount of Zēng in Zēng.
In general, when one's own people kill their ruler, it is called 'shì';
when outsiders do it, it is called 'qiāng'.
B7.18.4 King Zhuāng of Chǔ died,
and the Chǔ army did not set out.
Later, troops from Jìn were used,
and it was then that Chǔ had the campaign of Shǔ.
B7.18.5 Gōngsūn Guīfù, because Xiāng Zhòng had established the Duke,
was favored,
and wished to remove the Three Huán,
in order to strengthen the ducal house.
He plotted with the Duke,
and then went on a diplomatic mission to Jìn,
intending to use the men of Jìn to remove them.
In winter,
the Duke passed away.
Jì Wénzǐ spoke at court,
saying:
"The one who caused us to kill the rightful heir and establish a concubine's son, thereby losing great support,
was Zhòng, was he not!"
Zāng Xuānshū angrily said:
"At that time, you could not deal with it;
what crime do later generations bear?
If you wish to remove him,
I, Xǔ, request to remove him."
Thereupon, they expelled the Dōngmén clan.
Zǐjiā (i.e., Gōngsūn Guīfù) returned,
and upon reaching Shēng,
he set up an altar with curtains,
and reported his mission completion to his deputy.
After completing his report,
he bared his shoulder, bound up his hair,
took his position and wailed,
leaped three times, and then departed.
Thereupon, he fled to Qí.
The record says, "Guīfù returned from Jìn,"
praising him.
A8.1 《The First Year of Chénggōng, the Classic》
A8.1.1 First year, spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A8.1.2 In the second month, on Xīnyǒu,
we buried our lord, Duke Xuān.
A8.1.3 There was no ice.
A8.1.4 In the third month,
they instituted the Qiū Jiǎ.
A8.1.5 In summer,
Zāngsūn Xǔ and the Marquis of Jìn made a covenant at Chìjí.
A8.1.6 In autumn,
the royal army was utterly defeated at Máo Róng.
A8.1.7 In winter, the tenth month.
B8.1 《The First Year of Chénggōng, the Commentary》
B8.1.1 First year, spring.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Xiá Jiā to make peace with the Róng for the King.
Dān Xiànggōng went to Jìn to thank them for the peace.
Liú Kānggōng sought to take advantage of the Róng,
and was about to attack them.
Shūfú said:
"To break a covenant and deceive a great state,
this is certain to bring defeat.
Breaking a covenant is inauspicious;
deceiving a great state is unrighteous;
neither spirits nor men will assist,
how then can you achieve victory?"
He did not listen,
and thereupon attacked the Máo Róng.
In the third month, on Guǐwèi,
they were utterly defeated at Xúwúshì.
B8.1.2 Because of the threat from Qí,
they instituted the Qiū Jiǎ.
B8.1.3 Hearing that Qí was about to send forth a Chǔ army,
in summer,
they made a covenant at Chìjí.
In autumn,
a man from the King came to report the defeat.
In winter,
Zāng Xuānshū ordered the preparation of levies,
the repair of defenses, and the readiness of guard preparations,
saying:
"Qí and Chǔ have formed an alliance,
we have newly covenanted with Jìn,
Jìn and Chǔ contend for covenants,
a Qí army is certain to come.
Even if the men of Jìn attack Qí,
Chǔ will certainly rescue them,
meaning Qí and Chǔ are united against us.
Knowing the difficulty and being prepared, only then can one succeed."
A8.2 《The Second Year of Chénggōng, the Classic》
A8.2.1 Second year, spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern borders.
A8.2.2 In summer, the fourth month, on Bǐngxū,
Wèi's Sūn Liángfū led an army and fought with the Qí army at Xīnzhù,
the Wèi army was utterly defeated.
A8.2.3 In the sixth month, on Guǐyǒu,
Jìsūn Xíngfù,
Zāngsūn Xǔ,
Shūsūn Qiáorú,
Gōngsūn Yīngqí led an army to join with Jìn's Xì Kè,
Wèi's Sūn Liángfū,
Cáo's Gōngzǐ Shǒu, and fought with the Marquis of Qí at Ān,
the Qí army was utterly defeated.
A8.2.4 In autumn, the seventh month,
the Marquis of Qí sent Guó Zuǒ to the army.
On Jǐyǒu,
they made a covenant with Guó Zuǒ at Yuánlóu.
A8.2.5 In the eighth month, on Rénwǔ,
the Duke of Sòng, Bào, died.
A8.2.6 On Gēngyín,
the Marquis of Wèi, Sù, died.
A8.2.7 They took the fields of Wènyáng.
A8.2.8 In winter,
a Chǔ army,
a Zhèng army invaded Wèi.
A8.2.9 In the eleventh month,
the Duke met with Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Yīngqí at Shǔ.
A8.2.10 On Bǐngshēn,
the Duke and men of Chǔ,
men of Qín,
men of Sòng,
men of Chén,
men of Wèi,
men of Zhèng,
men of Qí,
men of Cáo,
men of Zhū,
men of Xuē,
men of Zēng made a covenant at Shǔ.
B8.2 《The Second Year of Chénggōng, the Commentary》
B8.2.1 Second year, spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern borders,
and besieged Lóng.
The favorite of Duke Qǐng, Lúpú Jiùkuí, attacked its gate.
The men of Lóng captured him.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Do not kill him,
I will make a covenant with you,
and will not enter your borders."
They did not listen,
killed him and displayed his corpse on the city wall.
The Marquis of Qí personally beat the drum,
and the soldiers scaled the walls.
After three days,
they took Lóng.
Thereupon, they advanced south to invade,
reaching Cháoqiū.
B8.2.2 The Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū, Shí Jì, Nìng Xiàng, Xiàng Qín to invade Qí,
and they encountered the Qí army.
Shízi (Shí Jì) wished to retreat.
Sūnzi (Sūn Liángfū) said:
"That cannot be.
To lead an army to attack others,
and upon encountering their army to retreat,
what will you say to the ruler?
If you knew you were incapable,
then you should not have set out.
Now that we have already encountered them,
it is better to fight."
In summer,
there was.
Shí Chéngzǐ (Shí Jì) said:
"The army is defeated,
if you, sir, do not wait a little,
the multitude fears complete destruction.
If you, sir, lose the army,
how will you report back on your mission?"
None replied.
He also said:
"You, sir,
are a minister of the state.
If you, sir, are lost,
it would be a disgrace.
You, sir, retreat with the multitude,
I will stay here."
And he reported
that many chariots were coming.
The Qí army then halted,
and encamped at Jūjū.
A man of Xīnzhù, Zhòngshū Yúxī,
rescued Sūn Huánzǐ (Sūn Liángfū),
and Huánzǐ was thereby spared.
Afterwards,
the people of Wèi rewarded him with a city,
but he declined it
and requested instead to have the curved chime-stand and
the decorated horse trappings for his court appearances.
This was granted to him.
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"What a pity!
It would have been better to give him more cities.
For vessels and titles
must not be lent to others—
they are what the ruler administers.
Titles give rise to trust,
trust preserves the vessels,
vessels embody ritual,
ritual carries out righteousness,
righteousness generates benefit,
benefit brings peace to the people—
these are the great principles of governance.
If they are lent to others,
it is giving away governance.
Once governance is lost,
the state will follow,
and it cannot be stopped."
B8.2.3 Sūn Huánzǐ returned to Xīnzhù,
but did not enter,
and proceeded to Jìn to request troops.
Zāng Xuānshū also went to Jìn
to request troops.
Both relied on Xì Xiànzǐ.
The Marquis of Jìn granted them seven hundred chariots.
Xìzǐ said:
"This is the levy of Chéngpú.
With the wisdom of the former ruler and the diligence of the former ministers,
we achieved victory.
Compared to the former ministers,
I am not fit to serve;
I request eight hundred chariots."
This was granted.
Xì Kè commanded the central army,
Shì Xiè assisted the upper army,
Luán Shū commanded the lower army,
Hán Jué served as Minister of War,
to rescue Lǔ
and Wèi.
Zāng Xuānshū met the Jìn army,
and guided them.
Jì Wénzǐ led troops to join them.
When they reached Wèi territory,
Hán Xiànzǐ was about to execute a man,
and Xì Xiànzǐ galloped over
to save him.
Upon arrival,
he had already been executed.
Xìzǐ then ordered the body to be displayed quickly,
and told his attendant:
"I did this to share the blame."
The army pursued the Qí army to Shēn.
On the rénshēn day of the sixth month,
the army reached the foot of Míjī.
The Marquis of Qí sent a request for battle,
saying:
"You have brought your ruler's army to our humble state;
our meager forces
request to meet you tomorrow morning."
The reply was:
"Jìn, Lǔ, and Wèi are brothers.
They came and reported:
'The great state constantly
vents its grievances on our land.'
Our ruler could not bear it,
and sent us, his ministers, to request from the great state
that we not allow our army to linger in your land.
We can advance but not retreat;
you need not trouble to command."
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Your agreement, sir,
is my wish;
if you do not agree,
we shall still meet."
Qí's Gāo Gù entered the Jìn army,
lifted a stone and threw it at someone,
captured him and mounted his chariot,
tied a mulberry root to it,
and paraded it around the Qí camp,
saying:
"Those who want courage, buy my leftover courage!"
On the guǐyǒu day,
the armies arrayed at Ān.
Bǐng Xià drove for the Marquis of Qí,
and Péng Chǒufǔ served as the right-hand guard.
Jìn's Xiè Zhāng drove for Xì Kè,
and Zhèngqiū Huǎn served as the right-hand guard.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"I will first wipe out these
and then eat breakfast."
He drove his horses without armor.
Xì Kè was wounded by an arrow,
and blood flowed to his shoes,
but he did not stop the drumbeat,
saying:
"I am wounded!"
Zhāng Hóu said:
"From the start of the engagement,
an arrow pierced my hand and elbow,
but I broke it and kept driving.
The left wheel is stained dark red—
how dare I speak of being wounded?
You must endure it!"
Huǎn said:
"From the start of the engagement,
whenever there was danger,
I always got down to push the chariot—
did you not notice?
But you are wounded!"
Zhāng Hóu said:
"The eyes and ears of the army
are on our flags and drums,
advancing and retreating follow them.
If one person holds this chariot steady,
we can accomplish our task.
How can we
let wounds ruin our ruler's great affair?
We donned armor and took up weapons
precisely to face death.
Wounded but not yet dead—
you must press on!"
He took the reins with his left hand,
and with his right hand took the drumstick and beat the drum.
The horses galloped uncontrollably,
and the army followed.
The Qí army was defeated.
They pursued them,
circling Huábùzhù three times.
Hán Jué dreamed that Zǐyú
said to him:
"Avoid the left and right at dawn!"
So he drove from the center
and pursued the Marquis of Qí.
Bǐng Xià said:
"Shoot the driver—
he is a nobleman."
The Duke said:
"To call him a nobleman and then shoot him
is against ritual."
They shot his left guard,
who fell beneath the chariot.
They shot his right guard,
who died in the chariot.
Qíwú Zhāng lost his chariot
and followed Hán Jué, saying:
"Allow me to ride with you!"
He tried to stand on the left or right,
but Hán Jué nudged him with his elbow,
making him stand behind.
Hán Jué bent down
and secured the body of his right guard.
Péng Chǒufǔ and the Duke switched places.
As they neared Huáquán,
the trace horse became entangled in a tree
and stopped.
Chǒufǔ had once slept in a narrow cart,
and a snake emerged from beneath it.
He struck it with his arm,
was wounded, and hid it,
so he could not push the chariot
and was caught.
Hán Jué held the reins before the horses,
bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
presented a cup and added a jade disc, saying:
"Our ruler sent us, his ministers,
to make a request for Lǔ and Wèi,
saying:
'Do not let our army intrude into your land.'
I, your humble servant, am unfortunate
to be in the path of your army,
with nowhere to hide.
Moreover, I fear that fleeing would
disgrace both rulers.
I am unworthy to be a soldier,
but dare to report my incompetence
and temporarily fill this official role."
Chǒufǔ made the Duke descend
to fetch water from Huáquán.
Zhèng Zhōufǔ
drove the auxiliary chariot,
with Wǎn Fèi as the right-hand guard,
and carried the Marquis of Qí to safety.
Hán Jué presented Chǒufǔ,
Xì Xiànzǐ was about to execute him,
when he cried out:
"From now on, there will be no one to bear hardship in place of his lord.
There is one here now,
yet he is to be executed?"
Xìzǐ said:
"A man who does not shrink from death to save his lord—
if I execute him,
it would be inauspicious.
I shall pardon him,
to encourage those who serve their lords."
So he was spared.
The Marquis of Qí, having escaped,
sought Chǒufù,
going in and out three times.
Each time he came out,
the Qí army used it to lead the retreat.
Entering among the Dí troops,
the Dí troops all drew their spears
and shielded him with their bucklers.
He then entered among the Wèi troops,
and the Wèi troops spared him.
He then entered through Xúguān.
The Marquis of Qí saw the defenders,
and said:
"Exert yourselves!
The Qí army is defeated!"
He made way for a woman.
The woman said:
"Has our lord escaped?"
He replied:
"He has escaped."
She said:
"Has the Commandant of the Vanguard escaped?"
He replied:
"He has escaped."
She said:
"If our lord and my father have escaped,
what more could be done?"
Then she ran off.
The Marquis of Qí considered her to be well-mannered.
Later, upon inquiry,
she was the wife of the Commandant of the Fortifications.
He bestowed upon her Shíliù.
The Jìn army pursued the Qí army,
entering from Qiūyú.
They attacked Mǎxíng.
The Marquis of Qí sent Bīn Mèirén to bribe them
with the Jì yǎn,
a jade qìng, and territory.
"If they do not accept,
then let the guests do as they will."
Bīn Mèirén presented the bribes.
The men of Jìn would not accept,
saying:
"You must give Xiāo Tóngshūzǐ as a hostage,
and also make all the fields within Qí's borders
run east-west."
He replied:
"Xiāo Tóngshūzǐ is no other
than the mother of our humble lord.
If we speak in terms of equals,
then she is also the mother of the lord of Jìn.
You, sir, proclaim great commands to the feudal lords,
yet say you must take his mother as a hostage
to ensure good faith—
what does this do to the king's command?
Moreover, this is to order with unfiliality.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The filial son's supply never fails;
forever he confers it on his kind.'
If you order the feudal lords with unfiliality,
is that not contrary to virtuous kinship?
The former kings demarcated and ordered the world,
assessing the suitability of the land,
and distributing its benefits.
Therefore the *Book of Songs* says:
'We demarcate, we order,
making the fields run south and east.'
Now you, sir, demarcate and order the feudal lords,
yet say merely 'make all the fields run east-west'—
considering only the advantage for your war chariots,
with no regard for the land's suitability—
is that not contrary to the former kings' command?
To oppose the former kings is unrighteous;
how then can you be the leader of the covenant?
Truly, Jìn is at fault.
When the Four Kings ruled,
they cultivated virtue and satisfied common desires;
when the Five Hegemons dominated,
they toiled and pacified,
to serve the king's command.
Now you, sir, seek to assemble the feudal lords
to gratify boundless desires.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'His governance is generous and ample,
and all blessings gather to him.'
You, sir, are truly not generous,
and cast away all blessings—
what harm would that be to the feudal lords?
If not,
our humble lord's command to his envoy
included these words:
He said:
'You have brought your lord's army to disgrace our humble city.
Our meager resources
are to reward your followers.
Fearing your lord's might,
our troops have been routed.
If you, sir, graciously seek fortune for Qí,
and do not extinguish its altars of soil and grain,
allowing us to continue the old friendship,
we dare not begrudge these old vessels of our former lords
and territory.
If you still do not consent,
we beg to gather the remaining embers,
and stake one last fight with our backs to the city wall.
If our humble city is fortunate,
we will still follow you;
how much more if we are unfortunate—
would we dare not obey your command?'"
Lǔ and Wèi remonstrated, saying:
"Qí resents us.
Those who have died
were all close kin.
If you do not consent,
they will surely hate us bitterly.
As for you, sir,
what more do you seek?
You obtain their state treasures,
we also obtain territory,
and are relieved from calamity—
the glory is great indeed.
Qí and Jìn both depend on Heaven's grant;
must it necessarily be Jìn?"
The men of Jìn consented,
replying:
"We ministers led the army and chariots
to make this request for Lǔ and Wèi.
If there is a pretext
to report back to our humble lord,
it will be his grace.
How dare we not obey your command?"
Qín Zhèng came from the army
to welcome the duke.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the Jìn army and Qí's Guó Zuǒ made a covenant at Yuánlóu.
They made the men of Qí return
our fields of Wènyáng.
The duke met the Jìn army at Shàngmíng.
He bestowed upon the three commanders ceremonial carriages
and robes for the three-rank command.
The Minister of War, Minister of Works, Chariot Commander,
Chief of Scouts, and Assistant Commanders
all received robes for the one-rank command.
B8.2.4 In the eighth month,
Duke Wén of Sòng died.
For the first time, there was lavish burial:
using clamshells and charcoal,
increasing chariots and horses,
beginning the use of human sacrifices,
and multiplying grave goods.
The outer coffin had four sloping sides,
the inner coffin had painted decorations
and cypress wood.
The gentleman says of Huà Yuán and Yuè Jǔ
that "in this they were not ministers.
Ministers
are those who govern troubles and remove delusions;
therefore they remonstrate even at risk of death.
Now these two men,
while the lord lived, indulged his delusions,
and after his death increased his extravagance—
this is to abandon the lord to evil.
What kind of ministers are they?"
B8.2.5 In the ninth month,
Duke Mù of Wèi died.
The three commanders of Jìn, returning from campaign,
went to offer condolences,
weeping outside the main gate.
The men of Wèi welcomed them,
and the women wept inside the gate.
The farewell was also like this.
This then became the customary practice for funerals.
B8.2.6 When Chǔ was punishing the Xià clan of Chén,
King Zhuāng wished to take Xià Jī for himself.
Shēngōng Wūchén said:
"It cannot be.
My lord summoned the feudal lords
to punish crime;
now to take Xià Jī
is to covet her beauty.
Coveting beauty is licentiousness.
Licentiousness brings great punishment."
The Book of Zhou says,
'Cultivate virtue and be cautious in punishments.'
This is how King Wen founded the Zhou dynasty.
'Cultivate virtue' means
to strive to exalt it;
'be cautious in punishments' means
to strive to eliminate them.
If you raise an army among the feudal lords
to incur great punishment,
that is not being cautious.
May Your Majesty consider this!"
The king then desisted.
Zǐ Fǎn wanted to take her,
but Wū Chén said,
"This is an inauspicious woman.
She caused the early death of Zǐ Mán,
brought about the killing of Yù Shū,
instigated the murder of Lord Líng,
led to the execution of Xià Nán,
drove out Kǒng and Yí,
and caused the loss of the state of Chén.
Could there be anything more inauspicious than this?
Human life is truly difficult;
might she not meet an unnatural death?
Under heaven there are many beautiful women;
why must it be this one?"
Zǐ Fǎn then desisted.
The king gave her to Liányǐn Xiāng Lǎo.
Xiāng Lǎo died at Bì,
and his body was not recovered.
His son Hēi Yāo then had an illicit relationship with her.
Wū Chén sent her a message,
saying,
"Return [to your homeland],
and I will take you as my wife."
He also had someone summon her from Zhèng,
saying,
"The body can be obtained;
you must come to receive it."
Jī informed the king of this.
The king questioned Qū Wū about it.
He replied,
"It is credible.
Zhì Yīng's father
was a favorite of Duke Chéng,
and is the youngest brother of Zhōngháng Bó.
He has recently been assisting the commander of the central army,
and is on good terms with Zhèng's Huáng Xū.
He dearly loves this son.
He will certainly use Zhèng to return our prince
and the body of Xiāng Lǎo in exchange for him.
The people of Zhèng are fearful because of the battle of Bì,
and wish to curry favor with Jìn;
they will certainly agree to it."
The king sent Xià Jī back.
As she was about to depart,
she said to those seeing her off,
"If I do not obtain the body,
I will not return."
Wū Chén sought her in marriage from Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng consented.
When King Gòng ascended the throne,
and was about to launch the campaign of Yángqiáo,
he sent Qū Wū on a diplomatic mission to Qí,
and to inform them of the army's schedule.
Wū Chén took his entire household and departed.
Shēn Shū Guì was accompanying his father,
and was going to Yǐng,
when he met him.
He said,
"How strange!
This gentleman has the grave responsibility of military affairs,
yet also has the joy of a secret rendezvous.
He must be planning to steal away with a wife."
When he reached Zhèng,
he sent his assistant back with the betrothal gifts,
and left with Xià Jī.
He intended to flee to Qí.
But the army of Qí had recently been defeated,
so he said,
"I will not reside in a country that cannot win."
He then fled to Jìn,
and through Xì Zhì,
entered the service of Jìn.
The people of Jìn made him a senior official of Xíng.
Zǐ Fǎn requested
to offer heavy bribes to have him permanently barred from office.
The king said,
"Stop!
In planning for himself he was at fault,
but in planning for our former lord he was loyal.
Loyalty
is what secures the altars of soil and grain;
its benefits are many.
Moreover, if he can benefit the state,
even with heavy bribes,
would Jìn agree?
If he is of no benefit to Jìn,
Jìn will cast him aside.
Why trouble to have him barred?"
B8.2.7 The Jìn army returned,
and Fàn Wénzǐ entered last.
Wǔzǐ said,
"Did you not think I was waiting for you?"
He replied,
"The army has achieved merit,
and the people of the state are joyously welcoming them.
To enter first
would certainly attract everyone's attention;
this would be to usurp the commander's fame.
Therefore I did not dare."
Wǔzǐ said,
"I know I can be spared [from calamity]."
When Xì Bó had his audience,
the duke said,
"This is due to your efforts!"
He replied,
"It is due to Your Lordship's instructions,
and the efforts of the other ministers.
What effort have I contributed?"
When Fàn Shū had his audience,
the duke commended him as he had Xì Bó.
He replied,
"It was due to Gēng's commands
and Kè's direction;
what effort has Xiè contributed?"
When Luán Bó had his audience,
the duke did likewise.
He replied,
"It was due to Xiè's instructions
and the officers obeying orders;
what effort has Shū contributed?"
B8.2.8 Duke Xuān had sent envoys to seek friendly relations with Chǔ.
King Zhuāng died,
Duke Xuān passed away,
and friendly relations could not be established.
When our duke ascended the throne,
he accepted a covenant with Jìn,
and joined Jìn in attacking Qí.
The people of Wèi did not send envoys to Chǔ,
and also accepted a covenant with Jìn,
joining in the attack on Qí.
Therefore, Chǔ's Prime Minister Zǐ Zhòng
launched the campaign of Yángqiáo to rescue Qí.
As he was about to raise the army,
Zǐ Zhòng said,
"Our ruler is young,
and we ministers are not equal to the former great officers.
We must have a large army to succeed.
The Book of Songs says:
'With many officers, well arrayed,
King Wen's realm was well secured.'
Even King Wen used a multitude;
how much more should we?
Moreover, our former lord King Zhuāng instructed us, saying:
'If you lack virtue to reach distant lands,
there is nothing better than to generously care for your people,
and employ them well.'"
Thereupon, they conducted a major household registration,
cancelled debts,
relieved the widowers,
aided the needy,
and pardoned offenses.
The entire army was mobilized,
and the king's personal troops all marched.
Péng Míng drove the command chariot,
with Duke Jǐng of Cài on the left,
and Duke Líng of Xǔ on the right.
Both rulers were young,
and were forcibly capped as adults.
In winter,
the Chǔ army invaded Wèi,
then invaded our state, encamping at Shǔ.
They sent Zāng Sūn to go.
He declined, saying,
"Chǔ is distant and the campaign is prolonged;
they will certainly withdraw.
To receive praise without merit—
I dare not."
When Chǔ invaded as far as Yángqiáo,
Mèng Sūn requested to go and bribe them
with craftsmen:
woodworkers, needleworkers, and weavers,
one hundred of each,
and with Gōng Héng as a hostage,
to request a covenant.
The people of Chǔ agreed to make peace.
In the eleventh month,

our duke, along with Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Yīng Qí, the Marquis of Cài, the Baron of Xǔ, Qín's Right Senior Official Shuō, Sòng's Huá Yuán, Chén's Gōngsūn Níng, Wèi's Sūn Liáng Fū, Zhèng's Gōngzǐ Qùjí, and a senior official of Qí, made a covenant at Shǔ.
The high ministers are not recorded [in the Spring and Autumn Annals]
because it was a 'deficient covenant.'
At that time, they feared Jìn and secretly made a covenant with Chǔ,
hence it is said
it was a 'deficient covenant.'
The Marquis of Cài and the Baron of Xǔ are not recorded
because they rode in Chǔ's chariots,
which is called losing their proper status.
The gentleman says:
"How can one not be cautious about one's position!
The rulers of Cài and Xǔ,
once they lost their positions,
could no longer be ranked among the feudal lords,
let alone those below them!
The Odes says:
'Not slack in their positions,
the people find rest.'
This is what it refers to."
The Chǔ army reached Sòng,
and Gōnghéng fled back.
Zāng Xuānshū said:
"Héngfù cannot bear a few years of discomfort,
and thus abandons Lǔ.
What will become of the state?
Who will be responsible?
Those who come after will surely bear the consequences!
The state is abandoned."
In this campaign,
Jìn avoided Chǔ,
fearing their multitude.
The gentleman says:
"The multitude cannot be dispensed with.
When great officers govern,
they still rely on the multitude to overcome,
how much more so a wise ruler who skillfully employs his multitude?
What the Great Oath calls 'the millions of Shāng people were divided,
while ten men of Zhōu were united'
refers to the multitude."
B8.2.9 The Marquis of Jìn sent Gǒng Shuò
to present the Qí captives to Zhōu.
The king did not receive him,
but sent Dān Xiānggōng to decline,
saying:
"The barbarians of the four quarters,
disobey the king's commands,
indulge in excess and destroy the constant norms.
When the king orders them attacked,
then captives are presented.
The king personally receives and rewards them,
to punish disrespect and encourage merit.
Brothers,
maternal uncles and nephews,
if they invade and ruin the king's plans,
and the king orders them attacked,
it is only to report the affair,
not to present their achievements,
so as to respect kinship and intimacy,
and prohibit wicked excess.
Now, uncle, you have succeeded,
achieving merit against Qí,
yet you did not send a commissioned minister
to pacify the royal house,
but sent someone to comfort me.
And Gǒng Bó indeed came,
who holds no office in the royal house,
and moreover violates the rites of the former kings.
Though I wish to favor Gǒng Bó,
how dare I abandon the old statutes and disgrace uncle?
Now Qí,
is a state of maternal uncles and nephews,
and the descendants of the Grand Master.
Was it not indeed indulging its desires
and angering uncle,
or could it not be admonished and instructed?"
Shì Zhuāngbó could not reply.
The king had the matter entrusted to the three officials,
treating it with the rites for when a marquis or count overcomes an enemy and sends a great officer
to announce the celebration,
one rank lower than the rites for a minister.
The king feasted Gǒng Bó,
and privately gave him gifts.
He had the master of ceremonies announce:
"This is not according to ritual,
do not record it!"
A8.3 The Annals of Duke Chéng, Third Year
A8.3.1 In the third year, spring,
the royal first month,
the duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and the Earl of Cáo to attack Zhèng.
A8.3.2 On Xīnhài,
buried Duke Mù of Wèi.
A8.3.3 In the second month,
the duke returned from attacking Zhèng.
A8.3.4 On Jiǎzǐ,
the new palace suffered a fire.
They wept for three days.
A8.3.5 On Yǐhài,
buried Duke Wén of Sòng.
A8.3.6 In summer,
the duke went to Jìn.
A8.3.7 Zhèng's Gōngzǐ Qùjí led troops to attack Xǔ.
A8.3.8 The duke returned from Jìn.
A8.3.9 In autumn,
Shūsūn Qiáorú led troops to besiege Jí.
A8.3.10 The great rain sacrifice was held.
A8.3.11 Jìn's Xì Kè
and Wèi's Sūn Liángfū attacked Qiánggāorú.
A8.3.12 In winter, the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Gěng to come on a friendly mission.
A8.3.13 The Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū to come on a friendly mission.
A8.3.14 On Bǐngwǔ,
made a covenant with Xún Gěng.
A8.3.15 On Dīngwèi,
made a covenant with Sūn Liángfū.
A8.3.16 Zhèng attacked Xǔ.
B8.3 The Commentary of Duke Chéng, Third Year
B8.3.1 In the third year, spring,
the feudal lords attacked Zhèng,
and encamped at Bóniú,
to punish the Bì campaign.
Then they advanced east to invade Zhèng.
Zhèng's Gōngzǐ Yǎn led troops to resist them,
and had the eastern border troops ambush them at Màn,
defeating them at Qiūyú.
Huángxū went to Chǔ to present the captives.
B8.3.2 In summer,
the duke went to Jìn,
to thank for the fields of Wènyáng.
B8.3.3 Xǔ relied on Chǔ and did not serve Zhèng,
so Zhèng's Zǐliáng attacked Xǔ.
B8.3.4 The people of Jìn returned Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Gǔchén and the corpse of Liányǐn Xiānglǎo to Chǔ,
to seek Zhì Yīng in exchange.
At this time, Xún Shǒu was assistant to the central army,
so the people of Chǔ agreed.
The king sent off Zhì Yīng,
saying:
"Do you resent me?"
He replied:
"Two states engaged in war,
I, your servant, lacking talent,
was unequal to the task,
and became a captive.
Your officers did not
use my blood to smear the drums,
but let me return to be executed,
this is your grace.
I truly lack talent,
who would I dare resent?"
The king said:
"Then are you grateful to me?"
He replied:
"Two states plan for their altars of soil and grain
and seek to relieve their people,
each restraining their anger,
to pardon each other.
Both release the bound prisoners,
to establish good relations.
The two states have good relations,
I, your servant, have no part in it,
who would I dare be grateful to?"
The king said:
"When you return,
how will you repay me?"
He replied:
"I bear no resentment,
nor does your grace bear any gratitude,
without resentment or gratitude,
I do not know what to repay."
The king said:
"Even so,
you must tell me."
He replied:
"By your grace's spirit,
this bound servant can return his bones to Jìn.
If my ruler considers me worthy of execution,
death will be immortal.
If following your grace's favor I am spared,
and given to your external minister Shǒu;
Shǒu will request my ruler,
and have me executed in the ancestral temple,
death will also be immortal."
If I do not receive your command,
and am made to succeed to the ancestral office,
and in order of precedence come to affairs of state,
and lead a flank army,
to guard the borders.
Even if I encounter your officers,
I dare not evade them,
but will exert all my strength until death,
without any disloyalty,
to fulfill the rites of a minister,
this is how I will repay you."
The king said:
"Jìn cannot be contended with."
He treated him with great ceremony and sent him back.
B8.3.5 In autumn,
Shūsūn Qiáorú besieged Jí,
and took the fields of Wènyáng.
Jí did not submit,
so he besieged it.
B8.3.6 Xì Kè of Jìn
and Sūn Liángfū of Wèi attacked Qiánggāorú,
to chastise the remnants of the Red Dí.
Qiánggāorú collapsed,
because its superiors had lost the people.
B8.3.7 In winter, in the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Gēng to come on a friendly mission,
and to renew the covenant.
The Marquis of Wèi sent Sūn Liángfū to come on a friendly mission,
and to renew the covenant.
The Duke asked Zāng Xuānshū about it, saying:
"Zhòng Xíngbó in Jìn,
his rank is the third;
Master Sūn in Wèi,
his rank is that of senior minister.
Whom should we receive first?"
He replied:
"The senior minister of a secondary state
corresponds to the middle minister of a great state,
the middle minister corresponds to its junior minister,
the junior minister corresponds to its senior grand officer.
The senior minister of a small state
corresponds to the junior minister of a great state,
the middle minister corresponds to its senior grand officer,
the junior minister corresponds to its junior grand officer.
High and low being thus,
is the ancient system.
Wèi compared to Jìn,
cannot be considered a secondary state.
Jìn being the covenant leader,
we should receive them first."
On Bǐngwǔ,
they covenanted with Jìn;
on Dīngwèi,
they covenanted with Wèi.
This was according to ritual.
B8.3.8 In the twelfth month, on Jiǎxū,
Jìn established six armies.
Hán Jué, Zhào Kuò, Gǒng Shuò, Hán Chuān,
Xún Zhuī, and Zhào Zhān all were made ministers,
as a reward for the achievement at Ān.
B8.3.9 The Marquis of Qí visited Jìn,
and was about to present the jade.
Xì Kè hurried forward and said:
"This journey of yours,
my lord, is because you were insulted by a woman's laughter,
my humble lord dares not accept it."
The Marquis of Jìn feasted the Marquis of Qí.
The Marquis of Qí looked at Hán Jué.
Hán Jué said:
"Does my lord recognize Jué?"
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Your attire has changed."
Hán Jué ascended,
raised his cup and said:
"The reason I did not dare to begrudge death,
was for the sake of the two lords being in this hall."
B8.3.10 When Xún Yīng was in Chǔ,
a merchant of Zhèng was about to hide him in a sack to get him out.
Having planned it,
before it was carried out,
the men of Chǔ sent him back.
The merchant went to Jìn,
Xún Yīng treated him well,
as if he had actually gotten him out.
The merchant said:
"I have no such merit,
how dare I accept the reality of it?
I am a petty man,
I cannot greatly deceive a gentleman."
Thereupon he went to Qí.
A8.4 "The Classic of Duke Chéng's Fourth Year"
A8.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the Duke of Sòng sent Huá Yuán to come on a friendly mission.
A8.4.2 In the third month, on Rénshēn,
the Earl of Zhèng, Jiān, died.
A8.4.3 The Earl of Qǐ came to court.
A8.4.4 In summer, in the fourth month, on Jiǎyín,
Zāngsūn Xǔ died.
A8.4.5 The Duke went to Jìn.
A8.4.6 They buried Duke Xiāng of Zhèng.
A8.4.7 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
A8.4.8 In winter,
they walled Yùn.
A8.4.9 The Earl of Zhèng attacked Xǔ.
B8.4 "The Commentary of Duke Chéng's Fourth Year"
B8.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
Huá Yuán of Sòng came on a friendly mission,
to announce the accession of the new ruler.
B8.4.2 The Earl of Qǐ came to court,
because of returning Shū Jī.
B8.4.3 In summer,
the Duke went to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn received the Duke,
but was not respectful.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"The Marquis of Jìn will certainly not escape misfortune.
The Odes say:
'Be reverent, be reverent!
Heaven is clear and bright,
its mandate is not easy!'
Now the mandate of the Marquis of Jìn lies with the feudal lords,
can he not be reverent!"
B8.4.4 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from Jìn,
and wished to seek peace with Chǔ
and betray Jìn.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"It cannot be done.
Although Jìn is without principle,
it cannot be betrayed.
Its state is large, its ministers harmonious,
and it is near to us,
the feudal lords obey it,
we cannot be disloyal.
The Records of Shǐ Yì has it:
'If they are not of our kind,
their hearts must be different.'
Although Chǔ is great,
it is not of our kind,
would it be willing to cherish us?"
The Duke then stopped.
B8.4.5 In winter, in the eleventh month,
Gōngsūn Shēn of Zhèng led troops
to demarcate the fields of Xǔ.
The men of Xǔ defeated them at Zhǎnpō.
The Earl of Zhèng attacked Xǔ,
and took the fields of Chúrén and Língdūn.
Luán Shū of Jìn commanded the central army,
Xún Shǒu assisted him,
Shì Xiè assisted the upper army,
to rescue Xǔ and attack Zhèng,
taking Fán and Zhài.
Zǐ Fǎn of Chǔ rescued Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng and the Baron of Xǔ disputed before him,
Huáng Xū presented the Earl of Zhèng's arguments.
Zǐ Fǎn could not decide,
and said:
"If you lords would deign to come to our humble lord,
our humble lord and his two or three ministers will together hear what the two lords desire,
and a settlement can be known.
Otherwise,
Cè is insufficient
to know the settlement of the two states."
B8.4.6 Zhào Yīng of Jìn
had illicit relations with Zhào Zhuāng Jī.
A8.5 "The Classic of Duke Chéng's Fifth Year"
A8.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
Shū Jī of Qǐ came back.
A8.5.2 Zhòngsūn Miè went to Sòng.
A8.5.3 In summer,
Shūsūn Qiáorú met with Xún Shǒu of Jìn at Gǔ.
A8.5.4 Mount Liáng collapsed.
A8.5.5 In autumn,
there was a great flood.
A8.5.6 In winter, in the eleventh month, on Jǐyǒu,
the Heavenly King died.
A8.5.7 In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and the Earl of Qǐ, and they formed an alliance at Chóngláo.
B8.5 The Commentary of Duke Chéng, Year Five
B8.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
Yuán and Píng exiled him to Qí.
Yīng said:
"While I am here,
the Luán clan will not act.
If I am gone,
my two elder brothers will have cause for worry.
Moreover, each person has abilities
and lacks others.
If you let me go,
what harm is there?"
They did not listen.
Yīng dreamed that a heavenly envoy said to him:
"Sacrifice to me,
and I will bless you."
He sent someone to ask Shì Zhēnbó about it.
Zhēnbó said:
"I do not know."
Afterwards, he told his
man, saying:
"The spirits bless the benevolent and bring calamity upon the licentious.
If one is licentious yet receives no punishment,
that is a blessing.
If he sacrifices,
can he escape?"
The day after
he sacrificed, he was gone.
B8.5.2 Mèng Xiànzǐ went to Sòng,
to repay Huà Yuán.
B8.5.3 In summer,
Xún Shǒu of Jìn went to Qí to fetch a bride,
therefore Xuān Bó sent provisions to him at Gǔ.
B8.5.4 Mount Liáng collapsed.
The Marquis of Jìn sent a relay carriage to summon Bó Zōng.
Bó Zōng ordered a heavy cart to make way,
saying:
"Make way for the relay carriage!"
The man with the heavy cart said:
"Waiting for me
is not as fast as taking a shortcut."
He asked him where he was from.
He said:
"I am from Jiàng."
He asked him about affairs in Jiàng.
He said:
"Mount Liáng has collapsed,
and they are going to summon Bó Zōng to deliberate on it."
He asked what should be done.
He said:
"When a mountain has rotten earth and collapses,
what can be done?
The state relies on its mountains and rivers,
therefore when mountains collapse and rivers dry up,
the ruler should abstain from rich foods,
wear plain clothes, ride in an unadorned carriage,
cease music, move out of his chamber,
have invocators present silk,
and scribes offer prayers,
all according to ritual.
That is all that can be done.
Even Bó Zōng,
what can he do?"
Bó Zōng requested to see him.
He would not agree.
So Bó Zōng reported his words,
and followed them.
B8.5.5 Duke Líng of Xǔ complained to the King of Chǔ about the Earl of Zhèng.
In the sixth month,
Duke Dào of Zhèng went to Chǔ to plead his case.
He did not prevail,
and the men of Chǔ detained Huáng Xū and Zǐ Guó.
Therefore, when the Earl of Zhèng returned,
he sent Gōngzǐ Yǎn to request peace with Jìn.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
the Earl of Zhèng and Zhào Tóng of Jìn formed an alliance at Chuíjí.
B8.5.6 Wéi Guī, a prince of Sòng,
returned after having been a hostage in Chǔ.
Huà Yuán hosted a feast for him.
He requested to go out with drums and clamor,
and to re-enter with drums and clamor,
saying:
"I am practicing an attack on the Huà clan."
The Duke of Sòng put him to death.
B8.5.7 In winter,
they formed an alliance at Chóngláo,
because Zhèng had submitted.
The feudal lords planned to meet again,
but the Duke of Sòng sent Xiàng Wéirén to decline
on account of the trouble with Zǐ Líng.
B8.5.8 In the eleventh month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
King Dìng passed away.
A8.6 The Spring and Autumn Annals of Duke Chéng, Year Six
A8.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
in the royal first month,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.6.2 In the second month, on the day Xīnsì,
a Wǔ palace was established.
A8.6.3 Zhuan was taken.
A8.6.4 Sūn Liángfū of Wèi led troops to invade Sòng.
A8.6.5 In summer, in the sixth month,
the Viscount of Zhū came for an audience.
A8.6.6 Gōngsūn Yīngqí went to Jìn.
A8.6.7 On the day Rénshēn,
the Earl of Zhèng, Fèi, passed away.
A8.6.8 In autumn,
Zhòngsūn Miè
and Shūsūn Qiáorú led troops to invade Sòng.
A8.6.9 Gōngzǐ Yīngqí of Chǔ led troops to attack Zhèng.
A8.6.10 In winter,
Jìsūn Xíngfú went to Jìn.
A8.6.11 Luán Shū of Jìn led troops to rescue Zhèng.
B8.6 The Commentary of Duke Chéng, Year Six
B8.6.1 In the spring of the sixth year,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn
to express gratitude for the peace,
with Zǐ Yóu as his assistant.
He received the jade token east of the eastern pillar.
Shì Zhēnbó said:
"The Earl of Zhèng will probably die!
He has abandoned himself.
His gaze is restless and his movements hasty,
he is not settled in his position,
so it is fitting he will not last long."
B8.6.2 In the second month,
Jì Wénzǐ established a Wǔ palace because of the achievement at Ān.
This was contrary to ritual.
To rely on others to rescue one from difficulty
does not warrant establishing a Wǔ palace.
Establishing a Wǔ palace should come from one's own achievements,
not from others.
B8.6.3 Zhuan was taken,
indicating it was easy.
B8.6.4 In the third month,
Bó Zōng of Jìn, Xià Yáng Shuō, Sūn Liángfū of Wèi,
Nìng Xiàng, men of Zhèng,
the Róng of Yī and Luò,
the Lùhún,
and the Mán clan invaded Sòng,
because it had declined the meeting.
The army was at Zhēn.
The people of Wèi did not guard their city.
Shuō wanted to attack Wèi by surprise,
saying:
"Even if we cannot enter,
we can take many captives and return.
The crime would not warrant death."
Bó Zōng said:
"It cannot be done.
Wèi trusts Jìn alone,
therefore, though our army is in its suburbs,
it has made no defensive preparations.
If we attack it by surprise, we would be abandoning trust.
Even if we capture many from Wèi,
Jìn would be without trust.
How then could we seek allegiance from the feudal lords?"
So they stopped.
When the army withdrew, the people of Wèi mounted the battlements.
B8.6.5 The people of Jìn planned to leave old Jiàng.
All the senior ministers said:
"We must dwell in the lands of the Xún and Xiá clans.
They are fertile and rich and close to the salt marshes.
The state benefits and the ruler is pleased.
This opportunity must not be lost."
Hán Xiànzǐ commanded the new central army,
and also served as the minister of attendants.
The Duke bowed and entered.
Xiànzǐ followed.
The Duke stood in the courtyard of the sleeping quarters,
and said to Xiànzǐ:
"What do you think?"
He replied:
"It would not be suitable.
The lands of Xún and Xiá have thin soil and shallow water,
and their impurities are easily encountered.
When impurities are easily encountered, the people become distressed;
when the people are distressed, they become worn down and impoverished,
and thus there arise diseases of edema and swollen limbs.
It is not as good as Xīntián,
where the soil is deep and the water is abundant,
and living there does not cause illness.
With the Fén and Kuài rivers to carry away impurities,
and moreover, the people are obedient to instruction—
it is a benefit for ten generations.
Mountains, marshes, forests, and salt ponds
are the treasures of the state.
When the state is rich,
the people become arrogant and indolent.
Being close to such treasures,
the ducal house will become poor.
This cannot be called a pleasure."
The duke was pleased
and followed his advice.
In the summer, on the dingchǒu day of the fourth month,
Jìn moved its capital to Xīntián.
B8.6.6 In the sixth month,
Duke Dào of Zhèng passed away.
B8.6.7 Zǐ Shū Shēngbó went to Jìn
and was ordered to attack Sòng.
B8.6.8 In autumn,
Mèng Xiànzǐ and Shūsūn Xuānbó invaded Sòng,
as ordered by Jìn.
B8.6.9 Chǔ’s Zǐ Zhòng attacked Zhèng,
because Zhèng had aligned with Jìn.
B8.6.10 In winter,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Jìn
to congratulate them on the move.
B8.6.11 Jìn’s Luán Shū came to rescue Zhèng
and encountered the Chǔ army at Rǎojiǎo.
The Chǔ army withdrew.
The Jìn army then invaded Cài.
Chǔ’s Gōngzǐ Shēn and Gōngzǐ Chéng led the armies of Shēn and Xī to rescue Cài
and defended against them at Sāngsuì.
Zhào Tóng and Zhào Kuò wanted to engage in battle
and requested permission from Wǔzǐ.
Wǔzǐ was about to grant it.
Zhī Zhuāngzǐ, Fàn Wénzǐ,
and Hán Xiànzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"It would not be suitable.
We came to rescue Zhèng;
the Chǔ army withdrew from us,
and we then proceeded here.
This is shifting the slaughter.
If the slaughter does not cease,
and we further provoke the Chǔ army,
we will surely not prevail in battle.
Even if we do prevail,
it will not be commendable.
To lead a full army out
and defeat two counties of Chǔ—
what glory is there in that?
If we cannot defeat them,
the disgrace will be even greater.
It would be better to withdraw."
So they withdrew.
At that time, many among the army commanders desired to fight.
Someone said to Luán Wǔzǐ:
"A sage shares the desires of the multitude;
thus, he accomplishes things.
Why do you not follow the multitude?
You are the chief minister,
and you should weigh the opinions of the people.
Among your eleven assistants,
those who do not wish to fight
are only three.
Those who wish to fight can be said to be the majority.
The *Shāngshū* says:
'When three diviners consult,
follow the two.'
This is because of the majority."
Wǔzǐ said:
"When opinions are equally good, follow the majority.
But what is good
is the master of the multitude.
With three ministers as masters,
they can be said to be the majority.
To follow them—
is that not appropriate?"
A8.7 *The Classic of Duke Chéng, Year Seven*
A8.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
in the royal first month,
mice gnawed the horns of the sacrificial ox for the suburban sacrifice,
and another ox was divined for.
The mice gnawed its horns as well,
so the ox was spared.
A8.7.2 Wú attacked Tán.
A8.7.3 In the summer, fifth month,
the Earl of Cáo came for an audience.
A8.7.4 The suburban sacrifice was not held,
but the three observations were still performed.
A8.7.5 In autumn,
Chǔ’s Gōngzǐ Yīngqí led an army to attack Zhèng.
A8.7.6 The duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and the Earl of Qǐ to rescue Zhèng.
On the wùchén day of the eighth month,
they formed an alliance at Mǎlíng.
A8.7.7 The duke returned from the meeting.
A8.7.8 Wú entered Zhōulái.
A8.7.9 In winter,
a great rain sacrifice was held.
A8.7.10 Wèi’s Sūn Línfǔ fled to Jìn.
B8.7 *The Commentary of Duke Chéng, Year Seven*
B8.7.1 In the spring of the seventh year,
Wú attacked Tán,
and Tán made peace.
Jì Wénzǐ said:
"The central states do not marshal their armies;
the barbarians invade,
and no one shows concern for them.
There is no one to pity us!
The *Shī* says:
'Unpitying Heaven above,
the chaos has no end.'
Is this not referring to this?
If those above show no pity,
who will not suffer from chaos?
Our downfall is not far off."
The gentleman said:
"To be aware of fear like this—
this means they will not perish."
B8.7.2 Zhèng’s Zǐ Liáng served as prime minister to Duke Chéng and went to Jìn,
where he had an audience
and also expressed gratitude for the army's assistance.
B8.7.3 In summer,
Duke Xuān of Cáo came for an audience.
B8.7.4 In autumn,
Chǔ’s Zǐ Zhòng attacked Zhèng
and stationed his army at Fàn.
The feudal lords came to rescue Zhèng.
Zhèng’s Gòng Zhòng and Hóu Yǔ attacked the Chǔ army,
captured Yún’s administrator Zhōng Yí,
and presented him to Jìn.
In the eighth month,
they formed an alliance at Mǎlíng,
renewing the alliance of Chóngláo,
and also because Jǔ had submitted.
The people of Jìn took Zhōng Yí back with them
and imprisoned him in the military storehouse.
B8.7.5 During Chǔ’s siege of Sòng,
when the army returned,
Zǐ Zhòng requested lands from Shēn
and Lǚ as reward fields.
The king agreed.
Shēn’s administrator Wūchén said:
"It would not be suitable.
These are the lands that make Shēn and Lǚ cities,
and they provide taxes
to defend against the north.
If they are taken,
it will be as if Shēn
and Lǚ no longer exist,
and Jìn and Zhèng will surely reach the Hàn River."
The king then stopped.
Zǐ Zhòng thus bore a grudge against Wūchén.
Zǐ Fǎn wanted to take Xià Jī as his wife,
but Wūchén stopped him,
and then took her himself
and left.
Zǐ Fǎn also bore a grudge against him.
When King Gòng ascended the throne,
Zǐ Zhòng and Zǐ Fǎn killed Wūchén’s clansmen Zǐ Yán, Zǐ Dàng, and Qīngyǐn Fújì, as well as Xiānglǎo’s son Hēi Yāo,
and divided their households.
Zǐ Zhòng took Zǐ Yán’s household,
had Shěnyǐn and Wángzǐ Pí divide Zǐ Dàng’s household,
and Zǐ Fǎn took Hēi Yāo and Qīngyǐn’s household.
Wǔ Chén sent a letter from Jìn to the two men,
saying:
"You have served your lord with slander, wickedness, greed, and avarice,
and have killed many innocent people.
I will surely make you exhausted from rushing about on military campaigns
until you die."
Wǔ Chén requested to be sent as an envoy to Wú,
and the Marquis of Jìn granted his request.
Shòu Mèng, the ruler of Wú, was pleased with him.
He then established relations between Wú and Jìn,
and went to Wú with a contingent of troops,
leaving behind one detachment of chariots.
He provided them with archers and charioteers,
taught the people of Wú how to drive chariots,
instructed them in battle formations,
and taught them to rebel against Chǔ.
He left his son Hú Yōng there,
appointing him as an official envoy in Wú.
Wú then began to attack Chǔ, attack Cháo, and attack Xú,
and Zǐ Zhòng was exhausted from rushing about on campaigns.
At the meeting of Mǎlíng,
Wú entered Zhōulái,
and Zǐ Zhòng rushed from Zhèng to respond to the emergency.
Thus, Zǐ Zhòng and Zǐ Fǎn had to rush about on seven military campaigns in one year.
The barbarian tribes that had been subordinate to Chǔ
were all taken by Wú,
and because of this, Wú began to grow powerful
and established relations with the Central States.
B8.7.6 Duke Dìng of Wèi hated Sūn Línfǔ.
In winter,
Sūn Línfǔ fled to Jìn.
The Marquis of Wèi went to Jìn,
and Jìn returned Qī to him.
A8.8 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Eighth Year of Duke Chéng*
A8.8.1 In the eighth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Chuān to come and discuss the fields of Wènyáng,
returning them to Qí.
A8.8.2 Luán Shū of Jìn led troops to invade Cài.
A8.8.3 Gōngsūn Yīngqí went to Jǔ.
A8.8.4 The Duke of Sòng sent Huá Yuán to come on a friendly visit.
A8.8.5 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng sent Gōngsūn Shòu to come and present betrothal gifts.
A8.8.6 Jìn executed its great officers Zhào Tóng
and Zhào Kuò.
A8.8.7 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the Son of Heaven sent Shào Bó to come and confer a mandate on the Duke.
A8.8.8 In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Shū Jī of Qǐ died.
A8.8.9 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Xiè to come on a friendly visit.
A8.8.10 Shūsūn Qiáorú joined with Shì Xiè of Jìn,
men of Qí,
and men of Zhū to attack Tán.
A8.8.11 Men of Wèi came with accompanying brides.
B8.8 *The Commentary of Zuo, Eighth Year of Duke Chéng*
B8.8.1 In the eighth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Chuān to come and discuss the fields of Wènyáng,
returning them to Qí.
Jì Wénzǐ gave him a farewell feast,
and spoke with him privately,
saying:
"A great state establishes righteousness,
and thereby becomes the leader of the covenant.
Thus, the feudal lords
cherish its virtue and fear its punishments,
and have no disloyal thoughts.
As for the fields of Wènyáng,
they were originally the territory of our humble state,
and when you used military force against Qí,
you made them return them to our humble state.
Now there is a second command,
saying
'Return them to Qí.'
Good faith is used to carry out righteousness,
and righteousness is used to fulfill commands.
This is what small states look to and cherish.
If good faith cannot be known,
and righteousness finds no establishment,
then among the feudal lords of the four quarters,
who will not fall away?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The maiden was not at fault;
the man was double in his conduct.
The man was without constancy,
changing in his virtue.'
Within seven years,
one grant and one seizure—
what could be more changeable than this?
If a man is changeable,
he will still lose his spouse;
how much more so a hegemon?
A hegemon relies on virtue to act,
but if he is changeable,
how can he long retain the feudal lords?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'If your plans are not far-reaching,
therefore I greatly admonish you.'
I, Xíngfǔ, fear that Jìn's plans are not far-reaching
and that it will lose the feudal lords.
Therefore, I dare to speak these words privately."
B8.8.2 Luán Shū of Jìn invaded Cài,
and then invaded Chǔ,
capturing Shēn Lí.
When the Chǔ army was returning,
Jìn invaded Shěn,
capturing the ruler of Shěn, Jīchū,
following the advice of Zhì, Fàn, and Hán.
A gentleman said:
"Following good advice is like flowing water—
how fitting!
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Affable and courteous gentlemen,
why do they not nurture men?'
They seek goodness!
Nurturing men—
this is how achievements are made."
On this campaign,
the Earl of Zhèng was about to join the Jìn army,
and attacked the east gate of Xǔ,
capturing much booty.
B8.8.3 Shēng Bó went to Jǔ,
to fetch a bride.
B8.8.4 Huá Yuán of Sòng came on a friendly visit,
to arrange the marriage of Gòng Jī.
B8.8.5 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng sent Gōngsūn Shòu to come and present betrothal gifts—
this was according to ritual.
B8.8.6 Zhào Zhuāng Jī of Jìn,
because of Zhào Yīng's exile,
slandered them to the Marquis of Jìn,
saying:
"Yuán and Píng are about to rebel."
Luán and Xì served as witnesses.
In the sixth month,
Jìn punished Zhào Tóng and Zhào Kuò.
Wǔ, following his mother, was kept
in the ducal palace.
Their fields were given to Qí Xī.
Hán Jué spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"The achievements of Chéng Jì
and the loyalty of Xuān Mèng—
if they are left without posterity,
those who do good will be afraid.
The enlightened kings of the three dynasties
all preserved Heaven's blessings for several hundred years.
Were there no wicked kings among them?
They relied on the wisdom of former sages
to avoid disaster.
The *Book of Zhou* says:
'They did not dare to insult the widowers and widows.'
This is how they made their virtue clear."
Then they established Wǔ
and returned his fields to him.
B8.8.7 In autumn,
Shào Huángōng came to confer a mandate on the Duke.
B8.8.8 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shēngōng Wǔ Chén to go to Wú,
passing through Jǔ.
He stood by a pond with the Duke of Qúqiū,
and said:
"Your city walls are in poor condition."
The ruler of Jǔ said:
"Our remote and humble state is among the barbarians—
who would take us as a target?"
He replied:
"Those who cunningly think to open up borders
to benefit their altars of soil and grain—
what state does not have them?
It is precisely because of this
that there are many great states.
It is only a matter of some thinking and some neglecting.
A brave man takes care to double-lock his doors;
how much more should a state?"
B8.8.9 In winter,
Shū Jī of Qǐ died.
She had returned from Qǐ,
so it was recorded.
B8.8.10 Shì Xiè of Jìn came on a friendly visit,
to discuss attacking Tán,
because it had served Wú.
The Duke bribed him,
requesting to delay the army.
Wénzǐ refused,
saying:
"A lord's command allows no second thoughts;
to break faith is to lose one's standing.
In ritual, there is no adding of gifts;
in affairs, there is no achieving two outcomes.
If you, my lord, lag behind the other feudal lords,
then our humble ruler will be unable to serve you.
Xiè will report this back."
Jì Sūn was afraid,
and sent Xuān Bó to lead troops to join in attacking Tán.
B8.8.11 Men of Wèi came to escort Gòng Jī as a secondary bride,
which was in accordance with ritual.
Whenever a feudal lord married off a daughter,
those of the same surname would escort her as secondary brides,
but those of a different surname would not.
A8.9 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Ninth Year of Duke Chéng*
A8.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
the royal first month,
the Earl of Qǐ came to receive the remains of Shū Jī and return with them.
A8.9.2 The Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
and the Earl of Qǐ,
and they formed an alliance at Pú.
A8.9.3 The Duke returned from the meeting.
A8.9.4 In the second month,
Bó Jī went to her marital home in Sòng.
A8.9.5 In summer,
Jì Sūn Xíngfǔ went to Sòng to escort the bride.
A8.9.6 Men of Jìn came to escort as secondary brides.
A8.9.7 In autumn, on the bǐngzǐ day of the seventh month,
the Marquis of Qí, Wú Yě, died.
A8.9.8 Men of Jìn seized the Earl of Zhèng.
A8.9.9 Luán Shū of Jìn led troops to attack Zhèng.
A8.9.10 In winter, in the eleventh month,
Duke Qǐng of Qí was buried.
A8.9.11 The Chǔ nobleman Yīng Qí led troops to attack Jǔ.
On the gēngshēn day,
Jǔ collapsed.
Men of Chǔ entered Yùn.
A8.9.12 Men of Qín
and the Bái Dí attacked Jìn.
A8.9.13 Men of Zhèng besieged Xǔ.
A8.9.14 The inner city walls were built.
B8.9 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, Ninth Year of Duke Chéng*
B8.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
Duke Huán of Qǐ came to receive the remains of Shū Jī,
