having been requested to do so.
Shū Jī of Qǐ died
because of Qǐ.
Receiving Shū Jī
was for our sake.
B8.9.2 Because of the return of the fields of Wènyáng,
the feudal lords became disloyal to Jìn.
The men of Jìn were afraid,
and met at Pú
to renew the alliance of Mǎlíng.
Jì Wénzǐ said to Fàn Wénzǐ:
"If virtue is not contended for,
what is the use of renewing alliances?"
Fàn Wénzǐ said:
"Be diligent in comforting them,
lenient in treating them,
firm and strong in controlling them,
and use the bright spirits to bind them.
Be gentle with those who submit and attack those who are disloyal—
this is the next best thing to virtue."
On this journey,
they were to meet with Wú for the first time,
but the men of Wú did not arrive.
B8.9.3 In the second month,
Bó Jī went to her marital home in Sòng.
B8.9.4 The men of Chǔ sought Zhèng with heavy bribes,
and the Earl of Zhèng met with the Chǔ nobleman
Chéng at Dèng.
B8.9.5 In summer,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Sòng to escort the bride.
Upon reporting back on his mission,
the Duke feasted him.
He recited the fifth stanza of "Hán Yì."
Mù Jiāng came out from her chamber,
bowed twice,
and said:
"You, sir, have toiled and endured disgrace,
not forgetting our former lord,
and extending this to the successor lord,
bestowing it even upon this widow.
Our former lord would still have had hopes.
I dare to bow in acknowledgment of your double diligence."
She then recited the final stanza of "Lǜ Yī" and went back inside.
B8.9.6 Men of Jìn came to escort as secondary brides,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B8.9.7 In autumn,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn.
The men of Jìn, investigating his disloyalty
toward Chǔ,
seized him at Tóngtī.
B8.9.8 Luán Shū attacked Zhèng.
The men of Zhèng sent Bó Juān to negotiate peace,
but the men of Jìn killed him,
which was contrary to ritual.
When armies clash,
envoys may be allowed between them.
Zǐ Zhòng of Chǔ invaded Chén to rescue Zhèng.
B8.9.9 The Marquis of Jìn inspected the military storehouse
and saw Zhōng Yí.
He asked, saying:
"Who is that man wearing a southern cap and bound?"
The officer in charge replied:
"He is a Chǔ prisoner presented by the men of Zhèng."
He ordered him to be released.
Summoning him, he condoled with him.
Zhōng Yí bowed twice and touched his head to the ground.
The Marquis asked about his clan.
He replied: "I am a musician."
The Duke said:
"Can you play music?" He replied:
"It was my late father's official duty;
how dare I engage in other affairs?"
He was given a zither and played southern tunes.
The Duke said:
"What is your king like?"
He replied:
"That is not something a petty man like me can know."
Pressed further,
he replied:
"When he was crown prince,
his tutors and guardians attended him,
and he paid morning visits to Yīng Qí
and evening visits to Cè.
I know nothing else."
The Duke told this to Fàn Wénzǐ.
Wénzǐ said:
"This Chǔ prisoner
is a gentleman.
He speaks of his father's office—
he does not turn his back on his roots;
he plays native music—
he does not forget the old;
he speaks of the crown prince—
showing no partiality;
he names his two high ministers—
showing respect for his ruler.
Not turning his back on his roots is benevolence;
not forgetting the old is faithfulness;
showing no partiality is loyalty;
respecting his ruler is acuity.
With benevolence he handles affairs,
with faithfulness he maintains them,
with loyalty he accomplishes them,
with acuity he carries them out.
Even great affairs
will surely succeed.
Why not send him back,
to bring about an agreement between Jìn
and Chǔ?"
The Duke followed this advice,
treated him with great courtesy,
and sent him back to seek an agreement.
B8.9.10 In winter, in the eleventh month,
Zǐ Zhòng of Chǔ attacked Jǔ from Chén,
besieging Qúqiū.
The walls of Qúqiū were weak,
and the defenders fled in disarray,
running to Jǔ.
On the wùshēn day,
Chǔ entered Qúqiū.
The men of Jǔ imprisoned the Chǔ nobleman Píng.
The men of Chǔ said:
"Do not kill him,
I will return your captives."
The people of Jǔ killed him, and the army of Chǔ besieged Jǔ.
The walls of Jǔ were also in poor condition,
on Gēngshēn day,
Jǔ collapsed.
Chǔ then entered Yùn,
because Jǔ was unprepared.
The gentleman says:
"Relying on poor defenses and being unprepared,
is the greatest of faults;
preparing for unforeseen events,
is the greatest of virtues.
Jǔ relied on its poor defenses,
and did not repair its city walls,
within twelve days,
Chǔ captured its three cities,
all due to lack of preparation!
The Book of Songs says:
'Although you have silk and hemp,
do not discard coarse grasses;
although you have beautiful women,
do not discard the plain ones;
all gentlemen,
must prepare for times of shortage.'
This means that preparation cannot be neglected."
B8.9.11 The people of Qín and
Báidí attacked Jìn,
because the feudal lords were disloyal.
B8.9.12 The people of Zhèng besieged Xǔ,
to show Jìn that they were not anxious about their ruler.
This was planned by Gōngsūn Shēn,
who said:
"If we send troops to besiege Xǔ,
pretending that we are about to install a new ruler,
and delay Jìn's envoy,
Jìn will surely return our ruler."
B8.9.13 The inner city wall was built,
recorded
because it was timely.
B8.9.14 In the twelfth month,
the ruler of Chǔ sent Prince Chén to Jìn,
to reciprocate Zhōng Yí's mission,
and to request the restoration of friendly relations and the conclusion of an alliance.
A8.10 The Annals of Duke Chéng, Year Ten
A8.10.1 In the tenth year, spring,
the younger brother of the ruler of Wèi, Hēibèi, led an army to invade Zhèng.
A8.10.2 In summer, the fourth month,
five divinations were made for the suburban sacrifice,
but the results were unfavorable,
so the sacrifice was not performed.
A8.10.3 In the fifth month,
the Duke met with the ruler of Jìn,
the ruler of Qí,
the ruler of Sòng,
the ruler of Wèi,
and the ruler of Cáo to attack Zhèng.
A8.10.4 People from Qí came with a bride's escort.
A8.10.5 On Bǐngwǔ day,
the ruler of Jìn, Nòu, died.
A8.10.6 In autumn, the seventh month,
the Duke went to Jìn.
A8.10.7 In winter, the tenth month.
B8.10 The Commentary on Duke Chéng, Year Ten
B8.10.1 In the tenth year, spring,
the ruler of Jìn sent Dí Fá to Chǔ,
to reciprocate the mission of Grand Steward Zǐ Shāng.
B8.10.2 Wèi's Zǐ Shū Hēibèi invaded Zhèng,
on Jìn's orders.
B8.10.3 Zhèng's Prince Bān heard of Shū Shēn's plan.
In the third month,
Zǐrú installed Prince Xū as ruler.
In summer, the fourth month,
the people of Zhèng killed Xū,
and installed Kūnwán,
Zǐrú fled to Xǔ.
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"The people of Zhèng have installed a ruler,
if we detain one person,
what good will it do?
It would be better to attack Zhèng and return their ruler,
in order to seek peace."
The ruler of Jìn fell ill,
in the fifth month,
Jìn installed the crown prince, Zhōupú, as ruler,
and met with the feudal lords to attack Zhèng.
Zhèng's Zǐ Hǎn bribed them with the Xiāng bell,
Zǐrán made a covenant at Xiūzé,
and Zǐsì served as a hostage.
On Xīnsì day,
the ruler of Zhèng returned.
B8.10.4 The ruler of Jìn dreamed of a great demon,
with disheveled hair reaching the ground,
beating its chest and leaping,
saying:
"You killed my descendant,
unjustly.
I have obtained permission from the Emperor!"
It broke through the main gate and the inner gate and entered.
The Duke was terrified,
and went into the inner chamber.
It then broke through the door.
The Duke woke up,
and summoned the shaman of Sāngtián.
The shaman's words matched the dream.
The Duke said:
"What will happen?"
He said:
"You will not eat the new grain."
The Duke's illness worsened,
and he sought a physician from Qín.
The ruler of Qín sent Physician Huǎn to treat him.
Before he arrived,
the Duke dreamed that his illness took the form of two boys,
saying:
"He
is a skilled physician,
I fear he will harm us,
where can we escape to?"
One of them said:
"Reside above the huāng,
below the gāo,
what can he do to us?"
When the physician arrived,
he said:
"The illness cannot be treated,
it is above the huāng,
below the gāo,
neither cauterization nor acupuncture can reach it,
medicine cannot penetrate there,
it cannot be treated."
The Duke said:
"A skilled physician indeed."
He gave him rich gifts and sent him back.
On the Bǐngwǔ day of the sixth month,
the ruler of Jìn wanted to eat wheat,
he had the diànrén present wheat,
and the kuìrén prepared it.
He summoned the shaman of Sāngtián,
showed him the wheat and killed him.
As he was about to eat,
he felt bloated,
went to the toilet,
fell in and died.
A minor servant had dreamed in the morning of carrying the Duke
and ascending to heaven,
and at noon,
he carried the ruler of Jìn out of the toilet,
and was subsequently buried alive with him.
B8.10.5 The ruler of Zhèng punished those who had installed the ruler,
on Wùshēn day,
he killed Shū Shēn and Shū Qín.
The gentleman says:
"Loyalty is a fine virtue,
but if it is directed at the wrong person, it is still unacceptable,
how much more so if it is not fine?"
B8.10.6 In autumn,
the Duke went to Jìn.
The people of Jìn detained the Duke,
and had him attend the funeral.
At that time, Dí Fá had not yet returned.
B8.10.7 In winter,
the funeral of Duke Jǐng of Jìn was held.
The Duke attended the funeral,
but no other feudal lords were present.
The people of Lǔ felt humiliated,
so it was not recorded,
to conceal it.
A8.11 The Annals of Duke Chéng, Year Eleven
A8.11.1 In the eleventh year, spring,
in the king's third month,
the Duke returned from Jìn.
A8.11.2 The ruler of Jìn sent Xì Chōu on a mission,
on Jǐchǒu day,
he made a covenant with Xì Chōu.
A8.11.3 In summer,
Jìsūn Xíngfǔ went to Jìn.
A8.11.4 In autumn,
Shūsūn Qiáorú went to Qí.
A8.11.5 In winter, the tenth month.
B8.11 The Commentary on Duke Chéng, Year Eleven
B8.11.1 In the spring of the eleventh year,
in the royal third month,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
The men of Jìn
considered the Duke to be duplicitous towards Chǔ,
and therefore detained him.
The Duke requested to accept a covenant,
and only then was he sent back.
B8.11.2 Xì Chōu came on a diplomatic visit,
and also to oversee the covenant.
B8.11.3 Shēng Bó's mother
was not betrothed with proper ceremony.
Mù Jiāng said:
"I will not treat a concubine as a sister-in-law."
She gave birth to Shēng Bó and was then sent away.
She was married to Qí's Guǎn Yúxī,
bore two children and was widowed,
and then returned to Shēng Bó.
Shēng Bó made his maternal half-brother a senior officer,
and married his maternal half-sister to Shī Xiàoshū.
Xì Chōu came on a diplomatic visit,
and sought a wife from Shēng Bó.
Shēng Bó took the wife from the Shī family and gave her to him.
The woman said:
"Even birds and beasts do not lose their mates;
what will you do?"
He said:
"I cannot face death or exile."
The woman then went.
She bore two sons in the Xì family.
When the Xì clan perished,
the men of Jìn returned her to the Shī family.
Shī Xiàoshū met her at the Yellow River,
and drowned her two sons.
The woman angrily said:
"You could not protect your own spouse
and lost her,
and you could not nurture another's orphans
but killed them;
how will you end?"
She then swore an oath against the Shī family.
B8.11.4 In summer,
Jì Wénzǐ went to Jìn,
to reciprocate the diplomatic visit,
and also to oversee the covenant.
B8.11.5 Zhōu Gōng Chǔ resented
the pressure from Huì and
Xiāng,
and moreover contended for governance with Bóyǔ.
Not victorious,
he left in anger.
Reaching Yáng Fán,
the King sent Liúzǐ to restore him,
and they covenanted at Juàn before he entered.
After three days he left again,
and fled to Jìn.
B8.11.6 In autumn,
Xuān Bó went on a diplomatic visit to Qí,
to renew the former friendship.
B8.11.7 Jìn's Xì Zhì
contended with Zhōu over the fields of Hóu.
The King commanded Liú Kānggōng and
Shàn Xiānggōng to litigate the matter at Jìn.
Xì Zhì said:
"Wēn
is our old territory,
therefore we dare not lose it."
Liúzǐ and
Shànzǐ said:
"In the past, when Zhōu conquered Shāng,
they enfeoffed the various lords to pacify the borders.
Sū Fènshēng was made Minister of Justice with Wēn,
and was enfeoffed by the river with Tán Bódá.
The Sū clan then allied with the Dí,
and, not getting along with the Dí, fled to Wèi.
King Xiāng rewarded Duke Wén
and bestowed Wēn upon him.
The Hú clan and
Yáng clan first resided there,
and only later did it come to you.
If we trace its origins,
then it is a city of the royal officials;
how can you possess it?"
The Marquis of Jìn ordered Xì Zhì
not to dare contend further.
B8.11.8 Sòng's Huá Yuán was on good terms with Lìngyǐn Zǐzhòng,
and also on good terms with Luán Wǔzǐ.
Hearing that the men of Chǔ had already agreed to Jìn's Dí Fá's peace proposal,
and had sent him back to report,
in winter,
Huá Yuán went to Chǔ,
and then proceeded to Jìn,
to bring about an agreement between Jìn
and Chǔ.
B8.11.9 Qín and
Jìn made peace,
and were to meet at Lìnghú.
The Marquis of Jìn arrived there first.
The Earl of Qín was unwilling to cross the river,
and encamped at Wángchéng.
He sent Shǐ Kě to covenant with the Marquis of Jìn
east of the river.
Jìn's Xì Chōu covenanted with the Earl of Qín
west of the river.
Fàn Wénzǐ said:
"What benefit is this covenant?
A solemn covenant
is to secure good faith.
The meeting place
is the beginning of trust.
If one does not comply from the start,
what security can there be?"
The Earl of Qín returned and broke the peace with Jìn.
A8.12 *The Twelfth Year of Duke Chéng, Spring and Autumn Annals*
A8.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
Zhōu Gōng fled to Jìn.
A8.12.2 In summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn and
the Marquis of Wèi at Suǒzé.
A8.12.3 In autumn,
the men of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jiāogāng.
A8.12.4 In winter, the tenth month.
B8.12 *The Twelfth Year of Duke Chéng, Commentary*
B8.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
the King sent someone to report the difficulties of Zhōu Gōng.
It was written:
"Zhōu Gōng fled to Jìn."
Generally, from Zhōu there is no 'fleeing out',
but Zhōu Gōng fled out on his own account.
B8.12.2 Sòng's Huá Yuán succeeded in bringing about an agreement between Jìn
and Chǔ.
In summer, in the fifth month,
Jìn's Shì Xiè met with Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Pí and
Xǔ Yǎn.
On Guǐhài day,
they covenanted outside the western gate of Sòng,
saying:
"Henceforth, Jìn and Chǔ shall not impose warfare upon each other,
sharing likes and dislikes,
jointly sympathizing with calamity and danger,
preparing to rescue from misfortune and distress.
If anyone harms Chǔ,
then Jìn shall attack them;
if in Jìn,
Chǔ shall do likewise.
Envoys bearing gifts shall come and go,
the roads unobstructed;
they shall consult on matters of disagreement,
and punish those who do not attend court.
Whoever violates this covenant,
may the bright spirits strike them,
causing their armies to fall,
and may they not long enjoy their state."
The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn to hear the terms of the agreement,
and they met at Suǒzé,
because of the agreement.
B8.12.3 The Dí, taking advantage of the Sòng covenant,
invaded Jìn,
but did not take precautions.
In autumn,
the men of Jìn defeated the Dí at Jiāogāng.
B8.12.4 Jìn's Xì Zhì went to Chǔ on a diplomatic visit,
and also to oversee the covenant.
The Master of Chǔ hosted a feast for him,
with Zǐfǎn as assistant.
They prepared an underground chamber
and suspended bells there.
As Xì Zhì was about to ascend,
metallic music began playing below,
and he was startled and ran out.
Zǐfǎn said:
"The day is growing late,
our ruler is waiting;
please, sir, enter!"
The guest said:
"Your lord does not forget the friendship of his predecessor,
extending it to your humble servant,
bestowing a grand ceremony,
and adding to it with full music.
If by heaven's blessing,
the two lords were to meet,
what could replace this?
Your humble servant dares not."
Zǐfǎn said:
"If by heaven's blessing,
the two lords were to meet,
would it not be merely with an arrow added to the exchange?
What use for music?
Our lord is waiting;
please, sir, enter!"
The guest said:
"If you yield to him by one arrow,
it would be a great calamity;
what kind of blessing would that be?
When the world is well-governed,
the feudal lords, in the intervals between their duties to the Son of Heaven,
pay visits to each other,
and on such occasions there are the ceremonies of the xiǎng feast and the yàn feast.
The xiǎng feast is to teach respect and frugality;
the yàn feast is to demonstrate kindness and generosity.
Respect and frugality are used to conduct ceremonies,
and kindness and generosity are used to administer governance.
Governance is accomplished through ritual,
and thus the people find rest.
The hundred officials carry out their duties,
attending court in the morning and not in the evening;
this is how the dukes and marquises protect their people like a shield and wall.
Therefore, the Odes says:
'Valiant are the warriors,
the dukes and marquises' shield and wall.'
When it falls into disorder,
the feudal lords become greedy and covetous,
invading and desiring without restraint,
fighting over trivial lands and exhausting their people,
and enlisting their warriors
to serve as their own heart and belly, arms and legs, claws and teeth.
Therefore, the Odes says:
'Valiant are the warriors,
the dukes and marquises' heart and belly.'
When the Way prevails under heaven,
then the dukes and marquises can act as shield and wall for the people,
and control their own heart and belly.
In disorder, it is the opposite.
Now your words
are the way of disorder,
and cannot be taken as a model.
However, you, my lord,
are the host,
so how dare I not comply?"
He then entered,
completed the affair,
and upon returning, reported it to Fàn Wénzǐ.
Wénzǐ said:
"Without ritual,
he is sure to go back on his word;
my death is not far off!"
In winter,
Chǔ's prince Bà went to Jìn on a diplomatic mission,
and also attended a covenant.
In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Jìn and Chǔ's prince Bà made a covenant at Chìjí.
A8.13 The Classic of Duke Chéng's Thirteenth Year
A8.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Qí to come and request troops.
A8.13.2 In the third month,
the Duke went to the capital.
A8.13.3 In summer, in the fifth month,
the Duke, from the capital,
then joined the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the men of Zhū,
and the men of Téng in attacking Qín.
A8.13.4 The Earl of Cáo, Lú, died in the army.
A8.13.5 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the Duke arrived back from the attack on Qín.
A8.13.6 In winter,
the burial of Duke Xuān of Cáo took place.
B8.13 The Commentary of Duke Chéng's Thirteenth Year
B8.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Qí to come and request troops,
and in handling the affair he was not respectful.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"The Xì clan is about to perish!
Ritual
is the trunk of the person;
respect
is the foundation of the person.
Master Xì has no foundation.
Moreover, he is a minister inherited from a former ruler,
who received a command to seek troops,
intending to defend the altars of soil and grain,
yet he is negligent;
this is to abandon the ruler's command.
If he does not perish, what will?"
B8.13.2 In the third month,
the Duke went to the capital.
Xuān Bó wanted to receive gifts,
and requested to be sent ahead.
The king treated him with the ritual due to a messenger.
Mèng Xiànzǐ accompanied him.
The king considered him an assistant
and bestowed heavy gifts upon him.
The Duke and the feudal lords had an audience with the king,
and then followed Liú Kānggōng and Chéng Sùgōng
to join the Marquis of Jìn in attacking Qín.
Chéngzǐ received the sacrificial meat at the altar of soil,
but was not respectful.
Master Liú said:
"I have heard it said:
The people receive the mean of heaven and earth to be born;
this is what is called destiny.
Therefore, there are rules for action, ritual, righteousness, dignity, and demeanor,
to stabilize destiny.
Those who are capable nurture it to obtain blessing;
those who are incapable ruin it and bring calamity upon themselves.
Therefore, the gentleman is diligent in ritual,
and the small man exhausts his strength.
In diligence to ritual, nothing is like showing utmost respect;
in exhausting strength, nothing is like being sincere and steadfast.
Respect lies in nourishing the spirits;
steadfastness lies in guarding one's duties.
The great affairs of a state
are sacrifice and war.
In sacrifice, there is the receiving of the cooked meat;
in war, there is the receiving of the raw meat;
these are the great ceremonies for the spirits.
Now Chéngzǐ is negligent;
he has abandoned his destiny.
Will he not return?"
B8.13.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on the wǔwǔ day,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Lǚ Xiàng to break off relations with Qín,
saying:
"In the past, from the time of our Duke Xiàn and your Duke Mù, they were friendly with each other,
joining forces and uniting their hearts,
binding it with covenants and oaths,
and reinforcing it with marriage alliances.
Heaven brought calamity upon the state of Jìn,
and Duke Wén went to Qí,
while Duke Huì went to Qín.
Unfortunately,
Duke Xiàn passed away.
Duke Mù did not forget the former virtue,
and enabled our Duke Huì thereby to continue the sacrifices in Jìn.
Yet he was unable to accomplish a great achievement,
and there was the battle of Hán.
He also repented in his heart,
and thereby established our Duke Wén;
this was Duke Mù's accomplishment.
Duke Wén personally donned armor and helmet,
traversed mountains and rivers,
crossed over dangerous obstacles,
subdued the feudal lords of the east,
the descendants of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu,
and made them pay court to Qín;
thus he had already repaid the former virtue.
The people of Zhèng provoked your borders,
and our Duke Wén led the feudal lords and Qín to besiege Zhèng.
The great officers of Qín did not consult with our humble ruler,
but arbitrarily made a covenant with Zhèng.
The feudal lords resented this,
and were about to deliver a fatal blow to Qín.
Duke Wén was fearful,
pacified and calmed the feudal lords,
and the Qín army was able to return unharmed;
this was a great service we rendered to the west.
Unfortunately,
Duke Wén passed away,
and Duke Mù showed no condolences,
disparaged our deceased ruler,
treated our Duke Xiāng as insignificant,
invaded our territory at Xiáo,
cut off our friendly relations,
attacked our fortified cities,
exterminated our Fèi Huá,
scattered and separated our brothers,
disrupted and confused our allies,
and overturned our state.
Our Duke Xiāng had not forgotten your former merits,
but feared the fall of the altars of soil and grain,
and therefore there was the battle of Xiáo.
He still wished to seek pardon for the offense from Duke Mù.
Duke Mù would not listen,
but instead turned to Chǔ to plot against us.
Heaven guided his heart,
and King Chéng met his death,
so Duke Mù was unable to fulfill his ambitions against us.
Dukes Mù and Xiāng passed away,
and Dukes Kāng and Líng ascended the throne.
Duke Kāng
was born of our line,
yet he also wanted to weaken and cut down our ducal house,
overturn our altars of soil and grain,
led our pests and vermin,
to come and shake our borders;
therefore we had the battle of Línghú.
Kānggōng still did not repent,
invaded our Héqū,
attacked our Sùchuān,
captured our Wángguān,
and seized our Jīmǎ.
This is why we had the battle of Héqū.
The reason the eastern route was blocked
was because Kānggōng severed our friendly relations.
"When you, my lord, succeeded to the throne,
our lord Jǐnggōng craned his neck looking westward and said:
'Perhaps he will comfort us!'
But you, my lord, also did not kindly agree to an alliance.
Taking advantage of our troubles with the Dí,
you entered our Héxiàn,
burned our Jī and Gào,
destroyed our agricultural work,
and slaughtered our border people.
This is why we gathered at Fǔshì.
You, my lord, also regretted the prolongation of hostilities
and wished to seek blessings from the former lords Xiàn and Mù.
You sent Bóchē to command our lord Jǐnggōng, saying:
'I and you shall join in friendship, abandon enmity,
restore the old virtue,
and recall former merits.'
Before the oath was completed,
Jǐnggōng passed away,
and thus our humble lord had the meeting at Línghú.
You, my lord, again proved inauspicious,
betraying the alliance oath.
The Báidí and you, my lord, share the same region;
they are your enemies,
yet they are our relatives by marriage.
You, my lord, came with a command, saying:
'I and you shall attack the Dí.'
Our humble lord dared not consider the marriage ties,
but fearing your might,
he accepted the command from your officer.
Yet you, my lord, had duplicitous intentions toward the Dí,
saying:
'Jìn is about to attack you.'
The Dí, though responding, felt hatred,
and therefore informed us.
The people of Chǔ also detested your fickleness in virtue,
and came to inform us, saying:
'Qín betrayed the alliance of Línghú
and came seeking an alliance with us:
"Solemnly announcing to the August Heaven God,
the three dukes of Qín,
and the three kings of Chǔ,
I say: 'Although I have dealings with Jìn,
I look only to profit.'
I, the unworthy one, detest their lack of constant virtue,
and therefore proclaim this,
to punish inconsistency."'
The feudal lords have all heard these words,
and thus are pained to the heart and aggrieved,
drawing close to me, the humble one.
I lead them to heed your command,
seeking only friendship.
If you, my lord, kindly regard the feudal lords,
pity me, the humble one,
and grant an alliance,
then it is the wish of me, the humble one,
to receive and pacify the feudal lords
and withdraw,
daring not to seek turmoil.
If you, my lord, do not bestow great kindness,
I, the humble one, though incompetent,
will not be able to withdraw the feudal lords.
I dare to fully lay this before your officer,
that your officer may truly consider what is beneficial.'"
Qín Huángōng
had already made the alliance of Línghú with Jìn Lìgōng,
but then summoned the Dí and Chǔ,
intending to lead them to attack Jìn.
Therefore, the feudal lords became friendly with Jìn.
Jìn Luán Shū commanded the central army,
with Xún Gēng assisting him;
Shì Xiè commanded the upper army,
with Xì Qí assisting him;
Hán Jué commanded the lower army,
with Xún Yīng assisting him;
Zhào Zhān commanded the new army,
with Xì Zhì assisting him.
Xì Gǔ drove the war chariot,
with Luán Zhēn as the right-hand guard.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"The Jìn commanders and troops are harmonious;
the army is sure to achieve great merit."
On the dīnghài day of the fifth month,
the Jìn army, together with the armies of the feudal lords,
fought the Qín army at Másù.
The Qín army was defeated,
and Chéng Chā of Qín and the Bùgēng Nǚfù were captured.
Cáo Xuāngōng died in the army.
The army then crossed the Jīng River,
reached Hóulì and returned.
They welcomed the Jìn lord at Xīnchǔ.
Chéng Sùgōng died at Xiá.
B8.13.4 On the dīngmǎo night of the sixth month,
Zhèng's prince Bān from Zī
sought entry into the great temple,
but failed.
He killed Zǐyìn
and Zǐyǔ,
then turned his army to the market.
On the jǐsì day,
Zǐsì
led the people of the state to swear an oath in the great temple,
then followed and burned it all,
killing Zǐrú, Zǐmáng,
Sūnshū, and Sūnzhī.
B8.13.5 The people of Cáo sent prince Fùchú to guard,
and sent prince Xīnshí to meet the funeral of the Cáo lord.
In autumn,
Fùchú killed the heir apparent
and established himself.
The feudal lords then requested to punish him.
The people of Jìn, because of the toil of their campaign,
asked to wait until another year.
In winter,
they buried Cáo Xuāngōng.
After the burial, Zǐzāng was about to flee,
and all the people of the state were going to follow him.
Chénggōng then became afraid,
admitted his fault,
and pleaded with him.
Zǐzāng then returned
and presented his city.
A8.14 "The Classic of the Fourteenth Year of Duke Chéng"
A8.14.1 In the fourteenth year, spring,
in the king's first month,
the viscount of Jǔ, Zhū, died.
A8.14.2 In summer,
Wèi's Sūn Línfù returned from Jìn to Wèi.
A8.14.3 In autumn,
Shūsūn Qiáorú went to Qí to meet the bride.
A8.14.4 Zhèng's prince Xǐ led an army to attack Xǔ.
A8.14.5 In the ninth month,
Qiáorú arrived from Qí with the lady, wife Jiāngshì.
A8.14.6 In winter, on the gēngyín day of the tenth month,
the lord of Wèi, Zāng, died.
A8.14.7 The earl of Qín died.
B8.14 "The Commentary of the Fourteenth Year of Duke Chéng"
B8.14.1 In the fourteenth year, spring,
the lord of Wèi went to Jìn,
and the lord of Jìn insisted on having Sūn Línfù presented.
Dìnggōng would not agree.
In summer,
after the lord of Wèi had returned,
the lord of Jìn sent Xì Chōu to escort Sūn Línfù
and have him presented.
The lord of Wèi wanted to decline.
Dìng Jiāng said:
"Do not.
He is the heir of our former lord's ancestral minister,
and the great state also makes this request.
If you do not agree,
we will perish.
Although you dislike him,
is it not still better than perishing?
My lord, endure it!
Pacify the people and pardon the ancestral minister—
is that not acceptable?"
The lord of Wèi received him and restored him.
The lord of Wèi feasted Kǔchéng Shū,
with Nìng Huìzǐ assisting.
Kǔchéng Shū was arrogant.
Nìngzǐ said:
"Kǔchéng Shū's house will likely perish!
In ancient times, at feasts and meals,
they observed dignity and demeanor,
and examined fortune and misfortune.
Therefore, the Odes say:
'The rhinoceros cups are curved,
the fine wine is mild.
Not haughty nor arrogant,
ten thousand blessings come seeking.'
Now this man is arrogant—
it is the way to invite misfortune."
B8.14.2 In autumn,
Xuān Bó went to Qí to meet the bride.
He is referred to by his clan name,
to honor the lord's command.
B8.14.3 In the eighth month,
Zǐ Hǎn of Zhèng attacked Xǔ,
but was defeated.
On the Wùxū day,
the Earl of Zhèng attacked Xǔ again.
On the Gēngzǐ day, he entered its outer city.
The people of Xǔ sought peace
by agreeing to the boundaries set by Shū Shēn.
B8.14.4 In the ninth month,
Qiáorú arrived from Qí with the lady, the wife Jiāng.
He omitted his clan name,
to honor the lady.
Therefore, the gentleman said:
"The terminology of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
is subtle yet clear,
records yet is profound,
tactful yet forms a complete text,
exhaustive yet not excessive,
punishes evil and encourages good.
If not a sage,
who could have compiled it?"
B8.14.5 The Marquis of Wèi was ill,
and sent Kǒng Chéngzǐ
and Nìng Huìzǐ
to establish Kàn, the son of Jìng Sì, as the heir apparent.
In the tenth month of winter,
Duke Dìng of Wèi died.
The lady Jiāng, after weeping, rested,
and seeing that the heir apparent showed no grief,
she did not partake of the sacrificial wine,
and sighed, saying:
"This man,
will not only bring ruin to the state of Wèi,
but it will surely begin with me, the widow.
Alas!
Heaven is bringing calamity upon Wèi!
That I could not get Zhuān
to preside over the altars of soil and grain."
The great officers, hearing this,
were all filled with awe and fear.
Sūn Wénzǐ from then on did not dare
to leave his precious vessels in Wèi,
but placed them all in Qī,
and was very friendly with the great officers of Jìn.
A8.15 The Classic of Duke Chéng, Year Fifteen
A8.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
in the king's second month,
Duke Dìng of Wèi was buried.
A8.15.2 In the third month, on the Yǐsì day,
Zhòng Yīngqí died.
A8.15.3 On the Guǐchǒu day,
the duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
Chéng, the heir apparent of Sòng,
Guó Zuǒ of Qí,
and a man of Zhū, and they formed an alliance at Qī.
The Marquis of Jìn seized the Earl of Cáo and took him back to the capital.
A8.15.4 The duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.15.5 In summer, in the sixth month,
Duke Gù of Sòng died.
A8.15.6 The Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng.
A8.15.7 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the Gēngchén day,
Duke Gòng of Sòng was buried.
A8.15.8 Huà Yuán of Sòng fled to Jìn.
A8.15.9 Huà Yuán of Sòng returned from Jìn to Sòng.
A8.15.10 Sòng put to death its great officer Shān.
A8.15.11 Yú Shí of Sòng fled to Chǔ.
A8.15.12 In winter, in the eleventh month,
Shūsūn Qiáorú met with Shì Xiè of Jìn,
Gāo Wújiù of Qí,
Huà Yuán of Sòng,
Sūn Línfǔ of Wèi,
Gōngzǐ Qiū of Zhèng,
and a man of Zhū, and they met with Wú at Zhōnglí.
A8.15.13 Xǔ moved its capital to Yè.
B8.15 The Commentary of Duke Chéng, Year Fifteen
B8.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
they met at Qī,
to condemn Duke Chéng of Cáo.
He was seized and taken back to the capital.
The record says
"the Marquis of Jìn seized the Earl of Cáo,"
because he had not involved his people.
Whenever a ruler is unjust towards his people,
and the feudal lords condemn and seize him,
it is recorded as
"so-and-so seized such-and-such a marquis,"
otherwise it is not.
The feudal lords were about to present Zǐ Zāng to the king
and establish him.
Zǐ Zāng declined, saying:
"The former records have it:
'The sage attains the proper measure,
the next best maintains the proper measure,
the lowest loses the proper measure.'
To become a ruler is not my proper measure.
Though I cannot be a sage,
how dare I lose what I should maintain?"
Thereupon he fled and went to Sòng.
B8.15.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
Duke Gòng of Sòng died.
B8.15.3 Chǔ was about to send an army north.
Zǐ Náng said:
"We have newly made an alliance with Jìn and now betray it;
is this not improper?"
Zǐ Fǎn said:
"When the situation is advantageous against the enemy, we advance;
what does an alliance matter?"
Shēn Shū Shí was old,
and was in Shēn.
Hearing this,
he said:
"Zǐ Fǎn will certainly not escape calamity.
Good faith is used to uphold propriety,
propriety is used to protect one's person.
When good faith and propriety are lost,
to wish to escape calamity,
is it possible?"
The Viscount of Chǔ invaded Zhèng,
reaching Bàosuì.
Then he invaded Wèi,
reaching Shǒuzhǐ.
Zǐ Hǎn of Zhèng invaded Chǔ,
and took Xīnshí.
Luán Wǔzǐ wished to retaliate against Chǔ.
Hán Xiànzǐ said:
"There is no need.
Let them increase their crimes,
and the people will turn against them.
Without the people,
with whom will they fight?"
B8.15.4 In autumn, in the eighth month,
Duke Gòng of Sòng was buried.
At that time, Huà Yuán was the Right Marshal,
Yú Shí was the Left Marshal,
Dàng Zé was the Minister of War,
Huà Xǐ was the Minister of Education,
Gōngsūn Shī was the Minister of Works,
Xiàng Wéirén was the Chief Minister of Justice,
Lín Zhū was the Junior Minister of Justice,
Xiàng Dài was the Grand Steward,
Yú Fǔ was the Junior Steward.
Dàng Zé weakened the ducal house,
and killed Gōngzǐ Féi.
Huà Yuán said:
"I am the Right Marshal;
the instruction of ruler and minister,
is what my office oversees.
Now the ducal house is humbled,
and I cannot rectify it;
my crime is great.
Unable to manage my office,
how dare I cling to favor?"
Thereupon he fled to Jìn.
The two Huà
were of the Dài clan;
the Minister of Works
was of the Zhuāng clan;
the six officers were all of the Huán clan.
Yú Shí was about to stop Huà Yuán.
Yú Fǔ said:
"If the Right Marshal returns,
he will certainly exact punishment;
this will mean the end of the Huán clan."
Yú Shí said:
"If the Right Marshal does get to return,
even if we allow him to exact punishment,
he certainly will not dare.
Moreover, he has many great achievements,
and the people of the state are with him.
If he does not return,
I fear the Huán clan will have no sacrifices
in Sòng.
If the Right Marshal exacts punishment,
there is still Xū.
Even if the Huán clan perishes,
it will only be partially."
Yú Shí himself intercepted Huà Yuán on the riverbank.
He requested permission to attack,
which was granted,
and then he returned.
He sent Huà Xǐ and Gōngsūn Shī to lead the men of the capital
to attack the Dàng clan,
killing Zǐshān.
The record says, "Sòng killed its senior officer Shān,"
indicating that he turned against his own clan.
Yú Shí, Xiàng Wéirén, Lín Zhū, Xiàng Dài,
and Yú Fǔ went out and took up quarters on the banks of the Suī River.
Huà Yuán sent someone to stop them,
but they would not listen.
In winter, the tenth month,
Huà Yuán personally went to stop them,
but they would not listen,
so he returned.
Yú Fǔ said:
"If we do not follow him now,
we will not be able to re-enter the capital.
The Right Marshal looked hurried and spoke hastily,
indicating he has other intentions.
If he does not admit us,
he will now gallop away."
They climbed a hill and watched him,
and indeed he galloped off.
They whipped their horses and followed him,
but he had already breached the Suī River embankment
and closed the gates, ascending the ramparts.
The Left Marshal,
the two Directors of Crime,
and the two Stewards then fled to Chǔ.
Huà Yuán appointed Xiàng Xū as Left Marshal,
Lǎo Zuǒ as Minister of War,
and Yuè Yì as Director of Crime,
to pacify the men of the capital.
B8.15.5 The three Xì clans of Jìn hated Bó Zōng,
slandered him, and killed him,
along with Luán Fújì.
Bó Zhōulí fled to Chǔ.
Hán Xiànzǐ said:
"The Xì clan will surely not escape calamity!
Good men are
the guiding principles of Heaven and Earth,
yet they repeatedly exterminate them.
If they do not perish,
what are they waiting for?"
Earlier,
whenever Bó Zōng went to court,
his wife would always warn him, saying:
"'Thieves hate their master;
the people detest those above them.'
You, sir, are fond of speaking bluntly,
and will surely meet with disaster."
B8.15.6 In the eleventh month,
they met with Wú at Zhōnglí,
marking the beginning of communications with Wú.
B8.15.7 Duke Líng of Xǔ, fearing pressure from Zhèng,
requested to move to Chǔ.
On the xīnchǒu day,
Prince Shēn of Chǔ moved Xǔ to Yè.
A8.16 The Classic of Duke Chéng's Sixteenth Year
A8.16.1 In the sixteenth year, spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
it rained, and the trees were covered in ice.
A8.16.2 In summer, the fourth month, on the xīnwèi day,
the Viscount of Téng died.
A8.16.3 Prince Xǐ of Zhèng led an army to invade Sòng.
A8.16.4 In the sixth month, on the bǐngyín day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
A8.16.5 The Marquis of Jìn sent Luán Yǎn to request troops.
A8.16.6 On the jiǎwǔ day, the last day of the month,
the Marquis of Jìn and the Viscount of Chǔ,
along with the Earl of Zhèng, fought at Yānlíng.
The Viscount of Chǔ
and the army of Zhèng were defeated.
A8.16.7 Chǔ executed its senior officer, Prince Cè.
A8.16.8 In autumn,
our duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Marquis of Wèi,
Huà Yuán of Sòng,
and a man from Zhū at Shásuí,
but they did not receive our duke.
A8.16.9 Our duke returned from the meeting.
A8.16.10 Our duke met with Master Yǐn,
the Marquis of Jìn,
Guó Zuǒ of Qí,
and a man from Zhū to attack Zhèng.
A8.16.11 The Earl of Cáo returned from the royal capital.
A8.16.12 In the ninth month,
the men of Jìn arrested Jìsūn Xíngfǔ
and detained him at Tiáoqiū.
A8.16.13 In winter, the tenth month, on the yǐhài day,
Shūsūn Qiáorú fled to Qí.
A8.16.14 In the twelfth month, on the yǐchǒu day,
Jìsūn Xíngfǔ and Xì Chōu of Jìn made a covenant at Hù.
A8.16.15 Our duke returned from the meeting.
A8.16.16 On the yǐyǒu day,
Prince Yǎn was assassinated.
B8.16 The Commentary of Duke Chéng's Sixteenth Year
B8.16.1 In the sixteenth year, spring,
the Viscount of Chǔ, from Wǔchéng, sent Prince Chéng
to offer the lands south of the Rǔ River to seek peace with Zhèng.
Zhèng rebelled against Jìn,
and Zǐsì followed the Viscount of Chǔ to make a covenant at Wǔchéng.
B8.16.2 In summer, the fourth month,
Duke Wén of Téng died.
B8.16.3 Zǐhǎn of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
Jiàng Chú
and Yuè Jù of Sòng defeated him at Zhuóbēi.
They retreated
and encamped at Fúqú,
without taking precautions.
The men of Zhèng ambushed them,
defeating them at Zhuólíng,
and capturing Jiàng Chú
and Yuè Jù.
Sòng had relied on its victory.
B8.16.4 The Marquis of Wèi attacked Zhèng,
reaching Míngyàn,
for the sake of Jìn.
B8.16.5 The Marquis of Jìn was about to attack Zhèng.
Fàn Wénzǐ said:
"If we fulfill our wishes,
and all the feudal lords rebel,
Jìn can then fulfill its ambitions.
If only Zhèng rebels,
the troubles for the state of Jìn
will arrive immediately."
Luán Wǔzǐ said:
"We cannot, in our generation, lose the feudal lords.
We must attack Zhèng."
So they raised an army.
Luán Shū commanded the central army,
with Shì Xiè as his assistant;
Xì Qí commanded the upper army,
with Xún Yǎn as his assistant;
Hán Jué commanded the lower army;
Xì Zhì assisted the new army.
Xún Yīng remained to guard the state.
Xì Chōu went to Wèi,
then proceeded to Qí,
requesting troops in both places.
Luán Yǎn came to request troops.
Mèng Xiànzǐ said:
"There will be victory."
On the wùyín day,
the Jìn army set out.
When the men of Zhèng heard that the Jìn army was coming,
they sent word to Chǔ,
with Yáo Jù'ěr accompanying the messenger.
The Viscount of Chǔ went to rescue Zhèng.
The Minister of War commanded the central army,
the Prime Minister commanded the left,
and the Right Minister, Zǐxīn, commanded the right.
Passing through Shēn,
Zǐfǎn went in to see Shēn Shūshí,
and said, "How will the army fare?"
He replied:
"Virtue, punishment, reverence, righteousness,
ritual, and good faith
are the instruments of war.
Virtue is for bestowing kindness,
punishment for correcting evil,
reverence for serving the spirits,
righteousness for creating benefit,
ritual for obeying the seasons,
and good faith for preserving things.
When the people's livelihood
is abundant and virtue is upright,
resources are used beneficially and affairs are regulated,
the seasons are followed and things are accomplished,
superiors and inferiors are harmonious and amiable,
actions are smooth and unopposed,
needs are all met,
and each knows his proper limits.
Therefore, the Odes say:
'You established our multitudes of people;
none fails to take your standard as his rule.'"
Thus, the gods bestowed blessings upon them,
and there were no disasters at that time.
The people's lives were prosperous and abundant,
harmonious and united in their obedience,
all exerting their utmost effort
to follow the commands of their superiors,
even willing to die to make up for any deficiencies.
This is why they were victorious in battle.
Now, the state of Chǔ internally neglects its people,
and externally severs its alliances;
it violates solemn covenants,
and breaks its promises;
it acts at inopportune times,
and exhausts its people to satisfy its own desires.
The people do not know where trust lies,
and whether they advance or retreat, they are deemed guilty.
Everyone is concerned about their own safety,
so who would be willing to fight to the death?
You must strive hard!
I will not see you again."
Yáo Jù'ěr returned first,
and Zǐ Sì asked him about the situation.
He replied:
"Their march is hasty,
and when passing through dangerous terrain, they are disorganized.
Haste leads to loss of composure,
and disorganization
means the loss of formation.
With composure lost
and formation broken,
how can they fight?
The Chǔ army is not to be feared."
In the fifth month,
the Jìn army crossed the Yellow River.
Hearing that the Chǔ army was approaching,
Fàn Wénzǐ wanted to turn back,
saying:
"If we pretend to flee from Chǔ,
we can alleviate our worries.
As for uniting the feudal lords,
that is not something we are capable of,
so we should leave it to those who can.
If we, as ministers, can live in harmony
and serve our ruler,
that is more than enough."
Wǔzǐ said:
"That cannot be done."
In the sixth month,
the armies of Jìn and Chǔ met at Yānlíng.
Fàn Wénzǐ did not wish to engage in battle.
Xì Zhì said:
"In the battle of Hán,
Duke Huí did not return with his army intact;
in the campaign at Jī,
Xiān Zhěn did not return alive;
in the battle of Bì,
Xún Bó did not bring back his troops.
These are all shames for Jìn.
You have also witnessed the affairs of our former rulers.
Now, if we avoid Chǔ,
we will only add to our shame."
Wénzǐ said:
"Our former rulers frequently engaged in war
for a reason.
Qín, Dí,
Qí, and Chǔ were all strong,
and if they had not exerted their full effort,
their descendants would have become weak.
Now, three of the strong states have submitted,
and only Chǔ remains as our enemy.
Only a sage can ensure there are no troubles both internally and externally.
Since we are not sages,
external peace will inevitably lead to internal troubles.
Why not spare Chǔ
to serve as an external threat?"
On the last day of the month, Jiǎwǔ,
the Chǔ army pressed close to the Jìn army at dawn and formed their battle lines.
The Jìn officers were troubled by this.
Fàn Gài hurried forward,
saying:
"Fill in the wells and level the stoves,
form our battle lines within the camp,
and spread out the front ranks.
Whether Jìn or Chǔ prevails depends on Heaven's will.
What is there to worry about?"
Wénzǐ took up a spear and chased him away,
saying:
"The survival or fall of a state
is determined by Heaven.
What does a youth like you know?"
Luán Shū said:
"The Chǔ army is rash and reckless.
If we fortify our positions and wait,
they will surely retreat within three days.
When they retreat, we can attack them,
and we will certainly achieve victory."
Xì Zhì said:
"There are six weaknesses in the Chǔ army,
and we must not miss this opportunity.
Their two high ministers are at odds with each other,
the king's troops are composed of old soldiers,
the Zhèng army is in formation but disorganized,
the Mán troops are present but not in formation,
they have formed their lines on the last day of the month,
there is clamor within their ranks,
and when they gather, the noise increases.
Each is concerned about their own safety,
and none have the will to fight.
Old soldiers are not necessarily skilled,
and they have violated a heavenly taboo.
We are sure to defeat them."
The king of Chǔ ascended a watchtower chariot
to observe the Jìn army.
Zǐ Zhòng had the Grand Steward Bó Zhōulí stand behind the king.
The king asked:
"Why are they galloping left and right?"
Bó Zhōulí replied:
"They are summoning their officers."
"They have all gathered in the central army."
He said:
"They are planning together."
"They have set up tents."
He said:
"They are reverently divining before their ancestors."
"They have taken down the tents."
He said:
"They are about to issue orders."
"There is great clamor,
and dust is rising."
He said:
"They are about to fill in the wells and level the stoves
to form their ranks."
"They have all mounted their chariots,
and the left and right are descending with weapons in hand."
He said:
"They are listening to the oath."
"Are they going to fight?"
He said:
"It is not yet certain."
"They have mounted their chariots, and both left and right have descended."
He said:
"They are praying before battle."
Bó Zhōulí reported the movements of the Jìn army to the king.
Miáo Bēnhuáng was by the side of the marquis of Jìn,
and he also reported the movements of the king's troops.
Both said:
"The elite troops are there,
and they are numerous.
They are not to be confronted."
Miáo Bēnhuáng said to the marquis of Jìn:
"The elite troops of Chǔ
are only in the central army, the king's own clan.
I suggest dividing our elite troops
to attack their left and right wings,
while our four armies concentrate on the king's troops.
We will surely inflict a great defeat on them."
The marquis performed a divination.
The diviner said:
"It is auspicious.
The hexagram encountered is 'Fù' (Return)
and it says:
'The southern state is distressed,
shoot its great king,
and hit his eye.'
With the state distressed and the king wounded,
how can they avoid defeat?"
The marquis followed this advice.
There was a muddy area ahead,
so they all moved left and right to avoid it.
Bù Yù drove the chariot for Jìn Lìgōng,
with Luán Zhēn as the right-hand guard.
Péng Míng drove for Chǔ Gòngwáng,
with Pān Dǎng as the right-hand guard.
Shí Shǒu drove for Zhèng Chénggōng,
with Táng Xún as the right-hand guard.
The Luán and Fàn clans flanked the marquis as they advanced.
They became stuck in the mud.
Luán Shū was about to take the marquis onto his chariot.
Luán Zhēn said:
"Shū, step back!
The state has entrusted you with great responsibilities.
How can you take charge of everything?
Moreover, to encroach on another's duties
is presumptuous,
to neglect one's own duties
is negligent,
and to leave one's post
is treacherous.
You would commit three offenses.
This must not be done."
So he lifted the marquis out of the mud.
On the guǐsì day,
Pān Wāng's partisans and Yǎng Yóujī
piled up armor and shot at it,
penetrating seven layers.
They showed this to the king,
saying:
"With two ministers like these,
what worry is there in battle?"
The king angrily said:
"A great disgrace to the state!
Tomorrow morning when you shoot,
you will die by your skill."
Lǚ Qí dreamed of shooting the moon,
hitting it,
then retreated into mud.
It was divined,
and the interpretation said:
"The Jī surname
is the sun;
other surnames
are the moon.
This must be the king of Chǔ.
Shooting and hitting it,
then retreating into mud—
he too will certainly die."
When battle came,
he shot at King Gòng, hitting his eye.
The king summoned Yǎng Yóujī,
gave him two arrows,
and ordered him to shoot Lǚ Qí.
He hit his neck,
and Lǚ Qí fell upon his bow case.
Yǎng Yóujī returned with one arrow to report.
Xì Zhì three times encountered the troops of the Chǔ ruler,
and whenever he saw the Chǔ ruler,
he would dismount,
remove his helmet and hasten like the wind.
The Chǔ ruler sent the artisan-official Xiāng to present him with a bow,
saying:
"In the heat of the affair,
there was a gentleman in leather leg-guards.
He is a nobleman.
Having seen my humble self and hastened away,
was he perhaps wounded?"
Xì Zhì met the envoy,
removed his helmet and received the command,
saying:
"Your servant from abroad, Zhì,
following my ruler in military affairs,
by your grace,
am temporarily clad in armor,
and dare not bow to receive your command.
I venture to report that I am unharmed,
and am honored by your command.
For the sake of the affair,
I venture to salute the envoy."
He saluted the envoy three times and withdrew.
Jìn's Hán Jué pursued the earl of Zhèng,
and his charioteer Dù Hùnluó said:
"Quickly pursue him?
His charioteer frequently looks back,
his attention not on the horses—
he can be overtaken."
Hán Jué said:
"I cannot disgrace a ruler of a state twice."
So he stopped.
Xì Zhì pursued the earl of Zhèng,
and his right-hand man Fú Hànhú said:
"Send a scout to intercept his chariot,
I will follow and board it,
and capture him alive."
Xì Zhì said:
"To injure a ruler of a state is punishable."
He too stopped.
Shí Shǒu said:
"Duke Yì of Wèi only failed to remove his banner,
and thus was defeated at Yíng."
So he stored his banner inside its case.
Táng Gǒu said to Shí Shǒu:
"You are at the ruler's side—
in defeat, the great matter is one.
I am not as good as you.
You ensure the ruler's escape,
I request to stay behind."
Then he died.
The Chǔ army was pressed in a narrow place,
and Shūshān Rǎn said to Yǎng Yóujī:
"Though the ruler gave an order,
for the state's sake,
you must shoot."
So he shot,
fired twice,
and killed them all.
Shūshān Rǎn seized men and threw them,
hitting a chariot,
and breaking its front rail.
The Jìn army then halted.
They captured the Chǔ prince Fá.
Luán Zhēn saw Zǐ Chóng's banner,
and requested:
"The Chǔ people call that banner
Zǐ Chóng's command flag—
that must be Zǐ Chóng.
Formerly, when your servant was envoy to Chǔ,
Zǐ Chóng asked about Jìn's courage.
Your servant replied:
'We excel at being orderly in masses.'
He said:
'What else?'
Your servant replied:
'We excel at being leisurely.'
Now two states conduct warfare,
envoys are not sent—
this cannot be called orderly;
facing affairs
and breaking one's word—
this cannot be called leisurely.
I request to offer him a drink."
The duke permitted it.
He sent an envoy holding a vessel with drink,
who went to Zǐ Chóng,
saying:
"My ruler lacks men to send,
so Zhēn serves holding a spear,
and thus cannot feast your followers.
He sends me to offer a drink."
Zǐ Chóng said:
"That gentleman once spoke with me in Chǔ—
this must be the reason.
Is he not thoughtful?"
He accepted and drank it,
dismissed the envoy, and resumed drumming.
They fought from dawn
until stars appeared, not yet ceased.
Zǐ Fǎn ordered army officers to inspect the wounded,
replenish foot soldiers and chariots,
repair armor and weapons,
check chariots and horses,
eat at cockcrow,
and be ready to obey orders.
The Jìn people were troubled by this.
Miáo Bēnhuáng announced:
"Inspect chariots, replenish troops,
feed horses, sharpen weapons,
repair formations, solidify ranks,
eat early, offer prayers again—
tomorrow we fight once more!"
Then they released Chǔ prisoners.
The king heard of this,
and summoned Zǐ Fǎn to consult.
Gǔyáng Shù offered drink to Zǐ Fǎn,
and Zǐ Fǎn became drunk and could not appear.
The king said:
"Heaven is defeating Chǔ!
I cannot wait."
So he fled overnight.
The Jìn entered the Chǔ camp,
and feasted for three days.
Fàn Wénzǐ stood before the army horses,
saying:
"The ruler is young,
and we ministers are not talented—
how did we achieve this?
May the ruler be cautious!
The Zhōu Shū says:
'The Mandate is not constant.'
This refers to having virtue."
The Chǔ army returned,
and reaching Xiá,
the king sent word to Zǐ Fǎn, saying:
"When the late great officer caused the army's defeat,
the ruler was not present.
You need not take it as your fault—
it is my crime."
Zǐ Fǎn bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"If the ruler grants me death,
death will be immortal.
Your servant's troops indeed fled—
it is your servant's crime."
Zǐ Chóng again said to Zǐ Fǎn:
"The one who first lost the army—
you have heard of him too.
Why not consider it!"
He replied:
"Even without the precedent of the late great officer having done so,
if you, great officer, command Cè,
how dare Cè act unrighteously?
Cè has destroyed the ruler's army—
how dare he forget death?"
The king sent to stop him,
but before they arrived, he died.
On the day of battle,
Qí's Guó Zuǒ and Gāo Wújiù arrived with the army,
the marquis of Wèi set out from Wèi,
and the duke set out from Huàituí.
Xuān Bó had an affair with Mù Jiāng,
and wanted to remove Jì and Mèng
and take their households.
As he was about to depart,
Mù Jiāng saw Duke Chéng off
and urged him to expel the two ministers.
The duke explained the difficulties with Jìn,
saying:
"I request to return and obey your command."
Jiāng was angry.
When the dukes' sons Yǎn and Chú hurried past,
she pointed at them and said:
"If you do not do this,
these will both become rulers."
The duke waited at Huàituí,
inspected the palace,
strengthened the defenses, set up guards,
and only then departed,
thus he was late.
He sent Mèng Xiànzǐ to guard the ducal palace.
B8.16.6 In autumn,
a meeting was held at Shāsuí,
to plan an attack on Zhèng.
Xuān Bó sent a message to Xì Chōu, saying:
"The Marquis of Lǔ is waiting at Huàituí,
to await the victors."
Xì Chōu commanded the new army
and also served as a senior minister of the ducal clan,
overseeing the eastern feudal lords.
He accepted bribes from Xuān Bó
and slandered the duke to the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn refused to see the duke.
B8.16.7 The people of Cáo petitioned Jìn, saying:
"Since our late ruler Duke Xuān ascended the throne,
the people of the state have said:
'What is to be done?
Our worries have not yet ceased.'
And now you punish our humble ruler,
causing the loss of the guardian of the Cáo state's altars of soil and grain—
the ducal son.
This is to utterly destroy Cáo.
Did our late ruler perhaps have some crime?
If he had a crime,
then you, my lord, placed him among the meetings.
My lord, only by not neglecting virtue and punishments
have you become hegemon of the feudal lords.
How could you neglect only our humble state?
We dare to privately state this."
B8.16.8 In the seventh month,
the duke joined Duke Wǔ of Yǐn and the feudal lords in attacking Zhèng.
As he was about to depart,
Jiāng again ordered the duke as before.
The duke again strengthened the guards and then departed.
The armies of the feudal lords were stationed west of Zhèng,
while our army was stationed at Dūyáng,
not daring to pass Zhèng.
Zǐshū Shēngbó sent Shūsūn Bào
to request to meet the Jìn army,
and prepared food in the suburbs of Zhèng.
The army came to meet them.
Shēngbó went without food for four days waiting for them,
and only ate after feeding the envoys.
B8.16.9 The feudal lords moved to Zhìtián.
Zhì Wǔzǐ assisted the lower army
and led the armies of the feudal lords to invade Chén,
reaching Mínglù.
Then they invaded Cài.
Before they returned,
the feudal lords moved to the banks of the Yǐng River.
On the wùwǔ day,
Zhèng's Zǐ Hǎn attacked them at night,
and Sòng, Qí, and Wèi all lost their armies.
B8.16.10 The people of Cáo again petitioned Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn said to Zǐ Zāng:
"Return,
and I will restore your ruler."
Zǐ Zāng returned,
and the Earl of Cáo was restored.
Zǐ Zāng completely surrendered his towns and ministerial rank
and did not take office.
B8.16.11 Xuān Bó sent a message to Xì Chōu, saying:
"The presence of Jì and Mèng in Lǔ
is like the presence of Luán and Fàn in Jìn.
Government orders are thereby accomplished.
Now they are plotting, saying:
'Jìn's government has many factions;
it cannot be followed.
We would rather serve Qí and Chǔ,
even if it means destruction,
and not follow Jìn.'
If you wish to succeed in Lǔ,
I request that you detain Xíngfǔ and kill him.
I will eliminate Mǐ,
and serve Jìn.
Mǐ will have no disloyalty.
If Lǔ is not disloyal,
the small states will surely be harmonious.
Otherwise,
when he returns he will surely rebel."
In the ninth month,
the men of Jìn arrested Jì Wénzǐ at Tiáoqiū.
The duke returned
and waited at Yùn,
sending Zǐshū Shēngbó to request Jì Sūn from Jìn.
Xì Chōu said:
"If you remove Zhòngsūn Mǐ
and detain Jì Sūn Xíngfǔ,
I will give you a state
more intimate than the ducal house."
He replied:
"As for Qiáorú's situation,
you must have heard of it.
If you remove Mǐ and Xíngfǔ,
this is to greatly abandon Lǔ
and condemn our humble ruler.
If you do not abandon us,
but graciously seek the blessings of Duke Zhōu,
enabling our humble ruler to serve the ruler of Jìn,
then these two men
are ministers of the altars of soil and grain of Lǔ.
If they are lost in the morning,
Lǔ will perish by evening.
With Lǔ so close to your enemies,
if it perishes and becomes an enemy,
how can you deal with it?"
Xì Chōu said:
"I will request a town for you."
He replied:
"Yīngqí
is a constant servant of Lǔ.
How dare I rely on a great state to seek enrichment?
I have received our humble ruler's command to make this request.
If my request is granted,
your gift to me is great indeed.
What more could I seek?"
Fàn Wénzǐ said to Luán Wǔzǐ:
"Jì Sūn in Lǔ
has served as minister to two rulers.
His concubines do not wear silk,
his horses do not eat grain.
Can he not be called loyal?
If we trust slanderers and abandon the loyal and good,
what will the feudal lords think?
Zǐshū Yīngqí, in carrying out his ruler's command,
was without selfishness,
planned for the state without disloyalty,
and considered his own person without forgetting his ruler.
If we void his request,
we abandon a good man.
You should consider this!"
Then they made peace with Lǔ
and pardoned Jì Sūn.
In winter, the tenth month,
they expelled Shūsūn Qiáorú
and made a covenant with him.
Qiáorú fled to Qí.
In the twelfth month,
Jì Sūn and Xì Chōu made a covenant at Hù.
Upon returning,
they assassinated the duke's son Yǎn.
They summoned Shūsūn Bào from Qí
and established him.
Qí's Shēng Mèngzǐ
had illicit relations with Qiáorú
and had him placed between the Gāo and Guó clans.
Qiáorú said:
"I cannot incur guilt again."
Then he fled to Wèi,
where he was also placed among the ministers.
B8.16.12 The Marquis of Jìn sent Xì Zhì to present the spoils from Chǔ to Zhōu.
He spoke with Duke Xiāng of Shàn,
repeatedly boasting of his achievements.
The Viscount of Shàn said to the senior ministers:
"Wēn Jì
will likely perish!
His position is below seven others,
yet he seeks to surpass those above him.
Where resentments gather,
there is the root of disorder.
Accumulating many resentments and creating steps to disorder—
how can he remain in his position?
The Xià Shū says:
'Are resentments only in the open?
What is not seen should be considered.'
This means to be cautious about the small things.
Now he makes them obvious.
Is this acceptable?"
A8.17 The Chénggōng 17th Year Classic
A8.17.1 In the seventeenth year, spring,
Wèi's Běigōng Kuò led an army to invade Zhèng.
A8.17.2 In summer,
the duke met with the Viscount of Yǐn,
the Viscount of Shàn,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
and a man of Zhū
to attack Zhèng.
A8.17.3 In the sixth month, on Yǐyǒu,
they formed an alliance at Kēlíng.
A8.17.4 In autumn,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A8.17.5 Gāo Wújiù of Qí fled to Jǔ.
A8.17.6 In the ninth month, on Xīnchǒu,
the Suburban Sacrifice was performed.
A8.17.7 The Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Yīng to request troops.
A8.17.8 In winter,
the Duke, together with Prince Shàn,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Cáo,
men of Qí,
and men of Zhū, attacked Zhèng.
A8.17.9 In the eleventh month,
the Duke arrived from the attack on Zhèng.
A8.17.10 On Rénshēn,
Gōngsūn Yīngqí died at Líshèn.
A8.17.11 In the twelfth month, on Dīngsì, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A8.17.12 Juéqiě, the Viscount of Zhū, died.
A8.17.13 Jìn put to death its great officers Xì Qí,
Xì Chōu,
and Xì Zhì.
A8.17.14 The men of Chǔ extinguished Shūyōng.
B8.17 The Commentary for the 17th Year of Duke Chéng
B8.17.1 In the 17th year, in spring, in the royal first month,
Zǐsì of Zhèng invaded Xū
and Huá of Jìn.
Běigōng Kuò of Wèi came to the aid of Jìn,
invaded Zhèng,
and reached Gāoshì.
In summer, in the fifth month,
Kūnwán, the heir-apparent of Zhèng,
and Hóu Nòu went as hostages to Chǔ,
and the Chǔ princes Chéng
and Yín
were sent to guard Zhèng.
B8.17.2 The Duke, together with Duke Wǔ of Yǐn, Duke Xiāng of Shàn, and the other princes, attacked Zhèng,
from Xìtóng to Qūwěi.
B8.17.3 Fàn Wénzǐ of Jìn, having returned from Yānlíng,
ordered his invocator and temple director to pray for his death,
saying:
"Our ruler is arrogant and extravagant, yet he has overcome the enemy.
This is Heaven increasing his malady.
Calamity is about to arise.
Let those who love me pray for me,
that I may die quickly,
and not be involved in the calamity. That would be the good fortune of the Fàn clan."
In the sixth month, on Wùchén,
Shì Xiè died.
B8.17.4 On Yǐyǒu,
they formed an alliance at Kēlíng,
renewing the covenant made at Qī.
B8.17.5 Zǐzhòng of Chǔ came to the aid of Zhèng,
and encamped his army at Shǒuzhǐ.
The princes then withdrew.
B8.17.6 Qìng Kè of Qí had illicit relations with Shēng Mèngzǐ.
Disguised in women's clothes, he entered the palace gate
in a carriage.
Bào Qiān saw him
and reported it to Guó Wǔzǐ.
Wǔzǐ summoned Qìng Kè and spoke to him about it.
Qìng Kè stayed indoors for a long time afterwards,
and then told the lady, saying:
"Guózǐ has reprimanded me."
The lady was angry.
Guózǐ was acting as assistant to Duke Líng at a meeting,
while Gāo and Bào remained to guard the state.
When he was returning,
and was about to arrive,
they closed the gates
and searched for suspicious persons.
Mèngzǐ accused them, saying:
"Gāo
and Bào intended not to admit you, my lord,
but to set up Prince Jiǎo.
Guózǐ knew of it."
In autumn, in the seventh month, on Rényín,
they cut off the feet of Bào Qiān
and banished Gāo Wújiù.
Wújiù fled to Jǔ.
Gāo Ruò rebelled with Lú.
The people of Qí sent for Bào Guó
and set him up in his place.
Formerly,
Bào Guó had left the Bào clan
and become a retainer of Shī Xiàoshū.
When the Shī family divined about appointing a steward,
Kuāng Jùxū proved auspicious.
The steward of the Shī family had an estate of a hundred families.
When they offered Kuāng Jùxū the estate
and wished to make him steward,
he yielded it to Bào Guó and gave him the estate.
Shī Xiàoshū said:
"You are indeed the auspicious one."
He replied:
"To be able to yield to one who is loyal and good—
what auspiciousness could be greater than this?"
Bào Guó served the Shī family loyally,
therefore the people of Qí fetched him
to be the successor of the Bào clan.
Zhòngní said:
"The wisdom of Bào Zhuāngzǐ
was inferior to that of the mallow,
for the mallow can still protect its roots."
B8.17.7 In winter,
the princes attacked Zhèng.
In the tenth month, on Gēngwǔ,
they besieged Zhèng.
Prince Shēn of Chǔ came to the aid of Zhèng,
and encamped his army on the Rǔ River.
In the eleventh month,
the princes withdrew.
B8.17.8 Formerly,
Shēng Bó dreamed that he crossed the Huán River,
and someone gave him pieces of jade. He ate them,
and his tears became pieces of jade,
filling his bosom.
Thereupon he sang, saying:
"The waters of the Huán River
gave me pieces of jade.
To return, to return,
pieces of jade fill my bosom!"
He was afraid and did not dare to divine the dream.
On his return from Zhèng,
on Rénshēn,
when he reached Líshèn, he divined about it,
saying:
"I feared death,
therefore I did not dare to divine it before.
But now my followers are many,
and they have followed me for three years.
There will be no harm."
Having said this,
in the evening he died.
B8.17.9 The Marquis of Qí made Cuī Zhù
a great officer,
and appointed Qìng Kè to assist him,
to lead an army and besiege Lú.
Guó Zuǒ, who was with the princes besieging Zhèng,
requested leave on account of this trouble
and returned.
He then went to the army at Lú,
killed Qìng Kè,
and rebelled with Gǔ.
The Marquis of Qí made a covenant with him at Xúguān
and restored him.
In the twelfth month,
Lú surrendered.
He sent Guó Shèng to report the trouble to Jìn,
and await orders at Qīng.
B8.17.10 The Jìn ruler, Duke Lì, was extravagant
and had many favorite male attendants.
Returning from Yānlíng,
he wished to get rid of all the great officers,
and set up those around him in their places.
Xú Tóng, because of the dismissal of Xú Kè,
bore a grudge against the Xì clan,
and was a favorite of Duke Lì.
Xì Qí had seized the fields of Yí Yángwǔ,
and Wǔ was also a favorite of Duke Lì.
Xì Chōu and Chángyú Jiǎo contended over fields.
Xì Chōu seized him and put him in fetters,
binding him together with his parents, wife, and children to the same cart-pole.
Afterwards, Jiǎo also became a favorite of Duke Lì.
Luán Shū bore a grudge against Xì Zhì,
because he had not followed his advice
and yet defeated the Chǔ army,
and wished to ruin him.
He sent the Chǔ prince Fá
to tell the Duke, saying:
"In this battle,
it was really Xì Zhì who summoned our ruler,
because the eastern army had not arrived,
and the army commanders were not all present.
He said:
'This battle is sure to be lost.
I will then take the opportunity to support Sūn Zhōu
and serve you, my lord.'"
He reported this to Luán Shū.
Shū said:
"There may be something to it.
Otherwise,
how could he be so unconcerned about his own death
as to accept an envoy from the enemy?
Why does Your Majesty not try sending him on a mission to Zhōu
and observe him?"
Xì Zhì went on a diplomatic mission to Zhōu,
and Luán Shū arranged for Sūn Zhōu to meet with him.
The Duke sent someone to spy on him,
and it was confirmed.
He then bore a grudge against Xì Zhì.
Duke Lì was on a hunt,
and with women he first hunted and drank,
afterward ordering the great officers to hunt.
Xì Zhì presented a boar,
but the eunuch Mèng Zhāng seized it,
and Xì Zhì shot and killed him.
The Duke said:
"Jìzǐ has deceived me!"
Duke Lì was about to launch a purge,
Xū Tóng said:
"We must first deal with the three Xìs.
Their clan is large
and has many enemies.
Removing a large clan
will relieve pressure;
confronting many enemies
will bring merit."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
The Xì clan heard of this,
Xì Qí wanted to attack the Duke,
saying:
"Even if we die,
the ruler will certainly be endangered."
Xì Zhì said:
"What enables a man to stand firm
is trustworthiness, wisdom, and courage.
Trustworthiness means not betraying one's ruler,
wisdom means not harming the people,
courage means not creating disorder.
If one loses these three qualities,
who will stand with me?
To die and leave many enemies,
what use would that be?
If the ruler indeed has ministers and kills them,
what will be said of the ruler?
If I am guilty,
I will die afterward.
If he kills the innocent,
he will lose the support of the people.
Wanting stability,
how can he achieve it?
We can only await our fate.
Having received the ruler's emoluments,
we have thereby gathered a faction.
To use that faction to resist his orders—
what crime could be greater?"
On Rénwǔ,
Xū Tóng
and Yí Yángwǔ led eight hundred armored soldiers
to attack the Xì clan.
Chángyú Jiǎo requested not to use a large force,
and the Duke sent Qīng Fèituí to assist him.
They drew their spears and tucked in their lapels,
pretending to be disputants.
The three Xìs were about to deliberate in a pavilion,
when Jiǎo killed Jū Bó
and Kǔchéng Shū at their positions with a spear.
Wēn Jì said:
"He is avoiding authority."
He then hurried away.
Jiǎo caught up with him at his carriage,
and killed him with a spear.
All their corpses were exposed at the court.
Xū Tóng used armored soldiers to seize Luán Shū
and Zhōngháng Yǎn at court.
Jiǎo said:
"If you do not kill these two men,
trouble will surely reach you, my lord."
The Duke said:
"In one morning, three ministers have been exposed as corpses;
I cannot bear to add more."
Jiǎo replied:
"Others will bear to harm you, my lord.
I have heard that disorder outside is called treachery,
and inside is called rebellion.
Treachery is controlled by virtue,
rebellion is controlled by punishment.
To kill without first applying virtue
cannot be called virtue;
when ministers press upon you and you do not punish them,
it cannot be called punishment.
If virtue and punishment are not established,
treachery and rebellion will arrive together.
I beg to take my leave."
He then fled to the Dí.
The Duke sent a message to the two men, saying:
"I have punished the Xì clan,
and the Xì clan has already paid for its crimes.
There is no need for you, ministers, to suffer humiliation;
return to your positions!"
Both bowed twice and touched their heads to the ground, saying:
"The ruler has punished the guilty,
and spared your ministers from death;
this is the ruler's kindness.
Even if we two ministers die,
how dare we forget the ruler's virtue?"
They then both returned.
The Duke appointed Xū Tóng as a minister.
The Duke went on an excursion to the house of Jiàng Lìshì,
where Luán Shū and Zhōngháng Yǎn seized him.
They summoned Shì Gài,
but Shì Gài declined.
They summoned Hán Jué,
and Hán Jué also declined,
saying:
"In the past, I was raised by the Zhào clan.
When Mèng Jī slandered them,
I was able to avoid taking up arms.
The ancients had a saying:
'No one dares to be responsible for killing an old ox.'
How much more so with a ruler?
If you few cannot serve your ruler,
what use is Jué?"
B8.17.11 The Shūyōng people, because of the Chǔ army's defeat,
guided the Wú people to besiege Cháo,
attack Jià,
and besiege Lí and Huī,
and thus relied on Wú and made no preparations.
The Chǔ prince Tuó Shī attacked Shūyōng,
and destroyed it.
B8.17.12 In the intercalary month, on the last day Yǐmǎo,
Luán Shū and Zhōngháng Yǎn killed Xū Tóng.
The people did not support the Xì clan,
and Xū Tóng had led the ruler into disorder,
therefore the record in both cases says
"Jìn killed its great officer."
A8.18 The Annals of Duke Chéng, Year 18
A8.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
Jìn killed its great officer Xū Tóng.
A8.18.2 On Gēngshēn,
Jìn assassinated its ruler, Zhōu Pú.
A8.18.3 Qí killed its great officer Guó Zuǒ.
A8.18.4 The Duke went to Jìn.
A8.18.5 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ
and the Earl of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
Sòng's Yú Shí re-entered Péngchéng.
A8.18.6 The Duke arrived from Jìn.
A8.18.7 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Gài on a diplomatic mission.
A8.18.8 In autumn,
the Earl of Qǐ came for an audience.
A8.18.9 In the eighth month,
the Viscount of Zhū came for an audience.
A8.18.10 The Lù garden was built.
A8.18.11 On Jǐchǒu,
the Duke passed away in the main chamber.
A8.18.12 In winter,
men of Chǔ
and men of Zhèng invaded Sòng.
A8.18.13 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Fáng to request troops.
A8.18.14 In the twelfth month,
Zhòngsūn Miè met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Viscount of Zhū,
and Qí's Cuī Zhù, and they formed an alliance at Xūtīng.
A8.18.15 On Dīngwèi,
we buried our ruler, Duke Chéng.
B8.18 The Commentary on Duke Chéng, Year 18
B8.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
on the first month, Gēngshēn day,
Lǚan Shū and Zhōngháng Yǎn of Jìn sent Chéng Huá
to assassinate Duke Lì.
He was buried outside the east gate of Yì,
with only one chariot.
They sent Xún Yīng and Shì Fáng to welcome the Zhōu heir from the capital
and established him as ruler.
He was fourteen years old at birth.
The senior officials welcomed him at Qīngyuán.
The Zhōu heir said:
"I never originally aspired to reach this position.
Even though I have reached it,
is it not Heaven's will?
Moreover, when people seek a ruler,
it is to issue commands.
If established but not followed,
then what use is a ruler?
Whether you gentlemen employ me today,
or reject me today,
let us be respectful and follow our ruler,
for that is what the spirits will bless."
They replied:
"It is the wish of your ministers,
how dare we not obey your command?"
On Gēngwǔ day,
they swore a covenant and entered,
lodging at the residence of Bózǐ Tóng.
On Xīnsì day, he held court at the Wǔ Palace.
He expelled seven disloyal ministers.
The Zhōu heir had an elder brother who was unintelligent,
unable to distinguish beans from wheat,
and therefore could not be established.
B8.18.2 Because of the troubles caused by the Qìng clan in Qí,
on the last day of the month, Jiǎshēn,
the Marquis of Qí sent Shì Huá Miǎn
to kill Guó Zuǒ with a dagger-axe
in the court of the inner palace.
The guards fled to the quarters of the lady.
The record says
"Qí killed its senior official Guó Zuǒ,"
because he abandoned commands,
arrogated the power to kill,
and rebelled with Gǔ.
He sent men from Qīng to kill Guó Shèng.
Guó Ruò came fleeing.
Wáng Qiū fled to Lái.
Qìng Fēng was made a senior official,
and Qìng Zuǒ was made Minister of Justice.
Afterwards,
the Marquis of Qí restored Guó Ruò,
making him succeed to the Guó lineage,
which was according to ritual.
B8.18.3 On the first day of the second month, Yǐyǒu,
Duke Dào of Jìn assumed his position in court.
He began by appointing all officials,
bestowing gifts and remitting debts,
reaching out to widows and widowers,
reviving the neglected,
relieving the destitute,
aiding disaster victims,
prohibiting excess and wickedness,
lightening taxes,
pardoning crimes,
economizing on utensils, using the people seasonably,
wishing not to violate the seasons.
He appointed Wèi Xiāng, Shì Fáng, Wèi Jié,
and Zhào Wǔ as ministers;
Xún Jiā, Xún Huì, Luán Yǎn, Hán Wújì
as Masters of the Ducal Clan,
to instruct the sons and younger brothers of the ministers
in respect, frugality, filial piety, and fraternal duty.
He appointed Shì Wòzhuó as Grand Tutor,
to revise the laws of Fàn Wǔzǐ;
Yòuháng Xīn as Minister of Works,
to revise the laws of Shì Wěi.
Biàn Jiū was made charioteer for the ruler's war chariot,
with the chariot master subordinate to him,
to instruct all charioteers in righteousness.
Xún Bīn was made the right-hand guard,
with the master of knights subordinate to him,
to train the brave and strong for timely use.
Ministers did not have personal charioteers;
army commandants were established to oversee them.
Qí Xī was made commandant of the central army,
with Yángshé Zhí as his assistant;
Wèi Jiàng was made marshal,
and Zhāng Lǎo was made scout commander.
Duó Èkòu was made commandant of the upper army,
with Jí Yǎn as his marshal,
to train the foot soldiers and charioteers,
to be harmonious and obey commands.
Chéng Zhèng was made master of the horses,
with the six grooms subordinate to him,
to instruct all grooms in ritual.
All the heads of the six offices
were men praised by the people.
Appointments did not miss their duties,
officials did not change their methods,
ranks did not exceed virtue,
division commanders did not oppress their superiors,
brigade commanders did not pressure their division commanders,
the people had no slanderous words.
This is how he restored hegemony.
B8.18.4 Our duke went to Jìn,
to pay court to the new ruler.
B8.18.5 In the summer, sixth month,
the Earl of Zhèng invaded Sòng,
reaching outside the Cáo Gate.
Then he joined the Viscount of Chǔ in attacking Sòng,
capturing Zhāo Jiá.
Zǐ Xīn of Chǔ and Huáng Chén of Zhèng
invaded Chéng Gào,
capturing Yōuqiū.
Together they attacked Péngchéng,
installing the men of Sòng, Yú Shí, Xiàng Wéirén,
Lín Zhū, Xiàng Dài,
and Yú Fǔ there,
leaving three hundred chariots to garrison it before returning.
The record says "returned and entered."
In general, when someone leaves his state,
and the state welcomes and establishes him,
it is called
"entered";
if he is restored to his position,
it is called
"returned to his place";
if the feudal lords install him,
it is called
"returned";
if it is with ill intent, it is called "returned and entered."
The men of Sòng were troubled by this.
Xī Chúwú said:
"Why?
If the men of Chǔ share our hatred,
and show us virtue,
we would certainly serve them,
not daring to be disloyal.
But a great state is never satisfied;
even making us a border state would leave them regret.
Otherwise,
they gather those we hate,
to assist their government,
to spy on our weaknesses,
which would also trouble us.
Now they are elevating the traitors of the feudal lords
and dividing their lands,
blocking the peaceful roads.
Indulging traitors and alienating the submissive,
poisoning the feudal lords
and alarming Wú
and Jìn,
our gain is great,
it is not our worry.
Moreover, why serve Jìn?
Jìn will certainly pity us."
B8.18.6 Our duke returned from Jìn.
Fàn Xuānzǐ of Jìn came on a friendly mission,
and also to acknowledge our court visit.
The gentleman says that Jìn in this acted ritually.
B8.18.7 In autumn,
Duke Huán of Qǐ came to our court,
inquired after our duke,
and asked about the affairs of Jìn.
Our duke told him about the ruler of Jìn.
The Earl of Qǐ then repeatedly paid court to Jìn
and requested a marriage alliance.
B8.18.8 In the seventh month,
Lǎo Zuǒ
and Huá Xǐ of Sòng besieged Péngchéng,
and Lǎo Zuǒ died there.
B8.18.9 In the eighth month,
Duke Xuān of Zhū came to our court,
because he had just assumed his position and came to visit.
B8.18.10 The Lù park was built;
the record
says it was not the proper season.
B8.18.11 On Jǐchǒu day,
our duke died in the main chamber,
which is said to be the proper way.
B8.18.12 In winter, eleventh month,
Zǐ Zhòng of Chǔ relieved Péngchéng,
and attacked Sòng.
Huá Yuán of Sòng went to Jìn to report the emergency.
Hán Xiànzǐ was in charge of government,
and said:
"To wish to gain men's allegiance,
one must first exert oneself for them.
To achieve hegemony and secure borders,
it should start with Sòng."
The Marquis of Jìn led his army to Táigǔ
to relieve Sòng.
They encountered the Chǔ army at Míjiǎo Valley,
and the Chǔ army withdrew.
B8.18.13 Shì Fáng of Jìn came to request troops.
Jì Wénzǐ asked Zāng Wǔzhòng about the number of troops,
who replied:
"In the campaign against Zhèng,
Zhì Bó actually came,
he was the assistant of the Lower Army.
Now Zhì Jì is also the assistant of the Lower Army,
so following the precedent of the campaign against Zhèng is acceptable.
In serving a great state,
do not deviate from the order of rank and show added respect,
this is propriety."
They followed this.
B8.18.14 In the twelfth month,
Mèng Xiànzǐ met at Xūtīng,
to plan rescuing Sòng.
The people of Sòng declined the help of the feudal lords
and requested troops to besiege Péngchéng.
Mèng Xiànzǐ requested from the feudal lords
and returned first to attend the funeral.
B8.18.15 On Dīngwèi,
we buried our ruler, Duke Chéng. The record follows the proper sequence.
