Chǔ's Zǐnáng and Qín's grandee Wúdì attacked Sòng,
stationing troops at Yángliáng
to retaliate for Jìn's taking of Zhèng.
B9.12.5 King Líng sought a queen from Qí.
The Marquis of Qí consulted Yàn Huánzǐ about the reply.
Huánzǐ replied:
"The ritual formulas of the former kings have provisions for this.
When the Son of Heaven seeks a queen from a feudal lord,
the feudal lord replies:
'There are so many daughters born to my wife,
and so many born to my concubines.'
If he has no daughters but has sisters or paternal aunts,
then he says:
'There are so many daughters left by the former ruler, Duke So-and-so.'"
The Marquis of Qí consented to the marriage.
The King sent Yīnlǐ to conclude it.
B9.12.6 The Duke went to Jìn to pay court,
and also to acknowledge Shì Fáng's visit—
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.12.7 Qín Yíng returned to Chǔ.
The Chǔ Minister of War, Zǐgěng, visited Qín
to inquire after his wife's well-being—
this was in accordance with ritual.
A9.13 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 13 of Duke Xiāng
A9.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Duke returned from Jìn.
A9.13.2 In summer,
we took Shī.
A9.13.3 In autumn, in the ninth month, on the gēngchén day,
the Viscount of Chǔ, Shěn, died.
A9.13.4 In winter,
we fortified Fáng.
B9.13 The Commentary, Year 13 of Duke Xiāng
B9.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Duke returned from Jìn.
Mèng Xiànzǐ recorded the merit in the temple—
this was in accordance with ritual.
B9.13.2 In summer,
Shī was in disorder,
divided into three parts.
Our army relieved Shī
and then took it.
Whenever the Annals record 'took,'
it means it was easy.
If a great army is used, it is called 'annihilated';
if no territory is seized, it is called 'entered.'
B9.13.3 Xún Yīng and Shì Fáng died.
The Marquis of Jìn held a review at Miánshàng
to drill the troops.
He ordered Shì Gài to command the central army,
but he declined, saying:
"Bóyóu is senior.
In the past, I was accustomed to assisting Zhì Bó,
so I served as his assistant—
not because I was worthy.
I beg to follow Bóyóu."
So he ordered Xún Yǎn to command the central army,
with Shì Gài as his assistant.
He ordered Hán Qǐ to command the upper army,
but he declined in favor of Zhào Wǔ.
He then ordered Luán Yǎn,
but he declined, saying:
"I am not equal to Hán Qǐ.
Hán Qǐ wishes to yield to Zhào Wǔ above him—
I beg you to heed him."
So he ordered Zhào Wǔ to command the upper army,
with Hán Qǐ as his assistant;
Luán Yǎn commanded the lower army,
with Wèi Jiàng as his assistant.
The new army had no commander.
The Marquis of Jìn found it difficult to choose someone,
so he ordered its ten officers
to lead its troops, chariots, and officials
to follow the lower army—
this was in accordance with ritual.
Thus, the people of Jìn were greatly harmonious,
and the feudal lords became amicable.
A gentleman said:
"Yielding
is the essence of ritual.
Fàn Xuānzǐ yielded,
and those below him all yielded.
Though Luán Yǎn was arrogant,
he did not dare to go against it.
Jìn was thereby pacified,
and for several generations relied on this—
When one person practices goodness,
the hundred clans enjoy harmony and peace;
how can this not be earnestly pursued!
The *Book of Documents* says:
'When the one man has cause for celebration,
the myriad people rely on him,
and his tranquility is enduring.'
This is probably what it means!
When the Zhōu dynasty was rising,
its *Odes* said:
'Take King Wén as your model and pattern,
and the myriad states will place their trust.'
This speaks of practicing goodness.
When it was declining,
its *Odes* said:
'The great officers are not equitable,
and I, who serve, alone am deemed worthy.'
This speaks of not yielding.
When the age is well-governed,
the noble man esteems ability
and yields to those below him,
while the lesser man labors diligently
to serve those above him.
Therefore, superiors and inferiors observe ritual,
slanderers and evil-doers are dismissed and kept at a distance,
all because there is no contention.
This is called beautiful virtue.
When it is in disorder,
the noble man boasts of his merit
to lord it over the lesser man,
and the lesser man flaunts his skill
to encroach upon the noble man.
Therefore, superiors and inferiors lack ritual,
disorder and cruelty arise together,
all because of contention over being good.
This is called benighted virtue.
The ruin of a state
must always come from this."
B9.13.4 The King of Chǔ was ill
and informed his great officers, saying:
"I, the unworthy one, lack virtue,
and became master of the altars of soil and grain at a young age.
I was born for ten years and then lost my late lord,
before I had time to learn the instructions of my tutors and guardians
yet I received manifold blessings.
Therefore, lacking virtue,
I lost our army at Yān;
thus disgracing the altars of soil and grain,
and causing worry for you, my great officers.
This is indeed great.
If, through the spiritual power of you, my great officers,
I am able to preserve my head and neck and be buried in the earth,
regarding only the affairs of the spring and autumn sacrifices and burials,
and the means by which I am to follow my late lord in the temple of my father,
I ask to be given
the posthumous title 'Líng' or 'Lì'.
You, my great officers, choose."
None replied.
Only after he had given the command five times
did they consent.
In autumn,
King Gòng of Chǔ died.
Zǐ Náng consulted about the posthumous title.
The great officers said:
"Our lord already gave his command."
Zǐ Náng said:
"Our lord commanded with the word 'gòng' (reverent),
how can we defame him?
The majestic state of Chǔ,
and our lord ruled over it,
pacifying and possessing the Mán and Yí tribes,
extending his campaigns to the southern sea,
bringing it into the fold of the Xià states.
Yet he knew his own faults;
can he not be called 'gòng' (reverent)?
I ask to give him the posthumous title 'Gòng'."
The great officers followed him.
B9.13.5 Wú invaded Chǔ.
Yǎng Yóujī hastened to meet the emergency,
and Zǐ Gēng followed with an army.
Yǎng Shū said:
"Wú is taking advantage of our mourning period,
thinking we cannot raise an army.
They will certainly underestimate us and be unprepared.
You set up three ambushes and wait for me;
I request to lure them."
Zǐ Gēng followed his plan.
They fought at Yōngpǔ,
greatly defeated the Wú army,
and captured Prince Dǎng.
The noble man considered Wú as lacking in due reverence.
The *Odes* say:
"Heaven is not reverenced,
and disorder has no end."
B9.13.6 In winter,
they walled Fáng.
It was recorded because
it was the appropriate season.
They were about to wall it early,
but Zāng Wǔzhòng requested to wait until the farming tasks were finished;
this was according to ritual.
B9.13.7 Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng and the Grand Steward Shí Chuò were still in Chǔ.
Shí Chuò said to Zǐ Náng:
"The former kings divined for campaigns over five years,
and each year repeated the auspicious signs;
when the auspicious signs were repeated, then they acted.
If they were not repeated,
they increased their cultivation of virtue and divined again.
Now Chǔ is truly not strong,
so what fault have the envoys?
Detaining one minister of Zhèng
to remove pressure from them,
causing them to be harmonious and hate Chǔ,
so they become firm towards Jìn—
what use is that?
If you send them back and they fail in their mission,
they will resent their ruler
and hate their great officers,
and they will drag each other down;
is that not still better?"
The men of Chǔ sent them back.
A9.14 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 14 of Duke Xiāng*
A9.14.1 In the fourteenth year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
Jì Sūn Sù
and Shū Lǎo met with Shì Gài of Jìn,
men of Qí,
men of Sòng,
men of Wèi,
Gōngsūn Chài of Zhèng,
men of Cáo,
men of Jǔ,
men of Zhū,
men of Téng,
men of Xuē,
men of Qǐ,
and men of Xiǎozhū to meet with Wú at Xiàng.
A9.14.2 On the first day of the second month, yǐwèi,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.14.3 In summer, in the fourth month,
Shū Sūn Bào met with Xún Yǎn of Jìn,
men of Qí,
men of Sòng,
Běigōng Kuò of Wèi,
Gōngsūn Chài of Zhèng,
men of Cáo,
men of Jǔ,
men of Zhū,
men of Téng,
men of Xuē,
men of Qǐ,
and men of Xiǎozhū to attack Qín.
A9.14.4 On the jǐwèi day,
the Marquis of Wèi fled to Qí.
A9.14.5 Men of Jǔ invaded our eastern borders.
A9.14.6 In autumn,
Prince Zhēn of Chǔ led an army to attack Wú.
A9.14.7 In winter,
Jì Sūn Sù met with Shì Gài of Jìn,
Huá Yuè of Sòng,
Sūn Línfǔ of Wèi,
Gōngsūn Chài of Zhèng,
men of Jǔ,
and men of Zhū at Qī.
B9.14 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, Year 14 of Duke Xiāng*
B9.14.1 In spring of the fourteenth year,
Wú reported its defeat to Jìn.
The meeting at Xiàng
was held for Wú's sake to plan against Chǔ.
Fàn Xuānzǐ enumerated Wú's lack of virtue
and thereby dismissed the men of Wú.
They arrested Prince Wùlóu of Jǔ
because he had communicated with Chǔ's envoy.
They were about to arrest the Róng leader Jūzhī.
Fàn Xuānzǐ personally enumerated his faults at court,
saying:
"Come here,
Jiāng Róng clan!
Formerly, the men of Qín pursued and drove your ancestor Wúlí from Guāzhōu.
Your ancestor Wúlí, clad in rush coverings
and covered with thorns,
came to submit to our late lord.
Our late lord, Duke Huì, had some not-so-fertile land,
which he divided and shared with you to eat from.
Now the affairs of the various lords with our unworthy ruler are not like in former times.
This is probably because words have leaked out,
and the responsibility for this lies with you.
For tomorrow morning's affairs,
you are not to participate.
If you participate,
we will arrest you."
He replied:
"In the past, the people of Qín relied on their multitudes,
greedy for territory,
and drove out our various Róng tribes.
Duke Huì displayed his great virtue,
saying of our various Róng tribes,
'They are the descendants of the Four Peaks,
they should not be cut off and abandoned.'
He granted us the fields of the southern border,
where foxes dwelt,
and jackals and wolves howled.
We, the various Róng tribes, cleared away its thorns and brambles,
drove out its foxes, jackals, and wolves,
and became ministers to the former lord, neither invading nor rebelling,
and have remained without duplicity to this day.
In the past, Duke Wén joined Qín in attacking Zhèng,
but the people of Qín secretly made a covenant with Zhèng,
and left troops to garrison there,
and thus there was the battle of Xiáo.
Jìn resisted them from above,
and the Róng opposed them from below,
so the Qín army did not return;
this was truly due to us, the various Róng tribes.
Thus,
it was like capturing a deer:
the men of Jìn seized it by the horns,
the various Róng tribes pulled it by the legs,
and together with Jìn, we brought it down.
Why then are we, the Róng, not spared?
From that time onward,
in all the campaigns of Jìn,
we, the various Róng tribes, have followed one after another in timely succession,
obeying the commands of your officers,
just as at Xiáo,
how dare we deviate?
Now, is it not rather that the officers and armies of your state truly have some deficiency,
which causes the feudal lords to waver,
and yet you blame us, the various Róng tribes!
We, the various Róng tribes, in food and drink, clothing and attire,
are not the same as the Huá,
we do not exchange ceremonial gifts,
our languages are not mutually intelligible,
what harm could we possibly do?
If we are not included in the meeting,
we will also feel no shame."
He recited the "Qīng Yíng" and withdrew.
Xuānzǐ apologized,
and had him attend to affairs at the meeting,
thus achieving harmony and amity.
Thereupon, Zǐ Shū Qízǐ
served as deputy to Jì Wǔzǐ at the meeting,
and from then on, the people of Jìn slighted Lǔ's gifts
but increasingly respected its envoys.
B9.14.2 When Wúzǐ Zhūfán had completed the mourning period,
he intended to establish Jì Zhá.
Jì Zhá declined, saying:
"At the death of Duke Xuān of Cáo,
the feudal lords and the people of Cáo considered the Cáo ruler unrighteous,
and intended to establish Zǐ Zāng.
Zǐ Zāng left,
and so they did not proceed,
thus completing the establishment of the Cáo ruler.
The gentleman said
'He was able to maintain integrity.'
You, my lord,
are the rightful successor;
who would dare to oppose you?
To possess the state
is not my integrity.
Though Zhá lacks talent,
I wish to follow Zǐ Zāng
so as not to lose integrity."
They firmly insisted on establishing him,
but he abandoned his household and went to plow the fields,
so they gave up.
B9.14.3 In summer,
the great officers of the feudal lords followed the Marquis of Jìn to attack Qín,
in retaliation for the defeat at Lì.
The Marquis of Jìn remained at the border,
and had the six ministers lead the armies of the feudal lords to advance.
When they reached the Jīng River,
they did not cross.
Shū Xiàng met Shūsūn Mùzǐ,
and Mùzǐ recited the "Páo Yǒu Kǔ Yè";
Shū Xiàng withdrew and prepared boats.
The men of Lǔ and Jǔ crossed first.
Zhèngzǐ Jiǎo met Wèi's Běigōng Yìzǐ and said:
"To ally with others but not firmly,
brings upon oneself the greatest hatred;
what then of the altars of soil and grain?"
Yìzǐ was pleased.
The two men saw the armies of the feudal lords
and urged them to cross.
They crossed the Jīng River and encamped.
The people of Qín poisoned the upper reaches of the Jīng River,
and many in the army died.
Zhèng's Minister of War Zǐ Jiǎo led the Zhèng army forward,
and the whole army followed him,
reaching Yùlín,
but they did not achieve a settlement.
Xún Yǎn gave the order:
"At the crow of the cock, harness the chariots,
fill in the wells and level the hearths,
and only look to where my horse's head turns."
Luán Yǎn said:
"The orders of the state of Jìn
have never been like this.
My horse's head wishes to turn east."
So he returned.
The lower army followed him.
The Left Historian said to Wèi Zhuāngzǐ:
"Will you not wait for Zhōngháng Bó?"
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Our commander ordered us to follow our leader;
Luán Bó
is my leader,
and I will follow him.
To follow one's leader
is how to obey our commander."
Bó Yóu said:
"My command was indeed mistaken;
what use is regret now?
It will only leave many to be captured by Qín."
So he ordered a general withdrawal.
The people of Jìn called this
"the campaign of delay."
Luán Zhēn said:
"This campaign
was to avenge the defeat at Lì.
Yet the campaign has achieved no merit;
this is a disgrace to Jìn.
I hold two positions in the army,
how dare I not feel ashamed?"
He and Shì Yāng charged the Qín army,
and died there.
Shì Yāng returned.
Luán Yǎn said to Shì Gài:
"My younger brother did not wish to go,
but your son summoned him.
My younger brother died,
and your son came back;
this means your son killed my younger brother.
If you do not drive him out,
I will also kill him."
Shì Yāng fled to Qín.
At this time, Qí's Cuī Zhù, Sòng's Huá Yuè, and Zhòng Jiāng joined in attacking Qín.
They were not recorded,
due to their indolence.
The same was true at the meeting at Xiàng.
Wèi's Běigōng Kuò was not recorded at Xiàng,
but was recorded in the attack on Qín,
because he exerted himself.
The Earl of Qín asked Shì Yāng:
"Among the great officers of Jìn, who will perish first?"
He replied:
"It will be the Luán clan!"
The Earl of Qín said:
"Because of their arrogance?"
He replied: "Yes.
Luán Yǎn's arrogance and cruelty are extreme,
yet he might still escape;
it will be with Yíng!"
The Earl of Qín said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"The virtue of Wǔzǐ remains among the people,
like the Zhōu people's remembrance of Duke Shào,
who loved his gāntáng tree;
how much more so his son?
When Luán Yǎn dies,
Yíng's goodness will not yet have reached others;
the benefits bestowed by Wǔzǐ will be exhausted,
while the resentment against Yǎn will truly become manifest,
and it will rest upon him."
The Earl of Qín considered this wise speech,
and interceded for him with Jìn to have him restored.
B9.14.4 Duke Xiàn of Wèi invited Sūn Wénzǐ and Nìng Huìzǐ to a meal,
and both dressed in court attire and attended court,
but as the day grew late, he did not summon them,
instead shooting geese in the park.
The two men went to him,
but he did not remove his leather cap when speaking to them.
The two men were angry.
Sūn Wénzǐ went to Qī,
and Sūn Kuǎi entered on a mission.
The duke gave him wine to drink,
and ordered the Grand Musician to sing the final stanza of "Qiǎo Yán."
The Grand Musician declined.
Shī Cáo requested to do it.
Earlier,
the duke had a favored concubine,
and had Shī Cáo teach her the qín,
but Shī Cáo whipped her.
The duke was angry,
and whipped Shī Cáo three hundred times.
Therefore, Shī Cáo wished to sing it,
to anger the Sūn clan,
and thus repay the duke.
The duke had him sing it,
and so he recited it.
Kuǎi was afraid,
and informed Wénzǐ.
Wénzǐ said:
"The ruler resents me.
If I do not act first,
I will surely die."
He gathered his family at Qī and entered,
met Qú Bóyù,
and said:
"The ruler's tyranny,
you are aware of.
I greatly fear the collapse of the altars of soil and grain.
What is to be done?"
He replied:
"The ruler governs his state;
how dare a minister oppose him?
Even if one opposes him,
how can one know it will be better?"
He then departed,
leaving through the nearest pass.
The duke sent Zǐ Jiǎo, Zǐ Bó,
and Zǐ Pí to make a covenant with Sūnzǐ at Qiūgōng, but Sūnzǐ killed them all.
On the jǐwèi day of the fourth month,
Zǐ Zhǎn fled to Qí,
and the duke went to Juàn.
He sent Zǐ Xíng to make a request of Sūnzǐ,
but Sūnzǐ killed him as well.
The duke fled to Qí,
and the Sūn clan pursued him,
defeating the duke's followers at Āzé,
where the people of Juàn captured him.
Earlier,
Yǐn Gōngtuó had learned archery from Yǔ Gōngchā,
and Yǔ Gōngchā had learned archery from Gōngsūn Dīng.
The two pursued the duke,
while Gōngsūn Dīng drove the duke's chariot.
Zǐyú said:
"To shoot would be to betray my teacher;
not to shoot would mean execution.
Shall I shoot in accordance with ritual?"
He shot two arrows at the yoke-ends and turned back.
Yǐn Gōngtuó said:
"He is your teacher,
but mine is more distant."
He then turned back to pursue them.
Gōngsūn Dīng handed the reins to the duke and shot at him,
piercing his arm.
Zǐ Xiān followed the duke.
When they reached the border, the duke sent the invocator to announce his flight,
and also to declare his innocence.
Dìng Jiāng said:
"If there are no spirits,
whom to inform?
If there are,
they cannot be deceived.
If guilty,
how can one declare innocence?
Abandoning the great ministers and consulting with petty ones—
that is one crime.
Our former ruler had a chief minister as his mentor and guardian, yet you treated him with contempt—
that is the second crime.
I served the former ruler with towel and comb,
yet you treated me like a lowly concubine—
that is the third crime.
Announce your flight,
but do not declare your innocence!"
The duke sent Hòu Chéngshū to offer condolences in Wèi,
saying:
"My humble ruler sends me, Jí,
having heard that you do not comfort the altars of soil and grain,
but have crossed into another state's territory.
How can we not offer condolences?
Due to our alliance,
my ruler dares to speak privately to your officers,
saying:
'If a ruler is not mourned,
and ministers are not diligent;
if the ruler does not pardon,
and ministers do not fulfill their duties—
increasing excess and venting grievances,
what is to be done?'"
The people of Wèi sent Tàishū Yí to reply,
saying:
"The ministers, lacking talent,
have offended our humble ruler.
Our humble ruler did not subject them to punishment,
but in his grief cast them aside,
causing you concern.
You, not forgetting the friendship of our former rulers,
have condescended to console the ministers,
and further shown them compassion.
We dare to bow in acknowledgment of your gracious command,
and again bow in gratitude for your great kindness."
Hòu Sūn returned,
reported back,
and said to Zāng Wǔzhòng:
"The ruler of Wèi will surely return!
With Tàishū Yí guarding within,
and his own younger brother Zhuān managing affairs abroad—
some pacifying the interior,
others managing the exterior—
how can he not return?"
The people of Qí placed the Wèi ruler in Lái.
When he was restored,
he took the grain of Lái with him.
Yòuzǎi Gǔ followed
but then fled back,
and the people of Wèi were about to kill him.
He pleaded:
"I did not approve from the start.
I am like a fox-fur robe with lamb-skin sleeves."
They then pardoned him.
The people of Wèi set up Gōngsūn Piào,
with Sūn Línfǔ and Nìng Zhí as his ministers,
to heed the commands of the feudal lords.
The Wèi ruler was in Lái,
and Zāng Hé went to Qí to console him.
The Wèi ruler spoke with him,
and was abusive.
Withdrawing, Zāng Hé told his followers:
"The Wèi ruler will likely not re-enter.
His words are like dung and dirt.
In exile and unchanged,
how can he restore his state?"
Zǐ Zhǎn and Zǐ Xiān heard of this,
went to see Zāng Hé,
spoke with him,
and were reasonable.
Zāng Sūn was pleased,
and told his followers:
"The Wèi ruler will surely re-enter.
These two men—
one pulls him,
the other pushes him.
Even if he wished not to enter,
could he avoid it?"
B9.14.5 The army returned from attacking Qín.
The marquis of Jìn disbanded the new army,
which was according to ritual.
A fully established state should not exceed half the Son of Heaven's army.
Zhōu had six armies;
the greatest among the feudal lords
may have three armies.
At this time, Zhì Shuò
died after giving birth to Yíng,
and Yíng was six years old when Wǔzǐ died.
Zhì Qiú was also young;
none could be established.
The new army had no commander,
so it was disbanded.
B9.14.6 Shī Kuàng attended the marquis of Jìn.
The marquis of Jìn said:
"The people of Wèi expelled their ruler—
is that not excessive?"
He replied:
"Perhaps it is the ruler who was truly excessive.
A good ruler rewards the good and punishes the licentious,
nourishes the people like children,
covers them like heaven,
and contains them like earth.
The people serve their ruler,
loving him like parents,
looking up to him like the sun and moon,
revering him like spirits,
fearing him like thunder—
how could they expel him?
The ruler is
the host of the spirits and the hope of the people.
If he impoverishes the people's host,
deprives the spirits of sacrifices,
leaves the common people without hope,
and the altars of soil and grain without a master—
what use is he?
If not removed, what then?
Heaven gave birth to the people and set up rulers for them,
to shepherd them,
so they do not lose their nature.
Having a ruler, there are deputies for him,
to mentor and guard him,
so he does not exceed the proper measure.
Thus, the Son of Heaven has dukes,
feudal lords have ministers,
ministers have collateral branches,
great officers have secondary clans,
officers have friends,
and commoners, artisans, merchants, servants, grooms, shepherds, and stablemen all have intimates,
to assist one another.
Good is rewarded,
errors are corrected,
calamities are rescued,
and failures are reformed.
From the king down,
each has fathers, brothers, sons, and younger brothers
to supplement and scrutinize his governance.
The scribes wrote the records,
the blind musicians composed the poems,
the artisans recited admonitions,
the senior officials offered guidance and warnings,
the lower officials conveyed opinions,
the common people voiced criticisms,
the merchants discussed matters in the markets,
and the various artisans presented their skills.
Therefore, the *Book of Xia* says:
'The herald with his wooden bell patrolled the roads,
officials and instructors admonished each other,
and artisans used their skills to remonstrate.'
In the first month of early spring,
this was practiced,
to correct deviations from the norm.
Heaven loves the people deeply;
how could it allow one man to act recklessly over the people,
indulging his excesses,
and abandoning the nature of Heaven and Earth?
This certainly cannot be so."
B9.14.7 In autumn,
the Viscount of Chǔ, because of the battle at Yōngpǔ,
sent Zǐ Náng to lead troops at Táng
to attack Wú.
Wú did not come out, and they returned.
Zǐ Náng commanded the rear guard,
thinking Wú incapable and therefore not taking precautions.
The men of Wú, from the narrow pass of Gāozhōu,
intercepted and attacked them.
The men of Chǔ could not rescue each other,
and the men of Wú defeated them,
capturing the Chǔ prince Yígǔ.
B9.14.8 The king sent Liú Dìnggōng
to confer a mandate upon the Marquis of Qí,
saying:
"In the past, our maternal uncle, the Grand Duke,
assisted our former kings,
serving as the limbs and bones of the Zhōu house,
protecting and instructing the myriad people.
Generation after generation, he was enfeoffed as Grand Master,
to manifest authority over the Eastern Sea.
That the royal house has not crumbled
relies entirely on our maternal uncle.
Now I command you, Huán:
follow the statutes of your maternal uncle's house,
succeed your ancestors,
and do not disgrace your heritage.
Be reverent!
Do not abandon my command!"
B9.14.9 The Marquis of Jìn asked Zhōngxíng Xiànzǐ about the situation in Wèi.
He replied:
"It would be best to take advantage of the situation to stabilize it.
Wèi already has a ruler;
attacking it
would likely not achieve our aim,
and would trouble the other lords.
Shǐ Yì has said:
'Take advantage of a weighty situation to pacify it.'
Zhònghuǐ has said:
'Destroy those who are arrogant,
seize those who are in chaos.
Topple the perishing and strengthen the surviving—
this is the way of states.'
My lord, you should stabilize Wèi
and await the right time!"
In winter,
they met at Qì,
to plan the stabilization of Wèi.
B9.14.10 Fàn Xuānzǐ borrowed feathers and plumes from Qí
and did not return them,
and the people of Qí began to be disloyal.
B9.14.11 Chǔ's Zǐ Náng returned from attacking Wú
and died.
As he was dying,
he left a message for Zǐ Gēng:
"You must fortify Yǐng!"
The gentleman says:
"Zǐ Náng was loyal.
When his lord died,
he did not forget to enhance his name;
when he himself was dying,
he did not forget to guard the altars of soil and grain.
Can he not be called loyal?
Loyalty—
it is what the people hope for.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'His conduct returns to Zhōu,
the hope of the myriad people'—
this is loyalty."
A9.15 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, 15th Year of Duke Xiāng*
A9.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
the Duke of Sòng sent Xiàng Xū on a friendly mission.
In the second month, on Jǐhài,
he made a covenant with Xiàng Xū at Liú.
A9.15.2 Liú Xià went to Qí to meet the queen.
A9.15.3 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern borders,
besieging Chéng.
Our duke went to relieve Chéng,
reaching Yù.
A9.15.4 Jìsūn Sù
and Shūsūn Bào led troops to build the outer wall of Chéng.
A9.15.5 In autumn, in the eighth month, on Dīngsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
A9.15.6 The men of Zhū attacked our southern borders.
A9.15.7 In winter, in the eleventh month, on Guǐhài,
the Marquis of Jìn, Zhōu, died.
B9.15 *The Zuo Commentary, 15th Year of Duke Xiāng*
B9.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
Sòng's Xiàng Xū came on a friendly mission,
and also to renew the covenant.
He visited Mèng Xiànzǐ,
and criticized his house,
saying:
"You have a fine reputation, yet you beautify your house—
this is not what one would expect."
He replied:
"When I was in Jìn,
my elder brother did this.
To destroy it would be a great labor,
and moreover, I dare not find fault with my brother."
B9.15.2 The official instructor accompanied Shàn Jìnggōng to Qí to meet the queen.
A high minister did not go—
this was contrary to ritual.
B9.15.3 Chǔ made Prince Wǔ its Prime Minister,
Prince Píróng its Right Minister,
Wěi Zǐféng its Grand Marshal,
Prince Tuóshī its Right Marshal,
Prince Chéng its Left Marshal,
Qū Dào its Mò'áo,
Prince Zhuīshū its Zhēnyǐn,
Qū Dàng its Liányǐn,
and Yǎng Yóujī its Gōngjiùyǐn,
to pacify the people of the state.
The gentleman says:
"In this, Chǔ was able to appoint officials appropriately.
Appointing officials appropriately—
this is a state's urgent matter.
When officials are appointed appropriately,
then the people have no covetous thoughts.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Alas for the one I long for,
placed in that Zhōu rank'—
this is about appointing officials appropriately.
The king, and the dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, barons, the Diàn, Cǎi, and Wèi domains, and the senior officials—each occupies his proper position;
this is what is called the Zhōu ranks."
B9.15.4 Regarding the rebellion of the Wèi and Sī clans in Zhèng,
the remaining rebels were in Sòng.
The people of Zhèng, because of Zǐ Xī, Bó Yǒu, and Zǐ Chǎn,
sent bribes to Sòng,
consisting of forty teams of horses, along with Shī Fá and Shī Huì.
In the third month,
Gōngsūn Hēi served as a hostage there.
The Minister of Works, Zǐ Hǎn,
handed over Dǔ Nǚfù, Wèi Piān, and Sī Qí to them,
but considered Sī Chén a good man and let him escape,
entrusting him to Jì Wǔzǐ.
Wǔzǐ placed him at Biàn.
The people of Zhèng made the three men into mincemeat.
Shī Huì passed by the Sòng court,
and was about to relieve himself.
His guide said:
"This is the court."
Huì said:
"There is no one here."
The guide said:
"This is the court;
why do you say there is no one?"
Huì said:
"There certainly is no one here.
If there were still someone,
how could they exchange the minister of a state of a thousand chariots for a blind musician of lewd songs?
It must be because there is no one here."
Zǐ Hǎn heard this,
and firmly requested and sent him back.
B9.15.5 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí besieged Chéng,
because he had become disloyal to Jìn.
Thereupon, they built the outer wall of Chéng.
B9.15.6 In autumn,
the men of Zhū attacked our southern borders,
and we sent word to Jìn.
Jìn was about to hold a meeting to punish Zhū and Jǔ,
but the Marquis of Jìn fell ill,
and so it was stopped.
In winter,
Jìn's Duke Dào died,
and so the meeting could not be held.
B9.15.7 Zhèng's Gōngsūn Xià went to Jìn for the funeral,
and Zǐ Jiǎo accompanied the burial procession.
B9.15.8 A man of Sòng obtained a piece of jade,
and presented it to Zǐ Hǎn.
Zǐ Hǎn would not receive it.
The presenter of the jade said:
"I showed it to a jade-worker,
who pronounced it a gem,
and therefore I venture to present it."
Zǐ Hǎn replied:
"I consider freedom from covetousness my gem,
while you consider jade your gem.
If you were to give it to me,
we should both lose our gems.
It is better that each should keep his own gem."
The other bowed his head to the ground and said:
"A humble man, carrying a piece of jade,
cannot cross the countryside safely.
I present this to beg that you might save me from death."
Zǐ Hǎn placed him in his own village,
had a jade-worker work the jade for him,
and when he was enriched, sent him back to his own place.
B9.15.9 In the twelfth month,
a man of Zhèng took away the wife of Dǔ Gǒu,
and returned her to the Fàn family.
A9.16 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 16 of Duke Xiāng
A9.16.1 In the sixteenth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
we buried Duke Dào of Jìn.
A9.16.2 In the third month,
our duke had a meeting with the marquis of Jìn,
the duke of Sòng,
the marquis of Wèi,
the earl of Zhèng,
the earl of Cáo,
the viscount of Jǔ,
the viscount of Zhū,
the earl of Xuē,
the earl of Qǐ,
and the viscount of Xiǎo Zhū at Jú Liáng.
On Wùyín,
the great officers took an oath.
A9.16.3 Men of Jìn seized the viscount of Jǔ
and the viscount of Zhū and carried them back with them.
A9.16.4 The marquis of Qí invaded our northern borders.
A9.16.5 In summer,
our duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.16.6 In the fifth month, on Jiǎzǐ,
there was an earthquake.
A9.16.7 Shū Lǎo, together with the earl of Zhèng,
Xún Yǎn of Jìn,
Nìng Zhí of Wèi,
and men of Sòng, invaded Xǔ.
A9.16.8 In autumn,
the marquis of Qí invaded our northern borders,
and laid siege to Chéng.
A9.16.9 There was a great rain sacrifice.
A9.16.10 In winter,
Shūsūn Bào went to Jìn.
B9.16 The Commentary, Year 16 of Duke Xiāng
B9.16.1 In spring of the sixteenth year,
Duke Dào of Jìn was buried.
Duke Píng ascended the throne,
with Yángshé Xī as his tutor,
Zhāng Jūnchén as commander of the central army's Sima,
Qí Xī, Hán Xiāng, Luán Yíng, and Shì Yǎng as Dukes' Clan Great Officers,
and Yúqiū Shū as charioteer for the royal horses.
They changed their mourning garments, repaired the official residences,
and performed the Zhēng sacrifice at Qūwò.
After posting guards, they descended south,
and met at Jú Liáng.
They ordered the return of invaded lands.
Because of our state,
they seized Duke Xuān of Zhū and Duke Líbǐ of Jǔ,
saying:
"They communicated with envoys from Qí and Chǔ."
The marquis of Jìn feasted with the princes at Wēn,
and made the great officers dance,
saying:
"The songs you chant must be appropriate."
The song chanted by Gāo Hòu of Qí was not appropriate.
Xún Yǎn was angry,
and said:
"The princes have different intentions."
He made the great officers take an oath with Gāo Hòu,
but Gāo Hòu fled back home.
Thereupon, Shūsūn Bào, Xún Yǎn of Jìn, Xiàng Xū of Sòng, Nìng Zhí of Wèi, Gōngsūn Chài of Zhèng, and the great officers of Xiǎo Zhū took an oath,
saying:
"We will jointly punish those who do not attend court."
B9.16.2 The baron of Xǔ requested to move to Jìn.
The princes then moved Xǔ,
but the great officers of Xǔ would not agree,
so the men of Jìn sent the princes back.
Zǐ Jiǎo of Zhèng heard they were about to attack Xǔ,
and thereupon acted as assistant to the earl of Zhèng
to follow the armies of the princes.
Mù Shū followed our duke.
Qí Zǐ led troops to join Xún Yǎn of Jìn.
The record says "joined the earl of Zhèng,"
because he was treated as an equal.
In summer, in the sixth month,
they halted at Yùlín.
On Gēngyín,
they attacked Xǔ,
and halted at Hánshì.
B9.16.3 Xún Yǎn and Luán Yǎn of Jìn led troops to attack Chǔ,
in retaliation for the battle at Yáng Liáng of Sòng.
Prince Gé of Chǔ led troops,
and fought with the Jìn army at Zhànbǎn.
The Chǔ army was severely defeated.
The Jìn army then invaded beyond Fāngchéng,
attacked Xǔ again, and returned.
B9.16.4 In autumn,
the marquis of Qí laid siege to Chéng,
and Mèng Rúzǐ Sù intercepted him.
The marquis of Qí said:
"This man is fond of bravery;
let us withdraw to give him fame."
Sù then blocked the Hǎixíng pass and returned.
B9.16.5 In winter,
Mù Shū went to Jìn on a friendly mission,
and spoke about the affair with Qí.
The men of Jìn said:
"Because our ruler has not yet performed the Dì sacrifice, and the people have not yet rested,
otherwise,
we would not dare forget."
Mù Shū said:
"Because the men of Qí morning and evening vent their resentment on the lands of our humble state,
therefore we make this urgent request.
The urgency of our humble state
is such that morning cannot wait for evening.
We crane our necks looking westward, saying:
'Perhaps help will come!'
If we wait until you, the officers in charge, are at leisure,
we fear it will be too late."
He went to see Xiànzǐ of Zhōngháng,
and recited the poem "Qífù."
Xiànzǐ said:
"Yǎn knows his fault;
how dare I not follow you, the officers in charge,
to jointly care for the altars of soil and grain,
and allow Lǔ to come to this!"
He went to see Xuānzǐ of Fàn,
and recited the final stanza of the poem "Hóngyàn."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Gài is here;
how dare I allow Lǔ to be without peace!"
A9.17 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 17 of Duke Xiāng
A9.17.1 In the seventeenth year, in spring,
in the king's second month, on Gēngwǔ,
the viscount of Zhū, Kēng, died.
A9.17.2 Men of Sòng invaded Chén.
A9.17.3 In summer,
Shí Mǎi of Wèi led troops to invade Cáo.
A9.17.4 In autumn,
the marquis of Qí invaded our northern borders,
and laid siege to Táo.
Gāo Hòu led troops to invade our northern borders,
and laid siege to Fáng.
A9.17.5 In the ninth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice.
A9.17.6 Huà Chén of Sòng fled to Chén.
A9.17.7 In winter,
men of Zhū invaded our southern borders.
B9.17 The Commentary, Year 17 of Duke Xiāng
B9.17.1 In spring of the seventeenth year,
Zhuāng Cháo of Sòng invaded Chén,
captured Minister of Education Áng,
because Chén despised Sòng.
B9.17.2 Sūn Kuǎi of Wèi was hunting in the fields at Cáo Suì,
watered his horse at Chóngqiū,
and broke their water jars.
The people of Chóngqiū shut their gates and reviled him,
saying:
"You personally drove out your ruler,
and your father acted cruelly.
You do not worry about this,
so what are you doing hunting here?"
In summer,
Shí Mǎi and Sūn Kuǎi of Wèi attacked Cáo,
capturing Zhòngqiū.
The people of Cáo complained to Jìn.
B9.17.3 Because the people of Qí had not achieved their aims against us,
in autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern borders,
besieging Táo.
Gāo Hòu besieged Zāng Hé at Fáng.
Our troops from Yángguān went to meet Zāng Sūn,
reaching Lǚsōng.
Zōu Shū Hé, Zāng Chóu, and Zāng Jiǎ, leading three hundred armored soldiers,
made a night attack on the Qí army,
escorted him back, and then returned.
The Qí army withdrew from there.
The men of Qí captured Zāng Jiān.
The Marquis of Qí sent Sùshā Wèi to console him,
and said, "Do not die."
Jiān bowed his head to the ground and said:
"I acknowledge the disgrace of your command.
However, the ruler's favor did not reach its end,
and he further sent his mutilated official to show courtesy to a gentleman."
He then used a wooden stake to pick at his wound and died.
B9.17.4 In winter,
the people of Zhū attacked our southern borders,
for the sake of Qí.
B9.17.5 Huà Yuè of Sòng died.
Huà Chén weakened the household of Gāobǐ,
and sent assassins to kill its steward, Huà Wú.
Six assassins killed him with spears at the Lú Gate,
behind the residence of Hé Zuǒshī.
Zuǒshī was afraid,
and said:
"This old man is without guilt."
The assassins said:
"Gāobǐ privately sought to punish Wú."
They then imprisoned his wife,
saying:
"Give me your large jade disc."
The Duke of Sòng heard of this,
and said:
"Chén not only violently oppressed his own clan,
but greatly disrupted the governance of the state of Sòng.
He must be expelled."
Zuǒshī said:
"Chén
is also a minister.
For a great minister to be disobedient
is a disgrace to the state.
It would be better to cover it up."
So they let him be.
Zuǒshī made a short whip for himself,
and whenever he passed Huà Chén's gate,
he would gallop.
On the jiǎwǔ day of the eleventh month,
the people of the capital chased a mad dog.
The mad dog entered the residence of Huà Chén,
and the people followed it.
Huà Chén was afraid,
and fled to Chén.
B9.17.6 Huáng Guófù of Sòng was the Grand Steward.
He built a terrace for Duke Píng,
which hindered the agricultural harvest.
Zǐ Hǎn requested to wait until the farming work was finished,
but the duke did not permit it.
The builders sang:
"The pale one from Zémén
truly started our labor.
The dark one from within the city
truly comforts our hearts."
Zǐ Hǎn heard this,
personally took a whip,
went among the builders,
and struck those who were not diligent,
saying:
"We common people
all have houses
to shelter from dryness, dampness, cold, and heat.
Now our ruler is building a single terrace,
and if you do not complete it quickly,
how can you be considered laborers?"
The singing then stopped.
Someone asked him the reason.
Zǐ Hǎn said:
"Sòng is a small state,
yet it has both curses and blessings;
this is the root of calamity."
B9.17.7 Yàn Huánzǐ of Qí died.
Yàn Yīng wore coarse hempen mourning garments with unhemmed edges,
a headband and girdle of dark hemp, and a staff,
straw sandals,
ate gruel,
lived in a mourning hut,
slept on a straw mat with a grass pillow.
His steward said:
"This is not the ritual for a senior official."
He said:
"Only a minister is considered a senior official."
A9.18 The Classic of the Eighteenth Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the White Dí came.
A9.18.2 In summer,
the men of Jìn seized the Wèi messenger Shí Mǎi.
A9.18.3 In autumn,
the Qí army attacked our northern borders.
A9.18.4 In winter, in the tenth month,
our duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎozhū,
and together they besieged Qí.
A9.18.5 The Earl of Cáo, Fùchú, died in the army.
A9.18.6 The Chǔ prince Wǔ led an army to attack Zhèng.
B9.18 The Commentary of the Eighteenth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
the White Dí first came.
B9.18.2 In summer,
the men of Jìn seized the Wèi messenger Shí Mǎi at Zhǎngzǐ,
and seized Sūn Kuǎi at Chúnliú,
for the sake of Cáo.
B9.18.3 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked our northern borders.
Xiànzǐ of Zhōngháng was about to attack Qí.
He dreamed that he was disputing with Duke Lì,
and did not win.
The duke struck him with a dagger-axe,
his head fell in front of him,
he knelt and placed it on his head,
and holding it, he ran away.
He saw the shaman Gāo of Gěngyáng.
Another day,
he saw him on the road,
spoke with him,
and it was the same.
The shaman said:
"This year, my lord will certainly die.
If there are affairs in the east,
then you can succeed."
Xiànzǐ agreed.
The Marquis of Jìn attacked Qí.
When they were about to cross the river,
Xiànzǐ tied two pairs of jades with red silk,
and prayed, saying:
"Qí Huán relies on his perilous terrain,
depends on his multitude of people,
abandons friendship and breaks covenants,
and violently mistreats the spirits' hosts.
Your subject Biāo will lead the feudal lords to punish him,
and your official servant Yǎn will truly precede and follow him.
If we are successful and achieve merit,
do not let it bring shame to the spirits.
Your official servant Yǎn dares not cross again.
May you, the spirits, judge it."
He sank the jades and crossed.
In winter, in the tenth month,
they met at the Lǔ crossing of the Jì River,
renewing the words of the Júliáng covenant,
and together attacked Qí.
The Marquis of Qí defended against them at Píngyīn,
digging a moat at the Fáng Gate and guarding it,
a width of one lǐ.
Sùshā Wèi said:
"If we cannot fight,
it would be better to guard a strategic point."
He did not listen.
The officers of the feudal lords attacked the gate,
and many men of Qí died.
Xuānzǐ of Fàn told Wénzǐ of Xī,
saying:
"I know you,
dare I conceal the truth?
The men of Lǔ and Jǔ have both requested to enter with a thousand chariots from their own directions,
and we have already agreed.
If they enter,
you, my lord, will certainly lose the state.
Why do you not plan for it!"
Zǐ Jiā reported this to the duke.
The duke was afraid.
Yàn Yīng heard of it,
and said:
"The ruler was originally without courage,
and now he has heard this; he cannot last long."
The Marquis of Qí ascended Mount Wū to observe the Jìn army.
The men of Jìn sent their Minister of War to reconnoiter the dangerous mountain and marsh terrain.
Even in places they could not reach,
they unfurled banners and deployed troops in a sparse formation.
They had the charioteers
place real soldiers on the left and dummies on the right,
with banners leading the way,
and the chariots dragging brushwood behind them.
When the Marquis of Qí saw this,
he feared their numbers,
and so slipped away to return.
On the last day of the month, Bǐngyín,
the Qí army fled by night.
Shī Kuàng reported to the Marquis of Jìn:
"The cries of the birds and crows are joyful;
the Qí army must have fled."
Xíng Bó reported to Zhōngháng Bó:
"There is the sound of neighing horses;
the Qí army must have fled."
Shū Xiàng reported to the Marquis of Jìn:
"There are crows on the city walls;
the Qí army must have fled."
On the first day of the eleventh month, Dīngmǎo,
they entered Píngyīn,
and then pursued the Qí army.
Sùshā Wèi linked large carts
to block the narrow path and served as the rear guard.
Zhí Chuò
and Guō Zuì said:
"For you to serve as the rear guard of the state's army
is a disgrace to Qí.
You should go ahead first!"
So they replaced him as the rear guard.
Wèi killed horses at the narrow pass
to block the road.
Zhōu Chuò of Jìn caught up with them,
shot Zhí Chuò,
hitting his shoulder,
with two arrows pinning his neck,
and said:
"Stop,
and you will be captured by the three armies;
if you do not stop,
I will aim for your heart."
Zhí Chuò looked back and said:
"Swear a private oath."
Zhōu Chuò said: "I swear by the sun!"
Then he loosened his bow and bound him from behind.
His right-hand man, Jù Bǐng, also laid down his weapons
and bound Guō Zuì.
Both were bound in their armor
and made to sit beneath the drum of the central army.
The men of Jìn wanted to pursue those retreating,
but Lǔ and Wèi requested to attack the dangerous positions.
On Jǐmǎo,
Xún Yǎn and Shì Gài with the central army captured Jīngzī.
On Yǐyǒu,
Wèi Jiàng and Luán Yíng with the lower army captured Shì.
Zhào Wǔ
and Hán Qǐ with the upper army besieged Lú,
but did not capture it.
On the twelfth month, Wùxū,
they reached Qínzhōu,
and cut down the catalpas at Yōngmén.
Fàn Yāng attacked the Yōngmén gate,
and his charioteer, Zhuī Xǐ, killed a dog in the gateway with a halberd.
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ cut down a camphor tree
to make a qín for the lord.
On Jǐhài,
they burned Yōngmén and the western and southern outer walls.
Liú Nán
and Shì Ruò led the armies of the various lords to burn the bamboo and trees at Shēnchí.
On Rényín,
they burned the eastern and northern outer walls.
Fàn Yāng attacked the Yángmén gate.
Zhōu Chuò attacked the Dōnglǘ gate.
His left outer horse was pressed,
and he circled back within the gate,
counting the door panels with a whip.
The Marquis of Qí harnessed his carriage,
preparing to flee to Yóutáng.
The crown prince and Guō Róng seized the horses' bridles,
saying:
"The army is swift and fierce,
but they are only plundering.
They are about to retreat.
Why should you, my lord, fear?
Moreover, the ruler of the state must not act lightly;
acting lightly will cause you to lose the people.
You must wait for them!"
The Marquis was about to push past them.
The crown prince drew his sword and cut the traces,
and so he stopped.
On Jiǎchén,
they advanced eastward to the Wéi River,
and southward to the Yí River.
B9.18.4 Zǐ Kǒng of Zhèng wanted to remove the great officers,
and planned to rebel against Jìn and raise a Chǔ army
to eliminate them.
He sent word to Zǐ Gēng,
but Zǐ Gēng did not agree.
The King of Chǔ heard of this,
and sent Yángtún Yǐn Yí to inform Zǐ Gēng, saying:
"The people of the state say that I preside over the altars of soil and grain
but do not send out armies,
and that even in death I will not follow the rites.
Since I ascended the throne,
it has now been five years,
and the army has not marched out.
People must think that I am indulging in ease
and have forgotten the enterprise of the former lords.
Consider this, great officer.
What should be done?"
Zǐ Gēng sighed and said:
"Does the king think that Wǔ seeks comfort and ease?
I act for the benefit of the altars of soil and grain."
He received the messenger,
kowtowed, and replied:
"The various lords are currently friendly with Jìn.
I request to test them.
If it is feasible,
you, my lord, may follow up.
If it is not feasible,
I will withdraw the army and retreat.
This can cause no harm,
and you, my lord, will also suffer no disgrace."
Zǐ Gēng led the army and drilled the troops at Fén.
At that time, Zǐ Jiǎo, Bó Yǒu, and Zǐ Zhāng followed the Earl of Zhèng to attack Qí,
while Zǐ Kǒng, Zǐ Zhǎn, and Zǐ Xī remained to guard.
The latter two knew of Zǐ Kǒng's plot,
so they strengthened the defenses and entered the stronghold.
Zǐ Kǒng did not dare to join the Chǔ army.
The Chǔ army attacked Zhèng,
and encamped at Yúlíng.
The right army fortified Shàngjí,
and then crossed the Yǐng River.
They encamped at Zhānrán.
Wěi Zǐ Féng and Prince Gé led a crack force
to invade Fèihuá, Xūmí, Xiànyú, and Yōngliáng,
turned right around Méishān,
invaded the northeast of Zhèng,
and reached Chóngláo before returning.
Zǐ Gēng attacked the Chúnmén gate,
camped beneath the city walls, and then withdrew,
crossing below Yúchǐ.
Heavy rain caught up with them.
Many in the Chǔ army froze,
and the laborers were nearly all lost.
When the men of Jìn heard that there was a Chǔ army,
Shī Kuàng said:
"It is no harm.
I repeatedly sang songs of the north wind,
and also sang songs of the south wind.
The south wind is not strong;
it has many notes of death.
Chǔ will surely achieve nothing."
Dǒng Shū said:
"The way of heaven lies mostly in the northwest.
The southern army acts out of season;
they will surely achieve nothing."
Shū Xiàng said:
"It lies in the virtue of their ruler."
A9.19 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Nineteenth Year of Duke Xiāng*
A9.19.1 In the nineteenth year, spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the various lords made a covenant at Zhùkē.
The men of Jìn seized the Viscount of Zhū.
A9.19.2 The duke arrived from attacking Qí.
A9.19.3 They took fields from Zhū,
from the Guō River.
A9.19.4 Jìsūn Sù went to Jìn.
A9.19.5 They buried Duke Chéng of Cáo.
A9.19.6 In summer,
Sūn Línfǔ of Wèi led an army to attack Qí.
A9.19.7 In autumn, the seventh month, Xīnmǎo,
the Marquis of Qí, Huán, died.
A9.19.8 Shì Gài of Jìn led an army to invade Qí.
He reached Gǔ,
heard that the Marquis of Qí had died,
and then returned.
A9.19.9 In the eighth month, Bǐngchén,
Zhòngsūn Miè died.
A9.19.10 Qí killed its great officer Gāo Hòu.
A9.19.11 Zhèng killed its great officer Prince Jiā.
A9.19.12 In winter,
they buried Duke Líng of Qí.
A9.19.13 The outer city wall of the western capital was fortified.
A9.19.14 Shūsūn Bào met with Jìn's Shì Gài at Kē.
A9.19.15 The city of Wǔchéng was fortified.
B9.19 The Commentary for the Nineteenth Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.19.1 In the spring of the nineteenth year,
the feudal lords returned from the banks of the Yí River,
and made a covenant at Dūyáng,
saying:
"The great shall not invade the small."
The Duke of Zhū, Dào, was seized,
because he had attacked us.
They then encamped on the banks of the Sì River,
and demarcated our fields.
They took fields from Zhū,
and restored them to us from the Huò River.
The Marquis of Jìn returned first.
Our duke entertained the six ministers of Jìn at Púpǔ,
and bestowed upon them robes of the third rank;
the army commanders, marshals, ministers of works, chariot commanders, and scouts all received robes of the first rank;
he presented Xún Yǎn with bundles of fine silk, an additional jade disc, and a team of horses,
preceding the tripod of Wú's Shòu Mèng.
Xún Yǎn suffered from a carbuncle,
which developed into an ulcer on his head.
Crossing the Yellow River,
when they reached Zhùyōng,
he fell ill,
and his eyes bulged out.
The great officers who had returned earlier all came back.
Shì Gài requested an audience,
but was not admitted.
He asked about a successor,
and [Xún Yǎn] said:
"The Zhèng-born nephew is suitable."
On the jiǎyín day of the second month,
he died,
but his eyes remained open,
and the jade could not be placed in his mouth.
Xuānzǐ washed his hands and stroked the corpse,
saying:
"How dare I not serve Wú as I served my lord!"
The eyes still stared.
Luán Huáizǐ said:
"Is it because the affair with Qí is not yet finished?"
He then stroked it again and said:
"If you, my lord, end here,
if I do not continue the affair with Qí,
may the River bear witness!"
Only then did the eyes close,
and he accepted the jade.
Xuānzǐ went out,
and said:
"I was shallow in my understanding of what makes a true man."
B9.19.2 Jìn's Luán Fáng led troops to follow Wèi's Sūn Wénzǐ in attacking Qí.
B9.19.3 Jì Wǔzǐ went to Jìn to thank them for the army,
and the Marquis of Jìn entertained him.
Fàn Xuānzǐ was in charge of government,
and recited the "Shǔ Miáo".
Jì Wǔzǐ rose,
bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
saying:
"A small state looks up to a great state,
as all grains look up to the nourishing rain.
If it is constantly nourished,
all under heaven will be harmonious,
not just our humble state."
He recited the "Liù Yuè".
B9.19.4 Jì Wǔzǐ used the weapons obtained from Qí to cast a Lín bell
and inscribe upon it the achievements of Lǔ.
Zāng Wǔzhòng said to Jìsūn:
"This is contrary to ritual.
As for inscriptions,
the Son of Heaven records virtue,
the feudal lords speak of timely achievements and reckon merit,
and the great officers record campaigns.
Now, to record a campaign is of the lowest rank;
to reckon merit,
then it is borrowed from others;
to speak of timeliness,
then the harm to the people was great.
On what grounds is this inscription made?
Moreover, when a great state attacks a small one,
taking what it has gained,
to make sacrificial vessels,
inscribing their meritorious deeds,
to show to sons and grandsons,
is to display illustrious virtue
and punish those without ritual.
Now, we are borrowing the strength of others to save ourselves from death,
how can we inscribe this?
For a small state to be fortunate against a great state,
and to display what was gained, thereby angering them,
is the way to perish."
B9.19.5 The Marquis of Qí took a wife from Lǔ,
named Yán Yìjī,
who had no sons.
Her niece, Zòng Shēngjī,
bore Guāng,
who was made heir apparent.
Among his concubines were Zhòngzǐ and Róngzǐ,
and Róngzǐ was favored.
Zhòngzǐ bore Yá,
and entrusted him to Róngzǐ.
Róngzǐ requested that Yá be made heir apparent,
and it was granted.
Zhòngzǐ said:
"It cannot be.
To abandon the regular order
is inauspicious;
to cause discord among the feudal lords
is difficult.
Guāng's establishment
has been announced to the feudal lords.
Now to depose him without cause
is to arbitrarily disgrace the feudal lords,
and to use difficulty to confront inauspiciousness.
My lord will certainly regret it."
The duke said:
"It is up to me alone."
He then sent the heir apparent Guāng east.
He appointed Gāo Hòu as tutor to Yá,
making him heir apparent,
and Sùshā Wèi as junior tutor.
The Marquis of Qí fell ill,
Cuī Zhù secretly brought Guāng back,
and when the illness became critical, he established him.
Guāng killed Róngzǐ,
and exposed her corpse in the court,
which was contrary to ritual.
Women are not subject to public punishments.
Even if punished,
it should not be in the court or marketplaces.
In the summer, on the last day of the fifth month, rénchén,
Duke Líng of Qí died.
Duke Zhuāng succeeded to the throne.
He seized Prince Yá at Gōudòu Hill.
Because Sùshā Wèi had plotted against him,
Wèi fled to Gāotáng and rebelled.
B9.19.6 Jìn's Shì Gài invaded Qí,
and reached Gǔ.
Hearing of the mourning, he returned,
which was according to ritual.
B9.19.7 In the fourth month, on the dīngwèi day,
Zhèng's Gōngsūn Chài died,
and the announcement was sent to the great officers of Jìn.
Fàn Xuānzǐ spoke to the Marquis of Jìn,
because he had been good in the campaign against Qín.
In the sixth month,
the Marquis of Jìn made a request to the king,
and the king posthumously bestowed upon him a grand chariot,
to be used in the funeral procession,
which was according to ritual.
B9.19.8 In autumn, the eighth month,
Qí's Cuī Zhù killed Gāo Hòu at Sǎlán,
and took over his household.
The record says, "Qí killed its great officer,"
because he followed his lord in folly.
B9.19.9 When Zǐ Kǒng of Zhèng was in charge of government, he was autocratic,
and the people of the state were troubled by it.
They then investigated the disaster at the Western Palace and the army at Chúnmén.
Zǐ Kǒng was held accountable for the crime,
and with his own armor and that of the houses of Zǐ Gé and Zǐ Liáng, he defended himself.
On the jiǎchén day,
Zǐ Zhǎn
and Zǐ Xī led the people of the state to attack him,
killed Zǐ Kǒng,
and divided his household.
The record says
"Zhèng killed its great officer,"
because of his autocracy.
Zǐ Rán and Zǐ Kǒng
were sons of Sòngzǐ;
Shì Zǐ Kǒng
was the son of Guī Guī.
Guī Guī's rank was below Sòngzǐ's,
but they were close;
the two Zǐ Kǒngs were also close.
In the fourth year of Duke Xī,
Zǐ Rán died;
in the first year of Duke Jiǎn,
Shì Zǐ Kǒng died.
The minister Zǐ Kǒng actually managed the households of Zǐ Gé and Zǐ Liáng,
and the three households were as one,
therefore they were involved in the disaster.
Zǐ Gé
and Zǐ Liáng fled to Chǔ.
Zǐ Gé became the Right Minister.
The people of Zhèng appointed Zǐ Zhǎn to oversee the state,
Zǐ Xī to administer the government,
and established Zǐ Chǎn as a minister.
B9.19.10 Qí's Qìng Fēng besieged Gāotáng,
but did not capture it.
In winter, in the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Qí besieged it.
Seeing Wèi on the city wall,
he called out to him,
and Wèi came down.
(The Marquis) asked him about the city's defenses,
and Wèi reported there were none.
(The Marquis) bowed to him,
and (Wèi) then ascended (back to the wall).
Hearing the army was about to attack,
(Wèi) had the people of Gāotáng feast.
Zhí Chuò and Gōng Lóu Huì let down ropes at night to admit the (besieging) army,
and Wèi was made into mincemeat in the army.
B9.19.11 (Lǔ) built an outer wall on the west side of the city,
out of fear of Qí.
B9.19.12 Qí made peace with Jìn,
and they swore a covenant at Dàsuì.
Therefore, Mù Shū met Fàn Xuānzǐ at Kē.
Mù Shū met Shū Xiàng,
and recited the fourth stanza of the "Zài Chí".
Shū Xiàng said:
"Xī dares not refuse your command!"
Mù Shū returned and said:
"Qí's situation is not yet settled,
we cannot be without fear."
They then fortified the city of Wǔchéng.
B9.19.13 Wèi's Shí Gòngzǐ died,
but his son Dàozǐ did not mourn.
Kǒng Chéngzǐ said:
"This is called uprooting one's foundation,
he will certainly not preserve his clan."
A9.20 《The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 20 of Duke Xiāng》
A9.20.1 In the twentieth year, in spring,
in the royal first month, on the Xīnhài day,
Zhòngsūn Sù met with a man from Jǔ and swore a covenant at Xiàng.
A9.20.2 In summer,
in the sixth month, on the Gēngshēn day,
our Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎozhū, and swore a covenant at Chányuān.
A9.20.3 In autumn,
our Duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.20.4 Zhòngsūn Sù led an army to attack Zhū.
A9.20.5 Cài killed its senior minister, Prince Xiè.
Cài's Prince Lǚ fled to Chǔ.
A9.20.6 The younger brother Huáng of the Marquis of Chén fled to Chǔ.
A9.20.7 Shū Lǎo went to Qí.
A9.20.8 In winter, in the tenth month, on the Bǐngchén day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.20.9 Jìsūn Sù went to Sòng.
B9.20 《The Commentary of Zuo, Year 20 of Duke Xiāng》
B9.20.1 In the twentieth year, in spring,
(Lǔ) made peace with Jǔ.
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ met with a man from Jǔ and swore a covenant at Xiàng,
because of the covenant at Dūyáng.
B9.20.2 In summer,
(they) swore a covenant at Chányuān,
because Qí had made peace.
B9.20.3 The men of Zhū repeatedly made incursions,
and because of the affairs of the various lords, (Lǔ) could not retaliate.
In autumn,
Mèng Zhuāngzǐ attacked Zhū in retaliation.
B9.20.4 Cài's Prince Xiè wished to make Cài follow Jìn,
and the men of Cài killed him.
Prince Lǚ was his full younger brother,
so he fled to Chǔ.
Chén's Qìng Hǔ and Qìng Yín feared the pressure from Prince Huáng,
and accused him before Chǔ, saying:
"He conspired with Cài's Minister of War."
The men of Chǔ used this as a pretext for action,
and Prince Huáng fled to Chǔ.
Earlier,
Cài's Duke Wén wished to serve Jìn,
saying:
"Our former lord participated in the covenant at Jiàntǔ,
Jìn cannot be abandoned,
and moreover they are our brothers."
But he feared Chǔ,
and could not carry it out before he died.
The men of Chǔ made demands on Cài without constancy,
Prince Xiè sought to follow the former lord's will
for the benefit of Cài,
but could not and died.
The record says
"Cài killed its senior minister Prince Xiè",
meaning he was not in accord with the people's desires;
"The younger brother Huáng of the Marquis of Chén
fled to Chǔ",
meaning it was not his crime.
Prince Huáng was about to flee,
and cried out in the capital, saying:
"The Qìng clan is without principle,
seeking to monopolize the state of Chén,
violently disregarding their ruler,
and removing his relatives;
if they are not destroyed within five years,
it is because Heaven has no eyes."
B9.20.5 Qízǐ made his first diplomatic visit to Qí,
which was according to ritual.
B9.20.6 In winter,
Jì Wǔzǐ went to Sòng,
to return Xiàng Xū's diplomatic visit.
Chǔshī Duàn welcomed him and received the feast,
and (Jì Wǔzǐ) recited the seventh and final stanzas of the "Chángdì".
The men of Sòng gave him rich gifts.
Upon returning,
he reported back,
our Duke feasted him,
and he recited the final stanza of the "Yú Lí".
Our Duke recited the "Nánshān Yǒu Tái".
Wǔzǐ left his mat,
and said:
"Your servant cannot bear this."
B9.20.7 Wèi's Nìng Huìzǐ was ill,
and summoned his son Dàozǐ, saying:
"I offended our ruler,
and regret is too late.
My name is recorded in the annals of the various lords,
saying
'Sūn Línfù and Nìng Zhí expelled their ruler'.
If the ruler returns,
then cover it up.
If you can cover it up,
then you are my son.
If you cannot,
and if ghosts and spirits exist,
I will starve,
and will not come to partake of the offerings."
Dàozǐ promised,
and Huìzǐ then died.
A9.21 《The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 21 of Duke Xiāng》
A9.21.1 In the twenty-first year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
our Duke went to Jìn.
A9.21.2 Zhū's Shùqí brought Chī and
Lǚqiū and came fleeing (to Lǔ).
A9.21.3 In summer,
our Duke arrived from Jìn.
A9.21.4 In autumn,
Jìn's Luán Yíng fled to Chǔ.
A9.21.5 In the ninth month, on the Gēngxū day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.21.6 In winter, in the tenth month, on the Gēngchén day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.21.7 The Earl of Cáo came for an audience.
A9.21.8 Our Duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
and the Viscount of Zhū at Shāngrén.
B9.21 《The Commentary of Zuo, Year 21 of Duke Xiāng》
B9.21.1 In the twenty-first year, in spring,
our Duke went to Jìn,
to thank them for the army and for taking the fields of Zhū.
B9.21.2 Zhū's Shùqí brought Chī and Lǚqiū and came fleeing (to Lǔ),
and Jì Wǔzǐ gave him a sister of our Duke as a wife,
and also bestowed gifts on his followers.
At this time, Lǔ had many robbers.
Jìsūn said to Zāng Wǔzhòng:
"Why do you not investigate the robbers?"
Wǔzhòng said:
"It cannot be investigated.
Hé is also incapable."
Jìsūn said:
"I have four borders,
and investigate the thieves therein,
why is it impossible?
You are the Minister of Justice,
and should be devoted to eliminating thieves,
how can you be incapable?"
Wǔzhòng said:
"You summon external thieves
and treat them with great courtesy,
how can you stop our own thieves?
You are the chief minister,
yet you welcome external thieves;
to make Hé remove them,
how could he be capable?
Shǔqí stole a city from Zhū and came here,
you gave him a daughter of the Jī clan as wife,
and bestowed upon him a city,
and his followers all received rewards.
If great thieves are treated with courtesy by giving them the ruler's aunts or sisters along with large cities,
the next rank receives grooms, herdsmen, carriages, and horses,
and the lesser ones receive clothing, swords, and belts,
this is rewarding thieves.
To reward them and then remove them,
perhaps it is difficult.
Hé has heard that
those in high positions cleanse their hearts,
and are consistent in treating others;
they regulate their trustworthiness,
which can be clearly verified,
and only then can they govern others.
What those above do,
the people follow.
What those above do not do,
yet the people sometimes do,
therefore punishments are applied,
and none dare not be warned.
If what those above do,
the people also do,
then it is as it should be,
how can it be prohibited?
The *Xiàshū* says:
'Think of this, be in this,
release this, be in this,
speak of this, be in this,
sincerely issue from this, be in this,
only the Emperor thinks of merit.'
This means it should come from one's own consistency.
Trustworthiness comes from one's own consistency,
and only then can merit be considered."
Shǔqí was not a minister,
but came with land,
though lowly,
it must be recorded,
to emphasize the land.
B9.21.3 The Marquis of Qí sent Qìng Zuǒ to be a senior official,
again to deal with the faction of Prince Yá,
and arrested Prince Mǎi at Gōudòu Hill.
Prince Chú fled here.
Shūsūn Huán fled to Yān.
B9.21.4 In summer,
Chǔ Zǐgēng died.
The King of Chǔ sent Wěi Zǐféng to be the Prime Minister,
and consulted Shēn Shūyù.
Shūyù said:
"The state has many favorites and the king is weak,
the state cannot be governed."
Thereupon he declined due to illness.
It was the height of summer,
he dug a pit,
placed ice beneath and a bed on top.
Wearing double-layered garments,
dressed in furs,
he ate little and slept.
The King of Chǔ sent a physician to examine him.
The physician reported:
"He is extremely emaciated,
but his vital energy is unaffected."
Thereupon he made Zǐnán the Prime Minister.
B9.21.5 Luán Huánzǐ married a daughter of Fàn Xuānzǐ,
and gave birth to Huáizǐ.
Fàn Yāng, because of his exile,
resented the Luán clan,
so although he and Luán Yíng both served as Ministers of the Ducal Clan,
they could not get along.
Huánzǐ died,
Luán Qí had an affair with her steward Zhōu Bīn,
nearly ruining the household.
Huáizǐ was troubled by this.
Qí, fearing he would punish her,
accused him to Xuānzǐ, saying:
"Yíng is about to rebel,
thinking that the Fàn clan caused the death of his master Huán
and monopolized power, saying:
'My father expelled Yāng,
who showed no anger but repaid it with favor,
and now shares the same office with me yet monopolizes it.
My father died and he grew richer.
He caused my father's death and monopolizes the state,
I would rather die
than follow him.'
His plans are like this,
I fear harm will come to you, my lord,
I dared not remain silent."
Fàn Yāng corroborated this.
Huáizǐ was generous in giving,
and many men rallied to him.
Xuānzǐ, fearing his many followers,
believed the accusation.
Huáizǐ was a junior minister,
Xuānzǐ had him fortify Zhù
and then expelled him.
In autumn,
Luán Yíng fled to Chǔ.
Xuānzǐ killed Jī Yí, Huáng Yuān, Jiā Fù, Sīkōng Jìng, Bǐng Yù, Dǒng Shū, Bǐng Shī, Shēn Shū, Yángshé Hǔ, and Shū Pí,
and imprisoned Bó Huá, Shūxiàng, and Jí Yǎn.
Someone said to Shūxiàng:
"You have fallen into crime,
is it not due to lack of wisdom?"
Shūxiàng said:
"Compared with death or exile, how is this?
The *Shī* says,
'Leisurely, leisurely,
I pass the year in idleness,'
this is wisdom."
Yuè Wángfù visited Shūxiàng,
saying:
"I will plead for you."
Shūxiàng did not respond.
When he left,
Shūxiàng did not bow.
His attendants all blamed Shūxiàng.
Shūxiàng said:
"It must be Minister Qí."
The household steward heard this,
saying:
"When Yuè Wángfù speaks to the ruler,
nothing fails;
he sought to pardon you, sir,
yet you, sir, did not consent.
Minister Qí is incapable of this,
yet you say it must be through him,
why?"
Shūxiàng said:
"Yuè Wángfù
is one who follows the ruler's wishes,
how can he accomplish it?
Minister Qí, when recommending externally,
does not reject enemies,
and when recommending internally,
does not overlook kin;
would he alone leave me out?
The *Shī* says:
'With upright virtue and conduct,
all states obey him.'
That man is upright."
The Marquis of Jìn asked Yuè Wángfù about Shūxiàng's crime.
He replied:
"He does not abandon his kin,
there may be something to it."
At this time, Qí Xī was already old,
but hearing of it,
he rode a post carriage to see Xuānzǐ,
saying:
"The *Shī* says:
'Bestow boundless grace upon us,
that our descendants may preserve it.'
The *Shū* says:
'The sage has plans and merits,
clearly verified and firmly preserved.'
One who plans with few errors
and tirelessly imparts kind instruction—
Shūxiàng has these qualities.
He is a pillar of the state;
even ten generations of his descendants should be pardoned,
to encourage the capable.
Now for a single fault, he is not spared,
thereby abandoning the state's interests—
is this not deluded?
Gǔn was executed yet Yǔ rose;
Yīyǐn exiled Tàijiǎ yet served as his minister,
and in the end bore no resentment;
Guǎn and Cài were executed,
yet Zhōugōng assisted the king.
How can we, for the sake of Hǔ,
abandon the state's interests?
If you do good,
who would dare not strive?
What use is much killing?"
Xuānzǐ was pleased,
rode with him,
and spoke to the duke to pardon Shūxiàng.
He did not see Shūxiàng before returning,
and Shūxiàng also did not announce his pardon
but went to court.
Initially,
Shū Xiàng's mother
(corr=was jealous of Shū Hǔ's mother's beauty
and did not allow her to serve,
her sons all admonished their mother.
Their mother said:
"In deep mountains and great marshes,
truly are born dragons and serpents.
That beauty of hers,
I fear she will give birth to dragons and serpents
to bring calamity upon you.
You are a declining clan.
The state has many great favorites;
if unrighteous men intervene,
is it not difficult?
Why should I cherish her?"
She sent her to attend in the bedchamber,
and she bore Shū Hǔ,
handsome and possessing courage and strength.
Luán Huáizi favored him,
hence the Yángshé clan
met with disaster.
Luán Yíng passed through Zhōu,
and the western borderlands of Zhōu plundered him.
He addressed the messenger, saying:
"The Son of Heaven's attendant minister Yíng
has offended Your Majesty's guardian minister,
and is about to flee from punishment.
If my crime is further aggravated within the suburbs,
I will have nowhere to hide or flee.
I dare to lay bare my fate:
Formerly, attendant minister Shū
was able to devote his strength to the royal house,
and the king bestowed favor upon him.
His son Yǎn was unable to preserve the merits of his father's labors.
If the great lord does not discard Shū's contributions,
this fleeing minister may yet have a place to escape.
If you discard Shū's contributions,
and consider Yǎn's crime,
I, your minister,
am one who should have been executed,
and will return to die before the commandant.
I dare not return.
I dare to bare my limbs,
awaiting only the command of the great lord."
The king said:
"To imitate one's own fault-finding,
would be even worse."
He ordered the Minister over the Masses to prohibit plundering the Luán clan,
and to return what had been taken.
He sent a border guard to escort him out through Huányuán.
B9.21.6 In winter,
Duke Wǔ of Cáo came to court,
for the first audience.
B9.21.7 A meeting was held at Shāngrén,
to confine the Luán clan.
The Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi were disrespectful.
Shū Xiàng said:
"These two rulers will certainly not escape calamity.
Meetings and court appearances
are the warp of ritual;
ritual
is the carriage of governance;
governance
is the guardian of one's person.
To neglect ritual
is to lose governance;
to lose governance
is to lack stability,
hence disorder arises."
B9.21.8 Zhī Qǐ, Zhōngháng Xǐ, Zhōu Chuò, and Xíng Kuǎi
fled to Qí,
all being partisans of the Luán clan.
Yuè Wángfù said to Fàn Xuānzǐ:
"Why not recall Zhōu Chuò and Xíng Kuǎi?
They are brave warriors."
Xuānzǐ said: "They are the bravery of that Luán clan;
what would I gain from them?"
Wángfù said:
"If you act as their Luán clan,
then they will also be your bravery."
Duke Zhuāng of Qí held court,
and pointing to Zhí Chuò and Guō Zuì, said:
"These are my champions."
Zhōu Chuò said:
"If my lord considers them champions,
who dares not to consider them so?
However, your servant is not clever;
at the battle of Píngyīn,
I crowed before these two gentlemen."
Duke Zhuāng established a rank for bravery.
Zhí Chuò and Guō Zuì wished to be included.
Zhōu Chuò said:
"At the battle of Dōnglǘ,
your servant's left trace-horse was hard-pressed,
and I circled back within the gate,
and could count the studs on it.
Can I perhaps be included in this?"
The duke said:
"You acted for the ruler of Jìn."
He replied:
"Your servant is but a new subordinate,
yet these two men,
compared to birds and beasts,
I have eaten their flesh and slept upon their skins."
A9.22 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Xiāng, 22nd Year*
A9.22.1 In the 22nd year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
the duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.22.2 In summer, in the fourth month.
A9.22.3 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the xīnyǒu day,
Shǔlǎo died.
A9.22.4 In winter,
the duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎozhū at Shásuí.
A9.22.5 The duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.22.6 Chǔ put to death its great officer, Prince Zhuīshū.
B9.22 *The Commentary of Zuo, Duke Xiāng, 22nd Year*
B9.22.1 In the 22nd year, in spring,
Zāng Wǔzhòng went to Jìn.
It rained,
and he passed by Yù Shū.
Yù Shū was in his town,
about to drink wine,
and said:
"What use is a sage?
I am about to drink wine,
and that is all.
To travel in the rain—
what makes one a sage?"
Mù Shū heard of this,
and said:
"He is unfit for service,
yet he arrogantly treats a messenger,
he is a pest of the state."
He ordered his tax to be doubled.
B9.22.2 In summer,
the men of Jìn demanded court attendance from Zhèng.
The men of Zhèng sent the junior minister Gōngsūn Qiáo to reply,
saying:
"In the ninth year of your former ruler, Duke Dào of Jìn,
our humble ruler thereupon ascended the throne.
In the eighth month of his accession,
our former great officer Zǐsì
followed our humble ruler to attend upon your officers.
Your officers showed no courtesy to our humble ruler,
and our humble ruler was afraid.
Because of that journey,
in the sixth month of our second year we attended upon Chǔ,
and Jìn therefore had the battle of Xì.
The men of Chǔ were still strong,
and extended courtesy to our humble state.
Our humble state wished to follow your officers,
but feared to incur great blame,
saying:
'Jìn will surely say we do not share in respect for the rites,'
and therefore dared not be disloyal to Chǔ.
In the third month of our fourth year,
our former great officer Zǐjiǎo again followed our humble ruler
to observe the situation in Chǔ,
and Jìn then had the battle of Xiāoyú.
Considering our humble state,
close to the state of Jìn,
likened to plants and trees,
we are of the same scent,
so how dare we be at variance?
Chǔ also was not strong,
and our humble ruler exhausted the products of his land,
adding to them the vessels of the ancestral temple,
to receive the covenant of alliance.
Thereupon he led his ministers to follow your officers,
to meet at year's end.
Those who were disloyal to Chǔ,
Zǐhóu and Shíyú,
we returned and punished them.
In the year after Júliáng,
Zǐjiǎo was old,
and Gōngsūn Xià followed our humble ruler to attend upon you, my lord,
was received at the autumn sacrifice with aged wine,
and participated in presenting the roast meat."
After two years,
we heard that you were about to pacify the Eastern Xia,
and in the fourth month,
we again attended court to hear of the matter.
In the intervals between court attendances,
there was not a year without a diplomatic mission,
nor a campaign without our participation.
Due to the inconstancy of the great state's government orders,
our state is exhausted and afflicted,
with unforeseen calamities repeatedly arriving,
and not a day passes without apprehension.
How dare we neglect our duties?
"If the great state would stabilize it,
we would be at court morning and evening—
what need would there be for such a command?
But if you have no compassion for our distress,
and instead use it as a pretext,
would that not make us unable to bear your appointments,
and turn us into enemies?
Our humble city fears this,
and how dare we forget your command?
We entrust this to your officers,
and hope your officers will seriously consider it."
B9.22.3 In autumn,
Luán Yíng went from Chǔ to Qí.
Yàn Píngzhòng said to the Marquis of Qí:
"At the meeting at Shāngrén,
we received orders from Jìn.
Now if we accept the Luán clan,
how will we use them?
The means by which the small serve the great
is good faith.
To lose good faith
is to lose one's standing.
I hope you will consider this."
He did not listen.
Withdrawing, he told Chén Wénzǐ:
"A ruler should hold to good faith,
and a minister should hold to reverence.
Loyalty, good faith, sincerity, and respect—
these should be shared by high and low alike;
this is the Way of Heaven.
Our ruler is abandoning himself,
and will not last long."
B9.22.4 In the ninth month,
Zhèng's Gōngsūn Hēigōng fell ill,
returned his fief to the duke,
summoned his steward
and clan officer
to establish Duàn,
and ordered him to reduce offices and curtail sacrifices.
Sacrifices were to use a single sheep,
and the seasonal sacrifices a lesser offering,
sufficient for the sacrifices, and he returned all his remaining fiefs,
saying:
"I have heard that
in a chaotic age,
to be noble yet able to be poor,
so that the people seek nothing from you,
allows one to perish later.
Reverently serve the ruler and the several ministers.
Life lies in vigilance and caution,
not in wealth."
On Jǐsì,
Bó Zhāng died.
The gentleman says:
"Well cautioned.
The Book of Songs says:
'Be careful of your noble measure,
to guard against the unforeseen.'
Zhèng's Zǐ Zhāng had this."
B9.22.5 In winter,
they met at Shāsuí,
to reaffirm the proscription of the Luán clan.
Luán Yíng was still in Qí.
Yànzǐ said:
"Disaster is about to arise.
Qí will attack Jìn,
and we cannot but be apprehensive."
B9.22.6 In Chǔ, Guàn Qǐ was favored by the Lingyǐn Zǐ Nán,
and though his stipend was not increased,
he had several tens of chariots and horses.
The people of Chǔ were troubled by this,
and the king was about to punish him.
Zǐ Nán's son Qìjí was the king's charioteer,
and whenever the king saw him,
he would weep.
Qìjí said:
"You have wept before me three times;
may I ask whose fault it is?"
The king said:
"The Lingyǐn's incompetence
is known to you.
The state is about to punish him;
will you remain?"
He replied: "If a father is executed and a son remains,
how could you use him?
To divulge orders and impose heavy punishments—
I would not do that either."
The king then killed Zǐ Nán at court,
and had Guàn Qǐ torn apart by chariots
in the four borders.
Zǐ Nán's retainers said to Qìjí:
"We request to move your father's body from court."
He said: "There is ritual between ruler and minister;
it is up to you few gentlemen."
After three days,
Qìjí requested the body.
The king permitted it.
After the burial,
his followers said:
"Shall we leave?"
He said: "I participated in killing my father;
where would I go?"
They said:
"Then will you serve the king?"
He said:
"To abandon my father and serve his enemy—
I cannot bear it."
He then hanged himself and died.
Again, Wěi Zǐ Féng was made Lingyǐn,
Gōngzǐ Qí was made Sīmǎ,
and Qū Jiàn was made Mò'áo.
There were eight men favored by Wěi Zǐ,
all without stipends but with many horses.
One day, at court,
he spoke to Shēn Shū Yù,
who did not reply but withdrew.
He followed him,
and he entered among the crowd.
He followed him again,
and he then went home.
After court,
he went to see him,
saying:
"You three times embarrassed me at court;
I was afraid,
and dared not not see you.
I have faults;
please tell me,
why do you shun me?"
He replied: "I fear I cannot avoid it;
how dare I tell you?"
He said: "Why?"
He replied:
"Formerly, Guàn Qǐ was favored by Zǐ Nán;
Zǐ Nán incurred guilt,
and Guàn Qǐ was torn apart by chariots.
Why should I not fear?"
He drove himself home,
unable to stay on the road.
Upon arrival,
he said to the eight men:
"I have seen Shēn Shū;
that master is what is called one who gives life to the dead
and puts flesh on bones.
If those who understand me are like that master, it is acceptable;
otherwise,
I ask you to stop."
He dismissed the eight men,
and thereafter the king was at ease with him.
B9.22.7 In the twelfth month,
Zhèng's Yóu Pàn was about to go to Jìn,
but before leaving the border,
he encountered a man fetching his wife,
seized her,
and lodged with her in a town.
On Dīngsì,
her husband attacked Zǐ Míng,
killed him,
and took his wife away.
Zǐ Zhǎn deposed Liáng and established Tàishū,
saying:
"A state minister
is the ruler's deputy
and the people's master;
