he cannot be careless.
I ask to abandon those like Zǐ Míng."
He sought the man who had lost his wife,
and restored him to his place.
He ordered the Yóu clan not to resent it,
saying:
"Do not publicize evil."
A9.23 The Annals of the Twenty-third Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.23.1 In the twenty-third year, in spring,
in the royal second month, on Guǐyǒu, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.23.2 In the third month, on Jǐsì,
the Earl of Qǐ, Gài, died.
A9.23.3 In summer,
Zhū's Bì Wǒ came fleeing.
A9.23.4 They buried Duke Xiào of Qǐ.
A9.23.5 Chén killed its great officers Qìng Hǔ and Qìng Yín.
A9.23.6 The younger brother of Marquis Chén, Huáng, returned from Chǔ to Chén.
A9.23.7 Jìn's Luán Yíng re-entered Jìn,
entering Qūwò.
A9.23.8 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Wèi,
and subsequently attacked Jìn.
A9.23.9 In the eighth month,
Shūsūn Bào led troops to rescue Jìn,
and halted at Yōngyú.
A9.23.10 On the jǐmǎo day,
Zhòngsūn Sù died.
A9.23.11 In winter, on the yǐhài day of the tenth month,
Zāngsūn Hé fled to Zhū.
A9.23.12 The men of Jìn killed Luán Yíng.
A9.23.13 The Marquis of Qí made a surprise attack on Jǔ.
B9.23 The Commentary for the Twenty-third Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.23.1 In the spring of the twenty-third year,
Duke Xiào of Qǐ died.
The wife of Duke Dào of Jìn mourned for him.
Duke Píng did not suspend his music,
which was contrary to ritual.
According to ritual,
one should suspend it for a neighboring state.
B9.23.2 The Marquis of Chén went to Chǔ.
Gōngzǐ Huáng accused the two Qìngs before Chǔ,
and the men of Chǔ summoned them.
They sent Qìng Lè to go,
and he was killed.
The Qìng clan rebelled with Chén.
In summer,
Qū Jiàn
followed the Marquis of Chén and besieged Chén.
The people of Chén were building the city walls,
but when a plank fell, they killed people.
The laborers gave each other orders,
each killing their overseer,
and subsequently killed Qìng Hǔ and Qìng Yín.
The men of Chǔ installed Gōngzǐ Huáng.
The gentleman said of the Qìng clan:
"Being unrighteous,
they could not be allowed to act with impunity.
Therefore, the *Shū* says:
'The Mandate is not constant.'"
B9.23.3 Jìn was about to marry a daughter to Wú.
The Marquis of Qí sent Xī Guīfǔ to accompany her as a secondary bride,
and used a curtained carriage to transport Luán Yíng and his men,
installing them in Qūwò.
Luán Yíng went at night to see Xū Wǔ
and informed him.
He replied: "It cannot be done.
Whom Heaven discards,
who can raise up?
You will surely not escape.
It is not that I love life,
but I know the plan will not succeed."
Yíng said:
"Even so,
if I die because of you,
I will have no regrets.
It is truly I who am not favored by Heaven,
you bear no blame."
He gave his consent.
He concealed him and then feasted the men of Qūwò.
When the music began,
Wǔ said:
"What if we now obtain the young master Luán?"
They replied:
"To have obtained a master and die for him,
is as if we did not die."
All sighed,
and some wept.
When the cups went round,
he spoke again.
All said:
"Having obtained a master,
how could there be any disloyalty!"
Yíng came out,
and bowed to them all.
In the fourth month,
Luán Yíng led the armored men of Qūwò,
relying on Wèi Xiànzǐ,
and entered Jiàng by daylight.
Earlier,
Luán Yíng had assisted Wèi Zhuāngzǐ in the Lower Army,
and Xiànzǐ had a private connection with him,
so he relied on him.
The Zhào clan bore a grudge against the Luán clan because of the disaster of Yuán and Píng.
Hán and Zhào were on good terms.
The Zhōngháng clan bore a grudge against the Luán clan because of the campaign against Qín,
and were firmly allied and friendly with the Fàn clan.
Zhī Dàozǐ was young,
and followed the Zhōngháng clan.
Chéng Zhèng was favored by the duke.
Only the Wèi clan and the seven carriage officers were with him.
Yuè Wángfù was in attendance sitting with Fàn Xuānzǐ.
Someone reported:
"The Luán clan has arrived."
Xuānzǐ was afraid.
Huánzǐ said:
"Escort the lord to the fortified palace,
and there will surely be no harm.
Moreover, the Luán clan has many enemies,
you are in charge of the government,
the Luán clan is from outside,
you are in position,
the advantages are many.
Since you have the advantageous position,
and also hold the handle over the people,
what is there to fear?
What the Luán clan has obtained,
is it only the Wèi clan?
And they can be taken by force.
To overcome disorder lies in authority,
do not slacken!"
The duke had a mourning in his affinal family,
Wángfù had Xuānzǐ wear dark mourning garments,
a hood, and a mourning band,
and with two women in a carriage
they went to the duke,
and escorted the duke to the fortified palace.
Fàn Yā went to meet Wèi Shū,
and found the ranks already formed and mounted,
about to go to meet the Luán clan.
He hurried forward,
and said:
"The Luán clan is leading rebels to enter,
Yā's father and several others are with the lord,
he sent Yā to meet you.
Yā requests to be your chariot companion."
He grasped the strap,
and then leaped onto the chariot.
With his right hand he rested on his sword,
with his left he took hold of the strap,
and ordered to drive out.
The driver asked,
Yā said: "To the duke."
Xuānzǐ met him at the steps,
took his hand,
and bribed him with Qūwò.
Earlier,
Fěi Bào,
was a menial, recorded in the red register.
The Luán clan's strong retainer was called Dū Róng,
the people of the state feared him.
Fěi Bào said to Xuānzǐ:
"If you burn the red register,
I will kill Dū Róng."
Xuānzǐ was pleased,
and said:
"If you kill him,
if I do not request from the lord to burn the red register,
may I be as the sun!"
Then he sent Bào out and shut the gate.
Dū Róng followed him.
He crossed over a low wall and waited for him,
Dū Róng crossed over and entered,
Bào struck from behind and killed him.
The followers of the Fàn clan were behind the terrace,
the Luán clan ascended the duke's gate.
Xuānzǐ said to Yā: "If arrows reach the lord's house,
you die!"
Yā used his sword to lead the soldiers,
the Luán clan retreated,
he mounted a chariot and pursued them.
He encountered Luán Yuè,
and said:
"Yuè, stop.
If I die,
I will accuse you before Heaven."
Yuè shot at him,
but did not hit;
he fitted another arrow,
then his chariot hit a locust tree root and overturned.
Someone hooked him with a halberd,
breaking his elbow, and he died.
Luán Fáng was wounded.
Luán Yíng fled to Qūwò.
The men of Jìn besieged him.
B9.23.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Wèi.
For the vanguard,
Gǔ Róng drove for Wángsūn Huī,
with Zhào Yáng as the right;
for the second force,
Chéng Zhì drove for Jǔ Héng,
with Shēn Xiānyú's tutor Zhì as the right.
Cáo Kāi drove the ruler's chariot,
with Yànfù Róng as the right.
The second chariot:
Shàng Zhīdēng drove for Lord Xíng,
with Lú Púguǐ as the right-hand guard;
the third chariot:
Láo Chéng drove for Xiāng Píshī,
with Láng Qúshū as the right-hand guard;
the fourth chariot:
Shāng Zǐchē drove for Hóu Cháo,
with Huán Tiào as the right-hand guard;
the rear chariot:
Shāng Zǐyóu drove for Xià Zhīyùkòu,
with Cuī Rú as the right-hand guard;
Zhú Yōngzhīyuè rode as the fourth man in a chariot.
From Wèi, they intended to attack Jìn.
Yàn Píngzhòng said:
"Our lord relies on courage and strength
to attack the leader of the covenant alliance.
If he does not succeed,
it will be a blessing for the state.
To lack virtue yet achieve merit
will surely bring trouble upon our lord."
Cuī Zhù remonstrated, saying:
"This cannot be done.
I have heard it said:
'When a small state takes advantage of a large state's defeat
to inflict harm upon it,
it is certain to suffer retribution.'
May our lord consider this."
He did not listen.
Chén Wénzǐ went to see Cuī Wǔzǐ
and said:
"What will become of our lord?"
Wǔzǐ said:
"I spoke to our lord,
but he would not listen.
He regards the leader of the covenant alliance
as an opportunity to profit from its difficulties.
If the ministers become desperate,
what will become of our lord?
You should let the matter rest."
Wénzǐ withdrew
and told his followers:
"Cuīzǐ is about to die!
He speaks of our lord with severity yet exceeds him in wrongdoing;
he will not die a natural death.
To surpass one's lord in righteousness
is still a form of self-restraint,
how much more so when surpassing him in wickedness?"
The Marquis of Qí then attacked Jìn
and captured Zhāogē.
Dividing his army into two columns,
he entered Mèngmén,
ascended Tàiháng.
He displayed his martial array at Yíngtíng,
garrisoned Píshào,
and piled up corpses at Shǎoshuǐ,
to avenge the defeat at Píngyīn,
before returning.
Zhào Shèng led the army of Dōngyáng in pursuit
and captured Yàn Máo.
In the eighth month,
Shūsūn Bào led troops to rescue Jìn
and encamped at Yōngyú,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B9.23.5 Jì Wǔzǐ had no legitimate heir;
Gōng Mí was the eldest,
but he favored Dàozi
and wished to establish him.
He consulted Shēn Fēng, saying:
"I love both Mí and Hé
and wish to choose the more talented to establish."
Shēn Fēng hurriedly withdrew,
returned home,
and prepared to depart with his entire household.
Another day,
he consulted him again.
Shēn Fēng replied:
"If that is the case,
I will prepare my humble carriage and depart."
He then desisted.
He consulted Zāng Hé.
Zāng Hé said:
"Host a drinking feast for me,
and I will establish him for you."
The Jì family hosted a feast for the high officials,
with Zāng Hé as the guest of honor.
After the offerings were presented,
Zāngsūn ordered a mat to be spread facing north,
with a new vessel purified.
He summoned Dàozi,
descended,
and welcomed him.
All the high officials rose.
When it came to the general toast,
he summoned Gōng Chú
and had him take his place according to age.
Jìsūn changed color.
The Jì family appointed Gōng Chú as Master of the Horse,
but he was resentful and did not appear.
Mǐn Zǐmǎ went to see him
and said:
"Do not act this way.
Fortune and misfortune have no gate;
they are summoned only by men.
As a son,
worry about being unfilial,
not about having no position.
Reverently obey your father's commands;
what is constant about them?
If you can be filial and respectful,
you may become twice as wealthy as the Jì family.
If you are treacherous and disobedient,
you may suffer twice the misfortune of the common people."
Gōng Chú accepted this,
reverently served morning and evening,
and diligently performed his official duties.
Jìsūn was pleased
and had him host a drinking feast,
bringing along his own utensils
and leaving them all there.
Thus, the Gōng Chú family became wealthy,
and he was further appointed as the Left Steward of the ducal house.
Mèngsūn disliked Zāngsūn,
while Jìsūn favored him.
The groom Fēng Diǎn of the Mèng family favored Jié
and said:
"Follow my words,
and you will surely become the head of the Mèng family."
He repeated this several times,
and Jié followed his advice.
When Mèng Zhuāngzǐ fell ill,
Fēng Diǎn said to Gōng Chú:
"If Jié is established,
I ask that you make an enemy of the Zāng family."
Gōng Chú said to Jìsūn:
"The child Zhì is certainly the rightful heir.
If Jié is established,
then the Jì family will truly have influence over the Mèng family."
He did not respond.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Mèngsūn died.
Gōng Chú supported Jié
and stood by the door.
When Jìsūn arrived,
he entered,
mourned,
and then came out,
asking:
"Where is Zhì?"
Gōng Chú said:
"Jié is here."
Jìsūn said: "The child is the elder."
Gōng Chú said: "What does seniority matter?
It is only talent that counts.
Moreover, this was the master's command."
Thus, Jié was established.
Zhì fled to Zhū.
Zāngsūn entered to mourn,
with great sorrow,
and many tears.
When he came out,
his charioteer said:
"Mèngsūn disliked you,
yet you grieve like this.
If Jìsūn were to die,
what would you do?"
Zāngsūn said:
"Jìsūn's fondness for me
is like a disease;
Mèngsūn's dislike of me
is like medicine and stone.
A pleasant disease is not as good as harsh medicine.
The stone can still save my life,
but a pleasant disease,
its poison is all the greater.
With Mèngsūn dead,
my own end is not far off."
The Mèng family closed their gates
and reported to Jìsūn:
"The Zāng family is planning a rebellion
and will not allow us to conduct the burial."
Jìsūn did not believe it.
When Zāngsūn heard of this,
he took precautions.
In the tenth month of winter,
when the Mèng family was about to clear the path for the funeral,
they borrowed laborers from the Zāng family.
Zāngsūn sent regular laborers to assist them,
clearing the path at the east gate,
with armored men following him to observe.
The Mèng family again reported to Jìsūn.
Jìsūn became angry
and ordered an attack on the Zāng family.
On the day Yǐhài,
Zāng Hé broke the bar of the Lù Gate
and fled, escaping to Zhū.
Initially,
Zāng Xuānshū married a woman from Zhù,
who gave birth to Jiǎ and Wéi and then died.
He took her niece as his second wife,
who was the daughter of Mù Jiāng’s sister,
and she gave birth to Hé,
who was raised in the ducal palace.
Lady Jiāng loved him,
so he was established as heir.
Zāng Jiǎ and Zāng Wéi went out and resided in Zhù.
Zāng Wǔzhòng sent a messenger from Zhū to inform Zāng Jiǎ,
and also presented a large tortoise shell,
saying:
“Hé is unworthy,
and has failed to maintain the ancestral temple.
I dare to report this misfortune.
Hé’s crime
does not extend to the cessation of sacrifices.
If you use the large tortoise shell to request the succession,
it may be permissible.”
Jiǎ said:
“This is the family’s misfortune,
not your fault.
Jiǎ has heard your command.”
He bowed twice and accepted the tortoise shell,
but sent Wéi to make the request for succession,
and thus it was Wéi who succeeded.
Zāngsūn went to Fáng,
and sent a messenger to report, saying:
“Hé is not capable of causing harm,
but lacks wisdom.
I dare not make a private request.
If only the ancestral sacrifices can be preserved,
and the achievements of the two ancestors are not abandoned,
how dare I not relinquish the city!”
Thus, Zāng Wéi was established.
Zāng Hé surrendered Fáng and fled to Qí.
His followers said:
“Will they make a covenant against us?”
Zāngsūn said:
“There is no pretext.”
When they were about to make a covenant against the Zāng clan,
Jìsūn summoned the external historian
in charge of wicked ministers
and inquired about the wording of the covenant.
He replied:
“When covenanting against the Dōngmén clan,
it was said:
‘Let none be like Dōngmén Suì,
who disobeyed the duke’s command,
killing the rightful heir and establishing a concubine’s son.’
When covenanting against the Shūsūn clan,
it was said:
‘Let none be like Shūsūn Qiáorú,
who sought to abolish the state’s constants,
and overturned the ducal house.’”
Jìsūn said:
“Zāngsūn’s crimes do not reach this level.”
Mèng Jiāo said:
“Why not use his breaking through the gates
and smashing the bolts?”
Jìsūn adopted this,
and thus covenanted against the Zāng clan,
saying:
“Let none be like Zāngsūn Hé,
who violated the state’s laws,
breaking through the gates and smashing the bolts!”
Zāngsūn heard of this,
and said:
“There are capable men in the state.
Who could it be?
It must be Mèng Jiāo!”
B9.23.6 The men of Jìn defeated Luán Yíng at Qūwò,
and exterminated all the clansmen and partisans of the Luán family.
Luán Fáng fled to Sòng.
The record says:
“The men of Jìn killed Luán Yíng,”
not mentioning him as a senior official,
to indicate that he was an outsider.
B9.23.7 The Marquis of Qí returned from Jìn,
but did not enter the capital,
and instead launched a surprise attack on Jǔ.
He attacked the gate at Qiěyú,
but was wounded in the thigh and withdrew.
The next day,
he prepared to fight again,
setting the rendezvous at Shòushū.
Qí Zhí and
Huá Huán, carrying armor, entered the pass at Qiěyú by night,
and camped in the outskirts of Jǔ.
The next day,
they first encountered the Viscount of Jǔ at Púhóushì.
The Viscount of Jǔ offered them generous bribes,
urging them not to fight to the death,
saying:
“I request that we make a covenant.”
Huá Zhōu replied:
“To covet goods and abandon one’s duty
is also something you, my lord, would despise.
We received our orders at dusk,
and before midday we would abandon them—
how could we serve our lord?”
The Viscount of Jǔ personally beat the drum,
and his troops advanced to attack them,
capturing Qí Liáng.
The men of Jǔ sought peace.
The Marquis of Qí returned,
and encountered Qí Liáng’s wife in the outskirts,
so he sent someone to offer condolences.
She declined, saying:
“If Zhí was guilty,
why trouble with condolences?
If he was exempt from guilt,
there are still the humble dwellings of his ancestors,
and this lowly concubine cannot receive condolences in the outskirts.”
The Marquis of Qí then offered condolences at her home.
B9.23.8 The Marquis of Qí intended to grant fields to Zāng Hé.
Zāngsūn heard of this,
went to see the Marquis of Qí,
and spoke with him about attacking Jìn.
The Marquis replied:
“Your achievements are many indeed,
but you, my lord, resemble a rat.
A rat
hides by day and moves by night,
not daring to burrow in the ancestral temples,
because it fears people.
Now you, my lord, upon hearing of the disorder in Jìn,
only then take action.
If you were truly going to serve them,
how are you not like a rat?”
Thus, he did not grant him the fields.
Zhòngní said:
“Wisdom is difficult.
With the wisdom of Zāng Wǔzhòng,
he was still not tolerated in the state of Lǔ.
There must be a reason for this:
his actions were not upright,
and his conduct was not forgiving.
The *Xiàshū* says:
‘Think of this in this,’
meaning upright actions
and forgiving conduct.”
A9.24 *The Classic of the Twenty-Fourth Year of Duke Xiāng*
A9.24.1 In the twenty-fourth year, in spring,
Shūsūn Bào went to Jìn.
A9.24.2 Zhòngsūn Jié led an army to invade Qí.
A9.24.3 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Wú.
A9.24.4 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the first day jiǎzǐ,
there was an eclipse of the sun,
which was total.
A9.24.5 Cuī Zhù of Qí led an army to attack Jǔ.
A9.24.6 There was a great flood.
A9.24.7 In the eighth month, on the first day guǐsì,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A9.24.8 The duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎozhū at Yíyí.
A9.24.9 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Marquis of Chén,
and the Baron of Xǔ attacked Zhèng.
A9.24.10 The duke returned from the meeting.
A9.24.11 Chén Zhēnyíjiù fled to Chǔ.
A9.24.12 Shūsūn Bào went to the royal capital.
A9.24.13 There was a great famine.
B9.24 *The Commentary of the Twenty-Fourth Year of Duke Xiāng*
B9.24.1 In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
Shū of Mù went to Jìn.
Xuānzǐ of Fàn went to meet him,
asked him,
and said:
"The ancients had a saying:
'To die and not decay' —
what does it mean?"
Shū of Mù did not reply.
Xuānzǐ said:
"In the past, my ancestor,
from Yú and above, was the Táotáng clan;
in Xià, he was the Yùlóng clan;
in Shāng, he was the Shǐwéi clan;
in Zhōu, he was the Tángdù clan;
and now, with Jìn as the leader of the Xià alliance, we are the Fàn clan.
Is this not what it means?"
Shū of Mù said:
"According to what Bào has heard,
this is called hereditary emolument,
not 'not decaying.'
In Lǔ, there was a former senior official named Zāng Wénzhòng.
After his death,
his words endured.
That is what it means!
Bào has heard:
'The highest is to establish virtue;
the next is to establish achievements;
the next is to establish words.'
Even after a long time, they are not abandoned.
This is called 'not decaying.'
As for preserving the surname and receiving the clan name,
guarding the ancestral temple,
with sacrifices unbroken through generations,
there is no state without this.
Even the greatest emolument
cannot be called 'not decaying.'"
B9.24.2 When Xuānzǐ of Fàn was in charge of the government,
the tributes from the feudal lords were heavy,
and the people of Zhèng were troubled by it.
In the second month,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn.
Zǐchǎn sent a letter through Zǐxī
to inform Xuānzǐ,
saying:
"You govern the state of Jìn,
but the neighboring feudal lords do not hear of your excellent virtue;
instead, they hear of heavy tributes.
Qiáo is perplexed by this.
Qiáo has heard that a gentleman who leads a state
does not worry about lacking wealth,
but finds it difficult to lack a good reputation.
If the wealth of the feudal lords is gathered in the ducal house,
then the feudal lords will become disloyal.
If you, sir, rely on it,
then the state of Jìn will become disloyal.
If the feudal lords are disloyal,
then the state of Jìn will be ruined.
If the state of Jìn is disloyal,
then your household will be ruined.
How can you be so oblivious!
What use is wealth?
"A good reputation
is the carriage of virtue;
virtue
is the foundation of the state.
With a foundation, there is no ruin.
Should you not devote yourself to this?
With virtue, there is joy;
with joy, there can be longevity.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The joyful gentleman
is the foundation of the state.'
This is because of his excellent virtue!
'God is watching over you;
do not be disloyal in your heart.'
This is because of his good reputation!
With considerate thoughts to illuminate virtue,
then a good reputation carries it forward,
so that those from afar come and those nearby are at peace.
Would you rather have people say of you,
'You truly gave me life,'
or say
'You drained me to live'?
An elephant is burned for its tusks
because of its wealth."
Xuānzǐ was pleased
and reduced the tributes.
On this journey,
the Earl of Zhèng paid court to Jìn,
because of the heavy tributes,
and also requested to attack Chén.
The Earl of Zhèng kowtowed,
and Xuānzǐ declined.
Zǐxī, acting as assistant,
said:
"Because the state of Chén relied on a great state
and oppressed our humble city,
our ruler therefore requests to punish them.
How dare he not kowtow?"
B9.24.3 Xiàobó of Mèng invaded Qí,
because of Jìn.
B9.24.4 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ raised a naval force to attack Wú,
but did not enforce military discipline,
and returned without success.
B9.24.5 The Marquis of Qí, after attacking Jìn, became fearful
and wished to meet the Viscount of Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěi Qǐqiáng to Qí on a diplomatic mission,
and to request a date.
In Qí, they held a sacrifice to the soil god,
displayed military equipment,
and had the guest observe it.
Wénzǐ of Chén said:
"Qí will face invaders.
I have heard that if weapons are not stored away,
they will surely bring harm to one's own clan."
B9.24.6 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí heard that Jìn troops would come,
so he sent Chén Wúyǔ to follow Wěi Qǐqiáng to Chǔ,
to decline the meeting,
and to request troops.
Cuī Zhù led troops to escort him,
then attacked Jǔ,
invading Jiègēn.
B9.24.7 They met at Yíyí,
intending to attack Qí.
There was flooding,
and they could not proceed.
B9.24.8 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ attacked Zhèng to rescue Qí,
attacked the east gate,
and encamped at Jízé.
The feudal lords turned back to rescue Zhèng.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Zhāng Gé and Fǔ Lì to challenge the Chǔ army,
and sought a charioteer from Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng divined
about Wǎn Shèquǎn,
and it was auspicious.
Zǐtàishū warned him, saying:
"One cannot be equal to men from a great state."
He replied:
"Regardless of numbers,
their superiors are the same."
Tàishū said:
"A small mound has no pines or cypresses."
The two men were in the tent,
and made Shèquǎn sit outside.
After they had eaten,
they then gave him food.
They had him drive a large chariot and set out,
while they themselves rode in a light chariot.
When they were about to reach the Chǔ army,
they then got into his chariot,
both squatting on the crossbar and playing the qin.
As they drew near,
without warning, he whipped the horses and charged.
They both took helmets from their bags and put them on.
Entering the enemy camp,
they both dismounted,
seized men and threw them,
gathered captives and bound prisoners.
Without waiting for him, they rushed out.
Both leaped onto the chariot,
drew their bows and shot.
Once they were safe,
they again squatted on the crossbar and played the qin,
saying: "Gōngsūn!
Riding together,
we are like brothers.
Why twice without consultation?"
He replied:
"The first time, my mind was only on entering;
this time, I was afraid."
They both laughed,
and said:
"Gōngsūn is indeed hasty!"
The Viscount of Chǔ returned from Jízé
and sent Wěi Qǐqiáng to lead troops
to escort Chén Wúyǔ.
B9.24.9 The people of Wú, because of the Chǔ naval campaign,
summoned the Shūjiū people.
The Shūjiū people rebelled against Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ stationed troops at Huāngpǔ
and sent Shěn Yǐn Shòu and Shī Qí Lí to reprimand them.
The ruler of Shūjiū respectfully welcomed the two men
and told them there was no such thing,
and requested to accept a covenant.
The two men reported back.
The king wished to attack them.
Wěizi said:
"That cannot be done.
They have declared they are not rebelling,
and have requested to accept the covenant,
yet we attack them—
that is attacking the innocent.
Let us return for now to give the people rest,
and await their final outcome.
If in the end they remain loyal,
what more could we seek?
If they still rebel against us, they will have no justification,
and then we will have grounds [to act]."
Thereupon they withdrew.
B9.24.10 The people of Chén again pursued the partisans of the Qìng clan,
and Zhēn Yíjiù fled to Chǔ.
B9.24.11 The people of Qí fortified Jiá.
Mù Shū went to Zhōu on a courtesy visit,
and also to congratulate them on the fortification.
The king praised him for his propriety,
and bestowed upon him a grand carriage.
B9.24.12 The Marquis of Jìn favored Chéng Zhèng,
and made him assistant commander of the lower army.
When Zhèng's envoy Gōngsūn Huī went to Jìn on a courtesy visit,
Chéng Zhèng asked him,
saying:
"May I presume to ask by what means one lowers one's rank?"
Zǐyǔ was unable to reply,
and upon returning, reported this to Ránmíng.
Ránmíng said:
"This man is about to die.
If not,
he will flee.
When one is noble yet knows fear,
and through fear considers lowering oneself,
then one finds the proper step.
It is merely a matter of humbling oneself before others—
what need is there to ask about it?
Moreover, one who, having already ascended, seeks the steps to descend—
is a man of wisdom,
which Chéng Zhèng is not.
Perhaps he has the omen of flight!
If not,
perhaps he is afflicted by a delusion,
and is anxious because he is about to die."
A9.25 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, 25th Year of Duke Xiāng*
A9.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
Cuī Zhù of Qí led an army to attack our northern borders.
A9.25.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on the day Yǐhài,
Cuī Zhù of Qí assassinated his ruler, Guāng.
A9.25.3 The duke met with the Marquis of Jìn,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Lesser Viscount of Zhū at Yíyí.
A9.25.4 In the sixth month, on the day Rénzǐ,
Gōngsūn Shězhī of Zhèng led an army and entered Chén.
A9.25.5 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day Jǐsì,
the feudal lords made a covenant together at Chóngqiū.
A9.25.6 The duke arrived from the meeting.
A9.25.7 The Marquis of Wèi entered Yíyí.
A9.25.8 Qū Jiàn of Chǔ led an army and destroyed Shūjiū.
A9.25.9 In winter,
Gōngsūn Xià of Zhèng led an army to attack Chén.
A9.25.10 In the twelfth month,
the Viscount of Wú, È, attacked Chǔ,
attacked the gate of Cháo,
and died.
B9.25 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, 25th Year of Duke Xiāng*
B9.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
Cuī Zhù of Qí led an army to attack our northern borders,
in retaliation for the army of Xiàobó.
The duke was troubled by this,
and sent word to Jìn.
Mèng Gōngchuò said:
"Cuī Zǐ is about to have a great ambition,
it does not lie in harming us.
He is certain to return quickly—
what cause for worry is there?
His coming is not as a marauder;
he drives his people not harshly—
different from other times."
The army of Qí returned without achieving anything.
B9.25.2 The wife of the Lord of Táng of Qí
was the elder sister of Dōngguō Yǎn.
Dōngguō Yǎn served Cuī Wǔzǐ.
When the Lord of Táng died,
Yǎn drove Wǔzǐ's carriage to offer condolences.
He saw Táng Jiāng
and considered her beautiful,
and had Yǎn take her for him.
Yǎn said:
"Men and women are distinguished by surname.
Now you, my lord, descend from Dīng,
and I, your servant, descend from Huán—
it cannot be done."
Wǔzǐ performed a divination by milfoil about it,
and obtained the hexagram *Kùn* (困) changing to *Dàguò* (大過)
The scribes all said, "Auspicious."
He showed it to Chén Wénzǐ,
and Wénzǐ said:
"The husband follows the wind,
the wind makes the wife fall—
she cannot be taken.
Moreover, its verse says:
'Beset by stones,
leaning on thorns and brambles;
entering his house,
he does not see his wife—
inauspicious.'
'Beset by stones'—
going will not succeed;
'leaning on thorns and brambles'—
what one relies on will cause injury;
'entering his house,
he does not see his wife'—
inauspicious,
nowhere to return to."
Cuī Zǐ said:
"She is a widow—
what harm is there?
Her former husband has already borne the omen."
Thereupon he took her.
Duke Zhuāng had an affair with her,
and frequently went to the Cuī residence,
and gave Cuī Zǐ's cap to others.
An attendant said:
"That cannot be done."
The duke said:
"If it were not for Cuī Zǐ,
would he have no cap?"
Cuī Zǐ, because of this,
and also because of the interval when he attacked Jìn,
said:
"Jìn is certain to retaliate."
He wished to assassinate the duke to please Jìn,
but had not yet found an opportunity.
The duke had whipped the attendant Jiǎ Jǔ,
but later drew close to him again,
and so he became Cuī Zǐ's opportunity against the duke.
In summer, in the fifth month,
because of the former campaign at Jūyú,
the Viscount of Jǔ paid a court visit to Qí.
On the day Jiǎxū,
a feast was held for him in the northern outer city.
Cuī Zǐ pleaded illness,
and did not attend to affairs.
On the day Yǐhài,
the duke inquired after Cuī Zǐ,
and thereupon followed Jiāng Shì.
Jiāng entered the inner chamber,
and with Cuī Zǐ went out through a side door.
The duke tapped the pillar and sang.
The attendant Jiǎ Jǔ stopped the various followers
and entered,
then closed the gate.
The armored men rose up.
The duke climbed a terrace and begged for his life—
it was not granted;
he begged to make a covenant—
it was not granted;
he begged to kill himself in the ancestral temple—
it was not granted.
They all said:
"Your servant Zhù is gravely ill,
and cannot receive your commands.
Since we are near the duke's palace,
we, your servants guarding the watch, are dealing with a lecher,
and know no other orders."
The duke climbed over the wall,
and they shot at him again,
hitting him in the thigh.
He fell back down,
and they thereupon assassinated him.
Jiǎ Jǔ, Zhōu Chuò, Bǐng Shī, Gōngsūn Áo, Fēng Jù, Duó Fù, Xiāng Yī, and Lóu Yīn all died.
Zhù Tuófù had been performing sacrifices at Gāotáng;
he arrived,
and was reporting his mission when, without removing his ceremonial cap, he died at the Cuī residence.
Shēn Kuǎi,
a supervisor of fisheries,
withdrew [from court]
and said to his steward:
"You may escape with my family,
but I will die."
His steward said:
"To escape
would be contrary to your sense of duty."
And so he died with him.
The Cuī clan killed Zōng Miè at Píngyīn.
Yànzǐ stood outside the gate of the Cuī residence.
His attendants said:
"Will you die?"
He replied: "Is he my ruler alone,
that I should die for him?"
They said:
"Will you flee?"
He said:
"Is it my crime,
that I should flee?"
They said:
"Will you return home?"
He said:
"The ruler is dead;
to what home can I return?
One who rules the people,
how can he oppress them?
His charge is the altars of soil and grain.
One who serves a ruler,
is it merely for his sustenance?
His duty is to nurture the altars of soil and grain.
Therefore, if a ruler dies for the altars of soil and grain,
then one dies with him;
if he flees for the altars of soil and grain,
then one flees with him.
But if he dies for himself,
or flees for himself,
unless one is his personal favorite,
who would dare to take responsibility for it?
Moreover, someone had a ruler and murdered him;
how can I die for him?
And how can I flee for him?
Yet to what place can I return?"
The gate opened and he entered,
placed the corpse's head on his lap and wept.
He rose,
leaped three times [in mourning], and went out.
Someone said to Cuīzǐ:
"You must kill him!"
Cuīzǐ said:
"He is the hope of the people.
To spare him
will win the people."
Lú Pú Guǐ fled to Jìn,
and Wáng Hé fled to Jǔ.
When Shūsūn Xuānbó was in Qí,
Shūsūn Huán presented his daughter to Duke Líng.
She became a favorite
and gave birth to Duke Jǐng.
On Dīngchǒu,
Cuī Zhù established him [as ruler] and became his minister,
while Qìng Fēng became left minister.
They made a covenant with the people of the state in the Grand Temple,
saying:
"Those who do not side with Cuī and Qìng—"
Yànzǐ looked up to heaven and sighed, saying:
"If I, Yīng, do not side only with those who are loyal to the ruler and beneficial to the altars of soil and grain,
may the High God witness it!"
Then he smeared the blood [on his lips].
On Xīnsì,
the Duke [of Lǔ] and his great officers made a covenant with the Viscount of Jǔ.
The Grand Historiographer wrote:
"Cuī Zhù murdered his ruler."
Cuīzǐ killed him.
His younger brother continued the record,
and two more died.
His younger brother again wrote it,
and then [Cuīzǐ] spared him.
The Historian of the South heard that the Grand Historiographers had all died,
took his bamboo slips and went [to the court].
Hearing that it had already been recorded,
he returned.
Lǘqiū Yīng bound his wife with curtains and placed her in a carriage,
and fled with Shēn Xiānyú.
Xiānyú pushed her down [from the carriage],
saying:
"When the ruler was benighted, you could not correct him;
when he was in danger, you could not save him;
when he died, you could not die for him.
Yet you know only to hide your favorite;
who will take you in?"
Traveling until they reached Yǎnzhōng,
they were about to lodge.
Yīng said:
"Cuī and Qìng are probably pursuing us."
Xiānyú said:
"One against one,
who can intimidate us?"
So they lodged,
slept with their heads pillowed on the reins,
fed the horses and ate themselves,
then harnessed the horses and departed.
Upon exiting Yǎnzhōng,
he said to Yīng:
"Drive quickly!
The multitude of Cuī and Qìng
cannot be withstood."
Then they came fleeing [to Lǔ].
The Cuī clan interred Duke Zhuāng at the northern outer wall.
On Dīnghài,
they buried him at Shìsūn's village.
Four feather fans [were used],
there was no clearing of the way,
seven carriages followed the coffin,
and no weapons or armor [were used].
B9.25.3 The Marquis of Jìn crossed from Pàn,
met [the allies] at Yíyí,
and attacked Qí
to avenge the battle of Zhāogē.
The men of Qí offered Duke Zhuāng's death as an excuse,
sent Xí Chú to request peace,
and Qìng Fēng went to the army.
Men and women were presented in separate groups.
They bribed the Marquis of Jìn with ancestral vessels and musical instruments.

From the six ministers, the five officers, the thirty commanders, the great officers of the three armies, the heads of the hundred offices, the army divisions, down to those left in charge of defense, all were bribed.
The Marquis of Jìn agreed.
He sent Shū Xiàng to inform the feudal lords.
The Duke [of Lǔ] sent Zǐfú Huìbó to reply, saying:
"You, my lord, have pardoned the guilty,
thereby bringing peace to a small state;
this is your grace.
My humble ruler has heard your command."
B9.25.4 The Marquis of Jìn sent Wèi Shū and Wǎn Mò to meet the Marquis of Wèi,
intending to give Wèi Yíyí.
Cuīzǐ detained his family,
to demand Wǔlù.
B9.25.5 Earlier,
the Marquis of Chén joined the Viscount of Chǔ
in attacking Zhèng.
Along the route through Chén,
wells were filled and trees felled,
and the men of Zhèng resented this.
In the sixth month,
Zhèng's Zǐzhǎn and Zǐchǎn led seven hundred chariots to attack Chén,
made a night assault on the walls of Chén,
and entered it.
The Marquis of Chén, supporting his heir apparent Yǎnshī, fled toward the tombs.
He encountered Minister of War Huánzǐ
and said:
"Carry me!"
He replied:
"I am about to inspect the walls."
He encountered Jiǎ Huò,
who was carrying his mother and wife.
He made them get down,
and gave the ducal carriage [to the Marquis].
The Duke said:
"Leave your mother [in the carriage]."
He declined, saying:
"It would be inauspicious."
He and his wife supported his mother and fled toward the tombs,
and thus also escaped.
Zǐzhǎn ordered the army not to enter the ducal palace,
and together with Zǐchǎn personally guarded the gates.
The Marquis of Chén sent Minister of War Huánzǐ to bribe them with ancestral vessels.
The Marquis of Chén, wearing mourning garb,
embraced the altar of soil,
had his men and women separated and bound,
and waited in the court.
Zǐzhǎn took the reins and appeared before him,
bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, then received a drink
and presented it [to the Marquis].
Zǐměi entered,
counted the captives, and went out.
The invocator purified the altar of soil,
the minister of the masses presented the people,
the minister of war presented the tallies,
the minister of works presented the lands,
and then they returned.
B9.25.6 In autumn, the seventh month, on Jǐsì,
they made a covenant together at Chóngqiū, because Qí had made peace.
B9.25.7 Zhào Wénzǐ was in charge of government.
He ordered that the contributions from the feudal lords be reduced,
while their courtesies were increased.
Mù Shū went to see him.
[Zhào Wénzǐ] said to Mù Shū:
"From now on,
warfare will likely diminish somewhat.
Qí's Cuī and Qìng have newly gained power,
and will seek good relations with the feudal lords.
I, Wǔ, know the Lingyǐn of Chǔ.
If they respectfully perform the rites,
guide [others] with cultured speech,
and bring peace to the feudal lords,
warfare can be diminished."
B9.25.8 Chǔ's Wěi Zǐféng died,
Qū Jiàn became Lingyǐn,
and Qū Dàng became Mó'áo.
The people of Shūjiū ultimately rebelled against Chǔ.
The Prime Minister Zǐmù attacked them.
When he reached Líchéng,
the people of Wú came to their rescue.
Zǐmù hastily led the right army
to advance first,
while Zǐqiáng, Xī Huán, Zǐjié, Zǐpián, and Zǐyú commanded the left army to retreat.
The Wú forces occupied the area between them for seven days.
Zǐqiáng said:
"If we remain long, we will become exhausted and distressed.
Once distressed, we will be captured.
It is better to engage in battle quickly.
I request to use my private troops to lure them,
while you select and array your forces,
and form your battle lines to await me.
If we prevail, we will advance;
if they flee, we will observe them,
and only then can we avoid disaster.
Otherwise,
we will surely be captured by Wú."
They followed his plan.
The five commanders led their private troops to attack the Wú army first.
The Wú army fled;
but upon climbing a hill to observe,
they saw that the Chǔ forces were not reinforced,
so they turned back and pursued them,
closing in on their army.
The selected Chǔ forces joined the battle.
The Wú army was greatly defeated.
Subsequently, they besieged Shūjiū,
and Shūjiū collapsed.
In the eighth month,
Chǔ annihilated Shūjiū.
B9.25.9 Duke Xiàn of Wèi entered Yíyí.
B9.25.10 Zǐchǎn of Zhèng presented the spoils of victory to Jìn,
wearing military attire to conduct the affairs.
The people of Jìn inquired about the crime of Chén.
He replied:
"In the past, Yú Èfǔ served as the Director of Pottery for Zhōu,
and served our former kings.
Our former kings relied on his excellent tools and implements,
and because he was a descendant of divine sages,
they married their eldest daughter, Dàjī, to Húgōng,
and enfeoffed him in Chén,
to serve as one of the three honored states.
Thus, Chén originated from our Zhōu,
and to this day relies on us.
During the turmoil of Duke Huán,
the people of Cài wished to establish one of their own,
but our former lord Duke Zhuāng supported Wǔfǔ and established him.
The people of Cài killed him,
and we again joined with the people of Cài in supporting Duke Lì.
As for Dukes Zhuāng and Xuān,
both were established by us.
During the turmoil of the Xià clan,
Duke Chéng was displaced,
and it was again through us that he was restored,
as you, my lord, know.
Now Chén has forgotten the great virtue of Zhōu,
disregarded our great kindness,
abandoned our marital ties,
relied on the multitude of Chǔ,
to encroach upon our humble city,
with insatiable ambitions,
which is why we had the declaration of the previous year.
Before we received a conclusive command,
there was the battle at our eastern gate.
Along the paths of Chén,
wells were blocked and trees were felled.
Our humble city greatly feared its inability to compete,
and was shamed before Dàjī.
Heaven guided our hearts,
and enlightened our humble city's resolve.
Chén realized its crime,
and surrendered to us.
Therefore, we dare to present our achievements."
The people of Jìn said:
"Why did you invade a smaller state?"
He replied:
"According to the command of the former kings,
wherever guilt lies,
each should receive its punishment.
Moreover, in the past, the land of the Son of Heaven was one qí,
and the feudal states each had one tóng,
diminishing from there.
Now the great states often have several qí;
if they did not invade smaller states,
how could they have reached this?"
The people of Jìn said:
"Why are you wearing military attire?"
He replied:
"Our former lords, Duke Wǔ and Duke Zhuāng, served as ministers for Kings Píng and Huán.
During the battle of Chéngpú,
Duke Wén issued a command,
saying:
'Each shall resume their former duties.'
He commanded our Duke Wén to wear military attire to assist the king,
and to present the spoils from Chǔ.
We dare not disregard the king's command."
Shì Zhuāngbó was unable to refute him,
and reported back to Zhào Wénzǐ.
Wénzǐ said:
"His words are reasonable.
To oppose what is reasonable,
is inauspicious."
Thus, they accepted it.
In the tenth month of winter,
Zǐzhǎn accompanied Duke Bó of Zhèng to Jìn,
to pay respects for the achievement over Chén.
Zǐxī again attacked Chén,
and Chén made peace with Zhèng.
Zhòngní said:
"The Records say:
'Words are to fully express one's intent,
and literary elegance is to fully adorn one's words.'
Without speaking, who would know one's intent?
If words lack literary elegance,
they will not travel far.
Jìn being the hegemon,
and Zhèng entering Chén,
would not have succeeded without eloquent rhetoric.
Be cautious with words."
B9.25.11 Wěi Yǎn of Chǔ served as Minister of War.
Zǐmù ordered him to manage the levies,
and count the armor and weapons.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Wěi Yǎn recorded the land and fields:
surveying the mountains and forests,
gathering from the marshes and lakes,
distinguishing the high hills and mounds,
marking the saline and barren lands,
counting the waterlogged and flooded areas,
planning the reservoirs and ponds,
dividing the level fields and embankments,
pasturing on the low wetlands,
well-fielding the fertile plains,
measuring the income to adjust the levies,
levying chariots and registering horses,
and counting the numbers of chariot soldiers, infantry, armor, and shields.
After completing this,
he presented it to Zǐmù,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B9.25.12 In the twelfth month,
Zhūfán, the Viscount of Wú, attacked Chǔ,
to retaliate for the naval campaign.
He attacked the gate of Cháo.
Niú Chén of Cháo said:
"The King of Wú is brave but reckless.
If we open the gate for him,
he will personally approach the gate.
If I can shoot him,
he will surely die.
If this ruler dies,
our borders will be somewhat pacified."
They followed his plan.
When the Viscount of Wú attacked the gate,
Niú Chén hid behind a short wall and shot him,
and he died.
B9.25.13 The Viscount of Chǔ rewarded Zǐmù for annihilating Shūjiū.
Zǐmù declined, saying:
"It was the achievement of the late senior minister, Wěizi."
Thus, it was given to Wěi Yǎn.
B9.25.14 Chéng Zhèng of Jìn died.
Zǐchǎn then came to know Ránmíng,
and asked him about governance.
He replied:
"Treat the people as your own children.
When you see the unrighteous,
punish them,
like hawks chasing small birds."
Zǐchǎn was pleased,
and told Zǐdàshū about it,
saying:
"In the past,
I only saw Miè's face,
but now I see his heart."
Zǐdàshū asked Zǐchǎn about governance.
Zǐchǎn said:
"Governance is like farming.
Think about it day and night,
consider its beginning
and ensure its completion,
and act on it morning and evening.
Do not act beyond your thoughts,
just as farming has its boundaries.
Then errors will be few."
B9.25.15 Duke Xiàn of Wèi, from Yíyí, sent a message to Níng Xǐ to speak,
and Níng Xǐ agreed.
Dàshū Wénzǐ heard of this,
and said:
"Alas!
As the Odes say,
'I myself am not accepted,
how can I care for what comes after?'"
Nìng Xǐ can be said to have shown no concern for his future.
Could it possibly be acceptable?
It is certainly not acceptable.
In the actions of a noble man,
he considers their conclusion,
he considers their recurrence.
The Book of Documents says:
'Be cautious at the beginning and respectful at the end,
so that in the end you will not be distressed.'
The Book of Songs says:
'Morning and night, without slacking,
to serve one man.'
Now Nìng Xǐ regards his ruler
as no more than a game of chess;
how can he avoid calamity?
In chess, if a player moves his pieces indecisively,
he cannot defeat his opponent;
how much more so when setting up a ruler
and not settling it decisively?
He is certain to be unable to avoid calamity.
A ministerial clan of nine generations,
wiped out in a single move—
how lamentable indeed!"
B9.25.16 In the year of the meeting at Yíyí,
the people of Qí fortified Jiá.
In the fifth month of that year,
Qín and Jìn made peace.
Jìn's Hán Qǐ went to Qín to attend the covenant,
and Qín's Bó Jū went to Jìn to attend the covenant.
They made peace but did not solidify it.
A9.26 The Spring and Autumn Annals, 26th Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.26.1 In the 26th year, in spring,
in the second month of the royal calendar, on the xīnmǎo day,
Wèi's Nìng Xǐ assassinated his ruler, Piāo.
A9.26.2 Wèi's Sūn Línfǔ entered Qì and rebelled.
A9.26.3 On the jiǎwǔ day,
the Marquis of Wèi, Kàn, returned to Wèi.
A9.26.4 In summer,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Wú to come on a friendly visit.
A9.26.5 Our duke met with men of Jìn,
Zhèng's Liáng Xiāo,
men of Sòng,
and men of Cáo at Chányuān.
A9.26.6 In autumn,
the Duke of Sòng killed his heir apparent, Cuó.
A9.26.7 Men of Jìn arrested Wèi's Nìng Xǐ.
A9.26.8 In the eighth month, on the rénwǔ day,
the Viscount of Xǔ, Nìng, died in Chǔ.
A9.26.9 In winter,
the Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Cài,
and the Marquis of Chén attacked Zhèng.
A9.26.10 The funeral of Duke Líng of Xǔ was held.
B9.26 The Commentary of Zuo, 26th Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.26.1 In the 26th year, in spring,
the younger brother of the Earl of Qín, Zhēn, went to Jìn to renew the peace agreement.
Shū Xiàng ordered to summon the diplomatic officer Zǐ Yuán.
The diplomatic officer Zǐ Zhū said:
"Zhū is currently on duty."
He said it three times,
but Shū Xiàng did not respond.
Zǐ Zhū became angry,
and said:
"Our ranks and titles are the same;
why do you slight Zhū at court?"
He grasped his sword and approached him.
Shū Xiàng said:
"Qín and Jìn have been at odds for a long time.
Today's affair,
if it fortunately succeeds,
the state of Jìn will benefit from it.
If it does not succeed,
the three armies will be exposed to bones on the battlefield.
Zǐ Yuán conveys the words of the two states
without selfishness,
while you often change them.
Those who serve their ruler with deceitful intent—
I am able to deal with them."
He flicked his sleeves and approached him.
Others intervened to stop them.
Duke Píng said:
"Jìn is indeed near to excellence!
What my ministers contend over is of great importance."
Shī Kuàng said:
"The ducal house is in danger of decline.
When ministers do not contend with their hearts
but strive with force,
not cultivating virtue but contending for advantage,
their private desires are already excessive—
how can it not decline?"
B9.26.2 The exiled Duke Xiàn of Wèi sent Zǐ Xiān to arrange his restoration,
but he declined.
Jìng Sì insisted and ordered him.
He replied:
"The ruler lacks good faith;
I fear I will not escape calamity."
Jìng Sì said:
"Even so,
do it for my sake."
He then agreed.
Earlier,
Duke Xiàn had sent someone to speak with Nìng Xǐ,
and Nìng Xǐ said:
"It must be Zǐ Xiān who comes.
Otherwise,
it is sure to fail."
Therefore, the duke sent Zǐ Xiān.
Zǐ Xiān, having received no permission from Jìng Sì,
went with the duke's command to speak with Nìng Xǐ,
saying:
"If I return,
government affairs will be managed by the Nìng clan,
but the sacrifices will be performed by me."
Nìng Xǐ informed Qú Bóyù.
Bóyù said:
"Yuàn did not hear of the ruler's departure;
dare I hear of his return?"
He then left,
exiting through the nearest pass.
Nìng Xǐ informed Yòuzǎi Gǔ.
Yòuzǎi Gǔ said:
"It cannot be done.
To offend two rulers—
who in the world would harbor him?"
Dào Zǐ (Nìng Xǐ) said:
"I received the command from my ancestors,
and cannot betray it."
Gǔ said:
"I request to go as an envoy and observe."
He then went to see the duke at Yíyí.
Returning,
he said:
"The ruler has been distressed abroad for twelve years,
yet shows no look of sorrow,
nor any words of leniency—
he is still the same man.
If we do not stop,
death is not far off."
Dào Zǐ said:
"Zǐ Xiān is involved."
Yòuzǎi Gǔ said:
"Even with Zǐ Xiān involved,
what good is it?
If he is numerous yet can perish,
what does it matter to us?"
Dào Zǐ said:
"Even so,
we cannot stop."
Sūn Wénzǐ was in Qì,
Sūn Jiā was on a mission to Qí,
and Sūn Xiāng remained in charge at home.
In the second month, on the gēngyín day,
Nìng Xǐ and Yòuzǎi Gǔ
attacked the Sūn clan,
but did not succeed, and Bó Guó was wounded.
Nìng Zǐ went out
and camped in the suburbs.
Bó Guó died,
and the Sūn clan wailed at night.
The people of the capital summoned Nìng Zǐ,
and Nìng Zǐ again attacked the Sūn clan,
defeating them.
On the xīnmǎo day,
he killed Zǐ Shū and the heir apparent, Jiǎo.
The record says
"Nìng Xǐ assassinated his ruler, Piāo,"
indicating that the crime lies with the Nìng clan.
Sūn Línfǔ went with Qì to Jìn.
The record says "entered Qì and rebelled,"
blaming the Sūn clan.
A minister's emolument
truly belongs to the ruler.
If it is righteous, he advances;
if not, he withdraws with his person.
To monopolize the emolument and maneuver with it
is deserving of punishment.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
the Marquis of Wèi entered.
The record says "returned,"
indicating the state accepted him.
To those ministers who met him at the border,
he took their hands and spoke with them;
to those who met him on the road,
he bowed to them from his carriage;
to those who met him at the gate,
he merely nodded.
The Duke arrived,
and sent a reproach to Dàshū Wénzǐ, saying:
"I have long been distressed abroad,
and all of you ministers have kept me informed morning and evening
of the affairs of Wèi,
yet you alone have not been with me.
The ancients had a saying:
'Do not resent those who are not to be resented.'
I have resented you."
He replied:
"Your servant acknowledges his guilt.
I am not talented,
and was unable to bear the halter and tether
to follow and guard the herds and pastures;
this is my first offense.
Some went out,
some remained;
I could not be of two minds,
communicating the words of those inside and outside to serve my lord;
this is my second offense.
Having these two offenses,
how dare I forget that I deserve death?"
He then departed,
leaving through the nearest pass.
The Duke sent someone to stop him.
B9.26.3 The people of Wèi invaded the eastern borders of Qī.
The Sūn clan complained to Jìn,
and Jìn garrisoned Máoshì.
Zhí Chuò attacked Máoshì,
killing three hundred Jìn garrison troops.
Sūn Kuǎi pursued him,
but did not dare to attack.
Wénzǐ said:
"You are worse than a coward."
He then followed the Wèi army,
and defeated them at Yǔ.
Yōng Chú captured Zhí Chuò.
They again complained to Jìn.
B9.26.4 The Earl of Zhèng rewarded the merit of entering Chén.
In the third month, on the first day, jiǎyín,
he feasted Zǐzhǎn,
bestowing upon him a carriage of the first rank and robes for a three-command appointment,
preceding eight cities;
he bestowed upon Zǐchǎn a carriage of the second rank
and robes for a two-command appointment,
preceding six cities.
Zǐchǎn declined the cities,
saying:
"From the highest down,
decreasing by two levels is the rule of ritual.
Your servant's rank is fourth,
and moreover, it was Zǐzhǎn's merit;
I dare not partake of the reward according to ritual,
I beg to decline the cities."
The Duke firmly insisted on giving them,
so he accepted three cities.
Gōngsūn Huī said:
"Zǐchǎn will likely come to know governance.
His yielding does not lose propriety."
B9.26.5 The people of Jìn, because of the Sūn clan's affair,
summoned the feudal lords,
intending to attack Wèi.
In summer,
Zhōngháng Mùzǐ came on a mission,
to summon the Duke.
B9.26.6 The King of Chǔ and the people of Qín invaded Wú,
reaching Yúlóu,
but hearing that Wú was prepared, they turned back.
They then invaded Zhèng.
In the fifth month,
they reached Chéngjūn.
Huáng Xié of Zhèng was defending it;
he went out,
engaged the Chǔ army in battle,
and was defeated.
Chuān Fēngxū captured Huáng Xié,
and Prince Wéi contended with him for the captive,
appealing to Bózhōulí for judgment.
Bózhōulí said:
"Let us ask the prisoner."
They then had the prisoner stand.
Bózhōulí said:
"The one contended over
is a nobleman;
how could he not know?"
Raising his hand,
he said:
"This gentleman is Prince Wéi,
the honored younger brother of our ruler."
Lowering his hand,
he said:
"This man is Chuān Fēngxū,
a county magistrate beyond the Fāngchéng Mountains.
Who captured you?"
The prisoner said:
"I encountered the Prince,
and was overpowered."
Xū was enraged,
drew his spear and pursued Prince Wéi,
but did not catch him.
The people of Chǔ took Huáng Xié back with them.
Yìn Jǐngfù and Huáng Xié had been defending Chéngjūn; the Chǔ people captured them
and presented them to Qín.
The people of Zhèng sought goods from the Yìn clan
to request their release,
with Zǐtàishū as the official in charge of documents,
preparing the request.
Zǐchǎn said:
"They will not be obtained.
To receive the merit from Chǔ
and take goods from Zhèng
cannot be called acting for the state;
Qín would not do so.
If it were said:
'We thank your lord for his diligence toward Zhèng.
Were it not for your lord's favor,
the Chǔ army would still be at the walls of our humble city,'
that might be acceptable."
They did not follow his advice,
and proceeded.
The people of Qín did not give them up.
Changing the gifts,
they followed Zǐchǎn's advice,
and only then obtained them.
B9.26.7 In the sixth month,
the Duke met with Zhào Wǔ of Jìn, Xiàngxū of Sòng, Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng, and a man from Cáo at Chányuān,
to attack Wèi,
and demarcate the fields of Qī.
They took sixty
from the western border of Wèi at Yìshì and gave it to the Sūn clan.
Zhào Wǔ was not recorded,
out of respect for the Duke.
Xiàngxū was not recorded,
because he was late.
Zhèng preceded Sòng,
because they did not lose their place.
At this time, the Marquis of Wèi joined the meeting.
The people of Jìn arrested Níng Xǐ and Běigōng Yí,
and sent Nǚ Qí to take them back first.
The Marquis of Wèi went to Jìn,
and the people of Jìn arrested and imprisoned him at the residence of Shì Ruò.
In autumn, the seventh month, the Marquis of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng, on account of the Marquis of Wèi, went to Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn feasted them together.
The Marquis of Jìn recited "Jiā Lè".
Guó Jǐngzǐ, assisting the Marquis of Qí,
recited "Liǎo Xiāo".
Zǐzhǎn, assisting the Earl of Zhèng,
recited "Zī Yī".
Shūxiàng instructed the Marquis of Jìn to bow to the two rulers,
saying:
"My ruler dares to bow to the ruler of Qí for pacifying the ancestral temple of our former rulers,
and dares to bow to the ruler of Zhèng for his lack of duplicity."
Guózǐ sent Yàn Píngzhòng to speak privately with Shūxiàng,
saying:
"The ruler of Jìn has displayed his bright virtue among the feudal lords,
sympathizing with their troubles and making up for their deficiencies,
correcting their errors and ordering their disorders;
this is why he is the leader of the covenant.
Now, for the sake of a minister, he arrests a ruler;
how is this?"
Shūxiàng reported this to Zhào Wénzǐ,
and Wénzǐ reported it to the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn stated the crimes of the Marquis of Wèi,
and sent Shūxiàng to inform the two rulers.
Guózǐ recited "Pèi Zhī Róu Yǐ",
Zǐzhǎn recited "Jiāng Zhòngzǐ Xī",
and the Marquis of Jìn then agreed to return the Marquis of Wèi.
Shūxiàng said:
"Of the seven Mù clans of Zhèng,
the Hǎn clan will be the last to perish;
Zǐzhǎn is frugal and single-minded."
B9.26.8 Earlier,
Ruì Sītú of Sòng gave birth to a girl,
who was red and hairy,
and was abandoned beneath a dike.
A concubine of Gòngjī picked her up and brought her in,
naming her Qì.
She grew up beautiful.
When Duke Píng entered for evening audience,
Gòngjī gave him food.
The Duke saw Qì,
and gazed at her,
finding her exceptional.
The Lady presented her among his attendants,
and she became favored,
giving birth to Zuǒ,
who was ugly but gentle.
The crown prince Cuó was handsome but cruel,
and Hé Zuǒshī feared and hated him.
The eunuch Huìqiáng Yīlì was the crown prince's inner tutor
but was not favored.
In autumn,
a guest from Chǔ was sent on a diplomatic mission to Jìn,
passing through Sòng.
The crown prince learned of this,
and requested to entertain him in the countryside.
The duke sent him to go.
Yī Lì requested to accompany him.
The duke said:
"Does he not dislike you?"
He replied:
"When a petty man serves a gentleman,
even if disliked, he dares not distance himself;
even if favored, he dares not draw too close.
He respectfully awaits orders,
how dare he harbor disloyalty?
Even if there are those who serve him outwardly,
none serve him inwardly.
I beg to go."
He was sent.
Upon arrival,
he dug a pit,
used a sacrificial animal,
placed a document,
and performed a divination.
Then he galloped back to report to the duke,
saying:
"The crown prince is about to rebel,
and has already sworn an alliance with the guest from Chǔ."
The duke said:
"He is my son,
what more could he seek?"
He replied: "He desires speed."
The duke sent someone to investigate,
and indeed found evidence.
He inquired of the lady and the left marshal,
and both said:
"We have indeed heard of it."
The duke imprisoned the crown prince.
The crown prince said:
"Only Zuǒ can save me."
He summoned him and asked him to plead,
saying:
"If he does not come by noon,
I know I will die."
The left marshal heard of this,
and chattered with him to delay him.
When the time passed,
he hanged himself and died.
Zuǒ became the crown prince.
The duke later learned of his innocence,
and boiled Yī Lì alive.
The left marshal saw the lady's horse trainer,
and questioned him.
He replied:
"It is the lady of the ruler."
The left marshal said:
"Who is the lady of the ruler?
Why do I not know?"
The groom returned,
and reported this to the lady.
The lady sent him brocade and a horse as gifts,
presenting jade first,
saying:
"The ruler's concubine, Qì, sends someone to present these."
The left marshal changed the address to "the lady of the ruler,"
and then bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and accepted them.
B9.26.9 The earl of Zhèng returned from Jìn,
and sent Zǐ Xī to Jìn on a diplomatic mission.
He declined, saying:
"Our ruler has troubled your officers,
fearing he may not escape blame.
He sends Xià to apologize for his lack of discernment."
The gentleman said:
"He is skilled in serving a great state."
B9.26.10 Earlier,
Wǔ Shēn of Chǔ was friends with the grand tutor of Cài, Zǐ Cháo.
His son, Wǔ Jǔ, was close with Shēngzǐ.
Wǔ Jǔ married the daughter of Prince Móu.
Prince Móu, as the lord of Shēn, fled,
and the people of Chǔ said:
"Wǔ Jǔ indeed aided his escape."
Wǔ Jǔ fled to Zhèng,
intending to then flee to Jìn.
Shēngzǐ was about to go to Jìn,
and met him in the outskirts of Zhèng.
They spread grass and ate together,
discussing how to return to their former state.
Shēngzǐ said:
"You go ahead,
I will surely restore you."
When Xiàng Xū of Sòng was about to mediate peace between Jìn and Chǔ,
Shēngzǐ was sent as an envoy to Jìn,
and returned to Chǔ.
The prime minister, Zǐ Mù, spoke with him,
inquiring about affairs in Jìn,
and said:
"Are the great officers of Jìn more worthy than those of Chǔ?"
He replied:
"The ministers of Jìn are not as good as those of Chǔ,
but their great officers are worthy,
all fit to be ministers.
Like fine wood and leather,
they come from Chǔ.
Though Chǔ has talent,
Jìn actually uses it."
Zǐ Mù said:
"Do they not have their own clans and in-laws?"
He replied:
"Though they do,
they use much talent from Chǔ.
Guīshēng has heard:
Those skilled in governing a state
do not over-reward or over-punish.
Over-rewarding risks benefiting the wicked;
over-punishing risks harming the good.
If misfortune leads to excess,
it is better to over-reward
than to over-punish.
Rather than lose the good,
it is better to benefit the wicked.
Without good people,
the state will follow suit.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'When good men are lost,
the state is ruined.'
This speaks of having no good people.
Thus, the *Xià Shū* says:
'Rather than kill the innocent,
it is better to err on the side of mercy.'
This fears losing the good.
The *Shāng Sòng* says:
'Not over-rewarding, not over-punishing,
not daring to be idle or hasty.
Commanding the lower states,
establishing his blessings.'
This is how Tāng obtained heavenly blessings.
Those who governed the people in ancient times
encouraged rewards and feared punishments,
tirelessly caring for the people.
Rewards were given in spring and summer,
punishments in autumn and winter.
Thus, when about to reward,
they increased the feasts,
and increased feasts meant generous gifts.
This shows they encouraged rewards.
When about to punish,
they reduced the feasts,
and reducing feasts meant removing music.
This shows they feared punishments.
Rising early and retiring late,
attending to governance morning and night,
this shows they cared for the people.
These three
are the great principles of ritual.
With ritual, there is no defeat.
Now, Chǔ has excessive punishments,
and its great officers flee to all directions,
becoming chief strategists
to harm Chǔ.
It is beyond cure,
what is called incapability.
During the rebellion of Zǐ Yí,
Xī Gōng fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn placed him in the rear of the war chariots,
making him chief strategist.
At the battle of Rǎojiǎo,
the Jìn army was about to flee,
but Xī Gōng said:
'The Chǔ army is light and rash,
easily shaken.
If we beat many drums uniformly,
and attack them at night,
the Chǔ army will surely flee.'
The people of Jìn followed this,
and the Chǔ army fled overnight.
Jìn then invaded Cài,
attacked Shěn,
captured its ruler,
defeated the armies of Shēn and Xī at Sāngsuì,
captured Shēn Lì, and returned.
Zhèng then dared not face south.
Chǔ lost the central states,
all due to Xī Gōng's actions.
Yōngzǐ's father and brothers slandered him,
and the ruler and great officers did not rectify this.
Yōngzǐ fled to Jìn,
and the people of Jìn gave him Chù,
making him chief strategist.
At the battle of Péngchéng,
Jìn and Chǔ met at the valley of Míjiǎo.
The Jìn army was about to flee,
but Yōngzǐ issued orders to the army:
'Send back the old and young,
return the orphans and disabled,
if two are serving,
send one back.'
They selected troops and inspected chariots,
fed the horses and prepared meals,
the army formed ranks and burned their encampments,
preparing to fight the next day.
They released those returning home,
and let the Chu prisoners escape.
The Chu army fled overnight,
Jìn descended upon Péngchéng and returned it to Sòng,
taking Yú Shí back with them.
Chǔ lost the eastern barbarians,
Zǐ Xīn died because of it,
all this was the doing of Yōngzǐ.
Zǐ Fǎn and Zǐ Líng contended for Xià Jī,
and he obstructed and harmed the affair,
so Zǐ Líng fled to Jìn,
the people of Jìn gave him Xíng,
making him their chief strategist,
he defended against the northern Dí,
opened communications between Wú and Jìn,
taught Wú to rebel against Chǔ,
instructed them in chariot driving, archery, charioteering, and raiding,
and sent his son Hú Yōng
to serve as Wú’s envoy.
Thereupon Wú attacked Cháo, captured Jià,
overcame Jí, and entered Zhōulái,
Chǔ was exhausted from rushing to meet threats,
and to this day it remains a trouble,
all this was the doing of Zǐ Líng.
During the Ruò’áo rebellion,
Bó Fén’s son Fén Huáng fled to Jìn,
the people of Jìn gave him Miáo,
making him their chief strategist.
At the battle of Yānlíng,
Chǔ pressed upon the Jìn army at dawn and formed ranks.
The Jìn were about to flee,
when Miáo Fén Huáng said:
‘The elite of the Chǔ army are only in the
center division, the royal clan;
if we fill the wells and level the stoves,
form our ranks to face them,
have Luán and Fàn exchange positions to lure them,
Zhōng Háng and the two Xì will surely defeat the two Mù,
then we can concentrate our four divisions against their royal clan,
and are sure to inflict a great defeat.’
The people of Jìn followed this,
the Chǔ army was greatly defeated,
the king was wounded and the army annihilated,
Zǐ Fǎn died because of it.
Zhèng rebelled, Wú rose,
Chǔ lost the feudal lords,
all this was the doing of Miáo Fén Huáng.”
Zǐ Mù said:
“These are all indeed so.”
Shēngzǐ said:
“Now there is one even worse than these.
Jiāo Jǔ married the daughter of Shēn Gōngzǐ Móu,
Zǐ Móu incurred guilt and fled,
the ruler and great officers said to Jiāo Jǔ:
‘You truly sent him away.’
In fear, he fled to Zhèng,
craning his neck to look south,
saying:
‘Perhaps they will pardon me.’
But they gave it no thought.
Now he is in Jìn.
The people of Jìn are about to give him a county,
ranking him with Shū Xiàng.
If he then schemes to harm the state of Chǔ,
will it not become a trouble?”
Zǐ Mù was alarmed,
spoke of it to the king,
increased his salary and rank and restored him.
Shēngzǐ sent Jiāo Míng to welcome him back.
B9.26.11 Duke Líng of Xǔ went to Chǔ,
requesting an attack on Zhèng,
saying:
“If the army is not raised,
I shall not return.”
In the eighth month,
he died in Chǔ.
The ruler of Chǔ said:
“If we do not attack Zhèng,
how shall we seek the allegiance of the feudal lords?”
In winter, the tenth month,
the ruler of Chǔ attacked Zhèng,
the people of Zhèng prepared to resist him.
Zǐ Chǎn said:
“Jìn and Chǔ are about to make peace,
the feudal lords are about to be harmonious,
the king of Chǔ is therefore making this one visit in obscurity.
It would be better to let him have his way and return,
then peace will be easier to achieve.
The nature of petty men,
is to be stirred by courage,
to crave calamity,
to satisfy their nature,
and seek fame thereby;
this is not beneficial to the state,
why should we follow them?”
Zǐ Zhǎn was pleased,
and did not resist the invaders.
In the twelfth month, on yǐyǒu day,
they entered Nánlǐ,
destroyed its walls,
crossed at Yuèshì,
and attacked the Shīzhīliáng gate.
The hanging gate was lowered,
and they captured nine men.
They crossed at Fàn and returned.
Afterward, they buried Duke Líng of Xǔ.
B9.26.12 The people of Wèi sent Wèi Jī to Jìn,
and only then released the marquis of Wèi.
The gentleman therefore knew that Duke Píng had lost proper governance.
B9.26.13 Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn paid a courtesy visit to Zhōu,
the king sent to inquire his business.
He replied:
“Jìn’s Shì Qǐ is about to present the seasonal tribute to the minister’s subordinates,
there is no other business.”
The king heard this,
and said:
“The Hán clan will surely flourish in Jìn!
His words do not lose the old ways.”
B9.26.14 In the year the people of Qí fortified Jiá,
that summer,
Wū Yú of Qí fled to Jìn with Lǐnqiū,
attacked Yángjiǎo of Wèi,
and captured it;
then attacked our Gāoyú.
There was heavy rain,
he entered through its drain,
took armor from its armory,
and climbed its walls,
overcame and captured it.
He also took a town from Sòng.
At that time, Fàn Xuānzǐ had died,
and the feudal lords could not bring him to order.
When Zhào Wénzǐ took charge of government,
he finally brought him to order.
Wénzǐ spoke to the marquis of Jìn, saying:
“Jìn is the leader of the covenant,
if the feudal lords encroach upon each other,
then we should chastise them and make them return the land.
Now Wū Yú’s towns
are all of the kind that should be chastised,
yet if we covet them,
this is no way to be leader of the covenant.
I request that we return them.”
The duke said:
“Agreed.
Who can be sent?”
He replied:
“Xū Liáng Dài can do it without using troops.”
The marquis of Jìn sent him.
A9.27 The Classic of the Twenty-Seventh Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.27.1 In the twenty-seventh year, spring,
the marquis of Qí sent Qìng Fēng to pay a courtesy visit.
A9.27.2 In summer,
Shūsūn Bào met with Zhào Wǔ of Jìn,
Qū Jiàn of Chǔ,
Gōngsūn Guīshēng of Cài,
Shí È of Wèi,
Kǒng Huàn of Chén,
Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng,
a man of Xǔ,
and a man of Cáo in Sòng.
A9.27.3 Wèi killed its great officer Níng Xǐ.
A9.27.4 The younger brother of the marquis of Wèi, Zhuān, fled to Jìn.
A9.27.5 In autumn,
the seventh month, on xīnsì day,
Bào and the great officers of the feudal lords made a covenant in Sòng.
A9.27.6 In winter, the twelfth month, on yǐhài day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
B9.27 The Commentary of the Twenty-Seventh Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.27.1 In the twenty-seventh year, spring,
Xū Liáng Dài made those who had lost towns
prepare chariots and followers to receive land,
and it had to be done completely.
He made Wū Yú prepare chariots and followers
to receive his fief.
Wū Yú came out with his multitude,
then he made the feudal lords pretend to be those presenting fiefs to Wū Yú
and thereupon seized him,
capturing all of them.
He took all their towns,
and returned them to the feudal lords.
The feudal lords therefore were harmonious with Jìn.
B9.27.2 Qìng Fēng of Qí came on a courtesy visit,
his chariot was fine.
Méngsūn said to Shūsūn:
“Qìng Jì’s chariot,
is it not fine indeed!”
Shūsūn said:
"Bào has heard:
'Fine attire that is not fitting,
will surely end in misfortune.'
What use is a fine carriage?"
Shūsūn dined with Qìng Fēng,
who was disrespectful.
They performed the ode "Xiàng Shǔ" for him,
but he did not understand it either.
B9.27.3 Nìng Xǐ of Wèi monopolized power,
and the duke was troubled by it.
Gōngsūn Miǎnyú requested to kill him.
The duke said:
"Without Master Nìng,
I would not have reached this position.
I have given him my word.
The outcome is uncertain,
and it would only create an evil reputation—
let it be."
He replied:
"Your servant will kill him,
and Your Lordship need not be involved."
So he plotted with Gōngsūn Wúdì and Gōngsūn Chén,
and sent them to attack the Nìng clan.
They did not succeed,
and both died.
The duke said:
"My ministers were without fault,
yet father and son died for me!"
In summer,
Miǎnyú again attacked the Nìng clan,
killing Nìng Xǐ and Right Steward Gǔ,
and displayed their corpses in the court.
Shí È was about to attend the covenant meeting in Sòng,
and having received his orders, he set out.
He clothed their corpses,
laid his head upon their thighs and wept for them.
He wished to encoffin them and flee,
but feared he would not escape,
and said:
"I have received my orders."
So he departed.
Zǐ Xiān said:
"Those who drove me out are gone,
and those who brought me back are dead.
Rewards and punishments are without rule—
how can they deter or encourage?
The lord has lost his trustworthiness,
and the state lacks proper penalties—
is this not difficult?
Moreover, Zhuān truly caused this."
Thereupon he fled to Jìn.
The duke sent to stop him,
but could not.
When he reached the river,
the duke again sent to stop him.
He detained the messenger and made a covenant by the river.
He took refuge in Mùmén,
and would not face toward Wèi when he sat.
The grandee of Mùmén urged him to take office,
but he refused,
saying:
"To take office and neglect its duties
is a crime;
to carry them out
would make clear the reason for my departure.
To whom could I complain?
I cannot stand in another's court."
He never took office for the rest of his life.
The duke mourned him as if wearing mourning garments for life.
The duke offered Miǎnyú sixty towns,
but he declined, saying:
"Only a minister is entitled to a hundred towns;
I already have sixty.
For a subordinate to have the emolument of a superior
is disorder.
I dare not hear of it.
Moreover, it was precisely because Master Nìng had many towns
that he died.
I fear death will quickly reach me."
The duke insisted on giving them to him,
and he accepted half.
He was made Junior Tutor.
The duke wanted to make him a minister,
but he declined, saying:
"Dàshū Yí is unwavering
and capable of assisting in great affairs—
Your Lordship should command him."
So he made Wénzǐ a minister.
B9.27.4 Xiàng Xū of Sòng was on good terms with Zhào Wénzǐ of Jìn,
and also with Língyǐn Zǐ Mù of Chǔ.
He wished to end the warfare among the feudal lords to make a name for himself.
He went to Jìn
and informed Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng consulted with the senior officials.
Hán Xuānzǐ said:
"Warfare
harms the people,
consumes resources,
and is a great calamity for small states.
If someone intends to end it,
even if we say it cannot be done,
we must still agree.
If we do not agree,
Chǔ will agree to it,
and will summon the feudal lords,
then we will lose our position as covenant leader."
The people of Jìn agreed.
He went to Chǔ,
and Chǔ also agreed.
He went to Qí,
and the people of Qí found it difficult.
Chén Wénzǐ said:
"Jìn
and Chǔ have agreed to it—
how can we refuse?
Moreover, if others speak of
'ending warfare,'
and we do not agree,
we will surely alienate our people—
what use would that be?"
The people of Qí agreed.
He informed Qín,
and Qín also agreed.
All the small states were informed,
and a meeting was arranged in Sòng.
On the jiǎchén day of the fifth month,
Zhào Wǔ of Jìn arrived in Sòng.
On the bǐngwǔ day,
Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng arrived.
On the dīngwèi day, the first day of the sixth month,
the people of Sòng feasted Zhào Wénzǐ,
with Shū Xiàng as his assistant.
The Minister of War set out the carved meat stands—
this was according to ritual.
Zhòngní had this ceremony recorded,
considering it rich in elegant words.
On the wùshēn day,
Shūsūn Bào, Qìng Fēng of Qí, Chén Xūwú, and Shí È of Wèi arrived.
On the jiǎyín day,
Xún Yíng of Jìn arrived following Zhào Wǔ.
On the bǐngchén day,
Duke Dào of Zhū arrived.
On the rénxū day,
Prince Hēigōng of Chǔ arrived first
and reached an agreement with Jìn.
On the dīngmǎo day,
Xiàng Xū of Sòng went to Chén,
following Zǐ Mù to reach an agreement with Chǔ.
On the wùchén day,
Duke Chéng of Téng arrived.
Zǐ Mù said to Xiàng Xū
that he requested the followers of Jìn and Chǔ to meet each other.
On the gēngwǔ day,
Xiàng Xū reported back to Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said:
"Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Qín
are peers.
Jìn's inability to command Qí
is like Chǔ's inability to command Qín.
If the ruler of Chǔ can make the ruler of Qín deign to visit our humble state,
would our ruler dare not firmly request the same of Qí?"
On the rénshēn day,
the Left Master again spoke to Zǐ Mù.
Zǐ Mù sent a courier to report to the king.
The king said:
"Set aside Qí and Qín—
let the other states meet each other."
In autumn, on the wùyín day of the seventh month,
the Left Master arrived.
That night,
Zhào Mèng and Zǐ Xī made a covenant,
agreeing on uniform terms.
On the gēngchén day,
Zǐ Mù arrived from Chén.
Kǒng Huàn of Chén and Gōngsūn Guīshēng of Cài arrived.
The senior officials of Cáo and Xǔ all arrived.
They used fences as army encampments.
Jìn and Chǔ each occupied their respective sides.
Bó Sù said to Zhào Mèng:
"The atmosphere from Chǔ is very ominous—
I fear trouble."
Zhào Mèng said:
"If I turn left,
I enter Sòng—
what can they do to me?"
On the xīnsì day,
they were to make a covenant outside the western gate of Sòng.
The men of Chǔ wore armor under their clothes.
Bó Zhōulí said:
"Assembling the armies of the feudal lords
and acting without good faith—
is this not improper?
The feudal lords look to Chǔ for good faith,
and thus submit.
If we are not trustworthy,
we abandon what makes the feudal lords submit."
He firmly requested the removal of armor.
Zǐ Mù said:
"Jìn and Chǔ have been without trust for a long time;
it is only a matter of advantage.
If one can achieve one's aim,
what use is there for trust?"
The Grand Steward withdrew
and told someone:
"The Lìngyǐn will die;
it will be within three years.
To seek to gratify one's ambition and abandon trust—
can ambition then be gratified?
Ambition gives rise to words;
words produce trust;
trust establishes ambition.
These three together determine it.
If trust is lost,
how can one last until the third year?"
Zhào Mèng was troubled that Chǔ had concealed armor under their robes,
and told Shū Xiàng about it.
Shū Xiàng said:
"What harm is there?
If a common man once acts without trust,
it is still unacceptable,
and he alone will meet his death.
But if the ministers of the assembled states
act without trust,
they certainly will not succeed.
Those who break their word do not prosper;
this is not your concern.
To summon people with trust
and then assist them with deceit—
certainly no one will support them;
how can they harm us?
Moreover, we rely on Sòng to guard against trouble,
and they are capable of fighting to the death.
If we and Sòng fight to the death,
even if Chǔ were twice as strong it would be acceptable;
what do you fear?
And it will not even come to that.
They speak of disarming to summon the states,
yet raise troops to harm us—
our advantage is great;
it is not something to worry about."
Jì Wǔzǐ sent a message to Shūsūn in the name of the Duke, saying:
"Regard Zhū and Téng as your models."
Afterwards, the men of Qí requested [the inclusion of] Zhū,
and the men of Sòng requested [the inclusion of] Téng,
but both were not included in the covenant.
Shūsūn said:
"Zhū and Téng
are the private possessions of others;
we
are a ranked state.
Why should we regard them as models?
Sòng and Wèi
are our equals."
Then he made the covenant.
Therefore, his clan name was not recorded,
indicating that he disobeyed orders.
Jìn and Chǔ contended for precedence.
The men of Jìn said:
"Jìn has long been the leader of the covenant among the states;
none has ever preceded Jìn."
The men of Chǔ said:
"You said Jìn and Chǔ are equals;
if Jìn always takes precedence,
this means Chǔ is weak.
Moreover, Jìn and Chǔ have alternately presided over the covenants of the states for a long time;
how can it belong exclusively to Jìn?"
Shū Xiàng said to Zhào Mèng:
"The states turn to Jìn's virtue,
not to its presiding over the covenant.
You should devote yourself to virtue,
and not contend for precedence.
Moreover, in covenants among the states,
a small state must certainly preside;
for Chǔ to be the minor to Jìn's major,
is that not acceptable?"
So they let Chǔ take precedence.
The record gives precedence to Jìn,
because Jìn had trust.
On the rénwǔ day,
the Duke of Sòng hosted a joint feast for the great officers of Jìn and Chǔ.
Zhào Mèng was the guest of honor.
Zǐ Mù spoke with him,
but he could not respond;
he had Shū Xiàng attend and speak for him,
but Zǐ Mù also could not respond.
On the yǐyǒu day,
the Duke of Sòng and the great officers of the states made a covenant outside the Méng Gate.
Zǐ Mù asked Zhào Mèng:
"What was the virtue of Fàn Wǔzǐ like?"
He replied:
"The affairs of that master's household were well ordered;
he spoke to the state of Jìn without concealing the truth;
his invocators and scribes presented trustworthiness to the spirits and ghosts,
without words that would cause shame."
Zǐ Mù returned and reported this to the king.
The king said:
"How noble!
