Able to please spirits and men,
it is fitting that he gloriously assisted five rulers
to become leader of the covenant."
Zǐ Mù also said to the king:
"It is fitting that Jìn is hegemon;
with Shū Xiàng assisting its minister,
Chǔ has no one to match him,
and cannot contend with them."
Then Xún Yíng of Jìn went to Chǔ to oversee the covenant.
B9.27.5 The Earl of Zhèng feasted Zhào Mèng
at Chuílǒng.
Zǐ Zhǎn, Bó Yǒu, Zǐ Xī, Zǐ Chǎn, Zǐ Tàishū, and the two Zǐ Shí attended.
Zhào Mèng said:
"The seven masters attend their lord,
to honor Wǔ.
I ask that you all recite odes,
to complete your lord's kindness,
and Wǔ may also observe the aspirations of the seven masters."
Zǐ Zhǎn recited "Grasshoppers."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Excellent!
A master of the people!
But I, Wǔ,
am not worthy to match it."
Bó Yǒu recited "The Bustard's Plume."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Words of the bedchamber should not pass the threshold;
how much less in the wilds?
These are not words an envoy should hear."
Zǐ Xī recited the fourth stanza of "Millet Sprouts."
Zhào Mèng said:
"My humble lord is present;
what can Wǔ do?"
Zǐ Chǎn recited "The Lowland Mulberry Tree."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Wǔ asks to receive its final stanza."
Zǐ Tàishū recited "In the Wilds Is Creeping Grass."
Zhào Mèng said:
"This is your kindness." ;
Yìn Duàn recited "The Cricket."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Excellent!
A master who preserves his family!
I have hope."
Gōngsūn Duàn recited "The Mulberry Guardian."
Zhào Mèng said:
"'Not forward, not arrogant'—
where will good fortune go?
If you preserve these words,
even if you wished to decline fortune and emolument,
could you?"
When the feast ended,
Wénzǐ told Shū Xiàng:
"Bó Yǒu will be executed.
The odes express aspirations;
his aspiration slanders his superior
and publicly resents him,
considering it an honor for the guest—
can he last long?
It will be fortunate if he perishes later."
Shū Xiàng said:
"Yes,
he is already extravagant;
what is called 'not reaching five harvests'
refers to that master."
Wénzǐ said:
"The others are all masters for several generations.
Zǐ Zhǎn will be the last to perish;
in high position, he does not forget to lower himself.
The Yìn clan will be next;
joyful but not dissolute.
Joy to comfort the people,
not excessive in employing them—
to perish later,
is that not acceptable?"
B9.27.6 The Left Marshal of Sòng requested a reward,
saying:
"I request a city to avoid death."
The duke gave him sixty cities
and showed [the grant] to Zǐ Hǎn.
Zǐ Hǎn said:
"All small states among the feudal lords
are militarily intimidated by Jìn and Chǔ;
through fear, their high and low are then kind and harmonious;
through kindness and harmony, they can then pacify and stabilize their states and families,
to serve the great states—
this is how they survive.
Without intimidation, they become arrogant;
arrogance gives rise to disorder;
disorder arising inevitably leads to destruction—
this is how they perish.
Heaven produced the five materials,
and the people use them all together;
to abandon one is impossible—
who can eliminate arms?
The establishment of arms has been long;
Therefore, it is used to awe the unruly
and display civil virtue.
The sage rises by it,
the troublemaker is ruined by it.
The methods of ruin and rise, survival and destruction,
darkness and brightness,
all come from military affairs.
Yet you seek to abolish it—
is that not deluded?!
To delude and mislead the feudal lords
is a crime of the greatest magnitude.
Even if you escape major punishment,
to then seek reward
is the height of insatiability."
He scraped off the writing and threw it away.
The Left Marshal declined the city.
Xiàng Shù wanted to attack the Minister of Works.
The Left Marshal said:
"I was about to perish,
but that gentleman preserved me.
No greater kindness exists.
How could I attack him?"
A gentleman said:
"'That man,
is the upholder of rectitude in the state.'
This refers to Yuè Xǐ!
'What will comfort me,
I will accept.'
This refers to Xiàng Shù!"
B9.27.7 In Qí, Cuī Zhù begot Chéng and Qiáng, but after being widowed,
he married Dōngguō Jiāng,
who bore Míng.
Dōngguō Jiāng entered the household with an orphan,
named Táng Wújiù,
who, together with Dōngguō Yǎn, managed the Cuī clan's affairs.
Cuī Chéng had an illness
and was set aside,
and Míng was established in his place.
Chéng requested to retire to Cuī,
and Cuī Zhù agreed.
But Yǎn and Wújiù would not give it,
saying:
"Cuī
is the ancestral city;
it must remain with the clan head."
Chéng and Qiáng were enraged.
They planned to kill them
and informed Qìng Fēng, saying:
"Our master's person
is also known to you, sir.
He only follows Wújiù and Yǎn;
no clansman or elder can gain access.
We greatly fear harm will come to our master,
and dare to report this."
Qìng Fēng said:
"You may withdraw for now.
I will consider it."
He informed Lúpú Piè.
Lúpú Piè said:
"They
are our lord's enemies.
Heaven may be about to abandon them.
They are truly causing disorder in their own house;
what trouble is it to you?
The weakening of Cuī
is the strengthening of Qìng."
Another day, they informed him again.
Qìng Fēng said:
"If it benefits your master,
you must remove them.
If there is difficulty,
I will help you."
In the ninth month, on the day Gēngchén,
Cuī Chéng and Cuī Qiáng killed Dōngguō Yǎn and Táng Wújiù in the Cuī clan's court.
Cuī Zhù was furious and went out.
His followers all fled.
He sought someone to harness his carriage,
but found none.
He had a groom harness it,
and a eunuch drove him out.
Moreover, he said:
"If the Cuī clan has fortune,
let it stop with me and that will suffice."
He then went to see Qìng Fēng.
Qìng Fēng said:
"Cuī and Qìng are one.
How dare they act thus?
Allow me to punish them for you."
He sent Lúpú Piè to lead armored troops
to attack the Cuī clan.
The Cuī clan fortified their walls and defended them.
They could not overcome them,
so they had the men of the capital assist,
and thus destroyed the Cuī clan,
killing Chéng and Qiáng,
and capturing all their households.
Cuī Zhù's wife hanged herself.
Piè reported back to Cuī Zhù,
and moreover drove him back.
Upon arrival,
he had nowhere to return to.
He then hanged himself.
Cuī Míng fled by night and hid among the great tombs.
On Xīnsì,
Cuī Míng came fleeing.
Qìng Fēng took control of the state.
B9.27.8 Chǔ's Wěi Pí went to Jìn to attend a covenant.
The Marquis of Jìn entertained him.
As he was about to leave, he recited the ode "Jì Zuì".
Shū Xiàng said:
"That the Wěi clan will have posterity in Chǔ
is fitting indeed!
He received his lord's command
and did not forget to be diligent.
Zǐ Dàng will come to know governance.
Diligence in serving his lord
will surely enable him to nurture the people.
Where else would governance go?"
B9.27.9 Due to the disorder in the Cuī clan,
Shēn Xiānyú came fleeing.
He hired himself out as a servant in the fields
to mourn for Duke Zhuāng.
In winter,
the people of Chǔ summoned him,
and he then went to Chǔ,
becoming the Right Assistant.
B9.27.10 In the eleventh month, on the first day Yǐhài,
there was a solar eclipse.
The celestial stem was in Shēn,
due to the error of the calendar officers,
who had twice missed intercalary months.
A9.28 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, 28th Year of Duke Xiāng*
A9.28.1 In the 28th year, in spring,
there was no ice.
A9.28.2 In summer,
Wèi's Shí È fled to Jìn.
A9.28.3 The Earl of Zhū came for an audience.
A9.28.4 In autumn, in the eighth month,
there was a great rain-seeking sacrifice.
A9.28.5 Zhòngsūn Jié went to Jìn.
A9.28.6 In winter,
Qí's Qìng Fēng came fleeing.
A9.28.7 In the eleventh month,
the duke went to Chǔ.
A9.28.8 In the twelfth month, on the day Jiǎyín,
the Son of Heaven passed away.
A9.28.9 On the day Yǐwèi,
Chǔ's Zǐ Zhāo (King Kāng of Chǔ) died.
B9.28 *The Zuo Tradition, 28th Year of Duke Xiāng*
B9.28.1 In the 28th year, in spring,
there was no ice.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"This year Sòng and Zhèng will likely suffer famine!
The year-star is in Xīngjì,
but has trespassed into Xuánxiāo.
Because there are seasonal disasters,
yin cannot withstand yang.
The snake rides the dragon.
The dragon is the star of Sòng
and Zhèng.
Sòng and Zhèng are sure to suffer famine.
Xuánxiāo
has emptiness at its center.
Xiāo means exhaustion.
When the earth is empty and the people exhausted,
how can they not suffer famine?"
B9.28.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí, the Marquis of Chén, the Marquis of Cài, the Earl of Běiyān, the Earl of Qǐ, the Viscount of Hú, the Viscount of Shěn, and the Báidí had an audience in Jìn,
due to the covenant of Sòng.
As the Marquis of Qí was about to depart,
Qìng Fēng said:
"We did not join the covenant.
Why go to Jìn?"
Chén Wénzǐ said:
"First serve, then receive gifts—
that is ritual.
The small serving the great,
if they have not yet obtained service,
they follow them according to their will—
that is ritual.
Even though we did not join the covenant,
dare we betray Jìn?
The covenant of Chóngqiū
cannot be forgotten.
You should urge him to go!"
B9.28.3 The people of Wèi attacked the partisans of the Nìng clan,
so Shí È fled to Jìn.
The people of Wèi established his nephew Shí Pǔ,
to maintain the sacrifices of the Shí clan,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B9.28.4 Duke Dào of Zhū came to court,
a seasonal courtesy.
B9.28.5 In autumn, the eighth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice,
due to drought.
B9.28.6 The Marquis of Cài returned from Jìn,
and entered Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng hosted a feast for him,
but he was disrespectful.
Zǐchǎn said:
"The Marquis of Cài will likely not escape calamity!
Previously, when he passed through here,
our lord sent Zǐzhǎn to greet and entertain him outside the eastern gate,
yet he was arrogant.
I said he might still change.
Now, upon his return, he receives a feast yet is indolent,
this reveals his true disposition.
For the lord of a small state,
serving a great state,
yet to make indolence and arrogance his disposition,
can he expect to die a natural death?
If he does not escape calamity,
it will surely come through his son.
As a ruler,
he is licentious and does not act as a father should.
I, Qiáo, have heard that,
in such cases,
there is always trouble from a son."
B9.28.7 Mèng Xiàobó went to Jìn,
to announce that, because of the covenant at Sòng,
he would go to Chǔ.
B9.28.8 When the Marquis of Cài went to Jìn,
the Earl of Zhèng sent Yóu Jí to Chǔ.
When he reached the Hàn River,
the men of Chǔ sent him back,
saying:
"At the covenant of Sòng,
your lord personally attended.
Now that you have come,
our humble lord asks that you return for now,
we will dispatch a courier to inquire of Jìn and then inform you."
Zǐtàishū said:
"At the covenant of Sòng,
your lord's command was to benefit the small states,
and also to enable them to stabilize their altars of state,
pacify and comfort their people,
and through ritual receive Heaven's blessings.
This was your lord's enlightened decree,
and the hope of the small states.
Therefore, our humble lord sent me, Jí, bearing gifts of furs and silks,
because the year has been troubled,
to pay court to your subordinate officers.
Now your officers command, saying:
'What business have you with our government's orders?
We must make your lord abandon his borders and duties,
trek across mountains and rivers,
endure frost and dew,
to satisfy our lord's wishes.'
The small state looks to your lord,
how dare we not obey your command?
But is this not contrary to the words of the covenant,
damaging your lord's virtue,
and is it not disadvantageous for your officers?
This is what the small state fears.
Otherwise,
what hardship would we dare shirk?"
Zǐtàishū returned,
and reported back.
He told Zǐzhǎn:
"The Viscount of Chǔ will die soon.
He does not cultivate his governance and virtue,
but covets and preys upon the feudal lords,
to satisfy his desires.
To wish for longevity,
can he attain it?
The Zhōu Yì has this,
in the hexagram Fù ䷗ changing to Yí
it says,
'Lost in return,
inauspicious.'
Is this not referring to the Viscount of Chǔ!
Wishing to fulfill his desires,
yet abandoning his foundation,
returning to find no place,
this is called 'lost in return'.
Can it be without inauspiciousness?
Our lord should go,
attend the funeral and return,
to gratify Chǔ's heart.
Within less than ten years, Chǔ
will be unable to trouble the feudal lords,
and we can then give our people rest."
Bízào said:
"This year, the King of Zhōu and the Viscount of Chǔ will both die.
The year-star has abandoned its station,
and wanders into next year's station,
harming the Bird Net,
Zhōu and Chǔ will suffer from this."
In the ninth month,
Yóu Jí of Zhèng went to Jìn,
to announce they would go to court in Chǔ
in accordance with the covenant of Sòng.
Zǐchǎn accompanied the Earl of Zhèng to Chǔ.
They lodged without building an altar-mound.
An attendant officer said:
"In the past, when senior ministers accompanied our former lords to the various states,
they never failed to build an altar-mound.
From then until now, this has always been followed.
Now you, sir, are lodging in a thatched hut,
is this not improper?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"When a great state goes to a small one,
then an altar-mound is built;
when a small state goes to a great one,
a simple lodging suffices,
what use is an altar-mound?
I, Qiáo, have heard that:
When a great state goes to a small one, there are five virtues:
forgiving its crimes and offenses,
pardoning its faults and errors,
relieving its disasters and calamities,
rewarding its virtue and punishments,
instructing it where it is deficient.
The small state is not oppressed,
feels cherished and submits as if returning home,
therefore an altar-mound is built
to display these achievements,
proclaim them to later generations,
and not neglect virtue.
When a small state goes to a great one, there are five evils:
explaining its crimes and offenses,
requesting what it lacks,
implementing its government affairs,
presenting its regular tribute,
obeying its seasonal commands.
Otherwise,
then increase its gifts of silks,
to congratulate its good fortune
and condole its misfortunes,
all these are calamities for the small state.
Why build an altar-mound to display these calamities?
What we tell our descendants,
is not to display calamities, and that is acceptable."
B9.28.9 Qìng Fēng of Qí loved hunting and was fond of drink.
He shared governance with Qìng Shě,
then moved his household and valuables to the house of Lúpú Piè,
exchanged wives and drank.
After several days,
the state officials held court there.
He ordered that those exiles who could identify thieves
should report, and they would be returned,
thus Lúpú Guǐ was returned.
Guǐ became a retainer of Zǐzhī (Qìng Shě),
was favored,
and was given a wife.
A retainer of Qìng Shě said to Lúpú Guǐ:
"Men and women should distinguish surnames,
you do not avoid your own clan,
why?"
He replied:
"My clan does not avoid me,
why should I alone avoid it?
When reciting poetry, one breaks off a stanza,
I take what I seek,
why should I recognize the clan?"
Guǐ spoke of Wáng Hé and had him returned,
both men were favored,
and were made to hold bedroom halberds and precede and follow him.
The ducal meals included a pair of chickens daily,
the cooks secretly replaced them with ducks.
The servers knew this,
then removed the meat,
and served only the broth.
Zǐyǎ and Zǐwěi were angry.
Qìng Fēng told Lúpú Piè.
Lúpú Piè said:
"They are like birds and beasts,
I will skin them and lie on their hides."
He sent Xīguīfǔ to inform Yàn Píngzhòng.
Píngzhòng said:
"My followers are insufficient for use,
my wisdom inadequate for planning.
I dare not speak out,
but I can swear an oath."
Zǐjiā said:
"Since you have spoken thus,
what need is there for an oath?"
He informed Běiguō Zǐchē.
Zǐchē said:
"Each man has his own way of serving his lord,
this is not what I, Zuǒ, can do."
Chén Wénzǐ said to Huánzǐ:
"Disaster is about to occur,
what can we gain from it?"
He replied:
"I have obtained one hundred cartloads of timber from the Qìng clan at Zhuāng."
Wénzǐ said:
"You must guard it carefully."
Lúpú Guǐ and
Wáng Hé divined about attacking the Qìng clan.
They showed the omen to Zǐzhī,
saying:
"Someone divined about attacking an enemy;
I dare to present the omen to you."
Zǐzhī said:
"You will overcome,
and there will be bloodshed."
In winter, the tenth month,
Qìng Fēng was hunting at Lái,
and Chén Wúyǔ accompanied him.
On the day Bǐngchén,
Wénzǐ sent someone to summon him,
and he requested:
"Wúyǔ's mother is gravely ill;
I request to return."
Qìng Jì divined about it,
showed him the omen,
and said:
"Death."
Wúyǔ held the tortoise shell and wept,
so they allowed him to return.
Qìng Sì heard of this,
and said:
"Disaster is about to occur."
He told Zǐjiā:
"Return quickly.
The disaster will certainly occur during the Cháng sacrifice.
If you return, you may still be in time."
Zǐjiā did not listen,
nor did he show any intention to repent.
Zǐxī said:
"He is lost!
If he is fortunate, he may survive in Wú or Yuè."
Chén Wúyǔ crossed the river,
then destroyed the boats and removed the bridge.
Lúpú Jiāng said to Guǐ:
"If you have plans and do not tell me,
you certainly will not succeed."
Guǐ told her.
Jiāng said:
"My husband is stubborn;
no one can stop him.
He will not go out.
I request to stop him."
Guǐ said:
"Agreed."
In the eleventh month, on the day Yǐhài,
the Cháng sacrifice was held in the temple of Tàigōng,
and Qìng Shè presided over the ceremony.
Lúpú Jiāng told him,
and tried to stop him,
but he would not listen,
saying:
"Who would dare?"
Then he went to the duke.
Má Yīng acted as the impersonator of the dead,
and Qìng Xié served as the chief presenter.
Lúpú Guǐ and Wáng Hé held sleeping spears.
The Qìng clan had their armored men surround the duke's palace.
The stablemen of the Chén and Bào clans performed as entertainers.
The horses of the Qìng clan were easily startled,
so the soldiers all removed their armor,
tied up their horses,
and drank wine,
watching the entertainers,
all the way to Yúlǐ.
The followers of Luán, Gāo, Chén, and Bào
put on the armor of the Qìng clan.
Zǐwěi pulled out a rafter,
and struck the door three times.
Lúpú Guǐ stabbed Zǐzhī from behind,
and Wáng Hé struck him with a spear,
severing his left shoulder.
He still clung to a temple rafter,
shaking the roof ridge.
He threw sacrificial vessels and pots,
killing people before he died.
Then they killed Qìng Shéng and Má Yīng.
The duke was frightened.
Bào Guó said:
"The ministers are acting for Your Grace's sake."
Chén Xūwú escorted the duke back,
removed his ceremonial robes, and entered the inner palace.
Qìng Fēng returned,
and encountered someone reporting the disorder.
On the day Dīnghài,
he attacked the west gate,
but did not take it.
He turned back and attacked the north gate,
and took it.
He entered,
attacked the inner palace,
but did not take it.
He retreated,
arrayed his forces at Yuè,
and requested battle,
but it was not granted.
Then he fled here.
He presented a chariot to Jì Wǔzǐ,
its beautiful gloss could serve as a mirror.
Zhǎn Zhuāngshū saw it,
and said:
"The chariot is very glossy,
but its owner must be haggard.
It is fitting that he perished."
Shūsūn Mùzǐ entertained Qìng Fēng to a meal,
and Qìng Fēng performed the sacrifice extravagantly.
Mùzǐ was displeased,
and had the musicians recite the "Máo Chī" for him,
but he did not understand.
Soon after, men of Qí came to reproach him,
and he fled to Wú.
Wú Jùyú gave him Zhūfāng,
where he gathered his clan and settled,
becoming richer than before.
Zǐfú Huìbó said to Shūsūn:
"Heaven seems to enrich the dissolute;
Qìng Fēng is rich again."
Mùzǐ said:
"When a good man becomes rich, it is called a reward;
when a dissolute man becomes rich, it is called a calamity.
Heaven is bringing calamity upon him,
and will gather them together and annihilate them."
B9.28.10 On the day Guǐsì,
the Heavenly King passed away.
The notice had not yet arrived,
so it was not recorded,
which was according to ritual.
B9.28.11 During the disorder of the Cuī clan,
the various princes were lost,
so Chú was in Lǔ,
Shūsūn Huán was in Yān,
and Jiǎ was at Gōudòu zhī Qiū.
When the Qìng clan perished,
they were all summoned back,
provided with their utensils and implements,
and their towns were returned to them.
They offered Yànzǐ the town of Bèidiàn
and its sixty border villages,
but he did not accept.
Zǐwěi said:
"Wealth
is what people desire.
Why do you alone not desire it?"
He replied:
"The Qìng clan's towns satisfied their desires,
so they perished.
My towns do not satisfy my desires;
if I add Bèidiàn to them,
then they would satisfy my desires.
If my desires are satisfied,
my perishing would not be far off.
If I am abroad,
I would not be able to govern even one of my towns.
I do not accept Bèidiàn
not because I dislike wealth,
but because I fear losing wealth.
Moreover, wealth
is like cloth and silk having a fixed width.
One sets a measure for it,
so that it does not change.
The people,
when their livelihood is ample and their resources abundant,
then correct virtue
is used to set a limit for them,
so that they are not arrogant or negligent;
this is called limiting profit.
Excessive profit leads to ruin.
I dare not be greedy for more;
this is what is meant by setting a limit."
They offered Běiguō Zuǒ a town of sixty households,
and he accepted it.
They offered Zǐyǎ a town,
but he declined most and accepted little.
They offered Zǐwěi a town,
and he accepted it but soon returned it.
The duke considered him loyal,
so he was favored.
They exiled Lúpú Piè to the northern border.
They sought Cuī Zhù's corpse,
intending to mutilate it,
but could not find it.
Shūsūn Mùzǐ said:
"It must be found.
King Wǔ had ten ministers of order;
does Cuī Zhù have them?
If not ten,
it is not enough for burial."
Later,
a retainer of the Cuī clan said:
"Give me his large round jade,
and I will present his coffin."
Then they obtained it.
On the first day of the twelfth month, which was yǐhài,
the men of Qí moved Duke Zhuāng’s coffin
and laid it in the great chamber.
They exposed Cuī Zhù’s corpse in the marketplace in his coffin.
The people of the state still recognized it,
and all said,
“It is Cuī Zǐ.”
B9.28.12 Because of the covenant at Sòng,
the Duke went with the Duke of Sòng, the Marquis of Chén, the Earl of Zhèng, and the Viscount of Xǔ to Chǔ.
When the Duke passed through Zhèng,
the Earl of Zhèng was not present.
Bó Yǒu went to meet and entertain him at Huángyá,
but was not respectful.
Shū Mù said:
“If Bó Yǒu does not suffer punishment in Zhèng,
Zhèng is sure to have great calamity.
Respect
is the master of the people;
if it is cast aside,
how can one continue to maintain [the state]?
If the people of Zhèng do not punish him,
they will certainly suffer the consequences.
The duckweed and algae
from the marshes and pools,
when placed in the ancestral temple,
are offered by Jì Lán—
this is respect.
Can respect be cast aside?”
When they reached the Hàn River,
King Kāng of Chǔ died.
The Duke wished to turn back.
Shūzhòng Zhāobó said:
“Our purpose is for Chǔ,
how can it be for one man?
Let us proceed!”
Zǐfú Huìbó said:
“A gentleman has long-term plans,
but a petty man follows the immediate.
If we do not attend to hunger and cold,
who will have leisure to think of what comes after?
It would be better to return for now.”
Shūsūn Mùzǐ said:
“Shūzhòngzǐ is the one to decide this matter;
Zǐfúzǐ
is just beginning his studies.”
Róng Chéngbó said:
“To plan for the long term
is loyalty.”
The Duke then proceeded.
Xiàng Xū of Sòng said:
“Our purpose is for our own state,
not for Chǔ.
If we do not attend to hunger and cold,
who can attend to Chǔ?
Let us return for now and rest the people,
wait until they have established a ruler,
and then make preparations.”
The Duke of Sòng then turned back.
B9.28.13 When Qū Jiàn of Chǔ died,
Zhào Wénzǐ mourned him
as an ally—
this was according to ritual.
B9.28.14 A royal messenger came to announce the mourning,
and when asked the date of the death,
he reported it as jiǎyín.
Therefore it was recorded thus,
to expose the error.
A9.29 The Spring and Autumn Annals, 29th Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.29.1 In the 29th year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the Duke was in Chǔ.
A9.29.2 In summer, in the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from Chǔ.
A9.29.3 On gēngwǔ,
the Marquis of Wèi, Kàn, died.
A9.29.4 A gatekeeper assassinated the Viscount of Wú, Yújì.
A9.29.5 Zhòngsūn Jié met with Xún Yíng of Jìn,
Gāo Zhǐ of Qí,
Huá Dìng of Sòng,
Shìshū Yí of Wèi,
Gōngsūn Duàn of Zhèng,
a man of Cáo,
a man of Jǔ,
a man of Téng,
a man of Xuē,
and a man of Xiǎozhū to wall the city of Qǐ.
A9.29.6 The Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Yǎng to come on a friendly mission.
A9.29.7 The Viscount of Qǐ came to covenant.
A9.29.8 The Viscount of Wú sent Zhá to come on a friendly mission.
A9.29.9 In autumn, in the ninth month,
Duke Xiàn of Wèi was buried.
A9.29.10 Gāo Zhǐ of Qí fled to Běiyān.
A9.29.11 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Jié went to Jìn.
B9.29 The Commentary of Zuǒ, 29th Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.29.1 In the 29th year, in spring, in the first month of the royal calendar,
the Duke was in Chǔ,
explaining why he did not attend the court ceremony in the ancestral temple.
The men of Chǔ made the Duke personally present the burial garments,
which troubled him.
Shū Mù said:
“If you purify the coffin and then present the garments,
it will be like presenting gifts.”
He then had a shaman first purify the coffin with peach branches and brooms.
The men of Chǔ did not stop him,
but later regretted it.
B9.29.2 In the second month, on guǐmǎo,
the men of Qí buried Duke Zhuāng outside the northern wall.
B9.29.3 In summer, in the fourth month,
King Kāng of Chǔ was buried.
The Duke and the Marquis of Chén, the Earl of Zhèng, and the Viscount of Xǔ escorted the funeral procession,
reaching outside the western gate,
while the great officers of the various lords all went to the tomb.
Jiá Áo of Chǔ ascended the throne,
and Prince Wéi became the lìngyǐn.
Zǐyǔ, the messenger of Zhèng, said:
“This is called improper;
he is sure to replace him and flourish.
Beneath the pines and cypresses,
the grass does not grow.”
B9.29.4 When the Duke was returning,
he reached Fāngchéng.
Jì Wǔzǐ seized Biàn
and sent Gōng Yě to inquire,
pursuing him with a sealed letter and giving it to him,
saying:
“I heard that the defender of Biàn was about to rebel,
so I led troops to attack him
and have already taken it.
I dare to report this.”
Gōng Yě delivered the message and withdrew.
When he reached his lodging,
he then heard about the seizure of Biàn.
The Duke said:
“He wanted it and spoke of rebellion—
this only shows his estrangement.”
The Duke said to Gōng Yě:
“May I enter?”
He replied:
“You indeed possess the state;
who would dare oppose you?”
The Duke gave Gōng Yě a ceremonial cap and robes.
He firmly declined,
but was forced to accept them.
The Duke wished not to enter.
Róng Chéngbó recited the poem “Shì Wēi,”
and so he returned.
In the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from Chǔ.
Gōng Yě returned his town to the Jì family
and never entered it thereafter.
He said:
“To deceive one’s lord—
why must he use me?”
When Jì Sūn saw him,
he spoke of the Jì family as on other days;
when he did not see him, he never spoke of the Jì family.
When he fell ill,
he gathered his retainers
and said:
“When I die,
be sure not to bury me in the ceremonial cap and robes—
they were not a reward for virtue.
And do not let the Jì family bury me.”
B9.29.5 When King Líng was buried,
the senior minister of Zhèng had duties [to attend to].
Zǐzhǎn sent Yìn Duàn to go.
Bó Yǒu said:
“He is too young;
it will not do.”
Zǐzhǎn said:
“Rather than no one going,
even if he is young,
is it not still better?
The Odes say:
‘The king’s affairs are never at rest,
I have no leisure to rest at home.’
East, west, south, north—
who dares to remain at ease?
We firmly serve Jìn and Chǔ
in order to protect the royal house.
The king’s affairs allow no neglect;
what constancy is there?”
He then sent Yìn Duàn to go to Zhōu.
B9.29.6 The people of Wú attacked Chǔ,
captured prisoners,
and made one of them a gatekeeper,
assigning him to guard the boats.
Wúzǐ Yújì went to inspect the boats,
and the gatekeeper assassinated him with a knife.
B9.29.7 Zhèng's Zǐ Zhǎn died,
and Zǐ Pí succeeded him.
At that time, Zhèng was suffering from famine,
and before the wheat could be harvested,
the people were in distress.
Zǐ Pí, in accordance with Zǐ Zhǎn's command, provided grain to the people of the state,
one zhōng per household.
Because of this, he won the hearts of Zhèng's people.
Hence, the Hǎn clan consistently held the reins of state government,
serving as the highest ministers.
Sīchéng Zǐ Hǎn of Sòng heard of this
and said:
"To be close to goodness
is the people's hope."
Sòng was also suffering from famine,
so he requested from Duke Píng
to release the state's grain for loans;
he also ordered the senior officials to make loans.
The Sīchéng clan lent grain without recording it,
providing loans for those senior officials who had none.
Thus, there were no starving people in Sòng.
Shū Xiàng heard of this
and said:
"The Hǎn of Zhèng
and the Lè of Sòng
will be the last to perish.
Both of them will likely gain control of their states!
The people turn to them.
They bestow benefits without claiming virtue,
and the Lè clan goes even further in this.
Perhaps they will rise and fall with Sòng!"
B9.29.8 Duke Píng of Jìn
was born of a Qí mother,
so he administered Qí's affairs.
In the sixth month,
Zhì Dàozǐ assembled the senior officials of the various states
to fortify Qí's city walls.
Mèng Xiàobó participated in the meeting,
and Zhèng's Zǐ Tàishū and Bó Shí went as well.
Zǐ Tàishū met with Tàishū Wénzǐ
and spoke with him.
Wénzǐ said:
"How excessive this fortification of Qí is!"
Zǐ Tàishū said:
"What can be done about it!
Jìn does not care about the deficiencies of the Zhōu lineage,
yet shields these remnants of the Xià.
That they are abandoning the various Jī-surnamed states
can also be understood.
If they abandon the various Jī-surnamed states,
to whom will they turn?
I, Jí, have heard that
to abandon one's own and draw close to strangers
is called forsaking virtue.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'In harmony with his neighbors,
his marriages are greatly esteemed.'
Jìn is no longer neighborly,
who will esteem them?"
B9.29.9 Gāo Zǐróng and the Sītú of Sòng went to see Zhì Bó,
with Nǚ Qí assisting in the ceremonies.
After the guests departed,
Sīmǎ Hóu said to Zhì Bó:
"Both of these men will inevitably meet with misfortune.
Zǐróng is autocratic,
the Sītú is extravagant,
both are masters who will ruin their families."
Zhì Bó said:
"How so?"
He replied:
"Autocracy leads to swift retribution,
extravagance will cause one to perish by his own strength,
autocracy means others will truly bring about his ruin;
it will happen soon."
B9.29.10 Fàn Xiànzǐ came on a diplomatic visit,
to acknowledge the fortification of Qí.
The Duke hosted a banquet for him,
and Zhǎn Zhuāngshū presented the ceremonial gifts.
There were three pairs of archers.
As the Duke's own officials were insufficient,
they selected from among the household officials.
Among the household officials,
Zhǎn Xiá and Zhǎn Wángfù formed one pair;
among the Duke's officials,
Gōngwū Zhàobó
and Zhòng Yán Zhuāngshū formed one pair,
Zēng Gǔfǔ and Dǎng Shū formed one pair.
B9.29.11 The Marquis of Jìn sent Sīmǎ Nǚ Shūhóu to
settle Qí's lands,
but he did not return them all.
The wife of Duke Dào of Jìn was displeased and said:
"Shūhóu has taken bribes.
If the former ruler were aware,
he would not approve of this."
The Duke informed Shūhóu.
Shūhóu said:
"Yú, Guó, Jiāo, Huá,
Huò, Yáng, Hán, Wèi
were all of the Jī surname,
and it was by annexing them that Jìn became great.
If we do not encroach upon the small,
from where shall we take land?
From Duke Wǔ and Duke Xiàn onward,
many states have been annexed.
Who has been able to govern them all?
Qí
is a remnant of the Xià,
and has aligned itself with the Eastern barbarians.
Lǔ,
being the descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
maintains friendly relations with Jìn.
It would be acceptable to grant Qí's lands to Lǔ,
so what concern is there?
As for Lǔ's relationship with Jìn,
its tributes are never lacking,
its rare treasures arrive seasonally,
its dukes, ministers, and senior officials come to our court in succession,
our historians never cease recording,
and our treasury receives goods every month.
This being the case is sufficient;
why must we impoverish Lǔ to enrich Qí?
Moreover, if the former ruler were aware,
he would surely side with the lady,
so why would he need an old minister like me?"
B9.29.12 Duke Wén of Qí came
to swear a covenant,
but the record refers to him as
"zǐ" (viscount),
showing contempt for him.
B9.29.13 The Wú prince Zhá came on a diplomatic visit,
met with Shūsūn Mùzǐ,
and was pleased with him.
He said to Mùzǐ:
"I fear you will not die a natural death!
You love goodness but cannot choose the right people.
I have heard that a gentleman's duty lies in selecting people.
You, sir, are the chief minister of the Lǔ lineage,
entrusted with its major governance.
If you are not careful in your recommendations,
how can you bear the responsibility?
Disaster is sure to befall you!"
He requested to observe the Zhōu music.
He had the musicians perform for him the songs of *Zhōunán* and *Shàonán*,
and said:
"Beautiful!
They mark the beginning of the foundation,
though not yet perfected, yet they reflect diligence without resentment."
When they performed for him the songs of *Bèi*, *Yōng*, and *Wèi*,
he said:
"Deeply beautiful!
They express worry but not despair.
I have heard that the virtue of Wèi Kāngshū
and Duke Wǔ was like this;
these must be the *Wèi Fēng*!"
When they performed for him the songs of *Wáng*,
he said:
"Beautiful!
They express longing but not fear;
they must be from the time of Zhōu's eastward move!"
When they performed for him the songs of *Zhèng*,
he said:
"Beautiful!
But they are overly intricate,
the people cannot endure it.
Perhaps Zhèng will be the first to perish!"
When they performed for him the songs of *Qí*,
he said:
"Beautiful,
vast and grand!
Truly the great airs!
To represent the Eastern Sea,
it must be Tàigōng!
The state's potential cannot be measured."
When they performed for him the songs of *Bīn*,
he said:
"Beautiful,
expansive!
Joyful but not excessive;
they must be from the Duke of Zhōu's eastern campaign!"
When they performed for him the songs of *Qín*,
he said: "This is what is called the Xià music.
To be able to embody Xià is to be great;
it is the ultimate greatness,
it must be the old music of Zhōu!"
When they performed for him the songs of *Wèi*,
he said:
"Beautiful,
harmonious and gentle!
Grand yet refined,
profound yet easy to follow.
If one were to assist this with virtue,
then one would be an enlightened ruler."
He performed the "Táng" song for him,
saying:
"How profound are its thoughts!
Does it not carry the lingering customs of the Táotáng clan?
If not,
why are its concerns so far-reaching?
If not the descendants of virtuous rulers,
who could be like this?"
He performed the "Chén" song for him,
saying:
"A state without a ruler,
how can it last long?"
From "Kuài" onward, he offered no criticism.
He performed the "Xiǎo Yǎ" for him,
saying:
"How beautiful!
Thoughtful yet without duplicity,
resentful yet without complaint.
Is this the decline of Zhōu's virtue?
Yet there still remain the people of the former kings."
He performed the "Dà Yǎ" for him,
saying:
"How vast,
how harmonious!
Graceful yet with an upright substance,
is this not the virtue of King Wén?"
He performed the "Sòng" for him,
saying:
"It is the utmost!
Upright yet not arrogant,
graceful yet not yielding,
close yet not oppressive,
distant yet not estranged,
changing yet not excessive,
repeating yet not tiresome,
sorrowful yet not grieving,
joyful yet not unrestrained,
used yet not exhausted,
broad yet not ostentatious,
bestowed yet not wasteful,
taken yet not greedy,
stationary yet not stagnant,
moving yet not drifting.
The five tones are harmonious,
the eight winds are balanced.
Rhythm has its measure,
order has its sequence—
these are shared by all great virtues."
Seeing the dance "Xiàng Xiāo"
and "Nán Yuè,"
he said:
"How beautiful,
yet still with regret."
Seeing the dance "Dà Wǔ,"
he said:
"How beautiful!
The prosperity of Zhōu,
is it not like this?"
Seeing the dance "Sháo Huò,"
he said:
"Great as the sage is,
he still had cause for shame—
such is the difficulty of being a sage."
Seeing the dance "Dà Xià,"
he said:
"How beautiful!
Diligent yet not claiming virtue—
if not Yǔ,
who could have achieved this?"
Seeing the dance "Sháo Xiāo,"
he said:
"Virtue has reached its peak,
how great!
Like heaven covering all,
like earth bearing all.
Even the greatest virtue
cannot surpass this.
This is the ultimate spectacle.
If there are other performances,
I dare not request them."
His mission abroad
was to announce the succession of the new ruler.
Thus, he proceeded to Qí,
where he took a liking to Yàn Píngzhòng,
and said to him:
"You must quickly surrender your fief and official duties.
Without fief or duties,
you can avoid disaster.
The governance of Qí will find its place,
but until it does,
disaster will not cease."
Thus, Yànzǐ, through Chén Huánzǐ,
surrendered his duties and fief,
thereby avoiding the disaster of Luán
and Gāo.
He visited Zhèng,
met Zǐchǎn,
and felt as if they were old acquaintances.
He gave Zǐchǎn a white silk belt,
and Zǐchǎn presented him with a linen garment.
He said to Zǐchǎn:
"The rulers of Zhèng are extravagant;
disaster is approaching.
Governance will surely fall to you.
When you govern,
be cautious and adhere to ritual.
Otherwise,
Zhèng will decline."
He went to Wèi,
and took a liking to Qú Yuàn, Shǐ Gǒu, Shǐ Qiū,
Gōngzǐ Jīng, Gōngshū Fā, and Gōngzǐ Cháo,
saying:
"Wèi has many noble men;
it will have no troubles."
From Wèi, he went to Jìn,
and was about to stay at Qī,
when he heard the sound of bells.
He said:
"How strange!
I have heard that
disputes without virtue
inevitably lead to punishment.
This master, having offended his lord, is here,
and fear is not enough—
what joy can there be?
For this master to be here
is like a swallow nesting on a tent.
Moreover, the lord is in mourning—
how can there be music?"
He then left.
Wénzǐ heard of this
and never listened to music again for the rest of his life.
He went to Jìn,
and took a liking to Zhào Wénzǐ, Hán Xuānzǐ,
and Wèi Xiànzǐ,
saying:
"The power of Jìn
will gather in these three clans!"
He also took a liking to Shūxiàng.
As he was about to depart,
he said to Shūxiàng:
"Strive hard!
The ruler is extravagant,
and there are many capable men;
the great officers are all wealthy.
Governance will shift to the families.
You are fond of uprightness—
you must think of how to avoid disaster."
B9.29.14 In autumn, the ninth month,
Qí's Gōngsūn Chài and Gōngsūn Zào
exiled their great officer Gāo Zhǐ to Běi Yān.
On Yǐwèi day,
he left.
It was recorded as "fled,"
to blame Gāo Zhǐ.
Gāo Zhǐ liked to take credit for affairs,
and was domineering,
so disaster befell him.
B9.29.15 In winter,
Mèng Xiàobó went to Jìn to repay Fàn Shū.
B9.29.16 Because of the Gāo clan's disaster,
Gāo Shù rebelled with Lú.
In the tenth month, on Gēngyín day,
Lǘqiū Yīng led troops to besiege Lú.
Gāo Shù said:
"If the Gāo clan can have descendants,
I will surrender the city."
The people of Qí established Yàn, the great-grandson of Jìngzhòng,
honoring Jìngzhòng.
In the eleventh month, on Yǐmǎo day,
Gāo Shù surrendered Lú and fled to Jìn.
The people of Jìn fortified Mián and placed him there.
B9.29.17 Zhèng's Bó Yǒu sent Gōngsūn Hēi to Chǔ,
but he declined, saying:
"Chǔ and Zhèng are currently hostile,
and sending me there
is to kill me."
Bó Yǒu said:
"It is a family tradition."
Zǐxī said:
"If it is feasible, go;
if difficult, stop.
What family tradition is this?"
Bó Yǒu tried to force him.
Zǐxī grew angry,
and prepared to attack Bó Yǒu's clan,
with the great officers mediating.
In the twelfth month, on Jǐsì day,
the great officers of Zhèng made a covenant at Bó Yǒu's clan.
Bì Chén said:
"This covenant,
how long will it last?
The 'Shī' says:
'When noblemen frequently covenant,
disorder grows.'
Now this is a path to growing disorder.
Disaster will not cease—
it will take three years to resolve."
Rán Míng said:
"Where will the government go?"
Pí Chén said:
"The good replacing the not-good,
is the Mandate of Heaven,
how can one avoid Zǐ Chǎn?
Promotion does not skip ranks,
thus his position is in order.
Selecting the good and promoting him,
then the age will be exalted.
Heaven moreover removes them,
takes away Bó Yǒu's spirit,
Zǐ Xī passes away,
how can one avoid it?
Heaven has afflicted Zhèng for long,
it must make Zǐ Chǎn bring it to rest,
then it can still be settled.
If not,
it will perish."
A9.30 The Annals of Duke Xiāng, Year 30
A9.30.1 In the thirtieth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěi Pí to come on a friendly mission.
A9.30.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
the crown prince Bān of Cài murdered his ruler Gù.
A9.30.3 In the fifth month, on the jiǎwǔ day,
there was a fire in Sòng,
and the Bó Jī of Sòng died.
A9.30.4 The Heavenly King killed his younger brother Nìngfū.
A9.30.5 Prince Xiá fled to Jìn.
A9.30.6 In autumn, in the seventh month,
Shū Gōng went to Sòng,
to bury the Gòng Jī of Sòng.
A9.30.7 Liáng Xiāo of Zhèng fled to Xǔ,
from Xǔ entered Zhèng,
and the people of Zhèng killed Liáng Xiāo.
A9.30.8 In winter, in the tenth month,
they buried Duke Jǐng of Cài.
A9.30.9 Men of Jìn,
Qí,
Sòng,
Wèi,
Zhèng,
Cáo,
Jǔ,
Zhū,
Téng,
Xuē,
Qǐ,
and Xiǎo Zhū met at Chányuān,
because of the fire in Sòng.
B9.30 The Commentary of Duke Xiāng, Year 30
B9.30.1 In the thirtieth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Wěi Pí to come on a friendly mission,
to announce the accession of the new ruler.
Mù Shū asked
how Prince Wéi conducted the government.
He replied:
"We petty men eat
and attend to our duties,
and still fear we cannot fulfill our orders,
and cannot avoid offenses,
how could we know about government?"
He pressed him,
but he did not tell.
Mù Shū told the great officers:
"The Chief Minister of Chǔ will have a great affair,
Zǐ Dàng will assist him in it,
he has concealed the truth."
B9.30.2 Zǐ Chǎn escorted Earl Zhèng to go to Jìn,
Shū Xiàng asked
about the government of Zhèng.
He replied:
"Whether I will get to see it or not,
depends on this year.
Sì and
Liáng are just now contending,
it is not yet known how it will be settled.
If it is settled,
I will get to see it,
then it can be known."
Shū Xiàng said:
"Are they not already reconciled?"
He replied:
"Bó Yǒu is extravagant and obstinate,
Zǐ Xī likes to be above others,
they cannot yield to each other.
Even if they are reconciled,
they still accumulate hatred,
the coming of hatred is not far off."
B9.30.3 In the second month, on the guǐwèi day,
the wife of Duke Dào of Jìn fed the workmen who were walling Qǐ,
a man of Jiàng County was already advanced in years,
having no sons he went,
and participated in the feeding.
Someone doubted his age,
and made him tell his age.
He said:
a petty man,
do not know how to count years.
In the year I was born,
the first month began on the jiǎzǐ day,
there have been four hundred and forty-five jiǎzǐ cycles,
and the last third of the cycle is now three days past."
The officer ran and asked about it at court.
Shī Kuàng said:
"It was the year when Shū Zhòng Huì Bó of Lǔ met Xì Chéngzǐ at Chéngkuāng.
In that year,
the Dí attacked Lǔ,
Shū Sūn Zhuāng Shū then defeated the Dí at Xián,
captured the tall Dí Qiáo Rú and Huǐ and Bào,
and named his sons after them.
That was seventy-three years ago."
Shǐ Zhào said:
"Hài has two heads and six bodies,
the lower two are like the body,
that is the number of days."
Shì Wén Bó said:
"Then it is twenty-six thousand six hundred and sixty days."
Zhào Mèng asked about the county's grand officer,
and it was his subordinate.
He summoned him
and apologized for the fault,
saying: "Wǔ is without talent,
entrusted with your great affairs,
and because Jìn has many troubles,
I could not follow your lead,
causing you to be humiliated in the mud for so long,
it is Wǔ's crime.
I dare apologize for my lack of talent."
Thereupon he gave him office,
making him assist in government.
He declined due to old age.
He gave him land,
made him the ruler's fù táo,
appointed him as the Jiàng County Master,
and dismissed his yù wèi.
At that time, an envoy from Lǔ was in Jìn,
returned, and told the great officers.
Jì Wǔzǐ said:
"Jìn cannot be taken lightly.
It has Zhào Mèng as its great officer,
Bó Xiá as his assistant,
Shǐ Zhào and Shī Kuàng
to consult and deliberate,
and Shū Xiàng and Nǚ Qí
to instruct and protect its ruler.
Its court has many noble men,
how can it be taken lightly!
Strive to serve it, and only then will it be possible."
B9.30.4 In summer, in the fourth month, on the jǐhài day,
the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant with his great officers.
The noble man therefore knew that the troubles of Zhèng would not cease.
B9.30.5 Duke Jǐng of Cài took a wife from Chǔ for Crown Prince Bān,
and had illicit relations with her.
The crown prince murdered Duke Jǐng.
B9.30.6 Formerly,
when Wáng Dān Jì died,
his son Kuò was about to see the king,
and sighed.
Shàn Gōngzǐ Qiānqī was a yù shì for King Líng,
met him in the court,
heard his sigh,
and said:
"Alas!
He must be aiming for this!"
He entered and told the king,
and said:
"You must kill him!
He shows no grief yet his desires are great,
his gaze is restless and his steps are high,
his mind is elsewhere.
If you do not kill him,
he will certainly cause harm."
The king said:
"What does a child know!"
When King Líng passed away,
Dān Kuò wanted to set up Prince Nìngfū.
Nìngfū did not know.
On the wùzǐ day,
Dān Kuò surrounded Wěi,
and drove out Chéng Qiān.
Chéng Qiān fled to Píngzhì.
In the fifth month, on the guǐsì day,
Yǐn Yánduō, Liú Yì, Shàn Miè,
Gān Guò, and Gǒng Chéng killed Nìngfū.
Kuò, Xiá, and Liào fled to Jìn.
The record says, "The Heavenly King killed his younger brother Nìngfū,"
placing the blame on the King.
B9.30.7 Someone cried out in the great temple of Sòng,
saying:
"Xīxī,
chūchū."
A bird cried at the Bó Shè,
as if saying
"Xīxī."
On the jiǎwǔ day,
a great disaster occurred in Sòng.
Sòng Bójī died,
because she waited for her governess.
The gentleman said of Sòng Gòngjī:
"She acted as a maiden, not as a married woman.
A maiden awaits others;
a married woman acts according to what is appropriate."
B9.30.8 In the sixth month,
Zhèng Zǐchǎn went to Chén to attend a covenant,
and upon returning,
reported back.
He informed the great officers, saying:
"Chén
is a state destined to perish,
and cannot be allied with.
They gather grain and millet,
repair their city walls,
rely on these two things,
yet do not comfort their people.
Their ruler is weak and indecisive,
the princes are extravagant,
the heir apparent is lowly,
the great officers are arrogant,
governance comes from many sources,
and they are situated between great states.
How can they avoid perishing?
It will be no more than ten years."
B9.30.9 In autumn, the seventh month,
Shū Gōng went to Sòng,
to bury Gòngjī.
B9.30.10 The Earl of Zhèng, Bóyǒu, was fond of drink.
He built an underground chamber,
and drank wine at night, striking bells there.
When the court arrived,
he had not yet finished.
Those at court said:
"Where is our lord?"
His attendants said:
"Our lord is in the ravine valley."
They all dispersed from court and left.
Later, at court,
he was about to send Zǐxī
to Chǔ,
and upon returning, drank wine.
On the gēngzǐ day,
Zǐxī, with the armor of the Sì clan,
attacked and burned it.
Bóyǒu fled to Yōngliáng,
and only after sobering up did he learn of it.
Then he fled to Xǔ.
The great officers gathered to deliberate.
Zǐpí said:
"The Zhònghuǐ Zhì says:
'Those who create disorder are to be seized;
those who are perishing are to be humiliated.
Pushing aside the perishing and securing the surviving
is beneficial to the state.'
Hǎn, Sì, and Fēng share the same lineage;
Bóyǒu was arrogant and extravagant,
so he could not avoid this."
People said that Zǐchǎn should align with the upright and assist the strong.
Zǐchǎn said:
"Are they really my companions?
In the state's calamities and difficulties,
who knows where the solution lies?
If someone upholds strength and uprightness,
difficulties will not arise.
Let me simply maintain my position."
On the xīnchǒu day,
Zǐchǎn collected the bodies of the dead from the Bóyǒu clan
and laid them out,
without consulting others
and then departed.
Yìn Duàn followed him.
Zǐpí stopped him.
The crowd said:
"If people do not follow us,
why stop him?"
Zǐpí said:
"Our master shows respect even for the dead,
how much more for the living?"
Then he stopped himself.
On the rényín day,
Zǐchǎn entered.
On the guǐmǎo day,
Zǐshí entered.
They both accepted the covenant at Zǐxī's residence.
On the yǐsì day,
the Earl of Zhèng and his great officers made a covenant at the Tài Gōng,
and made a covenant with the people outside Shīzhīliáng.
When Bóyǒu heard that the people of Zhèng had sworn a covenant against him,
he was angry;
hearing that Zǐpí's armor
had not joined in attacking him,
he was pleased,
and said:
"Zǐpí is with me."
On the guǐchǒu day,
at dawn,
he entered through the drain at the Mùmén,
and with the help of Mǎshī Jié
accessed the Xiāng armory,
to attack the old north gate.
Sì Dài led the people of the state to attack him.
They all summoned Zǐchǎn.
Zǐchǎn said:
"Brothers have come to this;
I will follow what Heaven favors."
Bóyǒu died in the sheep market.
Zǐchǎn draped a shroud over him,
laid his head on his thigh and wept for him,
collected and laid him out among Bóyǒu's servants
who were by the market,
and later buried him at Dǒuchéng.
The Zǐsì clan wanted to attack Zǐchǎn.
Zǐpí was angry with them,
saying:
"Ritual
is the backbone of the state.
To kill one who observes ritual,
there is no greater misfortune."
So they stopped.
At this time, Yóu Jí went to Jìn,
and upon returning,
hearing of the trouble,
did not enter.
He reported back through his deputy.
On the eighth month, jiǎzǐ day,
he fled to Jìn.
Sì Dài pursued him,
reaching Suānzǎo.
With Zǐshàng,
they used two jade guī to pledge in the river.
They sent Gōngsūn Xī to enter and make a covenant with the great officers.
On the jǐsì day,
he returned.
The record says, "The people of Zhèng killed Liáng Xiāo,"
not calling him a great officer,
indicating he entered from outside.
At the time of Zǐjiǎo's death,
when about to be buried,
Gōngsūn Huī and Pí Zào met early to handle affairs.
Passing by Bóyǒu's residence,
they saw weeds growing above his gate.
Zǐyǔ said:
"Are those weeds still there?"
At that time, the year-star was in Jiànglóu,
and Jiànglóu was at its zenith at dawn.
Pí Zào pointed to it,
saying:
"He can still last out the year,
but the year-star will not reach this position again."
When he perished,
the year-star was at the mouth of Jūzī,
and the next year it reached Jiànglóu.
Pú Zhǎn followed Bóyǒu,
and died with him.
Yǔ Jié fled to Jìn,
and became a great officer of Rèn.
At the Jīzé meeting,
Yuè Chéng of Zhèng fled to Chǔ,
and then went to Jìn.
Yǔ Jié relied on him,
allied with him and served Zhào Wénzǐ,
proposing plans to attack Zhèng.
Because of the Sòng covenant,
it was not permissible.
Zǐpí made Gōngsūn Chú the Master of Horses.
B9.30.11 The Chǔ prince Wéi killed the Grand Marshal Wěi Yǎn
and seized his household.
Shēn Wúyǔ said:
"The prince will certainly not escape misfortune.
Good men
are the pillars of the state.
The prince assists the state of Chǔ,
should be fostering such men,
yet he oppresses them,
which brings calamity to the state.
Moreover, the Marshal
is the assistant to the Lingyǐn,
and the four limbs of the king.
To cut off the pillars of the people,
remove one's own assistant,
sever the king's limbs,
and bring calamity to the state—
there is no greater inauspiciousness.
How can he escape?"
B9.30.12 Because of the disaster in Sòng,
the great officers of the various states held a meeting,
to plan the sending of aid to Sòng.
In winter, in the tenth month,
Shūsūn Bào met with Zhào Wǔ of Jìn, Gōngsūn Chài of Qí,
Xiàng Xū of Sòng, Běigōng Tuó of Wèi,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng, and the great officers of Xiǎo Zhū at Chányuān.
Afterwards, they did not send aid to Sòng,
therefore the text does not record their names.
The gentleman says:
"Is it not indeed necessary to be careful about good faith?
At the meeting of Chányuān,
the high ministers are not recorded,
because they were not trustworthy.
The chief ministers of the states,
meeting and yet not being trustworthy,
have abandoned both favor and reputation.
That one must not be untrustworthy is thus.
The Odes says:
'King Wén ascends and descends,
on the left and right of God.'
This speaks of trustworthiness.
It also says:
'Be careful and good in your demeanor,
do not bear your hypocrisy.'
This speaks of untrustworthiness."
The text says:
"So-and-so and so-and-so met at Chányuān,
because of the disaster in Sòng."
This is to blame them.
It does not record the great officer of Lǔ,
to conceal it.
B9.30.13 Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng handed over the government to Zǐchǎn.
He declined, saying:
"The state is small and pressed upon,
the clans are large and many hold favor;
it cannot be governed."
Hǎn Hǔ said:
"I, Hǔ, will lead them to obey you;
who would dare to oppose you?
You should skillfully assist them.
A state is not small;
if small, it can serve the great,
and the state will then be at ease."
Zǐchǎn took up the government.
When he had business with Bó Shí,
he bribed him with a city.
Zǐ Dàshū said:
"The state is the state of all;
why bribe him alone?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"To have no desires is truly difficult.
If they all get what they desire,
to follow their affairs,
and we demand their success.
If it is not I who achieve success,
is it then others?
Why begrudge a city,
where will the city go?"
Zǐ Dàshū said:
"What about the neighboring states?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"They are not opposing each other,
but are following each other;
what blame is there from the neighboring states?
The Zhèng Shū has it:
'To stabilize the state and family,
one must first attend to the great.'
Let us first pacify the great
and await their return."
Afterwards, Bó Shí became fearful
and returned the city,
but in the end it was given to him.
After Bó Yǒu died,
he had the Grand Scribe order Bó Shí
to become a minister.
He declined.
The Grand Scribe withdrew,
then he requested the order.
When the order was given again,
he declined again.
This happened three times,
then he accepted the tablet and entered to bow.
Zǐchǎn therefore disliked his character,
and placed him in a position below his own.
Zǐchǎn made the capital and countryside
have regulations,
and high and low have their proper duties;
fields had boundaries and ditches,
and hamlets and wells were organized into groups of five.
Among the great men, those who were loyal and frugal,
he followed and favored;
those who were extravagant and arrogant,
he thereby ruined.
Fēng Juàn was about to sacrifice,
and requested permission to hunt.
It was not permitted,
saying:
"Only the ruler uses fresh game,
the multitude have enough."
Zǐzhāng was angry,
withdrew and levied troops.
Zǐchǎn fled to Jìn,
Hǎn Hǔ stopped him,
and expelled Fēng Juàn.
Fēng Juàn fled to Jìn.
Zǐchǎn requested his fields and hamlets,
and after three years restored him,
returning his fields, hamlets, and their income.
After one year in government,
the common people chanted about him,
saying:
"He takes our clothes and caps and stores them,
he takes our fields and organizes them.
Who will kill Zǐchǎn,
we will join him."
After three years,
they chanted again,
saying:
"We have sons and younger brothers,
Zǐchǎn teaches them;
we have fields,
Zǐchǎn makes them productive.
If Zǐchǎn dies,
who will succeed him?"
A9.31 The Classic of the Thirty-first Year of Duke Xiāng
A9.31.1 In the thirty-first year, in spring,
the royal first month.
A9.31.2 In summer, in the sixth month, on Xīnsì,
the duke died in the Chǔ palace.
A9.31.3 In autumn,
in the ninth month, on Guǐsì,
Zǐyě died.
A9.31.4 On Jǐhài,
Zhòngsūn Jié died.
A9.31.5 In winter, in the tenth month,
the viscount of Téng came to attend the burial.
A9.31.6 On Guǐyǒu,
we buried our ruler, Duke Xiāng.
A9.31.7 In the eleventh month,
the people of Jǔ assassinated their ruler, Mìzhōu.
B9.31 The Commentary of the Thirty-first Year of Duke Xiāng
B9.31.1 In the thirty-first year, in spring,
the royal first month,
Mùshū arrived from the meeting.
He saw Mèng Xiàobó,
and said to him:
"Zhào Mèng is about to die.
His speech is careless,
not like a ruler of the people.
Moreover, he is not yet fifty years old,
yet he drones on like an eighty- or ninety-year-old;
he cannot last long.
If Zhào Mèng dies,
the one who will govern will be Hánzǐ!
Why don't you speak with Jìsūn about this,
so that we can establish good relations;
he is a gentleman.
The ruler of Jìn is about to lose his government.
If we do not establish relations,
and make early preparations for Lǔ,
afterwards when the government is with the great officers,
Hánzǐ is weak,
the great officers are mostly greedy,
their demands and desires are insatiable,
Qí and Chǔ are not sufficient to rely on,
Lǔ will be in fear!"
Xiàobó said:
"How long is a man's life?
Who can avoid being careless?
We cannot see from morning to evening;
what use is establishing relations?"
Mùshū went out,
and told people:
"Mèngsūn is about to die.
I told him about Zhào Mèng's carelessness,
and he is even worse."
He also spoke with Jìsūn about the affairs of Jìn,
but Jìsūn did not listen.
When Zhào Wénzǐ died,
the ducal house of Jìn was weakened,
and the government was with the extravagant families.
Hán Xuānzǐ governed,
but could not plan for the various states.
Lǔ could not bear the demands of Jìn,
slander and evil were widespread,
therefore there was the meeting of Píngqiū.
B9.31.2 Zǐ Wěi of Qí, who harbored ill will towards Lǘqiū Yīng,
wanted to kill him,
and sent him to lead troops to attack Yángzhōu.
Our state inquired about the reason for the army's action.
In the summer, in the fifth month,
Zǐ Wěi killed Lǘqiū Yīng,
to placate our army.
Gōnglóu Sǎ, Shěng Zào, Kǒng Huǐ,
and Jiǎ Yín fled to Jǔ.
The other princes were expelled.
B9.31.3 The Duke built a palace in the style of Chǔ.
Mù Shū said:
"The Great Oath states:
'What the people desire,
Heaven is sure to grant.'
Our lord desires Chǔ,
and therefore built its palace.
If he does not go to Chǔ again,
he is sure to die in this palace."
On the xīnsì day of the sixth month,
the Duke died in the Chǔ-style palace.
Shūzhòng Dài
secretly took the large jade disc
and gave it to a palace attendant,
placing it in his bosom,
and then retrieved it,
for which he incurred blame.
Zǐ Yě, the son of Jìngguī, a woman of Hú,
was established,
and resided with the Jì clan.
In autumn, on the guǐsì day of the ninth month,
he died,
due to excessive grief.
B9.31.4 On the jǐhài day,
Mèng Xiàobó died.
Gōngzǐ Chóu, the son of Qíguī, the younger sister of Jìngguī, was established.
Mù Shū disapproved,
saying:
"When the crown prince dies,
if there is a full brother,
he should be established; if not, the eldest should be established.
If the ages are equal, choose the worthy;
if virtue is equal,
then divine by oracle,
as is the ancient way.
Since he is not the proper heir,
why must it be the son of a younger sister?
Moreover, this man,
during mourning shows no sorrow,
and in grief has a cheerful countenance,
which is called lacking measure.
A person lacking measure
seldom avoids causing trouble.
If he is indeed established,
he will surely bring worry to the Jì clan."
Wǔzǐ did not listen,
and eventually established him.
By the time of the burial,
he had changed his mourning garments three times,
yet the lapels of the mourning robes were as worn as the old ones.
At this time, Duke Zhāo was nineteen years old,
yet still had a childish heart.
The gentleman therefore knew
that he would not come to a good end.
B9.31.5 In winter, in the tenth month,
Duke Chéng of Téng came to attend the burial,
but was negligent and shed many tears.
Zǐfú Huìbó said:
"The lord of Téng is about to die.
He is negligent in his duties,
yet his grief is excessive,
which is an omen of death.
How can he avoid following it?"
B9.31.6 On the guǐyǒu day,
Duke Xiāng was buried.
In the month of the Duke's death,
Zǐchǎn accompanied the Earl of Zhèng to Jìn,
but the Marquis of Jìn, due to our mourning,
did not receive them.
Zǐchǎn had
the walls of the guesthouse completely demolished
and brought in the carriages and horses.
Shì Wénbó reproached him,
saying:
"Our humble state, due to poor governance and lax laws,
is filled with bandits and robbers,
and we are unable to protect the envoys of the various lords who come to visit our ruler.
Therefore, we ordered officials to repair the guest quarters,
raising the gateways,
thickening the walls,
so that the envoys would have no worries.
Now you, sir, have destroyed them.
Even if your attendants can guard against danger,
what about other guests?
As our humble state is the leader of the alliance,
we repair and maintain the walls
to receive guests.
If all were to destroy them,
how could we fulfill our duties?
My ruler sent me, Gài, to inquire your intentions."
Zǐchǎn replied:
"Our humble state is small and narrow,
situated between great states,
and demands for tribute come at any time.
Therefore, we dare not rest in peace,
but gather all our resources,
to come and attend to affairs in a timely manner.
Encountering that your officials are occupied,
we have not been received;
nor have we received any instructions,
not knowing when we will be received.
We dare not deliver the tribute,
nor dare we leave it exposed.
If we deliver it,
it becomes the property of your ruler's treasury,
and unless it is properly presented,
we dare not deliver it.
If we leave it exposed,
we fear it may be damaged by untimely dryness or dampness
and rot or be eaten by insects,
thereby increasing the fault of our humble state.
I, Qiáo, have heard that when Duke Wén was the leader of the alliance,
his own palaces were low and humble,
with no towers or pavilions,
but he exalted and enlarged the guesthouses for the lords,
making them like his own sleeping quarters;
storehouses and stables were repaired,
the Minister of Works timely
leveled the roads,
and plasterers timely plastered the walls of the guesthouses;
when the lords' guests arrived,
the Diàn official set torches in the courtyard,
and servants patrolled the palace;
carriages and horses had their places,
guests' attendants were relieved of their duties,
the carriage official greased the axles,
and the servants, herdsmen, and grooms
each attended to their tasks;
the various officials
each displayed their wares;
the Duke did not detain guests,
yet no duties were neglected;
he shared their joys and sorrows,
and inspected affairs when necessary;
he instructed them in what they did not know,
and sympathized with their shortcomings.
Guests felt at home,
with no fear of disaster;
they neither feared bandits and robbers,
nor worried about dryness or dampness.
Now the palace at Tóngdī extends for miles,
yet the lords are lodged in servants' quarters,
the gates cannot admit carriages,
and one cannot pass over them;
robbers and thieves operate openly,
and epidemics are not guarded against.
Guests have no fixed time for audience,
and instructions are unpredictable.
If we do not demolish the walls,
we have no place to store the tribute
and will only increase our fault.
I venture to ask your officials:
what instructions do you have for us?
Although your ruler has the mourning of Lǔ,
it is also a sorrow for our humble state.
If we are allowed to present the tribute,
we will repair the walls and depart,
which would be your ruler's kindness,
and how would we dare fear toil?"
Wénbó reported back.
Zhào Wénzǐ said:
"He is right.
I am indeed lacking in virtue,
using servants' quarters to house the lords,
which is my fault."
He sent Shì Wénbó to apologize for his lack of discernment.
The Marquis of Jìn received the Earl of Zhèng,
with enhanced courtesy,
treated him generously with feasts and gifts, and sent him back.
Then he built guesthouses for the lords.
Shūxiàng said:
"The importance of rhetoric is indeed like this!
Zǐchǎn is skilled in rhetoric,
and the lords benefit from it.
How can one neglect rhetoric?
The Book of Songs says:
'When words are harmonious,
the people are united;
when words are pleasing,
the people are at peace.'
He understands this."
B9.31.7 Zǐ Pí of Zhèng sent Yìn Duàn to Chǔ,
to report his visit to Jìn,
which was according to ritual.
B9.31.8 The Jǔ ruler Líbǐgōng had sons Qùjí and Zhǎnyǔ.
After establishing Zhǎnyǔ as heir,
he deposed him.
Líbǐgōng was cruel,
and the people of the state were troubled by him.
In the eleventh month,
Zhǎnyǔ, relying on the people of the state, attacked the ruler of Jǔ,
killed him,
and then took the throne.
Qùjí fled to Qí,
for he was born of a Qí mother.
Zhǎnyǔ,
was born of a Wú mother.
The record says:
"The people of Jǔ killed their ruler Mǎizhūchú",
indicating where the guilt lies.
B9.31.9 The ruler of Wú sent Qū Húyōng
on a diplomatic mission to Jìn,
to open a route of communication.
Zhào Wénzǐ asked him,
saying:
"Will Jìzǐ of Yánzhōulái indeed be established?
Cháo caused the death of Zhūfán,
a gatekeeper murdered Dàiwú.
Heaven seems to be opening the way for him.
What do you think?"
He replied:
"He will not be established.
These were the fated ends of those two kings,
not an opening for Jìzǐ.
If Heaven is opening a way,
surely it is for the present heir!
He is very virtuous and measured.
Virtue does not lose the people,
measure does not fail in affairs.
The people are close and affairs are orderly,
this is what Heaven is opening the way for.
He who will possess the state of Wú,
must in the end be the descendants of this ruler.
Jìzǐ
is one who maintains integrity.
Even if he had the state,
he would not take the throne."
B9.31.10 In the twelfth month,
Běigōng Wénzǐ, accompanying Duke Xiāng of Wèi,
went to Chǔ,
because of the covenant at Sòng.
Passing through Zhèng,
Yìn Duàn went to meet and offer refreshments at Fěilín,
following the protocol of a diplomatic reception
but using words of greeting.
Wénzǐ entered to present his credentials.
Zǐyǔ acted as the reception officer,
Féng Jiǎnzǐ and Zǐ Tàishū went to meet the guests.
When the business was concluded and they came out,
Wénzǐ spoke to the Marquis of Wèi, saying:
"Zhèng has propriety.
This will be a blessing for several generations;
surely they will not incur the punitive expeditions of a great state!
The *Odes* say:
'Who can handle heat
without going to wash?'
Propriety in governance
is like having washing for heat.
Washing relieves the heat,
what trouble can there be?"
When Zǐchǎn conducted governance,
he selected the capable and employed them:
Féng Jiǎnzǐ could decide major affairs;
Zǐ Tàishū was handsome, elegant, and cultured;
Gōngsūn Huī could understand the actions of the four neighboring states,
and was discerning about the clan names,
ranks,
status,
and capabilities of their great officers,
and was also skilled at diplomatic speech;
Píchén could devise plans,
planning in the countryside he succeeded,
planning in the city he did not.
When the state of Zhèng was to have business with the feudal lords,
Zǐchǎn would then inquire
about the actions of the four states from Zǐyǔ,
and also have him draft much of the diplomatic correspondence;
he would take a carriage with Píchén to go to the countryside,
to have him plan what was feasible;
and then inform Féng Jiǎnzǐ to have him make the decision.
When the plan was formed,
he would then entrust it to Zǐ Tàishū to have him execute it,
to respond to the guests,
and therefore they rarely had failures.
This is what Běigōng Wénzǐ meant by
having propriety.
B9.31.11 The people of Zhèng would stroll in the village schools,
to discuss the administration.
Ránmíng said to Zǐchǎn:
"What about abolishing the village schools?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"Why?
People morning and evening, after their duties, go there to stroll,
and discuss what is good and bad in the administration.
What they approve of,
I then implement;
what they dislike,
I then change.
They are my teachers.
Why abolish them?
I have heard that loyalty and goodness reduce resentment,
not that authority is used to prevent resentment.
Could one not stop it quickly?
But it is like damming a river.
When a great breach occurs,
the harm to people is sure to be great,
and I cannot save it.
Better a small breach to channel it;
better I hear of it and take it as medicine."
Ránmíng said:
"From now on, I, Miè, know that you, sir, can indeed be relied upon.
I am truly without talent.
If this is indeed carried out,
the state of Zhèng will truly rely on it.
How could it be only for two or three ministers?"
Zhòngní heard these words,
and said:
"Judging from this,
when people say Zǐchǎn is not benevolent,
I do not believe it."
B9.31.12 Zǐpí wished to make Yǐn Hé administrator of a town.
Zǐchǎn said:
"He is young;
I do not know if he can."
Zǐpí said:
"He is honest;
I care for him,
he would not betray me.
Send him there to learn;
he will also come to know more about governance."
Zǐchǎn said:
"No.
When one cares for a person,
one seeks to benefit him.
Now you, sir, caring for a person
give him administration.
This is like not yet knowing how to wield a knife
and making him cut;
the harm would indeed be great.
Your caring for a person
only harms him;
who would then dare seek your affection?
You, sir, for the state of Zhèng,
are its pillar.
If the pillar breaks and the rafters collapse,
I, Qiáo, will be crushed.
How dare I not speak fully?
If you have fine brocade,
you would not have someone learn tailoring on it.
High office and large towns
are what one's person relies on for shelter,
yet you would have a learner tailor them?
Are they not of greater value than fine brocade?
I have heard one learns and then enters administration;
I have not heard one uses administration to learn.
If this is indeed done,
there will surely be harm.
It is like hunting:
skilled in archery and charioteering,
one can then catch game.
If one has never mounted a chariot to shoot or drive,
then one fears overturning and being crushed in defeat;
what leisure is there to think of catching game?"
Zǐpí said:
"Excellent!
I, Hǔ, am not perceptive.
I have heard that the nobleman strives to know the greater
and more distant things;
the petty man strives to know the smaller and nearer things.
I
am a petty man.
Clothes are attached to my person,
I know them and am careful with them;
high office and large towns are what shelter my person,
I distantly neglect them.
Without your words,
I would not have known.
Formerly I said,
you govern the state of Zhèng,
I govern my household,
to shelter myself,
that would suffice.
Now I know it is insufficient.
From now on I ask,
even my household affairs,
to follow your guidance."
Zǐchǎn said:
"People's minds differ just as their faces do;
how dare I say your face is like mine?
But if in my heart I deem something dangerous,
I also tell you of it."
Zǐpí considered him loyal,
and therefore entrusted the government to him.
Zǐchǎn was thus able to govern the state of Zhèng.
B9.31.13 The Marquis of Wèi was in Chǔ.
Běigōng Wénzǐ,
observing the demeanor of Lìngyǐn Wéi,
said to the Marquis of Wèi:
"The Lìngyǐn resembles a ruler;
he harbors other ambitions.
Even if he achieves his ambition,
he will not be able to maintain it to the end.
The Odes say:
'Nothing is without a beginning,
but few things can reach their end.'
To reach the end is truly difficult;
the Lìngyǐn will likely not escape misfortune."
The Duke said:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"The Odes say:
'Reverently careful in his dignified demeanor,
he is the pattern for the people.'
The Lìngyǐn lacks dignified demeanor;
the people have no pattern in him.
When the people do not take him as a pattern,
yet he occupies a position above them,
how can he last out his generation?"
The Duke said: "Excellent!
What is meant by 'dignified demeanor'?"
He replied:
"Having awe-inspiring authority is called 'wēi' (威);
having a proper, exemplary manner is called 'yí' (儀).
A ruler has the dignified demeanor of a ruler;
his ministers stand in awe of him and love him,
take him as their pattern and emulate him.
Therefore, he is able to possess his state and family,
and his good reputation lasts for generations.
A minister has the dignified demeanor of a minister;
his subordinates stand in awe of him and love him.
Therefore, he is able to maintain his office and duties,
preserve his clan, and bring harmony to his family.
Following this principle, all below are like this,
and thus superiors and inferiors
are able to secure each other.
The Odes of Wèi say:
'His dignified demeanor is abundant,
it cannot be chosen against.'
This speaks of how ruler and minister, superior and inferior, father and son,
elder and younger brother, inner and outer, great and small
all have their dignified demeanor.
The Odes of Zhōu say:
'Friends assist each other,
assisting with dignified demeanor.'
This speaks of how the way of friends must involve instructing each other
in dignified demeanor.
The Documents of Zhōu enumerate the virtues of King Wén,
saying:
'Great states feared his power,
small states cherished his virtue.'
This speaks of standing in awe and loving him.
The Odes say:
'Without knowledge or scheming,
he followed the rules of God.'
This speaks of taking him as a pattern and emulating him.
King Zhòu imprisoned King Wén for seven years;
the feudal lords all followed him into imprisonment.
Zhòu, because of this, became afraid and returned him to his state.
This can be called loving him.
King Wén attacked Chóng;
after a second campaign
they submitted and became his subjects.
The Mán and Yí tribes all followed and submitted.
This can be called fearing him.
The achievements of King Wén
were recited and celebrated with song and dance throughout the world.
This can be called taking him as a pattern.
The conduct of King Wén
remains a model to this day.
This can be called emulating him.
He possessed dignified demeanor.
Therefore, a nobleman in office inspires awe,
his acts of generosity inspire love,
his advances and withdrawals are measurable,
his social interactions are exemplary,
his appearance and bearing are admirable,
his actions are worthy of imitation,
his virtuous conduct is worthy of emulation,
his voice and spirit inspire delight;
his movements are cultured,
his speech is well-ordered.
When he presides over his subordinates in this manner,
he is said to possess dignified demeanor."
A10.1 The Classic, First Year of Zhāogōng
A10.1.1 First year, spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke took his seat.
A10.1.2 Shūsūn Bào met with Zhào Wǔ of Jìn,
Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Wéi,
Guó Ruò of Qí,
Xiàng Xū of Sòng,
Qí È of Wèi,
Chén's Gōngzǐ Zhāo,
Cài's Gōngsūn Guīshēng,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng,
a man of Xǔ,
and a man of Cáo at Guó.
A10.1.3 Third month,
took Yùn.
A10.1.4 Summer,
the younger brother of the Earl of Qín, Zhēn, fled to Jìn.
A10.1.5 Sixth month, dīngsì day,
the Viscount of Zhū, Huá, died.
A10.1.6 Xún Wú of Jìn led an army and defeated the Dí at Dàlǔ.
A10.1.7 Autumn,
Jǔ's Qùjí entered Jǔ from Qí.
Jǔ's Zhǎnyú fled to Wú.
A10.1.8 Shū Gōng led an army to demarcate the fields of Yùn.
A10.1.9 Buried Duke Dào of Zhū.
A10.1.10 Winter, eleventh month, jǐyǒu day,
the Viscount of Chǔ, Jūn, died.
A10.1.11 Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Bǐ fled to Jìn.
B10.1 The Commentary, First Year of Zhāogōng
B10.1.1 First year, spring,
Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Wéi went on a friendly mission to Zhèng,
and also to take a wife from the Gōngsūn Duàn family.
Wǔ Jǔ served as his assistant.
As they were about to enter the guesthouse,
the people of Zhèng disliked him,
and sent the Diplomat Zǐyǔ to speak with him.
They then lodged outside the city.
After the friendly visit,
he was about to enter with his multitude to receive the bride.
Zǐchǎn was troubled by this,
and sent Zǐyǔ to decline,
saying:
"Because our humble city is narrow and small,
it is insufficient to accommodate your followers.
We request to level a ground altar and await your commands there."
The Lìngyǐn ordered the Grand Steward Bózhōu Lí to reply,
saying:
"Our ruler has condescended to bestow upon our humble minister Wéi,
saying that Wéi will be sent to have the Lady of the Fēng clan as his wife.
Wéi has set out the mats and tables,
and reported in the ancestral temples of [Duke] Zhuāng and [Duke] Gòng before coming.
If you bestow her upon him in the wilds,
this is to cast our ruler's gracious gift into the weeds,
and it is to prevent our humble minister from being ranked among the high ministers.
Not only this,
but it also causes Wéi to deceive his former rulers,
and he will be unable to serve as an elder of our ruler,
and will have nothing with which to return.
We ask you, Great Officer, to consider this."
Zǐyǔ said:
"A small state is not at fault;
relying [on a great state] is truly its fault.
It intended to rely on a great state to pacify itself,
but could it be that you harbor treacherous intentions to plot against it?
If a small state loses what it relies on,
and this serves as a warning to the feudal lords,
causing none not to harbor resentment,
to resist and disobey your ruler's commands,
we fear this will lead to obstruction and your orders not being carried out.
If it were not so,
our humble city
is like a keeper of guesthouses for you;
how would we dare to begrudge the ancestral temple of the Fēng clan?"
Wǔ Jǔ, knowing they were prepared,
requested to enter with their quivers hanging empty.
They permitted it.
First month, yǐwèi day,
he entered,
received the bride, and came out.
Subsequently, they met at Guó,
renewing the covenant of Sòng.
Qí Wǔ said to Zhào Wénzǐ:
"At the covenant of Sòng,
the men of Chǔ got their way over Jìn.
Now, the Lìngyǐn's lack of good faith
is known among the feudal lords.
If you, Sir, are not on guard,
I fear it will be like Sòng again.
Zǐmù's good faith was praised by the feudal lords,
yet he still deceived Jìn and got the upper hand;
how much more one who is especially lacking in good faith?"
Chǔ having gained the upper hand over Jìn,
this is a disgrace to Jìn.
You have served as minister of Jìn,
acting as leader of the covenant alliance,
for seven years now.
Twice you have assembled the feudal lords,
thrice assembled their ministers,
subdued Qí and the Dí,
pacified the eastern Xià,
quelled the disorder of Qín,
fortified Chúnyú,
yet your armies have not been wearied,
the state has not been exhausted,
the people have not voiced slander or complaint,
the feudal lords bear no resentment,
and Heaven has sent no great calamities.
This is due to your efforts.
You have established a fine reputation,
yet to end it with disgrace—
this is what Wǔ fears.
You, sir, must certainly take warning."
Wénzǐ said:
"Wǔ accepts your instruction.
However, at the covenant of Sòng,
Zǐmù harbored a heart that brings harm to others,
while Wǔ possessed a heart of benevolence.
This is why Chǔ surpassed Jìn.
Now, Wǔ still holds to this heart,
while Chǔ again acts treacherously.
This is not what will cause harm.
Wǔ will take faithfulness as his foundation,
and follow it in his actions.
It is like a farmer
who weeds and mounds the soil.
Though there may be famine,
there will surely be abundant years.
Moreover, I have heard that
one who can be faithful will not be subordinate to others.
I have not yet achieved this.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Without deceit, without harm,
rarely does one not become a model.'
This is about faithfulness.
One who can be a model for others
will not be subordinate to others.
My difficulty lies in not being able to achieve this;
Chǔ does not pose a worry."
The Chǔ prime minister Wéi requested to use a sacrificial animal, read the old covenant document, and place it upon the animal, and that would be all.
The people of Jìn agreed.
On the jiǎchén day of the third month,
they made the covenant.
The Chǔ prince Wéi arranged his ceremonial attire and had his guards stand apart.
Shūsūn Mùzǐ said:
