"The Chǔ prince is splendid indeed,
like a ruler!"
Zhèng's Zǐpí said:
"Two halberd-bearers precede him."
Cài's Zǐjiā said:
"Having a Pú palace and a vanguard,
is that not permissible?"
Chǔ's Bó Zhōulí said:
"On this journey,
he borrowed these from our ruler by way of excuse."
Zhèng's diplomatic officer Huī said:
"Borrowed, but not returned."
Bó Zhōulí said:
"You should rather worry about Zǐxī's desire to rebel and act recklessly."
Zǐyǔ said:
"The one who faced the wall is still present.
If he borrows and does not return,
will you have no worries?"
Qí's Guózǐ said:
"I pity these two gentlemen."
Chén's prince Zhāo said:
"Without worry, how can there be accomplishment?
These two gentlemen are enjoying themselves."
Wèi's Qízǐ said:
"If one understands the situation,
even if worried, what harm is there?"
Sòng's Hé Zuǒshī said:
"The great state gives the orders,
the small states respectfully comply.
I only know to comply."
Jìn's Yuè Wángfù said:
"The final stanza of 'Xiǎo Mín' is excellent;
I follow it."
After withdrawing from the meeting,
Zǐyǔ said to Zǐpí:
"Shūsūn was incisive yet tactful,
Sòng's Zuǒshī was concise and proper,
Yuè Wángfù was respectful and reverent,
you and Zǐjiā maintained your positions,
all are lords capable of preserving their lineages.
The ministers of Qí, Wèi, and Chén will likely not escape trouble!
Guózǐ pities others on their behalf,
Zǐzhāo finds pleasure in worry,
Qízǐ, though worried, sees no harm.
To worry about what does not concern one,
and to take pleasure in what should be cause for worry,
and to worry yet see no harm—
these are all ways to invite worry,
and worry will surely reach them.
The *Great Declaration* says:
'What the people desire,
Heaven is sure to comply.'
These three ministers have given omens of worry;
can worry fail to arrive?
From words, one knows the outcome;
this saying refers to just this."
B10.1.2 Jì Wǔzǐ attacked Jǔ,
and took Yùn.
The people of Jǔ reported it at the meeting.
Chǔ reported to Jìn, saying:
"The renewal of the covenant is not yet concluded,
yet Lǔ attacks Jǔ,
defiling the covenant of alliance.
We request to execute their envoy."
Yuè Huánzǐ, assisting Zhào Wénzǐ,
sought goods from Shūsūn,
and made a plea on his behalf.
He sent someone to ask for a belt,
but it was not given.
Liángqí Jìng said:
"Goods are to protect one's person;
why do you begrudge them?"
Shūsūn said:
"The meeting of feudal lords
is to guard the altars of soil and grain.
If I use goods to escape punishment,
Lǔ will surely be attacked by armies.
This would bring disaster upon it;
what guarding would that be?
One has walls
to block out evil.
If the walls develop cracks and crumble,
whose fault is it?
To guard yet bring evil upon it,
I would be even worse.
Though I resent Jìsūn,
what crime has the state of Lǔ committed?
Shū going out while Jì stays at home
has been the practice for a long time;
whom else can I blame?
However, Fù is covetous of bribes;
if I do not give,
he will not stop."
He summoned the messenger,
tore a strip from his robe's silk and gave it to him,
saying:
"The belt is too narrow."
Zhào Mèng heard of this,
and said:
"Facing trouble yet not forgetting the state—
this is loyalty;
mindful of difficulty yet not overstepping one's office—
this is faithfulness;
planning for the state and forgetting death—
this is steadfastness;
considering these three as guiding principles—
this is righteousness.
Possessing these four qualities,
how can he be executed?"
He then made a request to Chǔ, saying:
"Though Lǔ is at fault,
its officer does not avoid difficulty,
but stands in awe of authority and reveres commands.
If you, sir, pardon him
to encourage your subordinates,
that would be permissible.
If your various officers
at home do not avoid disgrace,
and abroad do not flee from difficulty,
what worries could you have?
Worries arise
from disgrace left unaddressed,
and difficulty not defended against—
this is their origin.
If one can manage these two,
what worries remain?
If one does not pacify the capable,
who will follow?
Lǔ's Shūsūn Bào may be called capable;
I request to pardon him
to pacify the capable.
You, sir, presiding over the meeting, pardon the guilty,
and also reward the worthy;
which feudal lord would not rejoice, looking to Chǔ and turning to it,
viewing the distant as near?
Border towns
shift from one to the other;
what constancy is there?
Under the orders of kings and hegemons,
they delineate their borders,
and establish officials,
raise marker flags,
and set down regulatory commands,
If there is punishment for transgressions,
it still cannot be unified.
Thus, in the time of Yú, there were the Sān Miáo;
in the Xià dynasty, there were Guān and Hù;
in the Shāng dynasty, there were Shēn
and Pī;
in the Zhōu dynasty, there were Xú and Yǎn.
Since there have been no virtuous kings,
the feudal lords have vied for advancement,
taking turns presiding over alliances.
How can this be unified?
Attending to major matters while overlooking minor ones
is sufficient to be an alliance leader.
What need is there for more?
The loss of territory—
which state has not experienced it?
As for those who preside over alliances,
who can adjudicate them?
If Wú and Pú have conflicts,
would the officials of Chǔ care about the alliance?
Regarding the border affairs of Jǔ,
let Chǔ not interfere.
If the feudal lords are not troubled,
would that not be acceptable?
The dispute between Jǔ and Lǔ over Yùn
has lasted a long time.
As long as it does not greatly harm their altars of state,
there is no need to resist.
Eliminate troubles and pardon the good,
and all will strive to encourage one another.
Please consider this."
He firmly pleaded with Chǔ,
and the people of Chǔ agreed,
thus sparing Shūsūn.
B10.1.3 The Lìngyǐn entertained Zhào Mèng
and recited the first chapter of "Dà Míng."
Zhào Mèng recited the second chapter of "Xiǎo Wǎn."
After the ceremony,
Zhào Mèng said to Shū Xiàng:
"The Lìngyǐn considers himself a king.
What do you think?"
He replied:
"The king is weak,
and the Lìngyǐn is strong.
It is possible!
Even if possible,
it will not last."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"Using strength to overcome weakness and then finding peace in it
is unrighteous strength.
If one is unrighteous yet strong,
their downfall will surely be swift.
The *Shī* says:
'Majestic was the royal house of Zhōu,
yet Bāo Sì destroyed it.'
This is unrighteous strength.
If the Lìngyǐn becomes king,
he will surely seek the allegiance of the feudal lords.
Jìn has grown somewhat weak,
and the feudal lords will go to him.
If he gains the allegiance of the feudal lords,
his tyranny will intensify,
and the people will not endure it.
How then can it last?
To seize by strength,
to triumph through unrighteousness,
he will surely take it as his way.
A way of tyranny and cruelty
cannot last long."
B10.1.4 In the summer, the fourth month,
Zhào Mèng, Shūsūn Bào, and the senior official of Cáo entered Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng entertained them together.
Zǐ Pí informed Zhào Mèng of the ceremony.
After the ceremony concluded,
Zhào Mèng recited "Hù Yè."
Zǐ Pí then informed Mù Shū
and told him about it.
Mù Shū said:
"Zhào Mèng wishes for a single offering.
You should follow him."
Zǐ Pí said:
"Dare I?"
Mù Shū said:
"It is what the man desires.
Why would you not dare?"
At the feast,
five sets of offerings in bamboo baskets and wooden vessels were prepared under the tent.
Zhào Mèng declined,
privately saying to Zǐ Chǎn:
"Wǔ has already requested this from the Prime Minister."
Thus, a single offering was used.
Zhào Mèng was the guest of honor.
After the ceremony concluded, the banquet began.
Mù Shū recited "Què Cháo."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Wǔ cannot bear this."
He then recited "Cǎi Fán,"
saying:
"Small states are like the artemisia;
great states examine and use it sparingly.
How can this not be fate?"
Zǐ Pí recited the final chapter of "Yě Yǒu Sǐ Jūn."
Zhào Mèng recited "Cháng Dì,"
and said:
"If we brothers are close and at peace,
even the fierce dog can be made not to bark."
Mù Shū, Zǐ Pí, and the senior official of Cáo rose,
bowed,
raised their rhinoceros-horn cups,
and said:
"Small states rely on you,
knowing they can avoid calamity."
They drank joyfully.
Zhào Mèng went out and said:
"I will not experience this again."
B10.1.5 The Son of Heaven sent Liú Dìnggōng to greet Zhào Mèng at Yǐng,
lodging at Luò Ruì.
Liúzǐ said: "How magnificent are the achievements of Yǔ!
His bright virtue reaches far.
Without Yǔ,
would we not be fish?
You and I wear caps and robes,
governing the people and overseeing the feudal lords—
this is due to the efforts of Yǔ.
Why not also extend Yǔ's achievements and greatly protect the people?"
He replied:
"This old man fears his own crimes and faults.
How can he care for distant matters?
We, my kind, merely eat to survive,
with no plan for the morning in the evening.
How can we think of the long term?"
Liúzǐ returned
and reported to the king, saying:
"As the proverb says, 'The old general grows wise, but dotage overtakes him.'
This must refer to Zhào Mèng!
As the chief minister of Jìn,
overseeing the feudal lords,
yet equating himself with servants,
with no plan for the morning in the evening—
he has abandoned both spirits and people.
If the spirits are angry and the people rebel,
how can he last long?
Zhào Mèng will not live out the year.
If the spirits are angry,
they will not accept his sacrifices;
if the people rebel,
they will not perform their duties.
If sacrifices and duties are not followed,
how can he have long life?"
B10.1.6 Shūsūn returned,
and Zēng Yāo drove Jìsūn to greet him.
From morning until noon, he did not come out.
Zēng Yāo said to Zēng Fù:
"From morning until noon,
I know my offense.
Lǔ governs itself through mutual forbearance.
If we forbear externally
but not internally,
what use is it?"
Fù said:
"Months away,
and now a single morning like this—
what harm is there?
A merchant desires profit,
yet hates the noise?"
Fù said to Shūsūn:
"You may come out now."
Shūsūn pointed to the pillar
and said:
"Even if I dislike this,
can I leave it?"
Then he went out to meet them.
B10.1.7 The younger sister of Xú Wú Fàn of Zhèng was beautiful.
Gōngsūn Chǔ had already betrothed her,
but Gōngsūn Hēi also sent a forceful gift of betrothal fowl.
Fàn was afraid
and informed Zǐ Chǎn.
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"This shows the state lacks governance.
It is not your concern.
Do as you wish."
Fàn requested of the two men
to let the woman choose.
Both agreed.
Zǐ Xī entered in splendid attire,
laid out his gifts, and left.
Zǐ Nán entered in military dress,
shot arrows left and right,
leaped onto his chariot, and departed.
The woman observed them from her room,
and said:
"Zǐ Xī is indeed handsome,
but Zǐ Nán
is a true man.
When husband is husband and wife is wife,
that is what is called proper order."
She then went to Zǐ Nán's house.
Zǐ Xī was enraged.
Later, he donned armor beneath his robes and went to see Zǐ Nán,
intending to kill him and take his wife.
Zǐ Nán learned of this,
seized a halberd and pursued him.
Reaching the crossroads,
he struck him with the halberd.
Zǐ Xī, wounded, returned home
and reported to the senior officials, saying:
"I went to see him with good intentions,
not knowing he harbored treacherous designs,
and thus I was wounded."
All the senior officials discussed the matter.
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"When both sides are equally in the right,
the younger and lower-ranking one is at fault.
The fault lies with Chǔ."
They then arrested Zǐ Nán
and enumerated his offenses,
saying:
"There are five great principles for the state.
You have violated them all.
To stand in awe of the ruler's majesty,
to heed his governance,
to respect the noble,
to serve the elders,
and to support one's kin—
these five are the means by which the state is maintained.
Now, with the ruler in the state,
you resorted to arms;
this shows you do not stand in awe of his majesty.
You violated the laws of the state;
this shows you do not heed his governance.
Zǐ Xī
is a senior minister,
while you
are only a favored minister;
yet you did not defer to him;
this shows you do not respect the noble.
Being young, you showed no restraint;
this shows you do not serve your elders.
You took up arms against your elder cousin;
this shows you do not support your kin.
The ruler says:
'I cannot bear to put you to death,
so I pardon you by sending you into distant exile.'
Make an effort,
and depart quickly!
Do not compound your offenses!"
On the gēngchén day of the fifth month,
Zhèng exiled Yóu Chǔ to Wú.
When they were about to send Zǐ Nán away,
Zǐ Chǎn consulted with Dà Shū.
Dà Shū said:
"Jí cannot even protect himself,
how can he protect his clan?
That matter
concerns the governance of the state;
it is not a private difficulty.
You plan for the state of Zhèng;
if it is beneficial, then carry it out.
What doubt is there?
The Duke of Zhōu put Guǎn Shū to death and exiled Cài Shū;
was it that he did not love them?
It was for the sake of the royal house.
If Jí were to incur guilt,
you would carry out the punishment against him;
what consideration would you have for the various members of the Yóu clan?"
B10.1.8 Hòu Zǐ of Qín was favored by Duke Huán,
and under Duke Jǐng, he was like a second ruler.
His mother said:
"If you do not leave,
I fear you will be chosen [for punishment]."
On the guǐmǎo day,
Zhēn went to Jìn,
with a thousand chariots in his train.
The record says,
"Zhēn, younger brother of the Earl of Qín, fled to Jìn,"
placing the blame on the Earl of Qín.
Hòu Zǐ entertained the Marquis of Jìn.
He had boats placed side by side to form a bridge across the Hé River,
and stationed chariots every ten lǐ,
from Yōng to Jiàng.
He returned to fetch gifts for toasts,
and made eight round trips before the affair was concluded.
Sīmǎ Hóu asked him about it,
saying:
"Are all your chariots here, and that is all?"
He replied:
"This is what is called many.
If there were fewer than this,
how would I have been able to come and see you?"
Nǚ Shūqí reported this to the duke,
and moreover said:
"The Qín prince is sure to return.
Your servant has heard that when a nobleman is able to recognize his faults,
he is sure to have a good plan.
A good plan
is something Heaven assists."
Hòu Zǐ went to see Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said:
"When will you return, sir?"
He replied:
"Zhēn fears being chosen [for punishment] by my ruler,
and so I am here,
waiting for the next ruler."
Zhào Mèng said:
"What is the ruler of Qín like?"
He replied:
"He is without the Way."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Will he perish?"
He replied:
"Why would he?
For one generation to be without the Way
does not mean the state is exhausted.
A state stands between Heaven and Earth;
there are those who support its establishment.
Unless it is dissolute for several generations,
it cannot be overthrown."
Zhào Mèng said:
"Will he die young?"
He replied:
"That is possible."
Zhào Mèng said:
"How long [until then]?"
He replied:
"Zhēn has heard that
when a state is without the Way, yet the harvests are harmonious and ripe,
Heaven is assisting it.
Rarely does it last less than five years."
Zhào Mèng looked at the shadows [of the sun-dial]
and said:
"Morning and evening do not wait for each other;
who can wait for five years?"
Hòu Zǐ went out
and told others, saying:
"Zhào Mèng is about to die.
He who governs the people,
idling away the years and wasting the days—
how much longer can he last?"
B10.1.9 Because of the disorder caused by Yóu Chǔ in Zhèng,
on the dīngsì day of the sixth month,
the Earl of Zhèng and his senior officials made a covenant at Gōngsūn Duàn's house.
Hǎn Hǔ, Gōngsūn Qiáo, Gōngsūn Duàn,
Yìn Duàn, Yóu Jí,
and Sì Dài made a private covenant outside the inner gate,
at Xūn Suì.
Gōngsūn Hēi forcibly joined the covenant,
and had the Grand Historian record his name,
and moreover said
"the seven masters."
Zǐ Chǎn did not punish him.
B10.1.10 Zhōngxíng Mùzǐ of Jìn defeated Wúzhōng and the various Dí tribes at Tàiyuán,
by valuing infantry.
When about to engage in battle,
Wèi Shū said:
"They are on foot, while we have chariots;
the terrain we will meet on is also narrow.
If we match ten men against each chariot,
we are sure to overcome them.
If we trap them in the narrows,
we will overcome them again.
I request that we all fight on foot,
starting with me."
They then dismantled their chariots to form infantry lines,
making three squads of five men from five chariots.
Xún Wú's favorite retainer refused to join the infantry,
and was beheaded as a warning.
They formed five battle arrays, keeping them separate:
two in front,
a squad of five in the rear,
a concentrated force as the right horn,
a dispersed force as the left horn,
and a flanking force as the forward vanguard,
to lure them in.
The Dí people laughed at them.
Before they could form their battle lines, [Jìn's forces] pressed close and
routed them completely.
B10.1.11 When Zhǎn Yú of Jǔ was established,
he stripped the various princes of their stipends.
The princes summoned Qùjí from Qí.
In autumn,
Prince Chú of Qí installed Qùjí,
and Zhǎn Yú fled to Wú.
Shū Gōng led troops to demarcate the fields of Yùn,
taking advantage of the disorder in Jǔ.
At this time, Wù Lóu of Jǔ,
Mào Hú, and Prince Mièmíng fled to Qí with Dà Páng and Chángyí Mí.
The gentleman says:
"The failure of Zhǎn of Jǔ to establish himself
is because he abandoned people!
Can people be abandoned?
The Book of Songs says:
'Nothing is stronger than having people.'
How true this is."
B10.1.12 The Marquis of Jìn was ill.
The Earl of Zhèng sent Gōngsūn Qiáo to Jìn on a diplomatic mission,
and also to inquire about the illness.
Shū Xiàng asked him,
saying:
"Regarding our ruler's severe illness,
the diviner said:
'Shí Chén and
Tái Tái are causing the affliction.'
The historians do not know who they are.
May I venture to ask, what spirits are these?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"In ancient times, Gāo Xīn Shì had two sons.
The elder was called È Bó,
the younger was called Shí Chén.
They lived in Kuànglín,
and could not get along with each other,
daily seeking weapons
to attack one another.
The later emperor, disapproving of this,
moved È Bó to Shāngqiū,
where he was in charge of the constellation Chén.
The Shāng people followed him,
hence Chén became the star of Shāng.
He moved Shí Chén to Dàxià,
where he was in charge of the constellation Shēn.
The Táng people followed him,
and served the Xià and Shāng dynasties.
In their last generation was called Táng Shū Yú.
When King Wǔ and Yì Jiāng were pregnant with Tàishū,
she dreamed the emperor said to her:
'I name your son Yú,
and will give him Táng,
entrusting him to the constellation Shēn,
to multiply and nurture his descendants.'
When he was born,
there was the character 'Yú' on his hand,
so he was named accordingly.
When King Chéng destroyed Táng,
he enfeoffed Tàishū there,
hence Shēn became the star of Jìn.
From this we see,
then Shí Chén
is the spirit of Shēn.
In ancient times, Jīn Tiān Shì had a descendant named Mèi,
who was the master of Xuánmíng.
He begot Yǔn Gé and Tái Tái.
Tái Tái was able to continue his office,
dredging the Fén and Táo rivers,
damming the great marshes,
to settle in Tàiyuán.
The emperor praised him for this,
enfeoffing him in the Fén river region.
Shěn, Sì, Rù, and Huáng indeed maintained his sacrifices.
Now Jìn lords over the Fén and has extinguished them.
From this we see,
then Tái Tái
is the spirit of the Fén.
However, these two
do not affect your ruler's person.
For the spirits of mountains and rivers,
then disasters of flood, drought, plague, and pestilence are warded off by offering sacrifices to them;
for the spirits of the sun, moon, and stars,
then untimely frost, snow, wind, and rain
are warded off by offering sacrifices to them.
As for your ruler's person,
it is also a matter of activity and rest, eating and drinking, grief and joy.
What have the spirits of mountains, rivers, and stars to do with it?
I, Qiáo, have heard that
a gentleman has four periods of the day:
in the morning to attend to governance,
during the day to conduct inquiries and visits,
in the evening to review orders,
at night to settle his body.
Thereby he regulates and diffuses his vital energy,
not letting it become blocked, stagnant, or depressed to expose his body,
lest his mind become impaired,
and all measures fall into confusion.
Now perhaps he has unified them into one,
then illness arises.
I, Qiáo, have also heard that
inner officials should not be of the same surname,
for their offspring will not flourish.
When beauty is exhausted first,
then they generate illness in each other.
This is why gentlemen detest it.
Therefore, the Records say:
'If when buying a concubine you do not know her surname,
then divine it.'
To violate these two principles
was something the ancients were cautious about.
Distinguishing surnames between men and women
is a great principle of ritual.
Now within your ruler's household there are indeed four women of the Jī surname,
is it not perhaps because of this?
If it is due to these two causes,
nothing can be done.
If the four Jī women are reduced, it might still be possible;
if not, illness is sure to arise."
Shū Xiàng said:
"Excellent!
I, Xī, had not heard this,
but it is all true."
Shū Xiàng went out,
and the diplomatic officer Huī escorted him.
Shū Xiàng asked about affairs in Zhèng,
and also asked about Zǐ Xī.
He replied:
"How much longer can he last?
He is without propriety and fond of oppressing others,
relying on his wealth to belittle his superiors.
He cannot last long."
The Marquis of Jìn, hearing Zǐ Chǎn's words,
said:
"He is a gentleman of broad learning."
He sent him rich gifts.
The Marquis of Jìn sought a physician from Qín.
The Earl of Qín sent physician Hé to examine him.
He said:
"The illness cannot be cured.
This is called being close to women,
producing an illness like gu-poisoning.
It is not due to ghosts nor to food,
but to delusion which causes loss of will.
A good minister will die,
for Heaven's mandate does not protect him."
The duke said:
"May women not be approached?"
He replied:
"Regulate it.
The music of the former kings
was used to regulate all affairs,
hence it had five regulations;
slow and fast, root and branch followed each other,
reaching the middle pitch and then descending.
After five descents,
it could not be played further.
Then there arose complicated techniques and licentious sounds,
filling and clogging the heart and ears,
causing one to forget peace and harmony.
Gentlemen do not listen to such.
Other things are also like this.
When it reaches complexity,
one should then stop,
so as not to give rise to illness.
A gentleman's approach to the qín and sè
is for the sake of ritual regulation,
not to indulge the heart.
Heaven has six qi,
which descend to produce the five flavors,
manifest as the five colors,
and are verified as the five sounds.
Excess produces the six illnesses.
The six qi are called yīn, yáng, wind, rain, darkness, and brightness.
They divide to form the four seasons,
and are ordered into the five regulations.
Excess becomes calamity:
excess of yīn causes cold illnesses,
excess of yáng causes heat illnesses,
excess of wind causes limb illnesses,
excess of rain causes abdominal illnesses,
excess of darkness causes delusion illnesses,
excess of brightness causes heart illnesses.
Women
are yáng creatures but belong to darkness in time.
Excess with them produces internal heat and delusion gu-poisoning illnesses.
Now if your lordship does not regulate and is not timely,
can you avoid reaching this point?"
He went out
and reported to Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said:
"Who is the good minister?"
He replied:
"It refers to you, my lord.
You, my lord, have been minister of Jìn
for eight years now.
Jìn has had no disorder,
and the feudal lords have had no deficiencies.
You may be called good.
I, Hé, have heard that
a state's great ministers
glory in their favor and emolument,
and bear responsibility for its major principles.
When calamity and disaster arise,
and they do not change,
they are sure to suffer the blame.
Now the ruler has reached such excess that he has produced illness,
and will be unable to plan and care for the altars of soil and grain.
What disaster could be greater?
You, my lord, cannot prevent it.
This is why I said so."
Zhào Mèng said:
"What is meant by 'gǔ'?"
He replied:
"It is produced by excessive indulgence and confusion.
In terms of writing,
an insect in a vessel is 'gǔ'.
Grain that flies away is also called 'gǔ'.
In the Zhōu Yì,
a woman deluding a man,
wind blowing down a mountain is called 'Gǔ'䷑.
All are the same thing."
Zhào Mèng said:
"A good physician indeed."
He enriched his gifts and sent him back.
B10.1.13 Chǔ prince Wéi sent prince Hēigōng
and Bó Zhōulí to fortify the cities of Chōu, Lì, and Jiá.
The people of Zhèng were afraid.
Zǐchǎn said:
"No harm.
The Lìngyǐn is about to undertake a great affair,
and first removes these two men.
The calamity will not reach Zhèng,
what is there to worry about?"
In winter,
Chǔ prince Wéi was about to go on a mission to Zhèng,
with Wǔ Jǔ as his deputy.
Before they had left the border,
they heard that the king was ill and returned.
Wǔ Jǔ then went on the mission.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
prince Wéi arrived,
entered and inquired about the king's illness,
strangled and murdered him,
and then killed his two sons Mù and Píngxià.
The Right Yǐn Zǐgàn fled to Jìn,
the Palace Stable Yǐn Zǐxī fled to Zhèng,
and they killed the Grand Steward Bó Zhōulí at Jiá.
They buried the king at Jiá,
and called him Jiá Áo.
They sent a messenger to Zhèng,
and Wǔ Jǔ asked what words should be used for the successor.
The reply was:
"Our great officer Wéi."
Wǔ Jǔ changed it to say:
"Gòngwáng's son Wéi is the eldest."
Zǐgàn fled to Jìn,
with five chariots following him.
Shūxiàng made him eat with the Qín prince,
both receiving provisions for a hundred men.
Zhào Wénzǐ said:
"The Qín prince is wealthy."
Shūxiàng said:
"Rank is determined by virtue,
if virtue is equal by age,
if age is the same by seniority.
For a prince, it is by his state,
I have not heard it is by wealth.
Moreover, to leave his state with a thousand chariots,
is excessive in strength and power.
The Shī says:
'He does not insult the widowers and widows,
nor does he fear the strong and powerful.'
Qín and Chǔ
are peers."
He made Hòuzǐ and Zǐgàn take precedence by age,
but Hòuzǐ declined, saying:
"Qián fears being chosen,
the Chǔ prince has not attained his position,
therefore we have all come here,
and we will only follow orders.
Moreover, for your servant to take precedence by age with an exile,
is it not improper?
Shǐ Yì has a saying:
'If he is not an exile,
why be cautious?'"
B10.1.14 Chǔ Língwáng ascended the throne,
Wěi Pí became Lìngyǐn,
and Wěi Qǐqiáng became Grand Steward.
Zhèng Yóu Jí went to Chǔ,
to attend the burial of Jiá Áo,
and also to offer congratulations on the establishment of the new ruler.
Upon returning,
he said to Zǐchǎn:
"He has prepared his traveling vessels.
The Chǔ king is extravagant and arrogant
and delights in his own affairs,
he is sure to assemble the feudal lords,
I will have to go before many days."
Zǐchǎn said:
"He will not be able to do so for several years."
B10.1.15 In the twelfth month,
after the Zhēng sacrifice in Jìn,
Zhào Mèng went to Nányáng,
intending to meet Mèngzǐ Yú.
On the first day Jiǎchén,
he performed the Zhēng sacrifice at Wēn;
on the day Gēngxū,
he died.
The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn to offer condolences,
but when he reached Yōng he returned.
A10.2 The Second Year of Zhāogōng's Spring and Autumn Annals
A10.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Qǐ to come on a mission.
A10.2.2 In summer,
Shū Gōng went to Jìn.
A10.2.3 In autumn,
Zhèng put to death its great officer Gōngsūn Hēi.
A10.2.4 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn,
but when he reached the Hé River he returned.
A10.2.5 Jìsūn Sù went to Jìn.
B10.2 The Commentary for the Second Year of Zhāogōng
B10.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Hán Xuānzǐ to come on a mission,
and to announce that he had taken over the government
and had come to pay a visit,
which was according to ritual.
He examined the books at the Grand Historian's office,
and saw the Yì, the Xiàng, and the Lǔ Spring and Autumn Annals,
and said:
"The rituals of Zhōu are all preserved in Lǔ.
Now I know the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu and the reason why Zhōu became king."
The Duke entertained him,
and Jì Wǔzǐ recited the final stanza of Mián.
Hánzǐ recited Jiǎogōng.
Jì Wǔzǐ bowed,
and said:
"I dare to bow to you for mending the breaches of our humble city,
our ruler has hope."
Wǔzǐ recited the final stanza of Jié.
After the entertainment,
there was a feast at the Jì family.
There was a fine tree there,
which Xuānzǐ praised.
Wǔzǐ said:
"Sù dares not to cultivate and protect this tree,
so as not to forget Jiǎogōng."
He then recited Gāntáng.
Xuānzǐ said:
"Qǐ is not equal to this,
and cannot compare to Shàogōng."
Xuānzǐ then went to Qí to present betrothal gifts.
He met Zǐyǎ.
Zǐyǎ called Zǐqí,
and had him meet Xuānzǐ.
Xuānzǐ said:
"He is not one to preserve his family,
and is not a proper minister."
He met Zǐwěi.
Zǐwěi had Qiáng meet him,
and Xuānzǐ said of him the same as of Zǐqí.
Many of the great officers laughed at him,
but only Yànzǐ believed him,
saying:
"The Master
is a gentleman.
A gentleman is trustworthy,
he must have a way of knowing."
From Qí he went on a mission to Wèi,
and the Marquis of Wèi entertained him.
Běigōng Wénzǐ recited Qí'ào,
and Xuānzǐ recited Mùguā.
B10.2.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
Hán Xū went to Qí to fetch the bride.
Qí Chén Wúyǔ escorted the bride,
and delivered Shào Jiāng.
Shào Jiāng was favored by the Marquis of Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn called her Shàoqí.
He said that Chén Wúyǔ was not a minister,
and arrested him at Zhōngdū.
Shào Jiāng pleaded for him,
saying:
"The escort follows the rank of the one who fetched.
We feared the great state,
and yet made some changes,
therefore disorder arose."
B10.2.3 Shū Gōng went on a mission to Jìn,
to repay Xuānzǐ's visit.
The Marquis of Jìn sent someone to greet him at the outskirts,
but he declined, saying:
"Our ruler sent Gōng to renew the old friendship,
and firmly said
'you must not dare to act as a guest',
to convey his command to your officers,
our humble city is already greatly honored,
how dare we trouble the envoy from the outskirts?
I beg to decline."
He was offered a guesthouse,
but declined, saying:
"My ruler commanded his humble servant to come and renew the old friendship.
If this friendly mission is accomplished,
it will be my good fortune.
How dare I disgrace such a grand guesthouse!"
Shū Xiàng said:
"Master Zǐ Shū understands ritual indeed!
I have heard it said:
'Loyalty and trustworthiness
are the vessels of ritual;
humility and deference
are the essence of ritual.'
In declining, he did not forget his state—
that is loyalty and trustworthiness.
Putting his state before himself—
that is humility and deference.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Be reverent and careful in your dignified demeanor,
to draw near to those who have virtue.'
This gentleman draws near to virtue."
B10.2.4 In autumn,
Zhèng's Gōngsūn Hēi was about to start a rebellion,
wishing to remove the Yóu clan and take their place.
An old wound flared up, and he did not succeed.
The Sì clan and the various senior officials wanted to kill him.
Zǐ Chǎn was in the border regions;
hearing of it,
he feared he would not arrive in time,
and came by express carriage.
He sent an officer to enumerate his crimes,
saying:
"At the time of Bó Yǒu's rebellion,
because of matters involving the great state,
you were not yet punished.
You have a rebellious heart without satiety;
the state cannot bear you.
You arrogantly attacked Bó Yǒu—
that is crime one.
You contended with your brother over a wife—
that is crime two.
At the covenant of Xūnsuì,
you falsely assumed the ruler's position—
that is crime three.
Having three capital crimes,
how can you be endured?
If you do not die quickly,
great punishment will arrive."
He bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
pleading:
"Death is imminent morning and night;
do not assist Heaven in being cruel."
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"Who among men does not die?
That an evil man does not meet his end—
that is fate.
You committed evil deeds
and became an evil man.
If I do not assist Heaven,
would I then assist an evil man?"
He requested that Yìn be made a Chǔshī.
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"If Yìn has talent,
the ruler will employ him.
If he lacks talent,
he will follow you morning and night.
You show no concern for your own crimes,
and what request do you still make?
If you do not die quickly,
the Minister of Justice will arrive."
On the rěnyín day of the seventh month,
he was strangled.
His corpse was exposed at the crossroads of the Zhōu clan,
with a placard added.
B10.2.5 Jìn's Shào Jiāng died.
The Duke went to Jìn.
When he reached the Yellow River,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Wénbó to decline him,
saying:
"She was not a proper consort;
I beg you, my lord, not to trouble yourself."
The Duke returned.
Jìsūn Sù then sent the mourning garments.
Shū Xiàng spoke to the Marquis of Jìn about Chén Wúyǔ, saying:
"What crime did he commit?
You, my lord, sent a member of the ducal house to meet her,
while Qí sent a senior minister to escort her.
Yet you still said it was not respectful enough,
and my lord's demands were motivated by greed.
The state of Qí was not respectful,
and so you detained its envoy.
Your lordship's punishments are already biased;
how can you be the leader of covenants?
Moreover, Shào Jiāng had words about this."
In winter, the tenth month,
Chén Wúyǔ returned.
In the eleventh month,
Zhèng's Yìn Duàn went to Jìn to offer condolences.
A10.3 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Third Year of Duke Zhāo*
A10.3.1 In the third year, spring,
the first month, on the dīngwèi day,
the Viscount of Téng, Yuán, died.
A10.3.2 In summer,
Shū Gōng went to Téng.
A10.3.3 In the fifth month,
Téng Chénggōng was buried.
A10.3.4 In autumn,
the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū came for an audience.
A10.3.5 In the eighth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice.
A10.3.6 In winter,
there was heavy hail.
A10.3.7 The Earl of Northern Yàn, Kuǎn, fled to Qí.
B10.3 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, Third Year of Duke Zhāo*
B10.3.1 In the third year, spring,
the royal first month,
Zhèng's Yóu Jí went to Jìn
to attend Shào Jiāng's funeral.
Liáng Bǐng and Zhāng Tì saw him.
Liáng Bǐng said:
"How excessive it is,
that you, sir, have come for this!"
Zǐ Tàishū said:
"Could I help it?
In the past, when Wén and Xiāng were hegemons,
their affairs did not trouble the feudal lords.
They ordered the feudal lords to present themselves every three years,
and to come for an audience every five years.
When there were matters, they would assemble;
when there was discord, they would covenant.
When a ruler died,
a senior minister would offer condolences,
and a minister would attend the burial.
For a consort,
an officer would offer condolences,
and a senior minister would attend the burial.
This was sufficient to make ritual clear, to command affairs, and to plan for deficiencies—
there were no additional commands.
Now, for the funeral of a favorite,
we dare not choose the rank,
but the number exceeds that for the principal wife.
We only fear incurring offense;
how would we dare dread the trouble?
Shào Qí was favored and died;
Qí will certainly send a successor.
This year I will also come to congratulate;
it is not only this journey."
Zhāng Tì said:
"Excellent!
I have been able to hear this account!
However, from now on, you, sir, will have no more such business.
It is like fire:
when fire is at its zenith,
cold and heat then recede.
This is its extreme;
can it not recede?
Jìn will lose the feudal lords;
the feudal lords will seek trouble but not obtain it."
The two senior ministers withdrew.
Zǐ Tàishū told someone:
"Zhāng Tì has understanding;
he is still among the gentlemen, is he not?"
B10.3.2 On the dīngwèi day,
the Viscount of Téng, Yuán, died. They were covenant allies,
therefore his name was recorded.
B10.3.3 The Marquis of Qí sent Yàn Yīng to request sending a successor to Jìn,
saying:
"My ruler commanded Yīng to say:
'I wish to serve you, my lord, morning and evening without weariness,
and to present gifts and tokens without missing the proper time.
However, the state has many difficulties,
and therefore I have not been able to.
The unworthy daughter of my late father, to fill the inner chambers,
illuminated my hopes,
but again there was no good fortune—
she died early and lost her life,
and I am disappointed.
If you, my lord, do not forget the friendship of my late father,
and graciously regard Qí,
condescending to accept me,
to seek blessings from Tàigōng and Dīnggōng,
shining upon my humble city,
to pacify and comfort its altars of soil and grain,
then there are still daughters of my late father and surviving aunts and sisters, several such persons.'"
If you do not disdain our humble city,
but deign to have Dǒng Zhèn select
to serve as consorts,
that is my wish.'"
Hán Xuānzǐ sent Shū Xiàng to reply, saying:
"This is my ruler's desire.
My ruler cannot alone bear the affairs of his altars of soil and grain,
and having no spouse,
is in mourning garments,
thus he dared not request it.
That you have deigned to command,
there is no greater kindness.
If you kindly look upon our humble city,
and care for the state of Jìn,
bestowing an internal mistress,
how could it be only my ruler?
All the ministers indeed receive your bounty,
and from Táng Shū downward, they truly honor and praise it."
After the marriage was arranged,
Yànzǐ received the ceremony,
and Shū Xiàng accompanied him at the feast,
conversing together.
Shū Xiàng said:
"What of Qí?"
Yànzǐ said:
"This is a declining age.
I fear Qí will become the Chén clan.
The duke has abandoned his people,
and they turn to the Chén clan.
Qí's old four measures:
dòu, ōu, fǔ, zhōng.
Four shēng make a dòu,
each fourfold,
ascending to the fǔ.
Ten fǔ make a zhōng.
The Chén clan's three measures all add one,
so the zhōng is larger.
They lend by the private measure,
and collect by the public measure.
Mountain timber in the market,
is no more expensive than in the mountains;
fish, salt, clams, and mussels,
are no more expensive than by the sea.
The people's labor is divided three ways:
two go to the duke,
and one for clothing and food.
The duke's stores rot and are eaten by worms,
while the village elders freeze and starve.
In the state's markets,
shoes are cheap, but prosthetics are expensive.
The people suffer pain and illness,
and some comfort them.
They love them like parents,
and turn to them like flowing water.
Even if they wish not to gain the people,
how can they avoid it?
Jī Bó, Zhí Bǐng, Yú Suì, Bó Xì,
their spirits assisting Hú Gōng and Dà Jī are already in Qí."
Shū Xiàng said:
"Indeed.
Even our ducal house,
now is also in a declining age.
Warhorses are not harnessed,
ministers have no armies to lead,
the duke's chariots lack men,
the ranks lack leaders.
The common people are exhausted and worn,
while palaces grow more extravagant.
Corpses on the roads are seen everywhere,
and the women's wealth overflows excessively.
The people hear the duke's commands,
as if fleeing bandits and enemies.
Luán, Xì, Xū, Yuán, Hú,
Xù, Qìng, Bó have fallen to menial status.
Government is in the hands of great families,
the people have nowhere to rely.
The ruler daily does not reform,
using pleasure to cover worry.
The ducal house's decline,
how many days can it last?
The inscription on the Chán Dǐng says:
'Diligent at dawn to achieve glory,
later generations still grow idle.'
How can it last long?"
Yànzǐ said:
"What will you do?"
Shū Xiàng said:
"The Jìn ducal clan is finished.
Xī has heard:
when the ducal house declines,
its clan branches fall first,
then the duke follows.
Xī's clan has eleven branches,
only the Yángshé clan remains.
Xī also has no sons,
the ducal house has no measure,
if fortunate to die naturally, how could sacrifices be obtained?"
Earlier,
Duke Jǐng wanted to change Yànzǐ's residence,
saying:
"Your residence is near the market,
low, cramped, noisy, and dusty,
unfit to live in.
Please change to a high, dry place."
He declined, saying:
"Your servant's ancestors lived here,
your servant is unworthy to succeed them,
for your servant it is extravagant.
Moreover, being near the market,
morning and evening I obtain what I seek,
is your servant's benefit.
How dare trouble the neighborhood?"
The duke laughed, saying:
"You are near the market,
do you know what is expensive and cheap?"
He replied:
"Since it benefits me,
how dare I not know?"
The duke said:
"What is expensive?
What is cheap?"
At that time, Duke Jǐng had many punishments,
there were sellers of prosthetics,
so he replied:
"Prosthetics are expensive,
shoes are cheap."
Having already told the ruler,
he thus mentioned it when speaking with Shū Xiàng.
Duke Jǐng therefore reduced punishments.
The gentleman says:
"The words of a benevolent person,
their benefit is broad indeed!
Yànzǐ's one word
made the marquis of Qí reduce punishments.
The Odes say:
'If the gentleman is pleased,
disorder may quickly cease.'
Is this not referring to this?"
When Yànzǐ went to Jìn,
the duke changed his residence.
Returning,
it was already completed.
After bowing in thanks,
he had it demolished,
and rebuilt the neighborhood houses,
all as they were before,
then had the residents return,
saying:
"The proverb says:
'Do not divine about the house,
only divine about the neighbors.'
You gentlemen first divined about neighbors.
To go against divination is inauspicious.
Gentlemen do not violate propriety,
commoners do not violate inauspiciousness,
this is the ancient rule.
How dare I go against it?"
Finally restoring his old residence,
the duke did not permit it;
through Chén Huánzǐ he requested,
and then it was permitted.
B10.3.4 In summer, the fourth month,
the earl of Zhèng went to Jìn,
Gōngsūn Duàn assisting,
very respectful and humble,
with no breach of ritual.
The marquis of Jìn praised him,
granting him a tablet,
saying:
"Zǐ Fēng had merit for Jìn,
I have heard and not forgotten.
I grant you the fields of Zhōu,
to reward your old achievements."
Bó Shí bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
receiving the tablet and leaving.
The gentleman says:
"Ritual—
is it not urgent for a person?
Bó Shí was arrogant,
yet once performing ritual in Jìn,
still received its blessings,
how much more if one follows ritual from start to finish?
The Odes say:
'A person without ritual,
why not quickly die?'
Is this not referring to this?"
Earlier,
Zhōu County
was the fief of Luán Bào.
When the Luán clan perished,
Fàn Xuānzǐ, Zhào Wénzǐ, and Hán Xuānzǐ all desired it.
Wénzǐ said:
"Wēn
is my county."
The two Xuānzǐ said:
"Since Xì Chēng separated it,
three generations have passed.
Jìn's separated counties are not only Zhōu;
who can manage them?"
Wénzǐ was troubled by this,
and so he relinquished it.
The two Xuānzǐ said:
"We cannot uphold justice and yet take it for ourselves."
They all relinquished it.
When Wénzǐ was in power,
Zhào Huò said:
"We can take Zhōu now."
Wénzǐ said:
"Step back!
The words of those two gentlemen
were righteous.
To violate righteousness
is to invite disaster.
If I cannot manage my own county,
what use is Zhōu to me,
except to court disaster?
The gentleman says:
'Not knowing is truly difficult.
But knowing and not following,
no disaster is greater than that.'
Whoever speaks of taking Zhōu will surely die!"
The Fēng clan had formerly been hosts to the Hán clan;
when Bó Shí obtained Zhōu,
Hán Xuānzǐ made the request for him,
because he wanted to take it back again.
B10.3.5 In the fifth month,
Shū Gōng went to Téng,
to bury Duke Chéng of Téng,
with Zǐfú Jiāo as his deputy.
When they reached the outskirts,
it was the anniversary of Yì Bó's death,
so Jìngzǐ did not enter.
Huì Bó said:
"Public affairs have public benefit,
and no private taboos.
Jiāo requests to enter first."
So he first received lodging.
Jìngzǐ followed him.
B10.3.6 Hán Qǐ of Jìn went to Qí to fetch a bride.
Because Gōngsūn Chài saw that Shǎo Jiāng was favored,
he replaced the duke's daughter with his own,
and married off the duke's daughter.
Someone said to Xuānzǐ:
"Zǐ Wěi is deceiving Jìn;
why should Jìn accept it?"
Xuānzǐ said:
"We wish to win over Qí,
but if we alienate its favored ones,
will favor come to us in the future?"
B10.3.7 In autumn, the seventh month,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng went to Jìn,
to congratulate them on the marriage,
and reported:
"The people of Chǔ daily press our humble city for not paying court to the newly established king.
If our humble city goes,
we fear your officers will say our ruler has an ulterior motive;
if we do not go,
then there is the covenant of Sòng.
Whether we advance or retreat, it is a crime.
Our ruler has sent Hǔ to inform you."
Xuānzǐ had Shū Xiàng reply, saying:
"If your ruler shows regard for our ruler,
what harm is there in being in Chǔ?
It is to uphold the covenant of Sòng.
If your ruler truly thinks of the covenant,
our ruler will then know he is spared from blame.
If your ruler does not show regard for our ruler,
even if he comes morning and evening to our humble city,
our ruler will be suspicious.
If your ruler truly has the intention,
why trouble to send word?
Let your ruler go!
If he shows regard for our ruler,
being in Chǔ is like being in Jìn."
Zhāng Tì sent word to Tàishū, saying:
"Since you returned,
I have been cleaning the humble cottage of my ancestors,
saying:
'You will surely come again.'
Now Zǐ Pí has indeed come,
and I am disappointed."
Tàishū said:
"I, Jí, am lowly,
and did not get to come,
out of awe for the great state,
and respect for the lady.
Moreover, Mèng said
'and there will be no trouble,'
so I, Jí, am content."
B10.3.8 Duke Mù of Xiǎo Zhū came to court, and Jì Wǔzǐ wanted to treat him with disrespect.
Mù Shū said:
"It cannot be;
Cáo, Téng, and the two Zhū have not forgotten our friendship.
To receive them with respect,
we still fear they may be disloyal;
if we disrespect one friendly state,
how can we turn away a group of friends?
Treat them as before, but with added respect.
The Records say:
'Being respectful brings no disaster.'
And also:
'Respectfully receiving those who come,
is blessed by Heaven.'"
Jì Sūn followed his advice.
B10.3.9 In the eighth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice,
due to drought.
B10.3.10 The Marquis of Qí was hunting in Jǔ,
when Lú Pú Piè appeared,
weeping,
and pleaded:
"My hair is so sparse,
what can I do?"
The duke said:
"Very well.
I will tell the two gentlemen."
He returned and told them.
Zǐ Wěi wanted to restore him,
but Zǐ Yǎ would not allow it,
saying:
"His hair is short, but his mind is very long;
he might yet lie upon our skins."
In the ninth month,
Zǐ Yǎ exiled Lú Pú Piè to Běi Yān.
B10.3.11 Duke Jiǎn of Yān had many favorites,
and wanted to remove the great officers and establish his favorites.
In winter,
the great officers of Yān united to kill the duke's external favorites.
The duke was afraid,
and fled to Qí.
The record says
"Bó Kuǎn of Běi Yān fled to Qí,"
blaming him.
B10.3.12 In the tenth month,
the Earl of Zhèng went to Chǔ,
with Zǐ Chǎn as his minister.
The King of Chǔ feasted him,
and recited "Jí Rì."
After the feast,
Zǐ Chǎn prepared the hunting equipment,
and the king hunted in the Mèng marshes south of the river.
B10.3.13 Gōngsūn Zào of Qí died.
Simǎ Zào went to see Yànzǐ,
and said:
"We have lost Zǐ Yǎ again."
Yànzǐ said:
"A pity!
Zǐ Qí will not escape,
it is perilous!
The Jiāng clan is weakening,
while the Guī clan will begin to flourish.
If the two Huì had been equally strong, it might have been tolerable,
but now one more is weakened;
the Jiāng are in danger indeed!"
A10.4 The Classic of the Fourth Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.4.1 In the fourth year, spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
there was heavy hail.
A10.4.2 In summer,
the King of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Viscount of Xú,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Viscount of Dùn,
the Viscount of Hú,
the Viscount of Shěn,
the Viscount of Xiǎo Zhū,
the heir of Sòng, Zuǒ,
and the Huái Yí met at Shēn.
A10.4.3 The men of Chǔ seized the Viscount of Xú.
A10.4.4 In autumn, the seventh month,
the King of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Cài,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Baron of Xǔ,
the Viscount of Dùn,
the Viscount of Hú,
the Viscount of Shěn,
and the Huái Yí attacked Wú,
seized Qìng Fēng of Qí,
and killed him.
Then they destroyed Lài.
A10.4.5 In the ninth month,
they took Zēng.
A10.4.6 In winter, in the twelfth month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Shūsūn Bào died.
B10.4 The Commentary of Duke Zhāo, Year 4
B10.4.1 In the spring of the fourth year,
in the royal first month,
the Viscount of Xǔ went to Chǔ.
The Viscount of Chǔ detained him;
he then also detained the Earl of Zhèng.
They again hunted south of the Jiāng,
and the Viscount of Xǔ participated.
He sent Jiāo Jǔ to Jìn to request the attendance of the other lords,
and the two rulers waited for him.
Jiāo Jǔ delivered his message, saying:
"My ruler has sent me, Jǔ, to say:
'In the past, you showed favor,
granting a covenant at Sòng,
saying:
"The followers of Jìn and Chǔ shall meet with each other."
Due to the troubles of the year,
I wish to establish friendship with you, the two or three rulers,
and have sent Jǔ to request an opportunity.
If you, my lord, have no concerns from the four quarters,
then I hope to borrow your prestige to make a request of the other lords.'"
The Marquis of Jìn wished to refuse.
Simǎ Hóu said:
"You must not.
The King of Chǔ is currently arrogant and extravagant.
Heaven may perhaps wish to indulge his heart,
to deepen his poison,
and then bring punishment down upon him;
this is not yet known.
Whether his mission can be brought to a conclusion
is also not yet known.
Jìn and Chǔ depend only on whom Heaven assists;
we cannot contend with them.
My lord, you should grant his request,
and cultivate virtue to await its outcome.
If he turns to virtue,
we would still serve him,
how much more so the other lords?
If he goes to licentiousness and cruelty,
Chǔ will abandon him;
with whom then would we contend?"
The Duke said:
"Jìn has three things that make it unendangered;
what enemy could it have?
The state is strategically secure and has many horses;
Qí and Chǔ have many troubles.
Having these three things,
what direction could we not succeed in?"
He replied:
"To rely on strategic security and horses,
and to anticipate the troubles of neighboring states,
these are three sources of peril.
The Sì Yuè, Sān Tú, Yángchéng,
Dà Shì, Jīng Shān, and Zhōngnán
are the strategic points of the Nine Provinces,
yet they have not belonged to a single family.
The northern lands of Jì
are where horses are born,
yet no powerful state has arisen there.
To rely on strategic security and horses
cannot make a state secure;
it has been thus since antiquity.
Therefore, the former kings devoted themselves to cultivating virtuous influence to please spirits and men;
I have not heard that they devoted themselves to strategic security and horses.
The troubles of neighboring states
cannot be anticipated.
Some, through many troubles, have solidified their states
and opened up their territories;
others, without troubles, have lost their states
and forfeited their domains.
How can one anticipate troubles?
Qí had the troubles of Zhòngsūn,
yet obtained Duke Huán,
and relies on him to this day.
Jìn had the troubles of Lǐ and Pī,
yet obtained Duke Wén,
and thereby became leader of the covenants.
Wèi
and Xíng had no troubles,
yet their enemies also destroyed them.
Therefore, the troubles of others
cannot be anticipated.
To rely on these three things
and not cultivate governance and virtue,
one will perish without respite;
how then could one succeed?
My lord, you should grant his request!
Zhòu practiced licentious cruelty,
King Wén was benevolent and harmonious;
Yīn thereby fell,
Zhōu thereby rose.
Did they contend for the lords?"
He then granted the request of the Chǔ envoy.
He sent Shū Xiàng to reply, saying:
"My ruler has affairs of the altars of soil and grain,
and therefore cannot meet seasonally in spring and autumn.
The other lords—
you, my lord, truly possess them;
why trouble to command it?"
Jiāo Jǔ then requested a marriage alliance,
and the Marquis of Jìn granted it.
The Viscount of Chǔ asked Zǐ Chǎn:
"Will Jìn grant me the attendance of the lords?"
He replied: "They will grant it to you, my lord.
The ruler of Jìn is somewhat complacent;
his mind is not on the lords.
His great officers have many demands;
none correct their ruler.
Moreover, the covenant at Sòng said they would be as one.
If they do not grant you, my lord,
what use will it be?"
The King said:
"Will the lords come?"
He replied:
"They will certainly come.
Following the covenant at Sòng,
receiving your favor,
and not fearing the great state,
why would they not come?
Those who will not come are probably Lǔ, Wèi, Cáo, and Zhū!
Cáo fears Sòng;
Zhū fears Lǔ;
Lǔ and Wèi are pressed by Qí and are close to Jìn;
only for these reasons will they not come.
As for the rest,
they are within your reach,
who would dare not come?"
The King said:
"Then is there nothing I seek that will not be granted?"
He replied:
"To seek to impose one's will on others—
that cannot be done;
to share desires with others—
all will succeed."
B10.4.2 There was a great hailstorm.
Jì Wǔzǐ asked Shēn Fēng:
"Can hail be warded off?"
He replied:
"When a sage is above,
there is no hail.
Even if there is,
it does not become a disaster.
In ancient times, when the sun was in the northern constellation, they stored ice;
when it was in the western constellation and appeared at dawn, they brought it out.
When they stored the ice,
they took it from deep mountains and remote valleys,
places of solid shade and congealing cold.
When they brought it out,
for the stipends and ranks of the court,
for guests, feasts, funerals, and sacrifices,
they then used it.
When they stored it,
they used a black male and black millet to sacrifice to Sī Hán.
When they brought it out,
they used peachwood bows and thornwood arrows
to remove its calamities.
Its storage and removal were timely.
Those with stipends sufficient for meat,
all received ice.
Great officers and their wives used ice for washing the corpse in mourning.
They sacrificed to the cold and stored it;
they presented a lamb and opened it;
the duke began its use;
when the Fire Star appeared, the distribution was completed.
From titled officers and their wives down to the aged and infirm,
none did not receive ice.
The mountain men gathered it;
the district men transported it;
the cart men delivered it;
the servant men stored it.
Ice is strengthened by the wind,
and is brought out by the wind.
If its storage is thorough,
and its use is universal,
then in winter there is no excessive warmth,
in summer no hidden cold,
in spring no chill winds,
in autumn no bitter rains,
thunder does not issue with shocks,
there is no calamitous frost or hail,
pestilence does not descend,
and the people do not die prematurely.
Now, the ice of rivers and ponds is stored but not used;
the wind does not disperse but kills;
thunder does not issue but shocks.
Hail becoming a calamity—
who can ward it off?
The final stanza of the 'Seventh Month'
speaks of the way of storing ice."
B10.4.3 In summer,
the feudal lords went to Chǔ.
Lǔ, Wèi, Cáo, and Zhū did not attend.
Cáo and Zhū excused themselves on grounds of difficulty,
the Duke [of Lǔ] excused himself on grounds of the seasonal sacrifice,
and the Marquis of Wèi excused himself on grounds of illness.
The Earl of Zhèng first waited at Shēn.
On the bǐngwǔ day of the sixth month,
the Viscount of Chǔ assembled the feudal lords at Shēn.
Jiāo Jǔ said to the Viscount of Chǔ:
"Your servant has heard that feudal lords have no fixed allegiance,
but take propriety as their allegiance.
Now you, my lord, are for the first time gaining the allegiance of the feudal lords;
you must be careful regarding propriety.
The success or failure of your hegemony
lies in this assembly.
Xià Qǐ had the feast at Jūntái,
Shāng Tāng had the mandate at Jǐngbó,
Zhōu Wǔ had the oath at Mèngjīn,
King Chéng had the hunt at Qíyáng,
King Kāng had the court audience at Fēnggōng,
King Mù had the assembly at Túshān,
Duke Huán of Qí had the army at Zhàolíng,
and Duke Wén of Jìn had the covenant at Jiàntǔ.
Which will you, my lord, employ?
Xiàng Xū of Sòng and Gōngsūn Qiáo of Zhèng are present;
they are the excellent men among the feudal lords.
You, my lord, may choose from among them."
The King said:
"I will employ that of Duke Huán of Qí."
The King sent to inquire about the rites from the Left Minister and from Zǐchǎn.
The Left Minister said:
"A small state is practiced in them,
a great state employs them;
how dare I not present what I have heard?"
He presented the six rites for a duke assembling the feudal lords.
Zǐchǎn said:
"A small state fulfills its duties;
how dare I not present what I uphold?"
He presented the six rites for an earl, viscount, or baron meeting with a duke.
The gentleman says that the Left Minister was good at upholding the ways of former generations,
and Zǐchǎn was good at assisting a small state.
The King had Jiāo Jǔ stand behind him to watch for errors,
but when the proceedings ended, he had pointed out none.
The King asked the reason,
and he replied:
"Of the rites,
there were six that I had never seen before;
how then could I point out errors?"
The heir apparent Zuǒ of Sòng arrived late.
The King was hunting at Wǔchéng,
and after a long time still did not receive him.
Jiāo Jǔ requested that an excuse be sent.
The King sent a messenger,
who said:
"It happens that we have ancestral temple affairs at Wǔchéng;
our humble ruler is about to present the ceremonial silks.
We dare to apologize for meeting you later."
The Viscount of Xú,
being born of a Wú mother,
was suspected of disloyalty;
therefore he was seized at Shēn.
The Viscount of Chǔ displayed arrogance to the feudal lords.
Jiāo Jǔ said:
"The affairs of the six kings and two dukes
were all means by which they displayed propriety to the feudal lords,
and that is why the feudal lords obeyed their commands.
Xià Jié held the assembly at Réng,
and Yǒumín rebelled.
Shāng Zhòu held the hunt at Lí,
and the Eastern Yí rebelled.
Zhōu Yōu held the covenant at Dàshì,
and the Róng and Dí rebelled.
These were all means by which they displayed arrogance to the feudal lords,
and that is why the feudal lords abandoned their commands.
Now you, my lord, are acting with arrogance;
I fear you will not succeed!"
The King did not listen.
Zǐchǎn met the Left Minister and said:
"I no longer worry about Chǔ.
Arrogant and obstinately rejecting remonstrance,
it will not last ten years."
The Left Minister said:
"Yes.
If he is not arrogant for ten years,
his wickedness will not be far off.
When wickedness is far-reaching, then he will be abandoned.
It is the same with goodness;
when virtue is far-reaching, then he will flourish."
B10.4.4 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the Viscount of Chǔ led the feudal lords to attack Wú.
The heir apparent of Sòng and the Earl of Zhèng returned first;
Huá Fèisuì of Sòng and a senior official of Zhèng accompanied them.
He sent Qū Shēn to besiege Zhūfāng.
On the jiǎshēn day of the eighth month,
he captured it,
seized Qìng Fēng of Qí, and exterminated his entire clan.
As he was about to execute Qìng Fēng,
Jiāo Jǔ said:
"Your servant has heard that only one without flaw can execute others.
Qìng Fēng only because he defied his ruler's command
is here;
would he willingly submit to execution?
If this is broadcast among the feudal lords,
what use is it?"
The King did not listen.
He had him carry the axe and executioner's block on his back
and parade him before the feudal lords,
making him say:
"Let no one be like Qìng Fēng of Qí, who murdered his ruler,
weakened his orphan,
and forced his senior officials to swear allegiance!"
Qìng Fēng said:
"Let no one be like Wéi, the son by a concubine of King Gòng of Chǔ, who murdered his ruler—
his elder brother's son Jūn—and replaced him,
and forced the feudal lords to swear allegiance!"
The King ordered him killed quickly.
Then he led the feudal lords to destroy Lài.
The Viscount of Lài, with his hands bound behind his back and a jade disc in his mouth,
his officers baring their shoulders,
and a carriage bearing his coffin following him,
came to the central army.
The King asked Jiāo Jǔ about this,
who replied:
"When King Chéng conquered Xǔ,
Duke Xǐ of Xǔ acted thus.
The King personally loosened his bonds,
accepted his jade disc,
and burned his coffin."
The King followed this.
He moved Lài to Yān.
The Viscount of Chǔ wanted to move Xǔ to Lài,
and sent Dòu Wéiguī and the prince Qìjí to wall it and then returned.
Shēn Wúyǔ said:
"The beginning of Chǔ's calamities will lie here.
He summoned the feudal lords and they came;
he attacked a state and captured it;
he built walls, and no one in the borders opposed him.
The King's mind meets no opposition;
can the people dwell in peace?
If the people do not settle,
who can endure it?
If they cannot endure the King's commands,
then there will be calamity and disorder."
B10.4.5 In the ninth month,
they took Zēng.
This wording indicates it was easy.
Jǔ was in disorder;
Zhùqiūgōng was established but did not pacify Zēng,
so Zēng rebelled and came [to Lǔ].
Therefore it is said 'took'.
In general, when capturing a town
without using troops, it is called 'taking'.
B10.4.6 Zǐchǎn of Zhèng instituted the qiū tax.
The people of the state criticized him,
saying:
"His father died on the road;
he himself is a scorpion's tail
who gives orders to the state.
What will become of the state?"
Zǐkuān reported this.
Zǐchǎn said:
"What harm is there?
If it benefits the altars of soil and grain,
I will give my life for it.
Moreover, I have heard that one who does good does not change his measures;
therefore he can achieve success.
The people cannot be indulged;
measures cannot be changed.
The Odes say:
'If in ritual and righteousness one does not err,
why worry about what people say?'
I will not change."
Hún Hǎn said:
"The Guó clan will be the first to perish!
When a gentleman establishes laws with frugality,
their decay still leads to greed.
If he establishes laws with greed,
what will their decay be like?
Among the Jī states in the ranks,
Cài and Cáo, Téng will be the first to perish!
Pressured and without propriety.
Zhèng will perish before Wèi,
pressured and without law.
In government, he does not follow the law
but is controlled by his own mind.
The people each have their own minds;
what superiors will they have?"
B10.4.7 In winter,
Wú attacked Chǔ,
entered Jí,
Lì, and Má,
in retaliation for the campaign at Zhūfāng.
Shěn Yǐn Shè of Chǔ rushed to Xiàruì on urgent orders,
Zhēn Yǐn Yíjiù walled Zhōnglí,
Wěi Qǐqiáng walled Cháo,
and Rán Dān walled Zhōulái.
The eastern regions were flooded,
so they could not build walls.
Péngshēng disbanded the army at Lài.
B10.4.8 Initially,
Mùzǐ left the Shūsūn clan,
and when he reached Gēngzōng,
he met a woman,
whom he had privately prepare food for him and then spent the night with her.
She asked about his journey,
and he told her the reason.
She wept and saw him off.
He went to Qí,
married a woman from the Guó clan,
and had two sons, Mèng Bǐng and Zhòng Rén.
He dreamed that the sky was pressing down on him,
and he could not withstand it.
Looking around, he saw a man,
dark-skinned and hunchbacked,
with deep-set eyes and a snout-like mouth,
who called out to him:
"Niú!
Help me!"
Only then did he overcome it.
In the morning, he summoned all his followers,
but none matched the description.
He then said:
"Remember this!"
When Xuān Bó fled to Qí,
Mùzǐ sent him provisions.
Xuān Bó said:
"Because of our ancestors, Lǔ
will preserve our clan,
and will surely summon you.
If they summon you,
what will you do?"
He replied:
"I have long wished for it."
When the people of Lǔ summoned him,
he left without informing anyone and returned.
After he was established,
the woman from Gēngzōng, with whom he had stayed, presented him with a pheasant.
He asked about her clan,
and she replied:
"My son has grown up,
and can now present pheasants and follow me."
He summoned the son and saw him,
and it was the man from his dream.
Before asking his name,
he called out to him:
"Niú!"
The son replied:
"Yes."
He summoned all his followers to see him,
and then made him a page.
He became favored,
and when he grew up, he was put in charge of affairs.
Gōngsūn Míng knew Shūsūn in Qí.
When Shūsūn returned,
he did not send for Guó Jiāng,
and Zǐ Míng married her.
Therefore, Shūsūn was angry,
and only when his sons had grown up did he send for them.
While hunting at Qiūyóu,
he fell ill.
Shù Niú wanted to disrupt his household and take it over,
so he tried to force Mèng to swear an oath,
but Mèng refused.
Shūsūn had a bell cast for Mèng,
saying:
"You have not yet been introduced,
so feast the great officers to inaugurate it."
When everything was prepared,
he sent Shù Niú to request a date.
Shù Niú went in,
but did not report;
he came out,
and assigned a date.
When the guests arrived,
they heard the sound of the bell.
Niú said:
"Mèng has a guest from the northern woman."
Shūsūn was angry
and was about to go,
but Niú stopped him.
After the guests left,
he had Mèng seized and killed outside.
Niú again tried to force Zhòng to swear an oath,
but Zhòng refused.
Zhòng and the duke's charioteer, Lái Shū, were watching the duke,
and the duke gave Zhòng a jade ring,
ordering Niú to take it in and show it.
Niú went in,
but did not show it;
he came out,
and ordered Zhòng to wear it.
Niú said to Shūsūn:
"Why not summon Zhòng for an audience?"
Shūsūn said:
"Why?"
Niú said:
"If you do not summon him,
he has already seen himself,
and the duke gave him a ring, which he is wearing."
Shūsūn then expelled him,
and Zhòng fled to Qí.
As Shūsūn's illness worsened,
he ordered Zhòng to be summoned,
but Niú agreed but did not summon him.
Dù Xiè came to see him,
and Shūsūn told him he was hungry and thirsty,
handing him a spear.
Dù Xiè replied:
"If you seek him, he will come;
why then drive him away?"
Shù Niú said:
"The master is seriously ill
and does not wish to see anyone."
He had the food placed in a side room and withdrew.
Niú did not bring it in,
but instead had the empty dishes removed.
On the guǐchǒu day of the twelfth month,
Shūsūn ate nothing;
on the yǐmǎo day,
he died.
Niú established Zhāozǐ and served as his minister.
The duke sent Dù Xiè to bury Shūsūn.
Shù Niú bribed Shūzhòng Zhāozǐ and Nán Yí,
to slander Dù Xiè before Jìsūn and have him dismissed.
Dù Xiè intended to use the ceremonial carriage for the burial,
and to follow the full rites for a minister.
Nán Yí said to Jìsūn:
"Shūsūn never rode in the ceremonial carriage during his life;
why use it for his burial?
Moreover, the chief minister does not have such a carriage;
to bury a secondary minister with it,
is that not inappropriate?"
Jìsūn said:
"Indeed."
He ordered Dù Xiè to forgo the carriage.
Dù Xiè refused,
saying:
"The master received orders at court and was sent on a mission to the king.
The king, recalling his past merits, bestowed the carriage upon him.
Upon reporting back, he presented it to the ruler.
The ruler did not dare to oppose the king's command and bestowed it back upon him,
ordering three officials to record it.
You, sir, as Minister of Education,
recorded the name;
the master, as Minister of War,
together with the Minister of Works, recorded the insignia;
and Mèngsūn, as Minister of Public Works, recorded the merit.
Now that he is dead, if it is not used,
this is to disregard the ruler's command.
The record is in the ducal archives, yet it is not used;
this is to nullify the three officials.
As for ceremonial attire,
if one does not dare to wear it in life,
and does not use it in death either,
then what purpose does it serve?"
They then allowed it to be used for the burial.
Jìsūn planned to abolish the central army.
Shù Niú said:
"The master had long wished to abolish it."
A10.5 《The Fifth Year of Duke Zhāo's Spring and Autumn Annals》
A10.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
the central army was abolished.
A10.5.2 Chǔ executed its great officer Qū Shēn.
A10.5.3 The duke went to Jìn.
A10.5.4 In summer,
Móu Yí of Jǔ brought Móulóu, Fáng,
and Zī and fled to us.
A10.5.5 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the duke returned from Jìn.
A10.5.6 On the wùchén day,
Shū Gōng led troops and defeated the Jǔ army at Fěnquán.
A10.5.7 The earl of Qín died.
A10.5.8 In winter,
the viscount of Chǔ,
the marquis of Cài,
the marquis of Chén,
the baron of Xǔ,
the viscount of Dùn,
the viscount of Shěn,
the men of Xú,
and the men of Yuè attacked Wú.
B10.5 《The Fifth Year of Duke Zhāo's Commentary》
B10.5.1 In the spring of the fifth year,
in the royal first month,
the central army was abolished,
to humble the ducal house.
It was dismantled at the Shī family's place,
and the arrangements were completed at the Zāng family's place.
Initially, when the central army was established,
the ducal house was divided into three parts,
and each [of the three ministerial families] had one part.
The Jì family levied taxes from all [the people in their share].
The Shūsūn family made the younger generation serve as their retainers,
and the Mèng family took half [the people as retainers and levied taxes from the other half].
When they abolished it,
the ducal house was divided into four parts,
with the Jì family selecting two,
and the other two families each taking one.
They all levied taxes from all [the people in their shares],
and presented tribute to the Duke.
A written order was sent, instructing Dù Xiè to announce it before the coffin,
saying:
"You, sir, had always wished to dismantle the central army;
now that it has been dismantled,
we therefore announce it."
Dù Xiè said:
"Our master specifically did not wish to dismantle it,
therefore he swore an oath at the Xī Hóng gate,
and made a curse at the crossroads of Wǔfù."
He received the written order and threw it away,
then led the officers and wept.
Shúzhòng Zǐ said to Jìsūn:
"Dài received instructions from Zǐ Shūsūn, saying:
'Bury the one who died young through the western gate.'"
Jìsūn gave the order to Dù Xiè.
Dù Xiè said:
"For a minister's funeral, the procession departs from the court;
this is the ritual of Lǔ.
You, sir, administer the state's governance;
you have not changed the ritual but are now altering it.
The ministers fear death,
and dare not follow such an order."
After the burial, he departed.
Zhòng arrived from Qí,
and Jìsūn wished to install him [as head of the Shūsūn family].
Nán Yí said:
"If the Shūsūn family becomes strong,
then the Jì family will be weakened.
That is truly a family disorder;
you, sir, should not involve yourself in it.
Would that not be acceptable?"
Nán Yí had the men of the capital assist Shù Niú to attack [Zhòng] in the courtyard of the great treasury.
The Sīgōng shot at him,
hitting him in the eye, and he died.
Shù Niú took thirty towns from the eastern border and gave them to Nán Yí.
When Zhāozǐ [Shūsūn Chǒu] assumed his position,
he assembled the members of his household,
and said:
"Shù Niú brought disaster upon the Shūsūn family,
causing great disorder in its proper succession,
killing the rightful heir and establishing a concubine's son;
moreover, he divided its towns,
intending to pardon his crimes,
but no crime is greater than this.
He must be killed quickly!"
Shù Niú became afraid
and fled to Qí.
The sons of Mèng and Zhòng killed him outside the Sài Pass.
They threw his head onto the thorn bushes at Níngfēng.
Zhòngní said:
"For Shūsūn Zhāozǐ not to claim credit [for avenging his father],
is something hardly possible.
Zhōu Rén had a saying:
'Those who govern do not reward private services,
nor do they punish private grievances.'
The *Book of Songs* says:
'When one's virtuous conduct is upright,
all states in the four quarters submit to him.'"
Earlier,
when Mùzǐ [Shūsūn Bàozhū] was born,
Zhuāngshū [his father] used the *Zhōu Yì* to divine for him,
obtaining the hexagram *Míngyí* ䷣ changing to *Qiān* ䷎, and showed it to the diviner Chǔ Qiū.
Chǔ Qiū said:
"This one will go forth,
yet return to perform sacrifices for you.
He will enter with a slanderer,
whose name will be Niú [Ox],
and in the end will die of starvation.
*Míngyí*
is the sun.
The numbers of the sun are ten,
therefore there are ten time periods,
which also correspond to ten ranks.
From the king downward,
the second rank is that of a duke, the third is that of a minister.
The sun at its zenith is the first,
the sun at its eclipse is the second,
the sun at dawn is the third.
*Míngyí* changing to *Qiān*
indicates brightness that is not yet full;
it corresponds to dawn,
therefore it is said
'to perform sacrifices for you.'
The sun's *Qiān*
corresponds to a bird,
therefore it is said
'the darkening bird flies.'
Bright but not yet full,
therefore it is said
'it droops its wings.'
It images the movement of the sun,
therefore it is said
'the nobleman is on a journey.'
Corresponding to the third at dawn,
therefore it is said
'for three days he eats not.'
*Lí*
is fire,
*Gèn*
is mountain.
*Lí* represents fire,
fire burns the mountain,
the mountain is ruined.
In terms of humans, it represents speech.
Ruined speech is slander,
therefore it is said:
'There is a place to go.
The host has speech.'
The speech must be slanderous.
Pure *Lí* represents an ox,
in an age of disorder slander prevails,
the prevailing will correspond to *Lí*,
therefore it is said
'his name is Ox.'
*Qiān* indicates insufficiency,
flying but not soaring;
drooping, not lofty;
wings, not broad.
Therefore it is said
'he will be your successor.'
You, sir,
are an assistant minister,
but I fear he will not have a good end."
B10.5.2 The King of Chǔ considered Qū Shēn to be disloyal in favor of Wú,
and so killed him.
He appointed Qū Shēng as Mò'áo,
and sent him with the Lìngyǐn Zǐ Dàng to Jìn to fetch a bride.
Passing through Zhèng,
the Earl of Zhèng entertained Zǐ Dàng at Fàn,
and entertained Qū Shēng at Túshì.
The Marquis of Jìn escorted the bride to Xíngqiū.
Zǐ Chǎn attended the Earl of Zhèng to meet the Marquis of Jìn at Xíngqiū.
B10.5.3 The Duke [of Lǔ] went to Jìn.
From the welcoming ceremony at the outskirts to the presentation of farewell gifts,
he did not fail in any ritual.
The Marquis of Jìn said to Nǚ Shūqí:
"Is not the Marquis of Lǔ well-versed in ritual?"
He replied: "How would the Marquis of Lǔ know ritual!"
The Marquis said:
"Why so?
From the welcoming ceremony at the outskirts to the presentation of farewell gifts,
he did not violate any ritual. Why do you say he does not know it?"
He replied: "That is mere ceremony,
it cannot be called ritual.
Ritual
is that by which one preserves his state,
implements his governmental orders,
and does not lose his people.
Now governmental orders reside with the great families,
and he cannot take them back;
he has Zǐ Jiā Jī,
yet cannot employ him;
he violates covenants with great states,
oppresses and mistreats small states;
profits from others' difficulties,
unaware of his own perils.
The ducal house is divided into four parts,
and the people look to others for sustenance.
Their thoughts are not with the Duke,
and he does not plan for the end.
As the ruler of a state,
difficulties will reach his person,
yet he does not care for his position.
The root and branches of ritual lie in these matters,
yet he busies himself diligently practicing mere ceremonies.
To say he is well-versed in ritual,
is that not far from the truth?"
The gentleman says that Shūhóu [Nǚ Shūqí] in this showed his understanding of ritual.
B10.5.4 Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn went to Chǔ to escort the bride,
with Shū Xiàng as his deputy.
Zǐ Pí and Zǐ Tàishū of Zhèng entertained them at Suǒshì.
Tàishū said to Shū Xiàng:
"The King of Chǔ is excessively extravagant and arrogant,
you must be on your guard!"
Shū Xiàng said:
"If one is excessively extravagant,
it is a disaster to oneself;
how can it affect others?
If I present my silks and jades,
and am cautious in my dignified demeanor;
maintain them with sincerity,
and act in accordance with ritual;
respect the beginning and consider the end,
then in the end there will be no failure to recover.
Follow without losing decorum,
be respectful without losing dignity;
guide with instructive words,
uphold them with established laws,
examine them by the standards of former kings,
and measure them by the practices of two states,
even if others are extravagant,
what can they do to me?"
When they reached Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ held court with his high officials,
and said:
"Jìn
is our enemy.
If we can achieve our aim,
we need not worry about other matters.
Now those who have come
are the high minister and senior officials.
If we make Hán Qǐ a gatekeeper,
and Yáng Shí Xī a palace superintendent,
that would be enough to humiliate Jìn,
and we would also achieve our aim.
Is this permissible?"
None of the officials responded.
Wěi Qǐ Qiáng said:
"It is permissible.
If we have the preparations,
why would it not be permissible?
To disgrace a commoner, one cannot be unprepared,
let alone to disgrace a state?
Therefore, the sage kings devoted themselves to practicing ritual,
and did not seek to disgrace others.
For court visits there are jade tablets,
for ceremonial presentations there are jade scepters;
for minor matters there are reports on duties,
for major matters there are inspections of achievements.
Set out tables but do not lean on them,
fill cups but do not drink from them;
banquets have fine gifts,
feasts have supplementary tripods;
upon arrival there are welcomes at the suburbs,
upon departure there are parting gifts;
this is the height of ritual.
The decline of a state
is due to the loss of this way,
and then calamity and chaos arise.
In the battle of Chéngpú,
Jìn, having no preparations against Chǔ,
was defeated at Bì.
In the battle of Bì,
Chǔ, having no preparations against Jìn,
was defeated at Yān.
Since Yān,
Jìn has not neglected its preparations,
and has added ritual to them,
and emphasized harmony,
so Chǔ has been unable to retaliate,
and seeks kinship ties.
Having already obtained a marriage alliance,
you now wish to disgrace them,
thereby summoning enemies and foes;
what preparations do we have,
and who will bear the responsibility for this?
If we had such a person,
then disgracing them might be permissible.
But if we do not have one,
you should also consider this.
As for Jìn's service to you,
I say it is sufficient:
they sought the allegiance of the feudal lords, and they came in droves;
they sought a marriage alliance and presented a daughter,
you personally escorted her,
and the high minister and senior officials saw her off.
Yet you still wish to disgrace them;
you must also have preparations.
Otherwise,
what can be done?
Below Hán Qǐ,
there are Zhào Chéng, Zhōng Háng Wú, Wèi Shū, Fàn Yāng, and Zhī Yíng;
below Yáng Shí Xī,
there are Qí Wǔ, Zhāng Tì, Jí Tán, Nǚ Qí,
Liáng Bǐng, Zhāng Gé, Fǔ Lì, and Miáo Bēn Huáng,
all chosen men of the feudal lords.
Hán Xiāng is a minister of the ducal clan,
and Hán Xū has received orders and is on a mission;
Jī Xiāng, Xíng Dài, Shū Qín,
Shū Jiāo, and Zǐ Yǔ
are all from great families.
The Hán clan's seven fiefs
are all established counties.
The four clans of the Yáng Shí
are all powerful families.
If the people of Jìn were to lose Hán Qǐ and Yáng Xī,
the five ministers
and eight senior officials would assist Hán Xū and Yáng Shí,
relying on their ten families and nine counties,
with nine hundred war chariots,
and the remaining forty counties,
leaving four thousand for defense,
they would rouse their martial fury
to avenge their great disgrace.
Bó Huá would plan it,
Zhōng Háng Bó and Wèi Shū would lead it,
and there is nothing they would not accomplish.
You would exchange kinship for enmity,
indeed, act without ritual to hasten enemies,
and yet have no preparations,
sending your officials to be captured
to satisfy your heart's desire;
how could this not be permissible?"
The king said:
"This is my fault,
