let the officials not be disgraced."
He treated Hán Zǐ with great courtesy.
The king wished to show off to Shū Xiàng with what he did not know,
but could not,
and also treated him with great courtesy.
When Hán Qǐ returned,
the Earl of Zhèng welcomed him at Yǔ.
He declined, not daring to meet him,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B10.5.5 The Zhèng official Hǎn Hǔ went to Qí,
to marry a woman from the Zǐ Wěi clan.
Yàn Zǐ repeatedly visited him.
Chén Huán Zǐ asked the reason.
He replied:
"He who can employ good men
is a leader of the people."
B10.5.6 In summer,
the Jǔ official Móu Yí brought Móu Lóu, Fáng, and Zī and came fleeing.
Móu Yí was not a minister, yet he is recorded,
because the land was important.
The people of Jǔ complained to Jìn,
and the Marquis of Jìn wished to detain the Duke.
Fàn Xiàn Zǐ said:
"This cannot be done.
To detain someone when they come to court
is entrapment;
to punish without an army,
but to achieve it through entrapment,
is laziness.
To commit these two offenses as the leader of the covenant,
is it not unacceptable!
I ask that he be sent back,
and later punish with an army when there is an opportunity."
So they sent the Duke back.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the Duke arrived from Jìn.
B10.5.7 The people of Jǔ came to attack,
but did not set up defenses.
On Wùchén,
Shū Gōng defeated them at Fén Quán,
because Jǔ had not yet formed ranks.
B10.5.8 In winter, the tenth month,
the King of Chǔ led the feudal lords and the Eastern Yí to attack Wú,
to avenge the campaign of Jí, Lì, and Má.
Wěi Shè joined with the army of Fán Yáng at Xià Ruì.
The Yuè senior official Cháng Shòu Guò led his army to meet the King of Chǔ at Suǒ.
Hearing that the Wú army had set out,
Wěi Qǐ Qiáng led his army in pursuit,
but in haste did not set up defenses,
and the men of Wú defeated them at Què Àn.
The King of Chǔ traveled by post-horse to Luó Ruì.
The King of Wú sent his younger brother Jué Yóu to present gifts to the army,
and the men of Chǔ seized him,
intending to use his blood to anoint the drums.
The king sent someone to ask him,
saying:
"Did you divine that coming here would be auspicious?"
He replied:
"Auspicious.
My lord heard that you were about to mobilize troops against our humble state,
and divined with the tortoise shell,
saying:
'I urgently send someone to present gifts to the army,
to go and observe the speed of the king's anger,
and make preparations accordingly;
may I yet know it!'
The tortoise shell's cracks indicated auspiciousness,
saying:
'It can be known.'
If you, my lord, were to joyfully welcome the envoy,
it would increase our state's complacency and laxity,
and make us forget our peril,
and our downfall would be imminent.
Now you, my lord, are roused like thunder and lightning, in great rage,
cruelly seizing the envoy,
intending to use his blood to anoint the drums;
then Wú will know how to prepare."
Although our city is weak,
if we repair and complete our defenses early,
we can make the army rest.
Whether difficulties or ease arise, we are prepared—
this can be called auspicious.
Moreover, the state of Wú is divining for its altars of soil and grain;
how could it be for the sake of one man?
If your envoy were to have his blood smeared on the army drums,
and our city thereby knew to prepare,
to guard against the unforeseen,
would this not be auspicious?
What could be greater?
The state’s guardian tortoise shell—
for what affairs does it not divine?
Sometimes auspicious, sometimes inauspicious.
Who can determine which it will be?
The omen at Chéngpú,
its retribution came at Bì.
Now on this expedition,
how could there be a vengeful intent?”
Thus they did not kill him.
The Chǔ army crossed at Luóruì;
Shěn Yīnjī met with the King of Chǔ,
and encamped at Láishān.
Wěi Shè led the army from Fányáng and first entered Nánhuái;
the Chǔ army followed him,
reaching Rǔqīng.
Wú could not be entered.
The King of Chǔ then reviewed his troops at Zhǐjīzhīshān.
On this expedition,
Wú had prepared its defenses early;
Chǔ achieved no success and returned,
taking Jué Yóu back with them.
The King of Chǔ, fearing Wú,
sent Shěn Yīnshè to await orders at Cháo,
and Wěi Qǐqiáng to await orders at Yúlóu—
this was according to ritual.
B10.5.9 Qín Hòuzǐ returned to Qín,
because Duke Jǐng had died.
A10.6 The Sixth Year of Duke Zhāo (Classic)
A10.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
the Earl of Qǐ, Yìgū, died.
A10.6.2 The burial of Duke Jǐng of Qín took place.
A10.6.3 In summer,
Jìsūn Sù went to Jìn.
A10.6.4 The burial of Duke Wén of Qǐ took place.
A10.6.5 Huà Hébǐ of Sòng fled to Wèi.
A10.6.6 In autumn, in the ninth month,
a great rain sacrifice was held.
A10.6.7 Wěi Pí of Chǔ led an army to attack Wú.
A10.6.8 In winter,
Shū Gōng went to Chǔ.
A10.6.9 The Marquis of Qí attacked Northern Yān.
B10.6 The Sixth Year of Duke Zhāo (Commentary)
B10.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
Duke Wén of Qǐ died.
Condolences were offered as for an ally—
this was according to ritual.
B10.6.2 Great officers went to Qín
for the burial of Duke Jǐng—
this was according to ritual.
B10.6.3 In the third month,
the people of Zhèng cast penal statutes in bronze.
Shūxiàng sent a letter to Zǐchǎn,
saying:
“At first I had hopes for you,
but now that is over.
In the past, the former kings deliberated on affairs according to circumstances,
and did not make penal laws public,
fearing that the people would develop a contentious spirit.
Even then they could not entirely prevent or control it;
therefore they restrained them with righteousness,
regulated them with government,
guided their conduct with ritual,
maintained them with good faith,
and nurtured them with benevolence.
They established ranks and emoluments
to encourage obedience;
they strictly applied punishments
to overawe excess.
Fearing this was not enough,
they instructed them with loyalty,
exhorted them with good conduct,
taught them their duties,
employed them with harmony,
oversaw them with respect,
governed them with strength,
and decided matters with firmness.
Still they sought out sagely and wise superiors, clear-sighted officials,
loyal and trustworthy elders, and kind and benevolent teachers.
Only then could the people be employed and directed
without giving rise to calamity and disorder.
Once the people know there are penal laws,
they will not stand in awe of their superiors.
All will have a contentious spirit,
citing the written statutes,
and will try to succeed by luck—
this cannot be done.
“The Xià had disorderly government,
and thus created the ‘Penal Code of Yǔ’;
the Shāng had disorderly government,
and thus created the ‘Penal Code of Tāng’;
the Zhōu had disorderly government,
and thus created the ‘Nine Penalties’:
the rise of these three penal codes
all occurred in declining ages.
Now you, sir, assist the state of Zhèng:
you established field boundaries and ditches,
set up a government that invited criticism,
instituted a three-part penal code,
and cast penal statutes in bronze,
intending thereby to pacify the people—
is this not difficult?
The Odes say:
‘Model yourself on King Wén’s virtue,
daily bringing peace to the four quarters.’
They also say:
‘Take King Wén as your model,
and all states will trust you.’
If this is so,
what need is there for penal laws?
Once the people know the grounds for contention,
they will abandon ritual and cite the written statutes;
over the tip of an awl or knife,
they will contend to the utmost.
Disorderly lawsuits will multiply,
and bribery will become widespread.
By the end of your lifetime,
will Zhèng not be ruined?
Xī has heard it said:
‘When a state is about to perish,
it is sure to have many regulations’—
is this not referring to such a case!”
Zǐchǎn replied in a letter, saying:
“As for what you, sir, have said—Qiáo lacks talent,
and cannot plan for his descendants;
I am acting to save the age.
Since I cannot accept your instruction,
dare I forget your great kindness?”
Shì Wénbó said:
“When the Fire Star appears,
Zhèng will likely have a fire!
Before the Fire Star had emerged,
they used fire to cast penal vessels,
harboring contentious laws within them.
If the Fire Star symbolizes this,
how can they avoid a fire?”
B10.6.4 In summer,
Jìsūn Sù went to Jìn
to express thanks for the fields of Jǔ.
The Marquis of Jìn entertained him,
with extra dishes added.
Wǔzǐ withdrew,
and sent an envoy to announce:
“When a small state serves a great state,
if it merely avoids chastisement,
it does not dare seek gifts.
Even when receiving gifts, it does not exceed three presentations.
Now there are extra dishes;
your humble servant cannot bear this—
would it not be a transgression?”
Hán Xuānzǐ said:
“Our ruler considered it a gesture of pleasure.”
He replied:
“Even our ruler would not dare accept this,
how much less your humble servant,
who is but a subordinate of your lord—
how dare I hear of extra gifts?”
He firmly requested the removal of the extras,
and only then concluded the ceremony.
The people of Jìn considered him knowledgeable of ritual,
and valued his generous gifts.
B10.6.5 The eunuch Liǔ of Sòng was favored,
and the heir apparent, Zuǒ, disliked him.
Huà Hébǐ said:
“I will kill him.”
Liǔ heard of this,
and dug a pit, used a sacrificial animal, buried a document,
then reported to the duke, saying:
“Hébǐ is about to bring in the clans of fugitives;
they have already sworn a covenant north of the outer wall.”
The duke sent someone to investigate,
and it was found to be true,
so he expelled Huá Hébǐ.
Hébǐ fled to Wèi.
At this time, Huá Hài wanted to replace the Right Marshal,
so he colluded with the eunuch Liǔ,
who provided evidence for him,
saying:
"I have heard about this for a long time."
The duke sent him to replace him.
When he appeared before the Left Marshal,
the Left Marshal said:
"You, sir, are surely doomed to perish.
You have destroyed your own clan,
what do you have to offer others?
And what do others have to offer you?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The clan's sons are the city walls;
do not let the walls crumble,
do not stand alone in fear.'
You should be afraid!"
B10.6.6 On the bingxū day of the sixth month,
there was a fire in Zhèng.
B10.6.7 The Chǔ prince Qìjí went to Jìn,
to repay Hán Zǐ.
Passing through Zhèng,
Zhèng's Hǎn Hǔ, Gōngsūn Qiáo, and Yóu Jí
accompanied the Earl of Zhèng to greet him at Zhā,
but he declined, not daring to meet them.
They insisted,
and he met them.
He received them as if receiving a king.
He presented eight of his own horses as a private gift.
When meeting Zǐpí, he treated him as a high minister,
giving six horses;
when meeting Zǐchǎn, he gave four horses;
when meeting Zǐ Dàshū, he gave two horses.
He prohibited grazing, gathering firewood,
entering fields,
cutting down trees,
picking crops,
removing tiles from houses,
and forcibly demanding anything.
He swore an oath:
"Anyone who violates these orders,
if a noble, will be deposed;
if a commoner, will be demoted!"
His troops did not commit violence,
and the hosts did not trouble the guests.
Such was his conduct in coming and going,
and the three ministers of Zhèng all knew he would become king.
When Hán Xuānzǐ went to Chǔ,
the people of Chǔ did not welcome him.
When Prince Qìjí reached the border of Jìn,
the Marquis of Jìn was also about to not welcome him.
Shū Xiàng said:
"Chǔ is perverse,
but we are upright.
Why should we imitate perversity?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'When you teach,
the people all imitate.'
Let them follow us instead.
Why should we imitate others' perversity?
The *Book of Documents* says:
'The sage sets the example.'
Should we not take the good as our example,
rather than imitate others' perversity?
If an ordinary person does good,
the people still follow him,
how much more so a ruler of a state?"
The Marquis of Jìn was pleased,
and so he welcomed him.
B10.6.8 In autumn, the ninth month,
there was a great rain-seeking ceremony,
due to drought.
B10.6.9 Xú Yíchǔ paid a courtesy visit to Chǔ,
but the ruler of Chǔ detained him,
and he escaped back.
Fearing his rebellion,
Chǔ sent Wěi Xiè to attack Xú.
The people of Wú came to its rescue.
The Chief Minister Zǐ Dàng led troops to attack Wú,
stationed at Yùzhāng,
and then encamped at Gānxī.
The people of Wú defeated his army at Fángzhōng,
capturing the Palace Stable Master Qìjí.
Zǐ Dàng blamed Wěi Xiè for the defeat and had him killed.
B10.6.10 In winter,
Shū Gōng went to Chǔ,
on a courtesy visit and to offer condolences for the defeat.
B10.6.11 In the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Qí went to Jìn,
to request permission to attack Běi Yān.
Shì Fàn, assisting Shì Yǎng, welcomed him at the river,
as was proper.
The Marquis of Jìn agreed.
In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí then attacked Běi Yān,
intending to install Duke Jiǎn.
Yànzǐ said:
"He will not enter.
Yān already has a ruler,
and the people are not divided.
Our ruler is covetous of bribes,
his flatterers and sycophants,
undertaking great affairs without good faith—
this has never been acceptable."
A10.7 *The Annals of Duke Zhāo, Year Seven*
A10.7.1 In the seventh year, spring,
the royal first month,
peace was made with Qí.
A10.7.2 In the third month,
the duke went to Chǔ.
A10.7.3 Shūsūn Ruò went to Qí to oversee the covenant.
A10.7.4 In summer, the first day of the fourth month, jiǎchén,
there was a solar eclipse.
A10.7.5 In autumn, the eighth month, wùchén,
the Marquis of Wèi, È, died.
A10.7.6 In the ninth month,
the duke returned from Chǔ.
A10.7.7 In winter, the eleventh month, guǐwèi,
Jìsūn Sù died.
A10.7.8 In the twelfth month, guǐhài,
Duke Xiāng of Wèi was buried.
B10.7 *The Commentary of Duke Zhāo, Year Seven*
B10.7.1 In the seventh year, spring,
the royal first month,
peace was made with Qí,
at Qí's request.
On guǐsì,
the Marquis of Qí stationed his troops at Guó.
The people of Yān sought peace,
saying:
"Our humble state acknowledges its fault;
how dare we not obey your orders?
We beg to offer the former ruler's humble vessels as an apology."
Gōngsūn Xī said:
"Accept their submission and withdraw,
wait for an opportunity to act,
that would be acceptable."
On the wùwǔ day of the second month,
a covenant was made at Rúshàng.
The people of Yān presented a Yān princess,
and bribed with a jade jar, a jade casket, and a jade goblet.
They did not succeed and returned.
B10.7.2 When the ruler of Chǔ was Chief Minister,
he used a royal banner while hunting.
The Taro Officer Wú Yǔ cut it down,
saying:
"One state with two rulers—
who can endure that?"
When he ascended the throne,
he built the Zhānghuá Palace,
and gathered fugitives to fill it.
Wú Yǔ's gatekeeper entered there.
Wú Yǔ seized him,
but the officials would not hand him over,
saying:
"To seize someone in the king's palace—
the crime is great."
They seized him and presented him to the king.
The king was about to drink,
and Wú Yǔ argued:
"The Son of Heaven governs the realm,
the feudal lords administer their domains—
this is the ancient system.
Within the borders of the domain,
what land is not the ruler's?
Those who eat the produce of the land,
who are not the ruler's subjects?
Thus the *Book of Songs* says:
'Under the vast heaven,
all is the king's land;
to the shores of the land,
all are the king's subjects.'
Heaven has ten suns,
and men have ten ranks.
The lower serve the upper,
and the upper serve the spirits.
Thus the king rules the dukes,
the dukes rule the ministers,
the ministers rule the shì,
the shì rule the zào,
the zào rule the yú,
The charioteer has his subordinate,
the subordinate has his assistant,
the assistant has his servant,
the servant has his menial.
Horses have their grooms,
oxen have their herdsmen,
to attend to all affairs.
Now the officials say:
'Why did you arrest a man in the king's palace?'
Where else should he have been arrested?
The law of King Wén of Zhōu states,
'If there is a fugitive,
conduct a thorough search.'
This is how he obtained the empire.
Our former lord King Wén
established the law of Pú Ōu,
saying:
'Whoever conceals the stolen goods,
shares the same crime as the thief.'
This is how he enfeoffed you.
If we follow the officials,
then there is nowhere to arrest a fugitive servant.
If we let him escape and abandon him,
then there will be no menials.
Would not the king's affairs then be deficient?
In the past, King Wǔ enumerated Zhòu's crimes to inform the feudal lords, saying:
'Zhòu is the lord of fugitives for the empire,
the gathering place and deep pool.'
Therefore, men fought to the death against him.
If Your Majesty, in beginning to seek the feudal lords, imitates Zhòu,
would that not be unacceptable?
If we apply the laws of these two Wéns to take him,
the thief has a place to be found."
The king said:
"Take him and go with your servant.
The thief is favored,
and cannot be obtained."
Thereupon, he pardoned him.
B10.7.3 King Chǔ completed the Zhānghuá Terrace,
and wished to celebrate its completion with the feudal lords.
The Grand Steward Wěi Qǐqiáng said:
"I can get the Marquis of Lǔ to come."
Wěi Qǐqiáng came to summon the Duke,
and addressed him, saying:
"In the past, our former lord Duke Chéng commanded our former senior official Yīng Qí, saying:
'I have not forgotten the friendship of our former lord,
and will send Héngfǔ to shine upon the state of Chǔ,
to pacify and protect its altars of soil and grain,
so as to bring peace to your people.'
Yīng Qí received this command at Shǔ.
Upholding it since then,
I have not dared to neglect or lose it,
and have transmitted it to the ancestral temple.
Day by day, our former lord King Gòng stretched his neck gazing northward,
hoping month after month,
passing it on in succession,
and now it has been four kings.
Your gracious favor has not yet arrived,
only Duke Xiāng once honored us by attending our mourning.
I and my two or three ministers, grieving in heart and losing our plans,
have had no leisure even for the altars of soil and grain,
how much less could we cherish the memory of your lord's virtue?
Now if you would deign to move your jade-like steps,
and honor our humble lord with your presence,
bestowing glory upon the state of Chǔ,
to fulfill the covenant of Shǔ,
and bring about your gracious favor,
then our humble lord will have received your bounty,
what more could we dare hope for from Shǔ?
The ghosts and spirits of our former lords would truly rejoice and rely on it,
how much more our humble lord?
If you do not come,
send your minister to inquire about the date of your journey,
our humble lord will then receive the gifts and meet you at Shǔ,
to request the bounty of our former lord."
The Duke was about to go,
when he dreamed that Duke Xiāng performed the farewell sacrifice.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"You will not ultimately go.
When Duke Xiāng went to Chǔ,
he dreamed that the Duke of Zhōu performed the farewell sacrifice before he went.
Now Duke Xiāng actually performs the sacrifice,
you probably will not go."
Zǐfú Huìbó said:
"Go!
Our former lord had never been to Chǔ,
therefore the Duke of Zhōu performed the sacrifice to guide him;
Duke Xiāng had been to Chǔ,
and now performs the sacrifice to guide you.
If you do not go,
where will you go?"
In the third month,
the Duke went to Chǔ.
The Earl of Zhèng welcomed him at Shīzhī Liáng.
Mèng Xīzǐ acted as assistant,
but could not perform the ceremonies properly.
When they reached Chǔ,
he could not respond to the suburban welcome.
B10.7.4 In summer, the fourth month, on the first day, jiǎchén,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
The Marquis of Jìn asked Shì Wénbó, saying:
"Who will bear the brunt of the eclipse?"
He replied:
"Lǔ and Wèi will suffer from it.
Wèi will suffer greatly,
Lǔ slightly."
The Duke said: "Why is that?"
He replied: "The eclipse left the territory of Wèi and entered that of Lǔ,
and thus there will be disaster,
which Lǔ will actually receive.
The great misfortune will likely fall upon the lord of Wèi!
Lǔ will lose its senior minister."
The Duke said:
"What about the saying in the Odes,
'That sun is eclipsed,
in what way is it not bad?'
What does it mean?"
He replied:
"It refers to bad government.
If a state lacks good government,
and does not employ the good,
then it brings upon itself reproof from the disasters of the sun and moon,
therefore government cannot but be cautious.
There are three essentials:
first, selecting men;
second, following the people;
third, obeying the seasons."
B10.7.5 The men of Jìn came to settle the matter of Qǐ's lands,
and Jì Sūn was about to give them Chéng.
Xiè Xī was guarding it for Mèng Sūn,
and would not agree,
saying:
"There is a saying:
'Even with the knowledge of carrying a pitcher,
a guardian does not lend out the vessel,
that is propriety.'
My master follows the lord,
and if his guarding minister loses a city,
even you, sir, would have suspicions."
Jì Sūn said:
"Our lord's being in Chǔ
is a crime against Jìn.
If we also do not listen to Jìn,
Lǔ's crime will be heavy.
The army of Jìn will certainly come,
and we have no means to withstand them,
so it is better to give it to them.
Wait for an opportunity with Jìn and take it back from Qǐ.
I will give you Táo,
and when Chéng is returned,
who would dare to claim it?
Thus we gain two Chéngs.
Lǔ will be without worries,
and Mèng Sūn will gain a city,
what trouble is there for you?"
He declined on the grounds that there were no mountains,
so they gave him Lái and Zuò.
Then he moved to Táo.
The men of Jìn took Chéng for Qǐ.
B10.7.6 The King of Chǔ feasted the Duke at the New Terrace,
and had a man with long whiskers act as assistant.
He showed favor by presenting the Dàqū bow.
Afterwards, he regretted it.
Wěi Qǐqiáng heard of this,
and went to see the Duke.
The Duke told him about it,
and he bowed in congratulation.
The Duke said:
He replied:
"Qí, Jìn, and Yuè have long desired this.
Our humble lord had no one to give it to,
and passed it on to you.
You should prepare to defend against these three neighbors,
and carefully guard this treasure,
how dare I not congratulate you?"
The Duke became afraid,
and returned it.
B10.7.7 Zhèng's Zǐ Chǎn visited Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn was ill,
and Hán Xuānzǐ received the guest,
and spoke with him privately,
saying:
"Our humble lord has been bedridden ill,
for three months now,
and we have made offerings to all the mountains and rivers,
but his condition has worsened without improvement.
Now he dreams of a yellow bear entering the bedroom door,
what kind of fierce ghost is this!"
He replied:
"With your lord's intelligence,
and you, sir, as chief minister,
what fierce ghost could there be?
In the past, Yáo executed Gǔn at Yǔshān,
and his spirit transformed into a yellow bear,
and entered the depths of Yǔyuān,
He is actually the tutelary deity of Xià,
and was worshipped by the three dynasties.
Jìn is the leader of the alliance,
perhaps it has not yet worshipped him!
Hán Xuānzǐ performed sacrifices to the tutelary deity of Xià.
The Marquis of Jìn recovered from his illness,
and bestowed upon Zǐchǎn two square dǐng tripods from Jǔ.
B10.7.8 Zǐchǎn returned the land of Zhōu to Hán Xuānzǐ on behalf of Fēng Shī,
saying:
"Previously, our ruler considered that Gōngsūn Duàn was capable of fulfilling his duties,
and bestowed upon him the land of Zhōu.
Now he has passed away prematurely without fortune,
and could not long enjoy the ruler's kindness.
His son does not dare to possess it,
nor does he dare to report it to the ruler,
so he privately presents it to you."
Xuānzǐ declined.
Zǐchǎn said:
"The ancients had a saying:
'If the father splits the firewood,
the son may not be able to carry the load.'
Shī fears he cannot bear the fortune of his ancestors,
how much less can he bear the gifts of a great state?
Even if you, sir, in governing, find it acceptable,
if later generations have disputes over borders,
our humble city would incur guilt,
and the Fèng clan would suffer severe punishment.
If you, sir, take Zhōu,
it would spare our humble city from guilt,
and establish the Fèng clan.
I dare to make this request."
Xuānzǐ accepted it,
and reported it to the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn gave it to Xuānzǐ.
Xuānzǐ, because of his earlier words,
felt uneasy about possessing it,
and exchanged it for the county of Yuán with Yuè Dàxīn.
B10.7.9 The people of Zhèng frightened each other with Bó Yǒu,
saying:
"Bó Yǒu is coming!"
Then they all fled,
not knowing where to go.
In the second month of the year when the penal code was cast,
someone dreamed of Bó Yǒu wearing armor and walking,
saying:
"On the rénzǐ day,
I will kill Dài.
Next year on the rényín day,
I will also kill Duàn."
When the rénzǐ day arrived,
Sì Dài died,
and the people became even more fearful.
In the month when Qí and Yān made peace,
on the rényín day,
Gōngsūn Duàn died,
and the people grew even more terrified.
The following month,
Zǐchǎn established Gōngsūn Xiè and Liáng Zhǐ to appease them,
and it stopped.
Zǐ Dàshū asked the reason,
Zǐchǎn said:
"When ghosts have a place to return to,
they do not become malevolent.
I am giving them a place to return to."
Dàshū said: "Why Gōngsūn Xiè?"
Zǐchǎn said: "To please the people.
For oneself, without righteousness, yet seeking to please,
in governance, one sometimes acts contrary to principle,
to gain favor.
Without favor,
there is no trust;
without trust,
the people will not follow."
When Zǐchǎn went to Jìn,
Zhào Jǐngzǐ asked him,
saying:
"Can Bó Yǒu still become a ghost?"
Zǐchǎn said: "He can.
When a person is born and begins to transform, it is called pò;
once pò is born,
the yang aspect is called hún.
If the essence of things used is abundant,
then the hún and pò are strong,
hence there is refined essence reaching the level of spiritual intelligence.
When an ordinary man or woman dies a violent death,
their hún and pò can still attach to people,
to become malevolent spirits,
let alone Liáng Xiāo,
a descendant of our former ruler Mùgōng,
grandson of Zǐliáng,
son of Zǐ'ěr,
a minister of our humble city,
who has been in government for three generations.
Although Zhèng is not prosperous,
yet as the saying goes,
'a tiny state,'
but for three generations they have held the reins of government,
the things they used were vast,
the essence they took was abundant,
their clan is also large,
what they relied on was substantial,
and he died a violent death—
being able to become a ghost,
is it not fitting!"
B10.7.10 The clan of Zǐpí drank without restraint,
so the Mǎshī clan and the Zǐpí clan were on bad terms.
In the month when the Qí army returned from Yān,
Hǎn Shuò killed Hǎn Tuí.
Hǎn Shuò fled to Jìn.
Hán Xuānzǐ asked Zǐchǎn about his rank.
Zǐchǎn said:
"A wandering minister of your ruler,
if he can find refuge to escape death,
what rank dare he choose?
If a minister leaves his state,
he follows the rank of a senior official;
a criminal is demoted according to his crime,
this is the ancient system.
Shuò, in our humble city,
was a deputy senior official;
his office
was Mǎshī.
Having incurred guilt and fled,
it is entirely up to the ruler to place him.
If he can avoid death,
the kindness is great indeed,
how dare he seek rank?"
Xuānzǐ, impressed by Zǐchǎn's quick-wittedness,
made him follow the rank of a favored senior official.
B10.7.11 In autumn, the eighth month,
Duke Xiāng of Wèi passed away.
A senior official of Jìn said to Fàn Xiànzǐ:
"Wèi has served Jìn faithfully,
yet Jìn has not treated it with courtesy,
sheltering its criminals and taking its land,
so the various states have become disloyal.
The Book of Songs says:
'The wagtail on the plain,
brothers help in distress.'
It also says:
'The terror of death and mourning,
brothers are deeply concerned.'
If brothers are not harmonious,
then they do not show sympathy;
how much less for distant people—
who would dare to turn to them?
Now, not showing courtesy to the successor of Wèi,
Wèi is sure to rebel against us,
and this would cut us off from the states."
Xiànzǐ reported this to Hán Xuānzǐ.
Xuānzǐ was pleased,
and sent Xiànzǐ to Wèi to offer condolences,
and also to return the land of Qī.
Wèi's Qí È announced the mourning to Zhōu,
and requested a mandate.
The king sent Chéng Jiǎngōng to Wèi to offer condolences,
and to posthumously honor Duke Xiāng, saying:
"Uncle, ascending in reverence,
be at the side of our former kings,
to assist in serving the Lord on High.
How dare I forget Gāoyǔ and Yàyǔ?"
B10.7.12 In the ninth month,
the Duke returned from Chǔ.
Mèng Xīzǐ was distressed by his inability in rituals,
so he studied them,
and followed anyone who was skilled in rituals.
When he was about to die,
he summoned his senior officials,
and said:
"Ritual
is the trunk of a person.
Without ritual,
one has nothing to establish oneself.
I have heard that there will be an accomplished man named Kǒng Qiū,
a descendant of sages,
but his line was cut off in Sòng.
His ancestor Fúfù Hé could have had Sòng but yielded it to Duke Lì.
By the time of Zhèng Kǎofù,
he assisted Dukes Dài, Wǔ, and Xuān,
and with each appointment he became more reverent.
Therefore, the inscription on his dǐng tripod says:
'With one appointment, I bowed;
with a second appointment, I bent deeper;
with a third appointment, I stooped low.
I walked along the wall,
and no one dared to insult me.
With this, I ate congee;
with this, I ate gruel,
to fill my mouth.'
His reverence was like this.
Zāngsūn Hé once said:
'When a sage has brilliant virtue,
if he does not meet his time,
his descendants will surely have accomplished men.'
Now, is it not about to be in Kǒng Qiū!
If I die peacefully,
I must entrust Shuō and Héjì to the Master,
to serve him,
and learn ritual from him,
to stabilize their positions."
Therefore, Mèng Yìzǐ and Nángōng Jìngshū served as disciples of Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said:
"One who can rectify his faults
is a nobleman.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The nobleman is to be taken as a model and emulated.'
Mèng Xīzǐ can indeed be taken as a model and emulated."
B10.7.13 Dān Xiàngōng discarded his relatives and employed outsiders.
In winter, on the xīnyǒu day of the tenth month,
the clans of Xiāng and Qǐng killed Xiàngōng and established Chénggōng.
B10.7.14 In the eleventh month,
Jì Wǔzǐ died.
The Marquis of Jìn said to Bóxiá:
"The solar eclipse I inquired about,
has come to pass.
Can this be a constant rule?"
He replied:
"It cannot.
The six things are not the same,
the minds of the people are not uniform,
the order of affairs is not consistent,
the duties of offices are not fixed,
starting the same but ending differently—
how could it be constant?
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Some leisurely dwell at rest,
some toil and labor in service of the state.'
Such is the difference in their ends."
The Duke said:
"What are called the six things?"
He replied:
"Year, season, day, month, star, and celestial marker—
these are what is meant."
The Duke said:
"Many have spoken to me of celestial markers, yet none are the same.
What is meant by 'celestial marker'?"
He replied:
"The conjunction of the sun and moon is called a celestial marker,
therefore it is paired with the day."
B10.7.15 The wife of Duke Xiāng of Wèi, Lady Jiāng, had no sons.
A favored concubine, Zhōu È, gave birth to Mèng Zhí.
Kǒng Chéngzǐ dreamed that Kāngshū said to him:
"Establish Yuán.
I will have the grandson of Jī, Yǔ, and Shǐ Gǒu assist him."
Shǐ Cháo also dreamed that Kāngshū said to him:
"I will command your son Gǒu and the great-grandson of Kǒng Zhēngchú, Yǔ, to assist Yuán."
Shǐ Cháo went to see Chéngzǐ,
told him of the dream,
and the dreams matched.
In the year that Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn was in power and visited the various lords,
Zhōu È gave birth to a son,
and named him Yuán.
Mèng Zhí's feet were defective and he could not walk well.
Kǒng Chéngzǐ divined using the *Zhōu Yì*,
saying:
"May Yuán long enjoy the state of Wèi,
and preside over its altars of soil and grain."
He encountered the hexagram *Zhūn*
He then said:
"I would still establish Zhí;
may he be worthy and excellent."
He encountered the hexagram *Zhūn* ䷂ changing to *Bǐ*
He showed this to Shǐ Cháo.
Shǐ Cháo said:
"'Primacy and success'—
what further doubt is there?"
Chéngzǐ said: "Does this not refer to the eldest?"
He replied: "Kāngshū named him,
so he can be considered the eldest.
Mèng is not a proper man,
and will not be listed among the ancestors,
so he cannot be called the eldest.
Moreover, the oracle says:
'Beneficial to establish a lord.'
If succession were auspicious,
what need to establish?
Establishment means it is not succession.
Both hexagrams speak of it;
you should establish him!
Kāngshū commanded it,
the two hexagrams announced it,
the divination accords with the dream—
this is what King Wǔ employed;
why not follow it?
One with weak feet remains at home.
A lord presides over the altars of soil and grain,
oversees sacrifices,
serves the people,
attends to the spirits,
and attends meetings and court assemblies—
how could he remain at home?
Each according to what benefits him—
is this not acceptable?"
Therefore, Kǒng Chéngzǐ established Lord Líng.
On the guǐhài day of the twelfth month,
Duke Xiāng of Wèi was buried.
A10.8 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Eighth Year of Duke Zhāo*
A10.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
Zhāo, younger brother of the Marquis of Chén, killed Yǎnshī, heir apparent of Chén.
A10.8.2 In summer, on the xīnchǒu day of the fourth month,
the Marquis of Chén, Nì, died.
A10.8.3 Shū Gōng went to Jìn.
A10.8.4 The men of Chǔ arrested the envoy of Chén, Gān Zhēngshī, and killed him.
A10.8.5 Liú, a prince of Chén, fled to Zhèng.
A10.8.6 In autumn,
a hunt was held at Hóng.
A10.8.7 The men of Chén killed their senior minister, Prince Guò.
A10.8.8 A great rain sacrifice was held.
A10.8.9 In winter, on the rénwǔ day of the tenth month,
the army of Chǔ extinguished Chén.
They arrested Zhāo, a prince of Chén,
and exiled him to Yuè.
They killed Kǒng Huàn of Chén.
A10.8.10 Duke Āi of Chén was buried.
B10.8 *The Commentary of Zuo, Eighth Year of Duke Zhāo*
B10.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
a stone spoke in Wèiyú of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn asked Shī Kuàng:
"Why did the stone speak?"
He replied:
"The stone itself cannot speak.
Perhaps something relied upon it.
If not,
the people heard incorrectly.
Moreover, your servant has also heard it said:
'When affairs are undertaken untimely,
resentment and slander stir among the people,
then things that should not speak will speak.'
Now palaces and rooms are lofty and extravagant,
the people's strength is exhausted,
resentment and slander arise together,
and none can preserve their lives.
For a stone to speak—
is this not fitting?"
At that time, the Marquis of Jìn was just building the Palace of Sīqí.
Shū Xiàng said:
"The words of Zǐyě are indeed those of a nobleman!
The words of a nobleman
are trustworthy and have evidence,
therefore resentment stays far from his person.
The words of a petty man
are presumptuous and without evidence,
therefore resentment and blame come to him.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Alas for one who cannot speak!
It is not that his tongue is at fault,
but only that his person is wearied.
Happy is one who can speak!
His clever words flow like a stream,
and his person dwells in ease.'
Is this not referring to this?
When this palace is completed,
the feudal lords are sure to rebel,
and you, my lord, are sure to incur blame.
The Master knew this."
B10.8.2 Duke Āi of Chén's principal consort, Lady Zhèng Jī, gave birth to Yǎnshī, the heir apparent Dào.
His second consort gave birth to Prince Liú,
and his lesser consort gave birth to Prince Shèng.
The second consort was favored,
and Liú was doted upon.
He was entrusted to the Minister of Education, Zhāo, and Prince Guò.
Duke Āi suffered from a debilitating illness.
On the jiǎshēn day of the third month,
Princes Zhāo and Guò killed Dào, heir apparent Yǎnshī, and established Prince Liú.
In summer, on the xīnhài day of the fourth month,
Duke Āi hanged himself.
Gān Zhēngshī went to Chǔ to announce the death,
and also reported that a new ruler had been established.
Prince Shèng accused them before Chǔ.
The men of Chǔ arrested and killed him.
Prince Liú fled to Zhèng.
The record says:
"Zhāo, younger brother of the Marquis of Chén, killed Yǎnshī, heir apparent of Chén"—
the crime lies with Zhāo;
"The men of Chǔ arrested the envoy of Chén, Gān Zhēngshī, and killed him"—
the crime does not lie with the envoy.
B10.8.3 Shū Gōng went to Jìn
to congratulate them on the Palace of Sīqí.
Yóu Jí accompanied the Earl of Zhèng to Jìn,
also to congratulate them on the Palace of Sīqí.
Shǐ Zhào saw Zǐ Dàshū
and said:
"How extreme is this mutual deception!
It should be condoled,
yet you congratulate them."
Zǐ Tàishū said:
"How should we condole?
It is not only we who congratulate,
but the whole world will indeed congratulate."
B10.8.4 In autumn,
a great hunt was held at Hóng,
from Gēnmóu to Shāng and Wèi,
with a thousand chariots of war.
B10.8.5 On the jiǎxū day of the seventh month,
Qí's Zǐ Wěi died.
Zǐ Qí wanted to take control of his household.
On the dīngchǒu day,
he killed Liáng Yīng.
On the gēngxū day of the eighth month,
he expelled Zǐ Chéng, Zǐ Gōng, and Zǐ Chē,
who all fled here,
and established the steward of the Zǐ Liáng clan.
His minister said:
"The youth has grown up,
and yet he oversees our household,
desiring to annex us."
They distributed armor,
preparing to attack him.
Chén Huánzǐ was on good terms with Zǐ Wěi,
and also distributed armor,
preparing to assist him.
Someone reported this to Zǐ Qí,
but Zǐ Qí did not believe it,
then several people reported it.
As he was about to go,
several more people reported it on the road,
so he went to the Chén clan.
Huánzǐ was about to set out,
but upon hearing this, he returned,
changed into casual attire and went to meet him,
asking for instructions.
He replied:
"I heard that the Qiáng clan distributed armor and is about to attack you,
have you heard of it?"
He said:
"I have not heard."
"Why don't you also distribute armor,
Wú Yǔ requests to follow you."
Zǐ Qí said:
"Why do you say this?
He,
is but a youth.
I instruct him,
and still fear he will not succeed,
and I have also favored and ranked him.
How would I face my ancestors?
Why don't you speak to him?
The 'Zhōu Shū' says:
'Bestow favor where it is not bestowed,
encourage where it is not encouraged,'
this is how Kāng Shū achieved greatness."
Huánzǐ kowtowed and said:
"May Qǐng and Líng bless you,
I still have hope."
Thus they reconciled as before.
B10.8.6 Chén's Gōngzǐ Zhāo blamed Gōngzǐ Guò and killed him.
In the ninth month,
Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Qìjí led troops to support Sūn Wú in besieging Chén,
and Sòng's Dài È joined him.
In winter, on the rénwǔ day of the eleventh month,
Chén was destroyed.
The favored attendant Yuán Kè killed horses and destroyed jade to bury his lord.
The Chǔ people were about to kill him,
but he requested to be spared,
and then requested a private audience.
In private within the tent,
he placed mourning hemp on his forehead and escaped.
They appointed Chuān Fēngxū as the Duke of Chén,
saying:
"At the battle of Chéng Mí, he did not flatter."
While serving the king with drink,
the king said:
"At the battle of Chéng Mí,
if you had known I would come to this,
would you have avoided me?"
He replied:
"If I had known Your Majesty would come to this,
I would certainly have fought to the death to bring peace to Chǔ."
The Marquis of Jìn asked Shǐ Zhào:
"Will Chén then perish?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
The duke said:
He replied:
"Chén is a clan of Zhuānxū,
the year was in Chúnhuǒ,
thus it perished.
Chén will follow this.
Now it is at the ford of Xīmù,
and will still revive.
Moreover, the Chén clan will gain power in Qí before Chén finally perishes.
From Mù to Gǔsǒu, none disobeyed commands,
Shùn added to this with bright virtue,
and placed virtue in Suì.
Suì guarded it for generations.
When Húgōng did not indulge,
Zhōu bestowed him a surname,
and made him sacrifice to Emperor Yú.
I have heard that great virtue must be sacrificed to for a hundred generations.
The generations of Yú are not yet complete,
the succession will be in Qí,
the omen already exists."
A10.9 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: Ninth Year of Duke Zhāo"
A10.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Shū Gōng met the ruler of Chǔ at Chén.
A10.9.2 Xǔ moved to Yí.
A10.9.3 In summer, the fourth month,
Chén suffered a fire.
A10.9.4 In autumn,
Zhòngsūn Jué went to Qí.
A10.9.5 In winter,
the Láng park was built.
B10.9 "The Commentary of Zuǒ: Ninth Year of Duke Zhāo"
B10.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
Shū Gōng, Sòng's Huá Hài, Zhèng's Yóu Jí,
and Wèi's Zhào Yǎn met the ruler of Chǔ at Chén.
B10.9.2 On the gēngshēn day of the second month,
Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Qìjí moved Xǔ to Yí,
which was actually Chéngfù.
He took the fields of Zhōulái north of the Huái River to add to it,
and Wǔ Jǔ granted fields to the Earl of Xǔ.
Rán Dān moved the people of Chéngfù to Chén,
adding the fields west of Yí Pú to it.
He moved the people outside Fāngchéng to Xǔ.
B10.9.3 A man of Gān from Zhōu disputed with Jìn's Yán Jiā over Yán's fields.
Jìn's Liáng Bǐng and Zhāng Tì led the Yīnróng to attack Yǐng.
The king sent Zhàn Huánbó to reproach Jìn,
saying:
"Since Xià, we have had Hòujì,
Wèi, Tái, Ruì, Qí, and Bì,
these are our western lands.
When King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
Púgū and Shāngyǎn,
became our eastern lands;
Bā, Pú, Chǔ, and Dèng,
became our southern lands;
Sùshèn, Yān, and Bó,
became our northern lands.
How can we have narrow borders?
King Wén, King Wǔ,
King Chéng, and King Kāng established their own brothers,
to protect and screen Zhōu,
and also to prevent their decline,
how could they be like caps and hair,
and thus discard them?
The former kings placed Táowù in the four borders,
to guard against chīmèi,
thus the treacherous Yǔnxìng clan dwelled in Guāzhōu.
Elder Uncle Duke Huí returned from Qín,
and lured them here,
making them press upon our Jī clans,
enter our suburbs and outskirts,
and then the Róng took them.
The Róng possess the central states,
whose fault is it?
Hòujì planted and nurtured the world,
now the Róng control it,
is it not difficult?
Elder Uncle, consider this!
I am to Elder Uncle,
like the crown and cap to clothing,
the root and source to trees and water,
the strategist to the people.
If Elder Uncle tears the crown and destroys the cap,
uproots the source and blocks the spring,
and abandons the strategist entirely,
even the Róng and Dí,
what would they have to do with me?"
Shū Xiàng said to Xuānzǐ:
"When Duke Wén was hegemon,
could he change things?
He supported and upheld the Son of Heaven,
and added respect to it.
Since Duke Wén,
each generation has had declining virtue,
and have scorned the Zhōu royal house,
displaying their extravagance;
the disloyalty of the feudal lords,
is it not appropriate!
Moreover, the king's words are just,
you should consider it."
Xuānzǐ was pleased.
The king had a relative's funeral,
so he sent Zhào Chéng to Zhōu to offer condolences,
and also to present the Yán fields and burial garments,
returning the captives from Yǐng.
The king also sent Bīn Huá to arrest the Gān minister Xiāng to please Jìn,
and the Jìn people treated him with courtesy and sent him back.
B10.9.4 In the summer, in the fourth month,
a fire occurred in Chén.
Zhèng's Bì Zào said:
"In five years, Chén will be re-established as a state.
It will last for fifty-two years and then perish."
Zǐchǎn asked the reason.
He replied:
"Chén
belongs to the element water.
Fire
is the consort of water.
And Chǔ is the state that presides over it.
Now the Fire Star appears and Chén has a fire,
signifying that Chǔ will be driven out and Chén will be established.
The consort is completed with the number five,
hence it is said 'five years'.
When the year-star reaches the 'Quail Fire' constellation five times,
then Chén will finally perish,
and Chǔ will conquer and possess it.
This is the way of Heaven,
hence it is said 'fifty-two years'."
B10.9.5 Jìn's Xún Yíng went to Qí to fetch a bride.
On his return,
in the sixth month,
he died at Xìyáng.
His coffin was placed in Jiàng,
but he was not yet buried.
The Marquis of Jìn was drinking wine
and had music played.
The chief cook, Tú Kuǎi, hurried in
and requested to assist the duke in serving the wine.
The duke permitted it.
He then poured out wine and made the musicians drink,
saying:
"You are the ears of the ruler,
charged with overseeing hearing.
When the day is zǐ or mǎo,
it is called a day of abstinence.
The ruler refrains from feasting and music,
and students put aside their studies,
because of the abstinence.
The ruler's ministers and assistants
are called his limbs.
If a limb is impaired,
what sorrow is greater?
You have not heard of this and are playing music;
this is a failure of hearing."
He then made the favorite attendant Bì Shū drink,
saying:
"You are the eyes of the ruler,
charged with overseeing sight.
Attire is used to display ritual,
ritual is used to conduct affairs,
affairs have their proper substance,
and substance has its proper appearance.
Now the ruler's appearance
does not match the substance;
and you do not see it,
this is a failure of sight."
He also drank himself,
saying:
"Flavor serves to circulate the vital energy,
energy serves to fill the will,
the will serves to determine speech,
and speech serves to issue commands.
I am truly in charge of flavor.
The two attendants have failed in their duties,
and the ruler has not given the order;
this is my fault."
The duke was pleased,
and put away the wine.
Earlier,
the duke had wanted to depose the Zhì clan and establish his favorite in their place,
but because of this he repented and stopped.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
he appointed Xún Lì to assist the lower army to please him.
B10.9.6 Mèng Xīzǐ went to Qí for a grand diplomatic visit,
which was according to ritual.
B10.9.7 In winter,
they built the Láng park.
The record
indicates it was the proper season.
Jì Píngzǐ wanted it completed quickly.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'When beginning the work, do not be hasty;
the common people will come like sons.'
Why use haste,
which only oppresses the people?
To have no park is still possible;
to have no people,
is that possible?"
A10.10 *The Tenth Year of Duke Zhāo, the Classic*
A10.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
the royal first month.
A10.10.2 In summer,
Qí's Luán Shī came fleeing.
A10.10.3 In autumn, in the seventh month,
Jìsūn Yìrú,
Shū Gōng,
and Zhòngsūn Jué led troops to attack Jǔ.
A10.10.4 On Wùzǐ day,
the Marquis of Jìn, Biāo, died.
A10.10.5 In the ninth month,
Shūsūn Ruò went to Jìn,
to attend the burial of Jìn's Duke Píng.
A10.10.6 In the twelfth month, on Jiǎzǐ day,
the Duke of Sòng, Chéng, died.
B10.10 *The Tenth Year of Duke Zhāo, the Commentary*
B10.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
a star appeared in the constellation Wùnǚ.
Zhèng's Bì Zào said to Zǐchǎn:
"On the Wùzǐ day of the seventh month,
the ruler of Jìn will die.
This year the year-star is at the constellation of Zhuānxū's Void,
which is guarded by the Jiāng and Rén clans.
It occupies the head of the quadrant,
and now there is an ominous star there,
giving warning to Yì Jiāng.
Yì Jiāng is the ancestress of Jìn.
Heaven uses the number seven for its cycles.
On a Wùzǐ day, Duke Féng ascended;
the star thus appeared at that time.
I therefore predict this."
B10.10.2 The Qí clans of Huì's line, Luán and Gāo, were both fond of drink,
trusted their women, and had many enemies.
They were stronger than the Chén and Bào clans and hated them.
In summer,
someone informed Chén Huánzǐ,
saying: "Zǐqí and Zǐliáng are about to attack the Chén and Bào clans."
They also informed the Bào clan.
Huánzǐ armed his men and went to the Bào clan.
He encountered Zǐliáng drunk and galloping,
then went to see Wénzǐ (of the Bào clan),
who had also armed his men.
He sent someone to observe the two men (Zǐqí and Zǐliáng),
and they were both about to drink.
Huánzǐ said:
"Even if the report is untrue,
when they hear we have armed ourselves,
they will certainly drive us out.
While they are drinking,
should we attack them first?"
The Chén and Bào clans were then on good terms,
so they attacked the Luán and Gāo clans.
Zǐliáng said:
"If we get control of the duke first,
where can the Chén and Bào clans go?"
They then attacked the Tiger Gate.
Yàn Píngzhòng, in full court dress, stood outside the Tiger Gate.
The four clans summoned him,
but he went nowhere.
His followers said:
"Shall we assist Chén and Bào?"
He said:
"What is good about them?"
"Shall we assist Luán and Gāo?"
He said: "Are they any better?"
"Then shall we return home?"
He said:
"The ruler is under attack;
where can we return to?"
The duke summoned him,
and only then did he enter.
The duke divined about sending Wáng Hēi with the banner Línggū Pī,
and it was auspicious.
He requested to cut three feet off it and use it.
On the Gēngchén day of the fifth month,
they fought at Jì.
Luán and Gāo were defeated,
and were again defeated at Zhuāng.
The men of the capital pursued them,
and defeated them again at Lùmén.
Luán Shī and Gāo Qiáng fled here.
Chén and Bào divided their property.
Yànzǐ said to Huánzǐ:
"You must hand it over to the duke!
Yielding
is the master of virtue.
To yield is called excellent virtue.
All creatures with blood and breath
have a contentious heart.
Therefore, profit should not be seized by force;
it is better to think of righteousness.
Righteousness
is the root of profit.
Hoarding profit breeds calamity.
Let there be no hoarding for now!
Then it can grow."
Huánzǐ gave all his lands to the Duke,
and requested to retire to Jǔ.
Huánzǐ summoned Zǐ Shān,
privately provided him with tents, utensils, and clothing and shoes for his attendants,
and restored to him the territory of Jí.
He did the same for Zǐ Shāng,
and restored his city.
He did the same for Zǐ Zhōu,
and gave him Fūyú.
He restored the territories of Zǐ Chéng, Zǐ Gōng, and Gōngsūn Jié,
and increased their stipends.
For all the sons and
grandsons of the ducal house who had no stipends,
he privately divided and gave them cities.
For the impoverished, needy, orphaned, and widowed in the state,
he privately gave them grain.
It was said:
"The Book of Songs says,
'He displayed his bounty and founded Zhōu.'
This is about being able to bestow.
Duke Huán thus became hegemon."
The Duke offered Huánzǐ the neighboring cities of Jǔ,
but he declined.
Mù Mèngjī requested Gāotáng for him,
and the Chén clan began to grow powerful.
B10.10.3 In autumn, in the seventh month,
Píngzǐ attacked Jǔ,
and captured Gěng.
When presenting captives,
for the first time he used human sacrifices at the Bó Shè.
Zāng Wǔzhòng was in Qí,
and upon hearing of this,
said:
"How could the Duke of Zhōu enjoy the sacrifices of Lǔ!
The Duke of Zhōu enjoys righteousness,
but Lǔ has no righteousness.
The Book of Songs says:
'His virtuous fame is very bright,
showing the people not to be frivolous.'
This is called extreme frivolity,
and to uniformly use it thus,
upon whom will blessings be bestowed?"
B10.10.4 On Wùzǐ,
Duke Píng of Jìn died.
The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn,
but when he reached the Yellow River,
the people of Jìn declined him.
Yóu Jí then went to Jìn.
In the ninth month,
Shūsūn Ruò of Lǔ, Guó Ruò of Qí,
Huá Dìng of Sòng, Běigōng Xǐ of Wèi,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng, a man of Xǔ, a man of Cáo,
a man of Jǔ, a man of Zhū, a man of Téng, a man of Xuē, a man of Qǐ, and a man of Xiǎozhū went to Jìn,
to attend the burial of Duke Píng.
Zǐ Pí of Zhèng intended to take gifts with him,
but Zǐ Chǎn said:
"What use are gifts for a funeral?
Using gifts requires a hundred carriages,
and a hundred carriages require a thousand men.
When the thousand men arrive,
they will not be able to proceed.
If they cannot proceed,
the gifts will surely all be used up.
How can a state not perish with a thousand men?"
Zǐ Pí insisted on taking them.
After the burial,
the great officers of the various states wished to take the opportunity to see the new ruler.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said: "This is not according to ritual."
They did not listen.
Shū Xiàng declined them,
saying:
"The great officers' affairs are concluded,
and yet you command me, the orphan.
I, the orphan, am deeply in mourning garments,
if I meet you in festive attire,
then the mourning rites are not concluded;
if I meet you in mourning attire,
that would be to receive condolences again,
what are the great officers to do?"
All had no words to request an audience.
Zǐ Pí used up all his gifts.
Upon returning,
he said to Zǐ Yǔ:
"It is not that knowing is truly difficult,
but rather putting it into practice.
That master knew it,
but I was insufficient.
The Book of Documents says:
'Desires ruin measures,
indulgence ruins ritual.'
This refers to me.
That master knew measures and ritual.
I indeed indulged my desires,
and could not restrain myself."
Zhāozǐ arrived from Jìn,
and all the great officers came to see him;
Gāo Qiáng came but then withdrew.
Zhāozǐ said to the great officers:
"As a son, one cannot but be cautious!
In the past, when Qìng Fēng fled,
Zǐ Wěi received many cities,
but gradually gave them to the ruler.
The ruler considered him loyal,
and greatly favored him.
When he was about to die,
he fell ill in the ducal palace,
was carried back in a carriage,
and the ruler personally pushed it.
His son could not uphold this,
and thus is here.
Loyalty is a fine virtue,
but if his son cannot uphold it,
punishment still reaches him—
how can one not be cautious?
Losing the strength of that man,
abandoning virtue and neglecting the ancestral temple,
until it reaches his own person—
is that not harmful?
The Book of Songs says:
'Not before me,
not after me,'
does it not refer to this!"
B10.10.5 In winter, in the twelfth month,
Duke Píng of Sòng died.
Earlier,
Duke Yuán hated the eunuch Liǔ,
and wanted to kill him.
When the mourning period came,
Liǔ placed burning charcoal at the position,
and when the Duke was about to arrive,
he removed it.
By the time of the burial,
he was favored again.
A10.11 The Classic of the Eleventh Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.11.1 In the eleventh year, spring,
in the second month of the royal calendar,
Shū Gōng went to Sòng.
A10.11.2 They buried Duke Píng of Sòng.
A10.11.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on Dīngsì,
King Qián of Chǔ lured Cài Hóu Bān and killed him at Shēn.
A10.11.4 The Chǔ prince Qìjí led troops to besiege Cài.
A10.11.5 In the fifth month, on Jiǎshēn,
Lady Guīshì died.
A10.11.6 There was a great hunt at Bǐpú.
A10.11.7 Zhòngsūn Jué met with the Viscount of Zhū,
and made a covenant at Jìnxiáng.
A10.11.8 In autumn,
Jìsūn Yìrú met with Hán Qǐ of Jìn,
Guó Ruò of Qí,
Huá Hài of Sòng,
Běigōng Tuó of Wèi,
Hǎn Hǔ of Zhèng,
a man of Cáo,
and a man of Qǐ at Juéyìn.
A10.11.9 In the ninth month, on Jǐhài,
we buried our junior queen consort Qí Guī.
A10.11.10 In winter, in the eleventh month, on Dīngyǒu,
the Chǔ army destroyed Cài,
captured the Cài crown prince Yǒu and brought him back,
and used him as a sacrifice.
B10.11 The Commentary of the Eleventh Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.11.1 In the eleventh year, spring,
in the second month of the royal calendar,
Shū Gōng went to Sòng,
to attend the burial of Duke Píng.
B10.11.2 King Jǐng asked Cháng Hóng:
"This year, which of the feudal lords will actually have good fortune?
Which will actually have misfortune?"
He replied:
"Cài will have misfortune.
This is the year in which Cài Hóu Bān murdered his ruler.
The year star is in Shǐwéi,
it will not go beyond this.
Chǔ will possess it,
but it will be blocked.
When the year star reaches Dàliáng,
Cài will be restored,
and Chǔ will have misfortune—
this is the way of Heaven."
The King of Chǔ was at Shēn,
and summoned the Marquis Líng of Cài.
The Marquis Líng was about to go,
when a great officer of Cài said:
"The king is covetous and untrustworthy,
and bears a grudge only against Cài.
Now his gifts are heavy and his words are sweet,
to entice us.
It would be better not to go."
The Marquis of Cài would not listen.
On Bǐngshēn in the third month,
the King of Chǔ concealed armed men and feasted the Marquis of Cài at Shēn,
and when he was drunk, seized him.
On Dīngsì in the summer, the fourth month,
he put him to death,
and also executed seventy of his officers.
The prince Qìjí led an army and besieged Cài.
Xuānzǐ of Hán asked Shūxiàng,
"Will Chǔ be successful?"
He replied, "It will be successful!
The Marquis of Cài had offended against his ruler,
and could not secure the affection of his people.
Heaven is about to employ the hand of Chǔ to destroy him.
Why should it not be successful?
However, I have heard that
to succeed by being untrustworthy
cannot be done a second time.
The King of Chǔ supported Sūn Wú to punish Chén,
saying,
'I will settle your state.'
The people of Chén listened to his orders,
and then he made it a district.
Now he has again enticed Cài and killed its ruler,
and is besieging its capital.
Though he may fortunately succeed,
he is sure to suffer for it,
and will not be able to last long.
Jié succeeded against Yǒumín,
and thereby lost his kingdom.
Zhòu succeeded against the Eastern Yí,
and thereby brought ruin on himself.
Chǔ is small and its position low,
yet it is more violent than those two kings.
Can it escape calamity?
When Heaven assists the unworthy,
it is not blessing them,
but increasing their wickedness to bring down punishment on them.
Moreover, it is like Heaven having the five materials,
and being about to use them:
when their strength is exhausted, it casts them away.
Therefore there is no saving them;
they cannot be restored."
B10.11.3 In the fifth month,
Qí Guī died.
There was a great hunt at Bǐpú,
which was contrary to propriety.
B10.11.4 Mèng Xīzǐ had a meeting with Zhuāng, the duke of Zhū,
and made a covenant at Jìnxiáng,
renewing the friendly relations:—this was according to propriety.
A man of Quánqiū had a daughter,
who dreamt that she spread the curtains of her tent over the ancestral temple of the Mèng family.
She then fled to Xīzǐ,
and her companion followed her.
They made a covenant at the altar of Qīngqiū,
saying,
"If we have sons,
do not cast us off!"
Xīzǐ made them assist the concubine of the Wěi family.
On his return from Jìnxiáng,
he lodged with the Wěi family,
and by the woman of Quánqiū he had Yìzǐ and Nángōng Jìngshū.
Her companion had no son,
and she was made to bring up Jìngshū.
B10.11.5 The army of Chǔ being in Cài,
Xún Wú of Jìn said to Xuānzǐ of Hán,
"We have not been able to save Chén,
and now we cannot save Cài.
In such a state of things, we shall have no friends.
That Jìn is incompetent is thus made known.
Being the president of covenants, and not compassionate towards a perishing state,
what use is there in it?"
In autumn,
there was a meeting at Juéyìn,
to consult about saving Cài.
Zǐpí of Zhèng was about to go to it,
when Zǐchǎn said,
"You will not go far;
you will not be able to save Cài.
Cài is small and disobedient;
Chǔ is great and without virtue.
Heaven is about to abandon Cài to accumulate the guilt of Chǔ;
and when that is full, it will punish it.
Cài must perish.
Moreover, when a state has lost its ruler and yet can maintain itself, such a case is rare.
In three years,
the king will have his calamity.
Good and evil revolve in cycles, and must return.
The king's cycle of wickedness is completed."
A man of Jìn sent Húfǔ to ask Chǔ for Cài,
but the request was refused.
B10.11.6 The viscount of Shàn met Xuānzǐ of Hán at Qī.
He looked down, and spoke slowly.
Shūxiàng said,
"The viscount of Shàn will die!
At court there are the fixed positions;
at meetings there are the markers;
the robes have the cross-collar;
the girdle has the knot.
The words spoken at meetings and at court must be heard at the marked positions,
to show the order of business;
the looks must not go beyond the knot and cross-collar,
to guide the demeanor.
Words are to give the orders;
demeanor is to make them clear.
If there be any failure in these, there is a defect.
Now the viscount of Shàn is the chief of the king's officers,
and announces the business at the meeting.
He does not raise his looks to the girdle;
his words do not go beyond a single pace;
his looks do not guide his demeanor;
and his words do not make things clear.
Not guiding,
he is not reverent;
not making clear,
he is not followed.
He has lost the spirit of self-possession."
B10.11.7 In the ninth month,
Qí Guī was buried,
and the duke showed no sorrow.
An officer of Jìn who had accompanied the funeral,
on his return told the matter to Shǐ Zhào,
who said,
"He is sure to be driven to the suburbs of Lǔ."
An attendant said,
"Why so?"
He replied,
"Guī was his own mother.
He does not think of his parent,
and his ancestors will not receive him."
Shūxiàng said,
"The ducal house of Lǔ is becoming low!
The ruler has a great mourning,
and yet the state does not give up its hunting.
There is the three years' mourning,
and yet for a single day he shows no sorrow.
The state does not sympathize with the mourning,
showing no regard for its ruler;
the ruler shows no sorrowful countenance,
showing no regard for his parent.
If the state have no regard for its ruler,
and the ruler no regard for his parent,
can it avoid becoming low?
I am afraid it will lose the state."
B10.11.8 In winter, in the eleventh month,
the King of Chǔ extinguished Cài,
and sacrificed the heir-apparent Yǐn on Gāngshān.
Shēn Wúyǔ said,
"This is inauspicious.
The five victims are not used for one another;
how much less may feudal lords be so used!
The king will certainly repent of this."
B10.11.9 In the twelfth month,
Chéng, the viscount of Shàn, died.
B10.11.10 The King of Chǔ walled the cities of Chén, Cài, and Bùláng.
He made Qìjí governor of Cài.
The king asked Shēn Wúyǔ,
"How will Qìjí do in Cài?"
He replied,
"To choose a son, no one is like the father;
to choose a minister, no one is like the ruler.
Zhuāng, the duke of Zhèng, walled Lì, and placed Zǐ Yuán there,
which made Zhāo, the duke, not be established.
Huán, the duke of Qí, walled Gǔ, and placed Guǎn Zhòng there,
and to this day they profit by it.
I have heard that the five great officers should not be on the borders;
the five small ones should not be at court.
Relatives should not be abroad;
strangers should not be at home.
Now Qìjí is abroad,
and Zhèng Dān is at home;
let your majesty be a little on your guard."
The king said,
"If a state have great cities,
what then?"
He replied,
"In Zhèng, Jīng and Lì really killed Màn Bó;
in Sòng, Xiāo and Bó really killed Zǐyóu;
in Qí, Qúqiū really killed Wúzhī;
in Wèi, Pú and Qī really drove out duke Xiàn.
If we look at these cases,
they are injurious to the state.
When the branches are large, they break;
when the tail is large, it cannot be wagged:—
this is what your majesty knows."
A10.12 The twelfth year of Zhāogōng.
A10.12.1 In spring, in the twelfth year,
Gāo Yǎn of Qí led a force, and introduced the earl of Běiyàn into Yáng.
A10.12.2 In the third month, on Rénshēn,
the Earl of Zhèng, Jiā, died.
A10.12.3 In summer,
the Duke of Sòng sent Huá Dìng to come on a friendly mission.
A10.12.4 Our lord went to Jìn,
but when he reached the [Yellow] River he returned.
A10.12.5 In the fifth month,
the burial of Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng took place.
A10.12.6 Chǔ put to death its great officer Chéng Xióng.
A10.12.7 In autumn, in the seventh month.
A10.12.8 In winter, in the tenth month,
the prince Yìn fled to Qí.
A10.12.9 The Viscount of Chǔ invaded Xú.
A10.12.10 Jìn invaded Xiānyú.
B10.12 The Twelfth Year of Duke Zhāo - The Commentary
B10.12.1 In the spring of the twelfth year,
Gāo Yǎn of Qí escorted Běiyàn Earl Kuǎn into Táng,
relying on the support of its people.
B10.12.2 In the third month,
Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng died.
When they were about to clear the way for the funeral procession,
they came to the ancestral temple of the Yóu lineage,
and were about to demolish it.
Zǐtàishū made the workmen clearing the way stand holding their tools
but not proceed with the demolition,
saying:
"When Zǐchǎn passes by you,
and asks why you are not demolishing it,
then say:
'We cannot bear to destroy the temple.
Very well,
we are about to demolish it.'"
When it was thus,
Zǐchǎn then made them avoid it.
There was a house belonging to the officers of the grave-mounds that was in the way.
If they demolished it,
then the burial could take place in the morning;
if they did not demolish it,
then the burial would have to take place at midday.
Zǐtàishū requested to demolish it,
saying:
"What about the guests from the other states?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"If the guests from the other states are able to come and attend our funeral,
why should they mind midday?
There is no harm to the guests,
and the people are not injured,
why should we not do it?"
Accordingly, they did not demolish it,
and the burial took place at midday.
The gentleman says that Zǐchǎn in this showed his understanding of propriety.
Propriety
does not involve destroying others to complete oneself.
B10.12.3 In summer,
Huá Dìng of Sòng came on a friendly mission,
to announce the accession of his new ruler.
At the entertainment for him,
they performed for him the ode "Lù Xiāo".
He did not understand it,
nor did he respond with an ode.
Zhāozǐ said:
"He is sure to be ruined.
He does not cherish the friendly words of the banquet;
he does not proclaim the glory and favor [bestowed];
he does not know of virtuous commands;
he does not accept shared happiness;
how can he remain in his position?"
B10.12.4 The Marquis of Qí, the Marquis of Wèi, and the Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn,
to pay their court to the new ruler.
Our lord went to Jìn,
but when he reached the [Yellow] River,
he returned.
This was because of the affair of the capture of Gěng;
the people of Jǔ had complained to Jìn about it,
and Jìn, having the mourning for Duke Píng,
had not yet investigated the matter,
and therefore declined to receive our lord.
The prince Yìn then went to Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn entertained the various lords.
Zǐchǎn acted as assistant to the Earl of Zhèng,
and at the entertainment declined [to take part],
requesting that they be allowed to complete their mourning period before receiving orders.
The people of Jìn agreed to this,
which was according to propriety.
The Marquis of Jìn feasted with the Marquis of Qí,
and Zhōngháng Mùzǐ acted as assistant.
They played at pitch-pot.
The Marquis of Jìn threw first,
and Mùzǐ said:
"We have wine like the Huái River,
and meat like a lofty mound.
If our ruler hits this,
he will be the leader of the feudal lords."
He hit it.
The Marquis of Qí lifted his arrow,
and said:
"We have wine like the Shéng River,
and meat like a high hill.
If I hit this,
I will take Your Lordship's place in rising to power."
He also hit it.
Bóxiá said to Mùzǐ:
"You have made a mistake in your words.
We are already firmly the leaders of the feudal lords;
what has the pot to do with it?
Do you think hitting the mark makes one outstanding?
The ruler of Qí belittles our ruler;
he will go back and not come again."
Mùzǐ said:
"Our army commanders are strong and vigorous,
our foot soldiers and charioteers all strive and encourage each other;
today is just like ancient times;
what can Qí do about it?"
Gōngsūn Sǒu hurried forward,
and said:
"The day is late and the lords are weary,
it is time to withdraw!"
And he escorted the Marquis of Qí out.
B10.12.5 The Viscount of Chǔ said that Chéng Hǔ
was a remnant of the Ruò'áo [clan],
and accordingly put him to death.
Someone had slandered Chéng Hǔ to the Viscount of Chǔ.
Chéng Hǔ knew about it,
but could not take action.
The record says,
"Chǔ put to death its great officer Chéng Hǔ",
because he clung to favor.
B10.12.6 In the sixth month,
the burial of Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng took place.
B10.12.7 Xún Wú of Jìn pretended to be going to join the army of Qí,
and asked for a passage through Xiānyú,
and then entered Xīyáng.
In autumn, in the eighth month, on Rénwǔ,
he extinguished Féi,
and carried back Féizǐ Miángāo as a captive.
B10.12.8 Yuán Bó Jiǎo of Zhōu was cruel to his many officers,
causing them to flee.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the first day, Rénshēn,
the many officers of Yuán expelled Jiǎo,
and set up the prince Guìxún.
Jiǎo fled to Jiāo.
B10.12.9 Gān Jiǎngōng had no son,
and set up his younger brother Guò.
Guò was about to get rid of the families of [Dukes] Chéng and Jǐng.
The families of Chéng and Jǐng bribed Liú Xiàngōng,
and on Bǐngshēn,
they killed Gān Dàogōng,
and set up Qiū, grandson of Duke Chéng.
On Dīngyǒu,
they killed Guò, son of Yǔ Pí, the tutor of the Heir Apparent Xiàn,
killed Xiá Xīn in the marketplace, and also Gōng Bì Chuò, Wángsūn Mò, Liú Zhōujiū, Yīn Jì, and Lǎo Yángzǐ.
B10.12.10 Jì Píngzǐ having been set up,
treated Nán Kuǎi disrespectfully.
Nán Kuǎi said to Zǐzhòng:
"I will drive out the Jì family,
and restore their estates to the duke.
You will take their position,
and I will become a ducal officer with Fèi."
Zǐzhòng agreed to this.
Nán Kuǎi told Shūzhòng Mùzǐ about it,
and also explained his reasons.
When Jì Dàozǐ died,
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ, with a double appointment, became a minister.
And when Píngzǐ invaded Jǔ and conquered it,
he received a triple appointment.
Shūzhòngzǐ wanted to create discord between the two families,
and said to Píngzǐ:
"A triple appointment oversteps one's father and elder brothers;
it is contrary to propriety."
Píngzǐ said: "That is so."
He therefore made Zhāozǐ [reduce his appointment].
Zhāozǐ said:
"The Shūsūn family had domestic troubles,
killing the rightful heir and setting up a son by a concubine,
and therefore I, Ruò, have come to this.
If, because of these troubles, I am to be ruined,
then I have heard the command.
But if the ruler's command is not to be set aside,
then my position is already fixed."
Zhāozǐ went to court,
and commanded the clerk, saying:
"I, Ruò, am about to litigate with the Jì family;
write the documents without partiality."
Jìsūn became afraid,
and laid the blame on Shūzhòngzǐ.
Therefore, Shūzhòng Xiǎo, Nán Kuǎi, and the prince Yìn plotted against the Jì family.
Yìn informed the duke,
and then followed the duke to Jìn.
Nán Kuǎi, fearing he would not succeed,
rebelled with Fèi and went to Qí.
Zǐ Zhòng returned,
and reaching Wèi,
he heard of the disorder,
shed his escort and went ahead alone.
Arriving at the outskirts,
he heard that Fèi had rebelled,
and then fled to Qí.
When Nán Kuǎi was about to rebel,
some people of his district knew of it.
Passing by him, they sighed,
and said:
"How anxious,
how constrained and troubled!
Deep in thought but shallow in planning,
near in person but far in ambition,
a house officer yet scheming for his lord—
there is such a man indeed!"
Nán Kuǎi performed a divination by stalks without stating the matter,
and obtained the hexagram Kūn changing to Bǐ. It said:
"Yellow lower garment, supremely auspicious."
He considered it greatly auspicious.
He showed it to Zǐfú Huì Bó,
saying:
"If I wish to undertake an affair,
what about it?"
Huì Bó said:
"I have studied this.
For affairs of loyalty and good faith it is permissible;
otherwise,
it is sure to fail.
Strong outwardly and gentle inwardly—
that is loyalty;
harmonious and thereby leading to constancy—
that is good faith.
Therefore it is said,
'Yellow lower garment, supremely auspicious.'
Yellow—
is the color of the center;
lower garment—
is the adornment of the lower part;
supreme—
is the chief of excellences.
If the center is not loyal,
one does not obtain its color;
if the lower part is not respectful,
one does not obtain its adornment;
if affairs are not good,
one does not obtain the ultimate.
Outer and inner in harmony and response is loyalty;
leading affairs with good faith is respect;
nourishing the three virtues is goodness.
Unless these three are present, it is not fitting.
Moreover, the Yì
cannot be used to divine risky matters.
What affair are you about to undertake?
And can it be adorned?
The beauty of the center can be yellow,
the highest beauty is the supreme,
the lower beauty is the lower garment.
When these three are complete, divination is permissible.
If there is any deficiency,
even if the divination is auspicious,
it will not succeed."
When about to go to Fèi,
he gave wine to the people of his district.
Some among them sang, saying:
"I have a garden,
yet it grows wolfberries!
Those who follow me are gentlemen,
those who leave me are base!
To betray one's neighbor is shameful!
Enough, enough!
Are you not a man of our party?"
Píng Zǐ wanted to make Zhāo Zǐ expel Shū Zhòng Xiǎo.
Xiǎo heard of it,
and did not dare attend court.
Zhāo Zǐ ordered an officer to tell Xiǎo to wait for government business at court,
saying:
"I will not become a repository of resentment."
B10.12.11 The King of Chǔ hunted at Zhōulái,
and halted at Yǐngwěi.
He sent Dàng Hóu, Pān Zǐ, Sīmǎ Dū,
Xiāo Yǐn Wǔ, and Líng Yǐn Xǐ to lead troops and besiege Xú in order to intimidate Wú.
The King of Chǔ halted at Gānxī to serve as their support.
Snow was falling.
The king wore a leather cap,
a Qín-style fur-lined robe,
a kingfisher-feather cloak,
and leopard-
skin shoes. He came out holding a whip.
Pú Xīfǔ followed him.
The Right Minister Zǐ Gé came for evening audience.
The king saw him,
removed his cap and cloak,
laid aside his whip,
and spoke with him,
saying:
"In former times, our first king, Xióng Yì, along with Lǚ Jí, Wángsūn Móu, Xiè Fù, and Qín Fù, all served King Kāng.
Those four states all received sacrificial vessels,
but we alone received none.
Now if I send a man to Zhōu
to request a tripod as our portion,
will the king give it to me?"
He replied: "He will give it to Your Majesty!
In former times, our first king Xióng Yì dwelt secluded in the Jīng Mountains,
travelling in rough carts and ragged clothes, living amidst the wilds,
traversing mountains and forests to serve the Son of Heaven,
and only with peachwood bows and thornwood arrows did he supply the royal needs.
Qí—
was the king's maternal uncle;
Jìn, Lǔ, and Wèi were the king's brothers by the same mother.
Thus Chǔ had no portion,
while they all had.
Now Zhōu and those four states serve Your Majesty,
and will follow your commands alone.
How could they begrudge a tripod?"
The king said:
"In former times, my royal ancestor's elder brother Kūnwú
dwelt in old Xǔ.
Now the people of Zhèng covet and cling to its fields,
and do not give them to me.
If I request them,
will they give them to me?"
He replied:
"They will give them to Your Majesty!
If Zhōu does not begrudge a tripod,
how dare Zhèng begrudge fields?"
The king said:
"In former times, the feudal lords kept their distance from us and feared Jìn.
Now I have greatly fortified Chén, Cài, and Bùláng,
each capable of supplying a thousand chariots.
You, sir, had a hand in this labor.
Will the feudal lords now fear us?"
He replied:
"They will fear Your Majesty!
These four states alone
are sufficient to inspire fear.
Add to them Chǔ,
and how could they dare not fear Your Majesty?"
Gōng Yǐn Lù requested, saying:
"Your Majesty commanded to split a jade tablet to make the haft of a battle-axe.
I venture to request instructions."
The king went in to inspect it.
Xīfǔ said to Zǐ Gé:
"You, sir,
are the hope of the state of Chǔ.
Now when you speak with the king, it is like an echo.
What will become of the state?"
Zǐ Gé said:
"I have whetted my blade and wait.
When the king comes out,
my edge will strike."
The king came out,
and they spoke again.
The Left Scribe Yǐ Xiāng hurried past.
The king said:
"He is a good scribe.
You should treat him well!
He is able to read the Sānfén, Wǔdiǎn, Bāsuǒ, and Jiǔqiū."
He replied:
"I once asked him.
In former times, King Mù wished to indulge his heart's desires,
travelling all under heaven,
so that everywhere there would be the tracks of his chariot and horses.
Jì Gōng Móu Fǔ composed the poem 'Qí Zhāo' to check the king's heart.
Thus the king was able to die in his Zhī Palace.
I asked him about that poem, and he did not know it.
If one asks about distant matters,
how could he know them?"
The king said:
"Can you?"
He replied:
"I can.
The poem says:
'How tranquil is the Qí Zhāo,
displaying the virtuous sound.
Thinking of our king's measure,
it is like jade, it is like gold.
He shaped the people's strength,
yet had no drunken, sated heart.'"
The king bowed and went in.
He was offered food but did not eat,
lay down but did not sleep.
For several days he could not master himself,
and thus met with disaster.
Zhòngní said:
"In ancient times there was a record:
'To master oneself and return to propriety
is benevolence.'
How true and good!
If King Líng of Chǔ could have been like this,
would he have suffered disgrace at Gānxī?"
B10.12.12 Jìn attacked Xiānyú,
taking advantage of the campaign against Féi.
A10.13 The Spring and Autumn Annals, 13th Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
Shū Gōng led troops to besiege Fèi.
A10.13.2 In summer, in the fourth month,
the Chǔ prince Bǐ returned from Jìn to Chǔ,
and assassinated his ruler Qián at Gānxī.
A10.13.3 The Chǔ prince Qìjí killed Prince Bǐ.
A10.13.4 In autumn,
the Duke [of Lǔ] met with the Viscount of Liú,
the Marquis of Jìn,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Duke of Sòng,
the Marquis of Wèi,
the Earl of Zhèng,
the Earl of Cáo,
the Viscount of Jǔ,
the Viscount of Zhū,
the Viscount of Téng,
the Earl of Xuē,
the Earl of Qǐ,
and the Viscount of Xiǎozhū at Píngqiū.
A10.13.5 On the jiǎxū day of the eighth month,
they formed a covenant at Píngqiū.
The Duke did not participate in the covenant.
A10.13.6 Men of Jìn arrested Jìsūn Yìrú and took him back.
A10.13.7 The Duke arrived from the meeting.
A10.13.8 The Marquis of Cài, Lú, returned to Cài.
The Marquis of Chén, Wú, returned to Chén.
A10.13.9 In winter, in the tenth month,
they buried Duke Líng of Cài.
A10.13.10 The Duke went to Jìn,
but upon reaching the [Yellow] River, he turned back.
A10.13.11 Wú destroyed Zhōulái.
B10.13 The Commentary to the Thirteenth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
Shū Gōng besieged Fèi,
but did not capture it,
and was defeated there. Píngzǐ was angry,
and ordered that when people of Fèi were seen, they should be seized,
to be made prisoners and captives. Yě Qūfū said:
"This is not right.
If you see people of Fèi,
clothe those who are cold,
feed those who are hungry,
become their good ruler,
and supply their needs and deficiencies,
then Fèi will come to you as if returning home,
and the Nán clan will be lost.
The people will turn against them,
who will dwell with them in the city?
If you intimidate them with authority,
frighten them with anger,
the people will resent it and rebel,
gathering [support] for them.
If all the feudal lords act like this,
the people of Fèi will have nowhere to return to,
and if they do not side with the Nán clan,
where else will they go?"
Píngzǐ followed this advice,
and the people of Fèi rebelled against the Nán clan.
B10.13.2 When the Viscount of Chǔ was Prime Minister,
he killed the Grand Marshal Wěi Yǎn,
and took his household.
When he ascended the throne,
he seized the fields of Wěi Jū;
he relocated Xǔ and took Xǔ Wéi as a hostage.
Cài Wěi was favored by the King,
but when the King destroyed Cài,
his father died there,
yet the King made him participate in the guard and then departed.
At the meeting of Shēn,
a Yuè grandee was humiliated there.
The King seized Dòu Wéiguī's Zhōngchōu,
and also seized Chéngrán's city,
yet made him the Suburban Administrator.
Màn Chéngrán had formerly served the Lord of Cài.
Therefore, the clans of the Wěi family, and Wěi Jū, Xǔ Wéi, Cài Wěi, and Màn Chéngrán,
were all treated discourteously by the King.
Relying on the various clans that had lost their positions,
they incited the Yuè grandee Cháng Shòuguò to start a rebellion.
They besieged Gùchéng,
captured Xīzhōu,
fortified it, and dwelt there.
When Guān Qǐ died,
his son Cóng was in Cài,
serving Cháo Wú.
He said:
"If we do not restore Cài now,
Cài will never be restored.
I request to try it."
Using the Lord of Cài's name, he summoned Zǐ Gàn and Zǐ Xī.
When they reached the suburbs,
he told them the situation,
forced them to swear a covenant,
and entered to attack Cài.
The Lord of Cài was about to eat when he saw them and fled.
Guān Cóng made Zǐ Gàn eat,
dug a pit,
used a sacrificial animal,
placed a document [on it],
and hurried away.
He himself paraded through Cài,
saying:
"The Lord of Cài summoned the two lords,
intending to install them,
