swore a covenant with them and sent them off,
and will lead the army to follow them."
The people of Cài gathered,
intending to seize him.
He pleaded, saying:
"If you have lost the villain and an army is formed,
what good will killing me do?"
They then released him.
Cháo Wú said:
"If you gentlemen can face death or exile,
then you should oppose him,
and await the outcome.
If you seek stability,
then you should join him,
to achieve your desires.
Moreover, if you oppose your superior,
where can you go?"
The multitude said:
"Join him!"
They then supported the Lord of Cài,
summoned the two lords and swore a covenant at Dèng,
relying on the men of Chén and Cài to restore the state.
The Chǔ princes Bǐ, Hēigōng, and Qìjí, along with Màn Chéngrán and Cài's Cháo Wú, led the armies of Chén, Cài, Bùláng, Xǔ, and Yè,
and with the followers of the four clans,
entered Chǔ.
When they reached the suburbs,
Chén and Cài, wanting to make a name,
requested to build a martial rampart.
The Lord of Cài, knowing this,
said:
"We want speed,
and the laborers are already weary;
I ask merely for a fence."
They then made a fence as their military encampment.
The Lord of Cài sent Xū Wùmóu and Shǐ Pí to enter first,
who, through the chief steward, killed Crown Prince Lù and Prince Bádí.
Prince Bǐ was made King,
Prince Hēigōng was made Prime Minister,
and they encamped at Yúbēi.
Prince Qìjí was made Marshal,
and first cleared the royal palace.
He sent Guān Cóng to follow the army to Gānxī,
and thereupon informed them,
saying:
"Those who return first will have their positions restored;
those who come later will have their noses cut off."
The army reached Zīliáng and disintegrated.
When the King heard of the death of the princes,
he threw himself from his chariot,
saying:
"Do others love their sons
as much as I do?"
An attendant said:
"Even more so.
A commoner who grows old without a son
knows he will be cast into a ditch or ravine."
The King said:
"I have killed many men's sons;
can I avoid this?"
The Right Minister Zǐ Gé said:
"I ask to wait in the suburbs,
to listen to the people of the state."
The King said:
"The wrath of the multitude cannot be provoked."
[Zǐ Gé] said:
"Perhaps enter a major city,
and seek troops from the feudal lords."
The King said:
"They have all rebelled."
[Zǐ Gé] said:
"Perhaps flee to a feudal lord,
to listen to what a major state plans for you, my lord."
The King said:
"Great fortune does not come twice;
I would only bring disgrace upon myself."
Rán Dān then returned to Chǔ.
The King traveled along the Xià [River],
intending to enter Yān.
Shēn Hài, son of the Taro Administrator Wú Yǔ, said:
"My father twice violated the king's command,
yet the king did not execute him—
what greater kindness could there be?
A ruler's injustice cannot be endured,
but kindness cannot be cast aside.
I shall follow the king."
He then sought out the king
and encountered him at the Thorn Palace, bringing him back.
In the summer, on the guǐhài day of the fifth month,
the king hanged himself at the residence of Shěn Hài, the Taro Officer.
Shěn Hài buried him with his two daughters as sacrificial attendants.
Guàn Cóng said to Zǐ Gàn:
"If you do not kill Qìjí,
even if you gain the state,
you will still suffer calamity."
Zǐ Gàn said: "I cannot bear to do it."
Zǐ Yù said: "Others will bear to harm you;
I cannot bear to wait for that."
He then departed.
Every night, the capital was thrown into panic, with cries of:
"The king has entered!"
On the yǐmǎo night,
Qìjí had people run about shouting:
"The king has arrived!"
The people of the capital were greatly alarmed.
He sent Màn Chéngrán to run and inform Zǐ Gàn and Zǐ Xī:
"The king has arrived!
The people of the capital have killed your Minister of War
and are coming for you.
If you, my lords, make plans early for yourselves,
you may avoid disgrace.
The fury of the masses is like flood or fire—
it cannot be countered by schemes."
Then came another who ran shouting:
"The masses are here!"
Both men committed suicide.
On the bǐngchén day,
Qìjí ascended the throne,
taking the name Xióng Jū.
He buried Zǐ Gàn at Zī,
in fact calling him Zī Áo.
He had a prisoner killed,
dressed him in royal robes,
and floated the body on the Hàn River,
then retrieved and buried it,
to pacify the people of the capital.
He appointed Zǐ Qí as Prime Minister.
The Chǔ army, returning from Xú,
was defeated by the Wú at Yùzhāng,
which captured five of its commanders.
King Píng restored the states of Chén and Cài,
returned relocated cities,
distributed gifts to the multitude,
bestowed aid, eased the people's burdens,
pardoned offenses, and appointed officials to office.
He summoned Guàn Cóng,
and the king said:
"Whatever you desire, it shall be yours."
He replied:
"My ancestors assisted in divination."
He was then made Chief Diviner.
He sent Zhīrú Zǐgōng on a mission to Zhèng,
and to deliver the fields of Chōu and Lì.
After the mission was completed, he did not deliver them.
The people of Zhèng inquired:
"We have heard on the roads
that you were to command our ruler regarding Chōu and Lì;
we dare ask for your instructions."
He replied:
"I have not received such orders."
After his return,
the king asked about Chōu and Lì.
He removed his upper garment and replied:
"I erred in neglecting your command
and did not deliver them."
The king took his hand and said:
"Do not trouble yourself over this!
Return home for now.
If I, the unworthy one, have matters
I will inform you."
In another year,
Shěn Hài, the Taro Officer, reported the location of the king's coffin,
and he was reburied.
Earlier,
King Líng had divined, saying:
"May I yet obtain all under heaven!"
It was inauspicious.
He threw down the tortoise shell,
cursed Heaven, and cried out:
"If this petty thing you will not give me,
I will take it myself!"
The people resented the king's insatiability,
and so joined the rebellion as if returning home.
Earlier,
King Gòng had no designated heir among his principal wives;
he had five favored sons,
but none was designated to succeed.
He then held a grand ceremony to all the mountain and river spirits,
praying:
"I ask the spirits to choose from among the five,
to let one preside over the altars of soil and grain."
He then presented a jade disc to all the spirits, saying:
"He who bows over the disc
is the one established by the spirits—
who would dare oppose it?"
Afterward,
he secretly buried the disc in the courtyard of the Great Chamber with Bā Jī,
had the five sons fast,
and then enter in order of age to bow.
King Kāng stepped over it;
King Líng's elbow touched it;
Zǐ Gàn and Zǐ Xī both stood far from it.
King Píng was young;
he was carried in,
bowed twice,
and both times pressed upon the cord of the disc.
Dòu Wéiguī entrusted his son Chéngrán to this,
saying:
"To abandon ritual and defy fate—
will Chǔ not be in peril!"
When Zǐ Gàn returned,
Hán Xuānzǐ asked Shū Xiàng:
"Will Zǐ Gàn succeed?"
He replied: "It is difficult."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Those who share hatred seek each other out,
like merchants in the market—
why difficult?"
He replied:
"If none share his likes,
who will share his hatreds?
To seize a state, there are five difficulties:
to have favor but no men, the first;
to have men but no backing, the second;
to have backing but no strategy, the third;
to have strategy but no people, the fourth;
to have people but no virtue, the fifth.
Zǐ Gàn has been in Jìn
for thirteen years.
Among his followers from Jìn and Chǔ,
none are known to be distinguished—
he may be said to have no men.
His clan is gone, his kin have turned against him—
he may be said to have no backing.
To act without an opening—
he may be said to have no strategy.
A wanderer all his life—
he may be said to have no people.
In exile, he shows no signs of being loved—
he may be said to have no virtue.
The king is cruel but unrestrained;
the gentlemen of Chǔ with Zǐ Gàn,
facing five difficulties to slay the former ruler—
who can bring success?
He who will possess Chǔ—
is it not Qìjí?
He governs Chén and Cài,
and the lands beyond the walls are attached to him.
Harsh evils do not arise,
robbers and thieves lie hidden,
private desires are not transgressed,
and the people bear no resentment.
The spirits first commanded it;
the people of the state trust him.
When there is turmoil among the Mǐ surname,
it is always the youngest who is established—
such is Chǔ's constant practice.
To obtain the spirits' favor, first;
to have the people, second;
to possess admirable virtue, third;
to be favored and noble, fourth;
to accord with the constant practice, fifth.
With five advantages to overcome five difficulties,
who can harm him?
As for Zǐ Gàn's office,
he is but a Right Assistant;
counted by noble favor,
he is but a son of a concubine;
by the spirits' command,
he is far from it.
His nobility is gone;
his favor is cast aside.
The people do not cherish him;
the state does not support him.
On what will he stand?"
Xuānzǐ said:
“Weren’t Qí Huán and
Jìn Wén also like this?”
He replied:
“Qí Huán,
son of Wèi Jī,
was favored by Xí;
he had Bào Shūyá, Bīn Xūwú, and Xí Péng as his assistants;
he had Jǔ and Wèi as external supporters;
he had Guó and Gāo as internal supporters;
he followed good advice as a river follows its course,
and his goodness was uniform and solemn;
he did not hoard bribes,
nor did he indulge his desires;
he bestowed gifts tirelessly,
and sought goodness without weariness.
Thus, was it not fitting that he possessed the state?
Was it not appropriate?
Our former lord Wéngōng,
son of Hú Jì Jī,
was favored by Xiàn;
he was fond of learning and never borrowed;
at seventeen years of age,
he had five men of worth.
He had the former senior officials Zǐyú and Zǐfàn as his heart and mind,
and Wèi Chōu and Jiǎ Tuó as his limbs;
he had Qí, Sòng, Qín, and Chǔ as external supporters;
he had Luán, Xì, Hú, and Xiān as internal supporters;
he was in exile for nineteen years,
yet his resolve grew ever firmer.
Huì and Huái abandoned the people,
and the people followed and supported him.
Xiàn had no other close kin,
and the people had no other expectations.
Heaven was assisting Jìn—
how could anyone replace Wén?
These two lords
differed from Zǐgàn.
He had no favored son,
nor did the state have a hidden master;
he bestowed nothing upon the people,
and had no external support;
he left Jìn without being seen off,
and returned to Chǔ without being welcomed—
how could he hope for a state?”
B10.13.3 Jìn completed the Sīqí Palace,
and the feudal lords who returned from their court visits all harbored disloyal thoughts.
Because of the capture of Yùn, Jìn was about to lead the feudal lords to launch a punitive expedition.
Shūxiàng said:
“We must demonstrate our power to the feudal lords.”
So he summoned a joint meeting,
and informed Wú.
In autumn,
the Marquis of Jìn met with the Viscount of Wú at Liáng,
but the waterways were impassable,
so the Viscount of Wú declined and returned.
On the bǐngyín day of the seventh month,
they conducted military exercises south of Zhū.
There were four thousand armored chariots.
Yángshé Fù acted as Minister of War,
and then assembled the feudal lords at Píngqiū.
Zǐchǎn and Zǐ Dàshū accompanied the Earl of Zhèng to the meeting.
Zǐchǎn brought nine tents and canopies,
while Zǐ Dàshū brought forty.
Later, he regretted this,
and at each stop,
he reduced the number.
By the time of the meeting,
it was the same.
They encamped in Wèi territory,
and Shū Fù sought bribes from Wèi,
harassing the grass and firewood gatherers.
A man from Wèi sent Tú Bó to present Shūxiàng with a stew and a box of brocade,
saying:
“The feudal lords serve Jìn,
and dare not harbor disloyalty; how much more so for Wèi, which is under your lordship’s roof?
How would we dare have other intentions?
The grass and firewood gatherers are acting differently than before—
I venture to ask about this.”
Shūxiàng accepted the stew but returned the brocade,
saying:
“In Jìn, there is a man named Yángshé Fù,
insatiably greedy for bribes,
and he will soon meet his end.
For this matter,
if you, sir, bestow it upon him by your lord’s command,
it will stop.”
The messenger followed his advice,
and before he had even left, the harassment ceased.
The men of Jìn were about to renew the covenant,
but the men of Qí refused.
The Marquis of Jìn sent Shūxiàng to inform Liú Xiàngōng, saying:
“If the men of Qí do not join the covenant,
what should we do?”
He replied:
“A covenant is to establish trust.
If you, my lord, possess trust,
and the feudal lords are not disloyal,
what is there to worry about?
Inform them with eloquent words,
and oversee them with martial forces.
Even if Qí does not agree,
you, my lord, will have gained much.
This old servant of the Son of Heaven requests to lead the royal forces,
‘with ten great chariots
to lead the way.’
Whether slow or swift is up to you, my lord.”
Shūxiàng informed Qí,
saying:
“The feudal lords seek a covenant,
and are already gathered here.
If you, my lord, see no benefit in it,
our humble lord requests it.”
They replied:
“When the feudal lords punish disloyalty,
then they renew the covenant.
If all obey orders,
what need is there to renew the covenant?”
Shūxiàng said:
“When a state declines,
it has affairs but no established duties,
so affairs are not regulated;
it has duties but no ritual,
so regulation lacks order;
it has ritual but no authority,
so order lacks reverence;
it has authority but no display,
so reverence lacks clarity.
Without clarity, reverence is abandoned,
and all affairs are left unfinished—
this is the path to downfall.
Therefore, the system of the enlightened kings
made the feudal lords send annual visits to record their duties,
intervening court visits to discuss ritual,
a second court visit to assemble and demonstrate authority,
and a second assembly to covenant and display clarity.
Duties are recorded in friendship,
ritual is discussed in rank,
authority is demonstrated to the multitude,
and clarity is displayed to the spirits.
Since ancient times,
this has never been neglected.
The way of survival or destruction
always arises from this.
Jìn, as master of ritual for the covenant,
fears there may be disorder;
we present the Qí sacrificial animals
and lay them before you lords,
seeking to complete the affair.
If you, my lord, say
‘I will certainly abolish it,’
what covenant can there be with Qí?
We ask you, my lord, to consider this.
Our humble lord has heard your command.”
The men of Qí grew fearful,
and replied:
“A small state speaks,
a great state decides—
how dare we not obey?
Having heard your command,
we respectfully proceed,
whether slow or swift is up to you, my lord.”
Shūxiàng said:
“The feudal lords have grown lax,
we must demonstrate our power to them.”
On the xīnwèi day of the eighth month,
they conducted military exercises,
raising flags without streamers.
On the rénshēn day,
they added the streamers.
The feudal lords were awed.
The men of Zhū and Jǔ complained to Jìn, saying:
“Lǔ attacks us morning and night,
and we are nearly destroyed.
Our failure to pay tribute
is because of Lǔ.”
The Marquis of Jìn refused to see the Duke.
He sent Shūxiàng to decline, saying:
“The feudal lords will covenant on the jiǎxū day.
Our humble lord knows he cannot serve you, my lord,
so we ask you not to trouble yourself.”
Zǐfú Huìbó replied:
“If you, my lord, believe the complaints of barbarians,
and sever ties with a fraternal state,
abandoning the descendants of Zhōu Gōng—
that is up to you, my lord.
Our humble lord has heard your command.”
Shūxiàng said:
“Our humble lord has four thousand armored chariots here.
Even if he acted without principle,
he would surely be feared.
How much more so when he follows the Way—
what enemy could stand against him?
Even a lean ox,
falling upon a piglet,
would it not fear death?”
The troubles of Nán Kuǎi and Zǐ Zhòng,
how can they be abandoned?
If we lead the multitudes of Jìn,
employ the armies of the feudal lords,
and take advantage of the anger of Zhū, Jǔ, Qǐ, and Zēng,
to punish Lǔ for its crimes,
and exploit these two troubles,
what objective could we not achieve?"
The people of Lǔ were afraid,
and submitted to the command.
On the day Jiǎxū,
they formed an alliance at Píngqiū,
because Qí had submitted.
The feudal lords were ordered to arrive at the altar by midday.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
they withdrew from court.
Zǐ Chǎn ordered his outer attendants to quickly set up tents at the altar;
Zǐ Tàishū stopped him,
making him wait until the next day.
By evening,
when Zǐ Chǎn heard that they had not yet set up the tents,
he sent someone to hurry them,
but then there was no place left to set them up.
At the alliance ceremony,
Zǐ Chǎn contested the order of precedence,
saying:
"In former times, the Son of Heaven assigned tributes,
their weight according to rank.
High rank meant heavy tribute;
this was the system of Zhōu.
Low rank yet heavy tribute
was for the Diàn fiefs.
The Earl of Zhèng
is a Nán,
yet you make him follow the tribute of a Gōng or Hóu;
I fear he cannot supply it,
and dare to make this request.
The feudal lords have laid down arms,
and make friendship their business.
The commands of the messengers
arrive not a month without,
and the tribute has no fixed measure.
If a small state has deficiencies,
that is how it incurs offense.
The feudal lords repair alliances
to preserve small states.
If contributions are without limit,
their ruin can be awaited.
The system of preservation or ruin
will be decided now."
From midday he argued,
until dusk,
and the men of Jìn agreed.
After the alliance,
Zǐ Tàishū reproached him, saying:
"If the feudal lords were to chastise us,
could it be slighted?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"The government of Jìn has many doors;
they have no leisure to deal with disloyalty and negligence,
what leisure do they have to chastise?
A state that does not compete will also be oppressed;
what kind of state would that be?"
The Duke did not participate in the alliance.
The men of Jìn seized Jì Sūn Yìrú,
covered him with a curtain,
and had Dí men guard him.
Sīduó Shè, carrying brocade,
presented a pot of ice water,
and crawled forward.
The guards stopped him,
so he gave them the brocade and entered.
The men of Jìn took Píngzǐ back with them,
and Zǐfú Jiǎo followed.
Zǐ Chǎn returned,
but before arriving,
he heard that Zǐ Pí had died.
He wept,
and said:
"It is over for me!
There is no point in doing good anymore.
Only the Master knew me."
Zhòngní said of Zǐ Chǎn:
"In this action,
he was sufficient to be the foundation of a state.
The *Shī* says:
'Joyful is the gentleman,
the foundation of the state and family.'
Zǐ Chǎn
is a gentleman who seeks joy."
And he said:
"Assembling the feudal lords,
and regulating tribute affairs,
is ritual."
B10.13.4 The people of Xiānyú heard that the Jìn army had all been raised,
yet they did not alert their borders,
nor did they repair their defenses.
Xún Wú of Jìn, from Zhùyōng, led the Upper Army to invade Xiānyú,
reaching Zhōngrén,
drove chariots and competed,
and returned with great spoils.
B10.13.5 When Chǔ destroyed Cài,
King Líng moved Xǔ, Hú, Shěn,
Dào, Fáng, and Shēn to Jīng.
When King Píng ascended the throne,
he restored both Chén and Cài,
and returned them all,
which was ritual.
The son of the hidden heir, Lú, returned to Cài,
which was ritual.
The son of the mourning heir, Wú, returned to Chén,
which was ritual.
B10.13.6 In winter, the tenth month,
they buried Duke Líng of Cài,
which was ritual.
B10.13.7 The Duke went to Jìn.
Xún Wú said to Hán Xuānzǐ:
"When feudal lords visit each other,
it is to discuss old friendships.
To detain their minister and have their lord visit,
is not good friendship,
better to decline him."
So he sent Shì Jǐngbó to decline the Duke at the river.
B10.13.8 Wú destroyed Zhōulái.
Lìngyǐn Zǐ Qí requested to attack Wú.
The King did not permit it,
saying:
"I have not yet comforted the people,
not yet served the spirits and gods,
not yet repaired the defenses,
not yet stabilized the state and family,
and to employ the people's strength—
defeat would be irremediable.
Zhōulái being in Wú
is still as if in Chǔ.
You should wait for now."
B10.13.9 Jì Sūn was still in Jìn.
Zǐfú Huìbó privately said to Zhōngháng Mùzǐ:
"Lǔ serves Jìn;
why is it not like the small barbarian states?
Lǔ
is a brother state,
its territory is still large,
and it can fulfill what is commanded.
If you abandon it for barbarians,
making it serve Qí or Chǔ,
what benefit would that be for Jìn?
Cherishing kin and favoring the great,
rewarding the compliant and punishing the non-compliant,
is how one becomes an alliance leader.
Please consider this!
A proverb says:
'A minister has one lord, a lord has two choices.'
Do we not have a great state?"
Mùzǐ reported this to Hán Xuānzǐ,
and said:
"Chǔ destroyed Chén and Cài,
and we could not save them,
yet for barbarians we detain our kin;
what use is that?"
So they returned Jì Sūn.
Huìbó said:
"Our ruler does not know his crime;
you assembled the feudal lords and detained his elder.
If he still has a crime,
a death sentence is acceptable.
If you say he is innocent and kindly release him,
but the feudal lords do not hear of it,
this is escaping punishment;
what kind of release is that?
I request to follow our ruler's kindness at the assembly."
Xuānzǐ was troubled by this,
and said to Shū Xiàng:
"Can you get Jì Sūn to return?"
He replied:
"I cannot.
Fù can."
So he sent Shū Yú.
Shū Yú went to see Jì Sūn,
and said:
"Formerly, Fù offended the ruler of Jìn,
and fled to the ruler of Lǔ.
Without the grace of Wǔzǐ,
I would not have reached today.
Although I have returned my bones to Jìn,
you, sir, gave me flesh,
how dare I not be completely sincere?
If I let you return and you do not,
Fù hears from the officials
they will prepare lodgings for you at Xīhé;
what will you do then?"
And he wept.
Píngzǐ was afraid,
and returned first.
Huìbó awaited the ritual.
A10.14 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Zhāo, Fourteenth Year*
A10.14.1 In the fourteenth year, spring,
Yìrú arrived from Jìn.
A10.14.2 In the third month, the Earl of Cáo, Téng, died.
A10.14.3 In summer, the fourth month.
A10.14.4 In autumn,
the burial of Duke Wǔ of Cáo took place.
A10.14.5 In the eighth month,
the Viscount of Jǔ, Qùjí, died.
A10.14.6 In winter,
Jǔ put to death its nobleman, Yìhuī.
B10.14 The Commentary to the Fifteenth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.14.1 In spring of the fourteenth year,
Yìrú arrived from Jìn,
showing respect to Jìn
and blaming himself.
Showing respect to Jìn
and blaming oneself
was in accordance with ritual.
B10.14.2 When Nán Kuǎi was about to revolt,
he made a covenant with the people of Fèi.
The Minister of Works, Lǎo Qí, and Lǚ Guǐ pretended to be ill,
and sent a request to Nán Kuǎi, saying:
"We wish to receive the covenant, but our illness has flared up.
If, by your grace, we do not die,
we ask to wait until we recover and then covenant."
He agreed.
These two men, capitalizing on the people's desire to revolt,
requested to assemble the multitude in the morning and covenant.
They then seized Nán Kuǎi, saying:
"The multitude of officers have not forgotten their ruler,
and fearing you, have obeyed your commands
until now for three years.
If you do not consider this,
the people of Fèi, unable to bear the plight of their ruler,
will no longer be able to fear you.
Where is there any desire of yours that you cannot satisfy?
We ask to escort you away."
He requested a delay of five days.
He then fled to Qí.
He attended Duke Jǐng at a drinking party.
The Duke said:
"Traitor!"
He replied: "Your servant wished to strengthen the ducal house."
Zǐ Hán Xī said:
"A household officer wishing to strengthen the ducal house,
no crime is greater than this."
The Minister of Works Lǎo Qí and Lǚ Guǐ came to return Fèi,
and the Marquis of Qí sent Bào Wénzǐ to deliver it.
B10.14.3 In summer,
the Viscount of Chǔ sent Rán Dān to inspect the troops of the Upper States at Zōngqiū,
and also to comfort their people.
He distributed goods to the poor,
relieved the destitute;
cared for orphans and the young,
supported the aged and the sick;
gathered in the solitary,
aided those suffering calamity;
showed compassion to the widowed and orphaned,
pardoned crimes and offenses;
investigated the wicked and evil,
promoted those long neglected;
treated newcomers with courtesy,
gave positions to the old;
rewarded the meritorious,
united relatives;
employed the good,
and assigned offices appropriately.
He sent Qū Pí to inspect the troops of the Eastern States at Shàolíng,
and it was the same there.
He established good relations on the borders.
He gave the people five years of rest,
and only then used the army,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B10.14.4 In autumn, the eighth month,
Duke Zhùqiū of Jǔ died.
Duke Jiāo showed no grief,
and the people of the state were not obedient to him.
They wished to establish Duke Zhùqiū's younger brother, Gēng Yú.
Pú Yúhóu hated the nobleman Yìhuī,
but was friendly with Gēng Yú;
Duke Jiāo hated the nobleman Duó,
but was friendly with Yìhuī.
The nobleman Duó, through Pú Yúhóu, plotted with him,
saying:
"You kill Yìhuī,
and I will expel our ruler and bring in Gēng Yú."
He agreed.
B10.14.5 The Chief Minister of Chǔ, Zǐ Qí, had done favors for the King,
but did not know moderation.
He allied with the Yǎng clan,
and his demands were insatiable.
The King was troubled by this.
In the ninth month, on the jiǎwǔ day,
the Viscount of Chǔ killed Dòu Chéngrán,
and exterminated the Yǎng clan.
He made Dòu Xīn dwell in Yún,
so as not to forget past merits.
B10.14.6 In winter, the twelfth month,
Pú Yúhóu Zīfū killed the Jǔ nobleman Yìhuī.
Duke Jiāo fled to Qí.
The nobleman Duó went to Qí to welcome Gēng Yú.
Xí Dǎng and the nobleman Chú of Qí escorted him,
and he was given land as a bribe.
B10.14.7 The Jìn nobleman Xíng Hóu and Yōngzǐ disputed over the fields of Xù.
It dragged on for a long time without resolution.
Shì Jǐngbó went to Chǔ,
and Shū Yú acted as judge in his place.
Hán Xuānzǐ ordered him to adjudicate the old case,
and the fault lay with Yōngzǐ.
Yōngzǐ gave his daughter to Shū Yú,
and Shū Yú shifted the blame to Xíng Hóu.
Xíng Hóu was enraged,
and killed Shū Yú and Yōngzǐ at court.
Xuānzǐ asked Shū Xiàng about their crimes.
Shū Xiàng said:
"The three men are equally guilty;
it is permissible to execute the living and expose the corpses of the dead.
Yōngzǐ knew his own guilt,
yet bribed to purchase a favorable verdict;
Fù (Shū Yú) sold justice;
Xíng Hóu committed murder on his own authority.
Their crimes are one and the same.
To have evil oneself yet seize the good of others is 'hūn' (confusion/obscuration);
to be greedy and ruin one's office is 'mò' (corruption);
to kill without scruple is 'zéi' (banditry).
The *Xià Shū* says:
'For hūn, mò, zéi,
execute.
Such was the penalty of Gāo Yáo.'
I ask to follow this."
They then executed Xíng Hóu and exposed the corpses of Yōngzǐ and Shū Yú in the marketplace.
Zhòngní (Confucius) said:
"Shū Xiàng
possessed the straightforwardness of antiquity.
In governing the state and administering punishments,
he did not conceal the faults of his kin.
Three times he enumerated the evils of Shū Yú,
and did not make the slightest reduction.
He acted from righteousness,
truly he can be called straightforward!
At the meeting of Píngqiū,
he enumerated his (Shū Yú's) covetousness,
thereby easing the situation for Wèi,
and Jìn was not tyrannical.
In returning Jì Sūn to Lǔ,
he exposed his deceit,
thereby easing the situation for Lǔ,
and Jìn was not oppressive.
In the case of Xíng Hóu's trial,
he spoke of his greed,
thereby rectifying the penal code,
and Jìn was not unjust.
With three statements he removed three evils,
and added three benefits.
To kill one's kin yet increase one's honor,
this is indeed righteousness!"
A10.15 The Fifteenth Year of Duke Zhāo, the Classic
A10.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the Viscount of Wú, Yímò, died.
A10.15.2 In the second month, on the guǐyǒu day,
the great sacrifice was performed at the Wǔ Palace.
As the yuè players entered,
Shū Gōng died.
The music was removed,
and the ceremony was completed.
A10.15.3 In summer,
Cài Cháo Wú fled to Zhèng.
A10.15.4 In the sixth month, on the dīngsì day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A10.15.5 In autumn,
Xún Wú of Jìn led an army to attack the Xiānyú.
A10.15.6 In winter,
the Duke went to Jìn.
B10.15 The Commentary to the Fifteenth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.15.1 In spring of the fifteenth year,
when they were about to perform the dì sacrifice to Duke Wǔ,
the hundred officials were warned.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"On the day of the dì sacrifice, will there be misfortune?
I have seen a red and black baleful vapor,
which is not an auspicious sign for sacrifice,
but a sign of mourning.
Perhaps it will befall the presiding officer!"
On the guiyou day of the second month,
the Di sacrifice was held.
Shǔ Gōng was overseeing the ceremony,
but when the yuè players entered, he passed away.
The music was removed,
and the ceremony was completed,
which was in accordance with ritual.
B10.15.2 Chǔ’s Fèi Wújí, resenting Cháo Wú’s presence in Cài,
wanted to remove him.
He thus said to him:
"The king trusts only you,
which is why he placed you in Cài.
You are also of mature age,
yet you hold a low position—
this is humiliating.
You must seek advancement,
and I will assist you in making the request."
He also said to those above him:
"The king trusts only Wú,
which is why he placed him in Cài.
None of you gentlemen compare to him,
yet you are above him—
is this not difficult?
If you do not plan for this,
you will surely face calamity."
In summer,
the people of Cài expelled Cháo Wú,
and Cháo Wú fled to Zhèng.
The king was angry
and said:
"It is because I trusted Wú
that I placed him in Cài.
Moreover, without Wú,
I would not have reached this position.
Why did you remove him?"
Wújí replied:
"How could I not want Wú?
However, I knew beforehand that his character was unusual.
With Wú in Cài,
Cài would certainly fly away swiftly.
Removing Wú
is the means to clip its wings."
B10.15.3 On the yichou day of the sixth month,
the king’s crown prince, Shòu, passed away.
B10.15.4 In autumn, on the wuyin day of the eighth month,
King Mù’s queen passed away.
B10.15.5 Jìn’s Xún Wú led troops to attack Xiānyú,
besieging Gǔ.
Some people of Gǔ requested to surrender the city in rebellion,
but Mùzǐ did not permit it.
His attendants said:
"Our troops have not toiled,
yet we can obtain the city—
why not do it?"
Mùzǐ said:
"I heard from Shū Xiàng:
'If likes and dislikes are not excessive,
the people know where to turn,
and affairs will not fail.'
If someone were to betray our city,
it is what we greatly detest;
if others bring a city to us,
why should we alone favor it?
To reward what we greatly detest—
what then of what we favor?
If we do not reward it,
it would be breaking faith—
how then could we protect the people?
If our strength allows, we advance;
if not, we retreat—
acting according to our measure.
I cannot desire a city and thereby approach treachery—
the loss would be greater."
He had the people of Gǔ kill the traitors and repair their defenses.
After besieging Gǔ for three months,
some people of Gǔ requested to surrender.
He had their people appear
and said:
"They still have the appearance of having food—
let them repair their city for now."
The military officers said:
"To obtain a city and not take it,
to weary the people and halt the troops—
how is this serving the ruler?"
Mùzǐ said:
"It is how I serve the ruler.
To obtain one city and teach the people indolence—
what use is the city then?
A city bought with indolence

Ritual is the great guiding principle for kings.
With one action, two rituals are lost,
and there is no great guiding principle.
Words are used to examine the canons,
and the canons are used to record the guiding principles.
If one forgets the guiding principles and speaks excessively,
even if one cites the canons,
what use will it be?"
A10.16 *The Spring and Autumn Annals*, Year 16 of Duke Zhāo
A10.16.1 In the sixteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Xú.
A10.16.2 The Viscount of Chǔ lured the Róng Mánzǐ and killed him.
A10.16.3 In summer,
the duke arrived from Jìn.
A10.16.4 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the day Jǐhài,
the Marquis of Jìn, Yí, died.
A10.16.5 In the ninth month,
a great rain sacrifice was held.
A10.16.6 Jìsūn Yìrú went to Jìn.
A10.16.7 In winter, in the tenth month,
Duke Zhāo of Jìn was buried.
B10.16 *The Commentary of Zuǒ*, Year 16 of Duke Zhāo
B10.16.1 In the sixteenth year, in spring,
in the royal first month,
the duke was in Jìn,
and the people of Jìn detained the duke.
This was not recorded in the Annals,
as it was concealed out of discretion.
B10.16.2 The Marquis of Qí attacked Xú.
The Viscount of Chǔ, hearing of the disorder among the Mán people and the lack of good faith of the Mánzǐ,
sent Rán Dān to lure the Róng Mánzǐ, Jiā,
and killed him,
then seized the lands of the Mán.
Afterward, he reestablished the son of the Mánzǐ,
which was in accordance with ritual.
In the second month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
the army of Qí reached Púsuì,
and the people of Xú sought peace.
The Viscount of Xú, along with the people of Tán and Jǔ, met with the Marquis of Qí,
and they made a covenant at Púsuì,
presenting the Marquis with the Dǐng of Jiǎfù as a bribe.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"When the feudal lords lack a hegemon,
it is harmful indeed!
The ruler of Qí acts without principle,
raising armies to attack distant lands.
When they meet with him,
he achieves his aims and returns,
with no one able to resist him.
This is because there is no hegemon!
The *Book of Songs* says:
'When the royal house of Zhōu was destroyed,
there was nowhere to settle and find peace.
The chief ministers scattered and lived apart,
and none knew of our toil.'
Is this not referring to such a situation?"
B10.16.3 In the second month,
Hán Qǐ of Jìn paid a courtesy visit to Zhèng,
and the Earl of Zhèng hosted a banquet for him.
Zǐchǎn admonished his officials:
"If you hold a position at court,
you must not fail to be reverent and respectful!"
Kǒng Zhāng arrived late
and stood among the guests.
The master of ceremonies tried to move him;
he went behind the guests,
and again the master of ceremonies tried to move him;
so he went to stand among the hanging musical instruments.
The guests followed him with laughter.
After the affair concluded,
Fùzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"One must be cautious with people from great states.
They nearly laughed at us;
would they not then oppress us?
Even if we are all courteous,
they would still look down on us.
If a state lacks ritual,
how can it seek honor?
Kǒng Zhāng's loss of proper position
is a disgrace to you, sir."
Zǐchǎn angrily replied:
"Issuing commands that are not appropriate,
giving orders that are not trustworthy,
administering punishments that are biased and unjust,
allowing legal cases to become disordered and chaotic,
showing disrespect at meetings and court assemblies,
disobeying orders from missions,
bringing oppression from great states,
exhausting the people without achieving merit,
incurring guilt without realizing it—
these are the disgraces of Qiáo.
Kǒng Zhāng is the descendant of the ruler's elder brother,
the heir of a former minister,
a hereditary great officer;
he has received commands to serve as an envoy,
circulating among the feudal lords;
he is respected by the people of the state
and known to the feudal lords.
He stands at court and sacrifices at home;
he receives a salary from the state
and contributes to the army's provisions;
he has duties in mourning and sacrificial rites,
receiving and returning sacrificial meat.
When sacrifices are held in the ancestral temple,
he already has an established position.
For several generations, his family has held this position,
preserving their duties through the ages.
If he forgets his place,
how could Qiáo be disgraced by it?
If all deviant and improper actions were blamed on the minister in charge,
it would mean the former kings had no punishments.
You should rather admonish me with other matters."
Xuānzǐ had a pair of jade rings,
one of which was in the possession of a Zhèng merchant.
Xuānzǐ requested it from the Earl of Zhèng,
but Zǐchǎn refused to give it,
saying:
"This is not an object guarded by the government storehouses;
our humble ruler does not know of it."
Zǐtàishū and Zǐyǔ said to Zǐchǎn:
"Master Hán does not make many requests,
and we cannot be disloyal to the state of Jìn.
The state of Jìn and Master Hán must not be treated lightly.
If slanderers should arise and stir up conflict between them,
and even ghosts and spirits assist them,
rousing their fierce anger,
what would be the use of regret?
Why do you, sir, begrudge a single ring,
risking the hatred of a great state for it?
Why not seek it and give it to him?"
Zǐchǎn replied:
"I am not treating Jìn lightly or being disloyal;
I intend to serve them to the end,
and that is precisely why I do not give it—
out of loyalty and good faith.
Qiáo has heard that a gentleman does not worry about lacking wealth,
but worries about holding a position without a good reputation.
Qiáo has heard that in governing a state, the difficulty is not in being unable to serve the great and nurture the small,
but in the danger of lacking ritual to secure one's position.
If the people of a great state give orders to a small state,
and all their demands are met,
how will we be able to supply them?
Sometimes complying, sometimes refusing—
that would create even greater offense.
If the demands of a great state are not rejected on grounds of ritual,
what end will there be to their greed?
We would become a border town,
losing our proper status.
If Master Hán, on a mission by command,
seeks jade,
his greed and excess are extreme.
Is that not a crime?
To produce one piece of jade and give rise to two crimes—
we would lose our proper status,
and Master Hán would become guilty of greed.
What would be the use of that?
Moreover, if we incur offense because of jade,
would that not be foolish?"
Master Hán bought the ring from a merchant,
and the price was already settled.
The merchant said:
"You must inform the great officers of our state!"
Master Hán requested it from Zǐchǎn, saying:
"The other day, I requested the ring,
but you, the minister in charge, deemed it improper,
so I did not dare to ask again.
Now I have bought it from a merchant,
and the merchant says
'I must report it,'
so I venture to make this request."
Zǐchǎn replied:
"In the past, our former lord Duke Huán and the merchants all came from Zhōu.
Working together in pairs, they cleared this land,
cutting away the overgrowth of péng, hāo, lí, and diào,
and settled here together.
For generations, there have been covenants and oaths
to maintain mutual trust, saying:
'You shall not betray me,
and I shall not force unfair trade upon you,
nor seize or plunder anything.
You may have profitable markets and precious goods,
and I shall not interfere or seek to know of them.'
Relying on this solemn oath,
we have been able to protect each other, up to the present day.
Now you, sir, have come in friendship to honor us,
yet you say that our humble state forcibly seized the merchant's goods—
this would be teaching our humble state to violate the covenant and oath.
Would that not be unacceptable?
If you, sir, obtain the jade,
but lose the feudal lords,
you surely would not do so.
If a great state issues orders,
yet the tribute is without measure,
Zhèng is but a border town,
and we would not comply either.
If I, Qiáo, were to present the jade,
I would not know what it would accomplish.
I dare to privately state this. 」
Hán Zǐ declined the jade,
saying:
"Qǐ is not clever,
how dare I seek jade and invite two offenses?
I dare to decline it. "
In the fourth month of summer,
the six ministers of Zhèng gave Xuānzǐ a farewell feast in the suburbs.
Xuānzǐ said:
"May you gentlemen each recite a poem,
so that Qǐ may also understand Zhèng's intentions. "
Zǐ Cī recited "Wild Vines Grow in the Field."
Xuānzǐ said:
"The young man is excellent!
I have hope. "
Zǐ Chǎn recited Zhèng's "Lamb Fur."
Xuānzǐ said:
"Qǐ cannot bear it. "
Zǐ Tàishū recited "Lifting the Skirt."
Xuānzǐ said:
"With Qǐ here,
how dare I trouble you to turn to others? "
Zǐ Tàishū bowed.
Xuānzǐ said:
"Excellent!
Your words are true.
Without such matters,
could it last to the end? "
Zǐ Yóu recited "Wind and Rain."
Zǐ Qí recited "There Is a Lady in the Same Carriage."
Zǐ Liǔ recited "Falling Leaves."
Xuānzǐ was pleased,
saying:
"Zhèng is nearly prosperous!
You gentlemen, by your lord's command, have honored Qǐ,
reciting poems not beyond Zhèng's aspirations,
all expressing intimate friendship.
You gentlemen,
are masters for several generations,
and need not fear. "
Xuānzǐ presented horses to each,
and recited "I Will Offer."
Zǐ Chǎn bowed,
making the five ministers all bow,
saying:
"You, sir, bring peace to chaos,
how dare we not bow to your virtue! "
Xuānzǐ privately presented Zǐ Chǎn with jade and horses,
saying:
"You commanded Qǐ to abandon that jade,
this was granting me jade and sparing my life,
how dare I not offer thanks with these! "
B10.16.4 The Duke returned from Jìn.
Zǐfú Zhāobó said to Jì Píngzǐ:
"The ducal house of Jìn will likely decline.
The ruler is young and weak,
the six ministers are strong, extravagant, and arrogant.
They will thereby become accustomed to it,
and habit will become the norm.
How can it not decline! "
Píngzǐ said:
"You are young,
what do you know of state affairs? "
B10.16.5 In autumn, the eighth month,
Jìn Zhāogōng died.
B10.16.6 In the ninth month,
there was a great rain-seeking sacrifice,
due to drought.
In Zhèng, there was a great drought.
Tú Jī, Zhù Kuǎn, and Shù Fū were sent to perform rites at Sāng Shān.
They cut down its trees,
but no rain came.
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"To perform rites at the mountain,
is to nurture its forests;
yet they cut down its trees,
their offense is great. "
Their official fiefs were taken away.
B10.16.7 In winter, the tenth month,
Jì Píngzǐ went to Jìn,
to bury Zhāogōng.
Píngzǐ said:
"Zǐfú Huí's words were indeed trustworthy.
The Zǐfú clan has a worthy son! "
A10.17 "The Spring and Autumn Annals, Zhāogōng Year 17"
A10.17.1 In the seventeenth year, spring,
the ruler of Xiǎozhū came for an audience.
A10.17.2 In summer, the first day of the sixth month, jiǎxū,
there was a solar eclipse.
A10.17.3 In autumn,
the ruler of Tán came for an audience.
A10.17.4 In the eighth month,
Jìn Xún Wú led troops to destroy the Lùhún Róng.
A10.17.5 In winter,
a comet appeared at Dàchén.
A10.17.6 The people of Chǔ fought with Wú at Cháng'àn.
B10.17 "The Commentary of Zuǒ, Zhāogōng Year 17"
B10.17.1 In the seventeenth year, spring,
Xiǎozhū Mùgōng came for an audience,
and the Duke feasted with him.
Jì Píngzǐ recited "Gathering Beans,"
and Mùgōng recited "Lush Is the Artemisia."
Zhāozǐ said:
"If not for having a state,
could it last long? "
B10.17.2 In summer, the first day of the sixth month, jiǎxū,
there was a solar eclipse.
The invokers and scribes requested the silk to be used.
Zhāozǐ said:
"When there is a solar eclipse,
the Son of Heaven does not feast,
beats drums at the altar of soil,
feudal lords use silk at the altar of soil,
and beat drums at court—
this is ritual. "
Píngzǐ opposed this,
saying:
"Stop.
Only on the first day of the first month,
before evil arises,
if there is a solar eclipse,
then there is drum-beating and silk-use—
this is ritual.
At other times, it is not done. "
The Grand Scribe said:
"It is in this month.
The sun passes the equinox but has not reached the solstice,
the three luminaries bring disaster,
then all officials don plain garments;
the ruler does not feast,
withdraws for a time;
music is played and drums beaten,
invokers use silk,
scribes use words.
Thus the *Xià Shū* says:
'The luminaries do not gather in the chamber,
blind musicians beat drums,
overseers gallop,
commoners run'—
this refers to the first day of the month.
It corresponds to the fourth month of summer,
called Mèngxià. "
Píngzǐ did not comply.
Zhāozǐ withdrew,
saying:
"The master harbors different intentions,
he does not treat the ruler as ruler. "
B10.17.3 In autumn,
the ruler of Tán came for an audience,
and the Duke feasted with him.
Zhāozǐ asked him,
saying:
"Shàohào named officials after birds,
what was the reason? "
The ruler of Tán said:
"He is my ancestor,
I know of this.
In ancient times, Huángdì used clouds to mark,
thus had cloud masters and cloud names;
Yándì used fire to mark,
thus had fire masters and fire names;
Gònggōng used water to mark,
thus had water masters and water names;
Dàhào used dragons to mark,
thus had dragon masters and dragon names.
When my high ancestor Shàohào Zhì was established,
phoenixes happened to arrive,
thus he marked with birds,
having bird masters and bird names:
Fèngniǎo shì,
was the calendar regulator;
Xuánniǎo shì,
governed the equinoxes;
The Bózhào clan
oversaw the solstices;
the Qīngniǎo clan
oversaw the beginnings;
the Dānniǎo clan
oversaw the closures.
The Zhùjiū clan
was the Minister of Education;
the Jūjiū clan
was the Minister of War;
the Shījiū clan
was the Minister of Works;
the Shuǎngjiū clan
was the Minister of Justice;
the Gǔjiū clan
oversaw affairs.
These five Jiū clans
gathered the people.
The five Zhì clans served as the five Directors of Crafts,
improving tools and standardizing measures,
thereby equalizing the people.
The nine Hù clans served as the nine Directors of Agriculture,
preventing the people from excess.
Since the time of Zhuānxū,
they could not record the distant past,
so they recorded the recent.
To appoint people as teachers of the people and name them after the people's affairs
was something they could no longer do."
Zhòngní heard of this
and went to see Tánzǐ to learn from him.
Afterward, he told others:
"I have heard that
'When the Son of Heaven loses the official posts,
the official learning remains among the Four Barbarians,'
and this is indeed credible."
B10.17.4 The Marquis of Jìn sent Tú Kuǎi to Zhōu,
requesting to perform sacrifices at Luò and Sāntú.
Cháng Hóng said to Liúzǐ:
"The guest's demeanor is fierce;
this is not for a sacrifice,
but likely to attack the Róng!
The Lùhún clan is very close to Chǔ,
so this must be the reason.
My lord should prepare for it!"
They then alerted the defenses against the Róng.
In the ninth month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
Xún Wú of Jìn led his army across from Jíjīn,
first sending the sacrificial historian to offer animals at Luò.
The people of Lùhún were unaware,
and the army followed.
On the day Gēngwǔ,
they then destroyed Lùhún,
reproaching them for their disloyalty to Chǔ.
The ruler of Lùhún fled to Chǔ,
and his people fled to Gānlù.
Zhōu captured many.
Xuānzǐ dreamed that Duke Wén led Xún Wú by the hand and gave him Lùhún,
so he sent Mùzǐ to lead the army
and present the captives at the temple of Duke Wén.
B10.17.5 In winter,
a comet appeared at Dàchén,
reaching west to the Hàn River.
Shēn Xū said:
"The broomstar is used to sweep away the old and establish the new.
Heavenly affairs always have omens.
Now it sweeps away the fire,
so when fire appears, it will surely spread.
Will the feudal lords have fires?"
Zǐ Shèn said:
"Last year I saw it,
and that was its sign.
When fire appeared, it was seen;
this year, when fire appears, it will be prominent.
It must enter with the fire and then subside.
It has resided with the fire for a long time;
is this not so?
When fire appears,
in the Xià calendar it is the third month,
in the Shāng calendar the fourth month,
in the Zhōu calendar the fifth month.
The Xià calendar accords with Heaven.
If a fire occurs,
four states will bear it,
namely Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng!
Sòng
is the place of Dàchén;
Chén
is the place of Tàihào;
Zhèng
is the place of Zhùróng;
all are the abodes of fire.
The comet reached the Hàn River;
the Hàn
is an omen of water.
Wèi
is the place of Zhuānxū,
so it is called Dìqiū.
Its star is the great water;
water
is the mate of fire.
It will likely occur on Bǐngzǐ or Rénwǔ!
Water and fire combine thus.
If the fire enters and subsides,
it will surely be on Rénwǔ,
not beyond the month it appears."
Bì Zào of Zhèng said to Zǐchǎn:
"Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng will all have fires on the same day.
If we use guàn jiǎ and jade zàn,
Zhèng will surely not have a fire."
Zǐchǎn did not give them.
B10.17.6 Wú attacked Chǔ.
Yáng Gài was the Lìngyǐn;
he divined about the battle,
and it was not auspicious.
Sīmǎ Zǐyú said:
"We hold the upper river;
why is it not auspicious?
Moreover, according to Chǔ custom,
the Sīmǎ orders the tortoise shell;
I request to change the divination."
He ordered:
"If Fáng dies with his troops,
and the Chǔ army follows,
may we greatly overcome them!"
It was auspicious.
They fought at Cháng'àn.
Zǐyú died first,
and the Chǔ army followed.
They greatly defeated the Wú army,
capturing their flagship Yúhuáng.
They had men from Suí and those who arrived later guard it,
surrounding it with a moat,
digging to the springs,
filling the tunnel with charcoal,
and arraying troops to await orders.
Prince Guāng of Wú requested of his troops,
saying:
"Losing the former king's flagship
is not only my fault,
but also yours.
I ask to borrow strength to retrieve it and save ourselves from death."
The troops agreed.
He sent three men with long beards to hide by the side of the ship,
saying:
"When I call 'Yúhuáng,'
respond.
The army will follow at night."
He called three times,
and each time they responded in turn.
The Chǔ men followed and killed them.
The Chǔ army fell into chaos,
and the Wú men greatly defeated them,
retrieving Yúhuáng and returning.
A10.18 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Eighteenth Year of Duke Zhāo"
A10.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
in the king's third month,
the Earl of Cáo, Xū, died.
A10.18.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on Rénwǔ,
Sòng, Wèi,
Chén, and Zhèng had fires.
A10.18.3 In the sixth month,
the people of Zhū entered Yǔ.
A10.18.4 In autumn,
they buried Duke Píng of Cáo.
A10.18.5 In winter,
Xǔ moved to Báiyǔ.
B10.18 "The Commentary of Zuo: The Eighteenth Year of Duke Zhāo"
B10.18.1 In the eighteenth year, in spring,
in the king's second month, on Yǐmǎo,
Máo Dé of Zhōu killed Máo Bó Guò
and replaced him.
Cháng Hóng said:
"Máo Dé is sure to perish.
This is the day of Kūnwú's ripening,
due to his extravagance.
Yet Máo Dé achieves extravagance in the king's capital;
if he does not perish,
what is he waiting for?"
B10.18.2 In the third month,
Duke Píng of Cáo died.
B10.18.3 In summer, in the fifth month,
fire first appeared at dusk.
On Bǐngzǐ,
there was wind.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"This is called the Róng wind,
the beginning of fire;
in seven days,
the fire will occur!"
On the wùyín day,
the wind was very strong.
On the rénwǔ day,
it was even stronger.
Fires broke out in Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng.
Zǐ Shèn climbed the granary of the Dàtíng clan to observe,
and said:
"It is Sòng, Wèi, Chén, and Zhèng."
Several days later, they all came to report the fires.
Bì Zào said:
"If you do not heed my words,
Zhèng will suffer another fire."
The people of Zhèng requested to follow his advice,
but Zǐ Chǎn refused.
Zǐ Tàishū said:
"Treasures are meant to protect the people.
If there is a fire,
the state may be nearly destroyed.
If it can save us from destruction,
why do you begrudge it?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"The ways of Heaven are distant,
the ways of man are near.
They are not within our reach;
how can we know them?
How does Zào know the ways of Heaven?
He speaks a great deal,
and is it not possible that sometimes he is right?"
Thus, he did not comply.
And there was no further fire.
Before the disaster in Zhèng,
Lǐ Xī told Zǐ Chǎn:
"There will be a great omen,
the people will be shaken,
and the state may be nearly destroyed.
I myself will perish,
and will not live to see it.
If the capital were moved,
would that be feasible?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"Even if it were feasible,
I am not capable of deciding on a move."
When the fire occurred,
Lǐ Xī had already died,
and had not yet been buried.
Zǐ Chǎn sent thirty men with a carriage to move his coffin.
When the fire broke out,
Zǐ Chǎn dismissed the Jìn princes and nobles at the east gate,
ordered the Minister of Justice to send away new guests,
and forbade old guests from leaving the palace.
He sent Zǐ Kuān and Zǐ Shàng to patrol the screens and curtains,
all the way to the great temple.
He ordered Gōngsūn Dēng to move the great tortoise shell,
ordered the invocators and scribes to move the ancestral tablets to the Zhōu temple,
and reported to the former rulers.
He ordered the treasury and storehouse officials to each attend to their duties.
Shāng Chénggōng was ordered to alert the palace superintendent,
to evacuate the old palace women,
and place them where the fire could not reach.
The Minister of War and Minister of Justice stationed themselves along the fire's path,
to manage the areas affected by the fire.
People from below the walls formed ranks and ascended the walls.
The next day,
he ordered the rural magistrates to each protect their conscripts,
the suburban officials to assist the invocators and scribes,
to perform purification rites north of the capital,
to exorcise the fire with offerings to Xuánmíng and Huílù,
and to pray at the four city walls.
He recorded the burned houses and reduced their taxes,
and provided them with materials.
There was three days of mourning,
and the markets in the capital were closed.
He sent envoys to inform the various states.
Sòng and Wèi did the same.
Chén did not help fight the fire,
and Xǔ did not offer condolences for the disaster.
Thus, the noblemen knew that Chén and Xǔ would perish first.
B10.18.4 In the sixth month,
the people of Yǔ were transplanting rice,
and the people of Zhū attacked Yǔ.
The people of Yǔ were about to close the gates,
but a Zhū man named Yáng Luó seized the head of the gatekeeper,
and thus entered,
taking all captives back with him.
The ruler of Yǔ said:
"I have nowhere to return to."
He followed his family to Zhū.
Duke Zhuāng of Zhū returned the wife of the ruler of Yǔ,
but kept his daughter.
B10.18.5 In autumn,
Duke Píng of Cáo was buried.
Those who went there saw Yuán Bólǔ of Zhōu,
and spoke with him.
He expressed no interest in learning.
Upon returning, they told Mǐn Zǐmǎ.
Mǐn Zǐmǎ said:
"Zhōu is likely to fall into chaos!
There must be many who hold such views,
and then it reaches the great men.
The great men worry about losing and become confused,
and then say:
'One can do without learning,
lack of learning does no harm.'
If it does no harm, then they do not learn,
and then anything goes.
Thus, inferiors oppress superiors and superiors neglect their duties.
How can there not be chaos?
Learning
is like cultivation.
Without learning, one will decline.
The Yuán clan is likely to perish!"
B10.18.6 In the seventh month,
Zǐ Chǎn of Zhèng, because of the fire,
held a great sacrifice to the Earth God,
performed purification rites in all directions,
to dispel the fire disaster,
which was in accordance with ritual.
Then he selected troops for a grand hunt,
preparing to clear the grounds for the hunt.
Zǐ Tàishū's ancestral temple was south of the road,
and his residence was north of the road.
The courtyard was small.
After three days past the deadline,
he ordered the clearing crew to line up south of the road and north of the temple,
and said:
"When Zǐ Chǎn passes by you,
and orders you to clear quickly,
then demolish in the direction you are facing."
Zǐ Chǎn went to court,
passed by, and was angered by this.
The clearers demolished to the south.
When Zǐ Chǎn reached the intersection,
he ordered his attendants to stop them,
saying:
"Demolish to the north."
When the fire broke out,
Zǐ Chǎn distributed weapons and ascended the ramparts.
Zǐ Tàishū said:
"Will Jìn not take offense?"
Zǐ Chǎn said:
"I have heard that
a small state that forgets its defenses is in danger,
especially when there is a disaster.
A state cannot be treated lightly
precisely because it is prepared."
Later,
the border officials of Jìn reproached Zhèng, saying:
"When Zhèng had a disaster,
the ruler and ministers of Jìn did not dare rest at ease,
performed divinations and made offerings,
sparing no animals or jade.
Zhèng's disaster
was a source of worry for our ruler.
Now you, the officials, abruptly distribute weapons and ascend the ramparts.
Against whom is this directed?
The border people are fearful,
and we dare not fail to report this."
Zǐ Chǎn replied:
"As you have said,
the disaster of our humble state
is a worry for your ruler.
Our humble state has misgoverned,
and Heaven has sent down this disaster.
We also fear that slanderers and villains may seize the opportunity to plot,
inciting greedy men,
repeatedly acting against the interests of our humble state,
thereby increasing your ruler's worries.
If we are fortunate not to perish,
there is still an explanation;
if unfortunately we perish,
even if your ruler worries about it,
it will be too late.
Zhèng has other borders,
but we look to Jìn for support.
Since we serve Jìn,
how would we dare have disloyal thoughts?"
B10.18.7 The Left Minister of Chǔ, Prince Shèng, said to the King of Chǔ:
"Xǔ, to Zhèng,
is an enemy,
yet it resides in Chǔ territory,
and treats Zhèng with disrespect.
Jìn and Zhèng are currently on good terms.
If Zhèng attacks Xǔ,
and Jìn assists them,
Chǔ will lose territory.
Why does Your Majesty not move Xǔ?
Xǔ is not solely loyal to Chǔ.
Zhèng currently has good governance.
Xǔ says:
'We are an ancient state.'
Zhèng says:
'It is our captured city.'
Yè, in Chǔ territory,
is a shield outside the Fāngchéng Mountains."
The land cannot be exchanged,
the state cannot be diminished,
Xǔ cannot be captured,
enmity cannot be provoked—
may Your Majesty consider this!"
The King of Chǔ was pleased.
In winter,
the King of Chǔ sent Prince Shèng to relocate Xǔ to Xī,
which was actually Báiyǔ.
A10.19 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Nineteenth Year of Duke Zhāo"
A10.19.1 In the nineteenth year, in spring,
the Duke of Sòng attacked Zhū.
A10.19.2 In summer, on the wǔchén day of the fifth month,
Crown Prince Zhǐ of Xǔ assassinated his ruler, Mǎi.
A10.19.3 On the jǐmǎo day,
an earthquake occurred.
A10.19.4 In autumn,
Gāo Fā of Qí led troops to attack Jǔ.
A10.19.5 In winter,
Duke Dào of Xǔ was buried.
B10.19 "The Commentary: The Nineteenth Year of Duke Zhāo"
B10.19.1 In the nineteenth year, in spring,
Chǔ's Minister of Works, Chì, relocated Yīn to Xiàyīn,
while the Prime Minister Zǐxiá fortified Jiá.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"Chǔ is no longer concerned with the other feudal lords;
it merely seeks to preserve itself,
maintaining its position for generations to come."
B10.19.2 When the King of Chǔ was in Cài,
the daughter of the border official of Juéyáng fled to him,
and gave birth to Crown Prince Jiàn.
After ascending the throne,
he appointed Wǔ Shē as his tutor,
and Fèi Wújí as his junior tutor.
Fèi Wújí was not favored by the crown prince,
so he sought to slander him to the king,
saying:
"Jiàn is of age to marry."
The king arranged a marriage for him with Qín,
and Fèi Wújí accompanied the envoy to welcome the bride,
but he persuaded the king to take her for himself.
In the first month,
the Chǔ consort, Lady Yíng, arrived from Qín.
B10.19.3 The wife of the ruler of Yǔ
was the daughter of Xiàng Xū of Sòng,
so Xiàng Níng requested troops.
In the second month,
the Duke of Sòng attacked Zhū,
besieging Chóng.
In the third month,
they captured it,
and returned all the captives from Yǔ.
B10.19.4 In summer,
Duke Dào of Xǔ fell ill with malaria.
On the wǔchén day of the fifth month,
he drank the medicine given by Crown Prince Zhǐ and died.
The crown prince fled to Jìn.
The record states
"assassinated his ruler,"
and the gentleman remarked:
"To serve one's ruler with utmost effort and sincerity,
it is better to avoid administering medicine."
B10.19.5 Men of Zhū, Ní, and Xú met with the Duke of Sòng.
On the yǐhài day,
they formed an alliance at Chóng.
B10.19.6 The King of Chǔ raised a naval force to attack Pú.
Fèi Wújí said to the King of Chǔ:
"When Jìn was hegemon,
it was close to the Central States,
while Chǔ was remote and backward,
so it could not compete.
If we greatly fortify Chéngfù
and station the crown prince there,
to open communications with the north,
while Your Majesty secures the south,
then we will gain the world."
The king was pleased,
and followed his advice.
Thus, Crown Prince Jiàn resided in Chéngfù.
The Prime Minister Zǐxiá visited Qín,
to express gratitude for the consort.
B10.19.7 In autumn,
Gāo Fā of Qí led troops to attack Jǔ,
and the ruler of Jǔ fled to Jìzhāng.
He sent Sūn Shū to attack it.
Earlier,
there was a woman in Jǔ
whose husband was killed by the ruler of Jǔ,
and she became a widow.
In her old age,
she sought refuge in Jìzhāng,
where she spun thread to measure the city wall and then removed it.
When the army arrived,
she threw it outside.
Someone presented it to Zǐ Zhàn,
who had his troops climb the wall at night using ropes.
Sixty men ascended,
but the ropes broke.
The troops raised a clamor,
and the people on the walls also shouted.
Duke Gòng of Jǔ was terrified,
opened the western gate, and fled.
On the bǐngzǐ day of the seventh month,
the Qí army entered Jì.
B10.19.8 In this year,
Sì Yǎn of Zhèng died.
Zǐyóu had married the daughter of a Jìn minister,
and they gave birth to Sī,
who was still young.
His uncles and elder brothers installed Zǐxiá.
Zǐchǎn disliked his character,
and considered it improper,
so he did not approve,
but neither did he stop it.
The Sì clan was alarmed.
Another day,
Sī informed his maternal uncle.
In winter,
men from Jìn sent envoys with gifts to Zhèng,
to inquire about the reason for Sì Qǐ's installation.
The Sì clan was afraid,
and Sì Qǐ wanted to flee,
but Zǐchǎn did not allow him to leave;
he requested tortoise shells for divination,
but Zǐchǎn did not give them.
The ministers discussed how to respond,
but Zǐchǎn, without waiting, replied to the envoy:
"Zhèng has not been blessed by Heaven,
and several of our ruler's ministers have died from epidemics or premature deaths.
Now we have also lost our late senior minister Yǎn.
His son is young and weak,
and a few of his uncles and elder brothers, fearing the collapse of the ancestral line,
privately consulted within the clan,
and installed the eldest relative.
Our ruler and his senior ministers said:
'Perhaps Heaven itself has brought this disorder—
what do we know of it?'
The proverb says:
'Do not pass by the gate of disorder.'
When the people have weapons
and disorder, they still fear to pass by,
let alone dare to understand what Heaven has disordered?
Now, sir, you ask about the reason,
but our ruler truly does not dare to know,
and who indeed knows it?
At the meeting at Píngqiū,
you, sir, renewed the old covenant, saying:
'Let none neglect their duties!'
If, when several of our ruler's ministers
pass away,
Jìn ministers were to arbitrarily control their positions,
then Zhèng would be a mere district of Jìn.
What kind of state would that be?"
He declined the envoy's gifts but sent a reply to his mission,
and the men of Jìn let the matter drop.
B10.19.9 The men of Chǔ fortified Zhōulái.
Shěn Yǐnxū said:
"The men of Chǔ are sure to be defeated.
In the past, when Wú destroyed Zhōulái,
Zǐqí requested to attack them.
The king said:
'I have not yet pacified my people.'
Now it is the same,
yet they fortify Zhōulái to provoke Wú—
can they avoid defeat?"
An attendant said:
"The king tirelessly bestows gifts,
and has allowed the people to rest for five years.
This can be called pacifying them."
Xū said:
"I have heard that to pacify the people,
one must economize internally,
and cultivate virtue externally,
so that the people are content with their lives,
and have no enemies.
Now, the palaces are built without limit,
the people are daily alarmed,
exhausted to death or displaced,
forgetting sleep and food—
this is not pacifying them."
B10.19.10 There was a great flood in Zhèng,
and dragons fought in the Wěi Abyss outside the Shímén Gate.
The people requested to perform a yíng sacrifice.
Zǐchǎn did not allow it,
saying:
"When we fight,
the dragons do not appear to us;
Why should I alone see it?
To exorcise it,
then that is its dwelling.
I have no need of dragons,
nor do dragons have any need of me."
Thus he stopped.
B10.19.11 Prime Minister Zǐxiá spoke to the King of Chǔ about Juéyóu,
saying:
"What crime has he committed?
The proverb says,
'Angry at home, scowling in the marketplace,'
which describes Chǔ.
It would be well to abandon the previous resentment."
Thus they returned Juéyóu.
A10.20 The Spring and Autumn Annals, 20th Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.20.1 In the twentieth year, spring,
the first month of the royal calendar.
A10.20.2 Summer,
Gōngsūn Huì of Cáo fled from Mèng to Sòng.
A10.20.3 Autumn,
a bandit killed Zhí, the elder brother of the Marquis of Wèi.
A10.20.4 Winter, tenth month,
Huà Hài,
Xiàng Níng,
and Huà Dìng of Sòng fled to Chén.
A10.20.5 In the eleventh month, on the xīnmǎo day,
Marquis Lú of Cài died.
B10.20 The Commentary of Zuo, 20th Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.20.1 In the twentieth year, spring,
on the jǐchǒu day of the second month of the royal calendar,
the sun reached its southernmost point.
Zǐ Shèn observed the atmosphere and
said:
"This year Sòng will have turmoil,
the state will nearly perish,
and it will take three years to subside.
Cài will have a great mourning."
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ said:
"Then it is the Dài and
Huán clans.
They are extravagant and arrogant,
exceedingly without propriety,
so turmoil lies there."
B10.20.2 Fèi Wújí said to the King of Chǔ:
"Jiàn and Wǔ Shē are about to rebel with the area outside Fāngchéng,
considering themselves like Sòng
and Zhèng,
with Qí and Jìn both assisting them,
they intend to harm Chǔ,
and their plans are complete."
The king believed him,
and questioned Wǔ Shē.
Wǔ Shē replied:
"Your Majesty has already committed one fault,
why believe slander?"
The king arrested Wǔ Shē,
and sent Fènyáng, the Marshal of Chéngfù, to kill the crown prince.
Before he arrived,
he sent someone to warn him.
In the third month,
Crown Prince Jiàn fled to Sòng.
The king summoned Fènyáng,
and Fènyáng had the people of Chéngfù arrest him and bring him to court.
The king said:
"The words came from my mouth,
entered your ears,
who informed Jiàn?"
He replied:
"I informed him.
Your Majesty commanded me, saying:
'Serve Jiàn as you serve me.'
I am not talented,
but I cannot follow orders blindly.
Having received the initial command,
I could not bear the later order,
so I warned him.
Afterward I regretted it,
but it was too late."
The king said:
"Yet you dared to come,
why?"
He replied:
"Having been sent and failing the mission,
if summoned and not coming,
that would be a second offense.
There is nowhere to flee."
The king said:
"Return,
and attend to government as before."
Wújí said:
"Shē's sons are capable;
if they go to Wú,
they will surely trouble Chǔ.
Why not summon them by promising to spare their father?
They are righteous,
and will surely come.
Otherwise,
they will become a calamity."
The king sent to summon them,
saying:
"Come,
and I will spare your father."
Tángyǐn Shàng said to his brother Yuán:
"You go to Wú,
I will return to die.
My wisdom is inferior,
I can die,
you can take revenge.
Hearing the order to spare our father,
we cannot fail to go;
with relatives being killed,
we cannot fail to take revenge.
Going to die to spare our father is filial;
assessing merit and acting is benevolent;
choosing the task and going is wise;
knowing death and not avoiding it is courageous.
Our father cannot be abandoned,
our name cannot be ruined,
you must strive!
Following each other is better."
Wǔ Shàng returned.
Shē heard that Yuán did not come,
and said:
"The ruler and
great officers of Chǔ will have to eat late!"
The people of Chǔ killed them all.
Yuán went to Wú,
and spoke to Zhōuyú about the advantages of attacking Chǔ.
Prince Guāng said:
"His clan was killed,
and he wants to avenge them;
we cannot follow him."
Yuán said:
"He will have other intentions;
I will seek warriors for him,
and wait in the countryside."
Thus he introduced Zhuān Shèzhū,
and farmed in the countryside.
B10.20.3 Duke Yuán of Sòng was untrustworthy and selfish,
and hated the Huà and Xiàng clans.
Huà Dìng, Huà Hài, and Xiàng Níng plotted, saying:
"Exile is better than death,
shall we act first?"
Huà Hài feigned illness,
to lure the princes.
When the princes came to inquire,
he seized them.
In summer, the sixth month, on the bǐngshēn day,
he killed Prince Yín, Prince Yùróng,
Prince Zhū, Prince Gù,
Gōngsūn Yuán, and Gōngsūn Dīng,
and confined Xiàng Shèng and Xiàng Xíng in their granary.
The duke went to the Huà clan to plead,
but they refused,
and seized him.
On the guǐmǎo day,
they took Crown Prince Luán and his full brother Chén,
and Prince Dì as hostages.
The duke also took Huà Hài's son Wúqī,
Xiàng Níng's son Luó, and Huà Dìng's son Qǐ,
and made a covenant with the Huà clan,
taking them as hostages.
B10.20.4 Gōng Mèng Zhí of Wèi was familiar with Qí Bào,
but took away his position as Minister of Justice and his fief at Juàn.
When there was service, he returned them,
otherwise he took them.
Gōng Mèng disliked Běigōng Xǐ
and Chǔshī Pǔ,
and wanted to remove them.
Prince Cháo had an affair with Duchess Dowager Xuānjiāng,
and fearing exposure,
wanted to start a rebellion.
Thus Qí Bào, Běigōng Xǐ,
Chǔshī Pǔ, and Prince Cháo rebelled.
Earlier,
Qí Bào had introduced Zōng Lǔ to Gōng Mèng,
and he served as his chariot attendant.
When about to rebel,
he said to him:
"Gōng Mèng's lack of goodness
is known to you;
do not ride with him,
for I will kill him."
He replied:
"I served Gōng Mèng because of you;
you lent me your reputation,
so he did not distance himself from me.
Although he was not good,
I also knew it;
but for the sake of profit,
I could not leave,
which was my fault.
Now, hearing of the danger and fleeing,
would be betraying you.
You carry out your affairs,
I will die for it,
to serve you loyally,
and then return to die at the hands of Gōng Mèng,
that would be acceptable."
On Bǐngchén,
the Marquis of Wèi was at Píngshòu.
Gōng Mèng was conducting affairs outside the Gàihuò Gate,
the Qí family set up curtains outside the gate,
and concealed armed men there.
They had Zhù Wā place spears on a cart of firewood to block the gate,
and had one chariot follow Gōng Mèng as he went out;
they had Huá Qí drive Gōng Mèng's chariot,
with Zōng Lǔ as the right-hand attendant.
When they reached the middle of the lane,
the Qí family attacked Gōng Mèng with spears,
Zōng Lǔ shielded him with his back,
his arm was severed,
and the blow struck Gōng Mèng's shoulder.
Both were killed.
The Duke heard of the disorder,
mounted his chariot,
and drove in through the Yuè Gate.
Qìng Bǐ drove the Duke's chariot,
with Gōng Nánchǔ as the right-hand attendant.
He had Huá Yín ride in the second chariot.
When they reached the Duke's palace,
Hóng Liú Tuí joined as the fourth in the Duke's chariot.
The Duke loaded his treasures and left.
Chǔshī Zǐshēn encountered the Duke at the crossroads of Mǎlù,
and then followed him.
Passing by the Qí family,
he had Huá Yín bare his upper body
and hold a canopy to block the gap,
the Qí family shot at the Duke,
hitting Nánchǔ's back,
and the Duke then escaped.
Yín closed the outer gate,
climbed over it, and followed the Duke.
The Duke went to Sǐniǎo.
Xī Zhūchú slipped out through a drain at night,
and followed the Duke on foot.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gōngsūn Qīng on a diplomatic mission to Wèi.
After he had set out,
he heard of the disorder in Wèi,
and sent to ask where to present his credentials.
The Duke said:
"As long as he is within the borders,
he is the ruler of Wèi."
So he proceeded to carry out his duties,
and followed him to Sǐniǎo.
He requested to perform his duties.
The host declined, saying:
"This exile is unworthy,
having lost the altars of state,
and now dwelling in the wilds,
there is no place for you, sir, to carry out your lord's command without disgrace."
The guest said:
"My lord commanded me at court, saying:
'Humble yourself before the officer in charge.'
I dare not disobey."
The host said:
"If your lord graciously regards the friendship of our former rulers,
and shines his light upon our humble state,
to pacify and stabilize its altars,
then there are the ancestral temples for that."
So he stopped.
The Marquis of Wèi insisted on receiving him.
Unable to refuse the command,
he presented his fine horses,
because he had not yet delivered his credentials.
The Marquis of Wèi used them as carriage horses.
The guest was about to take up the night watch,
but the host declined, saying:
"The worries of an exile
should not extend to you, sir;
in the midst of the wilds,
it is not fitting to trouble your attendants.
I dare to decline."
The guest said:
"Your servant of my humble lord
is like a herdsman or groom to your lordship.
If I am not allowed to perform external duties,
it is as if I do not acknowledge my lord.
I fear I will not escape blame,
and beg to do this to avoid death."
He personally took up the bell,
and spent the whole night at the watchfires.
The steward of the Qí family, Qúzi, summoned Běigōngzi.
The steward of the Běigōng family did not inform his master,
plotted to kill Qúzi,
then attacked the Qí family,
and exterminated them.
On the last day of Dīngsì,
the Duke returned,
and made a covenant with Běigōng Xǐ on the banks of the Péng River.
In autumn, on the first day of the seventh month, Wùwǔ,
he then made a covenant with the people of the state.
On the Xīnhài day of the eighth month,
Gōngzǐ Cháo, Chǔshī Pǔ,
Zǐ Yùxiāo, and Zǐ Gāofáng fled to Jìn.
On the Wùchén day of the intercalary month,
Xuān Jiāng was killed.
The Marquis of Wèi granted Běigōng Xǐ the posthumous title Zhēnzǐ,
granted Xī Zhūchú the posthumous title Chéngzǐ,
and gave them the tombs of the Qí family.
The Marquis of Wèi reported the peace to Qí,
and also mentioned Zǐshí.
The Marquis of Qí was about to drink,
and generously rewarded his ministers, saying:
"This is due to the instruction of you gentlemen."
Yuàn Héjì declined,
saying:
"If I share in the reward for Qīng,
I must also share in his punishment.
In the 'Kāng Gào' it says,
between father and son, brothers,
guilt does not extend to one another,
how much less among ministers?
How dare I covet your lordship's reward
and offend against the former kings?"
Qín Zhāng heard of Zōng Lǔ's death,
and was about to go to mourn him.
Zhòngní said:
"Qí Bào was a thief,
and Mèng Zhí was a villain,
why do you mourn him?
A gentleman does not eat the bread of treachery,
does not accept disorder,
is not afflicted by profit to do wrong,
does not treat others with wrong,
does not cover up unrighteousness,
does not commit impropriety."
B10.20.5 In the disorder of the Huá and Xiàng families of Sòng,
Gōngzǐ Chéng, Gōngsūn Jì, Yuè Shě, Sīmǎ Qiáng, Xiàng Yí, Xiàng Zhèng, Chǔ Jiàn, and Ní Jiǎ fled to Zhèng.
Their followers fought with the Huá family at Guǐyán,
and defeated Zǐ Chéng.
Zǐ Chéng went to Jìn.
Huá Hài and his wife
would always wash their hands and feed the hostage princes before eating themselves.
The Duke and his consort would daily go to the Huá family,
feed the princes, and then return.
Huá Hài was troubled by this,
and wanted to return the princes.
Xiàng Nìng said:
"It is precisely because there is no trust
that we hold their sons hostage.
If we return them again,
death will not be far off."
The Duke requested of Huá Fèisuì
to attack the Huá family.
He replied:
"I dare not cherish my life,
but would this not seek to remove worry only to foster its growth?
I am therefore afraid,
but dare I not obey your command?"
The Duke said:
"Whether the sons live or die is fate,
but I cannot bear their disgrace."
In winter, the tenth month,
the Duke killed the hostages of the Huá and Xiàng families and attacked them.
On Wùchén,
the Huá and Xiàng families fled to Chén,
and Huá Dēng fled to Wú.
Xiàng Nìng wanted to kill the crown prince.
Huá Hài said:
"Having offended the ruler and fled,
if we also kill his son,
who will take us in?
Moreover, returning him may have merit."
He sent the Junior Minister of Justice Kēng to return him,
saying:
"You are of advanced age,
and cannot serve others.
With the three princes as hostages,
you will surely be spared."
After the princes entered,
Huá Kēng was about to leave through the gate.
The Duke hurriedly saw him,
took his hand,
and said:
"I know you are innocent,
enter,
and resume your position."
B10.20.6 The Marquis of Qí had a skin disease,
which then turned into a recurring fever,
and after a year he was still not cured.
Many envoys from the feudal lords were present inquiring about his illness.
Liángqiū Jù and Yì Kuǎn spoke to the lord, saying:
"We have served the ghosts and spirits with abundance,
exceeding what was done for the former lords.
Now our lord is gravely ill,
causing worry among the feudal lords;
this is the fault of the invocators and scribes.
If the feudal lords do not understand,
they will say we are not reverent.
Why does Your Lordship not execute Invocator Gù and Scribe Yín to dismiss the guests?"
The lord was pleased
and told Yànzǐ.
Yànzǐ said:
"During the covenant at Sòng,
Qū Jiàn asked Zhào Wǔ about Fàn Huì's virtue.
Zhào Wǔ said:
'The master's household affairs are well ordered;
when he speaks in the state of Jìn,
he exhausts his sincerity without selfishness.
His invocators and scribes, when performing sacrifices,
present sincerity without shame;
his household affairs are free of suspicion,
so his invocators
and scribes do not pray for anything.'
Jiàn reported this to King Kāng.
King Kāng said:
'With neither spirits nor men bearing resentment,
it is fitting that the master brilliantly assists five rulers to become leaders among the feudal lords.'"
The lord said:
"Jù and Kuǎn say that I am able to serve the ghosts and spirits,
and thus wish to execute the invocators and scribes.
You cite these words—for what reason?"
He replied:
"If there is a virtuous lord,
who does not neglect affairs inside and outside,
with no resentment between high and low,
whose actions are without transgression,
then his invocators and scribes present sincerity,
and have no shame in their hearts.
Therefore, the ghosts and spirits accept the offerings,
the state receives their blessings,
and the invocators and scribes share in them.
The reason they enjoy prosperity, felicity, old age, and longevity
is because they serve a sincere lord,
and their words are loyal and trustworthy to the ghosts and spirits.
If they happen to encounter a licentious lord,
with internal and external affairs perverse and crooked,
resentment and hatred between high and low,
actions depraved and transgressive,
following desires and indulging selfishness,
building high towers and deep pools,
striking bells and dancing with women,
cutting down the people's strength,
plundering and seizing their accumulations,
to accomplish his transgressions,
with no concern for later generations,
violent, cruel, licentious, and indulgent,
acting recklessly beyond measure,
with nothing to restrain or deter him,
not considering slander and resentment,
and not fearing the ghosts and spirits,
then the spirits are angry and the people suffer,
yet he feels no remorse in his heart.
If his invocators
and scribes present sincerity,
that is speaking of his crimes;
if they cover his faults and enumerate his virtues,
that is deception and falsehood.
With no proper words whether advancing or retreating,
they resort to empty flattery to seek favor.
Therefore, the ghosts and spirits do not accept the state's offerings but bring calamity upon it,
and the invocators and scribes share in it.
The reason they suffer premature death, confusion, orphanhood, and illness
is because they serve a tyrannical lord,
and their words are deceitful and disrespectful to the ghosts and spirits."
The lord said:
"If so, then what is to be done?"
He replied:
"It cannot be done:
the trees of the mountains and forests
are guarded by the Hélù;
the reeds and rushes of the marshes
are guarded by the Zhōujiāo;
