the firewood and kindling of the thickets
are guarded by the Yúhòu;
the salt
and clams of the sea
are guarded by the Qíwàng.
The people of the distant border regions
are forced into corvée labor;
at the oppressive border passes,
exactions are violently imposed on their private goods;
the hereditary great officers
forcibly exchange their bribes.
Regulations are constant but without measure,
levies and exactions are without limit;
palaces and chambers are daily renovated,
and licentious pleasures are not abandoned.
The favored concubines within
recklessly plunder in the markets;
the favored ministers outside
issue presumptuous orders in the borderlands.
Private desires and nurtured demands
are met if not supplied.
The people suffer and are distressed,
and husbands and wives all utter curses.
If invocations are beneficial,
curses are also harmful.
From Liáo and Shè eastward,
to Gū and Yóu westward,
the number of people is great indeed.
Even if the invocations are good,
how can they overcome the curses of millions upon millions of people?
If Your Lordship wishes to execute the invocators and scribes,
you must cultivate virtue first, and then it may be done."
The lord was pleased,
ordered the officials to relax governance,
dismantle the passes,
remove prohibitions,
reduce levies,
and cancel debts.
B10.20.7 In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí was hunting at Pèi,
and summoned the gamekeeper with a bow,
but he did not approach.
The lord ordered him seized.
He explained:
"In the past when our former lords hunted,
a plain banner was used to summon great officers,
a bow to summon officers,
and a leather cap to summon the gamekeeper.
Your servant did not see a leather cap,
and therefore dared not approach."
So he released him.
Zhòngní said:
"It is better to uphold one's duty than to uphold the Way."
The gentleman considered this right.
B10.20.8 The Marquis of Qí returned from the hunt,
and Yànzǐ attended him at Chuántái,
when Zǐyóu galloped over to visit.
The lord said:
"Only Jù is in harmony with me!"
Yànzǐ replied:
"Jù is merely agreeing,
how can that be called harmony?"
The lord said:
"Are harmony and agreement different?"
He replied:
"They are different.
Harmony is like a soup:
water, fire, vinegar, paste, salt, and plums
are used to cook fish and meat,
kindled with firewood,
the cook blends them,
balances the flavors,
supplements what is insufficient,
and reduces what is excessive.
The gentleman eats it,
and his heart is calmed.
So it is between ruler and minister.
If the ruler says something is acceptable but there is something unacceptable in it,
the minister presents the unacceptable to perfect the acceptable;
if the ruler says something is unacceptable but there is something acceptable in it,
the minister presents the acceptable to remove the unacceptable.
Thus governance is balanced and not contentious,
and the people have no contentious hearts.
Therefore, the *Odes* say:
'There is also harmonious soup,
both prepared and balanced.
Silent is the great offering,
and at that time there are no contentions.'
The former kings blended the five flavors and harmonized the five notes
to calm their hearts
and perfect their governance.
Notes are also like flavors:
one breath,
two forms,
three categories,
four materials,
five notes,
six pitch-pipes,
seven tones,
eight winds,
nine songs—
these complement each other;
clear and turbid, great
and small, short and long, fast and slow,
sorrowful and joyful, hard and soft,
delayed and quick, high and low,
entering and exiting, dense and sparse—
these balance each other.
The gentleman listens to them,
and his heart is calmed.
When the heart is calm,
virtue is harmonious.
Therefore, the *Book of Songs* says:
'His virtuous fame is without flaw.'
Now, Jù is not like this.
What the ruler says is acceptable,
Jù also says it is acceptable;
what the ruler says is not acceptable,
Jù also says it is not acceptable.
If one uses water to blend with water,
who can eat it?
If the qín and sè are only of one note,
who can listen to it?
That sameness cannot be tolerated is thus."
They drank wine and were merry.
The Duke said:
"If in ancient times there was no death,
how joyful it would be!"
Yànzǐ replied:
"If in ancient times there was no death,
then the joy would belong to the ancients,
how would you, my lord, obtain it?
Formerly, Shuǎngjiūshì first dwelt in this land,
Jìcè succeeded him,
Yǒuféng Bólíng succeeded him,
Púgūshì succeeded him,
and afterwards Tàigōng succeeded him.
If in ancient times there was no death,
the joy would belong to Shuǎngjiūshì,
which is not what you, my lord, would desire."
B10.20.9 Zhèng Zǐchǎn was ill,
and said to Zǐ Dàshū:
"After I die,
you will certainly be in charge of the government.
Only a virtuous man can use leniency to make the people submit;
next to that, nothing is better than severity.
Fire is fierce,
the people see it and fear it,
therefore few die by it;
water is weak,
the people become familiar with it and play with it,
and many die by it.
Therefore, leniency is difficult."
After several months of illness, he died.
Dàshū was in charge of the government,
and could not bear to be severe, so he was lenient.
In the state of Zhèng, there were many robbers,
who gathered in the marshes of Huánfú.
Dàshū regretted this,
and said:
"Had I earlier followed the master's words,
it would not have come to this."
He raised foot soldiers to attack the robbers of Huánfú,
and killed them all.
The robbers then somewhat ceased.
Zhòngní said:
"Excellent!
When government is lenient, the people become negligent;
when they are negligent, correct them with severity.
When government is severe, the people are injured;
when they are injured, apply leniency.
Use leniency to assist severity,
use severity to assist leniency,
and government is thereby harmonious.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'The people also are weary;
they may now have a little ease;
show kindness to this central kingdom,
to tranquilize the four quarters' —
this is applying leniency.
'Do not follow the crafty and flattering,
to restrain the unprincipled;
repress the oppressive and cruel,
who dare not fear the bright' —
this is correcting with severity.
'Be gentle to the distant and able to the near,
to establish our king' —
this is pacifying with harmony.
It also says:
'Not contentious, not hasty,
not hard, not soft,
his government is liberal and easy,
and all blessings gather around him' —
this is the perfection of harmony."
When Zǐchǎn died,
Zhòngní heard of it,
and shedding tears said:
"He was the legacy of ancient love."
A10.21 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, the Twenty-first Year of Duke Zhāo*
A10.21.1 In the twenty-first year, in spring,
in the king's third month,
we buried Duke Píng of Cài.
A10.21.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Yǎng on a mission of friendly inquiries.
A10.21.3 Huà Hài of Sòng,
Xiàng Níng,
and Huà Dìng from Chén entered Nánlǐ in Sòng and rebelled.
A10.21.4 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the first day, Rénwǔ,
the sun was eclipsed.
A10.21.5 In the eighth month, on Yǐhài,
Shū Zōu died.
A10.21.6 In winter,
Marquis Zhū of Cài fled to Chǔ.
A10.21.7 Our duke went to Jìn,
but when he reached the Hé River, he returned.
B10.21 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, the Twenty-first Year of Duke Zhāo*
B10.21.1 In the twenty-first year, in spring,
the king of Zhōu was about to cast the Wúyì bell.
Líng Zhōujiū said:
"The king will probably die of a heart disease!
Music
is the duty of the Son of Heaven.
Sound
is the carriage of music;
and bells
are the vessels of sound.
The Son of Heaven examines the winds to make music,
uses vessels to contain it,
and a carriage to convey it.
If the small is not too fine,
and the large not too coarse,
then there is harmony with things.
When things are harmonious, excellence is achieved.
Therefore harmonious sounds enter the ear and are stored in the heart;
when the heart is at ease, there is joy.
If too fine, it is not complete;
if too coarse, it cannot contain;
the heart is thereby affected,
and being affected indeed produces disease.
Now the bell is too coarse;
the king's heart cannot bear it;
how can it last long!"
B10.21.2 In the third month,
we buried Duke Píng of Cài.
The crown prince of Cài, Zhū, lost his position,
and his place was low.
The great officers who attended the funeral
returned,
and saw Zhāozǐ.
Zhāozǐ asked about the affairs of Cài,
and they told him.
Zhāozǐ sighed and said:
"Cài will probably perish!
If it does not perish,
this ruler will certainly not end well.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Not remiss in his position,
the people find their rest.'
Now the Marquis of Cài has just ascended the throne,
and has gone to a low position;
he himself will follow it."
B10.21.3 In summer,
Shì Yǎng of Jìn came on a mission of friendly inquiries,
and Shūsūn was in charge of the government.
Jìsūn wished to make Jìn dislike him,
and ordered the officer in charge to treat Shì Yǎng with the same ceremony as when Qí's Bào Guó returned Fèi.
Shì Yǎng was angry,
and said:
"Bào Guó's rank was low,
and his state small;
yet you make Yǎng follow his sacrificial offerings,
this is demeaning to our poor city,
and I will report it to my ruler."
The people of Lǔ were afraid,
and added four sets of offerings,
making eleven sets.
B10.21.4 Sòng's Huá Fèisuì begot Huá Chū, Huá Duōliáo, and Huá Dēng.
Chū was a junior minister of war,
Duōliáo was a charioteer,
and he and Chū hated each other.
He then slandered Chū to the duke, saying:
"Chū is about to bring in the fugitives."
He said this repeatedly.
The duke said:
"The minister of war, for my sake,
lost his good son.
Death and life are matters of fate;
I cannot cause him to lose another."
He replied:
"If you, my lord, love the minister of war,
then you should let him flee.
If death can be escaped,
what distance is too far?"
The duke was afraid,
and sent a chamberlain to summon the minister of war's chamberlain, Yíliáo,
gave him wine to drink,
and had him inform the minister of war.
The Minister of War sighed and said:
"It must be Duō Liáo.
I have a slanderous son,
yet I cannot kill him,
and I do not die.
Moreover, the ruler has given orders—
what can be done?"
He then plotted with the duke to expel Huà Chū,
intending to send him to hunt at Mèngzhū.
The duke gave him wine to drink,
generously rewarded him,
and bestowed gifts upon his attendants.
The Minister of War did the same.
Zhāng Gài found this excessive and said:
"There must be a reason."
He had Zǐ Pí hold a sword against Yí Liáo and interrogated him.
Yí Liáo told everything.
Zhāng Gài wanted to kill Duō Liáo.
Zǐ Pí said:
"The Minister of War is old.
To harm him would be too severe,
and if we add to his troubles,
it would be better to flee."
On the bǐngshēn day of the fifth month,
Zǐ Pí was about to see the Minister of War and then depart,
when he encountered Duō Liáo driving the Minister of War's chariot to court.
Zhāng Gài, unable to contain his anger,
joined with Zǐ Pí, Jiù Rén, and Zhèng Piān to kill Duō Liáo,
seized the Minister of War and rebelled,
and summoned the exiles.
On the rényín day,
Huà and Xiàng entered.
Yuè Dàxīn, Fēng Qiān, and Huà Kēng defended against them at Héng.
The Huà clan occupied the Lú Gate,
and rebelled from Nánlǐ.
On the gēngwǔ day of the sixth month,
Sòng fortified the old city walls and the Sānglín Gate to defend them.
B10.21.5 In autumn, on the first day of the seventh month, rényín,
there was a solar eclipse.
The duke asked Zǐ Shèn:
"What is this phenomenon?
What does it portend for fortune or disaster?"
He replied: "At the solstices and equinoxes,
if there is a solar eclipse,
it does not bring disaster.
The movements of the sun and moon
at the equinoxes
follow the same path;
at the solstices,
they cross each other.
In other months, it brings disaster,
for the yang force is overcome,
so it often brings floods."
At this, Shū Zhōu wept over the solar eclipse.
Zhāo Zǐ said:
"Shū Zhōu will die—
this is not something to weep over."
In the eighth month,
Shū Zhōu died.
B10.21.6 In winter, in the tenth month,
Huà Dēng led Wú troops to rescue the Huà clan.
Qí's Wū Zhīmíng garrisoned Sòng.
Chúrén Pú said:
"The *Military Records* state:
'To strike first is to seize the enemy's resolve;
to wait is to await their decline.'
Why not attack them while they are weary and not yet settled!
If they enter and fortify themselves,
the Huà clan will have many followers,
and regret will be too late."
They followed his advice.
On the bǐngyín day,
the Qí and Sòng armies defeated the Wú army at Hóngkǒu,
capturing their two commanders, Prince Kǔqián and Yǎnzhōu Yuán.
Huà Dēng led the remainder and defeated the Sòng army.
The duke wanted to flee,
but Chúrén Pú said:
"I am but a commoner—
I can die for you,
but I cannot escort you in flight.
I beg you to wait."
He then proclaimed:
"Those who raise the banners
are the duke's men."
The multitude followed him.
The duke saw them from the Yáng Gate,
descended and inspected them,
saying:
"If the state perishes and the ruler dies,
it is the shame of you all—
is it solely my fault?"
Qí's Wū Zhīmíng said:
"With few troops, nothing is better than fighting to the death;
to fight to the death, nothing is better than discarding defenses.
They have many soldiers—
I ask that we all use swords."
They followed his advice.
The Huà clan fled north,
and they pursued them again.
Chúrén Pú wrapped a head in his robe,
carried it on his shoulder, and ran,
shouting:
"I have captured Huà Dēng!"
They then defeated the Huà clan at Xīnlǐ.
Dí Lóuxīn lived at Xīnlǐ;
after the battle,
he removed his armor before the duke and returned home.
Huà Tǒu lived within the duke's precincts,
and did the same.
On the guǐwèi day of the eleventh month,
Prince Chéng arrived with the Jìn army.
Cáo Hànhú joined Jìn's Xún Wú,
Qí's Yuàn Héjì,
and Wèi's Prince Zhāo to rescue Sòng.
On the bǐngxū day,
they fought the Huà clan at Zhěqiū.
Zhèng Piān wished to form a 'stork' formation,
and his charioteer wished to form a 'goose' formation.
Zǐ Lù drove for Prince Chéng,
with Zhuāng Jǐn as the right-hand attendant.
Gàn Chōu drove for the Warden of Lǚ, Huà Bào,
with Zhāng Gài as the right-hand attendant.
They met,
and Chéng turned back.
Huà Bào shouted:
"Chéng!"
Chéng was angered
and turned back against him.
As he was about to draw his bow,
Bào had already shot.
Chéng said:
"By the spirit of Duke Píng,
may you still assist me!"
Bào shot,
but the arrow passed between them.
As Chéng was about to draw again,
Bào shot once more.
Chéng said:
"Not allowing me my turn—
how base!"
He drew an arrow,
shot Bào,
and killed him.
Zhāng Gài drew a club and descended,
shot at him,
and broke his thigh.
Crawling, he struck him,
breaking the chariot rail.
He shot again,
and killed him.
Gàn Chōu begged for an arrow,
but Chéng said:
"I will speak for you to the ruler."
Gàn Chōu replied:
"Not dying with one's comrades in the same chariot
is a great offense in the army.
To evade punishment and follow you—
how would the ruler use me?
Do it quickly!"
Chéng then shot him,
and killed him.
They heavily defeated the Huà clan,
and besieged them at Nánlǐ.
Huà Hài beat his chest and cried out,
seeing Huà Chū,
said:
"I have become like the Luán clan!"
Chū said:
"Do not frighten me—
if misfortune comes, we will flee later."
They sent Huà Dēng to Chǔ to seek troops.
Huà Chū, with fifteen chariots and seventy foot soldiers, broke through the siege and escaped,
ate by the Suī River,
wept as they saw him off,
and then returned inside.
Chǔ's Wěi Yuè led troops to meet the Huà clan,
but the Grand Minister Fàn advised:
"Among the states, only Sòng serves its ruler faithfully.
Now they are contending for the state—
to abandon the ruler and aid his ministers,
is that not improper?"
The king said:
"You told me too late—
I have already promised them."
B10.21.7 The Marquis of Cài, Zhū, fled to Chǔ.
Fèi Wújí took bribes from Dōngguó,
and said to the people of Cài:
"Zhū does not obey Chǔ's commands—
the king intends to establish Dōngguó.
If you do not first follow the king's wish,
Chǔ will surely besiege Cài."
The people of Cài feared,
Zhū Sù was in Chǔ,
and the Viscount of Chǔ was about to attack Cài.
Wújí said:
"Píng Hóu had a covenant with Chǔ,
therefore he was enfeoffed.
His son was of two minds,
therefore he was deposed.
King Líng killed the Crown Prince Yǐn,
and his son shares the same hatred as you, my lord,
and will certainly be deeply grateful to you.
Moreover, to have him established again,
would that not be acceptable!
Furthermore, deposing and establishing lie in your hands,
and Cài has no other course."
B10.21.8 The Duke went to Jìn,
and reached the Yellow River.
Gǔ rebelled against Jìn,
and Jìn was about to attack Xiānyú,
therefore they declined to receive the Duke.
A10.22 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Twenty-second Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.22.1 In the twenty-second year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Jǔ.
A10.22.2 Sòng's Huá Hài,
Xiàng Níng,
and Huá Dìng fled from Nánlǐ in Sòng to Chǔ.
A10.22.3 There was a great hunt at Chāngjiān.
A10.22.4 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
the Son of Heaven passed away.
A10.22.5 In the sixth month,
Shū Yāng went to the capital,
to bury King Jǐng.
A10.22.6 The royal house was in turmoil.
A10.22.7 Liúzi
and Shànzi took Wáng Měng and resided in Huáng.
A10.22.8 In autumn,
Liúzi
and Shànzi took Wáng Měng and entered Wángchéng.
A10.22.9 In winter, in the tenth month,
Prince Měng died.
A10.22.10 In the twelfth month, on the first day Guǐyǒu,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
B10.22 The Commentary, Twenty-second Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.22.1 In the twenty-second year, in spring,
in the king's second month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Qí's Běiguō Qǐ led troops to attack Jǔ.
The Viscount of Jǔ was about to give battle,
Yuànyáng Mùzhī remonstrated, saying:
"The Qí commander is of low rank,
his demands will not be great.
It would be better to submit to him.
A great state should not be provoked."
He did not listen,
and defeated the Qí army at Shòuyú.
The Marquis of Qí attacked Jǔ,
and the Viscount of Jǔ sought peace.
Simá Zào went to Jǔ to oversee the covenant;
the Viscount of Jǔ went to Qí to oversee the covenant,
and they made a covenant outside the Jímén Gate.
Jǔ then greatly resented its ruler.
B10.22.2 Chǔ's Wěi Yuè sent a message to Sòng, saying:
"My lord has heard that you have disobedient ministers causing you worry,
and that they are a disgrace to your ancestral temple.
My lord requests to receive and execute them."
He replied:
"I am unworthy,
and unable to please my elders,
causing you, my lord, concern.
I acknowledge the honor of your command.
However, ruler and ministers fight daily,
and if you, my lord, say
'I will certainly assist the ministers,'
I will also obey your command.
There is a saying:
'Only do not pass by the gate of disorder.'
If you, my lord, in your kindness protect our humble city,
do not support the disloyal,
thereby encouraging troublemakers—
that is my hope.
I ask you, my lord, to consider this!"
The men of Chǔ were troubled by this.
The garrison troops from the various states plotted, saying:
"If the Huá clan realizes it is cornered and fights to the death,
and Chǔ, ashamed of achieving nothing, launches a fierce attack,
it will not be to our advantage.
It would be better to let them leave,
making it a success for Chǔ,
and they will also be unable to do anything further.
We have saved Sòng and removed its harm,
what more do we seek?"
They then firmly requested to let them leave,
and the men of Sòng agreed.
On the day Jǐsì,
Sòng's Huá Hài, Xiàng Níng, Huá Dìng, Huá Chū, Huá Dēng, Huáng Yǎnshāng, Shěng Zāng, and Shì Píng fled to Chǔ.
The Duke of Sòng appointed Gōngsūn Jì as Grand Marshal,
Biān Áng as Grand Minister of Education,
Yuè Qí as Marshal,
Zhòng Jī as Left Army Commander,
Yuè Dàxīn as Right Army Commander,
and Yuè Wǎn as Grand Minister of Justice,
to pacify the people of the state.
B10.22.3 Prince Cháo and Bīn Qǐ were favored by King Jǐng.
The king and Bīn Mèng were pleased with him,
and wished to establish him.
Liú Xiàngōng's younger son Bó Fén served Shàn Mùgōng.
He hated Bīn Mèng's character,
and wished to kill him;
he also hated Prince Cháo's words,
considering them seditious,
and wished to remove him.
Bīn Mèng went to the outskirts,
and saw a rooster breaking off its own tail feathers.
He asked
his attendant, who said:
"It fears being used as a sacrificial victim."
He hurried back and reported to the king,
and said:
"Does the chicken fear being used by men!
Men are different from this.
The sacrificial victim is actually used by men;
for a man to be a victim is truly difficult,
but what harm is there in oneself being the victim?"
The king did not respond.
In summer, in the fourth month,
the king hunted on the northern hills,
ordering all the high ministers to accompany him,
intending to kill Shànzi and Liúzi.
The king had a heart ailment,
and on the day Yǐchǒu,
he died at the house of Róng Qí.
On the day Wùchén,
Liúzi Zhì died.
He had no son,
and Shànzi established Liú
Fén. On the fifth month, day Gēngchén,
he had an audience with the king,
then attacked Bīn Qǐ,
and killed him,
and made a covenant with the various princes at the house of Shàn.
B10.22.4 When Jìn captured Gǔ,
after presenting the captives they returned the Viscount of Gǔ.
He again rebelled and joined Xiānyú.
In the sixth month,
Xún Wú raided Dōngyáng,
and had his troops pretend to be grain buyers, carrying armor and resting outside the gate of Xīyáng,
then suddenly attacked Gǔ,
destroyed it,
and took the Viscount of Gǔ, Yuāndī, back with him,
leaving Shè Tuó to guard it.
B10.22.5 On the day Dīngsì,
King Jǐng was buried.
Prince Cháo, relying on old officials,
the various artisans who had lost their positions and salaries,
and the clans of Kings Líng and Jǐng, started a rebellion.
He led the armored troops of Jiāo, Yāo, and Jiàn,
to drive out Liúzi.
On the day Rénxū,
Liúzi fled to Yáng.
Shànzi welcomed King Dào from the Zhuāng Palace and returned with him.
Prince Huán took the king by night and went to the Zhuāng Palace.
On the day Guǐhài,
Shànzi left.
Prince Huán plotted with Zhào Zhuānggōng, saying:
"If we do not kill Shàn Qí,
we will not succeed.
If we make a solemn covenant with him,
he will certainly come.
There have been many who succeeded by breaking covenants."
They followed this plan.
Fán Qīngzǐ said:
"These are not proper words,
they will certainly not succeed."
They then escorted the king to pursue Shànzi.
Reaching Lǐng,
they made a grand covenant and then returned.
They killed Zhì Huāng to appease him.
Liúzi went to Liú,
and Shànzi fled.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
he fled to Píngzhì.
The various princes pursued him.
Shànzi killed Huán, Gū, Fā,
Ruò, Zōng, Yán, Dìng, and Chóu.
Prince Cháo fled to Jīng.
On the day Bǐngyín,
they attacked it.
The people of Jīng fled to the mountains.
Liǔzǐ entered the royal capital.
On Xīnwèi,
Gǒng Jiǎngōng was defeated at Jīng.
On Yǐhài,
Gān Pínggōng was also defeated there.
Shū Yāng arrived from the capital,
and spoke of the disorder in the royal house.
Mǐn Mǎfù said:
"Zǐ Cháo will certainly not prevail.
Those who side with him
are ones whom Heaven has abandoned."
Shànzǐ wished to report the emergency to Jìn.
In autumn, the seventh month, on Wùyín,
he took the king to Píngzhì,
then proceeded to Pǔchē,
and halted at Huáng.
Liǔzǐ went to Liú.
Shànzǐ sent Wángzǐ Chǔ to guard the royal capital.
He made a covenant with the various artisans at Píng Palace.
On Xīnmǎo,
Xún Xī attacked Huáng.
He was heavily defeated,
and Xún Xī was captured.
On Rénchén,
he was burned in the marketplace of the royal capital.
In the eighth month, on Xīnyǒu,
Minister of Education Chǒu was defeated with the royal army at Qiánchéng.
The various artisans rebelled.
On Jǐsì,
they attacked the residence of the Shàn clan,
but were defeated there.
On Gēngwǔ,
they counterattacked them.
On Xīnwèi,
they attacked Dōngyǔ.
In winter, the tenth month, on Dīngsì,
Jì Tán and Xún Lì of Jìn led the troops of the nine regions' Róng tribes and the armies of Jiāo, Xiá, Wēn, and Yuán,
to escort the king into the royal capital.
On Gēngshēn,
Shànzǐ and Liú Fén were defeated with the royal army at Jiāo,
and the men of Qiánchéng defeated the Lùhún at Shè.
In the eleventh month, on Yǐyǒu,
Wángzǐ Měng died.
No mourning ceremonies were held.
On Jǐchǒu,
King Jìng ascended the throne.
He lodged at Zǐlǚ's residence.
In the twelfth month, on Gēngxū,
Jì Tán, Xún Lì, and Jiǎ Xīn of Jìn,
and Minister of War Dū led troops and encamped at Yīn,
at Hóushì,
at Xīquán,
and halted at Shè.
The royal army encamped at Fàn,
at Xiè,
and halted at Rénrén.
In the intercalary month,
Jī Yí, Yuè Zhēng, and Yòuháng Guǐ of Jìn crossed with their army and took Qiánchéng,
encamping to its southeast.
The royal army encamped at Jīngchǔ.
On Xīnchǒu,
they attacked Jīng,
and destroyed its southwestern part.
A10.23 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Zhāo Year 23
A10.23.1 In the twenty-third year, in spring,
in the king's first month,
Shūsūn Ruò went to Jìn.
A10.23.2 On Guǐchǒu,
Shū Yāng died.
A10.23.3 The men of Jìn seized our messenger Shūsūn Ruò.
A10.23.4 The men of Jìn laid siege to Jiāo.
A10.23.5 In summer, the sixth month,
Marquis Dōngguó of Cài died in Chǔ.
A10.23.6 In autumn, the seventh month,
Lord Gēngyú of Jǔ came fleeing to us.
A10.23.7 On Wùchén,
Wú defeated the armies of Dùn,
Hú, Shěn,
Cài, Chén,
and Xǔ at Jīfù.
Lord Kūn of Hú and
Lord Chěng of Shěn perished,
and Xià Niè of Chén was captured.
A10.23.8 The Heavenly King resided at Díquán.
Yǐnshì set up Wángzǐ Cháo.
A10.23.9 In the eighth month, on Yǐwèi,
there was an earthquake.
A10.23.10 In winter,
our duke went to Jìn,
reached the Yellow River,
fell ill,
and then returned.
B10.23 The Commentary of Zuǒ, Duke Zhāo Year 23
B10.23.1 In the twenty-third year, in spring,
on the first day, Rényín, of the king's first month,
the two armies laid siege to Jiāo.
On Guǐmǎo,
Jiāo and Xún collapsed.
On Dīngwèi,
the Jìn army was at Píngyīn,
and the royal army was at Zéyì.
The king sent word that the crisis was over,
and on Gēngxū,
they returned.
B10.23.2 The men of Zhū fortified Yì,
and on their return,
intended to pass through Lí Gū.
Gōngsūn Chú said:
"Lǔ will intercept us."
They wished to return via Wǔchéng,
following the mountains southward.
Xú Chú, Qiū Ruò, and Máo Dì said:
"The road is low-lying,
and if we encounter rain,
we will not be able to get out,
meaning we will not return."
So they went via Lí Gū.
The men of Wǔchéng blocked their front,
and cut the trees behind them but did not sever them completely.
When the Zhū army passed through,
they pushed them over and felled them,
thus capturing the Zhū army,
and took Chú, Ruò, and Dì captive.
The men of Zhū complained to Jìn,
and the men of Jìn came to demand redress.
Shūsūn Ruò went to Jìn,
and the men of Jìn seized him.
The record says
"The men of Jìn seized our messenger Shūsūn Ruò,"
meaning he was an envoy.
The men of Jìn wanted him to sit in judgment with a Zhū grandee,
but Shūsūn said:
"A minister of a major state is equivalent to the ruler of a minor state;
this is indeed the Zhōu system.
Moreover, Zhū is a barbarian state.
My ruler's deputy envoy Zǐfú Huí is here;
I request that he take my place,
as I dare not disregard the Zhōu system."
So in the end he did not sit in judgment.
Hán Xuānzǐ had the men of Zhū gather their multitude,
intending to hand Shūsūn over to them.
Shūsūn heard of this,
dismissed his attendants and guards, and went to court.
Shì Mímóu said to Hán Xuānzǐ:
"If you do not plan well,
and hand Shūsūn over to his enemies,
Shūsūn will certainly die because of it.
If Lǔ loses Shūsūn,
it will certainly destroy Zhū.
If the lord of Zhū loses his state,
where will he go?
Even if you regret it then,
what good will it do?
What is called a covenant leader
is to punish violations of orders.
If everyone seizes each other,
what use is a covenant leader?"
So he did not hand him over.
He made them each stay in a separate lodging.
Shì Bó listened to their statements,
and reported them to Xuānzǐ,
whereupon he seized them all.
Shì Bó escorted Shūsūn,
with four attendants,
passing by the Zhū lodging to go to the officials.
He first sent the Zhū ruler back.
Shì Bó said:
"Due to the difficulty of obtaining fodder and firewood,
and the hardship for your attendants,
I will lodge you in the capital."
Shūsūn stood waiting at dawn,
awaiting the appointed time.
So he lodged him at Jī.
He put Zǐfú Zhāobó in another town.
Fàn Xiànzǐ sought goods from Shūsūn,
and had someone request a cap from him.
He took the pattern of his cap,
and gave him two caps,
saying:
"That is all."
For Shūsūn's sake,
Shēn Fēng went to Jìn with goods.
Shūsūn said:
"See me,
and I will tell you what goods to use."
He saw him,
but did not come out.
The officials who had lived with Shūsūn at Jī
requested his barking dog,
but he did not give it to them.
When he was about to return,
he killed it and prepared it for them to eat.
Wherever Shūsūn stayed,
even if only for a day,
he would always repair the walls
and houses,
and when he left, they looked as they did when he first arrived.
B10.23.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on Yǐyǒu,
Dǎnzǐ captured Zī,
and Liúzǐ captured Qiángrén and Zhírén.
In the sixth month, on Rénwǔ,
Wángzǐ Cháo entered Yǐn.
On Guǐwèi,
Yǐn Yǔ entrapped Liú Tuó and killed him.
On Bǐngxū,
Dǎnzǐ took the Bǎn road,
and Liúzǐ took the Yǐn road to attack Yǐn.
Dǎnzǐ arrived first but was defeated,
and Liúzǐ withdrew.
On Jǐchǒu,
Zhào Bó Huàn and Nángōng Jí led the men of Chéngzhōu to garrison Yǐn.
On Gēngyín,
Dǎnzǐ, Liúzǐ, and Fán Qí escorted the king to Liú.
On Jiǎwǔ,
Wángzǐ Cháo entered the royal capital,
and encamped at Zuǒxiàng.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on Wùshēn,
Xún Luó escorted him into the Zhuāng Palace.
Yǐn Xīn defeated the Liú army at Táng.
On Bǐngchén,
he again defeated them at Xún.
On Jiǎzǐ,
Yǐn Xīn captured Xīwéi.
On Bǐngyín,
he attacked Kuǎi,
and Kuǎi collapsed.
B10.23.4 Jǔzǐ Gēngyú was cruel and fond of swords.
Whenever a sword was cast,
he would test it on people.
The people of the state were troubled by this.
He also intended to rebel against Qí.
Wū Cún led the people of the state to drive him out.
As Gēngyú was about to leave,
he heard that Wū Cún was standing by the left side of the road holding a shū,
and he feared
he would be stopped and killed.
Yuàn Yáng Mùzhī said:
"My lord, pass by him!
Wū Cún is known for his strength, and that is enough;
why must he gain fame by killing his lord?"
So Gēngyú fled and came here.
The people of Qí installed Duke Jiāo.
B10.23.5 The men of Wú attacked Zhōulái.
Chǔ Wěi Yuè led his army and the armies of the various lords, rushing to the rescue of Zhōulái.
The men of Wú resisted them at Zhōnglí.
Zǐxiá died,
and the Chǔ army was demoralized.
Wú Prince Guāng said:
"The lords who follow Chǔ are many,
but they are all small states.
They fear Chǔ and have no alternative,
so they have come.
I have heard it said:
'In undertaking affairs, if authority overcomes affection,
though small,
one is sure to succeed.'
The lords of Hú and Shěn are young and reckless,
the Chén grand officer Niè is strong but stubborn,
and Dùn, Xǔ, and Cài resent Chǔ's government.
The Chǔ prime minister has died,
and their army is demoralized.
Their commander is lowly and many are favored,
so orders and commands are not unified.
Seven states share the campaign but are not of one mind;
their commander is lowly and cannot bring order,
and there is no great authority or command—
Chǔ can be defeated.
If we divide our army and first attack Hú, Shěn, and Chén,
they are sure to flee first.
When these three states are defeated,
the armies of the various lords will waver in heart.
When the lords are in discord and disorder,
Chǔ is sure to flee greatly.
I ask that the vanguard remove their defenses and diminish their awe,
while the rearguard strengthens their formations and arrays their troops."
The Wúzǐ followed this.
On Wùchén, the last day of the month,
they fought at Jīfù.
The Wúzǐ sent three thousand criminals to first attack Hú, Shěn, and Chén,
and the three states contended with them.
Wú formed three armies to follow behind them:
the center army followed the king,
Guāng commanded the right,
and Yǎnyú commanded the left.
The Wú criminals either fled or halted,
the three states fell into disorder,
the Wú army struck them,
the three states were defeated,
and the lords of Hú and Shěn and the Chén grand officer were captured.
They released the prisoners from Hú and Shěn and let them flee to Xǔ, Cài, and Dùn,
saying:
"Our lords are dead!"
The army shouted and pursued them,
the three states fled,
and the Chǔ army fled greatly.
The record says:
"Húzǐ Kūn and Shěnzǐ Chěng were destroyed,
and Xià Niè of Chén was captured"—
these are the terms for ruler and minister.
It does not say they fought,
because Chǔ had not arrayed its forces.
B10.23.6 In the eighth month, on Dīngyǒu,
Nángōng Jí was struck by lightning.
Cháng Hóng said to Liú Wéngōng:
"My lord, exert yourself!
The efforts of our former lord can succeed.
When Zhōu was about to perish,
its three rivers quaked.
Now the great minister of the Western King has also been struck by lightning—
Heaven has abandoned him.
The Eastern King is sure to greatly triumph."
B10.23.7 The mother of the Chǔ crown prince Jiàn was at Jué,
and she summoned the men of Wú and opened the city to them.
In winter, in the tenth month, on Jiǎshēn,
the Wú crown prince Zhūfán entered Jué,
took the Chǔ lady and her precious vessels, and returned.
The Chǔ minister of war Wěi Yuè pursued them,
but did not catch up.
He was about to die,
and the multitude said:
"We ask to attack Wú to seek a chance."
Wěi Yuè said:
"I have twice defeated our lord's army;
to die would be fitting, and I am guilty.
To have lost our lord's lady—
I cannot but die for this."
So he hanged himself at Wěishì.
B10.23.8 The duke went to Jìn on account of Shūsūn,
but when he reached the river,
he fell ill
and returned.
B10.23.9 Chǔ Náng Wǎ became prime minister,
and he walled Yǐng.
Shěn Yǐn Xū said:
"Zǐcháng is sure to lose Yǐng.
If one cannot defend it,
walling it is of no benefit.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven guarded himself with the four barbarians;
when the Son of Heaven was humbled,
he guarded himself with the various lords.
The various lords guarded themselves with their four neighbors;
when the various lords were humbled,
they guarded themselves within their four borders.
If one is careful about one's four borders,
forms alliances with the four sides,
the people are at ease in their fields,
and the three tasks are accomplished—
the people have no internal worries,
and moreover no external fears—
what use has the state for walls?
Now, in fear of Wú,
they wall Yǐng—
their guard has become small.
If they cannot achieve even this humbled state,
can they avoid perishing?
In the past, Liáng Bó dug a moat around his ducal palace, and the people dispersed;
when the people abandon their superiors,
if they do not perish,
what are they waiting for?
If one corrects one's borders,
cultivates one's fields,
secures one's outposts,
is close to one's people,
clarifies one's patrols and watches,
is trustworthy to neighboring states,
is careful in official duties,
maintains diplomatic rituals,
is neither presumptuous nor greedy,
neither cowardly nor aggressive,
completes one's defensive preparations,
and awaits the unexpected—
what is there to fear?
The Odes say:
'Think of your ancestors,
and cultivate their virtue.'
Should one not take as a mirror Ruò'áo, Fénmào, down to Wǔ and Wén?
Their territory did not exceed a tóng,
yet they were careful about their four borders,
and still did not wall Yǐng.
Now their territory is several qí,
yet they wall Yǐng—
is this not difficult?"
A10.24 The Classic of the Twenty-Fourth Year of Duke Zhāo
A10.24.1 In the twenty-fourth year, in spring,
in the second month of the royal calendar, on Bǐngxū,
Zhòngsūn Jué died.
A10.24.2 Ruò arrived from Jìn.
A10.24.3 In summer, in the fifth month, on the first day, Yǐwèi,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A10.24.4 In autumn, in the eighth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice.
A10.24.5 On Dīngyǒu,
the Earl of Qǐ, Yùlí, died.
A10.24.6 In winter,
Wú destroyed Cháo.
A10.24.7 The burial of Duke Píng of Qǐ took place.
B10.24 Commentary on the Twenty-fourth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.24.1 In the twenty-fourth year, in spring,
in the first month of the royal calendar, on Xīnchǒu,
Shào Jiǎngōng and Nángōng Yín took Gān Huángōng to see Prince Cháo.
Liúzǐ said to Cháng Hóng:
"The Gān clan has gone over there again."
He replied:
"What harm is there?
Those of shared virtue measure righteousness.
The 'Great Oath' says:
'Zhòu had millions of common people,
yet they were divided in virtue;
I have ten men of order,
united in heart and virtue.'
This is why Zhōu rose.
My lord, you should devote yourself to virtue,
and do not worry about lacking men."
On Wùwǔ,
Prince Cháo entered Wū.
B10.24.2 Jìn's Shì Mímóu went to meet Shūsūn at Jī.
Shūsūn had Liáng Qíjìng wait inside the gate,
saying:
"If I look to the left and cough,
then kill him.
If I look to the right and smile,
then stop."
Shūsūn met Shì Bó.
Shì Bó said:
"Our ruler, because of his role as leader of the covenant,
has therefore detained you for a long time.
The meager gifts of our humble city
will be presented to your followers,
and I, Mímóu, have been sent to welcome you."
Shūsūn accepted the gifts and returned.
In the second month,
the record "Ruò arrived from Jìn"
shows respect for Jìn.
B10.24.3 In the third month, on Gēngxū,
the Marquis of Jìn sent Shì Jǐngbó to go and inquire about the situation in Zhōu.
Shì Bó stood at Gānjì
and questioned the assembled crowd.
The men of Jìn then declined Prince Cháo,
not accepting his envoy.
B10.24.4 In summer, in the fifth month, on the first day, Yǐwèi,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
Zǐ Shèn said:
"There will be floods."
Zhāozǐ said:
"It will be drought.
The sun has passed the equinox, yet the yang force is still unable to overcome;
when it overcomes, it will be extreme,
how can there not be drought?
If the yang force does not overcome,
it will accumulate."
B10.24.5 In the sixth month, on Rénshēn,
the army of Prince Cháo attacked Xiá and Xìng,
and both were defeated.
B10.24.6 The Earl of Zhèng went to Jìn,
with Zǐ Tàishū as his assistant.
They met Fàn Xiànzǐ.
Xiànzǐ said:
"What about the royal house?"
He replied:
"This old man cannot even take care of his own state and family,
how dare I concern myself with the royal house?
However, people also have a saying:
'A widow does not worry about the weft of her loom,
but worries about the fall of the Zhōu dynasty,
fearing it will reach her.'
Now the royal house is truly in turmoil,
and we, a small state, are afraid;
but the worries of a great state,
what do we fellows know about them?
You, sir, should plan for it early!
The Odes say:
'When the bottle is empty,
it is the shame of the jar.'
The unrest of the royal house
is the shame of Jìn."
Xiànzǐ became fearful
and discussed it with Xuānzǐ.
They then summoned a meeting of the feudal lords,
scheduled for the next year.
B10.24.7 In autumn, in the eighth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice,
because of drought.
B10.24.8 In winter, in the tenth month, on Guǐyǒu,
Prince Cháo used the precious guī-jade of Chéngzhōu and sank it in the Hé River.
On Jiǎxū, a ferryman found it on the riverbank.
Yīn Bùnìng, leading men from Wēn, invaded southwards,
captured the man who had found the jade,
and took the jade from him.
When he was about to sell it,
it turned into stone.
When the king was settled, he presented it,
and was given Dōngzī.
B10.24.9 The Viscount of Chǔ prepared a naval force to raid the borders of Wú.
Shěn Yǐnxū said:
"On this campaign,
Chǔ is sure to lose cities.
Not comforting the people but making them toil,
Wú is not moving but we are hastening them;
Wú follows on Chǔ's heels,
yet the borders have no preparations.
Can the cities avoid being lost?"
The Yuè grandee Xū Àn entertained the king at the confluence of Yùzhāng,
and the Yuè prince Cāng presented the king with a boat.
Cāng and Shòumèng led troops to follow the king.
The king reached Yǔyáng and then returned.
The men of Wú followed on Chǔ's heels,
and the border guards were unprepared,
so they destroyed Cháo and Zhōnglí and then returned.
Shěn Yǐnxū said:
"The beginning of the loss of Yǐng lies here.
With one move, the king has lost the commanders of two clans;
if things continue like this, will it not reach Yǐng?
The Odes say:
'Who gave birth to this calamitous step?
It troubles us even now.'
This is surely said of the king!"
A10.25 The Twenty-fifth Year of Duke Zhāo, the Classic
A10.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
Shūsūn Ruò went to Sòng.
A10.25.2 In summer,
Shū Yì met with Jìn's Zhào Yǎng,
Sòng's Yuè Dàxīn,
Wèi's Běigōng Xǐ,
Zhèng's Yóu Jí,
a man of Cáo,
a man of Zhū,
a man of Téng,
a man of Xuē,
and a man of Xiǎozhū at Huángfù.
A10.25.3 There were quails that came and nested.
A10.25.4 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the first Xīn day,
there was a great rain sacrifice;
on the last Xīn day,
there was another rain sacrifice.
A10.25.5 In the ninth month, on Jǐhài,
the duke fled to Qí,
and halted at Yángzhōu.
The Marquis of Qí condoled with the duke at Yějǐng.
A10.25.6 In winter, in the tenth month, on Wùchén,
Shūsūn Ruò died.
A10.25.7 In the eleventh month, on Jǐhài,
Duke Āi of Sòng, Zuǒ, died at Qūjí.
A10.25.8 In the twelfth month,
the Marquis of Qí took Yùn.
B10.25 Commentary on the Twenty-fifth Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.25.1 In the twenty-fifth year, in spring,
Shūsūn Ruò went on a mission to Sòng.
The Right Master of Tóngmén met him.
In conversation,
he belittled the grandees of Sòng and disparaged the Sīchéng clan.
Zhāozǐ told his followers:
"The Right Master will likely perish!
A gentleman values himself,
and only then can he extend to others;
therefore he has ritual propriety.
Now this man belittles his grandees and disparages his own clan,
this is disparaging himself.
Can he have ritual propriety?
Without ritual propriety,
he is sure to perish."
The Duke of Sòng feasted Zhāozi (Shū Sūn Chǒu),
and recited the poem "New Palace."
Zhāozi recited the poem "Chariot Linchpin."
The next day, there was a banquet,
with drinking,
and music.
The Duke of Sòng made Zhāozi sit to his right,
and they spoke to each other, weeping.
Lè Qí assisted.
After withdrawing, he told someone:
"This year, both our lord and Shūsūn will likely die!
I have heard it said:
'To take joy in sorrow and sorrow in joy,
both are signs of a lost mind.'
The essence and clarity of the mind
are called the hún and pò.
If the hún and pò depart from it,
how can one last long?"
B10.25.2 Jì Gōngruò's elder sister was the wife of the ruler of Xiǎo Zhū.
She gave birth to the wife of Duke Yuán of Sòng,
who bore a daughter,
who was given in marriage to Jì Píngzǐ.
Zhāozi went to Sòng on a diplomatic mission,
and also to escort her back.
Gōngruò accompanied him,
and told the Cáo family not to give her away,
saying that Lǔ would expel him.
The Cáo family informed the Duke.
The Duke told Lè Qí.
Lè Qí said: "Give her.
If so, the ruler of Lǔ will certainly be driven out.
Governance has been in the hands of the Jì family for three generations,
and the rulers of Lǔ have lost governance for four dukes.
There has never been one who, lacking the people's support, could still achieve his ambitions.
This has never happened.
A ruler of a state therefore pacifies and cares for his people.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'When men are gone,
the heart is grieved.'
The ruler of Lǔ has lost the people;
how can he achieve his ambitions?
To remain tranquil and await fate is still possible;
any action will surely bring worry."
B10.25.3 In summer,
they met at Huángfù,
to deliberate on matters of the royal house.
Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào ordered the great officers of the various states to contribute grain for the king
and prepare garrison troops,
saying:
"Next year we will restore the king."
Zǐ Dàshū (Yóu Jí) met with Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào.
Jiǎnzǐ asked him about the rituals of bowing, yielding, and ceremonial movements.
He replied: "These are ceremonial forms,
not ritual propriety."
Jiǎnzǐ said: "May I ask,
what is meant by ritual propriety?"
He replied:
"I, Jí, heard from the late great officer Zǐchǎn:
'Ritual propriety
is the constant principle of Heaven,
the appropriate pattern of Earth,
and the conduct of the people.'
The constant principles of Heaven and Earth,
are what the people truly take as their model.
They model themselves on the brightness of Heaven,
and follow the nature of Earth.
They give rise to the six qì,
and employ the five phases.
The qì become the five flavors,
manifest as the five colors,
and are displayed as the five tones.
Excess leads to confusion and disorder,
and the people lose their inherent nature.
Therefore, ritual propriety is established to uphold these:
the six domestic animals, five sacrificial animals, and three pure sacrifices
are used to uphold the five flavors;
the nine patterns, six colors, and five ornamental designs
are used to uphold the five colors;
the nine songs, eight winds,
seven notes, and six pitch standards
are used to uphold the five tones.
The relationships between ruler and minister, superior and inferior
model the appropriate pattern of Earth;
the relationships between husband and wife, external and internal
regulate these two affairs;
the relationships between father and son, elder and younger brothers,
aunts and elder sisters, maternal uncles and nephews,
marriage connections, and affinal relations
symbolize the brightness of Heaven;
governmental affairs, labor services, and practical duties
follow the four seasons;
punishments, penalties, awe, and imprisonment
make the people fear and be cautious,
in imitation of Heaven's thunder, lightning, and killing;
warmth, kindness, beneficence, and harmony
emulate Heaven's generation, nurturing, growth, and fostering.
The people have likes and dislikes, joy and anger, sorrow and pleasure,
born from the six qì.
Therefore, one must carefully examine the proper models and appropriate categories
to regulate these six emotions.
Sorrow has weeping and wailing,
pleasure has singing and dancing,
joy has giving and bestowing,
anger has fighting and combat;
joy arises from liking,
anger arises from disliking.
Therefore, one must carefully implement trustworthy commands,
with misfortune and fortune, rewards and punishments,
to regulate life and death.
Life
is a thing liked,
death
is a thing disliked.
Liked things
bring pleasure;
disliked things
bring sorrow.
If sorrow and pleasure are not misplaced,
then one can harmonize with the nature of Heaven and Earth,
and thus endure long."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"How profound!
The greatness of ritual propriety!"
He replied: "Ritual propriety
is the guiding principle of superiors and inferiors, the warp and woof of Heaven and Earth.
It is that by which the people live.
Therefore, the former kings esteemed it.
Thus, one who can bend or straighten himself to conform to ritual propriety
is called a complete person.
Its greatness,
is it not indeed fitting!"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I, Yāng,
ask to hold to these words for life."
Lè Dàxīn of Sòng said:
"I will not contribute grain.
We of Sòng are guests to Zhōu;
how can you make a guest do this?"
Shì Bó of Jìn said:
"Since the covenant at Jiàntǔ,
what campaign has Sòng not joined,
and what covenant has it not participated in?
It was said
'to share in concern for the royal house';
how can you avoid it?
You, sir, have received your lord's command
to attend this great affair,
yet Sòng would break the covenant;
is this not unacceptable?"
The Yòushī did not dare reply,
but accepted the document and withdrew.
Shì Bó reported to Jiǎnzǐ, saying:
"The Yòushī of Sòng is sure to perish.
Having received his lord's command on a mission,
yet wishing to break the covenant and offend the covenant leader—
nothing could be more inauspicious."
B10.25.4 "'Magpies came and nested'
is a record of something unprecedented.
Shī Jǐ said:
"How strange!
I have heard that in the times of Dukes Wén and Chéng,
there was a children's rhyme,
which said:
'Magpie, oh magpie,
the duke goes forth, disgraced.
The feathers of the magpie,
the duke is in the wilds,
they go to send him horses.
The magpie hops about,
the duke is at Gānhóu,
seeking short and long garments.
The nest of the magpie,
far, oh so far away,
Duke Zhāo toils and is lost,
Duke Dìng is proud.
Magpie, oh magpie,
you go with song, return with weeping.'
The children's rhyme had this.
Now magpies have come and nested;
is it about to happen!"
B10.25.5 In autumn,
it is recorded that a second rain sacrifice was held,
because the drought was severe.
B10.25.6 Earlier,
Jì Gōngniǎo took a wife from the Bào family of Qí,
and she bore Jiǎ.
Gōngniǎo died,
and Jì Gōnghài, Gōngsī Zhǎn, and Gōngniǎo's retainer Shēn Yègū managed his household.
When Jì Sì had illicit relations with the cook Tán,
she became afraid,
and had her maid beat her,
to show it to the wife of Qín Chuán,
He said:
"If the lord wishes to employ me,
I cannot do so, and he will flog me."
He also complained to Gōngfǔ,
saying:
"Zhǎn and Yègū are going to seize me."
Qín Jī reported this to Gōngzhī.
Gōngzhī and Gōngfǔ informed Píngzǐ,
so Píngzǐ detained Zhǎn in Biàn,
and arrested Yègū,
intending to kill him.
Gōngruò wept and pleaded for him,
saying:
"To kill him
is to kill me."
He was about to plead for him,
but Píngzǐ ordered the attendant not to admit him,
and by midday he had not
been able to plead.
The officer in charge refused the order,
so Gōngzhī had him executed quickly.
Thus, Gōngruò resented Píngzǐ.
The Jì and Hòu families' cocks fought,
the Jì family armored their cock,
and the Hòu family fitted theirs with metal spurs.
Píngzǐ was angry,
seized more of the Hòu family's estates,
and reprimanded them.
Thus, Hòu Zhāobó also resented Píngzǐ.
Zāng Zhāobó's younger cousin Huì slandered the Zāng family,
and fled to the Jì family.
The Zāng family seized him.
Píngzǐ was angry,
and detained the Zāng family's steward.
When they were about to perform the dì sacrifice for Duke Xiāng,
only two dancers were present,
while the rest were dancing at the Jì family's.
Zāng Sūn said:
"This is what is called being unable to honor the temple of the former lord."
The grandees then resented Píngzǐ.
Gōngruò presented a bow to Gōngwéi,
and went out shooting with him,
plotting to remove the Jì family.
Gōngwéi told Gōngguǒ and Gōngbēn.
Gōngguǒ and Gōngbēn had the attendant Liáozhā inform the duke.
The duke was asleep,
and was about to strike him with a halberd,
so he fled.
The duke said:
"Seize him!"
But he gave no order.
Frightened, he did not come out,
and for several months did not appear.
The duke was not angry.
They sent him again to speak,
and the duke brandished a halberd to frighten him,
so he fled.
They sent him again to speak,
and the duke said:
"This is not something a petty man can manage."
Gōngguǒ spoke in person,
and the duke told Zāng Sūn,
but Zāng Sūn said it was difficult.
He told Hòu Sūn,
and Hòu Sūn said it was feasible,
and urged him on.
He told Zǐjiā Yìbó.
Yìbó said:
"Slanderers make the lord rely on luck;
if the affair does not succeed,
the lord bears the blame,
so it cannot be done.
For generations, we have neglected the people,
hoping to succeed in affairs,
but success is not certain.
Moreover, power lies with him,
so it is difficult to plot against him."
The duke dismissed him.
He declined, saying:
"Your servant has heard the command;
if the words leak out,
your servant will not escape death."
So he stayed at the duke's residence.
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ went to Kàn,
and the duke resided at the Chángfǔ.
On the wùxū day of the ninth month,
they attacked the Jì family,
killed Gōngzhī at the gate,
and then entered.
Píngzǐ ascended a tower and pleaded:
"My lord does not investigate your servant's crime,
but sends officers to attack your servant with weapons;
your servant requests to await at the Yí River to be investigated for his crime."
He was not permitted.
He requested to be imprisoned in Fèi,
but was not permitted.
He requested to leave with five chariots,
but was not permitted.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"My lord should permit him!
Power has issued from him for a long time;
many of the destitute depend on him for food,
and his followers are numerous.
When the sun sets, wickedness arises,
and it is impossible to know what will happen.
The anger of the masses cannot be stored up;
if stored and not managed,
it will accumulate.
When it accumulates,
the people will develop intentions.
When intentions arise,
those with the same goals will unite.
My lord will surely regret it!"
He did not listen.
Hòu Sūn said:
"He must be killed."
The duke sent Hòu Sūn to meet Mèng Yìzǐ.
The Sīmǎ of the Shūsūn family, Zōnglì, said to his followers:
"What should we do?"
No one replied.
He said again:
"I
am a family minister;
I dare not concern myself with state affairs.
In general, is it more beneficial for us
to have the Jì family or not?"
They all said:
"Without the Jì family,
there is no Shūsūn family."
Zōnglì said:
"Then let us rescue them!"
He led his followers there,
breaching the northwest corner to enter.
The duke's men had removed their armor and were sitting with their weapons,
so they were driven away.
The Mèng family had someone ascend the northwest corner,
to observe the Jì family.
Seeing the banners of the Shūsūn family,
they reported it.
The Mèng family seized Hòu Zhāobó,
killed him west of the south gate,
and then attacked the duke's men.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"Let your ministers pretend to have coerced the lord,
and bear the guilt as they leave;
the lord should stay.
Yìrú's service to the lord
will surely not dare remain unchanged."
The duke said:
"I cannot bear it."
He went with Zāng Sūn to the tombs to plan,
and then departed.
On the jǐhài day,
the duke fled to Qí,
and stopped at Yángzhōu.
The Marquis of Qí intended to console the duke at Píngyīn,
but the duke first arrived at Yějǐng.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"It is my fault.
I had officers wait at Píngyīn,
because it was closer."
The record says:
"The duke fled to Qí,
and stopped at Yángzhōu.
The Marquis of Qí consoled the duke at Yějǐng,"
which was according to ritual.
When one seeks something from others,
one should first humble oneself;
this is a good aspect of ritual.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"From the western border of Jǔ,
I offer a thousand shè,
to await my lord's command.
I will lead my humble forces to follow your officers,
obeying only your orders.
My lord's worries
are my worries."
The duke was pleased.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"Heaven's blessings do not come twice.
If Heaven favors my lord,
it will not exceed what was given to the Duke of Zhōu.
Having Lǔ is sufficient.
To lose Lǔ and become a minister with a thousand shè,
who will help you stand?
Moreover, the lord of Qí is untrustworthy;
it would be better to go to Jìn early."
He did not listen.
Zāng Zhāobó led the followers in making an oath,
and the covenant document said:
"Join forces with one heart,
sharing likes and dislikes.
Believe in whether there is guilt or not,
cling closely to the duke,
and do not communicate with outsiders or insiders!"
He showed the document to Zǐjiāzi on behalf of the duke's command.
Zǐjiāzi said:
"In this case,
I cannot join the covenant.
I, Jī, am not talented,
and cannot share the same heart with you gentlemen,
for I consider you all to be guilty.
Some wish to communicate between inside and outside,
and moreover wish to remove the ruler.
You gentlemen love ruin and hate stability—
how can I be the same as you?
To plunge the ruler into difficulty—
what crime could be greater?
If you communicate between inside and outside and remove the ruler,
the ruler will swiftly return.
If there is no communication, what is to be done?
And what are you guarding against?"
Thus he did not join the covenant.
Zhāozi returned from Kàn
and saw Píngzǐ.
Píngzǐ knocked his forehead to the ground
and said:
"What will you do with me?"
Zhāozi said:
"Who among men does not die?
But you have achieved fame by expelling the ruler—
your descendants will not forget it.
Is this not grievous?
What is to be done with you?"
Píngzǐ said:
"If only Yìrú could change and serve the ruler again,
it would be what is called giving life to the dead and putting flesh on bones."
Zhāozi followed the duke to Qí
and spoke with the duke.
Zǐjiāzi ordered that anyone going to the duke's lodging be seized.
The duke spoke with Zhāozi inside the tent,
saying:
"I intend to pacify the multitude and restore the duke."
The duke's followers were about to kill Zhāozi
and lay in ambush along the road.
Zuǒshī Zhǎn informed the duke,
and the duke had Zhāozi return from Zhù.
Píngzǐ had other intentions.
In winter, the tenth month, on Xīnyǒu,
Zhāozi fasted in his chamber
and had the invocator pray for death.
On Wùchén,
he died.
Zuǒshī Zhǎn intended to have the duke return by carriage,
but the duke's followers seized him.
B10.25.7 On Rénshēn,
Yǐn Wéngōng crossed the river at Gǒng,
burned Dōngzī,
but did not succeed.
B10.25.8 In the eleventh month,
Sòng Yuángōng intended to go to Jìn for the duke's sake.
He dreamed that Crown Prince Luán was assuming the position in the ancestral temple,
and he himself, along with Pínggōng, was robed and assisting him.
At dawn,
he summoned the six ministers.
The duke said:
"I, the unworthy one,
am unable to serve my father and elder brothers,
causing you gentlemen worry—
this is my crime.
If, by your divine favor,
I am able to protect my head and neck until death,
only the planks and supports used to prop up the trunk—
I ask that they not reach the level of the former rulers."
Zhòng Jī replied:
"If you, for the sake of the altars of soil and grain,
privately reduce intimate feasts,
we ministers dare not know of it.
But as for the laws of Sòng,
the measures of life and death,
the former rulers have already decreed them.
We ministers guard them unto death
and dare not deviate.
If I fail in my duty,
the regular punishments will not be pardoned.
I cannot bear to face death,
and your command would only be dishonored."
The Sòng duke then set out.
On Jǐhài,
he died at Qújí.
B10.25.9 In the twelfth month, on Gēngchén,
the marquis of Qí besieged Yùn.
B10.25.10 Earlier,
Zāng Zhāobó went to Jìn.
Zāng Huì stole his precious tortoise shell, Lóugōu,
and used it to divine about truth and falsehood.
Falsehood was auspicious.
When the elder of the Zāng clan was about to go to Jìn to inquire,
Huì requested to go instead.
Zhāobó asked about family affairs,
and he answered everything.
But when it came to his wife and younger brother Shūsūn,
he did not answer.
Asked again and again,
he did not answer.
On returning,
when they reached the outskirts,
Huì came to meet him.
Asked again,
he acted as before.
Upon arrival,
Zhāobó stayed outside and observed,
but found nothing.
He seized him and intended to kill him,
but Huì escaped
and fled to Hòu.
Hòu Fángjiǎ made him a market overseer.
When he submitted accounts to the Jì clan,
the Zāng clan sent five men with spears and shields to lie in ambush at the gate of Tóngrǔ.
When Huì came out,
they pursued him.
He turned and fled back,
and they seized him outside the middle gate of the Jì clan.
Píngzǐ angrily said: "Why have you entered my gate with weapons?"
He detained the elder of the Zāng clan.
The Jì and Zāng clans became enemies.
When Zhāobó followed the duke,
Píngzǐ installed Zāng Huì.
Huì said:
"Lóugōu did not deceive me."
B10.25.11 The king of Chǔ sent Wěi Shè to wall Zhōuqū,
and resettled the Qié people there;
he walled Qiūhuáng,
and moved the Zī people there.
He sent Xióngxiàng Méi to wall the outer city of Cháo,
and Jìrán to wall Juǎn.
Zǐtàishū heard of this
and said:
"The king of Chǔ is about to die.
Making the people unsettled in their land,
the people will surely grieve.
Grief will reach the king—
he cannot last long."
A10.26 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Twenty-sixth Year of Duke Zhāo"
A10.26.1 In the twenty-sixth year, in spring,
the royal first month,
we buried Duke Yuán of Sòng.
A10.26.2 In the third month,
the duke arrived from Qí
and resided in Yùn.
A10.26.3 In summer,
the duke besieged Chéng.
A10.26.4 In autumn,
the duke met with the marquis of Qí,
the viscount of Jǔ,
the viscount of Zhū,
and the earl of Qǐ,
and covenanted at Zhuānlíng.
A10.26.5 The duke arrived from the meeting
and resided in Yùn.
A10.26.6 In the ninth month, on Gēngshēn,
the king of Chǔ, Jū, died.
A10.26.7 In winter, the tenth month,
the Heavenly King entered Chéngzhōu.
Yǐnshì,
Shàobó,
and Máobó fled to Chǔ with Prince Cháo.
B10.26 "The Commentary: The Twenty-sixth Year of Duke Zhāo"
B10.26.1 In the twenty-sixth year, in spring,
in the royal first month, on Gēngshēn,
the marquis of Qí took Yùn.
B10.26.2 We buried Duke Yuán of Sòng,
according to the rites for former rulers—
this was proper.
B10.26.3 In the third month,
the duke arrived from Qí
and stayed in Yùn—
this indicates it was Lǔ territory.
B10.26.4 In summer,
the marquis of Qí intended to restore the duke
and ordered that no goods from Lǔ be accepted.
Shēn Fēng followed Nǚ Jiǎ,
with two bolts of brocade as gifts,
tied together like an earplug,
and went to the Qí army.
He said to Gāo Yǐ, a man of Zǐyóu:
"If you can bribe Zǐyóu,
to secure the future of the Gāo clan,
we offer five thousand yǔ of grain."
Gāo Yǐ showed silk brocade to Zǐ Yóu,
and Zǐ Yóu desired it.
Yǐ said:
"The men of Lǔ bought it,
paying a hundred liǎng per bolt.
Because the roads are impassable,
they sent the payment in advance."
Zǐ Yóu accepted it,
and said to the Marquis of Qí:
"The reason your ministers are not exerting their full strength for the ruler of Lǔ
is not that they are incapable of serving their lord.
However, Jù has a different view.
Duke Yuán of Sòng went to Jìn for the ruler of Lǔ,
and died at Qūjí;
Shūsūn Zhāozǐ sought to restore his lord,
and died without illness.
Is it that Heaven has abandoned Lǔ,
or is it that the ruler of Lǔ has offended the spirits and gods, hence this has come about?
If you, my lord, wait at Qūjí,
send your ministers to follow the ruler of Lǔ to test the omens.
If it is favorable,
the army will achieve success,
and you, my lord, can then follow up,
ensuring there will be no match for you.
If it does not succeed,
you, my lord, will not be disgraced."
The Marquis of Qí followed this advice,
and sent Gōngzǐ Chú to lead troops to follow the Duke.
The grand officer of Chéng, Gōngsūn Cháo, said to Píngzǐ:
"A city exists
to defend the state.
I request to receive the enemy army."
He granted it.
He requested to offer a hostage,
but it was not granted,
saying:
"We trust you,
that is enough."
He reported to the Qí army, saying:
"The Méng clan
is a declining house of Lǔ.
They have used Chéng excessively,
and we can no longer endure it.
We ask to shift our burden to Qí."
The Qí army besieged Chéng.
The men of Chéng attacked the Qí soldiers who were watering their horses at the Zī River,
saying:
"This is to satisfy the masses."
When Lǔ's defenses at Chéng were complete, they then reported, saying:
"We cannot overcome the masses."
The army fought the Qí army at Chuībí.
Zǐyuān Jié of Qí pursued Xiè Shēngzǐ,
shot at him,
hitting the shield's ridge,
the arrow passing from the throat groove, glanced off the chariot pole,
and the arrowhead penetrated three inches.
Shēngzǐ shot at his horse,
severed the breast strap,
and it died.
He changed chariots,
and people, thinking he was Zōng Lì,
came to assist him.
Zǐjū said:
"He is a man of Qí."
He was about to strike Zǐjū,
but Zǐjū shot him,
and he died.
His charioteer said:
"Again."
Zǐjū said:
"The multitude can be intimidated,
but should not be provoked."
Zǐnáng Dài pursued Yě Xiè,
and shouted at him.
Xiè said:
"In war, there is no private anger;
to retaliate is a private matter.
I will resist you."
He shouted at him again,
and the other also shouted back.
Rǎn Shǔ shot at Chén Wǔzǐ,
hitting his hand,
causing him to drop his bow and curse.
He reported this to Píngzǐ,
saying:
"There is a gentleman, fair-skinned with thick black beard and eyebrows,
very foul-mouthed."
Píngzǐ said:
"It must be Zǐ Qiáng.
Did you perhaps resist him?"
He replied: "Calling him a gentleman,
how would I dare resist him?"
Lín Yōng was ashamed to be Yán Míng's chariot right,
and descended.
Yuàn Héjì cut off his ear.
Yán Míng left him.
Yuànzǐ's charioteer said:
"Look down!"
He looked back.
Yuànzǐ struck Lín Yōng,
severed his foot,
and he was placed on another chariot and taken back.
Yán Míng entered the Qí army three times,
shouting:
"Lín Yōng, ride!"
B10.26.5 In the fourth month,
Dānzǐ went to Jìn to report the emergency.
On the wǔwǔ day of the fifth month,
the men of Liú defeated the army of Wángchéng at Shīshì.
On the wùchén day,
the men of Wángchéng and the men of Liú fought at Shīgǔ,
and the Liú army was defeated.
B10.26.6 In autumn,
they made a covenant at Zhuānlíng,
planning to restore the Duke.
B10.26.7 On the jǐsì day of the seventh month,
Liúzǐ escorted the King out.
On the gēngwǔ day,
they halted at Qú.
The men of Wángchéng burned Liú.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
the King lodged at Chǔshì.
On the dīngchǒu day,
the King halted at Huángǔ.
On the gēngchén day,
the King entered Xūmí.
On the xīnsì day,
the King halted at Huá.
Zhì Lì and Zhào Yǎng of Jìn led troops to escort the King,
and sent Rǔ Kuān to guard Quèsāi.
B10.26.8 In the ninth month,
King Píng of Chǔ died.
The Prime Minister Zǐ Cháng wanted to install Zǐ Xī,
saying: "The crown prince Rén is young,
and his mother is not the principal wife;
Prince Jiàn actually betrothed her.
Zǐ Xī is older and fond of goodness.
Installing the elder is in accordance with order,
establishing goodness brings good governance.
With the King in order and the state well-governed,
should this not be pursued?"
Zǐ Xī angrily said:
"This is to throw the state into disorder and defame our late king.
The state has external support,
which must not be defiled;
the King has a rightful heir,
which must not be disrupted.
To ruin kinship, hasten enmity, and disrupt the succession
is inauspicious.
I would bear the infamy.
Even if I were bribed with the whole world,
I would still refuse.
What would become of Chǔ?
The Prime Minister must be killed!"
The Prime Minister was afraid,
and so installed King Zhāo.
B10.26.9 In winter, on the bǐngshēn day of the tenth month,
the King raised an army at Huá.
On the xīnchǒu day,
they were at Jiāo,
and then halted at Shī.
On the xīnyǒu day of the eleventh month,
the Jìn army captured Gǒng.
Zhào Bó Yíng drove out Prince Cháo,
and Prince Cháo, along with the Zhào clan, Máo Bó Dé, Yǐnshì Gù, and Nángōng Yín, fled to Chǔ with the Zhou archives.
Yīn Jì fled to Jǔ and rebelled.
Zhào Bó welcomed the King at Shī,
and made a covenant with Liúzǐ and Dānzǐ.
Then they stationed troops at Yǔzé,
and halted at Dīshàng.
On the guǐyǒu day,
the King entered Chéngzhōu.
On the jiǎxū day,
they made a covenant at Xiānggōng.
The Jìn army left Chéng Gōng Bān to garrison Zhōu and then returned.
On the guǐwèi day of the twelfth month,
the King entered Zhuānggōng.
Prince Cháo sent a message to the feudal lords, saying:
"In the past, King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
King Chéng pacified the four quarters,
and King Kāng gave the people rest.
They all enfeoffed their maternal brothers,
to serve as a protective screen for Zhōu,
and also said:
'We do not exclusively enjoy the achievements of King Wén and
King Wǔ,
and for fear that later generations might become confused, degenerate, topple, and fall into calamity,
we will rescue them.'
Down to King Yí,
when the King suffered in his own person,
the feudal lords all hurried to their local altars,
to pray for the King's person.
Down to King Lì,
the King's heart was cruel and tyrannical,
and the myriad people could not endure it,
and placed the King at Zhì.
The feudal lords relinquished their positions,
to intervene in the royal government.
King Xuān had ambition,
and afterwards they returned their official duties.
As for King Yōu,
Heaven did not pity Zhōu,
the king was benighted and unrighteous,
thereby forfeiting his position.
King Xié usurped the mandate,
the feudal lords deposed him,
and established the royal heir,
moving to Jiárǔ.
— — This was the ability of brothers to exert strength for the royal house.
As for King Huì,
Heaven did not pacify Zhōu,
giving rise to Tuí's treacherous heart,
which extended to Shū Dài.
Huì and Xiāng avoided calamity,
fleeing from the royal capital.
Then there were Jìn and Zhèng, both of whom eliminated the unrighteous,
to pacify and stabilize the royal house.
This was the ability of brothers to uphold the former kings' commands.
In the sixth year of King Dìng,
the people of Qín reported an omen,
saying:
'Zhōu will have a bearded king,
who will also be able to fulfill his duties,
the feudal lords will submit and enjoy,
for two generations they will together perform their duties.
Should the royal house have one who intervenes in the kingship,
and the feudal lords do not plan,
they will suffer his chaotic disasters.'
As for King Líng,
he was born with
a beard.
The king was very divine and sagely,
doing no evil to the feudal lords.
King Líng,
King Jǐng were able to end their reigns.
"Now the royal house is in chaos,
Shàn Qí, Liú Dí disrupt and throw the world into disorder,
uniformly acting unrighteously,
saying
'What constancy did the former kings have?
Only what my heart commands,
who dares to punish it?'
Leading a crowd of unpitiable men,
to carry out disorder in the royal house.
Their encroaching desires are insatiable,
their scheming demands know no bounds,
they blaspheme and defile the ghosts and spirits,
neglect and discard the penal laws,
betray and violate the solemn covenants,
are arrogant and contemptuous of dignified ceremonies,
falsify and slander the former kings.
Jìn acts without principle,
is abetting and assisting them,
thinking to indulge their boundless excesses.
This unworthy one is shaken and tossed about,
hiding in Jīng Mán,
with no place to settle.
If my few brothers and nephews by marriage would encourage and follow Heaven's laws,
not aid the crafty and cunning,
to obey the former kings' commands,
not hasten Heaven's punishment,
pardon and plan for this unworthy one,
that would be my wish.
I dare to fully disclose my innermost thoughts and the former kings' constant principles,
and it is for the feudal lords to deeply consider them.
"In the past, the former kings' command said:
'If the queen has no legitimate son,
then choose and establish the eldest.
If age is equal, use virtue;
if virtue is equal, use divination.'
The king does not establish based on favor,
the dukes and ministers have no private interests,
this is the ancient institution.
Queen Mù and the crown prince Shòu died young and departed this world,
Shàn and Liú assisted in privately establishing a younger one,
to intervene against the former kings.
May the elder, second, third, and younger brothers consider this!"
Mǐn Mǎfù heard Zǐ Cháo's words,
and said:
"Eloquent words are to carry out ritual.
Zǐ Cháo violated King Jǐng's command,
distanced himself from Jìn's greatness
to concentrate his own will,
his lack of ritual is extreme,
what use are eloquent words?"
B10.26.10 In Qí there was a comet,
the Marquis of Qí ordered a sacrifice to avert it.
Yànzǐ said:
"It is of no benefit,
it only invites deception.
The Way of Heaven is not to be flattered,
it does not lend out its mandate,
how can one avert it by sacrifice?
Moreover, Heaven having a comet
is to sweep away filth.
If you, my lord, have no filthy virtue,
what need is there to avert it?
If your virtue is filthy,
what loss does averting it prevent?
The Odes say:
'Only this King Wén,
was careful and reverent.
Clearly serving the Lord on High,
thus he obtained much happiness.
His virtue was not devious,
thereby he received the myriad states.'
If you, my lord, have no deviant virtue,
the myriad states will come to you,
what worry is there about a comet?
The Odes say:
'I have nothing to look upon as a mirror,
but the Xià and the Shāng.
Because of the chaos of their times,
the people all fled and wandered.'
If virtue is deviant and chaotic,
the people will flee and wander,
what the invocators and scribes do
cannot make up for it."
The duke was pleased,
and stopped.
B10.26.11 The Marquis of Qí and Yànzǐ were sitting in the main hall.
The duke sighed and said:
"How beautiful this hall!
Who will possess it?"
Yànzǐ said: "May I ask,
what do you mean?"
The duke said: "I think it depends on virtue."
He replied:
"As you, my lord, say,
it will likely be the Chén family!
Although the Chén family has no great virtue,
they give to the people.
In the measures of dòu, ōu, fǔ, and zhōng,
what they take from the ducal store is little,
what they give to the people is much.
You, my lord, levy heavy taxes,
the Chén family gives generously,
the people turn to them.
The Odes say:
'Though I have no virtue for you,
yet you sing and dance.'
The Chén family's giving
makes the people sing and dance for them.
If later generations are somewhat negligent,
and the Chén family does not perish,
then the state will become their state."
The duke said: "Excellent!
What can be done about this?"
He replied:
"Only ritual can stop it.
According to ritual,
a family's giving does not extend to the state,
the people do not move,
farmers do not shift,
artisans and merchants do not change,
officers are not excessive,
officials are not negligent,
great officers do not take public benefits."
The duke said:
"I cannot do it.
From now on I know that ritual can govern a state."
He replied: "That ritual can govern a state is ancient,
it is coeval with Heaven and Earth.
The ruler gives orders, the ministers are reverent;
the father is kind, the son is filial;
the elder brother loves, the younger brother respects;
the husband is harmonious, the wife is gentle;
the mother-in-law is kind, the daughter-in-law is obedient;
this is ritual.
The ruler gives orders without transgression,
the ministers are reverent without duplicity;
the father is kind and teaches,
the son is filial and admonishes;
the elder brother loves and is friendly,
the younger brother respects and is compliant;
the husband is harmonious and righteous,
the wife is gentle and correct;
the mother-in-law is kind and yielding,
the daughter-in-law is obedient and gentle;
these are the good things of ritual."
The duke said: "Excellent,
I from now on have heard that ritual is supreme!"
He replied:
"Ritual is what the former kings received from Heaven and Earth to govern their people,
therefore the former kings held it supreme."
A10.27 The Twenty-seventh Year of Duke Zhāo, the Classic
A10.27.1 In the twenty-seventh year, spring,
the duke went to Qí.
A10.27.2 The duke arrived from Qí,
and resided in Yùn.
A10.27.3 In summer, the fourth month,
Wú assassinated its ruler Liáo.
A10.27.4 The state of Chǔ executed its senior official Xì Wǎn.
A10.27.5 In autumn,
Shì Yǎng of Jìn,
Yuè Qílí of Sòng,
Běigōng Xǐ of Wèi,
a representative from Cáo,
a representative from Zhū,
and a representative from Téng held a meeting at Hù.
A10.27.6 In winter, the tenth month,
the Earl of Cáo, Wǔ, died.
A10.27.7 Kuài of Zhū came fleeing [to Lǔ].
A10.27.8 The Duke [of Lǔ] went to Qí.
A10.27.9 The Duke arrived back from Qí
and resided in Yùn.
B10.27 The Commentary to the Twenty-seventh Year of Duke Zhāo
B10.27.1 In the spring of the twenty-seventh year,
the Duke [of Lǔ] went to Qí.
The Duke arrived back from Qí,
and took up residence in Yùn.
This indicates he was outside [the capital].
B10.27.2 The Prince of Wú wished to take advantage of Chǔ's mourning period to attack it.
He sent the princes Yǎnyú and Zhúyōng to lead troops and besiege Qián.
He sent Jìzǐ of Yánzhōulái on a diplomatic mission to the Central States,
and then to Jìn,
in order to observe the various lords.
Rán, the Yǒu-yǐn of Chǔ, and Jūn, the Wáng-yǐn, led troops to relieve Qián.
Shěn Yīnxū, the Left Minister of War, led the capital's gentlemen and the king's horse guard to reinforce the army.
They encountered the Wú army at Qióng.
The Prime Minister Zǐcháng led the naval forces to Shāruì and then turned back.
Xì Wǎn, the Left-yǐn, and Shòu, the Gōng-yǐn, led troops as far as Qián,
and the Wú army could not retreat.
Prince Guāng of Wú said:
"This is the moment,
it must not be lost."
He told Zhuān Shèzhū:
"In the Central States there is a saying:
'If one does not seek,
how can one obtain?'
I
am the rightful heir,
I wish to seek it.
If the affair succeeds,
even if Jìzǐ arrives,
he will not depose me."
Zhuān Shèzhū said:
"The king can be assassinated.
But my mother is old and my sons are young,
what will become of them?"
Guāng said:
"I
am as your own self."
In summer, the fourth month,
Guāng concealed armored soldiers in a cellar chamber and invited the king to a feast.
The king had soldiers in armor stationed along the road and at his gate.
The gate, the steps, the door, the mat—
all were attended by the king's personal guards,
flanking them with spears.
The servers presented themselves and changed their clothes outside the gate.
The servers entered crawling on their knees,
with spearmen flanking and supporting them,
so that the spears reached their bodies,
as they handed over the dishes.
Guāng feigned a foot ailment,
and went into the cellar chamber.
Zhuān Shèzhū placed a sword inside a fish and presented it.
He drew the sword and stabbed the king.
The spears crossed at his chest,
and thus he assassinated the king.
Hélú made his son a minister.
When Jìzǐ arrived,
he said:
"If the sacrifices to the former rulers are not abandoned,
if the people are not deprived of their lord,
if the altars of soil and grain receive offerings,
if the state and its altars are not overturned,
then he is my ruler.
Whom should I dare to resent?
I will mourn the dead and serve the living,
awaiting Heaven's decree.
The disorder did not arise from me.
I will follow the one who is established,
for this is the way of our forefathers."
He reported his mission at the tomb, weeping,
then resumed his post and awaited orders.
Prince Yǎnyú of Wú fled to Xú,
and Prince Zhúyōng fled to Zhōngwú.
The Chǔ army, hearing of the disorder in Wú, turned back.
B10.27.3 Xì Wǎn was upright and amiable,
and the people of the capital were pleased with him.
Yān Jiàngshī was the Right Commander,
and together with Fèi Wújí, he formed a clique and hated Xì Wǎn.
The Prime Minister Zǐcháng was covetous and believed slander.
Wújí slandered Xì Wǎn to him,
saying to Zǐcháng:
"Zǐ'è [i.e., Xì Wǎn] wishes to invite you to drink."
He also said to Zǐ'è:
"The Prime Minister wishes to drink at your house."
Zǐ'è said:
"I
am a humble man,
not worthy to trouble the Prime Minister.
If the Prime Minister must certainly come and trouble himself,
the favor would be too great.
I have nothing with which to reciprocate him.
What is to be done?"
Wújí said:
"The Prime Minister is fond of armor and weapons.
You bring some out,
and I will select them."
He took five sets of armor and five weapons,
and said:
"Place them at the gate.
When the Prime Minister arrives,
he is sure to look at them,
and you can then use them to reciprocate."
On the day of the feast,
they were placed behind a curtain to the left of the gate.
Wújí said to the Prime Minister:
"I nearly brought disaster upon you.
Zǐ'è intends to do you harm.
Armor is at his gate.
You must not go!
Moreover, in that campaign,
Wú could have achieved its aim.
Zǐ'è took bribes and withdrew;
he also misled the various commanders,
causing them to withdraw their troops,
saying
'To take advantage of disorder is inauspicious.'
Wú took advantage of our mourning;
we taking advantage of their disorder—
would that not be acceptable?"
The Prime Minister sent someone to inspect the Xì household,
and there was indeed armor there.
He did not go,
but summoned Yān Jiàngshī and told him.
Jiàngshī withdrew,
and then ordered an attack on the Xì family,
and to burn them out.
Zǐ'è heard of this,
and committed suicide.
The people of the capital would not set the fire,
so an order was issued:
"Whoever does not burn the Xì house
will share their crime."
Some took a bundle of reeds,
some took a handful of straw,
the people of the capital threw them [at the house],
but still did not set it ablaze.
