The Prime Minister burned them [the Xì family],
completely exterminating the Xì clan and its partisans.
He killed Yáng Lìngzhōng and his brother Wán, and Tuó, and Jìn Chén, and their sons and brothers.
The clan of Jìn Chén cried out in the capital,
saying:
"The Yān and Fèi clans consider themselves kings,
they bring disaster upon the state of Chǔ,
weaken and diminish the royal house,
and deceive the king and the Prime Minister for their own profit.
The Prime Minister believes them completely.
What will become of the state?"
The Prime Minister was troubled by this.
B10.27.4 In autumn,
they met at Hù,
to order the garrisoning of Zhōu,
and also to plan the restoration of the Duke [of Lǔ].
Sòng and Wèi both stood to gain from restoring the Duke,
so they firmly requested it.
Fàn Xiànzǐ [of Jìn] had taken bribes from Jìsūn,
and said to Sīchéng Zǐliáng [of Sòng] and Běigōng Zhēnzǐ [of Wèi]:
"Jìsūn does not know his crime,
yet your lords attacked him.
He asked to be imprisoned, asked to go into exile,
but in this he was not granted his wish.
Your lords were also unable to defeat him,
and he left of his own accord.
Could he have been able to make his lord leave without being prepared?
The restoration of the Jì family
was Heaven's rescue of them.
It calmed the anger of the Duke's followers,
and opened the hearts of the Shūsūn family.
Otherwise,
would they, when attacking others, have been leisurely taking off their armor and holding ice to play?
The Shūsūn family feared the overflow of disaster,
and so identified themselves with the Jì family.
This is the way of Heaven.
The lord of Lǔ defended Qí,
but after three years had not achieved success.
The Jì clan greatly gained the people's support,
the Huáiyí allied with them,
they had provisions for ten years,
had the aid of Qí and Chǔ,
had Heaven's assistance,
had the people's help,
had a resolute heart for defense,
had the authority among the various states,
yet dared not proclaim it,
serving their lord as if he were in the state.
Therefore, Yǎng considered it difficult.
The two gentlemen are both those who plan for the state,
and wish to bring in the lord of Lǔ,
this is Yǎng's desire,
I request to follow the two gentlemen to besiege Lǔ.
If we do not succeed,
I will die for it."
The two gentlemen were afraid,
and both declined.
Then they declined the small states,
and reported the difficulty.
B10.27.5 Mèng Yìzǐ and Yáng Hǔ attacked Yùn,
the people of Yùn prepared to fight.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"Heaven's mandate has not been doubted for a long time,
those who will cause our lord to perish,
are certainly this multitude.
Since Heaven has already brought disaster upon him,
yet he seeks blessings for himself,
is that not difficult indeed!
If there are still ghosts and spirits,
this will certainly lead to defeat.
Alas!
There is no hope left!
Will he die here?"
The lord sent Zǐjiāzǐ to Jìn.
The lord's followers were defeated at Qiězhī.
B10.27.6 In the disaster of Chǔ's Xì Wǎn,
the talk in the state had not ceased,
those presenting sacrificial meat all slandered the Prime Minister.
Shěn Yínxū said to Zǐcháng:
"The Left Minister and the Stable Minister,
no one knew their crimes,
yet you, sir, killed them,
thereby arousing slander and resentment,
which continues to this day without end.
Xū is perplexed by this:
a benevolent person might kill someone to cover up slander,
and still would not do it,
yet do not consider the consequences, is this not strange indeed!
That Wújí,
is a slanderer of Chǔ,
the people all know it.
He removed Cháo Wú,
expelled Càihóu Zhū,
caused the loss of Crown Prince Jiàn,
killed Liányín Shē,
blocked the king's ears and eyes,
making him unwise.
Otherwise,
with King Píng's gentle kindness, respectfulness, and frugality,
he surpassed Chéng
and Zhuāng,
and was not inferior in any aspect.
The reason he did not
gain the allegiance of the feudal lords,
was because Wújí was close to him.
Now he has again killed three innocent men,
arousing great slander,
which nearly reached you, sir.
If you, sir, do not consider this,
then what use are you?
That Yān Jiāngshī falsified your orders,
to exterminate three clans.
These three clans
were the finest of the state,
and had not erred in their positions.
Wú has a new ruler,
and the borders are daily alarmed.
If Chǔ encounters a major event,
you, sir, will be in danger!
A wise man removes slanderers to secure himself,
now you, sir, cherish slanderers and endanger yourself,
this is extreme,
how confused you are!"
Zǐcháng said:
"This is Wǎ's crime,
dare I not make good plans!"
In the ninth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
Zǐcháng killed Fèi Wújí and Yān Jiāngshī,
exterminating their entire clans,
to appease the state.
The slander then ceased.
B10.27.7 In winter,
the lord went to Qí,
the Marquis of Qí requested to host a feast for him.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"Morning and evening you stand in his court,
what need is there for a feast,
it is just drinking wine."
So they drank wine,
had the steward offer it,
and requested peace.
Zǐzhòng's daughter, named Zhòng,
was the wife of the Marquis of Qí,
said:
"Please let Zhòng have an audience."
Zǐjiāzǐ then led the lord out.
B10.27.8 In the twelfth month,
Jì's Jí Qín delivered the feudal lords' garrison troops to Zhōu,
the people of Lǔ declined due to difficulties.
A10.28 "The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Twenty-eighth Year of Duke Zhāo"
A10.28.1 In the twenty-eighth year, in spring,
in the king's third month,
Duke Dào of Cáo was buried.
A10.28.2 The duke went to Jìn,
and halted at Gānhóu.
A10.28.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Bǐngxū,
Duke Bó Níng of Zhèng died.
A10.28.4 In the sixth month,
Duke Dìng of Zhèng was buried.
A10.28.5 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Guǐsì,
Viscount Níng of Téng died.
A10.28.6 In winter,
Duke Dào of Téng was buried.
B10.28 "The Commentary of Zuo: The Twenty-eighth Year of Duke Zhāo"
B10.28.1 In the twenty-eighth year, in spring,
the duke went to Jìn,
intending to go to Gānhóu.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"When one seeks something from others,
and yet settles into comfort,
who will pity him?
He should go to the border."
The duke did not listen,
and sent a request to Jìn to welcome him.
The people of Jìn said:
"Heaven has brought disaster upon Lǔ,
and our lord lingers in distress abroad,
yet our lord has not sent a single messenger to humbly visit us,
but instead settled comfortably with his maternal uncle's state,
should we also send to welcome our lord?"
They made the duke return to the border,
and then welcomed him.
B10.28.2 Jìn's Qí Shèng and Wū Zāng exchanged wives.
Qí Yíng was about to arrest them,
and consulted Simǎ Shūyóu.
Shūyóu said:
"The 'Book of Zhèng' says:
'Those who hate the upright and detest the correct,
are indeed numerous.'
When there is no dao established,
you, sir, should fear not escaping harm.
The 'Book of Songs' says:
'When the people are full of wickedness,
do not set up laws yourself.'
Let it be for now,
what do you think?"
Yíng said:
"The Qí clan is conducting a private punishment,
what does the state have to do with it?"
So he arrested them.
Qí Shèng bribed Xún Lì,
Xún Lì spoke on his behalf to the Marquis of Jìn.
The Marquis of Jìn arrested Qí Yíng.
Qí Yíng's retainer said:
"Since we will all die equally,
we would rather let our lord hear of the deaths of Shèng and Zāng to find satisfaction."
So they killed them.
In summer, in the sixth month,
Jìn killed Qí Yíng and Yáng Shíwǒ.
Shíwǒ
was a partisan of Qí Yíng,
and assisted in the disorder,
so they killed him,
then exterminated the Qí clan
and the Yángshé clan.
Earlier,
Shūxiàng wanted to marry a woman from Shēngōng Wúchén's clan,
but his mother wanted him to marry a woman from her own clan.
Shūxiàng said:
"My mother has many relatives but few concubines,
I take warning from my maternal uncle's clan."
His mother said:
"Zǐ Líng's wife killed three husbands,
one lord, and one son,
and caused the loss of one state and two ministers,
should one not take warning from this?"
I have heard it said:
'Extreme beauty must be accompanied by extreme evil.'
This woman is the daughter of the junior concubine Yáozi of Duke Mù of Zhèng,
and the younger sister of Zǐhè.
Zǐhè died early,
leaving no heir,
and Heaven concentrated all this beauty in her.
Surely it will be through her that some great calamity will occur.
In ancient times, the clan of Yǒuréng had a daughter
with jet-black hair,
and of surpassing beauty;
her complexion was so radiant it could reflect light like a mirror.
She was named Xuánqī.
The Music Master Hòukuí took her as his wife,
and she bore Bófēng,
who truly had the heart of a pig:
insatiably greedy and avaricious,
boundlessly cruel and resentful.
He was called Fēngshǐ (the Great Boar).
Hòuyì of Yǒuqióng destroyed him,
and thus Kuí received no sacrifices.
Moreover, the downfalls of the three dynasties (Xià, Shāng, Zhōu) and the dismissal of Gòngzǐ (Shēnshēng of Jìn)
were all due to such things (i.e., beautiful women).
Why should you, sir, wish to have anything to do with her?
Now, the possession of a woman of extraordinary beauty
is sufficient to change a man.
Unless one is virtuous and righteous,
it is certain to bring disaster."
Shūxiàng was afraid
and did not dare to take her.
Duke Píng forced him to take her,
and she bore Bóshí.
When Bóshí was first born,
the mother of Zǐróng (Shūxiàng's mother) ran to tell her mother-in-law,
saying:
"The wife of the elder younger uncle (Shūxiàng's wife) has borne a son."
Her mother-in-law went to see him.
When she reached the hall,
she heard his cry and turned back,
saying:
"This is the voice of a jackal or wolf.
A wolf cub has the heart of a wild beast.
If not this one,
then no one will bring ruin to the Yángshé clan."
Thereupon she did not look at him.
B10.28.3 In autumn,
Hán Xuānzǐ of Jìn died.
Wèi Xiànzǐ took charge of the government.
He divided the lands of the Qí clan into seven counties,
and divided the lands of the Yángshé clan into three counties.
Sīmǎ Mímóu was made Administrator of Wū,
Jiǎ Xīn was made Administrator of Qí,
Sīmǎ Wū was made Administrator of Pínglíng,
Wèi Wù was made Administrator of Gěngyáng,
Zhī Xúwú was made Administrator of Túshuǐ,
Hán Gù was made Administrator of Mǎshǒu,
Mèng Bǐng was made Administrator of Yú,
Lè Xiāo was made Administrator of Tóngdī,
Zhào Cháo was made Administrator of Píngyáng,
and Liáo Ān was made Administrator of Yángshì.
It was said that Jiǎ Xīn and Sīmǎ Wū
had rendered service to the royal house, therefore they were promoted;
it was said that Zhī Xúwú, Zhào Cháo, Hán Gù, and Wèi Wù
were younger sons who had not failed in their duties and were able to preserve their inheritances;
the other four men
all received their counties and then were presented to Wèizi (Wèi Xiànzǐ),
having been promoted for their worthiness.
Wèizi said to Chéng Tuán:
"I have given Wù a county.
Will people think I am showing favoritism?"
He replied:
"Why would they?
Wù's character is such that
he does not forget his lord even when far away,
and does not press his peers when near;
in the face of profit he thinks of righteousness, in straitened circumstances he thinks of purity;
he has a steadfast heart and no dissolute conduct.
Even if you give him a county,
is it not indeed fitting?
In former times, King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
and brilliantly possessed all under Heaven.
Among the states he enfeoffed, fifteen were held by his brothers,
and forty were held by those of the Jī surname.
In all cases, he promoted his relatives.
Now, promotion has no other principle
than that goodness should be the criterion.
Whether close or distant, it is the same.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Only this King Wén,
God examined his heart.
He rectified his virtuous fame,
so that his virtue could shine forth.
He could shine forth and distinguish categories,
he could be a leader and a ruler.
Ruling over this great state,
he could be compliant and could follow.
Following after King Wén,
his virtue knew no regret.
Having received God's blessings,
he extended them to his sons and grandsons.'
'The mind's ability to control what is right is called examination (dù).'
'Virtue being correct and responding harmoniously is called rectification (mò).'
'Shining upon the four quarters is called shining forth (míng).'
'Diligently bestowing without selfishness is called distinguishing categories (lèi).'
'Instructing without weariness is called leadership (zhǎng).'
'Rewarding with bounty and punishing with awe is called rulership (jūn).'
'Being kind and harmonious, universally obeyed, is called compliance (shùn).'
'Choosing the good and following it is called following (bǐ).'
'Ordering Heaven and Earth is called culture (wén).'
When these nine virtues are without fault,
in undertaking affairs there is no regret.
Therefore, one inherits Heaven's blessings,
and sons and grandsons rely on them.
My lord's promotions
are close to cultured virtue.
Their influence will be far-reaching indeed!"
When Jiǎ Xīn was about to go to his county,
he went to see Wèizi.
Wèizi said:
"Come, Xīn!
In former times, Shūxiàng went to Zhèng.
Zōng Miè was ugly,
and wishing to observe Shūxiàng,
he followed among those who were collecting the vessels
and went,
standing below the hall.
With a single excellent remark,
Shūxiàng, who was about to drink,
hearing it,
said:
'This must be Zōng Míng!'
He descended,
took his hand and led him up,
saying:
'In former times, there was an ugly Grand Master Jiǎ
who took a wife of great beauty.
For three years she neither spoke nor laughed.
He took her driving to the marshlands,
shot a pheasant,
and got it.
Only then did his wife begin to laugh and speak.
Grand Master Jiǎ said:
"Ability is something one cannot do without.
Had I not been able to shoot,
you, madam, would never have spoken or laughed!"
Now you, sir, are not impressive in youth.
If you, sir, had not spoken,
I would have nearly missed knowing you.
That one cannot do without speaking is thus!'
Thereupon they became as old friends.
Now you have rendered service to the royal house,
therefore I have promoted you.
Go forth!
Be reverent!
Do not let your efforts decline!"
Zhòngní (Confucius), hearing of Wèizi's promotions,
considered them righteous,
saying:
"In close relations, he did not neglect his kin;
in distant relations, he did not neglect promotion.
This may be called righteous."
He also heard of his charge to Jiǎ Xīn,
and considered it loyal,
saying:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'Ever accord with the Mandate,
and seek much happiness for yourself.'
This is loyalty.
Wèizi's promotions were righteous,
and his charge was loyal.
Will he not long have descendants in the state of Jìn!"
B10.28.4 In winter,
a man of Gěngyáng was involved in a lawsuit.
Wèi Wù was unable to decide it,
and so submitted the case upward.
The senior branch of the clan offered a troupe of female musicians as a bribe,
and Wèizi was about to accept it.
Wèi Wù said to Yán Mò
and Nǚ Kuān:
"Our master is known among the feudal lords for not accepting bribes.
If he accepts from the man of Gěngyáng,
there could be no greater bribery.
You gentlemen must remonstrate!"
They both promised.
After retiring from court,
they waited in the courtyard.
When the food was brought in,
Wèizi summoned them.
Before the dishes were set out,
they sighed three times.
After they had eaten,
he had them sit.
Wèizi said:
"I have heard from my uncles,
the proverb says:
'Only when eating does one forget sorrow.'
Yet you, my lord, sighed three times during the meal,
why is that?"
They replied in unison:
"Someone gave us two humble men wine,
and we did not eat in the evening.
When the food first arrived,
we feared it would not be enough,
hence we sighed.
Midway through the meal,
we reproached ourselves, saying:
'How could the general's food be insufficient?'
Hence we sighed again.
When the meal was finished,
we wished that the bellies of humble men could be like the hearts of gentlemen,
satisfied and content."
Xiànzǐ declined the gift from the man of Gěngyáng.
A10.29 《The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 29 of Duke Zhāo》
A10.29.1 In the twenty-ninth year, in spring,
the duke arrived from Gānhóu,
and resided in Yùn.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gāo Zhāng to console the duke.
A10.29.2 The duke went to Jìn,
and halted at Gānhóu.
A10.29.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
Shū Yì died.
A10.29.4 In autumn, in the seventh month.
A10.29.5 In winter, in the tenth month,
Yùn fell.
B10.29 《The Commentary of Zuǒ, Year 29 of Duke Zhāo》
B10.29.1 In the twenty-ninth year, in spring,
the duke arrived from Gānhóu,
and stayed in Yùn.
The Marquis of Qí sent Gāo Zhāng to console the duke,
addressing him as "Lord."
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"Qí is belittling you, my lord,
you are only being humiliated here."
The duke went to Gānhóu.
B10.29.2 In the third month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
in the capital, Zhào Bó Yíng, Yǐnshì Gù, and the son of Yuán Bó Lǔ were killed.
When Yǐn Gù returned,
a woman encountered him in the outskirts of Zhōu,
reproached him,
saying:
"When at home, you incite others to cause trouble,
when traveling, you return after a few days,
this man,
will his life exceed three years?"
In summer, in the fifth month, on the day Gēngyín,
Prince Zhào Chē entered Liè to rebel,
Yīn Bùnìng defeated him.
B10.29.3 Píngzǐ each year bought horses,
prepared clothing and shoes for the attendants,
and sent them to Gānhóu.
The duke seized the man who delivered the horses,
sold him,
and then the horses were no longer sent.
The Marquis of Wèi came to present his carriage horses,
named Qǐfú,
which fell into a pit and died.
The duke intended to make a coffin for it.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"The attendants are suffering,
please let them eat it."
So they wrapped it in a curtain.
The duke bestowed a lamb-fur robe upon Gōng Yǎn,
and sent him to present a dragon-patterned jade to the Marquis of Qí,
and then presented the lamb-fur robe.
The Marquis of Qí was pleased,
and gave him Yánggǔ.
When Gōng Yǎn and Gōng Wéi were born,
their mothers went out together.
Gōng Yǎn was born first.
Gōng Wéi's mother said:
"Since we went out together,
let us announce it together."
After three days,
Gōng Wéi was born.
His mother announced it first,
so Gōng Wéi became the elder brother.
The duke privately rejoiced over Yánggǔ,
and reflected on Lǔ,
saying:
"Wùrén caused this disaster.
Moreover, being born later yet becoming the elder brother,
this falsehood has lasted long."
So he deposed him,
and made Gōng Yǎn the crown prince.
B10.29.4 In autumn,
a dragon appeared in the outskirts of Jiàng.
Wèi Xiànzǐ asked Cài Mò, saying:
"I have heard that,
among creatures, none is wiser than the dragon,
because it cannot be captured alive,
it is called wise,
is this true?"
He replied:
"It is actually humans who are not wise,
not that the dragon is truly wise.
In ancient times, dragons were kept,
so there were the Huànlóng clan in the state,
and the Yùlóng clan."
Xiànzǐ said:
"These two clans,
I have also heard of them,
but do not know the reason,
what does this mean?"
He replied:
"Formerly, there was Liào Shū'ān,
who had a descendant named Dǒng Fù,
who truly loved dragons,
and could seek their desires to feed them,
many dragons came to him,
so he tamed and kept dragons,
to serve Emperor Shùn,
the emperor bestowed upon him the surname Dǒng,
the clan name Huànlóng,
enfeoffed him at Zōngchuān,
the Zōngyí clan are his descendants.
Thus, the house of Emperor Shùn for generations kept dragons.
By the time of Kǒng Jiǎ of the Xià dynasty,
he was favored by the emperor,
the emperor bestowed upon him riding dragons,
two from the Hé River and two from the Hàn River,
each male and female.
Kǒng Jiǎ could not feed them,
and had not obtained the Huànlóng clan.
After the decline of the Táotáng clan,
there was Liú Lěi,
who learned dragon-taming from the Huànlóng clan,
to serve Kǒng Jiǎ,
and could feed them.
The Xià sovereign praised him,
and bestowed the clan name Yùlóng.
He replaced the descendants of Shǐwéi.
One female dragon died,
he secretly made it into minced meat to feed the Xià sovereign.
The Xià sovereign enjoyed it,
and later sent for more.
Fearing, he moved to Lǔxiàn,
the Fàn clan are his descendants."
Xiànzǐ said:
"Why are there none now?"
He replied:
"For all things,
there are officials in charge,
officials cultivate their methods,
and think of them morning and night.
Once they neglect their duties,
death befalls them.
Losing office means losing sustenance.
Officials diligently attend to their duties,
then those things appear.
If they are neglected and abandoned,
things hide and lie low,
depressed and unable to thrive.
Thus, there are officials of the five elements,
these are called the five offices,
they actually received surnames and clans,
were enfeoffed as high dukes,
and worshipped as noble spirits.
The sacrifices to the soil and grain and the five sacrifices,
are revered and upheld.
The wood official is called Gōumáng,
the fire official is called Zhùróng,
the metal official is called Rùshōu,
the water official is called Xuánmíng,
the earth official is called Hòutǔ.
The dragon,
is a creature of water,
the water official has been abandoned,
hence dragons cannot be captured alive.
Otherwise,
the Zhōuyì has it:
in the Qián hexagram changing to Gòu,
it says
'hidden dragon, do not act';
its Tóngrén hexagram says
'dragon appearing in the field';
its Dàyǒu hexagram says
'flying dragon in the sky';
its Guài hexagram says
'arrogant dragon has regret',
The Kūn hexagram ䷁ says,
'Seeing a flock of dragons without a head,
auspicious.'
The Kūn hexagram changing to the Bō hexagram ䷖ says,
'Dragons fight in the wilderness.'
If one does not see them morning and evening,
who can perceive such things?"
Xiànzǐ said,
"The sacrifices to the spirits of the land and grain and the five sacrifices,
to which clans' five officials do they belong?"
He replied,
"Shàohàoshì had four younger brothers,
named Zhòng, Gāi, Xiū, and Xī,
who truly mastered metal, wood, and water.
He appointed Zhòng as Jùmáng,
Gāi as Rùshōu,
and Xiū and Xī as Xuánmíng.
They never neglected their duties,
and thus brought prosperity to Qióngsāng.
These are three of the sacrifices.
Zhuānxūshì had a son named Lí,
who became Zhùróng;
Gònggōngshì had a son named Gōulóng,
who became Hòutǔ.
These are two of the sacrifices.
Hòutǔ is the spirit of the land;
Jì
is the overseer of the fields.
The son of Yǒulièshānshì, named Zhù, became Jì,
and was sacrificed to from the Xià dynasty and earlier.
Zhōu's Qì also became Jì,
and has been sacrificed to since the Shāng dynasty."
B10.29.5 In winter,
Jìn's Zhào Yǎng and Xún Yín led troops to build walls at the banks of the Rǔ River,
then levied a drum of iron from the state of Jìn,
to cast a penal cauldron,
inscribing upon it the penal code composed by Fàn Xuānzǐ.
Zhòngní said,
"Jìn is likely to perish!
It has lost its proper measure.
The state of Jìn should uphold the laws and measures received from Táng Shū,
to govern its people,
with the ministers and grandees maintaining them in order.
Thus, the people are able to respect their superiors,
and the superiors are able to preserve their estates.
When superiors and inferiors do not transgress,
this is what is called proper measure.
Duke Wén therefore established the office of the Zhízhì,
and created the laws of Bèilú,
thereby becoming the leader of the covenant.
Now, abandoning this measure,
and casting a penal cauldron,
the people will look to the cauldron,
how then will they respect their superiors?
What estates will the superiors preserve?
When superiors and inferiors lack order,
how can the state be governed?
Moreover, Xuānzǐ's penal code
was established during the muster at Yí,
a product of Jìn's disordered governance.
How can it be taken as law?"
Cài's historian Mò said,
"The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans are likely to perish!
Zhōngháng Yín is a lower minister,
yet he interferes with the orders of his superiors,
presumptuously creating penal vessels,
making them the law of the state.
This is to legalize villainy.
Moreover, he involves the Fàn clan in this,
changing it,
leading to their ruin.
It will also affect the Zhào clan,
for Zhào Měng participated in it.
However, he had no alternative,
if he cultivates virtue,
he may avoid calamity."
A10.30 The Classic of Duke Zhāo's Thirtieth Year
A10.30.1 In the thirtieth year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the duke was at Gānhóu.
A10.30.2 In summer, in the sixth month, on the Gēngchén day,
the Marquis of Jìn, Qùjí, died.
A10.30.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
the funeral of Jìn's Duke Qǐng was held.
A10.30.4 In winter, in the twelfth month,
Wú destroyed Xú,
and Xú's ruler, Zhāngyǔ, fled to Chǔ.
B10.30 The Commentary of Duke Zhāo's Thirtieth Year
B10.30.1 In the thirtieth year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the duke was at Gānhóu.
The reason for not first recording Yùn and Gānhóu
is not due to the duke,
but to indicate his fault.
B10.30.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
Jìn's Duke Qǐng died.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
the funeral was held.
Zhèng's Yóu Jí came to offer condolences,
and also attended the funeral.
Wèi Xiànzǐ sent Shì Jǐngbó to question him,
saying,
"At the funeral of Duke Dào,
Zǐxī offered condolences,
and Zǐjiǎo attended the funeral.
Now you alone perform both duties,
why is this?"
He replied,
"The reason the feudal lords submit to the ruler of Jìn
is due to ritual.
Ritual means
the small serving the great and the great cherishing the small.
Serving the great lies in fulfilling their seasonal commands,
cherishing the small lies in sympathizing with their lacks.
Our humble state lies between great states,
fulfilling its tribute duties,
and preparing against unforeseen calamities.
How could we forget to fulfill commands?
According to the former kings' regulations:
at the funerals of feudal lords,
a knight offers condolences,
and a grandee attends the funeral.
Only for joyous occasions, diplomatic visits, feasts, and military affairs are ministers sent.
In the funeral affairs of Jìn,
when our humble state is at leisure,
our former rulers have assisted in holding the funeral cords.
If we are not at leisure,
even knights
and grandees may not be available in full number.
The grace of a great state
should also rejoice in our added efforts,
and not reproach our deficiencies,
clearly understanding our situation,
accepting what is prepared,
as is proper according to ritual.
At the funeral of King Líng,
our former ruler Duke Jiǎn was in Chǔ,
and our former grandee Yìn Duàn actually went,
—he was a junior minister of our humble state.
The king's officials did not reproach,
sympathizing with our lack.
Now the grandee says,
'Why do you not follow the old ways?'
The old ways sometimes had more, sometimes less,
I do not know which to follow.
If we follow the more,
our ruler is young and weak,
and thus unable to fulfill it.
If we follow the less,
then I, Jí, am here.
I leave it to the grandee to consider!"
The men of Jìn could not refute him.
B10.30.3 The ruler of Wú ordered the men of Xú to seize Yǎnyú,
and the men of Zhōngwú to seize Zhúyōng.
The two princes fled to Chǔ.
The ruler of Chǔ generously enfeoffed them,
and settled their migration,
sending the Supervisor of Horses, Dàxīn, to welcome the princes of Wú,
and settling them at Yǎng.
Yǒuyǐn Rán
and Left Marshal Shěn Yǐnxū built walls for them;
they took lands from Chéngfù and Hú to give to them,
intending to use them to harm Wú.
Zǐxī remonstrated, saying,
"Wú Guāng has newly obtained the state,
and is close to his people,
treating them like his children,
sharing hardships with them,
and intends to employ them.
If we pacify our borders,
and make them submit softly,
we should still fear their arrival.
Now we strengthen their enemies,
thereby greatly angering them,
is this not unacceptable?
Wú
are descendants of the Zhōu,
but were abandoned by the seaside,
not communicating with the Jī clan.
Now they have begun to grow great,
comparable to the various Huá states.
Guāng is also very cultured,
and will align himself with the former kings.
We do not know whether Heaven intends to make him tyrannical,
causing the destruction of Wú and the enlargement of different surnames,
or whether it will ultimately bless Wú.
The outcome is not far off.
Why do we not simply rely on our ghosts and spirits,
and pacify our clans and surnames,
awaiting the outcome?
Why must we stir up trouble ourselves?"
The king did not listen.
B10.30.4 The Lord of Wú was enraged.
In winter, in the twelfth month,
the Lord of Wú seized the Lord of Zhōngwú.
He then attacked Xú,
damming up a mountain to flood it.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
he extinguished Xú.
Zhāngyǔ, the Lord of Xú, cut off his hair,
and leading his wife, went to meet the Lord of Wú.
The Lord of Wú offered condolences and sent him away,
ordering his close attendants to follow him.
He then fled to Chǔ.
Shěn Yínxū of Chǔ led troops to rescue Xú,
but did not arrive in time.
He then fortified the city of Yí,
and had the Lord of Xú reside there.
B10.30.5 The Lord of Wú asked Wǔ Yuán, saying:
"Earlier you spoke of attacking Chǔ.
I knew it was feasible,
but I feared they would send me to do it,
and I also disliked others claiming credit for my achievements.
Now I intend to claim it for myself.
What about attacking Chǔ?"
He replied:
"In Chǔ, those in power are many and at odds with each other;
none is fit to shoulder responsibility in times of trouble.
If we form three armies to harass them,
when one army arrives,
they will certainly all come out.
When they come out, we return;
when they return, we come out.
Chǔ will certainly be worn out on the roads.
Harass them repeatedly to exhaust them,
use many methods to mislead them.
Once they are exhausted, then follow up with our three armies,
and we will certainly achieve a great victory over them."
Hélú followed this advice,
and Chǔ from then on began to suffer.
A10.31 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year 31 of Duke Zhāo
A10.31.1 In the thirty-first year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the Duke was at Gānhóu.
A10.31.2 Jìsūn Yìrú met with Xún Lì of Jìn at Dílì.
A10.31.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on the Dīngsì day,
the Earl of Xuē, Gǔ, died.
A10.31.4 The Marquis of Jìn sent Xún Lì to offer condolences to the Duke at Gānhóu.
A10.31.5 In autumn,
the burial of Duke Xiàn of Xuē took place.
A10.31.6 In winter,
Hēigōng came fleeing, bringing Làn with him.
A10.31.7 In the twelfth month, on the Xīnhài day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
B10.31 The Commentary of Zuo, Year 31 of Duke Zhāo
B10.31.1 In the thirty-first year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the Duke was at Gānhóu.
This indicates he could not go either abroad or back to his state.
B10.31.2 The Marquis of Jìn intended to use troops to restore the Duke.
Fàn Xiànzǐ said:
"If we summon Jìsūn and he does not come,
then he truly shows himself disloyal.
After that, we attack him.
What about that?"
The men of Jìn summoned Jìsūn.
Xiànzǐ sent a private message to him,
saying:
"You must come.
I will ensure you come to no harm."
Jìsūn Yìrú met with Xún Lì of Jìn at Dílì.
Xún Lì said:
"My lord commanded me to say to you:
'Why did you drive out your lord?
Having a lord and not serving him
is subject to the constant punishments of Zhōu.
You should consider this!'"
Jìsūn, wearing a mourning cap
and hempen garments,
walked barefoot,
prostrated himself, and replied:
"To serve one's lord
is what a minister cannot but do.
How dare I evade the punishment decreed?
If my lord considers me guilty,
I beg to be imprisoned in Fèi,
to await my lord's investigation.
It is all as my lord wishes.
If, for the sake of my ancestors,
you do not cut off the Jì lineage,
but grant me death,
or if you neither kill me nor exile me,
that would be my lord's grace,
and I would die without decay.
If I could follow my lord and return,
that is certainly my wish.
How dare I harbor any other intention?"
In summer, in the fourth month,
Jìsūn followed Zhì Bó to Gānhóu.
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"My lord, go back with him.
If you cannot bear one moment of shame,
will you bear a lifetime of shame?"
The Duke said:
"Very well."
The attendants said:
"It rests on a single word.
My lord must drive him out!"
Xún Lì, on orders from the Marquis of Jìn, offered condolences to the Duke,
and said:
"My lord commanded me, in your name, to denounce Yìrú.
Yìrú did not dare flee death.
May my lord return!"
The Duke said:
"If my lord graciously remembers the friendship of my ancestors,
and extends it to this exile,
enabling me to return to sweep the ancestral temple and serve you,
then I cannot see that man.
If I ever see that man again,
may the River be my witness!"
Xún Lì covered his ears and ran off,
saying:
"My lord is fearful of being held guilty.
How dare I involve myself in the troubles of Lǔ!
I beg to report back to my lord."
Withdrawing, he said to Jìsūn:
"The Duke's anger has not abated.
You should return home for now to conduct the sacrifices."
Zǐjiāzǐ said:
"If my lord enters the Lǔ army with a single chariot,
Jìsūn is sure to return with you."
The Duke wished to follow this advice.
His attendants coerced the Duke,
and he was unable to return.
B10.31.3 The Earl of Xuē, Gǔ, died.
As he was an ally by covenant,
it is recorded.
B10.31.4 In autumn,
men of Wú invaded Chǔ,
attacked Yí,
and invaded Qián and Lù.
Shěn Yínxū of Chǔ led troops to rescue Qián,
and the Wú army withdrew.
The Chǔ army moved the people of Qián to Nángāng and then returned.
The Wú army besieged Xián.
The Left Minister of War, Xū, and the Right Minister of War, Jī, led troops to rescue Xián.
When they reached Yùzhāng,
the Wú army withdrew.
— — This was the beginning of the use of Zǐxū's strategies.
B10.31.5 In winter,
Hēigōng of Zhū came fleeing, bringing Làn with him.
Though a man of low rank, his name is recorded,
because of the importance attached to the territory.
The gentleman says:
"One cannot but be careful about names, is it not so?
There are cases where having a name is worse than having none.
To rebel, bringing territory,
even if the man is lowly,
the territory must be recorded,
and the man named.
In the end, it is unrighteous,
and cannot be erased.
Therefore, the gentleman, when acting, thinks of ritual;
when conducting himself, thinks of righteousness.
He does not turn aside for profit,
nor does he feel remorse over unrighteousness.
Some seek fame but do not attain it;
some wish to conceal their names, yet their names become illustrious.
This is to punish unrighteousness.
Qí Bào was Minister of Crime of Wèi,
a hereditary great officer.
Acting unrighteously,
he is recorded in the text as
'a robber'.
Shùqí of Zhū,
Móuyí of Jǔ,
and Hēigōng of Zhū, who left, bringing territory,
sought only sustenance,
not seeking fame.
Though lowly, they are necessarily recorded.
These two cases
serve to punish wantonness and remove greed.
If one endures hardship himself,
and through peril endangers his superiors,
yet his name becomes illustrious and widespread,
then men who stir up trouble will rush to do so.
If one steals a city and betrays his lord to seek great profit without gaining fame,
then greedy and reckless men will exert themselves for it.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals records Qí Bào as
'a robber',
and records the names of the three rebels,
to punish the unrighteous,
to censure evil and discourtesy,
this is its good intention.
Therefore it is said:
"The expressions of the Spring and Autumn Annals are subtle yet clear,
tactful yet discerning.
Those in high positions can make them manifest,
so that good men are encouraged,
and dissolute men are afraid,
hence the gentleman values them."
B10.31.6 In the twelfth month, on the Xīnhài day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
That night,
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ dreamed of a naked boy singing while turning around.
At dawn, he consulted the historian Mò about it,
saying:
"I had such a dream,
and now there is a solar eclipse,
what does it mean?"
He replied:
"Six years from now, in this month,
Wú will likely enter Yǐng,
but in the end will not conquer it.
The entry into Yǐng will certainly be on the Gēngchén day,
when the sun and moon are at the tail of Chén.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
the sun first showed an omen.
Fire overcomes metal,
therefore it will not conquer."
A10.32 The Classic of Duke Zhāo, Year 32
A10.32.1 In the thirty-second year, in spring,
the royal first month,
the duke was in Gānhóu.
A10.32.2 We took Kàn.
A10.32.3 In summer,
Wú attacked Yuè.
A10.32.4 In autumn, the seventh month.
A10.32.5 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Héjì met with Hán Bùxìn of Jìn,
Gāo Zhāng of Qí,
Zhòng Jī of Sòng,
Shìshū Shēn of Wèi,
Guó Cān of Zhèng,
men of Cáo,
men of Jǔ,
men of Xuē,
men of Qǐ,
and men of Xiǎozhū to fortify Chéngzhōu.
A10.32.6 In the twelfth month, on the Jǐwèi day,
the duke died in Gānhóu.
B10.32 The Commentary of Duke Zhāo, Year 32
B10.32.1 In the thirty-second year, in spring,
the royal first month,
the duke was in Gānhóu,
indicating that he could not handle affairs outside and inside,
nor could he employ his men.
B10.32.2 In summer,
Wú attacked Yuè,
this being the first use of troops against Yuè.
The historian Mò said:
"Within forty years,
Yuè will likely possess Wú!
Yuè has gained the year's influence, and Wú attacks it,
it will certainly suffer misfortune."
B10.32.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
the king sent Fù Xīn and Shí Zhāng to Jìn,
to request the fortification of Chéngzhōu.
The Son of Heaven said:
"Heaven has sent down calamity upon Zhōu,
causing my brothers all to have rebellious hearts,
bringing worry to my uncle.
My few close relatives, sons-in-law, and maternal uncles have had no leisure to settle,
for ten years now.
We have toiled at garrison duty for five years.
I myself have not forgotten it for a single day,
anxiously like a farmer hoping for the harvest,
waiting in fear for the time.
If my uncle would extend great kindness,
restore the achievements of the two Wén,
relieve the worries of the Zhōu house,
seek the blessings of King Wén and King Wǔ,
to solidify the alliance leader,
and proclaim and manifest a good name,
then I myself would have a great wish fulfilled.
In the past, King Chéng assembled the feudal lords to fortify Chéngzhōu,
making it the eastern capital,
to exalt civil virtue.
Now I wish to seek blessings and borrow the spiritual power from King Chéng,
to repair the walls of Chéngzhōu,
so that the garrison troops need not toil,
the feudal lords may be at peace,
and harmful elements be kept at a distance,
this is the strength of Jìn.
I entrust this to my uncle,
asking my uncle to seriously consider it,
so that I myself incur no resentment from the people,
and my uncle gains glory and merit,
which the former kings will reward."
Fàn Xiànzǐ said to Wèi Xiànzǐ:
"Rather than garrisoning Zhōu,
it is better to fortify it.
The Son of Heaven has indeed spoken,
even if there are later matters,
Jìn need not be involved, that is acceptable.
Following the king's command to relieve the feudal lords,
Jìn will have no worries,
if we do not attend to this,
then what else should we do?"
Wèi Xiànzǐ said:
"Good."
He sent Bó Yīn to reply, saying:
"The Son of Heaven has given a command,
how dare we not receive it and hasten to inform the feudal lords,
the speed or delay, the order of contributions,
lies in this."
In winter, in the eleventh month,
Wèi Shū of Jìn and Hán Bùxìn went to the capital,
assembled the great officers of the feudal lords at Díquán,
renewed the covenant,
and ordered the fortification of Chéngzhōu.
Wèizi faced south.
Wèi Biáoxī said:
"Wèizi will certainly have great misfortune.
To overstep his position and command great affairs,
is not his duty.
The Book of Songs says:
'Revere Heaven's anger,
dare not be frivolous or idle;
revere Heaven's change,
dare not gallop or drive.'
How much more dare he overstep his position to undertake great affairs?"
On the Jǐchǒu day,
Shì Mímóu planned the fortification of Chéngzhōu,
calculating the lengths in zhàng,
estimating heights and depths,
measuring thicknesses,
determining the depth of ditches,
assessing the earthworks,
discussing distances,
estimating the time required,
calculating labor and service,
considering materials,
recording provisions,
to order the labor from the feudal lords.
He assigned tasks and distributed measurements,
wrote them down and gave them to the commanders,
and presented them to Liúzǐ.
Hán Jiǎnzǐ oversaw it,
considering it an established order.
B10.32.4 In the twelfth month,
the duke fell ill,
and bestowed gifts on all the great officers,
but the great officers did not accept them.
He bestowed upon Zǐjiāzǐ a pair of tiger-shaped jades,
one ring, one disc,
and light garments,
and he accepted them.
Then all the great officers accepted their gifts.
On the Jǐwèi day,
the duke died.
Zǐjiāzǐ returned his gifts to the treasurer,
saying:
"I dared not disobey the lord's command."
All the great officers returned their gifts.
It is recorded
"the duke died in Gānhóu",
indicating he was not in his proper place.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked the historian Mò:
"The Jì clan expelled their lord,
yet the people submit to them,
and the feudal lords side with them;
the lord died abroad, and no one holds them guilty
for it."
He replied:
"In the birth of things, there are pairs, threes, fives, and assistants.
Thus heaven has the three luminaries,
earth has the five phases,
the body has left and right,
each has its mate,
the king has dukes,
feudal lords have ministers,
all have their assistants.
Heaven gave birth to the Jì clan,
to assist the lord of Lǔ,
and it has been a long time.
That the people submit to them,
is it not fitting!
The lords of Lǔ generation after generation followed their faults,
the Jì clan generation after generation cultivated their diligence,
The people have forgotten their ruler.
Even if he dies abroad,
who will pity him?
The altars of soil and grain have no constant worshipers,
rulers and ministers have no constant positions;
this has been so since ancient times.
Therefore, the *Book of Songs* says:
'High banks become valleys,
deep valleys become hills.'
The descendants of the three ancient sovereigns are now commoners—
this is known to you, my lord.
In the hexagrams of the *Book of Changes*,
when thunder rides over *Qián* (Heaven), it is called *Dà Zhuàng* (Great Strength)
which is the way of Heaven.
Formerly, Chéng Jì Yǒu
was the youngest son of Duke Huán
and the beloved son of Wén Jiāng.
When she first became pregnant, a divination was performed.
The diviner announced,
saying:
'He will be born with a fine reputation;
his name will be Yǒu,
and he will be a support to the ducal house.'
When he was born,
it was as the diviner had said:
there was a mark on his hand resembling the character
'Yǒu',
and so he was named accordingly.
Later, he achieved great merit for Lǔ,
and received Fèi as a high minister.
Down to Wénzǐ and Wǔzǐ,
each generation increased his estate,
without abandoning the old achievements.
When Duke Wén of Lǔ died,
Dōngmén Suì killed the rightful heir and established a concubine's son.
From then on, the ruler of Lǔ lost the state,
and governance lay with the Jì clan.
By this ruler's time, it has been four dukes.
If the people do not know their ruler,
how can he obtain the state?
Therefore, a ruler must be cautious with vessels and titles,
and must not lend them to others."
A11.1 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, First Year of Duke Dìng*
A11.1.1 First year, spring,
the royal first month.
A11.1.2 Third month,
a man of Jìn arrested Zhòng Jī of Sòng in the royal capital.
A11.1.3 Summer, sixth month, on the Guǐhài day,
the duke's coffin arrived from Gān Hóu.
A11.1.4 On the Wùchén day,
the duke took his position.
A11.1.5 Autumn, seventh month, on the Guǐsì day,
we buried our ruler, Duke Zhāo.
A11.1.6 Ninth month,
a great rain sacrifice was held.
A11.1.7 The Yáng temple was established.
A11.1.8 Winter, tenth month,
frost fell and killed the bean crops.
B11.1 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, First Year of Duke Dìng*
B11.1.1 In the first year, spring,
in the royal first month, on the Xīnsì day,
Wèi Shū of Jìn assembled the great officers of the various states at Díquán,
intending to wall the city of Chéngzhōu.
Master Wèi presided over the administration.
Biāo Xī of Wèi said:
"He is about to establish the Son of Heaven,
yet he changes positions to issue commands—
this is not righteous.
In great affairs, to violate righteousness
is certain to bring great calamity.
Even if Jìn does not lose the allegiance of the states,
Master Wèi will likely not escape!"
On this mission,
Wèi Xiànzǐ entrusted the duties to Hán Jiǎnzǐ and Yuán Shòuguò,
and went hunting at Dàlù,
where he set fire to the grasslands.
On his return,
he died at Níng.
Fàn Xiànzǐ removed his outer coffin of cypress wood,
because he had not yet reported back on his mission when he went hunting.
Mèng Yìzǐ joined in the work of walling Chéngzhōu.
On the Gēngyín day,
the planting of stakes began.
Zhòng Jī of Sòng refused to accept his assigned task,
saying:
"Téng, Xuē, and Ní
are our laborers."
The steward of Xuē said:
"Sòng acts without principle,
cutting off our small state from Zhōu,
and forcing us to go to Chǔ.
Therefore, we have always followed Sòng.
Duke Wén of Jìn made the covenant at Jiàntǔ,
saying:
'All of us who are in this alliance
shall each resume our former duties.'
If we follow the covenant of Jiàntǔ,
or if we follow Sòng,
we will obey orders."
Zhòng Jī said:
"The covenant of Jiàntǔ is indeed so."
The steward of Xuē said:
"Xuē's august ancestor Xī Zhōng dwelt in Xuē,
serving as the Director of Chariots for the Xià.
Xī Zhōng moved to Pī,
and Zhòng Huī dwelt in Xuē,
serving as the Left Minister to Tāng.
If we resume our former duties,
we shall receive appointments from the royal court.
Why then should we labor for the feudal lords?"
Zhòng Jī said:
"The Three Dynasties each had different arrangements;
how can Xuē claim to have former duties?
To labor for Sòng
is also your duty."
Shì Mímóu said:
"Jìn's administrator is new to his post;
you, sir, should for now accept the task.
When you return,
I will look into the old archives."
Zhòng Jī said:
"Even if you forget it,
will the spirits of the mountains and rivers forget it?"
Shì Bó was angered,
and said to Hán Jiǎnzǐ:
"Xuē appeals to men,
Sòng appeals to ghosts.
Sòng's offense is great.
Moreover, having no argument himself,
he tries to suppress me with spirits—
this is to deceive me.
'To invite favor is to invite insult'—
this is what it means.
Zhòng Jī must be punished."
Thereupon, they arrested Zhòng Jī and took him back.
In the third month,
they sent him to the royal capital.
The walling was completed in thirty days,
and then the guarding troops of the various states were sent home.
Gāo Zhāng of Qí arrived late,
not joining the other lords.
Nǚ Shūkuān of Jìn said:
"Cháng Hóng of Zhōu and Gāo Zhāng of Qí will both not escape misfortune.
Cháng Shū opposes Heaven,
Master Gāo opposes men.
What Heaven would ruin,
cannot be supported;
what the multitude does,
cannot be opposed."
B11.1.2 In summer,
Shūsūn Chéngzǐ went to Gān Hóu to meet the coffin of the duke.
Jìsūn said:
"Master Zǐjiā repeatedly spoke to me,
and never failed to match my intentions.
I wish to have him participate in governance;
you must detain him,
and moreover, listen to his counsel."
Master Zǐjiā did not see Shūsūn,
but changed the time for weeping.
Shūsūn requested to see Master Zǐjiā.
Master Zǐjiā declined,
saying:
"I, Jī, had not yet had an audience
when I followed the ruler out.
The ruler died without giving me orders,
and I, Jī, dare not have an audience."
Shūsūn sent a message to him, saying:
"Gōng Yǎn and Gōng Wéi truly caused the ministers to be unable to serve the ruler.
If the young lord Sòng presides over the altars of soil and grain,
that is the wish of the ministers.
As for all those who followed the ruler out and can return,
we will follow your decision.
The House of Zǐjiā has no heir;
Jìsūn wishes to have you participate in governance.
These are all Jìsūn's wishes,
which he has sent me to report."
He replied:
"If a ruler is to be established,
then there are the high ministers, great officers, and the divining tortoise-shell—
I, Jī, dare not presume to know.
As for those who followed the ruler,
those who left with their outward appearance,
may return;
those who left as enemies,
may depart."
If I were to flee,
then you, my lord, would know of my departure,
but not of my return;
I am about to escape."
When the funeral procession reached Huàituí,
Gōngzǐ Sòng entered first,
and all those who had followed the duke turned back from Huàituí.
B11.1.3 In the sixth month, on Guǐhài,
the duke's remains arrived from Gānhóu.
On Wùchén,
the duke ascended the throne.
Jì Sūn sent laborers to the burial grounds of the ducal house,
intending to dig a ditch around it.
Róng Jiā'é said:
"While he lived, you could not serve him;
now that he is dead, you would separate him from his ancestors—
is this to glorify yourself?
Even if you can bear to do this,
your descendants will surely be ashamed of it."
So he stopped.
Jì Sūn asked Róng Jiā'é:
"I wish to assign a posthumous title for our lord,
so that his descendants will know of it."
He replied:
"While he lived, you could not serve him;
now that he is dead, you would give him a bad name—
is this to show your sincerity?
What purpose would it serve?"
So he stopped.
B11.1.4 In autumn, the seventh month, on Guǐsì,
Duke Zhāo was buried south of the tomb path.
When Confucius served as Minister of Crime,
he had the ditch filled in and joined the tomb with the others.
B11.1.5 Because Duke Zhāo had been driven out,
Jì Píngzǐ prayed to Duke Yáng.
In the ninth month,
a temple to Duke Yáng was established.
B11.1.6 Zhōu's Duke Jiǎn of Gǒng discarded his own sons and younger brothers and favored employing outsiders.
A11.2 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year Two of Duke Dìng*
A11.2.1 In the second year, in spring,
the royal first month.
A11.2.2 In summer, the fifth month, on Rénchén,
the Pheasant Gate and its two watchtowers were destroyed by fire.
A11.2.3 In autumn,
the men of Chǔ attacked Wú.
A11.2.4 In winter, the tenth month,
the Pheasant Gate and its two watchtowers were newly built.
B11.2 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, Year Two of Duke Dìng*
B11.2.1 In the second year, in summer, the fourth month, on Xīnyǒu,
the sons and younger brothers of the Gǒng clan assassinated Duke Jiǎn.
B11.2.2 Tóng rebelled against Chǔ.
The viscount of Wú sent the Shūjiū clan to lure the men of Chǔ,
saying:
"If you bring an army to threaten us,
we will attack Tóng,
so that they will not be suspicious of us."
In autumn,
Chǔ's Náng Wǎ attacked Wú,
stationing his army at Yùzhāng.
The men of Wú displayed boats at Yùzhāng,
but secretly moved their army to Cháo.
In winter, the tenth month,
the army of Wú confronted the Chǔ army at Yùzhāng,
and defeated it.
Thereupon they besieged Cháo,
captured it,
and took Chǔ's Gōngzǐ Fán prisoner.
B11.2.3 Duke Zhuāng of Zhū drank with Yí Shègū,
and went out privately.
The gatekeeper asked him for meat,
and he seized the man's staff and beat him with it.
A11.3 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year Three of Duke Dìng*
A11.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
the royal first month,
the duke went to Jìn,
reached the Yellow River,
and then returned.
A11.3.2 In the second month, on Xīnmǎo,
the viscount of Zhū, Chuān, died.
A11.3.3 In summer, the fourth month.
A11.3.4 In autumn,
Duke Zhuāng of Zhū was buried.
A11.3.5 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Héjì and the viscount of Zhū made a covenant at Bá.
B11.3 *The Commentary of Zuǒ, Year Three of Duke Dìng*
B11.3.1 In the third year, in spring, the second month, on Xīnmǎo,
the viscount of Zhū was on the gate tower,
overlooking the courtyard.
The gatekeeper poured a bottle of water onto the courtyard,
and the viscount of Zhū saw it,
and became angry.
The gatekeeper said:
"Yí Shègū urinated here."
He ordered him seized.
When he was not found,
his anger increased,
and he threw himself onto his bed,
fell into the brazier coals,
was burned,
and subsequently died.
He was first buried with five chariots,
and five human sacrifices.
Duke Zhuāng was irritable and fond of cleanliness,
and so met this end.
B11.3.2 In autumn, the ninth month,
the men of Xiānyú defeated the Jìn army at Píngzhōng,
capturing Jìn's Guān Hǔ,
who had relied on his own courage.
B11.3.3 In winter,
a covenant was made at Tán, to restore good relations with Zhū.
B11.3.4 Marquis Zhāo of Cài brought two jade pendants and two fur robes to Chǔ,
and presented one pendant and one robe to King Zhāo.
King Zhāo wore them
when feasting the marquis of Cài.
The marquis of Cài also wore one of his.
Zǐ Cháng wanted them,
but he did not give them,
and so was detained for three years.
Duke Chéng of Táng went to Chǔ,
having two Sùshuǎng horses;
Zǐ Cháng wanted them,
but he did not give them,
and so was also detained for three years.
Some men of Táng plotted together,
asking to replace the earlier attendants,
and this was permitted.
They gave wine to the earlier attendants,
got them drunk,
stole the horses, and presented them to Zǐ Cháng.
Zǐ Cháng sent the marquis of Táng back.
They bound themselves and went to the Minister of Justice,
saying:
"Because of our lord's fondness for these horses,
he was endangered,
and the state was abandoned.
We, your ministers, ask to assist our lord's wife to compensate for the horses,
and we will surely do so."
The marquis of Táng said:
"This was my fault.
Do not disgrace yourselves, my ministers!"
And he rewarded them all.
When the men of Cài heard of this,
they insisted,
and presented the pendant to Zǐ Cháng.
Zǐ Cháng, at court,
saw the followers of the marquis of Cài,
and ordered the officials:
"The marquis of Cài has been here long,
and the officials have not provided for him.
If the farewell ceremony is not completed tomorrow,
you will die."
The marquis of Cài returned,
and when he reached the Hàn River,
he took the jade and sank it,
saying:
"If I ever cross the Hàn River and go south again,
may I be like this great river!"
The marquis of Cài went to Jìn,
offering his son Yuán and the sons of his high officials as hostages,
and requested an attack on Chǔ.
A11.4 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Year Four of Duke Dìng*
A11.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
the royal second month, on Guǐsì,
the marquis of Chén, Wú, died.
A11.4.2 In the third month,
the duke met with Prince Liú,
the marquis of Jìn,
the duke of Sòng,
the marquis of Cài,
the marquis of Wèi,
the viscount of Chén,
the earl of Zhèng,
the baron of Xǔ,
the earl of Cáo,
the viscount of Jǔ,
the viscount of Zhū,
the viscount of Dùn,
the viscount of Hú,
the viscount of Téng,
the earl of Xuē,
the earl of Qǐ,
the viscount of Xiǎozhū,
and Guó Xià of Qí at Shàolíng,
to invade Chǔ.
A11.4.3 In summer, in the fourth month, on Gēngchén,
Gōngsūn Xìng of Cài led troops to destroy Shěn,
took Shěnzǐ Jiā back,
and killed him.
A11.4.4 In the fifth month,
the Duke and the feudal lords made a covenant at Gāoyòu.
A11.4.5 The Earl of Qǐ, Chéng, died at the meeting.
A11.4.6 In the sixth month,
Duke Huì of Chén was buried.
A11.4.7 Xǔ moved to Róngchéng.
A11.4.8 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the Duke arrived from the meeting.
A11.4.9 Liǔ Juǎn died.
A11.4.10 Duke Dào of Qǐ was buried.
A11.4.11 The men of Chǔ laid siege to Cài.
A11.4.12 Shì Yǎng of Jìn and
Kǒng Yǔ of Wèi led troops to attack Xiānyú.
A11.4.13 Duke Wén of Liǔ was buried.
A11.4.14 In winter, in the eleventh month, on Gēngwǔ,
the Marquis of Cài, with the Viscount of Wú, fought the men of Chǔ at Bǎijǔ,
and the army of Chǔ was utterly defeated.
Náng Wǎ of Chǔ fled to Zhèng.
On Gēngchén,
Wú entered Yǐng.
B11.4 The Fourth Year of Duke Dìng - Commentary
B11.4.1 In spring, in the third month of the fourth year,
Duke Wén of Liǔ assembled the feudal lords at Shàolíng,
to plan an attack on Chǔ.
Xún Yín of Jìn sought goods from the Marquis of Cài,
but did not get them.
He spoke to Fàn Xiànzǐ, saying:
"Our state is in peril,
and the feudal lords are disloyal.
To use them to attack the enemy,
is that not difficult?
The floodwaters are just descending,
and epidemics are arising.
Zhōngshān is not submissive.
To abandon the covenant and incur resentment,
will do no harm to Chǔ,
and we will lose Zhōngshān.
It would be better to decline the Marquis of Cài."
Since we came from Fāngchéng,
we have not been able to achieve our aims against Chǔ,
and have only brought toil upon ourselves."
So they declined the Marquis of Cài.
The men of Jìn borrowed feathered banners from Zhèng,
and the men of Zhèng gave them.
The next day,
some attached them to their flags for the meeting.
Jìn thereby lost the feudal lords.
When they were about to meet,
Zǐháng Jìngzǐ of Wèi spoke to Duke Líng, saying:
"Meetings and assemblies are difficult;
there are many contentious words, and no one to manage them.
Let Zhù Tuó attend!"
The Duke said:
"Good."
So he sent Zǐyú.
Zǐyú declined,
saying:
"I stretch my four limbs
to carry out my old duties,
and still fear I will not suffice and will trouble the penal statutes.
If I also take on a second duty,
I will be inviting great crime.
Moreover, the Invocator
is a regular subordinate of the altars of soil and grain.
If the altars of soil and grain do not move,
the Invocator does not leave the borders—
such is the regulation of the office.
When the ruler marches with the army,
purifies the altar of soil and smears the drums with blood,
the Invocator accompanies him bearing [the tablets],
and thus leaves the borders.
But in matters of friendly visits,
when the ruler goes, a division follows;
when a minister goes, a brigade follows.
I have nothing to do with it."
The Duke said:
"Go!"
When they reached Gāoyòu,
they were about to give Cài precedence over Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi sent Zhù Tuó to speak privately with Cháng Hóng, saying:
"I have heard it on the roads,
but do not know if it is true.
If I hear that Cài is to precede Wèi,
is it true?"
Cháng Hóng said:
"It is true. Càishū
was the elder brother of Kāngshū.
For him to precede Wèi,
is that not permissible?"
Zǐyú said:
"Looking at it from the perspective of the former kings,
they valued virtue.
In the past, King Wǔ conquered Shāng,
and King Chéng settled it.
He selected and established those of illustrious virtue
to be a hedge and screen for Zhōu.
Therefore, the Duke of Zhōu assisted the royal house
and governed all under heaven.
With Zhōu, he was harmonious.
He allotted to the Duke of Lǔ the great carriage, the great banner,
the huáng jade of the Xiàhòu clan,
the Fányuò bow of Fēngfǔ,
and six clans of the Yīn people:
the Tiáo, Xú, Xiāo, Suǒ, Chángsháo, and Wěisháo clans.
He made them lead their main lineages,
gather their branch clans,
and lead their subordinate
multitudes, taking the Duke of Zhōu as their model.
They thereby received their charge from Zhōu.
He made them perform duties in Lǔ
to display the illustrious virtue of the Duke of Zhōu.
He allotted to them lands, fields, and appanages; Invocators, Ancestral Temple officers, Diviners, and Scribes;
full ritual paraphernalia and canonical writings;
officials and ritual vessels.
With the people of Shāngyǎn,
he charged them with the "Bóqín" and enfeoffed them at the ruins of Shàohào.
He allotted to Kāngshū the great carriage, the lesser white silk,
the crimson pennant, the feathered banners, and the Dàlǚ bell,
and seven clans of the Yīn people:
the Táo, Shī, and Fán clans,
the Qí, Fán, Jī,
and Zhōngkuí clans.
The boundaries of his territory
stretched from south of Wǔfù to the northern border of Pǔtián.
He took lands from Yǒuyán to supply the royal duties;
he took from the eastern capital of Xiàngtǔ to meet the king's eastern hunt.
Dān Jì presented the soil,
Táo Shū presented the people,
and he was charged with the "Kānggào" and enfeoffed at the ruins of Yīn.
For both, he initiated governance with Shāng institutions,
but demarcated boundaries with Zhōu's measures.
He allotted to Tángshū the great carriage, the drum of Mìxū,
the armor of Quègǒng, and the Gūxiǎn bell,
nine lineages of the Huái surname,
and five official directors.
He charged him with the "Tánggào" and enfeoffed him at the ruins of Xià,
initiating governance with Xià institutions,
and demarcating boundaries with the measures of the Róng.
These three were all younger brothers,
yet they had fine virtue.
Therefore, he distinguished them with the allotment of things.
Otherwise,
among the elder brothers of King Wén, King Wǔ, King Chéng, and King Kāng there were still many,
yet they did not receive these allotments—
it was simply because age was not valued.
Guǎn and Cài opened the way for Shāng,
plotting against the royal house.
The king thereupon killed Guǎnshū and banished Càishū,
with seven chariots and seventy foot soldiers.
His son, Cài Zhòng, reformed his conduct and followed virtue.
The Duke of Zhōu raised him up,
made him his own minister,
presented him to the king,
and charged him with Cài.
The charge document said:
'The king said:
"Hú!
Do not be like your father in disobeying the king's command!"'
How then can they make Cài precede Wèi?
King Wǔ had eight full brothers.
The Duke of Zhōu was Grand Steward,
Kāngshū was Minister of Justice,
Dān Jì was Minister of Works.
The five younger brothers had no office.
How could age have been valued?
Cáo
was a son of King Wén,
Jìn
was a son of King Wǔ.
Yet Cáo was a mere earl of the甸 region—
age was not valued.
If now you value it,
you go against the former kings.
Duke Wén of Jìn made the covenant at Jiàntǔ.
Duke Chéng of Wèi was not present,
but Yíshū,
his full brother,
still preceded Cài.
The covenant document said:
'The king says thus:
Jìn Chóng, Lǔ Shēn, Wèi Wǔ,
Cài Jiǎwǔ, Zhèng Jié, Qí Pān,
Sòng Wángchén, Jǔ Qī.'
The covenant is stored in the Zhōu court,
and can be reviewed.
If you, my lord, wish to restore the strategies of King Wén and King Wǔ,
yet do not rectify your virtue,
what is to be done?"
Cháng Hóng was pleased,
informed Liú Zǐ,
and plotted with Fàn Xiànzǐ.
As a result, they gave precedence to Marquis Wèi in the covenant.
B11.4.2 Upon returning from Zhàolíng,
Zǐ Dàshū of Zhèng died before reaching home.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ of Jìn attended his funeral,
deeply grieved,
and said:
"At the meeting at Huángfù,
the Master spoke to me nine words,
saying:
'Do not initiate disorder,
do not rely on wealth,
do not presume on favor,
do not oppose those in agreement,
do not be arrogant in ritual,
do not be proud of ability,
do not repeat anger,
do not plan what is contrary to virtue,
do not transgress what is contrary to righteousness.'"
B11.4.3 The people of Shěn did not attend the meeting at Zhàolíng,
so the people of Jìn ordered Cài to attack them.
In summer,
Cài destroyed Shěn.
In autumn,
Chǔ, because of Shěn,
besieged Cài.
Wǔ Yuán served as Wú's diplomatic officer to plot against Chǔ.
When Chǔ killed Xì Wǎn,
the Bó clan fled.
Pǐ, grandson of Bó Zhōulí, became Wú's Grand Steward to plot against Chǔ.
Since King Zhāo of Chǔ ascended the throne,
there was not a year without Wú armies.
The Marquis of Cài took advantage of this,
sending his son Qián and the sons of his senior officials as hostages to Wú.
In winter,
the Marquis of Cài, the Viscount of Wú, and the Marquis of Táng attacked Chǔ.
They left their boats at the bend of the Huái River,
and from Yùzhāng faced Chǔ across the Hàn River.
Left Sima Xū said to Zǐ Cháng:
"You follow the Hàn River and engage them upstream and downstream,
while I take all forces beyond Fāngchéng to destroy their boats,
then return to block the passes of Dàsuì, Zhíyuán, and Míng'è.
You then cross the Hàn to attack them,
and I will strike from behind,
surely inflicting a great defeat."
After planning, they set out.
Wǔchéng Hēi said to Zǐ Cháng:
"Wú uses wood [for armor],
we use leather,
which cannot last long,
so it is better to fight quickly."
Shǐ Huáng said to Zǐ Cháng:
"The people of Chǔ dislike you and favor the Sima.
If the Sima destroys Wú's boats on the Huái,
blocks the passes and enters,
he alone will have defeated Wú.
You must fight quickly!
Otherwise,
you will not escape blame."
So they crossed the Hàn and deployed their forces,
from Xiǎobié to Dàbié.
After three battles,
Zǐ Cháng knew it was hopeless,
and wanted to flee.
Shǐ Huáng said:
"In peace,
you sought this responsibility;
in difficulty you flee it,
where will you go?
You must fight to the death,
so that your initial faults may be fully excused."
On the gēngwǔ day of the eleventh month,
the two armies deployed at Bójǔ.
Fūgài Wáng, brother of Hélú, requested of Hélú at dawn:
"Chǔ's Wǎ is unrighteous,
and his officers have no will to die.
If we attack first,
his troops will surely flee;
then our main force can follow up,
and we will surely win."
Hélú did not consent.
Fūgài Wáng said:
"The saying
'A minister acts righteously without awaiting orders'
refers to this situation.
If I die today,
Chǔ can be entered."
With his own troops of five thousand, he first attacked Zǐ Cháng's forces.
Zǐ Cháng's troops fled,
the Chǔ army fell into chaos,
and the Wú army inflicted a great defeat.
Zǐ Cháng fled to Zhèng.
Shǐ Huáng died with his chariot unit.
Wú pursued the Chǔ army,
reaching Qīngfā,
and prepared to attack.
Fūgài Wáng said:
"A cornered beast still fights,
how much more so men?
If they know they cannot escape and fight to the death,
they will surely defeat us.
If we let those who cross first know they can escape,
those behind will envy them,
and they will have no will to fight.
We can attack when half have crossed."
They followed this,
and again defeated them.
The Chǔ men were preparing food,
the Wú men caught up,
and they fled.
After eating, Wú pursued,
defeating them at Yōngshì.
After five battles,
they reached Yǐng.
On the jǐmǎo day,
the King of Chǔ took his younger sister Jì Mǐ Bìwǒ and fled,
crossing the Jū River.
Zhēn Yǐngù was in the same boat as the king,
and the king had him drive fire-torched elephants to charge the Wú army.
On the gēngchén day,
Wú entered Yǐng,
and occupied the palaces according to rank.
Zǐ Shān occupied the Prime Minister's palace,
Fūgài Wáng wanted to attack him,
but Zǐ Shān, fearing, left it,
and Fūgài Wáng entered.
Left Sima Xū reached Xī and turned back,
defeated the Wú army at Yōngshì,
but was wounded.
Earlier,
the Sima had served Hélú,
so he was ashamed to be captured,
and said to his officers:
"Who can prevent my head from falling to the enemy?"
Wú Jūbēi said:
"I am lowly,
may I do it?"
The Sima said: "I indeed failed to recognize your worth,
you may!"
After being wounded in three battles,
he said: "I am of no more use."
Jūbēi spread a skirt,
cut off his head and wrapped it,
hid the body,
and escaped with the head.
The King of Chǔ crossed the Jū River,
then the Jiāng River,
and entered Yúnzhōng.
While the king was sleeping,
bandits attacked,
striking at the king with a dagger-axe.
Wángsūn Yóuyú shielded him with his back,
and was hit in the shoulder.
The king fled to Yún.
Zhōng Jiàn carried Jì Mǐ on his back and followed.
Yóuyú gradually revived and followed.
Huái, younger brother of Yún's lord Xīn, wanted to kill the king,
saying: "King Píng killed my father;
if I kill his son,
is that not fitting?"
Xīn said:
"When a ruler punishes a minister,
who dares to treat him as an enemy?
The ruler's command
is Heaven's will.
If one dies by Heaven's mandate,
whom should one oppose?
The Odes say:
'He does not devour the soft,
nor spit out the hard.
He does not insult the widowed and solitary,
nor fear the strong and forceful.'
Only the benevolent can do this.
To avoid the strong and bully the weak
is not courage;
to take advantage of others' distress
is not benevolence;
to destroy one's clan and abandon its sacrifices
is not filial piety;
to act without a good name
is not wisdom.
If you insist on committing these,
I will kill you."
Dòu Xīn and his brother Cháo fled with the king to Suí.
The Wú men pursued them,
and said to the people of Suí:
"The descendants of Zhōu dwelling in the Hàn River region
have all been wiped out by Chǔ.
Heaven has guided our hearts,
to bring punishment upon Chǔ,
yet you, lord, harbor their fugitive.
What crime has the house of Zhōu committed?"
If you, my lord, would consider repaying the Zhou royal house,
extending it to this humble person,
and thereby encouraging Heaven's favor,
it would be your grace.
The fields of Hànyáng,
you indeed possess them."
The King of Chǔ was in the northern part of the Duke's palace,
while the men of Wú were to the south.
Zǐqī resembled the king,
so he let the king escape,
and himself acted as the king,
saying:
"If you hand me over to them,
the king will surely be spared."
The people of Suí divined about handing him over,
but it was not auspicious,
so they declined to Wú, saying:
"Because Suí is remote and small
and close to Chǔ,
Chǔ has indeed preserved us.
For generations we have had covenants and oaths,
which remain unaltered to this day.
If we were to abandon them in times of trouble,
how could we serve our lord?
The trouble for your officers is not just one person;
if you pacify the entire territory of Chǔ,
how would we dare not obey your command?"
The men of Wú then withdrew.
Lǜ Jīn had initially served in the household of Zǐqī,
and he had actually made an agreement with the people of Suí.
The king sent for him to appear,
but he declined,
saying:
"I dare not seek profit from a covenant."
The king cut a piece from Zǐqī's heart and made a covenant with the people of Suí.
Earlier, Wǔ Yún and Shēn Bāoxū were friends.
When Wǔ Yún fled,
he said to Shēn Bāoxū:
"I will surely overturn the state of Chǔ."
Shēn Bāoxū said: "Strive for it!
If you can overturn it,
I will surely be able to restore it."
When King Zhāo was in Suí,
Shēn Bāoxū went to Qín to request troops,
saying: "Wú is like a great boar or a long snake,
repeatedly devouring the central states,
and its cruelty began with Chǔ.
Our ruler has lost his altars of soil and grain,
and is now in the wilderness,
so he has sent this humble minister to report the emergency,
saying:
'The nature of the barbarians is insatiable;
if they become your neighbors,
they will be a threat to your borders.
While Wú is not yet settled,
you, my lord, should take your share.
If Chǔ should perish,
it will be your land.
If by your divine power you assist us,
we will serve you for generations.'"
The Earl of Qín sent a message declining,
saying:
"I have heard your command.
You should first go to the guesthouse,
and I will consider the matter and inform you."
Shēn Bāoxū replied:
"Our ruler is in the wilderness,
and has not yet found a place to settle;
how dare this humble minister seek comfort?"
He stood,
leaning against the courtyard wall and weeping,
his cries unceasing day and night,
not taking a sip of water for seven days.
Duke Āi of Qín composed the poem "Wú Yī" for him.
Shēn Bāoxū bowed nine times and then sat down.
The Qín army then set out.
A11.5 《The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Fifth Year of Duke Dìng》
A11.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
in the third month of the royal calendar, on the first day, Xīnhài,
there was a solar eclipse.
A11.5.2 In summer,
grain was sent to Cài.
A11.5.3 The Yuè people entered Wú.
A11.5.4 In the sixth month, on Bǐngshēn,
Jìsūn Yìrú died.
A11.5.5 In autumn, in the seventh month, on Rénzǐ,
Shūsūn Bùgǎn died.
A11.5.6 In winter,
Shì Yǎng of Jìn led an army to besiege Xiānyú.
B11.5 《The Zuo Commentary: The Fifth Year of Duke Dìng》
B11.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
the king's men killed Zǐcháo in Chǔ.
B11.5.2 In summer,
grain was sent to Cài,
to relieve their urgent need,
pitying their lack of resources.
B11.5.3 The Yuè people entered Wú,
while Wú was in Chǔ.
B11.5.4 In the sixth month,
Jì Píngzǐ traveled to Dōngyě.
On his return,
before he arrived,
on Bǐngshēn,
he died in Fáng.
Yáng Hǔ intended to use the yúfán jade for the burial,
but Zhòngliáng Huái refused to give it,
saying:
"When the steps change, the jade changes."
Yáng Hǔ wanted to expel him,
and informed Gōngshān Bùniǔ.
Bùniǔ said:
"He is acting for the ruler;
why do you resent him?"
After the burial,
Huánzǐ traveled to Dōngyě,
and reached Fèi.
Zǐxiè was the steward of Fèi,
and went to meet and greet him in the suburbs;
Huánzǐ treated him with respect.
When he greeted Zhòngliáng Huái,
Zhòngliáng Huái did not show respect.
Zǐxiè was angry,
and said to Yáng Hǔ:
"Will you carry it out?"
B11.5.5 Shēn Bāoxū arrived with the Qín army.
Zǐ Pú and Zǐ Hǔ of Qín led five hundred chariots to rescue Chǔ.
Zǐ Pú said:
"I do not know the ways of Wú."
He had the men of Chǔ first engage the men of Wú in battle,
and then joined them from Jì,
defeating Fūgài Wáng greatly at Yí.
The men of Wú captured Wěi Shè at Bǎijǔ;
his son led fleeing soldiers to follow Zǐxī,
and defeated the Wú army at Jūnxiáng.
In autumn, in the seventh month,
Zǐqī
and Zǐ Pú destroyed Táng.
In the ninth month,
Fūgài Wáng returned,
and set himself up as ruler,
engaging the king in battle,
but was defeated,
fled to Chǔ,
and became the Tángxī clan.
The Wú army defeated the Chǔ army at Yōngshì.
The Qín army again defeated the Wú army.
The Wú army encamped at Jūn;
Zǐqī was about to set fire to it,
but Zǐxī said:
"The bones of our fathers and brothers are exposed there;
we cannot collect them,
and now we would burn them—
this cannot be done."
Zǐqī said:
"The state is lost;
if the dead have consciousness,
how could they enjoy the old sacrifices?
Why fear burning them?"
He set fire to it,
and then fought again;
the Wú army was defeated.
They fought again at Gōngxùzhīxī.
The Wú army was greatly defeated,
and the ruler of Wú then returned.
They captured Yīnyútí.
Yīnyútí requested to go first,
and then escaped back.
Hòuzāng, the younger brother of Shè Gōng Zhūliáng, followed his mother to Wú,
but returned without waiting for her.
Shè Gōng never looked at him directly again.
B11.5.6 On Yǐhài,
Yáng Hǔ imprisoned Jì Huánzǐ and Gōngfǔ Wénbó,
and expelled Zhòngliáng Huái.
In winter, in the tenth month, on Dīnghài,
he killed Gōnghé Miǎo.
On Jǐchǒu,
he made a covenant with Huánzǐ inside the Jì Gate.
On Gēngyín,
a great curse was performed.
He expelled Gōngfǔ Chù and Qín Chuán,
who both fled to Qí.
B11.5.7 The King of Chǔ entered Yǐng.
Earlier,
Dòu Xīn heard about the men of Wú contending over palaces,
and said:
"I have heard:
'Without yielding,
there is no harmony;
without harmony,
one cannot undertake distant campaigns.'"
When Wú contends with Chǔ,
there is certain to be disorder;
if there is disorder,
then they are certain to return,
so how can they settle Chǔ?"
When the king fled to Suí,
he was about to cross at Chéngjiù.
Lán Yǐn Wěi crossed with his family,
but did not give the king his boat.
When peace was restored,
the king wanted to kill him.
Zǐxī said:
"Zǐcháng was ruined precisely because he dwelt on old grudges;
why should you, my lord, imitate him?"
The king said:
"Well said.
Let him be restored to his post;
I shall use this to remember my former fault."
The king rewarded Dòu Xīn, Wángsūn Yóuyú,
Wángsūn Yǔ, Zhōng Jiàn, Dòu Cháo,
Shēn Bāoxū, Wángsūn Jiǎ, Sòng Mù, and Dòu Huái.
Zǐxī said:
"I beg that Huái be omitted."
The king said:
"Great virtue extinguishes small resentments—
this is the Way."
Shēn Bāoxū said:
"I acted for my lord,
not for myself.
Now that my lord is settled,
what more do I seek?
Moreover, I criticized Zǐqí;
how could I do the same?"
Thereupon he fled to avoid the reward.
The king was about to marry off Jì Mǐ,
but Jì Mǐ declined, saying:
"The reason a woman is a woman
is to keep her distance from men.
Yet Zhōng Jiàn has already carried me on his back."
So she was given in marriage to Zhōng Jiàn,
and he was made Master of Music.
When the king was in Suí,
Zǐxī used the king's carriage and robes to guard the roads,
and established a capital at Píxiè.
Upon learning where the king was,
he then followed the king.
The king sent Yóuyú to fortify Jūn,
and he returned to report.
Zǐxī asked about its height and thickness,
but he did not know.
Zǐxī said:
"If you cannot do something,
you should decline.
If you do not know the height and thickness of the walls,
how can you know their size?"
He replied:
"I firmly declined, saying I could not,
but you, sir, sent me.
Each person has things he can and cannot do.
When the king encountered bandits in Yúnzhōng,
I received a blow from their halberd—
the wound is still there."
Baring his back to show it,
he said:
"This is what I could do.
As for the affairs of Píxiè,
I could not do that either."
B11.5.8 Jìn's Shì Yǎng besieged Xiānyú,
in retaliation for Guānhǔ's defeat.
A11.6 The Classic of Duke Dìng's Sixth Year
A11.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
in the royal first month, on Guǐhài,
Zhèng's Yóu Sù led troops to destroy Xǔ,
and took the Earl of Xǔ, Sī, back with him.
A11.6.2 In the second month,
the duke invaded Zhèng.
A11.6.3 The duke returned from invading Zhèng.
A11.6.4 In summer,
Jìsūn Sī
and Zhòngsūn Héjì went to Jìn.
A11.6.5 In autumn,
men of Jìn seized the Sòng envoy Yuè Qílí.
A11.6.6 In winter,
they fortified the inner city wall.
A11.6.7 Jìsūn Sī
and Zhòngsūn Jì led troops to besiege Yùn.
B11.6 The Commentary of Duke Dìng's Sixth Year
B11.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
Zhèng destroyed Xǔ,
taking advantage of Chǔ's defeat.
B11.6.2 In the second month,
the duke invaded Zhèng,
taking Kuāng,
in order to punish Zhèng on behalf of Jìn for its attack on Xūmí.
On the way there, he did not request passage from Wèi;
and upon returning,
Yáng Hǔ made the Jì and Mèng clans enter through the south gate,
exit through the east gate,
and lodge at Túnzé.
The Marquis of Wèi was angry,
and sent Mí Zǐxiá to pursue them.
Gōngshū Wénzǐ was old,
but rode in a carriage to see the duke,
saying:
"To blame others and then imitate them
is contrary to ritual.
During the troubles of Duke Zhāo,
you, my lord, were willing to use the Shū tripod of Wén,
the Zhāo turtle-shell of Chéng,
or the pán mirror of Dìng—
if any of these could secure his return,
you would have chosen one to use.
As for the sons of the duke and of your various ministers,
if the other lords were concerned,
you would have sent them as hostages.
This is what all your ministers heard.
Now, on account of a small grievance, you would cover over old virtue—
is this not unacceptable?
Among the sons of Tàisì,
only Zhōugōng and Kāngshū were harmonious;
yet to imitate petty men and abandon this—
is that not a falsehood?
Heaven is about to multiply Yáng Hǔ's crimes and destroy him;
you, my lord, should simply wait—
what do you think?"
Thereupon he stopped.
B11.6.3 In summer,
Jì Huánzǐ went to Jìn,
to present captives from Zhèng.
Yáng Hǔ forced Mèng Yìzǐ to go to present gifts to the lady,
and the men of Jìn feasted them together.
Mèngsūn stood outside the chamber,
and said to Fàn Xiànzǐ:
"If Yáng Hǔ cannot remain in Lǔ,
and seeks rest in Jìn,
if you do not make him a Sima of the Central Army,
may the former lords be my witness!"
Xiànzǐ said:
"Our ruler has officials,
and will appoint the appropriate men;
what do I, Yǎng, know about it?"
Xiànzǐ said to Jiǎnzǐ:
"The men of Lǔ are troubled by Yáng Hǔ.
Mèngsūn knows his flaw,
and thinks he is certain to go to Jìn,
so he forcefully made this request for him,
in order to secure his entry there."
B11.6.4 On Jǐchǒu of the fourth month,
Wú's crown prince Zhōnglěi defeated the Chǔ naval forces,
capturing Pān Zǐchén, Xiǎowéizǐ, and seven great officers.
The state of Chǔ was greatly alarmed,
and feared destruction.
Zǐqī was also defeated with his land forces at Fányáng.
The Lingyǐn Zǐxī said joyfully:
"Now at last we can act."
Thereupon he moved the capital from Yǐng to Ruò,
and reformed its administration,
in order to stabilize the state of Chǔ.
B11.6.5 Zhōu Dānpiān, leading the followers of Prince Cháo,
planned with men of Zhèng to create disorder in Zhōu;
Zhèng thereupon attacked Féng, Huá,
Xūmí,
Fùshǔ,
Húrén,
and the area outside Què.
In the sixth month,
Jìn's Yán Méi garrisoned Zhōu,
and fortified Xūmí.
B11.6.6 In autumn, in the eighth month,
Sòng's Yuè Qí spoke to Duke Jǐng, saying:
"Among the lords, only we serve Jìn;
if we now send no envoy,
Jìn will surely resent it."
Yuè Qí informed his steward Chén Yín.
Chén Yín said:
"You must go yourself."
Another day,
the duke said to Yuè Qí:
"I alone am pleased with your words;
you must go!"
Chén Yín said:
"Establish your heir before going,
so that our house will not perish;
