moreover, the ruler will then also regard me as one who knows the difficulty yet proceeds."
He met Hùn and proceeded.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ welcomed him,
and offered him wine at Miánshàng,
presenting sixty poplar-wood shields to Jiǎnzǐ.
Chén Yín said:
"Formerly our master served the Fàn clan,
now you serve the Zhào clan,
and moreover you have presented gifts,
using poplar-wood shields to purchase calamity—
this cannot be done.
However, if you die for the state of Jìn,
your sons and grandsons will surely achieve their ambitions in Sòng."
Fàn Xiànzǐ spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"Having been sent across borders by his ruler's command,
before delivering his mission he privately drank wine,
showing disrespect to both rulers—
this cannot go unpunished."
Thereupon they seized Yuè Qí.
B11.6.7 Yáng Hǔ further swore a covenant with the Duke and the three Huán clans at the Zhōu altar,
swore a covenant with the men of the state at the Bó altar,
and performed a curse at the crossroads of Wǔfǔ.
B11.6.8 In winter, the twelfth month,
the Heavenly King resided at Gūyóu,
avoiding the rebellion of Dān Piān.
A11.7 《The Seventh Year of Duke Dìng's Classic》
A11.7.1 In the seventh year, spring,
the royal first month.
A11.7.2 In summer, the fourth month.
A11.7.3 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Xián.
A11.7.4 Men of Qí seized the messenger of Wèi, Běigōng Jié, to invade Wèi.
A11.7.5 The Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi made a covenant at Shā.
A11.7.6 The great rain sacrifice was held.
A11.7.7 Qí Guó Xià led an army to attack our western borders.
A11.7.8 In the ninth month,
the great rain sacrifice was held.
A11.7.9 In winter, the tenth month.
B11.7 《The Seventh Year of Duke Dìng's Commentary》
B11.7.1 In the seventh year, spring, second month,
Zhōu Dān Piān entered Yílì and rebelled.
B11.7.2 Men of Qí returned Yùn and Yángguān;
Yáng Hǔ occupied them and governed from there.
B11.7.3 In summer, the fourth month,
Shàn Wǔgōng and Liú Huángōng defeated the Yǐn clan at Qiónggǔ.
B11.7.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Xián,
summoning Wèi to a meeting.
The Marquis of Wèi wished to rebel against Jìn,
but the various great officers would not allow it.
He sent Běigōng Jié to Qí,
and privately said to the Marquis of Qí:
"Seize Jié to invade us."
The Marquis of Qí complied,
and they made a covenant at Suǒ.
B11.7.5 Qí Guó Xià attacked us.
Yáng Hǔ drove for Jì Huánzǐ,
Gōngliǎn Chǔfǔ drove for Mèng Yìzǐ,
and they planned to attack the Qí army by night.
The Qí army heard of this,
dismantled their defenses, and lay in ambush waiting for them.
Chǔfǔ said:
"Hǔ does not consider the calamity,
and will certainly die."
Jǔ Yí said:
"Hǔ has plunged these two masters into difficulty;
without waiting for the officers,
I will certainly kill you."
Hǔ became afraid,
and then turned back,
so they were not defeated.
B11.7.6 In winter, the eleventh month, on Wùwǔ,
Shànzǐ and Liúzǐ welcomed the King at the Qìng clan's.
Jìn's Jí Qín escorted the King.
On Jǐsì,
the King entered Wángchéng,
lodged at the Dǎng clan of the ducal lineage,
and afterwards paid court at the Zhuāng Palace.
A11.8 《The Eighth Year of Duke Dìng's Classic》
A11.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke invaded Qí.
A11.8.2 The Duke arrived from invading Qí.
A11.8.3 In the second month,
the Duke invaded Qí.
A11.8.4 In the third month,
the Duke arrived from invading Qí.
A11.8.5 The Earl of Cáo, Lù, died.
A11.8.6 In summer,
Qí Guó Xià led an army to attack our western borders.
A11.8.7 The Duke met with the Jìn army at Wǎ.
A11.8.8 The Duke arrived from Wǎ.
A11.8.9 In autumn, the seventh month, on Wùchén,
the Marquis of Chén, Liǔ, died.
A11.8.10 Jìn Shì Yǎng led an army to invade Zhèng,
and then invaded Wèi.
A11.8.11 They buried Duke Jìng of Cáo.
A11.8.12 In the ninth month,
they buried Duke Huái of Chén.
A11.8.13 Jìsūn Sī
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to invade Wèi.
A11.8.14 In winter,
the Marquis of Wèi
and the Earl of Zhèng made a covenant at Qūpú.
A11.8.15 They followed in sacrificing to the former dukes.
A11.8.16 Thieves stole the precious jade
and great bow.
B11.8 《The Eighth Year of Duke Dìng's Commentary》
B11.8.1 In the eighth year, spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke invaded Qí,
attacking the gate of Yángzhōu.
The officers all sat in ranks,
saying:
"Yán Gāo's bow is six jūn strong."
They all took it and passed it around to look at.
The men of Yángzhōu came out,
Yán Gāo seized someone's weak bow,
Jíqiū Zǐchú struck him,
and he fell together with another man.
Lying prone,
he shot at Zǐchú,
hitting his cheek,
and killed him.
Yán Xī shot a man in the eyebrow,
and retreating said:
"I lack courage,
I aimed for his eye."
The army retreated,
Rǎn Měng pretended to have a wounded foot and went first.
His elder brother Huì then shouted:
"Měng, bring up the rear!"
B11.8.2 In the third month, on Jǐchǒu,
Shànzǐ attacked Gǔchéng,
and Liúzǐ attacked Yílì.
On Xīnmǎo,
Shànzǐ attacked Jiǎnchéng,
and Liúzǐ attacked Yú,
to stabilize the royal house.
B11.8.3 Zhào Yǎng spoke to the Marquis of Jìn, saying:
"Among the feudal lords, only Sòng serves Jìn;
if we kindly receive their envoy,
we still fear he may not come;
now we have seized him again,
this is cutting off the feudal lords."
They were about to send Yuè Qí back,
but Shì Yǎng said:
"We have detained him for three years,
and now without reason send him back—
Sòng will certainly rebel against Jìn."
Xiànzǐ privately said to Zǐliáng:
"Our ruler fears he cannot serve the ruler of Sòng,
therefore he detained you.
You should let Hùn take your place for now."
Zǐliáng told this to Chén Yín.
Chén Yín said:
"Sòng is about to rebel against Jìn,
this is abandoning Hùn;
it is better to wait."
Yuè Qí returned,
and died at Tàiháng.
Shì Yǎng said:
"Sòng will certainly rebel;
it is better to detain his corpse to seek a settlement."
Thereupon they detained it at Zhōu.
B11.8.4 The Duke invaded Qí,
attacking the outer wall of Lǐnqiū.
The defenders set fire to the assault chariots,
but some soaked horse-hair cloths to extinguish the fires,
and thus destroyed them.
The defenders sallied forth,
and the army fled.
Yáng Hǔ pretended not to see Rǎn Měng,
saying:
"If Měng were here,
we would certainly be defeated."
Měng then charged after them,
but looking back saw no reinforcements,
and feigned a fall.
Hǔ said:
"All empty bravado."
B11.8.5 Jiǎ Yuè had a son,
and was waiting for an event to name him.
After capturing someone in the battle of Yángzhōu,
he named him
"Yángzhōu."
B11.8.6 In summer,
Guó Xià and Gāo Zhāng of Qí attacked our western borders.
Shì Yǎng, Zhào Yǎng, and Xún Yín of Jìn came to our rescue.
The Duke met the Jìn army at Wǎ.
Fàn Xiànzǐ held a lamb,
while Zhào Jiǎnzǐ and Zhōngháng Wénzǐ both held geese.
From then on, Lǔ began to esteem the lamb.
B11.8.7 The Jìn army was about to swear a covenant with the Marquis of Wèi at Zhuánzé.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Which of the ministers dares to covenant with the Lord of Wèi?"
Shè Tuó and Chéng Hé said:
"We can covenant with him."
The men of Wèi requested to hold the ox ear.
Chéng Hé said:
"Wèi
is like our territories of Wēn and Yuán;
how can it be regarded as a full state?"
As they were about to smear the blood,
Shè Tuó pushed the hand of the Marquis of Wèi,
and it reached his wrist.
The Marquis of Wèi was angry.
Wángsūn Jiǎ hurried forward
and said:
"A covenant is to establish trust through ritual.
If it were the Lord of Wèi,
how would he dare not uphold ritual and accept this covenant?"
The Marquis of Wèi wished to rebel against Jìn,
but was concerned about his senior ministers.
Wángsūn Jiǎ had him stay in the suburbs.
The ministers asked the reason.
The Duke told them of Jìn's insults,
and said:
"I have brought disgrace upon the altars of soil and grain.
You should choose another successor,
and I will follow."
The ministers said:
"This is Wèi's misfortune;
how could it be your fault?"
The Duke said:
"There is another concern:
they told me
'You must send your son and the ministers' sons as hostages.'"
The ministers said:
"If it is beneficial,
let the young lord go,
and how would the sons of your ministers dare not all take up the reins and follow?"
As they were about to depart,
Wángsūn Jiǎ said:
"If Wèi faces calamity,
the artisans and merchants have never failed to share the trouble.
They should all go as well."
The Duke informed the ministers,
and they were all to go.
A departure date was set.
The Duke appeared before the people of the capital,
and had Jiǎ ask them,
saying:
"If Wèi rebels against Jìn,
and Jìn attacks us five times,
how bad would it be?"
They all said:
"Even if they attack us five times,
we can still fight."
Jiǎ said:
"Then why not rebel now?
To wait until we are exhausted and then give hostages—
what delay is there?"
So they rebelled against Jìn.
The men of Jìn requested to renew the covenant,
but it was refused.
B11.8.8 In autumn,
Shì Yǎng of Jìn joined Duke Huán of Chéng in invading Zhèng,
besieging Chóngláo
in retaliation for Yīquē.
They then invaded Wèi.
B11.8.9 In the ninth month,
our army invaded Wèi,
because of Jìn.
B11.8.10 Jì Wù, Gōngchú Jí, and Gōngshān Bùniǔ
were all discontented in the Jì clan.
Shūsūn Zhé was not favored in the Shūsūn clan.
Shūzhòng Zhì was discontented in Lǔ.
Therefore, these five men allied with Yáng Hǔ.
Yáng Hǔ wanted to remove the Three Huán clans,
replacing the Jì clan with Jì Wù,
the Shūsūn clan with Shūsūn Zhé,
and himself replacing the Mèng clan.
In the tenth month of winter,
they performed the sacrifices to the former dukes in order and prayed.
On Xīnmǎo,
they held the dì sacrifice to Duke Xī.
On Rénchén,
they planned to feast Jì Sì at Púpǔ and kill him,
ordering the capital's chariots,
saying
"to arrive on Guǐsì."
The steward of Chéng, Gōngliǎn Chǔfǔ, informed Mèng Sūn,
saying:
"The Jì clan has ordered the capital's chariots;
what is the reason?"
Mèng Sūn said:
"I have not heard."
Chǔfǔ said:
"Then there will be disorder,
and it will certainly reach you.
Prepare for it first."
He and Mèng Sūn set Rénchén as the date.
Yáng Hǔ led the way.
Lín Chǔ drove for Huánzǐ,
with foresters flanking him with spears and shields,
and Yáng Yuè brought up the rear.
They were heading to Púpǔ.
Huánzǐ suddenly said to Lín Chǔ:
"Your ancestors were all good men of the Jì clan;
you continue this tradition."
He replied:
"I received the command too late.
Yáng Hǔ is in power,
and the state of Lǔ obeys him.
To disobey means seeking death,
and death would not benefit my master."
Huánzǐ said:
"What lateness is there?
Can you take me to the Mèng clan?"
He replied:
"I dare not cherish my life,
but fear I cannot save my master."
Huánzǐ said:
"Go!"
The Mèng clan selected three hundred strong grooms
to build a house outside the gate for Gōng Qī.
Lín Chǔ whipped the horses into a fury,
and galloped upon reaching the main road.
Yáng Yuè shot at him,
but missed.
The builders shut the gate.
Someone shot Yáng Yuè from between the gate leaves,
killing him.
Yáng Hǔ seized the Duke and Wǔ Shū,
to attack the Mèng clan.
Gōngliǎn Chǔfǔ led the men of Chéng in through the Upper East Gate,
and fought the Yáng clan inside the South Gate,
but did not prevail.
They fought again beneath the jujube trees,
and the Yáng clan was defeated.
Yáng Hǔ donned armor and went to the Duke's palace,
took the precious jade and great bow, and left,
stopping at the crossroads of Wǔfǔ,
where he slept before eating.
His followers said:
"Pursuers will likely come."
Hǔ said:
"When the men of Lǔ hear I have left,
they will rejoice at escaping death;
what leisure would they have to pursue me?"
A follower said:
"Alas!
Hurry and drive!
Gōngliǎn Yáng is here."
Gōngliǎn Yáng requested to pursue him,
but Mèng Sūn did not permit it.
Yáng wanted to kill Huánzǐ,
but Mèng Sūn, afraid, returned him.
Zǐyán arranged the wine vessels in the temple of the Jì clan and then left.
Yáng Hǔ entered Huān and Yángguān and rebelled.
B11.8.11 Zhèng Sì Chuán succeeded Zǐ Dàshū in governance.
A11.9 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Ninth Year of Duke Dìng*
A11.9.1 In the ninth year, spring,
the royal first month.
A11.9.2 In summer, on the fourth month, Wùshēn,
the Earl of Zhèng, Chài, died.
A11.9.3 The precious jade and
great bow were recovered.
A11.9.4 In the sixth month,
the burial of Zhèng Duke Xiàn.
The Marquis halted at Wǔshì.
A11.9.6 The Earl of Qín died.
A11.9.7 In winter,
the burial of Duke Āi of Qín took place.
B11.9 The Commentary to the Ninth Year of Duke Dìng
B11.9.1 In the spring of the ninth year,
the Duke of Sòng sent Yuè Dàxīn to make a covenant with Jìn,
and also to receive the body of Yuè Qí.
He declined,
feigning illness;
so they sent Xiàng Cháo to go to Jìn to make the covenant,
and also to receive the body of Zǐliáng.
Zǐmíng urged the Right Marshal of Tóngmén to come out,
saying:
"I am still wearing mourning garments,
yet you are striking bells.
Why is this?"
The Right Marshal said:
"Because the mourning is not here."
Later he told someone:
"He himself wore mourning garments and yet fathered a child.
Why should I abandon the bells?"
Zǐmíng heard this,
was angry,
and spoke to the Duke, saying:
"The Right Marshal will bring harm to the Dài clan.
He refuses to go to Jìn,
and is about to start a rebellion.
If not,
he has no illness."
Thereupon they expelled the Right Marshal of Tóngmén.
B11.9.2 Sì Chuán of Zhèng killed Dèng Xī,
yet employed his "Bamboo Penal Code."
The gentleman said of Zǐrán:
"In this he was not loyal.
If there is something that can benefit the state,
one may discard its evil aspects.
The three stanzas of 'The Quiet Maiden,'
take the red tube from it.
'The Banner with Ox-Tails,'
'What shall I tell him?'
take the loyalty from it.
Therefore, if one uses his methods,
one should not discard the man.
The Odes say:
'Luxuriant is the sweet pear tree;
Do not cut it, do not harm it;
For Lord Shào rested beneath it.'
In thinking of the man,
one still loves his tree;
how much more, when using his methods, should one not show compassion for the man!
Zǐrán has no way to encourage the capable."
B11.9.3 In summer,
Yánghǔ returned the precious jade and great bow.
The record says
"obtained,"
because they were vessels and implements.
In general, capturing vessels and implements is called
"obtained,"
while capturing something usable is called
"captured."
In the sixth month,
they attacked Yángguān.
Yánghǔ had them set fire to the Láimén gate.
The troops were thrown into confusion,
and he broke through them and went out, fleeing to Qí.
He requested troops to attack Lǔ,
saying:
"Three attacks,
and it will certainly be taken."
The Marquis of Qí was about to agree.
Bào Wénzǐ remonstrated, saying:
"I once served as a subordinate in the Shī clan,
and Lǔ cannot be taken.
High and low are still harmonious,
the multitude is still amicable,
they are able to serve the great states,
and they have no natural disasters.
How can they be taken?
Yánghǔ wishes to exhaust the Qí army.
When the Qí army is weary,
many great ministers will certainly die,
and he will then vigorously employ his deceitful schemes.
Now Yánghǔ was favored by the Jì clan,
yet he was about to kill Jì Sūn,
to the detriment of the state of Lǔ,
and sought acceptance here.
He is close to wealth, not to benevolence.
How can you, my lord, use him?
You, my lord, are richer than the Jì clan,
and greater than the state of Lǔ.
This is what Yánghǔ desires to overthrow.
Lǔ has rid itself of this affliction,
and you, my lord, take him in.
Would this not be harmful?"
The Marquis of Qí seized Yánghǔ,
intending to send him east.
Yánghǔ expressed a wish to go east,
so they imprisoned him in the western borderlands.
He borrowed all the chariots of the townspeople,
notched their axles,
He loaded a covered carriage,
slept inside it, and escaped.
They pursued and captured him,
imprisoning him in Qí.
Again he escaped using a covered carriage,
fled to Sòng,
then fled to Jìn,
and went to the Zhào clan.
Zhòngní said:
"The Zhào clan will likely have disorder for generations!"
B11.9.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Yíyí of Jìn.
Bì Wúcún's father was about to arrange a marriage for him.
He declined,
giving it to his younger brother,
saying: "In this campaign,
if I do not die,
and return,
I will certainly marry a woman from the Gāo or Guó clans."
He was the first to ascend,
sought to exit through the gate,
and died beneath the eaves.
Dōngguō Shū yielded the ascent,
Lí Mí followed him,
saying:
"You yield and go left,
I yield and go right,
so that those who ascend will be exhausted and then descend."
Shū went left,
Mí descended first.
Shū and Wáng Měng rested.
Měng said:
"I ascended first."
Shū gathered his armor,
saying:
"The difficulty just now,
and now another difficulty!"
Měng laughed and said:
"I follow you,
like the outer horse following the trace-horse."
Jìn had a thousand chariots at Zhōngmóu.
The Marquis of Wèi was about to go to Wǔshì.
They divined about passing through there,
and the tortoise shell cracked.
The Marquis of Wèi said:
"It is acceptable!
Wèi's chariots will face half of them,
and I will face half of them.
We are a match."
Thereupon they passed through Zhōngmóu.
The people of Zhōngmóu wanted to attack them.
Chǔ Shī Pǔ of Wèi, who was in exile at Zhōngmóu,
said:
"Although Wèi is small,
its ruler is present.
It cannot be defeated.
The Qí army, having captured the city, is arrogant,
and its commander is also lowly.
If we encounter them,
we will certainly defeat them.
It would be better to follow Qí."
Thereupon they attacked the Qí army,
and defeated it.
The Marquis of Qí presented Zhuó, Mèi, and Xìng to Wèi.
The Marquis of Qí rewarded Lí Mí.
Lí Mí declined,
saying:
"There was one who ascended first.
I followed him.
He had a pale turban and wore a fox-fur garment."
The Duke had someone look at Dōngguō Shū,
and said:
"It was this gentleman. I grant you the reward."
The Duke rewarded Dōngguō Shū.
He declined,
saying:
"He [Lí Mí]
is a guest from abroad."
Thereupon he rewarded Lí Mí.
When the Qí army was at Yíyí,
the Marquis of Qí said to the people of Yíyí:
"Whoever finds Bì Wúcún
will have five households exempted from service."
Thereupon they found his corpse.
The Duke enshrouded it three times,
gave it a rhinoceros-hide carriage and a straight canopy,
and sent it back first.
He made the pullers sit,
led the army in mourning for him,
and personally pushed the carriage three times.
A11.10 The Text of the Tenth Year of Duke Dìng
A11.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
in the royal third month,
[we] made peace with Qí.
A11.10.2 In summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí at Jiāgǔ.
A11.10.3 The Duke arrived from Jiāgǔ.
A11.10.4 Zhào Yāng of Jìn led troops to besiege Wèi.
A11.10.5 Men of Qí came to return the fields of Yùn,
Huān, and Guīyīn.
A11.10.6 Shūsūn Zhōuqiú
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led troops to besiege Hòu.
A11.10.7 In autumn,
Shūsūn Zhōuqiú
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led troops to besiege Hòu.
A11.10.8 Yuè Dàxīn of Sòng fled to Cáo.
A11.10.9 Gōngzǐ Dì of Sòng fled to Chén.
A11.10.10 In winter,
the Marquis of Qí,
the Marquis of Wèi,
and Yóu Sù of Zhèng met at Ānfǔ.
A11.10.11 Shūsūn Zhōuqiú went to Qí.
A11.10.12 Chén, the younger brother of the Duke of Sòng, together with Zhòng Tuó
and Shí Kōu, fled to Chén.
B11.10 The Commentary to the Tenth Year of Duke Dìng
B11.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
[we] made peace with Qí.
B11.10.2 In summer,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí at Zhùqí,
which was actually Jiāgǔ.
Kǒng Qiū acted as assistant.
Lí Mí said to the Marquis of Qí:
"Kǒng Qiū knows the rites but lacks courage.
If we have the Lái men use weapons to seize the Marquis of Lǔ,
we are sure to get our way."
The Marquis of Qí followed this advice.
Kǒng Qiū escorted the Duke to withdraw,
and said:
"Soldiers, take action!
Two rulers are meeting in friendship,
yet captives from the border Yi tribes are using weapons to disrupt it.
This is not how the ruler of Qí commands the feudal lords.
Border tribes do not plot against Xià,
Yi peoples do not disrupt Huá,
captives do not interfere with covenants,
and weapons do not threaten friendship. To the spirits, this is inauspicious;
in terms of virtue, it violates righteousness;
among men, it is a breach of ritual.
My lord certainly would not do this."
When the Marquis of Qí heard this,
he immediately ordered them to withdraw.
When about to take the covenant,
the men of Qí added to the covenant document:
"If the army of Qí marches out of its borders and [Lǔ] does not follow us with three hundred chariots of armored troops,
may [they suffer] as per this covenant!"
Kǒng Qiū had Zī Wúhuán bow and reply,
saying:
"If you do not return to us the fields of Wènyáng,
and we thereby supply your orders,
may [you suffer] likewise!"
The Marquis of Qí was about to host a feast for the Duke.
Kǒng Qiū said to Liángqiū Jù:
"Regarding the old practices of Qí and Lǔ,
have you, sir, not heard of them?
The business is already concluded,
and yet you host a feast,
this is to trouble your officers.
Moreover, sacrificial vessels and statues do not leave the gate,
and fine music is not performed in the wilds.
If the feast is fully prepared,
this is to abandon ritual;
if it is not fully prepared,
it is like using chaff and weeds.
Using chaff and weeds
brings disgrace to the ruler;
abandoning ritual
brings a bad name.
Why do you not consider this!
Now a feast
is to display virtue.
If it does not display it,
it is better not to hold it."
So the feast did not ultimately take place.
B11.10.3 Men of Qí came to return the fields of Yùn,
Huān, and Guīyīn.
B11.10.4 Zhào Yāng of Jìn besieged Wèi
in retaliation for Yíyí.
Earlier,
the Marquis of Wèi attacked Hándān Wǔ at Hánshì,
built fortifications to its northwest and guarded them,
but they were burned down at night.
When Jìn besieged Wèi,
Wǔ with seventy followers attacked the west gate of Wèi,
killing men within the gate,
and said:
"I request to repay the battle of Hánshì."
Shè Tuó said:
"Our master is indeed brave;
but if I go,
they certainly will not dare open the gate."
He also with seventy followers attacked the gate at dawn,
pacing left and right,
and all arrived,
and stood
as if planted.
By midday the gate was not opened,
so they withdrew.
After returning from the campaign,
the men of Jìn investigated the reason for Wèi's rebellion,
saying:
"It was due to Shè Tuó and Chéng Hé."
Thereupon they seized Shè Tuó,
seeking to make peace with Wèi.
The men of Wèi did not agree.
The men of Jìn then killed Shè Tuó,
and Chéng Hé fled to Yān.
A gentleman said:
"This is what is called abandoning ritual;
it certainly will not be equal.
The Odes say:
'If a man is without ritual,
why does he not quickly die?'
Shè Tuó indeed died quickly!"
B11.10.5 Earlier,
Shūsūn Chéngzǐ wished to establish Wǔshū,
Gōngruò Miǎo firmly remonstrated,
saying:
"It cannot be done."
Chéngzǐ established him and then died.
Gōngnán sent assassins to shoot him,
but they could not kill him.
Gōngnán was made Master of the Horse,
and had Gōngruò made Steward of Hòu.
After Wǔshū was settled,
he had Hóu Fàn, the Master of the Horse of Hòu, kill Gōngruò,
but he could not.
His stableman said:
"I will pass through the court with a sword,
and Gōngruò is sure to ask:
'Whose sword is this?'
I will tell him it is yours,
and he is sure to examine it.
I will pretend to be clumsy and hand it to him by the tip,
then he can be killed."
They had him do so.
Gōngruò said:
"Do you wish to make a Wú Wáng of me?"
They then killed Gōngruò.
Hóu Fàn rebelled with Hòu.
Wǔshū and Yìzǐ besieged Hòu,
but could not take it.
In autumn,
the two men, together with the army of Qí, again besieged Hòu,
but could not take it.
Shūsūn said to Sì Chì, the Artisan Master of Hòu:
"Hòu is not only a worry for the Shūsūn clan,
but a calamity for the altars of soil and grain.
What is to be done?"
He replied:
"My task lies in the four words of the final stanza of the 'Yáng Shuǐ'."
Shūsūn bowed his head to the ground.
Sì Chì said to Hóu Fàn:
"Living on the border between Qí and Lǔ and having no employment,
is certainly untenable.
Why do you not seek employment from Qí to oversee the people?
Otherwise,
they will rebel."
Hóu Fàn followed this.
An envoy from Qí arrived.
Sì Chì and the men of Hòu spread a rumor among Hòu, saying:
"Hóu Fàn is going to exchange Hòu with Qí,
and the men of Qí will relocate the people of Hòu."
The multitude was terrified.
Sì Chì said to Hóu Fàn:
"The talk of the multitude is different.
You would do better to exchange with Qí.
Compared with dying,
it is still this Hòu,
and you can gain relief.
Why must it be here?
The men of Qí wish to use this to pressure Lǔ,
they are sure to double the land given to you.
And why not store much armor at your gate to prepare for the unexpected?"
Hóu Fàn said, "Agreed."
He then stored a large quantity of armor there.
Hóu Fàn requested to exchange territory with Qí.
The Qí officials went to inspect Hòu.
As they were about to arrive,
Sì Chì had people run around shouting:
"The Qí army has arrived!"
The people of Hòu were greatly alarmed,
and donned the armor stored at Hóu Fàn's gate
to surround Hóu Fàn.
Sì Chì was about to shoot at them,
but Hóu Fàn stopped him,
saying:
"Devise a plan to spare me."
Hóu Fàn requested to leave,
and they agreed.
Sì Chì went first to Sù,
with Hóu Fàn bringing up the rear.
Each time they passed through a gate,
the people of Hòu closed it behind them.
When they reached the outer city gate,
they stopped him,
saying:
"You are taking out the armor of the Shūsūn clan.
If the officials investigate this,
we, your servants, fear for our lives."
Sì Chì said:
"The armor of the Shūsūn clan is marked.
I did not dare to take it out."
Hóu Fàn said to Sì Chì:
"You stay and count it with them."
Sì Chì stayed,
and let the Lǔ men in.
Hóu Fàn fled to Qí.
The people of Qí then returned Hòu.
B11.10.6 In Sòng, the prince Dì favored Qú Fùliè.
He divided his household property into eleven parts,
and gave five of them to him.
Prince Dì had four white horses.
The Duke favored Xiàng Tuí,
and Tuí wanted them.
The Duke took the horses, dyed their tails and manes red, and gave them to him.
Dì was angry,
and had his followers beat Tuí and seize the horses back.
Tuí was afraid
and was about to flee.
The Duke shut the gate and wept for him,
until his eyes were completely swollen.
His full brother Chén said:
"You divided your household property to give to Liè,
yet you alone slight Tuí.
There is also some partiality here.
If you observe the rites due to the ruler,
you should at most go beyond the borders.
The ruler is sure to stop you."
Prince Dì fled to Chén,
but the Duke did not stop him.
Chén pleaded for him,
but the Duke would not listen.
Chén said:
"It is I who deceived my elder brother.
If I leave with the men of the state,
with whom will the ruler remain?"
In winter,
his full brother Chén, along with Zhòng Tuó and Shí Kōu, fled to Chén.
B11.10.7 Wǔ Shū paid a courtesy visit to Qí.
The Marquis of Qí entertained him,
saying:
"Master Shūsūn!
If Hòu were located on another border of your ruler,
what would I, the humble one, know about it?
Since it borders our humble city,
I therefore dared to assist your ruler in his concern."
He replied:
"This is not what my humble ruler expected.
The means by which I serve you, my lord,
are for the sake of the borders and the altars of soil and grain.
How dare I trouble your lordship's officers with a servant of my family?
Those disobedient ministers
are detested by all under heaven.
Does your lordship perhaps consider them a gift to my humble ruler?"
A11.11 The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Eleventh Year of Duke Dìng
A11.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
Chén, the younger brother of the Duke of Sòng, and Zhòng Tuó,
Shí Kōu,
and Prince Dì entered from Chén into Xiāo to rebel.
A11.11.2 In summer, the fourth month.
A11.11.3 In autumn,
Yuè Dàxīn of Sòng entered from Cáo into Xiāo.
A11.11.4 In winter,
peace was made with Zhèng.
Shū Huán went to Zhèng to oversee the covenant.
B11.11 The Commentary: The Eleventh Year of Duke Dìng
B11.11.1 In the eleventh year, in spring,
Chén, the full brother of the Duke of Sòng, along with Zhòng Tuó,
Shí Kōu,
and Prince Dì, entered into Xiāo to rebel.
In autumn,
Yuè Dàxīn joined them,
causing great trouble for Sòng,
due to the favor shown to Xiàng Tuí.
B11.11.2 In winter,
peace was made with Zhèng,
marking the beginning of their rebellion against Jìn.
A11.12 The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Twelfth Year of Duke Dìng
A11.12.1 In the twelfth year, in spring,
the Earl of Xuē, Dìng, died.
A11.12.2 In summer,
the Earl Xiāng of Xuē was buried.
A11.12.3 Shūsūn Zhōuqiú led an army to dismantle the walls of Hòu.
A11.12.4 Gōng Mèng Kōu of Wèi led an army to attack Cáo.
A11.12.5 Jìsūn Sī
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to dismantle the walls of Bì.
A11.12.6 In autumn,
a great rain sacrifice was held.
A11.12.7 In winter, in the tenth month, on the guǐhài day,
the Duke met with the Marquis of Qí and made a covenant at Huáng.
A11.12.8 In the eleventh month, on the bǐngyín day, the first day of the month,
there was an eclipse of the sun.
A11.12.9 The Duke arrived from Huáng.
A11.12.10 In the twelfth month,
the Duke besieged Chéng.
A11.12.11 The Duke arrived from besieging Chéng.
B11.12 The Commentary: The Twelfth Year of Duke Dìng
B11.12.1 In the twelfth year, in summer,
Gōng Mèng Kōu of Wèi attacked Cáo,
and took Jiāo.
On the return,
Huá Luó brought up the rear.
Before they had left the enemy territory,
he did not withdraw from the ranks.
His chariot driver said:
"To be in the rear and yet remain in the ranks,
is that not cowardice?"
Luó said:
"Rather than being falsely fierce,
I would prefer to be considered cowardly."
B11.12.2 Zhòng Yóu was steward to the Jì clan.
He intended to dismantle the walls of the three capitals.
Thereupon, the Shūsūn clan dismantled the walls of Hòu.
The Jì clan was about to dismantle the walls of Bì,
when Gōngshān Bùniǔ and Shūsūn Zhé led the men of Bì to attack Lǔ.
The Duke and the three ministers entered the palace of the Jì clan
and ascended the terrace of Wǔzǐ.
The men of Bì attacked them,
but could not take it.
They entered and reached the Duke's side.
Zhòng Ní ordered Shēn Jùxū and Yuè Qí to descend
and attack them.
The men of Bì fled northward.
The men of the state pursued them
and defeated them at Gūmiè.
The two men fled to Qí,
and then the walls of Bì were dismantled.
When they were about to dismantle the walls of Chéng,
Gōngliǎn Chǔfǔ said to Mèngsūn:
"If we dismantle the walls of Chéng,
the men of Qí are sure to reach the northern gate.
Moreover, Chéng
is the protective barrier of the Mèng clan.
Without Chéng,
there is no Mèng clan.
You pretend not to know,
and I will not dismantle it."
In winter, in the twelfth month,
the Duke besieged Chéng,
but could not take it.
A11.13 The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Thirteenth Year of Duke Dìng
A11.13.1 In the thirteenth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi stationed their troops at Chuíjiā.
A11.13.2 In summer,
the Shéyuān Park was built.
A11.13.3 A great hunt was held at Bǐpú.
A11.13.4 Gōng Mèng Kōu of Wèi led an army to attack Cáo.
A11.13.5 Jin's Zhào Yǎng entered Jìnyáng in rebellion.
A11.13.6 In winter,
Jin's Xún Yín and
Shì Jíshè entered Zhāogē in rebellion.
A11.13.7 Jin's Zhào Yǎng returned to Jin.
A11.13.8 Xuē assassinated its ruler Bǐ.
B11.13 The Commentary of Duke Dìng's Thirteenth Year
B11.13.1 In the thirteenth year, spring,
the Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi stationed their troops at Chuíjiā, which was actually the Juéshì. They sent an army to attack Jin.
As they were about to cross the Yellow River,
all the senior ministers said it was not possible.
Bǐng Yìzī said:
"It is possible.
Send a crack force to attack Hénèi.
It will certainly take several days for the report to reach Jiàng.
Jiàng's forces will not be able to cross the river in less than three months.
By then, we will already have crossed the river."
So they attacked Hénèi.
The Marquis of Qí collected the carriages of all the senior ministers,
only Bǐng Yìzī was allowed to ride in a carriage.
The Marquis of Qí wished to ride with the Marquis of Wèi.
He feasted with him and harnessed the chariot 'Chéng Guǎng',
loading it with armor.
He sent a messenger to report:
"The Jin army has arrived!"
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Before Your Lordship's chariot is ready,
allow me to act as your substitute."
So he donned armor and rode with him,
driving the chariot.
Someone reported:
"There is no Jin army."
Then they stopped.
B11.13.2 Jin's Zhào Yǎng said to Hándān Wǔ:
"Return to me the five hundred households of tribute from Wèi,
and I will settle them in Jìnyáng."
Wǔ agreed.
Upon returning, he informed his elders.
The elders all said:
"It cannot be done.
Wèi sent these because of Hándān.
To place them in Jìnyáng
is to sever the way with Wèi.
It would be better to invade Qí and then devise a plan."
So they did this,
and then returned them to Jìnyáng.
Zhào Mèng was angry.
He summoned Wǔ
and imprisoned him in Jìnyáng.
He ordered Wǔ's attendants to remove their swords before entering.
Shè Bīn refused.
Then he sent word to the people of Hándān, saying:
"I have a private grievance to settle with Wǔ.
You gentlemen may choose whomever you wish to establish."
Thereupon, he killed Wǔ.
Zhào Jì and Shè Bīn rebelled with Hándān.
In summer, the sixth month,
the Commander of the Upper Army, Jí Qín, besieged Hándān.
Hándān Wǔ was
the nephew of Xún Yín.
Xún Yín was
related by marriage to Fàn Jíshè.
They were on friendly terms with each other.
Therefore, they did not participate in besieging Hándān
and were about to start a rebellion.
Dǒng Ānyú heard of this
and informed Zhào Mèng,
saying:
"Should we prepare first?"
Zhào Mèng said:
"In the state of Jin, there is a command:
'He who begins trouble shall die.'
It is better to act later."
Ānyú said: "Rather than harming the people,
it is better that I alone die.
I beg to offer myself as the scapegoat."
Zhào Mèng did not agree.
In autumn, the seventh month,
the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans attacked the residence of the Zhào clan.
Zhào Yǎng fled to Jìnyáng,
and the men of Jin besieged him there.
Fàn Gāoyí was not favored by Fàn Jíshè
and wished to cause trouble within the Fàn clan.
Liáng Yīngfù was favored by Zhì Wénzǐ,
and Wénzǐ wished to make him a minister.
Hán Jiǎnzǐ was on bad terms with Zhōngháng Wénzǐ.
Wèi Xiāngzǐ was also on bad terms with Fàn Zhāozǐ.
Therefore, these five men plotted
to expel Xún Yín
and replace him with Liáng Yīngfù;
to expel Fàn Jíshè
and replace him with Fàn Gāoyí.
Xún Lì spoke to the Marquis of Jin, saying:
"Your Lordship commanded the great ministers:
'He who begins trouble shall die.'
The covenant is deposited in the river.
Now three ministers have begun trouble,
yet only Yǎng is to be expelled.
The punishment is already unequal.
I beg that they all be expelled."
In winter, the eleventh month,
Xún Lì, Hán Bùxìn, and Wèi Mànduō
supported the duke to attack the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
but were not victorious.
The two masters (Fàn and Zhōngháng) were about to attack the duke.
Qí's Gāo Qiáng said:
"One who has broken his arm three times knows how to be a good physician.
Only attacking the ruler is not permissible,
for the people will not support it.
It is because I attacked my ruler that I am here.
The three families (Hán, Zhào, Wèi) are not yet harmonious.
They can all be overcome.
If you overcome them,
with whom will the ruler ally?
If you attack the ruler first,
this will cause them to become harmonious."
They did not listen.
Thereupon, they attacked the duke.
The people of the state aided the duke.
The two masters were defeated,
and (the duke's forces) pursued and attacked them.
On dīngwèi day,
Xún Yín and Shì Jíshè fled to Zhāogē.
Hán and Wèi pleaded on behalf of the Zhào clan.
In the twelfth month, on xīnwèi day,
Zhào Yǎng entered Jiàng
and made a covenant in the duke's palace.
B11.13.3 Earlier,
Wèi's Gōngshū Wénzǐ attended court
and requested to host a feast for Duke Líng.
Upon withdrawing,
he met Shǐ Qiú and told him.
Shǐ Qiú said:
"You are certain to meet with disaster!
You are wealthy, and the ruler is greedy.
Will it not reach you?"
Wénzǐ said: "Indeed.
That I did not inform you first
is my fault.
The ruler has already granted my request.
What can be done about it?"
Shǐ Qiú said: "It is harmless.
If you act as a minister should,
you can avoid it.
To be wealthy yet able to serve as a minister
is certain to escape calamity.
This principle is the same for both high and low.
Shù is arrogant.
Will he not perish?
Those who are wealthy and not arrogant are few.
I have only seen you as such.
Those who are arrogant and do not perish
have never existed.
Shù will certainly be involved."
When Wénzǐ died,
the Marquis of Wèi began to dislike Gōngshū Shù
because of his wealth.
Gōngshū Shù also intended to remove the faction of the ruler's wife.
The ruler's wife accused him, saying:
"Shù is about to start a rebellion."
A11.14 The Spring and Autumn Annals of Duke Dìng's Fourteenth Year
A11.14.1 In the fourteenth year, spring,
Wèi's Gōngshū Shù came fleeing.
Wèi's Zhào Yáng fled to Sòng.
A11.14.2 In the second month, on xīnsì day,
Chǔ's Prince Jié and
Chén's Gōngsūn Tuórén led an army to destroy Dùn
and took the Viscount of Dùn, Zāng, back with them.
A11.14.3 In summer,
Wèi's Běigōng Jié came fleeing.
A11.14.4 In the fifth month,
Yúyuè defeated Wú at Zuìlǐ.
A11.14.5 The Viscount of Wú, Guāng, died.
A11.14.6 The duke met with the Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi at Qiān.
A11.14.7 The duke arrived from the meeting.
A11.14.8 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Duke of Sòng met at Táo.
A11.14.9 The Son of Heaven sent Shí Shàng to come and present the sacrificial meat.
A11.14.10 Wèi's heir apparent Kuǎikuì fled to Sòng.
A11.14.11 Wèi's Gōng Mèng Kōu fled to Zhèng.
A11.14.12 The younger brother of the Duke of Sòng, Chén, fled from Xiāo to Lǔ.
A11.14.13 A great military review was held at Bǐpú.
A11.14.14 The Viscount of Zhū came to meet with the Duke.
A11.14.15 The walls of Jǔfǔ and Xiāo were fortified.
B11.14 Commentary on the Fourteenth Year of Duke Dìng
B11.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
the Marquis of Wèi expelled Gōngshū Shù and his faction,
so Zhào Yáng fled to Sòng,
and Shù fled to Lǔ.
B11.14.2 Liáng Yīngfù hated Dǒng Ānyú,
and said to Zhì Wénzǐ:
"If Ānyú is not killed,
and allowed to remain in charge of the Zhào clan's government until the end,
the Zhào clan will certainly gain control of Jìn.
Why not use the fact that he initiated the trouble to demand justice from the Zhào clan?"
Wénzǐ sent a message to Zhào Mèng, saying:
"Although the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans were indeed the ones who rebelled,
it was Ānyú who instigated it.
This means Ānyú was involved in plotting the rebellion.
In Jìn, there is a law:
'The one who initiates disaster shall die.'
Those two (Fàn and Zhōngháng) have already been punished for their crimes.
I dare to inform you of this."
Zhào Mèng was troubled by this.
Ānyú said:
"If my death brings peace to Jìn,
and stability to the Zhào clan,
what use is there for me to live?
Who among men does not die?
My death is timely."
He then hanged himself.
Zhào Mèng exposed his corpse in the marketplace,
and reported to the Zhì clan, saying:
"My lord commanded the execution of the criminal Ānyú.
He has already been punished for his crime.
I dare to inform you."
Zhì Bó made a covenant with Zhào Mèng,
and thereafter the Zhào clan was stabilized.
They sacrificed to Ānyú in the ancestral temple.
B11.14.3 The Viscount of Dùn, Zāng, wished to serve Jìn,
and turned his back on Chǔ, severing friendly relations with Chén.
In the second month,
Chǔ destroyed Dùn.
B11.14.4 In summer,
Běigōng Jié of Wèi fled to Lǔ,
due to the affair of Gōngshū Shù.
B11.14.5 Wú attacked Yuè.
The Viscount of Yuè, Gōujiàn, defended against them,
deploying his troops at Zuìlǐ. Gōujiàn was troubled by the orderly formation of the Wú army,
and sent death-defying warriors twice to capture men from their ranks,
but they did not move.
He then had three rows of criminals
place swords against their own necks,
and they addressed the army, saying:
"The two rulers are engaged in battle,
and we subjects have violated the military commands.
We were not alert in the presence of our lord,
and dare not escape punishment.
We dare to return to death."
They then cut their own throats.
The army watched them intently.
The Viscount of Yuè took advantage of this to attack,
and inflicted a great defeat on them.
Línggūfú struck Hé Lǘ with a dagger-axe,
wounding Hé Lǘ's big toe.
He took one of his shoes.
On the return journey,
Hé Lǘ died at Xíng,
seven lǐ from Zuìlǐ.
Fūchāi had a man stand in the courtyard,
and whenever he himself entered or exited,
the man was sure to say to him:
"Fūchāi!
Have you forgotten that the King of Yuè killed your father?"
He would then reply:
"Yes.
I dare not forget!"
After three years, he took revenge on Yuè.
B11.14.6 The men of Jìn besieged Zhāogē.
The Duke met with the Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi between Pí and Shàngliáng,
to plan the rescue of the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans.
Xīchéng Fù and Xiǎowáng Táojiǎ
led a Dí army to attack Jìn,
fighting at Jiàngzhōng.
They were unsuccessful and returned.
Shì Fù fled to Zhōu,
and Xiǎowáng Táojiǎ entered Zhāogē.
B11.14.7 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Duke of Sòng met at Táo,
because of the affair of the Fàn clan.
B11.14.8 The Marquis of Wèi summoned Cháo Zhāo for the sake of his wife Nánzǐ.
They met at Táo.
The heir apparent, Kuǎikuì, was presenting a sacrificial vessel called a yú to Qí,
and passed through the countryside of Sòng.
The country folk sang about him, saying:
"Since your sow is already satisfied,
why not return our boar?"
The heir apparent was ashamed by this.
He said to Xìyáng Sù:
"Accompany me to pay respects to the young mistress.
When the young mistress sees me,
I will look at you,
and then you kill her."
Sù said:
"Yes."
They then went to pay respects to the lady.
The lady saw the heir apparent.
The heir apparent looked at him three times,
but Sù did not advance.
The lady saw his expression,
cried out and ran away,
saying:
"Kuǎikuì is going to kill me."
The Duke took her hand and ascended the tower.
The heir apparent fled to Sòng.
All his partisans were expelled.
Therefore, Gōngmèng Kōu fled to Zhèng,
and from Zhèng fled to Qí.
The heir apparent told people:
"Xìyáng Sù brought disaster upon me."
Xìyáng Sù told people:
"The heir apparent brought disaster upon me.
The heir apparent is unprincipled.
He ordered me to kill his mother.
If I had not agreed,
he would have killed me.
If I had killed the lady,
he would have used me as a scapegoat.
Therefore, I agreed but did not act,
to delay my death.
The proverb says:
'The people are preserved by good faith.'
I acted according to good faith and righteousness."
B11.14.9 In winter, in the twelfth month,
the men of Jìn defeated the army of the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans at Lù,
capturing Jí Qín and Gāo Qiáng.
They also defeated a Zhèng army and the army of the Fàn clan at Bǎiquán.
A11.15 The Spring and Autumn Annals, Fifteenth Year of Duke Dìng
A11.15.1 In the fifteenth year, in spring,
the first month of the royal calendar,
the Viscount of Zhū came for an audience.
A11.15.2 A mole rat ate the ox for the border sacrifice,
and the ox died.
Another ox was divined for.
A11.15.3 In the second month, on the xīnchǒu day,
the Viscount of Chǔ destroyed Hú,
and took Húzǐ Bào back with him.
A11.15.4 In summer, in the fifth month, on the xīnhài day,
the border sacrifice was held.
A11.15.5 On the rénshēn day,
the Duke died in the Gāoqǐn chamber.
A11.15.6 Hǎn Dá of Zhèng led an army to attack Sòng.
A11.15.7 The Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi stationed their troops at Qúchú.
A11.15.8 The Viscount of Zhū came to attend the funeral.
A11.15.9 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the rénshēn day,
Lady Sì died.
A11.15.10 In the eighth month, on the gēngchén day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
A11.15.11 In the ninth month,
the Viscount of Téng came to attend the burial.
A11.15.12 On the dīngsì day,
our ruler Duke Dìng was to be buried,
but it rained, and the burial could not be completed.
On the wùwǔ day,
when the sun was declining in the afternoon,
the burial was finally completed.
A11.15.13 On the xīnsì day,
Dìng Sì was buried.
A11.15.14 In winter,
the walls of Qī were fortified.
B11.15 Commentary on the Fifteenth Year of Duke Dìng
B11.15.1 In the spring of the fifteenth year,
the Duke Yǐn of Zhū came to court.
Zǐgòng observed the ceremony.
The Viscount of Zhū held the jade token high,
with his face upturned;
the Duke (of Lǔ) received the jade low,
with his face bowed down.
Zǐgòng said:
"Judging by the rites,
these two rulers
will both face death or ruin.
For rites
are the embodiment of life and death, survival and ruin.
From one's movements to the left and right, turning and circling,
advancing and retreating, bowing and looking up—
these are taken from them;
from court audiences, sacrifices, funerals, and military affairs—these are observed through them.
Now in the first month they hold a court audience,
yet both fail to observe the proper measure.
Their minds are already lost.
If a joyous occasion lacks substance,
how can it long endure?
Holding high and looking up—
this is arrogance;
receiving low and bowing down—
this is decline.
Arrogance approaches disorder,
decline approaches sickness.
Since our ruler is the host,
he will likely perish first!"
B11.15.2 When Wú invaded Chǔ,
Hú Zǐ captured all the people of the Chǔ towns near Hú.
After Chǔ was stabilized,
Hú Zǐ Bào again did not serve Chǔ,
saying:
"Survival and ruin are matters of fate.
What is the use of serving Chǔ?
It only incurs more expenses."
In the second month,
Chǔ destroyed Hú.
B11.15.3 In the summer, on the rénshēn day of the fifth month,
the Duke (of Lǔ) passed away.
Zhòngní said:
"It is unfortunate that Cì's words proved accurate;
this will make Cì talk even more."
B11.15.4 Zhèng's Hǎn Dá defeated the Sòng army at Lǎoqiū.
B11.15.5 The Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi stationed their troops at Qúrú,
planning to rescue Sòng.
B11.15.6 In autumn, on the rénshēn day of the seventh month,
Lady Sì died.
She was not referred to as 'Lady,'
because no death announcement was sent,
and she was not enshrined with her husband.
B11.15.7 When Duke Dìng was buried,
it rained,
and the burial could not be completed.
This was in accordance with ritual.
B11.15.8 When Dìng Sì was buried,
she was not referred to as 'Lesser Lord,'
because the full funeral rites were not observed.
B11.15.9 In winter,
the walls of Qī were fortified.
It was recorded because the notification was not timely.
A12.1 *The Classic: First Year of Duke Āi*
A12.1.1 First year, spring, the royal first month,
the Duke ascended the throne.
A12.1.2 The Viscount of Chǔ,
the Marquis of Chén,
the Marquis of Suí,
and the Baron of Xǔ besieged Cài.
A12.1.3 A mole rat ate the ox for the border sacrifice;
another ox was divined for.
In summer, on the xīnsì day of the fourth month,
the border sacrifice was held.
A12.1.4 In autumn,
the Marquis of Qí
and the Marquis of Wèi attacked Jìn.
A12.1.5 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to attack Zhū.
B12.1 *The Commentary: First Year of Duke Āi*
B12.1.1 In the spring of the first year,
the Viscount of Chǔ besieged Cài,
to repay the defeat at Bǎijǔ.
They built a siege wall one lǐ out,
one zhàng wide and twice as high.
Men were stationed there day and night for nine days,
just as Zǐxī had planned.
The people of Cài, men and women, were separated.
They were made to settle between the Jiāng
and Rǔ rivers and then (Chǔ) withdrew.
Cài then requested to move to Wú.
B12.1.2 The King of Wú, Fūchāi, defeated Yuè at Fújiāo,
to repay the defeat at Zuìlǐ.
He then entered Yuè.
The Viscount of Yuè, with five thousand armored troops, defended himself at Kuàijī,
and sent his minister Zhǒng through Wú's Grand Steward Pǐ to sue for peace.
The Viscount of Wú was about to agree.
Wǔ Yuán said:
"It cannot be done.
I have heard it said:
'In cultivating virtue, nothing is better than causing it to grow;
in removing evil, nothing is better than making a clean sweep.'
In the past, Guó's Áo killed Zhēnguàn and attacked Zhēnxún,
exterminating Xià's sovereign Xiàng.
His consort Mín was then pregnant,
and escaped through a hole in the wall,
returning to Yǒuréng,
where she gave birth to Shàokāng.
He became the herdsman-officer of Réng,
and harbored hatred for Áo, taking precautions against him.
Áo sent Jiāo to seek him out,
so he fled to Yǒuyú,
where he became the kitchen-officer,
thereby escaping harm.
Yú Sī then gave him his two daughters, the Yáo sisters, in marriage,
and enfeoffed him at Lún,
where he had one chéng of land
and one lǚ of people.
He was able to spread his virtue
and begin his plans,
gathering the remnants of Xià,
and comforting its officials;
he sent Nǚ'ài to spy on Áo,
and sent Jìzhù to entice Yì.
He then destroyed Guó and Gé,
restored Yǔ's achievements,
sacrificed to Xià and matched Heaven,
not losing the old heritage.
Now Wú is not as strong as Guó was,
and Yuè is larger than Shàokāng was.
If we allow them to grow prosperous,
will it not be difficult for us?
Gōujiàn can be close to his people and is diligent in bestowing favors.
In bestowing favors, he does not miss anyone;
in being close, he does not reject the toilsome.
He shares borders with us,
and for generations has been our enemy.
If we defeat them yet do not take them,
and instead preserve them,
we would be defying Heaven and nurturing our enemy.
Later, even if we regret it,
it will be too late to undo.
The decline of the Jī clan
can be awaited day by day.
Wedged among the barbarians,
yet nurturing our enemy—
to seek hegemony in this way
will surely not succeed."
(The King) did not listen.
(Wǔ Yuán) withdrew and told others:
"In ten years, Yuè will multiply and gather strength;
in another ten years, it will be taught and trained.
In twenty years' time,
Wú will likely become a marsh!"
In the third month,
Yuè made peace with Wú.
Wú's entry into Yuè
was not recorded,
because Wú did not announce the victory, and Yuè did not announce the defeat.
B12.1.3 In summer, the fourth month,
the Marquis of Qí and the Marquis of Wèi came to rescue Hándān,
and besieged Wǔlù.
B12.1.4 When Wú invaded Chǔ,
it summoned Duke Huái of Chén.
Duke Huái assembled the people of the state and asked them,
saying:
"Those who wish to side with Chǔ, go to the right;
those who wish to side with Wú, go to the left."
The people of Chén followed their fields (i.e., landowners went right, landless went left),
those without fields followed their faction."
Féng Huá advanced straight toward the Duke and said:
"I have heard that
a state rises because of good fortune,
and falls because of calamity.
Now Wú has not shown good fortune,
and Chǔ has not shown calamity.
Chǔ cannot be abandoned,
and Wú cannot be followed.
Moreover, Jìn
is the leader of the covenant.
If we use Jìn as an excuse to decline Wú,
what would you think?"
The Duke said:
"The state is defeated and its ruler exiled—
if that is not calamity, what is it?"
He replied:
"For a state to have such things is common enough,
why must it not recover?
If even a small state can recover,
how much more a large one?
I have heard that
when a state rises to prosperity,
it regards the people as if they were wounded—
this is its blessing;
when it perishes,
it treats the people as dirt and weeds—
this is its calamity.
Although Chǔ lacks virtue,
it does not mow down and slaughter its people.
Wú daily wears itself out with warfare,
exposing bones like thickets,
yet no virtue is seen.
Heaven is perhaps giving Chǔ a proper lesson;
when calamity befalls Wú,
how long can it last?"
Lord Chén followed this advice.
When Fūchāi conquered Yuè,
he then revived the grievances of his late lord.
In autumn, in the eighth month,
Wú invaded Chén,
to settle old grievances.
B12.1.5 The lords of Qí and Wèi met at Gānhóu,
to aid the Fàn clan.
Their army, together with the Qí army, Wèi's Kǒng Yǔ, and the Xiānyú people, attacked Jìn,
capturing Jípú.
B12.1.6 The Wú army was in Chén,
and the great officers of Chǔ were all afraid,
saying:
"Hélǘ was able to use his people,
and defeated us at Bǎijǔ.
Now we hear his successor is even more so;
what shall we do?"
Zǐxī said:
"You gentlemen should worry about not being harmonious among yourselves,
and have no fear of Wú.
In the past, Hélǘ did not eat two flavors at a meal,
did not sit on double mats,
did not raise high foundations for his houses,
did not have vessels painted or carved,
had no ornamental towers in his palaces,
and did not adorn his boats or chariots;
for clothing and expenses,
he chose what was not costly.
In the state,
when Heaven sent disasters or epidemics,
he personally visited the orphaned and widowed to supply their needs.
In the army,
when cooked food was ready, he distributed it and only then dared to eat;
whatever delicacies he tasted,
the foot soldiers and charioteers shared in them.
He diligently cared for his people,
and shared their toil and ease;
thus the people did not become exhausted,
and they knew they would not die in vain.
Our late great officer Zǐcháng took the opposite approach,
which is why he defeated us.
Now we hear that Fūchāi,
wherever he stops has terraces, pavilions, ponds, and pools;
wherever he lodges has consorts, ladies, and attendants;
for a single day's journey,
whatever he desires must be achieved,
and his playthings must follow;
he gathers precious rarities,
and devotes himself to sights and pleasures;
he regards the people as enemies,
and uses them ever more harshly.
He will first defeat himself;
how can he defeat us?"
B12.1.7 In winter, in the tenth month,
Jìn's Zhào Yǎng attacked Zhāogē.
A12.2 The Classic of Duke Āi's Second Year
A12.2.1 In the second year, spring,
in the royal second month,
Jìsūn Sī,
Shūsūn Zhōuqiú,
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to attack Zhū,
taking the fields east of Kuò and west of Yí.
On Guǐsì,
Shūsūn Zhōuqiú,
Zhòngsūn Héjì, and the Viscount of Zhū made a covenant at Gōuyì.
A12.2.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on Bǐngzǐ,
Lord Wèi Yuán died.
A12.2.3 The Viscount of Téng came to court.
A12.2.4 Jìn's Zhào Yǎng led an army to escort Wèi's heir apparent Kuǎikuì into Qī.
A12.2.5 In autumn, in the eighth month, on Jiǎxū,
Jìn's Zhào Yǎng led an army and fought with Zhèng's Hǎn Dá, who led an army, at Tiě.
The Zhèng army was utterly defeated.
A12.2.6 In winter, in the tenth month,
Lord Wèi Líng was buried.
A12.2.7 In the eleventh month,
Cài moved to Zhōulái.
Cài killed its great officer, Prince Sì.
B12.2 The Commentary of Duke Āi's Second Year
B12.2.1 In the second year, spring,
they attacked Zhū,
intending to attack Jiǎo.
The people of Zhū cherished their land,
so they bribed them with the fields of Kuò and Yí and accepted the covenant.
B12.2.2 Earlier,
Lord Wèi was traveling in the suburbs,
with Zǐnán as his charioteer.
The lord said:
"I have no son,
and will establish you."
He did not reply.
On another day, the lord said it again,
and he replied:
"Yǐng is not worthy to disgrace the altars of soil and grain;
please, my lord, change your plan.
Your lady is in the hall,
and the three ranks of ministers are below;
your command would only bring disgrace."
In summer,
Lord Wèi Líng died.
The lady said:
"Command that Prince Yǐng be made heir apparent—
it is the lord's command."
He replied:
"Yǐng is different from the other sons,
and moreover, the lord died in my hands;
if there were such a command,
Yǐng would surely have heard of it.
Moreover, the son of the exile, Zhé, is here."
So they established Zhé.
In the sixth month, on Yǐyǒu,
Jìn's Zhào Yǎng escorted Wèi's heir apparent into Qī.
They lost their way at night,
and Yánghǔ said:
"Keep the river on the right and go south,
and you will surely arrive."
They had the heir apparent wear mourning garb,
with eight men in mourning clothes and hempen bands,
pretending to be a welcoming party from Wèi.
They announced themselves at the gate,
entered weeping,
and thus took up residence there.
B12.2.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
the people of Qí transported grain to the Fàn clan,
and Zhèng's Zǐyáo and Zǐbān escorted it.
Shì Jíshè went to meet them,
and Zhào Yǎng defended against them,
meeting at Qī.
Yánghǔ said:
"Our chariots are few;
let us take the banners of the war chariots and array them with the war chariots of Hǎn and Sì in front.
Hǎn and Sì will follow behind them,
and when the enemy sees our appearance,
they will surely be afraid;
then if we join battle,
we will surely greatly defeat them."
They followed this.
They divined about the battle,
and the turtle shell cracked.
Yuè Dīng said:
"The Odes say:
'Then we begin, then we plan,
then we notch our turtle.'
Since the plan is harmonious,
we may consult the old crack."
Jiǎnzǐ made an oath, saying:
"The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans have overturned Heaven's bright mandate,
cutting down and slaughtering the common people,
wishing to monopolize Jìn and destroy their lord.
Our humble lord relies on Zhèng to preserve himself.
Now Zhèng acts without principle,
abandoning the lord and aiding the ministers.
You gentlemen follow Heaven's bright mandate,
obey the lord's command,
uphold virtue and righteousness,
and wipe away shame and disgrace—
it is in this campaign.
Those who defeat the enemy: upper great officers will receive a county,
lower great officers will receive a commandery,
officers will receive 100,000 mu of land,
commoners, artisans, and merchants will achieve their status,
and servants, slaves, and grooms will be freed.
If Zhìfǔ is without fault,
the lord should consider it!
If he is at fault,
let him be strangled and executed,
with a coffin of tong wood three inches thick,
no inner coffin, plain carriage, and unadorned horses,
not to be buried in the ancestral cemetery—
this is the punishment for a lower minister."
On the jiǎxū day,
as they were about to engage in battle,
Yōu Wúxù drove for Jiǎnzǐ,
with the crown prince of Wèi as the chariot warrior.
They ascended Tiě Hill,
and upon seeing the multitude of the Zhèng army,
the crown prince became frightened
and threw himself down from the chariot.
Zǐliáng handed the crown prince the chariot strap,
helped him back onto the chariot,
and said:
"You are like a woman."
Jiǎnzǐ inspected the ranks
and said:
"Bì Wàn
was a common man,
yet in seven battles he captured prisoners each time,
and came to possess a hundred chariots.
He died peacefully in his bed.
All of you, exert yourselves!
Death does not necessarily come from the enemy."
Fán Yǔ drove for Zhào Luó,
with Sòng Yǒng as the chariot warrior.
Luó lacked courage,
so they bound him.
When an officer questioned them,
the driver replied:
"He is suffering from a malaria attack and is lying down."
The crown prince of Wèi prayed, saying:
"Your great-grandson Kuǎikuì dares to clearly report to the august ancestor King Wén,
the illustrious ancestor Kāngshū,
and the cultured ancestor Xiānggōng:
Zhèng Shèng has brought disorder upon the proper order,
and Jìn Wǔ is in distress,
unable to bring order to the chaos.
He has sent Yāng to punish him.
Kuǎikuì does not dare to indulge in ease,
but stands ready with his spear.
I dare to pray that I not have my sinews severed,
nor my bones broken,
nor my face wounded,
so that I may accomplish the great task,
and not bring shame upon my three ancestors.
I dare not ask for a long life,
nor do I begrudge my girdle jades."
A man of Zhèng struck Jiǎnzǐ, hitting his shoulder,
and he fell in his chariot.
They captured his banner with the bee emblem.
The crown prince rescued him with a dagger-axe.
The Zhèng army fled northward,
and they captured the grand officer of Wēn, Zhào Luó.
The crown prince again attacked them,
and the Zhèng army was greatly defeated.
They captured a thousand chariots of grain from Qí.
Zhào Mèng joyfully said:
"It is enough."
Fù Sǒu said:
"Although we have defeated Zhèng,
Zhī is still there,
so our worries are not yet over."
Earlier,
a man of Zhōu had given fields to the Fàn clan,
and Gōngsūn Lóng collected the taxes from them.
The Zhào clan captured him and presented him.
The officers requested to kill him.
Zhào Mèng said:
"He was acting for his master.
What crime is that?"
He spared him and gave him fields.
At the time of the battle of Tiě,
Gōngsūn Lóng led five hundred foot soldiers and attacked the Zhèng army by night,
taking the bee banner from beneath Zǐ Yáo's tent.
He presented it,
saying:
"I beg to repay my master's kindness."
When they pursued the Zhèng army,
Yáo, Bān, and Gōngsūn Lín covered the rear and shot arrows,
and many in the front ranks died.
Zhào Mèng said:
"No state is too small to be taken seriously."
After the battle,
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I lay prostrate over my bow-case, vomiting blood,
yet the sound of my drum did not weaken.
Today, I am the best."
The crown prince said:
"I rescued my lord on the chariot,
and drove back the enemy below.
I
am the best among the chariot warriors."
Yōuliáng said:
"The two traces of my team were about to break,
and I was able to stop them.
I
am the best among the drivers."
He then drove the chariot over some timber,
and both traces broke.
B12.2.4 Wú sent Xiè Yōng to Cài to present betrothal gifts,
and gradually introduced troops.
When the troops had all entered,
the multitude became aware of it.
The marquis of Cài informed his grand officers,
and killed Gōngzǐ Sì to appease them.
They wept and moved their ancestral graves.
In winter,
Cài moved to Zhōulái.
A12.3 The Classic of the third year of Duke Āi
A12.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
Qí Guó Xià
and Wèi Shí Màngū led armies to besiege Qī.
A12.3.2 In summer, in the fourth month, on the jiǎwǔ day,
there was an earthquake.
A12.3.3 In the fifth month, on the xīnmǎo day,
the temple of Duke Huán
and the temple of Duke Xī were destroyed by fire.
A12.3.4 Jìsūn Sī
and Shūsūn Zhōuqiú led armies to wall Qǐyáng.
A12.3.5 Sòng Yuè Kūn led an army to attack Cáo.
A12.3.6 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the bǐngzǐ day,
Jìsūn Sī died.
A12.3.7 The men of Cài exiled their grand officer Gōngsūn Liè to Wú.
A12.3.8 In winter, in the tenth month, on the guǐmǎo day,
the earl of Qín died.
A12.3.9 Shūsūn Zhōuqiú
and Zhòngsūn Héjì led armies to besiege Zhū.
B12.3 The Commentary of the third year of Duke Āi
B12.3.1 In the third year, in spring,
Qí and Wèi besieged Qī,
and sought aid from Zhōngshān.
B12.3.2 In summer, in the fifth month, on the xīnmǎo day,
a fire broke out in the Sīduó office.
The fire crossed over to the duke's palace,
and the temples of Huán and Xī were destroyed.
Those fighting the fire all said to look after the treasuries.
When Nángōng Jìngshū arrived,
he ordered the official in charge of documents to bring out the royal writings,
and wait in the palace,
saying:
"I entrust them to you.
If they are not here,
you will die."
When Zǐfú Jǐngbó arrived,
he ordered the steward to bring out the books on rites,
and wait for orders.
He said that failure to comply
would incur the regular punishment.
The master of the horse prepared the horses,
the master of the chariots greased the linchpins,
all officials attended to their duties,
the treasuries and storehouses were carefully guarded,
and the palace officers were respectfully supplied.
They soaked curtains and screens,
and followed with firefighting equipment.
They covered the duke's buildings with wet materials,
starting from the great temple,
working from the outside inward in order.
They assisted where supplies were insufficient.
If anyone disobeyed orders,
the regular punishment would be applied,
with no pardon.
When Gōngfù Wénbó arrived,
he ordered the master of the horse to harness the carriage.
When Jì Huánzǐ arrived,
he drove the duke's carriage and stood outside the Xiàngwéi gate,
ordering those fighting the fire to stop if there was risk of injury to people,
as property could be replaced.
He ordered the "Xiàngwéi" to be stored away,
saying:
"The old statutes must not be lost."
When Fùfù Huái arrived,
he said:
"To have officials manage things without preparation
is like trying to pick up spilled soup."
Thereupon, they removed the dry thatch from the markers,
and cleared the roads around the duke's palace.
Confucius was in Chén,
and when he heard about the fire,
he said:
"It must be the temples of Huán and Xī!"
B12.3.3 The Liú and Fàn clans had been intermarrying for generations,
and Cháng Hóng served Liú Wéngōng,
so Zhōu sided with the Fàn clan.
Zhào Yāng held this against them.
In the sixth month, on the guǐmǎo day,
the men of Zhōu killed Cháng Hóng.
B12.3.4 In autumn,
Jìsūn fell ill.
He commanded Zhèngcháng, saying:
"Do not die!
If the son born to the Nánrúzi
is a male,
then report it and establish him.
If it is a female,
then Féi can do."
Jìsūn died,
and Kāngzǐ assumed his position.
After the burial was completed,
Kāngzǐ was at court.
The Nán clan gave birth to a boy.
Zhèngcháng carried him and went to court,
and reported, saying:
"The Master left a dying command,
ordering this humble servant, saying:
'If the Nán clan gives birth to a boy,
then report it to the ruler and the great officers and establish him.'
Now he has been born,
a boy.
I dare to report it."
Thereupon, he fled to Wèi.
Kāngzǐ requested to retire.
The Duke sent Gòng Liú to look at the child,
but someone had already killed him.
Then they sought out the culprit.
They summoned Zhèngcháng,
but Zhèngcháng did not return.
B12.3.5 In winter, in the tenth month,
Jìn's Zhào Yāng besieged Zhāogē.
His army was to its south.
Xún Yín attacked its outer wall.
He made his followers enter from the north gate,
and he himself charged through the army and got out.
On Guǐchǒu day,
he fled to Hándān.
In the eleventh month,
Zhào Yāng killed Shì Gāoyí,
because he hated the Fàn clan.
A12.4 The Spring and Autumn Annals, the Fourth Year of Duke Āi
A12.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
in the royal second month, on the Gēngxū day,
bandits killed the Marquis of Cài, Shēn.
A12.4.2 Cài's Gōngsūn Chén fled to Wú.
A12.4.3 They buried Duke Huì of Qín.
A12.4.4 The men of Sòng seized the ruler of Xiǎozhū.
A12.4.5 In summer,
Cài killed its great officers Gōngsūn Xìng
and Gōngsūn Huò.
A12.4.6 The men of Jìn seized the Róng Mánzǐ Chì and sent him to Chǔ.
A12.4.7 They walled the western outer wall.
A12.4.8 In the sixth month, on the Xīnchǒu day,
the Bó Shrine suffered a fire.
A12.4.9 In autumn, in the eighth month, on the Jiǎyín day,
the ruler of Téng, Jié, died.
A12.4.10 In winter, in the twelfth month,
they buried Duke Zhāo of Cài.
A12.4.11 They buried Duke Qǐng of Téng.
B12.4 The Commentary of Zuo, the Fourth Year of Duke Āi
B12.4.1 In the fourth year, in spring,
Marquis Zhāo of Cài was about to go to Wú.
The various great officers, fearing he would move [the capital] again,
following Gōngsūn Piān, pursued and shot at him.
He entered a commoner's house and died.
[Piān] used two arrows to guard the gate,
and the multitude dared not advance.
Wén Zhīkǎi arrived later,
and said:
"Advance like a wall,
and at most he can kill two men."
Kǎi took up his bow and went first.
Piān shot at him,
hitting his elbow.
Kǎi then killed him.
Therefore, they drove out Gōngsūn Chén and killed Gōngsūn Xìng and Gōngsūn Xū.
B12.4.2 In summer,
the men of Chǔ, having already subdued the Yíhǔ,
then planned against the north.
The Left Minister of War Pàn, Shēngōng Shòuyú,
and Yègōng Zhūliáng assembled [the people of] Cài at Fùhán,
and assembled those outside the Fāngchéng [wall] at Zēngguān,
saying:
"Wú is about to ascend the river and enter Yǐng.
You will have to rush to its defense."
They set a one-night deadline,
and attacked Liáng and Huò.
Shàn Fúyú besieged the Mán clan,
and the Mán clan collapsed.
The Mánzǐ Chì fled to the Yīndì territory of Jìn.
The Minister of War raised troops from Fēng, Xī, and the Dí and Róng tribes,
and approached Shàngluò.
The left army encamped at Túhé,
the right army encamped at Cāngyě,
and they sent a message to the appointed great officer of Yīndì, Shì Miè, saying:
"Jìn and Chǔ have a covenant,
sharing likes and dislikes.
If this is not to be abandoned,
it is the wish of our humble ruler.
If not,
we will open a route through Shǎoxí to await your commands."
Shì Miè requested instructions from Zhào Mèng.
Zhào Mèng said:
"The state of Jìn is not at peace.
How can we incur the enmity of Chǔ?
You must quickly give him to them!"
Shì Miè then assembled the Róng of Jiǔzhōu,
intending to allocate fields to the Mánzǐ and build a walled city for him,
and was about to perform divination for him.
The Mánzǐ came to hear the divination,
whereupon [Shì Miè] seized him and his five great officers,
and handed them over to the Chǔ army at Sānhù.
The Minister of War presented him with a town and established a lineage for him there,
to lure his remaining people,
and then captured them all and returned.
B12.4.3 In autumn, in the seventh month,
Qí's Chén Qǐ, Xuán Shī, and Wèi's Níng Guì came to rescue the Fàn clan.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
they besieged Wǔlù.
In the ninth month,
Zhào Yāng besieged Hándān.
In winter, in the eleventh month,
Hándān surrendered.
Xún Yín fled to Xiānyú,
and Zhào Jì fled to Lín.
In the twelfth month,
Xuán Shī went to meet him,
and then razed Lín.
Guó Xià attacked Jìn,
capturing Xíng, Rén, Luán, Hào,
Nìzhì, Yīnrén, Yú, and Húkǒu.
He joined forces with Xiānyú,
and installed Xún Yín at Bóirén.
A12.5 The Spring and Autumn Annals, the Fifth Year of Duke Āi
A12.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
they walled Pí.
A12.5.2 In summer,
the Marquis of Qí attacked Sòng.
A12.5.3 Jìn's Zhào Yāng led an army to attack Wèi.
A12.5.4 In autumn, in the ninth month, on the Guǐyǒu day,
the Marquis of Qí, Chǔjiù, died.
A12.5.5 In winter,
Shū Huán went to Qí.
A12.5.6 In the intercalary month,
they buried Duke Jǐng of Qí.
B12.5 The Commentary of Zuo, the Fifth Year of Duke Āi
B12.5.1 In the fifth year, in spring,
Jìn besieged Bóirén.
Xún Yín and Shì Jíshè fled to Qí.
Earlier,
a retainer of the Fàn clan, Wángshēng, hated Zhāng Liǔshuò.
He spoke of him to Zhāozǐ,
recommending him to be [the governor of] Bóirén.
Zhāozǐ said:
"Is he not your enemy?"
He replied:
"Private enmity does not interfere with public affairs.
Fondness does not cover up faults,
hatred does not discard goodness.
This is the constant principle of righteousness.
How dare I violate it?"
When the Fàn clan was driven out,
Zhāng Liǔshuò said to his son:
"You follow the master.
Exert yourself!
I will stay and die.
Wángshēng entrusted me with this.
I cannot betray it."
Thereupon, he died at Bóirén.
B12.5.2 In summer,
Zhào Yāng attacked Wèi,
because of the Fàn clan affair,
and then besieged Zhōngmóu.
B12.5.3 Qí Yān Jī gave birth to a son,
but he did not survive and died.
Among the various sons, Yù Sì's son Tú was favored.
The senior officials feared he would be made crown prince,
and spoke to the Duke, saying:
"Your age is advanced,
and you have no crown prince.
What is to be done?"
The Duke said:
"If you gentlemen trouble yourselves with worries and anxieties,
then illness will arise.
Just seek pleasure for now.
Why worry about having no ruler?"
When the Duke fell ill,
he ordered Guó Huìzǐ and Gāo Zhāozǐ to establish Tú,
and placed the other princes in Lái.
In autumn,
Duke Jǐng of Qí died.
In winter, the tenth month,
Prince Jiā, Prince Jū, and Prince Qián fled to Wèi,
while Prince Chú and Prince Yángshēng came fleeing [to our state].
The people of Lái sang of it, saying:
"Duke Jǐng died, yet we had no part in his burial;
the affairs of the three armies, yet we had no part in their planning.
Oh, you multitude! Oh, you multitude!
To what faction do you belong?"
B12.5.4 Zhèng Sì Qín was wealthy and extravagant.
Though he was only a favored junior official,
he often displayed the carriages and robes of a minister in his courtyard.
The people of Zhèng despised him and killed him.
Zǐsī said:
"The *Book of Songs* says:
'Not remiss in their duties,
the people find their rest.'
Those who do not keep to their proper station and yet can last long are few indeed.
The *Shāng Odes* say:
'Not transgressing, not exceeding,
not daring to be idle or hasty,
they receive command of much happiness.'"
A12.6 *The Sixth Year of Duke Āi, the Classic*
A12.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
we walled Zhūxiá.
A12.6.2 Jìn Zhào Yǎng led an army to attack Xiānyú.
A12.6.3 Wú attacked Chén.
A12.6.4 In summer,
Qí Guó Xià and Gāo Zhāng came fleeing [to our state].
A12.6.5 Shū Huì met with Wú at Zhā.
A12.6.6 In autumn, in the seventh month, on the gēngyín day,
the Viscount of Chǔ, Zhěn, died.
A12.6.7 Qí Yángshēng entered Qí.
A12.6.8 Qí Chén Qǐ assassinated his ruler, Tú.
A12.6.9 In winter,
Zhòngsūn Héjì led an army to attack Zhū.
A12.6.10 Sòng Xiàng Cháo led an army to attack Cáo.
B12.6 *The Sixth Year of Duke Āi, the Commentary*
B12.6.1 In the sixth year, in spring,
Jìn attacked Xiānyú,
to settle the disorder caused by the Fàn clan.
B12.6.2 Wú attacked Chén,
resuming an old grievance.
The Viscount of Chǔ said:
"Our former ruler had a covenant with Chén;
we cannot fail to rescue them."
He then went to rescue Chén,
stationing his army at Chéngfù.
B12.6.3 Qí Chén Qǐ pretended to serve Gāo and Guó.
Every time he went to court,
he would invariably ride in the same carriage with them.
Wherever he accompanied them,
he would invariably say to the various senior officials:
"They are all arrogant and haughty,
and will cast aside your orders.
They all say:
'Gāo and Guó have gained the ruler's favor;
they are sure to oppress us.
Why not get rid of them?'
They are certainly planning against you.
You should plan early against them!
To plan against them,
nothing is better than to exterminate them all.
Hesitation
is the lowest form of action."
And when at court,
he would say:
"They
are tigers and wolves.
Seeing me at your side,
they will kill me any day now.
I beg to take my place among them."
He also said to the various senior officials:
"Those two men are heading for disaster.
Relying on having gained the ruler's favor, they wish to plot against you gentlemen,
saying:
'The many troubles of the state
arise from the honored and favored.
Only after removing them all can the ruler be secure.'
Their plan is already formed.
Why not, before they act,
strike first?
If we act only after they do,
regret will be of no avail."
The senior officials followed him.
In summer, in the sixth month, on the wùchén day,
Chén Qǐ, Bào Mù, and the various senior officials entered the ducal palace in armor.
Zhāozǐ heard of it,
and rode with Huìzǐ to the Duke.
They fought at Zhuāng,
and were defeated.
The men of the capital pursued them.
Guó Xià fled to Jǔ,
and subsequently, along with Gāo Zhāng, Yàn Yǔ, and Xián Shī, came fleeing [to our state].
B12.6.4 In autumn, in the seventh month,
the Viscount of Chǔ was at Chéngfù,
preparing to rescue Chén.
They divined about battle,
and it was not auspicious;
they divined about retreat,
and it was not auspicious.
The King said:
"Then it means death.
To be defeated again by the Chǔ army
is worse than death;
to abandon a covenant and flee from an enemy
is also worse than death.
Since death is the same in either case,
let me die facing the enemy!"
He ordered Prince Shēn to become king,
but he would not accept;
then he ordered Prince Jié,
but he also would not accept;
then he ordered Prince Qǐ,
who declined five times before consenting.
As they were about to engage in battle,
the King fell ill.
On the gēngyín day,
King Zhāo attacked Dàmíng,
and died at Chéngfù.
Zǐ Lǘ withdrew,
and said:
"The royal king set aside his own sons and yielded [the throne].
How dare we ministers forget our ruler?
To follow the ruler's command
is accord with duty;
to establish the ruler's son
is also accord with duty.
These two paths of duty must not be lost."
He plotted with Zǐ Xī and Zǐ Qī,
secretly moving troops, closing the fortifications,
and welcoming Zhāng, the son of the Yuè woman, establishing him,
and then they returned.
In this year,
there were clouds resembling many red birds,
flying on both sides of the sun for three days.
The Viscount of Chǔ sent to inquire of the Grand Historian of Zhōu.
The Grand Historian of Zhōu said:
"It likely portends something for the king's person!
If you perform the yíng sacrifice,
it can be transferred to the Prime Minister or the Minister of War."
The King said:
"To remove a disease from the heart and belly,
and place it on the limbs,
what good is that?
If I, the unworthy one, have not committed great faults,
would Heaven cut me off?
If I have committed offenses and deserve punishment,
then how can it be transferred?"
So he did not perform the yíng sacrifice.
Earlier,
when King Zhāo was ill,
the divination said:
"The Hé River is causing the affliction."
The King did not sacrifice to it.
The senior officials requested to sacrifice to it in the suburbs.
The King said:
"The three dynasties ordained the sacrifices;
sacrifices do not go beyond one's own borders.
The Jiāng, Hàn, Jū, and Zhāng rivers
are within the borders of Chǔ.
The arrival of fortune or misfortune
does not go beyond these.
Although I, the unworthy one, lack virtue,
the Hé River is not one for which I could incur offense."
So he did not sacrifice.
Confucius said:
"King Zhāo of Chǔ understood the great Way.
That he did not lose his state
is fitting indeed!"
The Book of Xia says:
'That Táng of Yáo,
following the constant ways of Heaven,
possessed this region of Jì.
Now having lost his proper course,
disordering his laws and principles,
he was thereby destroyed and perished.'
It also says:
'What is given out from this resides in this.'
To lead by following the constant ways oneself,
is acceptable."
B12.6.5 In the eighth month,
Bǐng Yìzī of Qí came fleeing.
B12.6.6 Chén Xīzǐ sent to summon the prince, Yángshēng.
Yángshēng harnessed a carriage and went to see Nánguō Qiěyú,
saying:
"I once presented horses to Jìsūn,
but they were not counted among the superior teams.
Therefore, I am presenting these again,
and I ask to try them out with you."
They went out the Lái gate, and he then told him the real reason.
Kàn Zhǐ knew about it,
and first waited for him outside.
The prince said: "The outcome of the affair is unknown.
Return,
and stay with Rén."
He gave him instructions,
and then proceeded.
Reaching nightfall, he arrived in Qí,
and the people of the state knew about it.
Xīzǐ had the mother of Zǐshì care for him,
and he entered along with those delivering provisions.
In winter, on the dīngmǎo day of the tenth month,
they set him up.
They were about to swear the covenant,
when Bàozi arrived drunk.
His minister, the chariot officer Bào Diǎn, said:
"Whose command is this?"
Chénzǐ said: "We received the command from Bàozi."
Thereupon he falsely accused Bàozi, saying:
"It was your command!"
Bàozi said:
"Have you forgotten how the ruler acted as a buffalo for the young boy and broke his tooth,
and now you betray him?"
Duke Dào bowed his head to the ground,
saying:
"You, sir,
are one who acts according to righteousness.
If I am acceptable,
there is no need to lose a single great officer;
if I am not acceptable,
there is no need to lose a single prince.
If it is righteous, advance;
if not, withdraw.
How dare I not follow you alone?
That neither setting aside nor raising up should cause disorder,
that is my wish."
Bàozi said:
"Who is not the ruler's son?"
He then accepted the covenant.
They sent Hú Jī to take the young boy Ān Rúzǐ to Lài,
removed Yù Sì,
killed Wáng Jiǎ,
arrested Jiāng Yuè,
and imprisoned Wáng Bào at the hill of Gōudòu.
The duke sent Zhū Máo to inform Chénzǐ,
saying:
"Without you, sir,
I would not have reached this position.
However, a ruler is different from a vessel;
there cannot be two.
With two vessels there is no shortage,
but with two rulers there is much trouble.
I venture to lay this before the great officers."
Xīzǐ did not reply but wept,
saying:
"Does the ruler in his actions not trust his ministers?
Because of Qí's difficulties,
and the further troubles amidst those difficulties,
the young ruler could not be consulted.
Therefore we sought an older ruler,
hoping he might also be able to accommodate his ministers!
If not, what crime did that young boy have?"
Máo reported back,
and the duke regretted it.
Máo said:
"For major matters, the ruler consults Chénzǐ,
