but for minor ones, he may plan them himself."
He sent Máo to move the young boy to Tái.
Before reaching it,
he killed him beneath a tent in the wilds,
and buried him at Shūmàochún.
A12.7 The Spring and Autumn Annals: The Seventh Year of Duke Āi
A12.7.1 In the seventh year, in spring,
Huáng Yuàn of Sòng led a force to invade Zhèng.
A12.7.2 Wèi Mànduō of Jìn led a force to invade Wèi.
A12.7.3 In summer,
the duke met with Wú at Zēng.
A12.7.4 In autumn,
the duke attacked Zhū.
In the eighth month, on the jǐyǒu day,
he entered Zhū,
and brought back the Viscount of Zhū, Yì.
A12.7.5 The men of Sòng besieged Cáo.
In winter, Sì Hóng of Zhèng led a force to rescue Cáo.
B12.7 The Commentary: The Seventh Year of Duke Āi
B12.7.1 In the seventh year, in spring,
the army of Sòng invaded Zhèng,
because Zhèng had turned against Jìn.
B12.7.2 The army of Jìn invaded Wèi,
because Wèi was not submissive.
B12.7.3 In summer,
the duke met with Wú at Zēng.
Wú came to demand one hundred sets of sacrificial animals.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó replied:
"The former kings never had such a thing."
The men of Wú said:
"Sòng gave us one hundred sets;
Lǔ cannot lag behind Sòng.
Moreover, Lǔ gave the great officers of Jìn over ten sets;
for the king of Wú to receive one hundred sets,
is that not acceptable?"
Jǐngbó said:
"Fàn Yāng of Jìn was greedy and abandoned ritual,
using his great state to intimidate our humble city.
Therefore, our humble city gave him eleven sets.
If you, sir, command the various lords according to ritual,
then there is a fixed number.
If you also abandon ritual,
then there are excesses.
When Zhōu ruled as king,
it established the rituals,
and the highest number of offerings did not exceed twelve,
considering that the great number of Heaven.
Now abandoning the rituals of Zhōu,
and saying it must be one hundred sets —
that is entirely up to you, the officers in charge."
The men of Wú would not listen.
Jǐngbó said:
"Wú is about to perish,
abandoning Heaven and turning its back on its roots.
If we do not give it,
they will certainly vent their anger on us."
So they gave it to them.
Grand Steward Pǐ summoned Jì Kāngzǐ,
and Kāngzǐ sent Zǐgòng to decline.
Grand Steward Pǐ said: "The ruler of a state travels a long road,
yet his great officer does not leave his gate.
What ritual is this?"
He replied:
"How could this be considered ritual?
It is from fear of a great state.
If a great state does not command the various lords according to ritual,
and if it does not act according to ritual,
how can its actions be measured?
Since our humble ruler has already complied with your command,
how would his senior minister dare abandon his state?
Tàibó wore the ceremonial cap and robes to administer the rituals of Zhōu;
Zhòngyōng succeeded him,
cut his hair and tattooed his body,
going naked as an ornament —
was that ritual?
There was a reason for it."
Returning from Zēng,
they considered Wú incapable of achieving anything.
B12.7.4 Jì Kāngzǐ wished to attack Zhū,
so he feasted the great officers to plan it.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó said:
"The means by which the small serve the great
is good faith;
the means by which the great protect the small
is benevolence.
To turn against a great state
is to lack good faith;
to attack a small state
is to lack benevolence.
The people are protected by the city walls,
the city walls are protected by virtue.
Losing these two virtues,
brings danger —
what then will there be to protect?"
Méngsūn said:
"What do you gentlemen think?
Which view is worthy, and which should we oppose?"
He replied:
"Yǔ assembled the feudal lords at Túshān,
and those who held jades and silks numbered ten thousand states.
Now those that remain
are not even several tens,
solely because the great do not nurture the small,
and the small do not serve the great.
Knowing it would certainly be perilous,
why did you not speak?
Lǔ's virtue is like Zhū's,
yet to attack it with a multitude—
is this permissible?"
He left displeased.
In autumn,
they attacked Zhū,
reaching Fànmén,
and still heard the sound of bells.
The great officers remonstrated,
but he did not listen.
Máo Chéngzǐ requested to inform Wú,
but it was not permitted.
He said:
"Lǔ's watchman's clappers are heard in Zhū;
Wú is two thousand lǐ away,
and cannot arrive in less than three months—
how can they reach us in time?
Moreover, is our state not sufficient within?"
Chéngzǐ rebelled with Máo,
and the army then entered Zhū,
occupying its ducal palace.
The troops plundered by day,
and the people of Zhū took refuge at Yì.
The army plundered by night,
and brought Zhūzǐ Yì back,
presenting him at the Bó Shè,
and imprisoning him at Fùxiá—
Fùxiá originally had Yì.
Zhū's Máo Yíhóng, with bolts of silk and teams of tanned leather, personally requested rescue from Wú,
saying:
"Lǔ belittles Jìn and distances Wú,
relying on its multitude,
and betraying your covenant,
avoiding your officers,
to oppress our small state.
Zhū does not dare to cherish itself,
but fears that your majesty's authority will not be established.
If your majesty's authority is not established,
it is a worry for small states.
If in summer they covenanted at Zēngyǎn,
and in autumn betrayed it,
achieving their demands without opposition,
how will the feudal lords of the four quarters serve you, my lord?
Moreover, Lǔ's levy is eight hundred chariots—
they are your second;
Zhū's levy is six hundred chariots—
they are your private possession.
To offer your private possession to your second—
may your lordship consider it!"
Wúzǐ followed this.
The men of Sòng besieged Cáo.
Zhèng's Huánzǐ Sī said:
"If the men of Sòng possess Cáo,
it will be a calamity for Zhèng—
we cannot not rescue them."
In winter,
the army of Zhèng rescued Cáo,
invading Sòng.
Earlier,
a man of Cáo dreamed that many gentlemen were standing at the shrine of the soil,
planning the destruction of Cáo.
Cáo Shū Zhènduó requested to wait for Gōngsūn Qiáng,
and they agreed.
At dawn he sought him
in Cáo, but he was not there.
He warned his son, saying:
"When I die,
if you hear that Gōngsūn Qiáng is in government,
you must leave."
When Cáo Bó Yáng ascended the throne,
he was fond of hunting and archery.
A man from the borders of Cáo, Gōngsūn Qiáng, was fond of archery;
he captured a white wild goose,
presented it,
and spoke of the methods of hunting and archery.
Yáng was pleased with him.
He then consulted him on affairs of government,
and was greatly pleased with him.
He gained favor,
and was made Sīchéng to administer government.
The son of the dreamer then departed.
Qiáng spoke to Cáo Bó about the way of hegemony,
and Cáo Bó followed him,
then betrayed Jìn and offended Sòng.
The men of Sòng attacked them,
and the men of Jìn did not rescue them.
They built five settlements in its outskirts,
called Shǔqiū, Yīqiū,
Dàchéng, Zhōng, and Yú.
A12.8 The Classic of the Eighth Year of Duke Āi
In the eighth year, spring,
the royal first month,
the Duke of Sòng entered Cáo,
and took Cáo Bó Yáng back with him.
Wú attacked us.
In summer,
the men of Qí took Huān and Chǎn.
They returned Zhūzǐ Yì to Zhū.
In autumn, the seventh month.
In winter, on the twelfth month, guǐhài day,
Qǐ Bó Guò died.
The men of Qí returned Huān and Chǎn.
B12.8 The Commentary of the Eighth Year of Duke Āi
In the eighth year, spring,
the Duke of Sòng attacked Cáo and was about to return,
with Chǔshī Zǐféi bringing up the rear.
The men of Cáo reviled him,
and he did not move.
The army waited for him.
The duke heard of this,
was angry,
ordered a return,
then destroyed Cáo,
capturing Cáo Bó Yáng and Sīchéng Qiáng to bring back,
and killed them.
Wú, for the sake of Zhū,
was about to attack Lǔ,
and asked Shūsūn Zhé.
Shūsūn Zhé replied:
"Lǔ has a name but no substance;
attacking it,
you will certainly achieve your aim."
He withdrew and told Gōngshān Bùniǔ.
Gōngshān Bùniǔ said:
"This is contrary to ritual.
When a nobleman leaves his state,
he does not go to a hostile state.
Not having submitted as a subject, yet to attack it—
if ordered to go,
he may die for it.
But if entrusted with a task, he should conceal himself.
Moreover, in a man's conduct,
he does not, because of what he dislikes, bring ruin to his homeland.
Now you, because of a small dislike, wish to overturn your ancestral state—is this not wrong?
If they make you lead,
you must decline.
The king will employ me."
Zǐzhāng disliked this.
The king asked Zǐxiè.
He replied:
"Although Lǔ has none to stand with it,
it certainly has some to perish with it.
The feudal lords will rescue it;
you cannot achieve your aim there.
Jìn and Qí, Chǔ will assist it—
these are four enemies.
Lǔ
is the lips to Qí and Jìn's teeth.
If the lips are gone, the teeth are cold—
this you, my lord, know.
Why would they not rescue it?"
In the third month,
Wú attacked us.
Zǐxiè led,
so he took a dangerous road,
passing through Wǔchéng.
Earlier,
some men of Wǔchéng had fields within the borders of Wú,
and detained men of Zēng who were steeping rushes,
saying:
"Why do you make our water turbid?"
When the Wú army arrived,
the detainers guided them to attack Wǔchéng,
and they captured it.
Wáng Fàn had once been its steward,
and Dàntái Zǐyǔ's father was on good terms with him,
so the people of the state were afraid.
Yìzǐ said to Jǐngbó:
"What is to be done?"
He replied:
"When the Wú army comes,
then fight them—
what worry is there?
Moreover, we summoned them and they came—
what more do we seek?"
The Wú army captured Dōngyáng and advanced,
The next day,
they encamped at the silkworm chamber.
Gōng Bīn Gēng,
Gōng Jiǎ Shūzǐ engaged in battle at Yí,
captured Shūzǐ and Xī Zhūchú,
and presented them to the king.
The king said:
"These men shared the same chariot,
so they must have been capable men.
The state cannot be underestimated."
The next day,
they encamped at Gēngzōng,
and then stationed at the banks of the Sì River.
Wēi Hǔ wanted to launch a night attack on the king's encampment,
and privately selected seven hundred men who leaped three times in the tent courtyard,
ultimately choosing three hundred men,
among whom was Yǒu Ruò.
When they reached inside the Jì Gate,
someone said to Jì Sūn:
"This is not enough to harm Wú,
but will only result in the death of many of our state's finest men.
It would be better to stop."
So he halted the attack.
When the ruler of Wú heard of this,
he relocated three times in one night.
The men of Wú sought peace,
and as they were about to make a covenant,
Jǐng Bó said:
"When the men of Chǔ besieged Sòng,
they exchanged children to eat,
and split bones to cook,
yet they still did not make a covenant under the city walls.
We have not yet reached such a state of depletion,
yet we would make a covenant under the city walls—
this is to abandon the state.
Wú is arrogant and far from home,
and cannot stay long.
They are about to return;
I ask that we wait a little longer."
They did not listen.
Jǐng Bó carried the covenant text on his back
and went to the Lái Gate.
He then requested that Zǐfú Hé be released to Wú,
and the men of Wú agreed,
offering Prince Gū Cáo in exchange,
and only then did they stop.
The men of Wú made the covenant and returned.
B12.8.3 When Qí Dào Gōng came,
Jì Kāngzǐ gave him his younger sister as a wife.
After he ascended the throne, he went to fetch her.
Jì Fánghóu had an affair with her,
and the woman told the truth,
so he did not dare to give her away.
The Marquis of Qí was angry.
In the summer, in the fifth month,
Bào Mù of Qí led troops to attack us,
and captured Huān and Chǎn.
B12.8.4 Someone slandered Hú Jī to the Marquis of Qí, saying:
"She is a partisan of Ān Rúzǐ."
In the sixth month,
the Marquis of Qí killed Hú Jī.
B12.8.5 The Marquis of Qí sent a messenger to Wú to request troops,
intending to attack us,
and so they returned the ruler of Zhū.
The ruler of Zhū again acted without principle,
so the ruler of Wú sent Grand Steward Zǐyú to punish him,
imprisoning him in a tower,
and surrounding it with thorns.
He ordered the various great officers to support Crown Prince Gé in governing.
B12.8.6 In autumn,
we made peace with Qí.
In the ninth month,
Zāng Bīnrú went to Qí to oversee the covenant.
Lǘqiū Míng of Qí came to oversee the covenant,
and also fetched Jì Jī to return with him,
and she became a favorite.
Bào Mù again said to the various princes:
"Shall I make you have a thousand chariots?"
The princes reported him.
The duke said to Bào Mù:
"Someone has slandered you.
You should temporarily reside in Lù to observe the situation.
If there is truth to it,
then divide the household and leave;
if there is not,
then return to your place."
When he left the gate,
he was ordered to take one-third of his household with him;
halfway there,
he was ordered to take only two chariots.
When he reached Lù,
they bound him and brought him in,
and then killed him.
B12.8.7 In winter, in the twelfth month,
the men of Qí returned Huān and Chǎn,
because Jì Jī had become a favorite.
A12.9 The Classic of the Ninth Year of Duke Āi
A12.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
in the king's second month,
we buried Qǐ Xī Gōng.
A12.9.2 Huáng Yuàn of Sòng led troops and captured the army of Zhèng at Yōngqiū.
A12.9.3 In summer,
the men of Chǔ attacked Chén.
A12.9.4 In autumn,
the Duke of Sòng attacked Zhèng.
A12.9.5 In winter, in the tenth month.
B12.9 The Commentary of the Ninth Year of Duke Āi
B12.9.1 In the ninth year, in spring,
the Marquis of Qí sent Gōng Mèng Chuò to decline troops from Wú.
The ruler of Wú said:
"Last year, I received your command;
now you have changed it again.
I do not know what to follow,
so I will advance and receive orders from you."
B12.9.2 The favorite of Zhèng Wǔzǐ Shèng, Xǔ Xiá, sought a city,
but he had none to give him.
He requested to take one from outside,
and he agreed,
so they besieged Sòng's Yōngqiū.
Huáng Yuàn of Sòng besieged the army of Zhèng,
moving his encampment daily,
until the fortifications were complete.
The army of Zhèng wept.
Zǐ Yáo came to rescue them,
but was greatly defeated.
On the jiǎxū day of the second month,
Sòng captured the army of Zhèng at Yōngqiū,
ordering that those with ability should not be killed,
and took Jiá Zhāng and Zhèng Luó back with them.
B12.9.3 In summer,
the men of Chǔ attacked Chén,
because Chén had allied with Wú.
B12.9.4 The Duke of Sòng attacked Zhèng.
B12.9.5 In autumn,
Wú built the city of Hán,
connecting the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
B12.9.6 Zhào Yǎng of Jìn divined about rescuing Zhèng,
and encountered water moving toward fire.
He consulted the diviners Shǐ Zhào, Shǐ Mò, and Shǐ Guī.
Shǐ Guī said:
"This is called 'sinking yang,'
and it is suitable for raising troops,
advantageous for attacking Jiāng,
but disadvantageous for aiding Shāng.
Attacking Qí is permissible,
but opposing Sòng is not auspicious."
Shǐ Mò said:
"Yíng
is the name of water,
and zǐ
is the position of water.
The name and position are opposed,
so they cannot be interfered with.
Yán Dì was the master of fire,
and the Jiāng surname are his descendants.
Water overcomes fire,
so attacking Jiāng is permissible."
Shǐ Zhào said:
"This is like a river being full,
and one cannot swim in it.
Zhèng is currently guilty,
and cannot be rescued.
Rescuing Zhèng is not auspicious,
and I do not know about other matters."
Yáng Hǔ used the Zhōu Yì to divine,
and encountered Tài changing to Xū.
He said: "Sòng is currently auspicious,
and we cannot oppose them.
Wēizǐ Qǐ
was the eldest son of Dì Yǐ.
Sòng and Zhèng
are uncle and nephew.
Zhǐ
means blessings.
If the eldest son of Dì Yǐ, marrying off his sister, had auspicious blessings,
how could we obtain auspiciousness?"
So they stopped.
B12.9.7 In winter,
the ruler of Wú sent a messenger to alert us to attack Qí.
A12.10 The Classic of the Tenth Year of Duke Āi
A12.10.1 In the tenth year, in spring,
in the king's second month,
the ruler of Zhū, Yì, fled to us.
A12.10.2 The duke joined Wú in attacking Qí.
A12.10.3 On the wùxū day of the third month,
the Marquis of Qí, Yángshēng, died.
A12.10.4 In summer,
the men of Sòng attacked Zhèng.
A12.10.5 Jin's Zhào Yāng led troops to invade Qí.
A12.10.6 In the fifth month,
the Duke arrived from the campaign against Qí.
A12.10.7 The burial of Qí Dàogōng took place.
A12.10.8 Wèi's Gōng Mèng Kōu returned from Qí to Wèi.
A12.10.9 The Earl of Xuē, Yí, died.
A12.10.10 In autumn,
the burial of Xuē Huìgōng took place.
A12.10.11 In winter,
Chǔ's prince Jié led troops to attack Chén.
A12.10.12 Wú rescued Chén.
B12.10 *The Commentary for the Tenth Year of Duke Āi*
B12.10.1 In the tenth year, spring,
Zhū Yǐngōng came fleeing;
he was a maternal nephew of Qí,
therefore he subsequently fled to Qí.
B12.10.2 The Duke met with the Viscount of Wú, the Viscount of Zhū,
and the Viscount of Tán to attack the southern borders of Qí,
and the army encamped at Xī.
B12.10.3 The men of Qí assassinated Dàogōng,
and reported it to the army.
The Viscount of Wú wailed for three days outside the army gate.
Xú Chéng led the naval fleet intending to enter Qí from the sea,
but the men of Qí defeated him,
and the Wú army then withdrew.
B12.10.4 In summer,
Zhào Yāng led troops to attack Qí.
The great officers requested to divine about it.
Zhào Mèng said:
"I divined about launching this military action,
matters should not be commanded twice,
divination does not repeatedly yield auspicious results.
Let us proceed!"
Thereupon they captured Lí and Yuán,
destroyed the outer wall of Gāotáng,
invaded as far as Lài and then returned.
B12.10.5 In autumn,
the Viscount of Wú sent a messenger to again alert for troops.
B12.10.6 In winter,
Chǔ's Zǐ Qī attacked Chén,
Wú's Yánzhōulái Jìzǐ rescued Chén,
and said to Zǐ Qī:
"The two rulers do not devote themselves to virtue,
but contend by force for the allegiance of the feudal lords,
what crime have the people committed?
I request to withdraw,
to give you, sir, a reputation,
so you may devote yourself to virtue and bring peace to the people."
He then withdrew.
A12.11 *The Spring and Autumn Annals for the Eleventh Year of Duke Āi*
A12.11.1 In the eleventh year, spring,
Qí's Guó Shū led troops to attack us.
A12.11.2 In summer,
Chén's Yuán Pō fled to Zhèng.
A12.11.3 In the fifth month,
the Duke joined with Wú to attack Qí.
On the jiǎxū day,
Qí's Guó Shū led troops and fought with Wú at Àilíng,
the Qí army was utterly defeated,
and Qí's Guó Shū was captured.
A12.11.4 In autumn, the seventh month, on the xīnyǒu day,
the Viscount of Téng, Yúmǔ, died.
A12.11.5 In winter, the eleventh month,
the burial of Téng Yǐngōng took place.
A12.11.6 Wèi's Shìshū Qí fled to Sòng.
B12.11 *The Commentary for the Eleventh Year of Duke Āi*
B12.11.1 In the eleventh year, spring,
because of the affair at Xī,
Guó Shū and Gāo Wúpī led troops to attack us,
reaching Qīng.
Jìsūn said to his steward Rǎn Qiú:
"The Qí army is at Qīng,
it must be because of Lǔ,
what should we do?"
Qiú said:
"Let one of you three defend, and the other two follow the Duke to resist them at the border."
Jìsūn said:
"That cannot be done." Qiú said:
"Then take a position within the borders."
Jìsūn informed the other two,
but the two would not agree.
Qiú said:
"If that cannot be done,
then the ruler should not go out.
Let one of you lead the army,
and fight with the city at your back.
Anyone who does not join in,
is not a man of Lǔ.
The various houses of Lǔ have more chariots than the army of Qí,
one house alone has more than enough chariots to oppose them,
what do you, sir, have to worry about?
It is natural that the two do not wish to fight,
for governance lies with the Jì family.
During your lifetime,
if the men of Qí attack Lǔ and we cannot fight,
it will be your disgrace,
and you will greatly not be ranked among the feudal lords."
Jìsūn had him follow to the court,
and wait at the ditch of the Dǎng family.
Wǔshū called out and asked him about the battle.
He replied:
"A gentleman has long-term plans,
what does a petty man know?"
Yìzǐ pressed him with questions,
and he replied:
"A petty man considers his ability before speaking,
and measures his strength before committing."
Wǔshū said:
"This means he thinks I am not a true man."
He withdrew and mustered his chariots.
Mèng Rúzǐ Xiè led the right army,
with Yán Yǔ as charioteer,
and Bǐng Xiè as the right-hand attendant.
Rǎn Qiú led the left army,
with Guǎn Zhōufù as charioteer,
and Fán Chí as the right-hand attendant.
Jìsūn said:
"Xū is too young."
Yǒuzǐ said:
"He will follow orders."
The Jì family had seven thousand armored soldiers,
Rǎn Yǒu used three hundred men from Wǔchéng as his personal infantry,
with the old and young guarding the palace,
and encamped outside the Yú Gate.
After five days,
the right army followed them.
Gōngshū Wùrén saw those guarding the city and wept,
saying:
"The corvée duties are excessive,
the taxes are heavy,
those above cannot devise plans,
the officers are not willing to die,
how can they govern the people?
Since I have already spoken of this,
how dare I not exert myself!"
The army engaged the Qí army in battle in the suburbs.
The Qí army came from Jìqū,
but our army would not cross the ditch.
Fán Chí said:
"It is not that they cannot,
but that they do not trust you, sir.
I request that you give the order three times and then cross it."
They did so,
and the multitude followed.
The army entered the Qí lines.
The right army fled,
and the men of Qí pursued them.
Chén Guàn and Chén Zhuāng crossed the Sì River.
Mèng Zhīcè entered last to act as rearguard,
drew an arrow and whipped his horse with it,
saying:
"The horse would not advance."
Lín Bùniǔ's squad said:
"Shall we flee?"
Bùniǔ said:
"Who is inferior?"
They said: "Then shall we stop?"
Bùniǔ said:
"What is worthy about that?"
He walked slowly and died.
The army captured eighty armored heads,
and the men of Qí could not maintain their formation.
That night, a spy reported:
"The men of Qí have fled."
Rǎn Yǒu requested three times to pursue them,
but Jìsūn did not permit it.
Mèng Rúzǐ said to someone:
"I am not as good as Yán Yǔ,
but I am worthier than Bǐng Xiè.
Zǐyǔ is sharp and keen,
I did not wish to fight but could remain silent,
while Xiè said
'Drive on!'"
Gōngwéi and his favored page Wāng Qí rode in the same chariot, and both died;
both were encoffined.
Confucius said:
"He who can grasp shield and spear to defend the altars of soil and grain
may not be treated as a premature death."
Rǎn Yǒu used a spear against the Qí army,
therefore he was able to enter their ranks.
Confucius said:
"This is righteousness."
B12.11.2 In summer,
Yuán Pō of Chén fled to Zhèng.
Earlier,
Yuán Pō had been the Minister of Land,
and had levied taxes on the fields to provide a dowry for the duke's daughter.
There was a surplus,
which he used to make large vessels for himself.
The people of the state drove him out,
and that is why he fled.
On the road, he was thirsty,
and a clansman of his, Yuán Xuǎn, presented him with sweet rice wine, millet cakes, and dried meat.
Pleased, he said:
"How well-provided you are!"
The reply was:
"When the vessels were completed, I prepared them."
He said: "Why did you not remonstrate with me?"
The reply was: "I was afraid I would be the first to go."
B12.11.3 Because of the battle at Jiāo,
the duke joined the Viscount of Wú in attacking Qí.
In the fifth month,
they took Bó.
On Rénshēn,
they reached Yíng.
The central army followed the king,
Xūmén Cháo commanded the upper army,
Prince Gū Cáo commanded the lower army,
and Zhǎn Rú commanded the right army.
Guó Shū of Qí commanded the central army,
Gāo Wúpī commanded the upper army,
and Zōng Lóu commanded the lower army.
Chén Xīzǐ said to his younger brother Shū:
"If you die,
I will certainly achieve my ambition."
Zōng Zǐyáng and Lǘqiū Míng encouraged each other.
Sāng Yǎnxū drove the chariot for Guózǐ.
Gōngsūn Xià said:
"These two men will certainly die."
As they were about to engage in battle,
Gōngsūn Xià ordered his followers to sing the "Yú Bìn."
Chén Zǐháng ordered his followers to prepare jade pieces for placing in the mouth.
Gōngsūn Huī ordered his followers, saying:
"Each man a length of rope,
for the men of Wú have short hair."
Dōngguō Shū said:
"Three battles and I must die;
this is the third."
He sent someone to ask Xián Duō for a qin,
saying:
"I shall not see you again."
Chén Shū said:
"On this campaign,
I shall only hear the drums,
and not the gongs."
On Jiǎxū,
they fought at Àilíng.
Zhǎn Rú defeated Gāozǐ,
Guózǐ defeated Xūmén Cháo,
but the king's troops came to his aid,
and they greatly defeated the army of Qí,
capturing Guó Shū, Gōngsūn Xià,
Lǘqiū Míng, Chén Shū, and Dōngguō Shū,
along with eight hundred chariots,
and three thousand armored heads,
which they presented to the duke.
Before the battle,
the Viscount of Wú called to Shūsūn,
saying:
"What is your duty?"
The reply was:
"To follow the Minister of War."
The king bestowed on him armor and a sword with a pointed blade,
saying:
"Attend to your lord's affairs,
and be reverent, do not disobey orders!"
Shūsūn was unable to reply.
Wèi Cì came forward,
and said:
"Zhōu Qiū receives the armor and follows his lord."
And he bowed.
The duke sent the Grand Scribe Gù to return the head of Guózǐ,
placing it in a new hamper,
wrapping it with black and crimson silk,
and adding a silk ribbon.
He placed a document on top of it,
saying:
"If Heaven does not recognize those who are not loyal,
how can it cause the lower states to submit?"
B12.11.4 When Wú was about to attack Qí,
the Viscount of Yuè led his multitude to pay court,
and the king and all his officers were presented with gifts.
The men of Wú were all pleased,
but only Zǐxū was fearful,
saying:
"This is fattening Wú!"
He remonstrated, saying:
"Yuè is to us
a disease in the heart and belly.
Our lands are adjacent,
and they have desires upon us.
Their submissive demeanor
is to seek the fulfillment of their desires.
It would be better to deal with them early.
Even if we achieve our ambition against Qí,
it is like obtaining a stony field,
of no use to us.
If Yuè is not made into a marsh,
Wú will be extinguished.
When one employs a physician to remove a disease,
and says
'you must leave some of it behind,'
such a thing has never been.
The "Announcement of Pángēng" says:
'If there are those who are rebellious and disobedient,
then I will cut them off and exterminate them, leaving no posterity,
not allowing them to propagate their seed in this city.'
This is how Shāng rose.
Now you, my lord, are doing the opposite,
and yet seek to achieve greatness;
is this not difficult!"
He did not listen.
When Zǐxū was sent to Qí,
he entrusted his son to the Bào clan,
and he became known as Wángsūn.
Upon returning from the campaign,
the king heard of this,
and sent him the sword Zhǔlòu with which to die.
As he was about to die,
he said:
"Plant a jiǎ tree at my grave;
the jiǎ will grow into timber.
Wú is about to perish!
In three years,
it will begin to weaken.
Fullness must be followed by destruction;
this is the way of Heaven."
B12.11.5 In autumn,
Jìsūn ordered defensive preparations to be made,
saying:
"For a small state to defeat a large one
is a calamity.
Qí's arrival is not far off."
B12.11.6 In winter,
Dàshū Jí of Wèi fled to Sòng.
Earlier,
Jí had married a daughter of Zǐ Cháo of Sòng,
and her younger sister was favored.
When Zǐ Cháo fled,
Kǒng Wénzǐ made Jí divorce his wife,
and gave him his own daughter in marriage.
Jí had a servant entice his former wife's younger sister and installed her in Lí,
and built a palace for her,
treating her as a second wife.
Wénzǐ was angry,
and wanted to attack him,
but Zhòngní stopped him.
He then took his daughter back.
Jí also had illicit relations in Wàizhōu,
and the people of Wàizhōu seized his carriage and presented it.
Ashamed of these two things,
he fled.
The people of Wèi established Yí,
and had him marry Kǒng Jí.
Jí became a retainer of Xiàng Tuí,
and presented him with fine pearls,
along with the city of Chéng Chú.
The Duke of Sòng demanded the pearls,
but Tuí would not give them,
and for this he incurred blame.
When the Huán clan fled,
the people of Chéng Chú attacked Dàshū Jí,
but Duke Zhuāng of Wèi restored him,
and had him reside in Cháo,
where he died.
He was laid in state at Yún,
and buried at Shǎo Dì.
Earlier,
Yìn, a son of Duke Dào of Jìn, was living in exile in Wèi,
and had his daughter drive his chariot while hunting.
Dàshū Yìzǐ stopped her and gave her wine to drink,
and subsequently betrothed her,
and she gave birth to Dàozǐ.
When Dàozǐ came to the throne,
Xià Wù therefore became a senior officer.
When Dàozǐ fled,
the people of Wèi reduced the power of Xià Wù.
When Kǒng Wénzǐ was about to attack Dàshū,
he consulted Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said:
"As for matters of sacrificial vessels,
I have indeed studied them;
but as for matters of armor and weapons,
I have not heard of them."
He withdrew,
ordered his carriage, and departed,
saying:
"The bird chooses the tree,
but how can the tree choose the bird?"
Wénzǐ hastily stopped him,
saying:
"How dare I consider my private affairs?
I am inquiring about the troubles of Wèi."
As he was about to stop,
the people of Lǔ summoned him with gifts,
so he returned.
B12.11.7 Jìsūn wished to implement the field tax,
and sent Rǎn Yǒu to inquire about it from Zhòngní.
Zhòngní said:
"Qiū does not understand."
After three inquiries,
he finally said:
"You are a senior statesman of the country,
and we await your advice to act.
Why do you not speak?"
Zhòngní did not reply,
but privately said to Rǎn Yǒu:
"In the conduct of a gentleman,
one measures by ritual:
bestowals should be generous,
affairs should be handled with moderation,
and levies should be light.
If so,
then even the current tax is sufficient.
If one does not measure by ritual,
but is greedy and insatiable,
then even with the field tax,
it will still be insufficient.
Moreover, if your master Jìsūn wishes to act according to law,
then the statutes of the Duke of Zhōu are present;
if he wishes to act arbitrarily,
why inquire further?"
He did not listen.
A12.12 The Annals of Duke Āi, Year 12
A12.12.1 In the twelfth year, spring,
the field tax was implemented.
A12.12.2 In summer, the fifth month, on the jiǎchén day,
Mèngzǐ died.
A12.12.3 The duke met with Wú at Tuógāo.
A12.12.4 In autumn,
the duke met with the Marquis of Wèi
and Huáng Yuàn of Sòng at Yún.
A12.12.5 Xiàng Cháo of Sòng led troops to attack Zhèng.
A12.12.6 In winter, the twelfth month,
there was a locust plague.
B12.12 The Commentary of Duke Āi, Year 12
B12.12.1 In the twelfth year, spring,
the royal first month,
the field tax was implemented.
B12.12.2 In summer, the fifth month,
Lady Mèngzǐ, wife of Duke Zhāo, died.
Duke Zhāo had married from Wú,
therefore her surname was not recorded.
Her death was not announced,
therefore she was not called "Lady."
The mourning rites were not performed,
therefore it was not stated that she was buried as a consort.
Confucius went to offer condolences,
and went to the Jì family.
The Jì family did not wear mourning headbands,
but removed their mourning girdles and bowed.
B12.12.3 The duke met with Wú at Tuógāo,
and the Prince of Wú sent Grand Steward Pǐ to request renewing the covenant.
The duke did not wish to,
and sent Zǐgòng to reply, saying:
"A covenant
is to secure good faith,
therefore the heart regulates it,
jades and silks are offered to it,
words bind it,
and bright spirits witness it.
Our ruler believes that if there is a covenant,
it cannot be altered.
If it can still be altered,
what use is a daily covenant?
Now you say
'we must renew the covenant.'
If it can be renewed,
it can also grow cold."
Thus they did not renew the covenant.
B12.12.4 Wú summoned a meeting with Wèi.
Earlier,
the people of Wèi had killed the Wú envoy Qiě Yáo and were afraid,
so they consulted with envoy Zǐyǔ.
Zǐyǔ said:
"Wú is currently without principle;
I fear it will disgrace our ruler.
It is better not to go."
Zǐmù said:
"Wú is currently without principle.
When a state is without principle,
it is sure to vent its malice on others.
Though Wú is without principle,
it is still enough to trouble Wèi.
Go!
When a tall tree falls,
nothing escapes being struck;
when a mad dog rages,
nothing escapes being bitten,
how much more a great state!"
In autumn,
the Marquis of Wèi met with Wú at Yún.
The duke and the Marquis of Wèi and Huáng Yuàn of Sòng made a covenant,
but finally declined to covenant with Wú.
The men of Wú fenced in the lodging of the Marquis of Wèi.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó said to Zǐgòng:
"When the lords meet,
after affairs are concluded,
the host presents courtesies,
the local lord provides provisions,
to bid farewell.
Now Wú shows no courtesy to Wèi,
but fences their ruler's lodging to trouble them.
Why do you not see Grand Steward
Pǐ?"
So he requested bundles of brocade and went.
When the conversation touched on the matter of Wèi,
Grand Steward Pǐ said:
"Our ruler wishes to serve the Lord of Wèi,
but the Lord of Wèi came slowly,
so our ruler was afraid,
and therefore detained him."
Zǐgòng said:
"When the Lord of Wèi came,
he must have consulted his people.
Some wished to come, some did not,
therefore he came slowly.
Those who wished to come
are your allies;
those who did not wish to come
are your enemies.
If you detain the Lord of Wèi,
you destroy your allies and elevate your enemies,
and those who destroy you will achieve their aim.
Moreover, to detain the Lord of Wèi when assembling the lords—
who would not be afraid?
Destroying allies, elevating enemies,
and frightening the lords—
perhaps it is difficult to achieve hegemony this way!"
Grand Steward Pǐ was pleased,
and released the Marquis of Wèi.
When the Marquis of Wèi returned,
he imitated the barbarian speech.
Zǐzhī was still young,
and said:
"Our ruler will surely not escape misfortune;
he will die among the barbarians!
He was detained and yet delights in their speech;
his following them is certain."
B12.12.5 In winter, the twelfth month,
there was a locust plague. Jìsūn asked Zhòngní about it.
Zhòngní said:
"Qiū has heard that
after the Fire Star sets, all creatures go into hibernation.
Now the Fire Star still flows westward;
the calendar officials have erred."
B12.12.6 Between Sòng and Zhèng there was a disputed territory,
called Mízuò, Qǐngqiū, Yùchàng, Yán, Gē, and Yáng.
Zǐchǎn made an agreement with the men of Sòng,
saying:
"Let neither have this."
When the clans of Duke Píng and Duke Yuán of Sòng fled from Xiāo to Zhèng,
the men of Zhèng built walls at Yán, Gē, and Yáng for them.
In the ninth month,
Xiàng Cháo of Sòng attacked Zhèng,
took Yáng,
killed the grandson of Duke Yuán,
and then besieged Yán.
In the twelfth month,
Hǎn Dá of Zhèng came to rescue Yán.
On the bǐngshēn day,
he besieged the Sòng army.
A12.13 The Annals of Duke Āi, Year 13
A12.13.1 In the thirteenth year, spring,
Hǎn Dá of Zhèng led troops and captured the Sòng army at Yán.
A12.13.2 In summer,
the Earl of Xǔ, Chéng, died.
A12.13.3 The duke met with the Marquis of Jìn and the Prince of Wú at Huángchí.
A12.13.4 Prince Shēn of Chǔ led troops to attack Chén.
A12.13.5 Yúyuè entered Wú.
A12.13.6 In autumn,
the duke returned from the meeting.
A12.13.7 Jìn's Wèi Mànduō led troops to invade Wèi.
A12.13.8 The funeral of Xǔ's Duke Yuán was held.
A12.13.9 In the ninth month,
locusts appeared.
A12.13.10 In winter, the eleventh month,
a comet appeared in the east.
A12.13.11 Bandits killed Chén's Xià Ōufū.
A12.13.12 In the twelfth month,
locusts appeared.
B12.13 The Commentary to the 13th Year of Duke Āi
B12.13.1 In the spring of the thirteenth year,
Sòng's Xiàng Tuí went to rescue his army.
Zhèng's Zǐ Shèng sent a proclamation saying:
"Whoever captures Huán Tuí will be rewarded."
Tuí fled back.
Subsequently, they captured the Sòng army at Yán,
capturing Chéng Huàn and Gào Yán.
They made the six cities empty.
B12.13.2 In summer,
the Duke met with Dān Pínggōng, Jìn Dìnggōng, and Wú's Fūchāi at Huángchí.
B12.13.3 On the bǐngzǐ day of the sixth month,
Yuèzǐ attacked Wú,
dividing into two columns,
Chóu Wúyú and Ōuyáng from the south,
first reaching the outskirts.
Wú's Crown Prince Yǒu, Prince Dì,
Wángsūn Míyōng, and Shòu Yúyáo observed them from Hóngshàng.
Míyōng saw the flag of Gūmiè,
and said:
"That is my father's flag.
I cannot see the enemy and not kill them."
The Crown Prince said:
"If we fight and do not win,
we will lose the state,
I ask to wait."
Míyōng did not agree,
gathered five thousand troops,
and Prince Dì assisted him.
On the yǐyǒu day,
they fought,
Míyōng captured Chóu Wúyú,
Dì captured Ōuyáng.
When Yuèzǐ arrived,
Prince Dì defended.
On the bǐngxū day,
they fought again,
greatly defeating the Wú army,
capturing Crown Prince Yǒu,
Wángsūn Míyōng,
and Shòu Yúyáo.
On the dīnghài day,
they entered Wú.
The people of Wú reported the defeat to the King.
The King hated that it would be heard,
and personally cut the throats of seven men under the tent.
B12.13.4 In autumn, on the xīnchǒu day of the seventh month, they swore a covenant,
Wú and Jìn contended for precedence.
The men of Wú said:
"Among the Zhōu royal house,
we are the eldest."
The men of Jìn said:
"Among the Jī surname,
we are the leader."
Zhào Yǎng called to Sīmǎ Yín, saying:
"The day is late,
the great affair is not yet accomplished,
it is the fault of us two ministers.
Set up the drums and array the ranks,
we two ministers will die in this,
and the order of precedence will surely be known."
He replied:
"I ask to go and observe for a moment."
He returned,
and said:
"Those who eat meat have no pallor.
Now the King of Wú has a pallor,
has the state been defeated?
Has the Crown Prince died?
Moreover, the virtue of the barbarians is light,
they cannot endure for long,
I ask to wait a little."
Then Jìn took precedence.
The men of Wú intended to have the Duke meet the Marquis of Jìn,
Zǐfú Jǐngbó replied to the messenger:
"When the King assembles the feudal lords,
then the leader leads the marquises and governors to see the King;
when the leader assembles the feudal lords,
then the marquis leads the viscounts
and barons to see the leader.
From the King down,
the jade and silk for court visits and missions differ;
therefore, the tribute duties of our humble state to Wú,
are richer than to Jìn,
none are lacking,
considering you as the leader.
Now the feudal lords are assembled,
and you, sir, intend to have our humble lord meet the Lord of Jìn,
then Jìn will become the leader,
and our humble state will change its tribute duties:
Lǔ's levy for Wú is eight hundred chariots,
if we become viscounts
and barons,
then we will take half of Zhū's levy to belong to Wú,
and serve Jìn like Zhū.
Moreover, you, the officers, summoned the feudal lords as leader,
but end it as a marquis,
what benefit is there in that?"
The men of Wú then stopped.
Afterwards, they regretted it,
and intended to imprison Jǐngbó.
Jǐngbó said:
"I have already established a successor in Lǔ,
I will take two chariots and six men to follow,
whether slow or fast, I obey your command."
They then imprisoned him and took him back.
When they reached Hùyǒu,
he said to the Grand Steward:
"Lǔ will in the tenth month, on the first xīn day, perform sacrifices to the Supreme God and the former dukes,
finishing on the last xīn day,
and I have held office for generations,
since Duke Xiāng,
it has not been changed.
If I do not participate,
the invocators and ancestral officers will say
'It was indeed Wú that caused it,'
and moreover say that Lǔ is not respectful,
and you detain seven of its lowly men,
what harm does it do?"
Grand Steward Pǐ spoke to the King, saying:
"It does no harm to Lǔ,
but only creates a reputation,
it is better to return him."
They then returned Jǐngbó.
Wú's Shēn Shūyí begged for grain from Gōngsūn Yǒushānshì,
saying:
"The pendant jades are dangling,
I have nothing to tie them to;
a vessel of fine wine,
I and the father in coarse cloth gaze at it."
He replied:
"Fine grain we have none,
coarse grain we have.
If you climb Shǒu Mountain and call out
'Gēngguǐ!'
then I will answer."
The King wanted to attack Sòng,
kill its men and imprison its women.
Grand Steward Pǐ said:
"We can win,
but cannot hold it."
They then returned.
B12.13.5 In winter,
Wú and Yuè made peace.
A12.14 The Spring and Autumn Annals of the 14th Year of Duke Āi
A12.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
a qílín was captured during a western hunt.
A12.14.2 Xiǎo Zhū's Shè came with Jǔyì to flee.
A12.14.3 In summer, the fourth month,
Qí's Chén Héng seized his lord,
and placed him in Shūzhōu.
A12.14.4 On the gēngxū day,
Shū Huán died.
A12.14.5 On the gēngshēn day, the first day of the fifth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
A12.14.6 Chén's Zōng Shù fled to Chǔ.
A12.14.7 Sòng's Xiàng Tuí entered Cáo to rebel.
A12.14.8 The ruler of Jǔ, Kuáng, died.
A12.14.9 In the sixth month,
Sòng's Xiàng Tuí fled from Cáo to Wèi.
A12.14.10 Sòng's Xiàng Cháo came fleeing.
A12.14.11 The men of Qí killed their lord Rén in Shūzhōu.
A12.14.12 In autumn,
Jìn's Zhào Yǎng led troops to attack Wèi.
A12.14.13 On the xīnchǒu day of the eighth month,
Zhòngsūn Héjì died.
A12.14.14 In winter,
Chén's Zōng Shù returned from Chǔ to Chén,
and the men of Chén killed him.
A12.14.15 Chén Yuánmǎi fled to Chǔ.
A12.14.16 A comet appeared.
A12.14.17 There was a famine.
B12.14 The Commentary to the Fourteenth Year of Duke Āi
B12.14.1 In the spring of the fourteenth year,
a hunt was conducted westwards in Dàyě.
Shūsūn Shì's charioteer Chú Shāng captured a qílín.
Considering it inauspicious,
he gave it to the gamekeeper.
Zhòngní saw it
and said:
"It is a qílín."
Only then was it taken.
B12.14.2 Xiǎo Zhū Shè came fleeing with Jǔyì,
saying:
"If Jìlù gives me his word,
I will have no need for a covenant."
Zǐlù was sent,
but Zǐlù declined.
Jì Kāngzǐ sent Rǎn Yǒu to say to him:
"A state of a thousand chariots
does not trust its covenant,
but trusts your word.
What disgrace is there for you?"
He replied:
"If Lǔ has a campaign against Xiǎo Zhū,
I would not dare inquire the reason,
but could die beneath its walls.
That man is disloyal,
yet if I fulfill his words,
it would mean endorsing his righteousness.
Yóu cannot do this."
B12.14.3 When Duke Jiǎn of Qí was in Lǔ,
Kǎn Zhǐ was favored by him.
Upon his accession,
he put him in charge of governance.
Chén Chéngzǐ feared him,
and frequently glanced at him in court.
The charioteer Yāng said to the duke:
"Chén and
Kǎn cannot coexist.
You, my lord, must choose between them."
He did not listen.
Zǐwǒ held an evening court session;
Chén Nì had killed a man,
and encountering him,
Zǐwǒ arrested him and took him inside.
The Chén clan was then harmonious;
they had him feign illness,
and sent him rice-water for washing,
along with wine and meat,
with which he entertained the guards,
got them drunk, killed them,
and escaped.
Zǐwǒ made a covenant with the Chén clan at the Chén ancestral temple.
Earlier,
Chén Bào wished to become Zǐwǒ's retainer.
He had Gōngsūn speak for him,
but there was a mourning period, so it stopped.
Afterwards,
he spoke of it, saying:
"There is a Chén Bào,
tall and stooped,
with an upward gaze.
In serving a gentleman, he is sure to succeed.
He wishes to become your servant.
I was wary of his character,
so delayed telling you."
Zǐwǒ said: "What harm?
It is within my control."
He made him a retainer.
Another day,
discussing governance with him,
he was pleased,
and grew fond of him,
saying to him:
"What if I expel all the Chéns and establish you?"
He replied:
"I am distant from the Chén clan.
Moreover, those who oppose you are only a few.
Why expel them all?"
He then informed the Chén clan.
Zǐháng said:
"He has gained the lord's favor.
If we do not act first,
he will surely bring disaster upon you."
Zǐháng took up residence in the duke's palace.
In summer, on the rénshēn day of the fifth month,
Chéngzǐ and his brothers, in four carriages, went to the duke.
Zǐwǒ was in a tent;
he came out,
met them,
then they entered
and closed the gates.
Attendants resisted them;
Zǐháng killed the attendants.
The duke was drinking with women on the Tántái;
Chéngzǐ moved him to the inner chamber.
The duke seized a halberd
and was about to strike him.
The Grand Scribe Zǐyú said:
"It is not to harm you,
but to remove a threat."
Chéngzǐ went out and lodged in the armory.
Hearing the duke was still angry,
he planned to leave,
saying:
"Where is there no lord?"
Zǐháng drew his sword
and said:
"Hesitation
ruins affairs.
Who is not of the Chén lineage?
If I do not kill you,
may the Chén ancestors be my witness!"
He then stopped.
Zǐwǒ returned,
assembled his followers,
attacked the side gate and the main gate,
but did not prevail,
so he fled.
The Chéns pursued him.
He lost his way in Yǎnzhōng,
and reached Fēngqiū.
The men of Fēngqiū captured him
and reported it;
he was killed at Guōguān.
Chéngzǐ was about to kill Dàlù Zǐfāng,
but Chén Nì pleaded and spared him.
Using the duke's order, he took a carriage on the road.
At Ér,
the crowd recognized him and made him go east.
Exiting Yōngmén,
Chén Bào offered him a carriage,
but he refused,
saying:
"Nì pleaded for me,
and Bào gives me a carriage.
This shows I have private dealings.
Having served Zǐwǒ yet having private dealings with his enemies—
how could I face the gentlemen of Lǔ and Wèi?"
Dōngguō Jiǎ fled to Wèi.
On the gēngchén day,
Chén Héng seized the duke at Shūzhōu.
The duke said:
"Had I followed Yāng's advice earlier,
I would not have come to this."
B12.14.4 Sòng Huán Tuí's favor was harming the duke.
The duke had the lady repeatedly invite him to a feast,
intending to move against him.
Before it happened,
Tuí first plotted against the duke,
requesting to exchange Ān for Bó.
The duke said:
"That cannot be.
Bó
is an ancestral town."
He then added seven towns to Ān,
and requested to feast the duke,
setting noon as the time,
with all his household troops going there.
The duke learned of it
and told Huáng Yě:
"I raised Tuí,
yet now he will bring disaster upon me.
I ask for immediate rescue."
Simǎ Zǐzhòng said:
"A minister who is disobedient
is hated by the spirits,
let alone by men.
How dare I not obey your command?
But without the Left Master, it cannot be done.
I ask to summon him by your order."
Whenever the Left Master ate,
bells were struck.
Hearing the bells,
the duke said: "The Master is about to eat."
After eating,
music was played again.
The duke said:
"Now it is possible."
He went in a carriage,
saying:
"The trackers have reported:
'In Féngzé there is a solitary elk.'
The duke said:
'Even though Tuí has not come,
if I get the Left Master,
I will go hunting with him.
What do you think?'"
The lord feared
to inform Zǐ,
and Yě said:
"I once had a private conversation with him."
The lord wished to hasten matters,
so he sent a carriage to fetch Zǐ.
He rode with him,
and upon arrival,
the duke explained the reason to him.
Zǐ bowed,
but could not rise.
The Minister of War said: "The lord should speak with him."
The duke said:
"What makes it difficult for you,
is that above there is Heaven,
and below there are the former lords."
He replied:
"Tuí's lack of reverence
is a calamity for Sòng,
how dare I not obey your command?"
The Minister of War requested the tally,
and ordered his followers to attack the Huán clan.
Their fathers, elder brothers, and old ministers said
"It cannot be done,"
while their new ministers said
"We follow our lord's command."
They then attacked them.
Zǐ Qí galloped to inform Minister of War Huán.
The Minister of War wished to enter,
but Zǐ Jū stopped him,
saying:
"You are unable to serve the lord,
and yet you attack the state;
the people will not support you,
you will only meet death."
Xiàng Tuí then entered Cáo to rebel.
In the sixth month,
he sent the Left Marshal Cháo to attack him,
wishing to take a senior official as a hostage to enter.
He was unable to do so,
and also entered Cáo,
to take a hostage.
Tuí said:
"It cannot be.
Since we are already unable to serve the lord,
and have also offended the people,
what shall we do?"
He then released him.
The people then rebelled against him.
Xiàng Tuí fled to Wèi.
Xiàng Cháo came fleeing,
and the Duke of Sòng sent someone to stop him,
saying:
"I have an agreement with you,
we cannot cut off the sacrifices of the Xiàng clan."
He declined, saying:
"My crime is great,
it would be fitting to exterminate the Huán clan entirely.
If, for the sake of the former ministers,
you allow them to have descendants,
that is the lord's kindness.
As for me,
I cannot enter."
Sīmǎ Niú presented his city and jade tablet, and went to Qí.
Xiàng Tuí came out from Wèi territory,
and Gōngwén shì attacked him,
demanding the jade disc of the Xiàhòu clan.
He gave him other jade,
and fled to Qí.
Chén Chéngzǐ made him a secondary minister,
and Sīmǎ Niú again presented his city,
and went to Wú.
The people of Wú disliked him,
and he returned.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ summoned him,
and Chén Chéngzǐ also summoned him.
He died outside the outer gate of Lǔ,
and the Kēng clan buried him at Qiūyú.
B12.14.5 On the jiǎwǔ day,
Chén Héng of Qí murdered his lord Rén at Shūzhōu.
Kǒng Qiū fasted for three days,
and three times requested to attack Qí.
The duke said:
"Lǔ has long been weakened by Qí;
if you attack them,
what will happen?"
He replied:
"Chén Héng murdered his lord,
half the people do not support him.
With the multitude of Lǔ added to half of Qí,
we can overcome them."
The duke said:
"You inform Jì Sūn."
Confucius declined,
and upon withdrawing told others:
"Because I follow after the senior officials,
I dared not remain silent."
B12.14.6 Earlier,
Mèng Rúzǐ Xiè was about to stable horses at Chéng,
but the steward of Chéng, Gōngsūn Sù, would not accept them,
saying:
"Because Chéng is impoverished,
Mèng Sūn does not stable horses here."
The Rúzǐ was angry,
attacked Chéng,
but his followers could not enter,
so he returned.
An official envoy from Chéng
was whipped by the Rúzǐ.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the xīnchǒu day,
Mèng Yìzǐ died.
The people of Chéng came for the funeral,
but were not admitted;
they bared their shoulders, removed their headgear,
and wept in the street,
offering their services,
but were not permitted;
they were afraid,
and did not return.
A12.15 *The Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Āi 15th Year*
A12.15.1 In the fifteenth year, spring,
the first month by the royal calendar,
Chéng rebelled.
A12.15.2 In summer, the fifth month,
Gāo Wúpī of Qí fled to Northern Yān.
A12.15.3 The Earl of Zhèng attacked Sòng.
A12.15.4 In autumn, the eighth month,
there was a great rain sacrifice.
A12.15.5 Zhào Yǎng of Jìn led an army to attack Wèi.
A12.15.6 In winter,
the Marquis of Jìn attacked Zhèng.
A12.15.7 They made peace with Qí.
A12.15.8 Gōngmèng Kōu of Wèi fled to Qí.
B12.15 *The Commentary of Zuo, Duke Āi 15th Year*
B12.15.1 In the fifteenth year, spring,
Chéng rebelled and went over to Qí.
Wǔ Bó attacked Chéng,
but did not overcome it,
so he fortified Shū.
B12.15.2 In summer,
Zǐ Xī and Zǐ Qī of Chǔ attacked Wú,
reaching Tóngruì.
The Marquis of Chén sent Gōngsūn Zhēnzǐ to offer condolences,
but he reached Liáng and died.
They were about to bring the corpse in.
The Lord of Wú sent Grand Steward Pǐ to greet them,
and declined, saying:
"Due to the untimeliness of the floods,
I fear the corpse of the senior official may decay and fall,
thereby increasing my lord's sorrow;
my lord dares to decline."
The chief deputy, Yùyǐn Gài, replied:
"My lord heard that Chǔ acts without principle,
repeatedly attacking the state of Wú,
exterminating its people.
My lord sent me, Gài, to serve as envoy,
to offer condolences to your lordship's subordinate officers.
Without fortune,
the envoy encountered Heaven's displeasure,
his great fate fell and ended,
his lineage was cut off at Liáng.
We wasted days gathering supplies,
moving camp each day.
Now your lordship commands, opposing the envoy, saying
'Do not bring the corpse to the gate,'
this is to cast my lord's command into the wilds.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
'Serve the dead as you serve the living,
this is ritual.'
Thus there is the ritual of a court visit or mission ending
with the corpse performing the duty,
and also the ritual of a court visit or mission encountering mourning.
If the corpse does not convey the command,
this is encountering mourning and returning,
is that not unacceptable!
Using ritual to guard the people,
some still overstep it;
now the senior official says
'When dead, discard him,'
this is to discard ritual,
how then can one be lord of the feudal lords?
The ancients had a saying:
'Do not defile the maltreated officer.'
I, the deputy envoy, present the corpse to convey the command.
If only my lord's command reaches your lordship's place,
even if I fall into a deep abyss,
then it is Heaven's mandate,
not the fault of your lordship or the boatmen."
The people of Wú admitted them.
B12.15.3 In autumn,
Chén Guàn of Qí went to Chǔ,
passing through Wèi.
Zhòng Yóu met him
and said:
"Heaven may be using the Chén clan as an axe,
having already hacked away the ducal house,
but whether others will possess it,
is unknowable;
whether it will allow them to finally enjoy it,
is also unknowable.
If you treat Lǔ well and await the right time,
would that not be acceptable!
Why must you incur hatred?"
Zǐ Yù said:
"Indeed.
I have received your command,
please have someone inform my younger brother."
B12.15.4 In winter,
[Lǔ] made peace with Qí.
Zǐfú Jǐngbó went to Qí,
with Zǐgòng as his deputy.
They met Gōngsūn Chéng,
and [Zǐgòng] said:
"All men serve others,
yet some harbor thoughts of betraying their lord.
How much more so the men of Qí, though they serve you,
can they be without duplicity?
You, sir,
are a descendant of the Duke of Zhōu,
having enjoyed great benefits,
yet still contemplate what is unrighteous.
If you gain no benefit,
and lose your ancestral state,
what use will it be?"
Chéng said:
"Well said!
Had I not heard this command earlier."
Chén Chéngzǐ received the guests in his residence,
saying:
"My humble lord sent Héng to announce:
'My humble lord wishes to serve your lord as he serves the lord of Wèi.'"
Jǐngbó motioned for Zǐgòng to step forward,
who replied:
"This is my humble lord's wish.
Formerly, when the men of Jìn attacked Wèi,
Qí, for Wèi's sake,
attacked Guànshì of Jìn,
losing five hundred chariots.
They then gave Wèi territory,
west of the Jì River,
south of Zhuó, Mèi, and Xìng,
five hundred registered communities.
When the men of Wú brought disorder upon our humble city,
Qí took advantage of our distress,
seizing Huān and Chǎn.
My humble lord was thus chilled to the heart.
If he can look upon serving your lord as Wèi serves him,
then that is indeed his wish."
Chéngzǐ was troubled by this,
and so returned Chéng.
Gōngsūn Sù entered Yíng with his troops and armor.
B12.15.5 Kǒng Yǔ of Wèi married the elder sister of the crown prince Kuǎikuì,
and she gave birth to Kuī.
A young servant of the Kǒng family, Hún Liángfū, grew tall and handsome.
After Kǒng Wénzǐ died,
he had relations with the lady of the household.
The crown prince was in Qī,
and Kǒng Jī sent him there.
The crown prince spoke with him, saying:
"If you enable me to enter and regain the state,
I will grant you the right to wear the official cap and ride in a high carriage,
and pardon you three death sentences."
He made a covenant with him,
and [Liángfū] made a request to Bó Jī.
In the intercalary month,
Liángfū and the crown prince entered,
and stayed in the outer garden of the Kǒng residence.
At dusk,
the two men covered themselves with clothing and rode,
with the eunuch Luó driving,
to the Kǒng residence.
The steward of the Kǒng family, Luán Níng, questioned them,
and they claimed to be female relatives of the family,
so they entered,
and went to Bó Jī's quarters.
After eating,
Kǒng Bó Jī, holding a spear, went first,
the crown prince and five men in armor,
followed with a sacrificial boar.
They cornered Kǒng Kuī in a privy,
forced him to swear a covenant,
and then compelled him to ascend a terrace.
Luán Níng was about to drink,
his roast meat not yet cooked,
when he heard of the disorder.
He sent someone to inform Jìzǐ;
summoned Huò to harness a carriage,
drank a cup, ate the roast meat,
and escorted Wèi Hóu Zhé to flee.
Jìzǐ was about to enter,
when he met Zǐgāo who was coming out.
[Zǐgāo] said: "The gates are already closed."
Jìzǐ said: "I shall go there nonetheless."
Zǐgāo said: "Do not get involved,
do not tread into their calamity!"
Jìzǐ said:
"Having eaten their salary,
I do not avoid their calamity."
Zǐgāo then went out, and Zǐlù entered.
Arriving at the gate, Gōngsūn Gǎn was guarding it,
saying: "Do not enter, it is useless."
Jìzǐ said:
"That is Gōngsūn,
seeking profit,
yet fleeing their calamity.
Yóu is not like that;
benefiting from their salary,
I must rescue them from their trouble."
When a messenger came out,
he then entered,
and said:
"Why does the crown prince need Kǒng Kuī?
Even if you kill him,
someone is sure to succeed him."
And he said:
"The crown prince lacks courage;
if you set fire to the terrace,
halfway, he is sure to release Kǒng Shū."
The crown prince heard this,
was afraid,
and sent Shí Qǐ and Yú Yǎn to fight Zǐlù.
They struck him with a halberd,
cutting his cap strings.
Zǐlù said:
"When a gentleman dies,
his cap must not be removed."
He tied his cap strings and died.
Confucius heard of the disorder in Wèi,
and said:
"Chái will likely come back,
but Yóu will die."
Kǒng Kuī established Duke Zhuāng.
Duke Zhuāng, resenting the old administration,
wished to remove them all.
He first said to the Minister of Education, Mán Chéng:
"I have long suffered illness abroad,
I ask you, sir, to also taste it."
[Mán Chéng] returned and told Chǔshī Bǐ,
wishing to join him in attacking the duke,
but it did not come to pass.
A12.16 *The Sixteenth Year of Duke Āi, Spring and Autumn Annals*
A12.16.1 In the sixteenth year, spring,
the first month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
the crown prince of Wèi, Kuǎikuì, entered Wèi from Qī,
and Wèi Hóu Zhé came fleeing [to Lǔ].
A12.16.2 In the second month,
Wèi Zǐ Huán Chéng fled to Sòng.
A12.16.3 In summer, the fourth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
Kǒng Qiū died.
B12.16 *The Sixteenth Year of Duke Āi, Commentary*
B12.16.1 In the sixteenth year, spring,
Mán Chéng and Chǔshī Bǐ fled to Sòng.
B12.16.2 The Marquis of Wèi sent Yān Wǔzǐ to announce to Zhōu, saying:
"Kuǎikuì offended his father and mother,
and fled to Jìn.
Jìn, for the sake of the royal house,
did not abandon a brother,
and placed him by the Hé River.
Heaven guided his heart,
enabling him to succeed in guarding the borders.
Your servant Xī dares to announce this to your attendants."
The king sent Shàn Pínggōng to reply,
saying:
"Xī has come to announce the good command to me alone.
Go and tell my uncle:
I commend your succession to the generation,
and restore your rank and stipend.
Be reverent!
Await Heaven's blessings.
Without reverence, there will be no blessings;
can regret be pursued?"
B12.16.3 In summer, the fourth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
Kǒng Qiū died.
The duke pronounced a eulogy for him, saying:
"Compassionate Heaven is unkind,
grudgingly leaving behind one elder,
to shield me alone in my position,
solitary, I remain in distress.
Alas, sorrowful! Nǐfù!
I have lost my model."
Zǐgòng said:
"I fear our lord will not die a natural death in Lǔ!"
The Master said:
'When ritual is lost, there is confusion;
when names are lost, there is transgression.'
To lose one's purpose is confusion;
to lose one's proper place is transgression.
Not to be able to employ him while alive,
and to eulogize him after death,
is contrary to ritual;
to call oneself 'the One Man,'
is a loss of proper names.
You, my lord, have lost both."
B12.16.4 In the sixth month,
the Marquis of Wèi entertained Kǒng Kuī with wine at Píngyáng,
and gave him rich presents.
All the great officers had something contributed to them.
When Kǒng Kuī was drunk, the marquis sent him away,
and at midnight dismissed him.
He carried Bó Jī with him from Píngyáng,
and when they reached the western gate,
he sent his second carriage back to the western park to fetch the stone tablet of his ancestor.
Zǐbó Jìzǐ had at first been an officer of the Kǒng family,
but had recently been advanced to the service of the marquis.
He asked leave to pursue Kǒng Kuī,
and met the man who was carrying the tablet.
He killed him, and mounted his carriage.
Xǔ Gōngwéi was returning with the tablet,
and met him,
saying,
"To contend with an unrighteous man,
one cannot but be victorious."
He made Zǐbó Jìzǐ shoot first,
who discharged three arrows,
all of which fell far from Xǔ Gōngwéi.
Xǔ Gōngwéi then shot him,
and killed him.
Some one followed with his carriage,
and got the tablet from the bag.
Kǒng Kuī then fled to Sòng.
B12.16.5 When the crown prince Jiàn of Chǔ encountered slander,
he fled from Chéngfù to Sòng.
He also avoided the disorder caused by the Huá family by going to Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng were very kind to him.
He then went to Jìn,
and plotted with the people of Jìn to make a surprise attack on Zhèng,
after which he sought to return to Zhèng.
The people of Zhèng received him as before.
The people of Jìn sent a spy to Zǐmù,
asking him to fix a time for the enterprise.
Zǐmù was oppressive and cruel in his own city,
and the people of the city complained of him.
The people of Zhèng made an investigation,
and discovered the spy from Jìn,
whereupon they put Zǐmù to death.
His son, named Shèng,
was in Wú,
and Zǐxī wished to summon him back.
Yègōng said,
"I have heard that Shèng is deceitful and disorderly;
is he not likely to do harm?"
Zǐxī said,
"I have heard that Shèng is trustworthy and brave,
and does nothing that is not advantageous.
Let him be placed on the borders,
to guard the frontiers."
Yègōng said,
"The observance of benevolence is what is called trustworthiness;
following righteousness is what is called bravery.
I have heard that Shèng is fond of keeping his word,
and seeks for men who will die for him;
is he not likely to have private ends?
Keeping one's word
is not trustworthiness;
expecting death
is not bravery.
You will certainly repent of this."
Zǐxī did not listen to him.
He summoned Shèng,
and made him reside on the borders,
as the Duke of Bái.
Shèng requested to invade Zhèng,
but Zǐxī said,
"Chǔ is not yet in a condition for military operations.
If it were otherwise,
I would not forget it."
Another day,
he repeated his request,
and Zǐxī agreed to it,
but did not send out an army.
When the people of Jìn invaded Zhèng,
Chǔ went to its relief,
and made a covenant with it.
Shèng was angry,
and said,
"The people of Zhèng are here;
my enemy is not far off."
Shèng then whetted his sword himself.
Píng, the son of Zǐqī, saw him,
and said,
"Why does the princely grandson whet his sword?"
Shèng replied,
"Shèng is known for his straightforwardness.
If I did not tell you,
how could that be straightforward?
I am going to kill your father."
Píng reported this to Zǐxī.
Zǐxī said,
"Shèng is like an egg;
I have sheltered and nurtured him.
In Chǔ,
when I die,
the offices of Prime Minister and Minister of War
will surely fall to Shèng, and to no one else."
Shèng heard this,
and said,
"The Prime Minister is mad!
If he gets to die a natural death,
I am not myself."
Zǐxī did not change his mind.
Shèng said to Shí Qǐ,
"The king and the two chief ministers—
if we had five hundred men to oppose them,
it would be sufficient."
Qǐ said,
"We cannot get so many."
Shèng said,
"There is one Xiōng Yíliáo in the southern market;
if we can get him,
he will be equal to five hundred men."
They then went with the Duke of Bái to see him.
They spoke with him,
and he was pleased.
They told him their purpose,
but he declined.
They presented a sword to him,
but he did not move.
Shèng said,
"He who is not tempted by gain,
not intimidated by authority,
and does not betray men's words to seek favor—
let us leave him."
When the people of Wú invaded Shèn,
the Duke of Bái defeated them.
He asked leave to present his spoils of war,
which was granted,
and then he raised an insurrection.
In autumn, in the seventh month,
he killed Zǐxī and Zǐqī at court,
and seized King Huì.
Zǐxī covered his face with his sleeve and died.
Zǐqī said,
"Formerly I served my prince with my strength;
I cannot but do so to the end."
He tore up a camphor tree and killed some with it before he died.
Shí Qǐ said,
"Burn the treasury and kill the king.
Otherwise,
we shall not succeed."
The Duke of Bái said,
"That will not do.
To kill the king
is inauspicious;
to burn the treasury
leaves no resources—
how then shall we defend ourselves?"
Qǐ said,
"When you possess Chǔ and govern its people,
and serve the spirits with reverence,
you may obtain auspiciousness,
and you will have resources;
what is there to fear?"
The Duke of Bái did not listen to him.
Yègōng was in Cài,
and all beyond the Fángchéng mountains said,
"You may enter now."
Zǐgāo said,
"I have heard that
those who seek good fortune through dangerous means
are never satisfied in their desires;
if they lean to one side, they are sure to become isolated."
When he heard that the Duke of Bái had killed Qí Guǎnxiū,
he then entered.
The Duke of Bái wished to make Zǐlǘ king,
but Zǐlǘ refused,
so he compelled him by force of arms.
Zǐlǘ said,
"If the princely grandson will pacify and settle Chǔ,
and rectify the royal house,
and then protect me,
it is what I desire;
how dare I not obey?
But if you intend to monopolize profit and overthrow the royal house,
disregarding Chǔ,
I would rather die than consent."
They then killed him,
and took the king to the Gāo mansion.
Shí Qǐ guarded the gate.
Yù Gōngyáng made a hole in the palace wall,
and carried the king on his back to the palace of Lady Zhāo.
Lord Yè also arrived,
and upon reaching the north gate,
someone encountered him,
saying:
"Why do you not wear your helmet?
The people of the state look to you as they look to their loving parents.
If the arrows of the thieves and robbers should wound you,
this would cut off the people's hopes.
How can you not wear your helmet?"
So he put on his helmet and advanced.
He encountered another person, who said:
"Why do you wear your helmet?
The people of the state look to you as they look forward to the harvest.
Day by day they hope for it.
If they see your face,
it will bring them comfort.
When the people know you are not dead,
they will also have a heart of zeal.
They will still raise your banner and parade it through the state;
but if you cover your face and cut off the people's hopes,
is that not excessive?"
So he removed his helmet and advanced.
He encountered Zhēn Yǐn Gù leading his subordinates,
who were about to join Lord Bái.
Zǐgāo said:
"If not for these two men,
Chǔ would not be a state.
To abandon virtue and follow a rebel,
can that be safeguarded?"
So he followed Lord Yè.
He was sent to join the people of the state in attacking Lord Bái.
Lord Bái fled to the mountains and hanged himself.
His followers concealed his body.
Shí Qì was captured alive and questioned about Lord Bái's death.
He replied:
"I know where he died,
but my elder instructed me not to speak."
They said:
"If you do not speak, you will be boiled."
Qì said:
"In such affairs, success makes one a minister,
failure leads to being boiled.
That is indeed its nature.
What harm is there?"
So they boiled Shí Qì.
Wángsūn Yàn fled to Kuíhuángshì.
Shěn Zhūliáng held both offices concurrently.
When the state was pacified,
he made Níng the Lìngyǐn,
made Kuān the Sīmǎ,
and retired in Yè.
B12.16.6 The Marquis of Wèi divined a dream.
A favorite sought wine from Tàishū Xīzǐ,
but did not get it.
He conspired with a diviner
and told the Marquis:
"Your lordship has a great minister in the southwestern corner.
If you do not remove him,
I fear he will cause harm."
So he expelled Tàishū Yí.
Yí fled to Jìn.
B12.16.7 The Marquis of Wèi said to Hún Liángfū:
"I succeeded the former lord but did not obtain his vessels.
What is to be done?"
Liángfū, taking the place of the torch-bearer, spoke,
saying:
"Jí and the exiled lord are both your sons.
Summon them and select the capable one—that is permissible.
If they are not capable,
the vessels can be obtained."
A page reported this to the heir.
The heir had five men carry a boar to follow him,
seized the Marquis and forced him to swear an oath,
and requested to kill Liángfū.
The Marquis said:
He said:
"I beg that after three days, if he is guilty, kill him."
The Marquis said:
"Agreed!"
B12.17 "The Commentary of Duke Āi, Seventeenth Year"
B12.17.1 In the spring of the seventeenth year,
the Marquis of Wèi built a tiger-patterned tent at Jiépǔ.
When it was completed,
he sought someone of good reputation to share the first meal with him there.
The heir requested that Liángfū be sent.
Liángfū rode in a chariot drawn by two stallions,
wearing purple robes and a fox-fur coat.
Upon arrival,
he bared his fur coat,
and ate without removing his sword.
The heir had him dragged away,
enumerated three crimes against him, and killed him.
B12.17.2 In the third month,
the Lord of Yuè attacked Wú.
The Lord of Wú defended against him at Lìzé,
arraying their forces on opposite sides of the river.
The Lord of Yuè formed left and right hook formations,
sending them at night, sometimes left, sometimes right,
advancing with drums and shouts;
the Wú army divided to defend against them.
The Lord of Yuè secretly crossed with three armies,
faced the center of the Wú army and drummed against them.
The Wú army fell into great disorder,
and was thus defeated.
B12.17.3 Zhào Yāng of Jìn sent a message to Wèi,
saying:
"When your lordship was in Jìn,
Zhìfǔ was your host.
I request that your lordship or the heir come,
to absolve Zhìfǔ.
Otherwise,
our lord will say it was Zhìfǔ's doing."
The Marquis of Wèi declined due to difficulties,
and the heir further slandered him.
In the summer, sixth month,
Zhào Yāng besieged Wèi.
Guó Guān and Chén Guàn of Qí came to rescue Wèi,
and captured a challenger from the Jìn army.
Zǐyù had him dressed and brought before him,
saying: "Guózǐ truly holds the authority of Qí,
and commanded Guàn, saying:
'Do not avoid the Jìn army!'
How dare I disobey the command?
And why do you trouble yourself?"
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"I divined about attacking Wèi,
but did not divine about fighting Qí."
So he withdrew.
B12.17.4 During the rebellion of Lord Bái of Chǔ,
the people of Chén, relying on their stores, invaded Chǔ.
After Chǔ was pacified,
they planned to seize the wheat of Chén.
The Lord of Chǔ asked about a commander from Grand Master Zǐgǔ and Lord Yè Zhūliáng.
Zǐgǔ said:
"Right Commander Chàchē and Left Historian Lǎo
both assisted the Lìngyǐn and Sīmǎ in attacking Chén.
They can be employed."
Zǐgāo said:
"Their rank is low,
the people disrespect them,
I fear they will not obey orders."
Zǐgǔ said:
"Guān Dīngfù
was a captive from Ruò.
King Wǔ made him an army commander,
and thus he overcame Zhōu and Liǎo,
subdued Suí and Táng,
and greatly opened up the many Mán tribes.
Péng Zhòngshuǎng,
was a captive from Shēn.
King Wén made him Lìngyǐn,
and he truly made Shēn
and Xī into counties,
made Chén and Cài pay court,
and extended the borders to the Rǔ River.
It is only their capability that matters.
What does lowliness have to do with it?"
Zǐgāo said:
"Heaven's mandate is not to be doubted.
The Lìngyǐn has a grievance against Chén.
If Heaven wishes to destroy it,
it will surely be with the Lìngyǐn's son.
Why does your lordship not set him aside?
I fear that the Right Commander and Left Historian have the lowliness of the two captives
but lack their virtuous command."
The King divined about it,
and Wǔchéng Yǐn was auspicious.
He was sent to lead the army and seize the wheat of Chén.
The people of Chén defended against them,
were defeated,
and Chén was then besieged.
In autumn, seventh month, on Jǐmǎo day,
Gōngsūn Cháo of Chǔ led an army and destroyed Chén.
The King and Lord Yè divined by lot about Zǐliáng becoming Lìngyǐn.
Shěn Yǐn Zhū said:
"Auspicious.
It exceeds his ambition."
Lord Yè said:
"A prince serving as minister of state,
what will he do if he exceeds it?"
Another day,
they divined again and made Zǐguó Lìngyǐn.
B12.17.5 The Marquis of Wèi dreamed in the northern palace.
He saw a man ascending the tower of Kūnwú,
with disheveled hair, facing north and shouting:
"Ascend this mound of Kūnwú,
where gourds grow in profusion.
I am Hún Liángfū,
calling to Heaven, innocent."
The Marquis personally performed a milfoil divination.
Xū Mí Shè interpreted it.
He said:
"It does no harm."
They gave him a town,
but he left it there and fled, running off to Sòng.
The Marquis of Wèi performed a divination,
and the oracle said:
"Like a fish with a red tail,
swimming across the current and wandering.
Bordering a great state,
it will be destroyed,
and about to perish.
Shut the gates and block the holes,
then climb over from the rear."
In winter, the tenth month,
Jìn again attacked Wèi,
entered its outer wall,
and was about to enter the city.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Stop!
Shūxiàng had a saying:
'Those who rely on chaos to destroy states will have no posterity.'"
The people of Wèi expelled Duke Zhuāng and made peace with Jìn.
Jìn set up Bānshī, the grandson of Duke Xiāng, and then withdrew.
In the eleventh month,
the Marquis of Wèi entered from Juàn,
and Bānshī fled.
Earlier,
the duke had climbed the city wall to look out,
and saw Róngzhōu.
He asked about it,
and they told him.
The duke said:
am of the Jī surname,
what Róng people are there here?"
And he cut it down.
The duke kept the artisans working for a long time.
The duke wanted to expel Shí Pǔ,
but before he could, trouble arose.
On Xīnsì,
Shí Pǔ used the artisans to attack the duke.
The duke shut the gates and pleaded,
but they did not agree.
He climbed over the northern wall and fell,
breaking his thigh.
The people of Róngzhōu attacked him,
and Crown Prince Jí and Prince Qīng climbed over to follow the duke,
but the people of Róngzhōu killed them.
The duke entered the house of Jǐshì of Róngzhōu.
Earlier,
the duke had seen from the city wall that Jǐshì's wife had beautiful hair,
and had made her shave it,
to use as a wig for Lǚ Jiāng.
After entering there,
he showed him a jade disk,
and said:
"Spare me,
and I will give you this disk."
Jǐshì said:
"If I kill you,
where will the disk go?"
So he killed him,
and took his disk.
The people of Wèi brought back Gōngsūn Bānshī and set him up.
In the twelfth month,
the people of Qí attacked Wèi,
the people of Wèi requested peace,
they set up Prince Qǐ,
seized Bānshī and took him back,
placing him in Lù.
B12.17.6 The duke met with the Marquis of Qí and made a covenant at Méng,
Mèng Wǔbó acted as assistant.
The Marquis of Qí performed the kowtow,
the duke bowed.
The people of Qí were angry.
Wǔbó said:
"Unless it is the Son of Heaven,
our ruler has no one to kowtow to."
Wǔbó asked Gāo Chái:
"When the feudal lords make a covenant,
who holds the ox ear?"
Jìgāo said:
"At the battle of Zēngyǎn,
it was Prince Gūcáo of Wú;
at the battle of Fāyáng,
it was Shí Tuí of Wèi."
Wǔbó said:
"Then it is Zhì."
B12.17.7 Huáng Yuàn of Sòng's son Mí had a friend named Tián Bǐng,
and he took a town from his elder brother Chán Bān and gave it to him.
Chán Bān was angry and left,
and told Zǐyí Kè, a retainer of Minister Huán.
Zǐyí Kè went to Sòng,
and told the lady:
"Mí is about to bring in the Huán clan."
The duke asked Zǐzhòng about it.
Earlier,
Zǐzhòng had intended to make Fēiwǒ, the son of Qǐ Sì, his heir.
Mí said:
"You must establish Bó,
he is excellent material."
Zǐzhòng was angry,
and did not follow his advice,
so he replied:
"The Right Marshal is old,
I do not know about Mí."
The duke seized him.
Huáng Yuàn fled to Jìn,
and they summoned him back.
B12.18 "The Commentary of Duke Āi, Eighteenth Year"
B12.18.1 In the spring of the eighteenth year,
Sòng killed Huáng Yuàn.
The duke heard the circumstances,
restored the Huáng clan,
and made Huáng Huǎn the Right Marshal.
B12.18.2 The Bā people attacked Chǔ,
and besieged Yōu.
Earlier,
when Right Minister Zǐguó divined,
Guān Zhān said:
"It matches your will."
So he was appointed.
When the Bā army arrived,
they were about to divine for a commander.
The king said:
"Since Níng matches the will,
why divine further?"
He sent him to lead the army and set out.
He requested a deputy,
the king said:
"The Chamberlain for the Bedchamber and the Minister of Works served the former ruler diligently."
In the third month,
Gōngsūn Níng of Chǔ, Wú Yóuyú,
and Wěi Gù defeated the Bā army at Yōu,
so he enfeoffed Zǐguó at Xī.
The gentleman said:
"King Huì knew the will.
The Xiàshū says:
'The official diviner must first determine the will,
then consult the great tortoise,'
is this not referring to this?
The Zhì says:
'The sage does not trouble with divination,'
King Huì had this quality."
B12.18.3 In summer,
Shí Pǔ of Wèi expelled his ruler Qǐ,
and Qǐ fled to Qí.
The Marquis of Wèi, Zhé, returned from Qí,
expelled Shí Pǔ,
and restored Shí Tuí and Tàishū Yí.
B12.19 "The Commentary of Duke Āi, Nineteenth Year"
B12.19.1 In the spring of the nineteenth year,
the Yuè people invaded Chǔ,
to mislead Wú.
In summer,
Prince Qìng and Gōngsūn Kuān of Chǔ pursued the Yuè army,
reached Míng,
but did not catch up,
and then returned.
B12.19.2 In autumn,
Shěn Zhūliáng of Chǔ attacked the Eastern Yí,
and the men and women of the three Yí tribes made a covenant with the Chǔ army at Áo.
B12.19.3 In winter,
Shū Qīng went to the capital,
because King Jìng had passed away.
B12.20 "The Commentary of Duke Āi, Twentieth Year"
B12.20.1 In the spring of the twentieth year,
the people of Qí came to summon a meeting.
In summer,
they met at Lǐnqiū,
for the sake of Zhèng,
to plan an attack on Jìn.
The people of Zhèng declined the feudal lords.
In autumn,
the army returned.
B12.20.2 Prince Qìngjì of Wú repeatedly remonstrated with the ruler of Wú,
saying:
"If you do not change,
you will surely perish."
He did not listen.
He left and resided in Ài,
then went to Chǔ.
Hearing that Yuè was about to attack Wú,
in winter,
he requested to return and make peace with Yuè,
and then returned.
He wanted to remove the disloyal to please Yuè.
The people of Wú killed him.
B12.20.3 In the eleventh month,
Yuè besieged Wú,
and Zhào Mèng reduced his mourning meals.
Chǔ Lóng said:
"The three-year mourning period,
is the utmost expression of closeness,
yet you, my lord, have further reduced it,
is there not a reason for this?"
Zhào Mèng said:
"At the Huángchí meeting,
our former ruler and the King of Wú exchanged hostages,
and said:
'We shall share likes and dislikes.'
Now Yuè has surrounded Wú,
and our heir has not abandoned the old alliance but opposes them;
this is beyond Jìn's power to assist,
and therefore I consider submission appropriate."
Chǔ Lóng said:
"If the King of Wú were to know of this,
what then?"
Zhào Mèng said: "Is that possible?"
Lóng said:
"Allow me to try."
He then went, first calling at the Yuè army,
saying:
"Wú has repeatedly offended and intruded upon our superior state,
and hearing that you, my lord, have personally come to chastise them,
all the people of the central states are overjoyed,
only fearing that your will might not be carried out;
I beg to enter and observe."
They permitted him.
He reported to the King of Wú, saying:
"My ruler's elder, Wúxù, has sent his attendant minister Lóng
to dare express apology for his inability to share the burden:
At the Huángchí meeting,
your predecessor, my ruler's minister Zhìfù, was able to join the covenant,
which said
'We shall share likes and dislikes.'
Now you, my lord, are in distress,
and Wúxù does not dare fear the toil,
but this is beyond Jìn's power to assist,
so he has sent his attendant minister to dare lay this before you."
The king bowed his head to the ground and said:
"I, the unworthy one,
am unable to serve Yuè,
causing concern for you, Great Officer,
and I bow to acknowledge your condescending message."
He gave him a basket of pearls,
and sent him to inquire of Zhào Mèng,
saying:
"Gōujiàn intends to cause me anxiety while I live,
and I shall not be allowed to die."
The king said:
"A drowning man must laugh;
I have a question.
Why was Shǐ Àn considered a gentleman?"
He replied: "Àn, in advancing, incurred no dislike;
in retiring, he received no slanderous words."
The king said: "Appropriate indeed!"
B12.21 The Twenty-first Year of Duke Āi
B12.21.1 In the summer, in the fifth month of the twenty-first year,
the Yuè people first came.
