B12.21.2 In autumn, in the eighth month,
the duke and the marquis of Qí and the viscount of Zhū made a covenant at Gù.
The men of Qí demanded the ceremonial bow,
and therefore sang of it, saying:
"The obtuseness of the men of Lǔ,
for several years unawakened,
has made us dance high.
Only because of their Ru books,
do they cause anxiety for the two states."
On this journey,
the duke first arrived at Yánggǔ.
Qí's Lǘqiū Xī said:
"You have condescended to raise your precious feet,
to come to our ruler's army;
the ministers will hasten by relay to inform our ruler.
By the time they return,
will you not be wearied, my lord?
As the servants' quarters are not yet prepared,
I beg to clear a lodging for you at Zhōudào."
He declined, saying:
"How dare I weary the servants?"
B12.22 The Twenty-second Year of Duke Āi
B12.22.1 In the summer, in the fourth month of the twenty-second year,
the viscount of Zhū, Duke Yǐn, fled from Qí to Yuè,
saying:
"Wú acts without principle,
detaining the father and establishing the son."
The Yuè people sent him back,
and the heir, Gé, fled to Yuè.
B12.22.2 In winter, in the eleventh month, on the dīngmǎo day,
Yuè destroyed Wú,
and requested the King of Wú to reside at Yǒngdōng.
He declined, saying:
"I am old;
how can I serve you, my lord?"
He then hanged himself.
The Yuè people returned with his body.
B12.23 The Twenty-third Year of Duke Āi
B12.23.1 In spring of the twenty-third year,
Jǐng Cáo of Sòng died.
Jì Kāngzǐ sent Rǎn Yǒu to offer condolences,
and to escort the funeral,
saying:
"Our humble city has affairs of the altars of soil and grain,
which keep Féi and his officers fully occupied;
therefore, we are unable to assist in holding the cords,
but have sent Qiú to follow among the carriage attendants,
saying:
'Because Féi had the honor to be a distant nephew by marriage,
he has some unworthy horses left by his ancestors,
and has sent Qiú to present them to your steward,
that they may perhaps be deemed worthy to bear tassels and trappings!'"
B12.23.2 In summer, in the sixth month,
Jìn's Xún Yáo invaded Qí,
and Gāo Wúpī led an army to resist him.
Zhì Bó observed the Qí army;
his horse took fright,
and he drove it forward,
saying:
"If the men of Qí recognize my banner,
they will say I was afraid and turned back."
He went up to the ramparts and then returned.
When about to engage in battle,
Cháng Wǔzǐ requested to divine.
Zhì Bó said:
"Our ruler reported to the son of Heaven,
and divined about it with the guardian tortoise in the ancestral temple;
it was auspicious,
so why should we divine again?
Moreover, the men of Qí seized our Yīngqiū;
our ruler commanded Yáo,
not daring to display martial prowess,
but to recover Yīngqiū.
With our just cause to punish the guilty, it is sufficient;
why must we divine?"
On the rénchén day,
they fought at Líqiū,
and the Qí army was severely defeated.
Zhì Bó personally captured Yán Gēng.
B12.23.3 In autumn, in the eighth month,
Shū Qīng went to Yuè,
being the first to be sent there.
Yuè's Zhū Yǎng came on a friendly mission,
in return for Shū Qīng's visit.
B12.24 The Twenty-fourth Year of Duke Āi
B12.24.1 In summer, in the fourth month of the twenty-fourth year,
the marquis of Jìn was about to invade Qí,
and sent to beg for troops,
saying:
"Formerly, Zāng Wénzhòng used the army of Chǔ to invade Qí,
and took Gǔ;
Xuān Shū used the army of Jìn to invade Qí,
and took Wènyáng.
Our ruler wishes to seek blessing from the Duke of Zhōu,
and hopes to borrow spiritual power from the Zāng clan."
Zāng Shí led troops to join him,
and took Lǐnqiū.
The army officers ordered preparations to be made,
to advance further.
Lái Zhāng said:
"Their ruler is base, their government oppressive;
last year they overcame the enemy,
this year they have again taken a city;
Heaven has bestowed much upon them,
how can they advance further?
This is boastful talk.
The campaign is about to be concluded."
The Jìn army then returned.
They presented Zāng Shí with an ox,
and the grand historian apologized,
saying:
"Because our ruler was with the army,
the sacrificial animals and ceremonies were not according to measure;
we dare to express our apologies."
B12.24.2 The viscount of Zhū again acted without principle,
and the Yuè people seized him and took him back,
establishing the prince Hé in his place.
Hé also acted without principle.
B12.24.3 The mother of prince Jīng was a favorite,
and the duke intended to make her his wife,
so he ordered the director of the ancestral temple, Xìn Xià, to present the ceremonies for it.
He replied:
"There are none."
The duke angrily said:
"You are the director of the ancestral temple;
establishing a wife
is a great ceremony of the state;
why do you say there are none?"
He replied:
"The Duke of Zhōu and Duke Wǔ married from Xuē,
Dukes Xiào and Huì married from Shāng,
and from Duke Huán downward, they married from Qí;
for these there are ceremonies.
But to make a concubine a wife,
there certainly are no ceremonies for that."
The duke finally established her,
and made Jīng heir,
and the people of the state began to detest him.
B12.24.4 In the intercalary month,
the Duke went to Yuè.
He met Crown Prince Shìyǐng,
who intended to give the Duke a wife and grant him much land.
Gōngsūn Yǒushān sent word to Jìsūn.
Jìsūn was afraid,
and sent a bribe through Grand Steward Pǐ,
and the matter was stopped.
B12.25 The Twenty-fifth Year of Duke Āi, Commentary
B12.25.1 In the summer, in the fifth month, on the Gēngchén day, in the twenty-fifth year,
the Marquis of Wèi fled to Sòng.
The Marquis of Wèi had built the Líng Terrace at the Jiè Gardens,
and was drinking there with his various great officers.
Chǔshī Shēngzǐ ascended the mat with his stockings on.
The Duke was angry.
He excused himself, saying:
"Your servant has an ailment
different from other people's.
If you were to see it,
you would surely gag,
and therefore I did not dare."
The Duke grew even angrier.
The great officers tried to excuse him,
but the Duke would not accept it.
Chǔshī withdrew.
The Duke pointed his hand like a halberd,
and said:
"I will certainly cut off your feet!"
Chǔshī heard this.
Chǔshī rode in a carriage with the Minister of Justice Hài,
and said:
"It is fortunate that today we escaped with our lives."
When the Duke had returned to the state,
he seized the city of the Nán clan
and stripped Minister of Justice Hài of his administration.
The Duke had a court attendant throw Gōngwén Yìzǐ's carriage into a pond.
Earlier,
the people of Wèi had exterminated the Xià Dīng clan,
and gave their families and property as a gift to Péng Fēng Mízi.
Mízi gave the Duke wine to drink,
and presented him with the daughter of Xià Wù.
She became a favorite,
and was made his principal wife.
Her younger brother, Qī,
was a great-grandnephew of Dàshū Jí,
had been raised in the Duke's household from a young age,
and was made Minister of the Multitude.
When the favor of the principal wife declined,
Qī incurred the Duke's displeasure.
The Duke kept the three groups of artisans at work for a long time.
The Duke had the entertainer Jiǎo swear an oath with Quán Mí,
and became very close to and trusting of him.
Therefore, Chǔshī Bǐ,
Gōngsūn Mímóu,
Gōngwén Yào,
Minister of Justice Hài,
and Minister of the Multitude Qī used the three groups of artisans and Quán Mí to start a revolt.
They all grasped sharp weapons,
and those without them grasped axes.
They sent Quán Mí into the Duke's palace,
and from the palace of Crown Prince Jí they raised a clamor and attacked the Duke.
Juànzǐ Shì requested to resist them,
but Mí seized his hand,
and said:
"You are certainly brave,
but what will you do about our lord?
Have you not seen what happened to the former lord?
Where could our lord not go to satisfy his desires?
Moreover, our lord has been abroad before;
is it certain he will not return?
To resist now is not possible;
the anger of the multitude is difficult to oppose.
When things calm down, they will be easier to separate."
So they left.
They were about to go to Pú,
but Mí said:
"Jìn is untrustworthy;
it will not do."
They were about to go to Juàn,
but Mí said:
"Qí
and Jìn contend for us; it will not do."
They were about to go to Líng,
but Mí said:
"Lǔ is not worth allying with.
I request we go to Chéngchú,
to establish a connection with Yuè.
Yuè has a proper ruler."
So they went to Chéngchú.
Mí said:
"The bandits of Wèi are unpredictable;
I request we hurry,
and let me take the lead."
Then he loaded up the treasures and returned.
The Duke organized his troops into a scattered formation,
and relying on the invocator and scribe Huī, invaded Wèi.
The people of Wèi were distressed by this.
Yìzǐ knew about it,
went to see Zǐzhī,
and requested to expel Huī.
Wénzǐ said:
"He has committed no offense."
Yìzǐ said:
"He is fond of monopolizing profit and is reckless.
When he sees the lord entering,
he will be the first to lead the way.
If we expel him,
he will certainly go out through the southern gate,
and go to where the lord is.
Now Yuè has newly gained the allegiance of the various lords,
and he will certainly request troops from them."
Huī was at court,
so they sent an officer to send him back to his home.
Huī went out,
spent the night,
and was not admitted.
After five days,
they lodged him at Wàilǐ,
whereupon he gained favor,
and was sent to Yuè to request troops.
B12.25.2 In the sixth month,
the Duke arrived from Yuè.
Jì Kāngzǐ and Mèng Wǔbó met him at Wǔwú.
Guō Zhòng was the charioteer.
He saw the two men,
and said:
"There has been much malicious talk;
I request you, my lord, to deal with it fully."
The Duke held a feast at Wǔwú.
Wǔbó offered a toast,
and, disliking Guō Zhòng,
said:
"Why so fat?"
Jìsūn said:
"I request you drink a penalty cup, Zhì!
Because Lǔ is so close to our enemies,
your servant therefore could not follow you, my lord,
and barely escaped a major journey.
And yet you say Zhòng is fat?"
The Duke said:
"He has eaten his words so often,
how could he not be fat?"
They drank without pleasure,
and the Duke and the great officers began to bear ill will.
B12.26 The Twenty-sixth Year of Duke Āi, Commentary
B12.26.1 In the summer, in the fifth month, in the twenty-sixth year,
Shūsūn Shū led troops to join Yuè's Gāorú,
Shé Yōng, and Sòng's Yuè Fá in escorting the Marquis of Wèi back.
Wénzǐ wished to admit him.
Yìzǐ said:
"The lord is stubborn and cruel.
If we wait a little,
he will certainly poison the people,
and then they will become friendly with you."
The army invaded Wàizhōu,
and took much booty.
When they came out to resist them,
they were badly defeated.
They dug up the grave of Chǔshī Dìngzǐ,
and burned it on Píngzhuāng.
Wénzǐ sent Wángsūn Qí to speak privately with Gāorú,
saying:
"Do you intend to greatly destroy Wèi?
Or merely to restore the lord?"
Gāorú said:
"The command of our humble ruler is nothing else
but to restore the lord of Wèi."
Wénzǐ assembled the multitude and asked them,
saying:
"The lord is using the Mán and Yí to attack the state.
The state is nearly lost.
I request we admit him."
The multitude said:
"Do not admit him."
He said:
"If my death would be beneficial,
I request to go out through the northern gate."
The multitude said: "Do not go out."
They heavily bribed the men of Yuè,
opened the gates twice, guarded the battlements, and offered to admit the Duke,
but the Duke did not dare enter.
The army withdrew.
They established Duke Dào,
and the Nán clan served as his minister.
They gave Chéngchú to the men of Yuè.
The Duke said:
"Qī was behind this."
He ordered that anyone who had a grievance against the principal wife should take revenge.
Minister of the Multitude Qī went on a friendly mission to Yuè.
The Duke attacked him and seized his gifts.
Qī reported to the King,
and the King ordered him to take them back.
Qī took them back with a multitude.
The Duke was angry,
killed Qī's nephew who was the crown prince,
and subsequently died in Yuè.
B12.26.2 Duke Jǐng of Sòng had no sons.
He took Dé and Qǐ, the sons of Gōngsūn Zhōu, and raised them in the ducal palace,
but had not yet designated an heir.
At that time, Huáng Huǎn was the Right Marshal,
Huáng Fēiwǒ was the Grand Marshal,
Huáng Huái was the Minister of Lands,
Líng Bùhuǎn was the Left Marshal,
Yuè Fá was the Minister of Works,
and Yuè Zhūchú was the Grand Minister of Justice.
The six ministers and the three clans collectively handled government affairs,
communicating through the Grand Steward.
The Grand Steward often did not report matters,
but instead issued orders in the ruler's name according to his own wishes.
The people of the state despised him.
The Minister of Works wished to remove the Grand Steward.
The Left Marshal said:
"Let him be.
Allow his crimes to accumulate.
When something is heavy but lacks a foundation,
can it avoid collapse?"
In winter, the tenth month,
the duke was traveling at Kōngzé.
On the Xīnsì day,
he died at Liánzhōng.
The Grand Steward mobilized a thousand armored soldiers from Kōngzé,
escorted the duke's body from Kōngtóng into Wò Palace,
and summoned the six ministers,
saying:
"I have heard there are troops below,
and the ruler requests that you six plan a strategy."
When the six ministers arrived,
he used the soldiers to seize them, saying:
"The ruler is ill, gravely so.
He requests that you, gentlemen, swear an oath."
So they swore an oath in the courtyard of the small resting chamber,
saying: "Do nothing detrimental to the ducal house!"
The Grand Steward installed Qǐ as ruler,
placed the coffin in the great temple,
and only after three days did the people of the state learn of it.
The Minister of Works, Fá, had a proclamation circulated in the state, saying:
"The Grand Steward deluded and manipulated his ruler
and monopolized the benefits.
Now the ruler has died without illness,
and his death was concealed.
This can mean nothing else
but the crime of the Grand Steward."
Dé dreamed that Qǐ was lying with his head to the north outside the Lú Gate,
while he himself was a crow perched upon him,
its beak pointing toward the South Gate,
and its tail toward the Tóng Gate.
He said: "My dream is auspicious;
I will surely be established."
The Grand Steward schemed, saying:
"I was not included in the oath.
Might they not expel me?
Let us renew the oath!"
He ordered the invocator to prepare a covenant document.
The six ministers were at Tángyú,
where they were to swear the covenant.
The invocator Xiāng informed Huáng Fēiwǒ of the covenant document.
Huáng Fēiwǒ, along with Zǐ Lù, Ményǐn Dé,
and the Left Marshal, plotted, saying:
"The people are with us.
Shall we expel him?"
They all returned to distribute armor
and had a proclamation circulated in the state,
saying:
"The Grand Steward deluded and manipulated his ruler,
oppressing and abusing the ducal house.
Those who are with us
are the ones saving the ruler."
The multitude said:
"We are with you!"
The Grand Steward circulated a proclamation, saying:
"The Dài and Huáng clans intend harm to the ducal house.
Those who are with me
need not worry about not becoming wealthy."
The multitude said:
"He shows no distinction!"
The Dài and Huáng clans wished to attack the duke.
Yuè Dé said:
"That cannot be done.
He was guilty of oppressing the duke;
if we attack the duke,
we would be worse."
They had the people of the state direct their actions against the Grand Steward.
The Grand Steward escorted Qǐ and fled to Chǔ.
Then Dé was established as ruler.
The Minister of Works became the Chief Minister.
They swore a covenant, saying:
"The three clans shall jointly administer the government,
and shall not harm one another!"
B12.26.3 Duke Chū of Wèi, from Chéngchú, sent a messenger with a bow to inquire of Zǐgòng,
and said:
"May I return to enter the state?"
Zǐgòng bowed his head to the ground and received the bow,
replying:
"Your servant does not know."
Privately, he said to the messenger:
"Formerly, Duke Chéng was exiled in Chén;
Nìng Wǔzǐ and Sūn Zhuāngzǐ made the covenant at Wǎnpú, and the ruler returned.
Duke Xiàn was exiled in Qí;
Zǐxiān and Zǐzhǎn made the covenant at Yíyí, and the ruler returned.
Now you, my lord, are in exile for a second time.
Internally, I have not heard of any relative like Duke Xiàn's,
nor externally of any minister like Duke Chéng's.
Therefore, Cì does not know by what means you may enter.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Be not contentious, but rely on men;
then all quarters will follow you.'
If you obtain the right men,
and all quarters regard you as their lord,
what difficulty would there be in regaining the state?"
B12.27 *The Commentary of the Twenty-seventh Year of Duke Āi*
B12.27.1 In the twenty-seventh year, spring,
the Viscount of Yuè sent Shéyōng to come on a friendly mission,
and to discuss the fields of Zhū,
setting the border at Táishàng.
In the second month,
they made a covenant at Píngyáng.
All three ministers accompanied him.
Kǎngzǐ was distressed by this,
and when the conversation turned to Zǐgòng,
he said:
"If he were here,
I would not have come to this!"
Wǔbó said:
"Indeed.
Why not summon him?"
He said:
"I certainly intended to summon him."
Wénzǐ said:
"Another day, remember this request."
B12.27.2 In summer, the fourth month, on the Jǐhài day,
Jì Kǎngzǐ died.
The duke went to offer condolences,
but with reduced ceremony.
B12.27.3 Xún Yáo of Jìn led troops to attack Zhèng,
and encamped at Tóngqiū.
Zhèng's Sì Hóng requested rescue from Qí.
The Qí army was about to set out.
Chén Chéngzǐ gathered the orphans of the state for an audience on the third day.
He prepared a carriage with two horses,
and attached the tallies of five towns to it.
He summoned Yán Zhuōjù's son, Jìn,
and said:
"At the battle of Xí,
your father died there.
Because the state faced many difficulties,
I have not yet shown concern for you.
Now our ruler commands you with these towns.
Ride in this carriage to attend court,
and do not abandon the former labors!"
Then they went to rescue Zhèng.
When they reached Liúshū,
they were seven *li* from Gǔ,
yet the people of Gǔ did not know.
When they reached the Pú River,
it rained,
and they did not cross.
Zǐsī said:
"A great state is right under the eaves of our humble city;
that is why we reported the emergency.
Now if your army does not advance,
I fear it will be too late."
Chéngzǐ put on his rain garment, leaned on his spear,
and stood on the slope.
For horses that would not go out, he helped by whipping them.
Zhìbó heard of this,
and then withdrew,
saying:
"I divined about attacking Zhèng,
but not about fighting Qí."
He sent a message to Chéngzǐ, saying:
"Great Officer Chénzǐ,
you are descended from Chén.
That Chén's sacrifices are not continued
is the crime of Zhèng.
Therefore, my humble ruler sent Yáo to investigate the true situation of Chén.
I would say, does the great officer perhaps feel concern for Chén?
If it is beneficial for the root to be toppled,
what concern is it of Yáo?"
Chéngzǐ angrily said:
"Those who frequently oppress others do not last long.
Can Zhìbó endure for long?"
Zhōngháng Wénzǐ reported to Chéngzǐ, saying:
"Someone from the Jìn army informed Yín
that they are preparing a thousand light chariots to press upon the gates of the Qí army,
so they could be completely destroyed."
Chéngzǐ said:
"My humble ruler commanded Héng, saying:
'Do not pursue the few,
and do not fear the many.'"
Even if a thousand chariots were to pass,
dare I avoid them?
I shall report your command to my lord."
Wénzǐ said:
"Only now do I understand why I was exiled.
When a nobleman plans something,
he considers its beginning, middle, and end thoroughly,
and only then proceeds with it.
Now I entered into it without knowing any of these three aspects—
wasn't that bound to be difficult!"
B12.27.4 The Duke was troubled by the excesses of the Three Huán clans,
and wanted to use the feudal lords to remove them;
the Three Huán clans were also troubled by the Duke's recklessness,
so there was much estrangement between ruler and ministers.
The Duke was wandering at Língbǎn,
when he met Mèng Wǔbó at the crossroads of the Mèng clan,
and said: "I beg to ask you a question:
Will I die a natural death?"
Mèng Wǔbó replied:
"Your servant has no way of knowing."
The Duke asked three times,
but in the end Mèng Wǔbó declined to answer.
The Duke wanted to use Yuè to attack Lǔ and remove the Three Huán clans.
In autumn, on the jiǎxū day of the eighth month,
the Duke went to Gōngsūn Yǒuxíngshì.
He then took refuge in Zhū,
and subsequently proceeded to Yuè.
The people of the state punished Gōngsūn Yǒushānshì.
B12.27.5 In the fourth year of Duke Dào,
Jìn's Xún Yáo led troops to besiege Zhèng.
Before he arrived,
Zhèng's Sì Hóng said:
"Zhì Bó is obstinate and fond of victory.
If we submit to him early,
then we can make him leave."
So they first defended Nánlǐ to wait for him.
Zhì Bó entered Nánlǐ,
and attacked the gate at Júdié's gate.
The Zhèng people captured Xí Kuí Lěi,
and tried to bribe him with a position in government,
but he kept his mouth shut and died.
As they were about to attack the gate,
"Charge in!"
He replied:
"The master is here."
Zhì Bó said:
"Ugly and without courage,
how can you be considered a man?"
He replied:
"Because I can endure shame,
perhaps I will not harm the Zhào clan!"
Zhì Bó did not reform,
and Zhào Xiāngzǐ henceforth resented Zhì Bó,
and eventually caused his downfall.
Zhì Bó was greedy and obstinate,
so Hán
and Wèi turned against him and caused his downfall.
